items.text: Opening Mishnah: Partners building a wall in a courtyard
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Partners building a wall in a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that partners who wish to make a partition in a courtyard build the wall in the middle. It specifies the thickness of the wall based on the building material (gwil, gazit, kfisin, leveinim) and rules that if the wall falls, the place and stones belong to both. It then distinguishes between a garden (where one can be compelled to fence) and a field (where not), and discusses cases where one builds alone or both agree.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that partners who wish to make a partition in a courtyard build the wall in the middle, and the building material (gvil, gazit, kfisin, or leveinim) follows local custom.
The Mishnah specifies the thickness each partner contributes for each material (e.g., three handbreadths each for gvil) and rules that if the wall falls, the place and stones belong to both.

items.text: פתיחת הגמרא: בירור המונח 'מחיצה'
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: What is 'mechitzah'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'mechitzah' means in the Mishnah, suggesting it refers to a 'guda' (a partition wall). It supports this by citing a baraita about a vineyard partition that, when breached, one tells the other to 'fence it'.
items.desc: הגמרא פותחת בבירור המונח 'מחיצה' המופיע במשנה, ומסבירה שהוא מתייחס לגדר או מחיצה. היא מביאה ברייתא העוסקת במחיצת הכרם שנפרצה, שבה בעל השדה יכול לומר לבעל הכרם לגדור, ואם נפרצה שוב, יכול לומר לו שוב לגדור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'מחיצה' (partition) and suggests it means a wall (גודא).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו המונח 'מחיצה' במשנה, ומשיבה שהוא גדר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'mechitzah' means in the Mishnah, suggesting it refers to a 'guda' (a partition wall).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו המונח 'מחיצה' במשנה, ומשיבה שהוא גדר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that uses the term 'מחיצת הכרם' (partition of a vineyard) to mean a wall, supporting the interpretation.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו המונח 'מחיצה' במשנה, ומשיבה שהוא גדר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a vineyard partition that, when breached, one tells the other to 'fence it', supporting the interpretation of 'mechitzah' as a partition.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו המונח 'מחיצה' במשנה, ומשיבה שהוא גדר.

items.text: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's language that if the neighbors did not agree to build a wall, they are not compelled, implying hezek re'iyah is not considered damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's language that if the neighbors did not agree to build a wall, they are not compelled, implying that hezek re'iyah (damage caused by seeing into a neighbor's property) is not considered damage.

items.text: Challenge from the term 'mechitzah'
items.text_en: Challenge from the term 'mechitzah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the inference by noting the Mishnah uses 'mechitzah' (partition), implying a wall is built even against one's will, which would mean hezek re'iyah is damage. The Gemara resolves the linguistic difficulty by explaining the Mishnah's wording.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the inference by noting the Mishnah uses 'מחיצה' (partition), implying a wall is built even against one's will, which would mean hezek re'iyah is damage.
The Gemara resolves the linguistic difficulty by explaining the Mishnah's wording: 'מחיצה' is used to teach that the wall is a proper wall (כותל), not just a simple partition.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's necessity
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that they build the wall in the middle, as it seems obvious. It explains the case is where one neighbor already agreed, and the other might claim the agreement was only for airspace, not for actual use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that they build the wall in the middle, as this seems obvious.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is necessary in a case where one neighbor already agreed, and the other might claim the agreement was only for airspace (אוירא), not for actual use (תשמישתא); the Mishnah teaches that the agreement covers actual use.

items.text: Introduction of the debate on hezek re'iyah
items.text_en: Introduction of the debate on hezek re'iyah
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a series of attempted proofs regarding whether hezek re'iyah is considered damage, with a mnemonic listing the sources to be examined.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the debate on whether hezek re'iyah (visual damage) is considered damage, listing a mnemonic of sources to be examined.

items.text: First proof from a garden (Ginah)
items.text_en: First proof from a garden (Ginah)
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove hezek re'iyah is damage from a baraita about a garden, but deflects by citing Rabbi Abba's teaching that one may not stand in a neighbor's field when it is standing grain, distinguishing the case. The 'vechein' (and similarly) is explained as referring to the materials, not the law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that hezek re'iyah is damage by citing a baraita that begins 'vechein baginah' (and similarly in a garden).

The Gemara deflects the proof by distinguishing a garden, citing Rabbi Abba's teaching that one may not stand in a neighbor's field when it is standing grain, implying the concern is theft of produce, not mere sight.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the word 'vechein' in the baraita refers to the materials (bricks and stones), not to the law of hezek re'iyah.

items.text: Second proof from a collapsed courtyard wall
items.text_en: Second proof from a collapsed courtyard wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from a baraita that one must rebuild a collapsed courtyard wall up to four cubits, but deflects by saying a collapsed wall is different (since it was already there). The latter part of the baraita is needed to teach the exemption above four cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that היזק ראייה (damage by sight) is considered damage by citing a baraita that requires rebuilding a collapsed courtyard wall up to four cubits.
The Gemara rejects the proof, arguing that a collapsed wall is different because it was already standing and the obligation to rebuild is based on restoring the prior state, not on היזק ראייה.
The Gemara explains that the latter part of the baraita is necessary to teach the exemption above four cubits, where one is not compelled to rebuild.

items.text: Third proof from forcing to build a gate and door
items.text_en: Third proof from forcing to build a gate and door
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from a baraita that one can force a neighbor to build a gate and door for the courtyard, but deflects by saying the damage from the public is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from a baraita that one can force a neighbor to build a gate and door for the courtyard, inferring that the damage of seeing (היזק ראייה) is considered damage.
The Gemara deflects the proof by distinguishing that the damage from the public (זיקא דרבים) is different from private damage.

items.text: Fourth proof from dividing a courtyard
items.text_en: Fourth proof from dividing a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from a mishnah about dividing a courtyard that a wall is required, but deflects by saying it refers only to a boundary marker (mesifas), not a wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a wall is required from a mishnah about dividing a courtyard, which states that division is only permitted if each party receives four cubits.
The Gemara deflects the proof by explaining that the mishnah refers only to a boundary marker (מסיפס), not a wall.

items.text: Fifth proof from windows
items.text_en: Fifth proof from windows
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from a baraita about windows that one must distance to prevent seeing, but deflects by saying the damage to a house (by darkening) is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about windows requiring a four-amah distance to prevent looking in and darkening, attempting to prove that היזק ראייה (damage by seeing) is considered damage.
The Gemara deflects the proof by distinguishing that damage to a house (by darkening) is different from היזק ראייה (damage by seeing) alone.

items.text: Sixth proof from Rav Nachman's ruling on a roof
items.text_en: Sixth proof from Rav Nachman's ruling on a roof
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a statement from Rav Nachman citing Shmuel that a roof near a neighbor's courtyard requires a four-cubit parapet, but deflects by distinguishing that the courtyard owner's use is fixed while the roof owner's use is not, so the courtyard owner cannot guard against the roof owner's sporadic appearances.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from Rav Nachman citing Shmuel that a roof near a neighbor's courtyard requires a four-cubit parapet, implying that היזק ראייה (damage by sight) is considered damage.

The Gemara deflects the proof by distinguishing that the courtyard owner's use is fixed (קביעא) while the roof owner's use is not fixed, so the courtyard owner cannot guard against the roof owner's sporadic appearances.

items.text: First interpretation of 'mechitzah' as partition
items.text_en: First interpretation of 'mechitzah' as partition
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a first version of a dispute: one side interprets 'mechitzah' as a partition (plughta), citing the verse 'vat'hi mechetzat ha'edah'. Since the Mishnah says they build the wall against their will if they agree, this implies that hezek re'iyah is considered a damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a first version of the dispute: 'mechitzah' means partition (פלוגתא), citing the verse 'ותהי מחצת העדה', and since the Mishnah says they build the wall against their will if they agree, this implies that hezek re'iyah is considered a damage.

items.text: Second interpretation of 'mechitzah' as wall
items.text_en: Second interpretation of 'mechitzah' as wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative interpretation: 'mechitzah' means a wall (guda), citing the Mishnah about a vineyard partition. If they do not agree, they are not compelled, proving that hezek re'iyah is not considered a damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that 'mechitzah' means a wall (guda), citing the Mishnah about a vineyard partition to support this interpretation.
The Gemara concludes that if they do not agree, they are not compelled, proving that hezek re'iyah is not considered a damage.

items.text: Linguistic objection to both interpretations
items.text_en: Linguistic objection to both interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to both interpretations based on the Mishnah's language: if 'mechitzah' means wall, it should say 'bonin oto'; if it means partition, it should say 'lachatzot'. It resolves that people colloquially say 'ta na'avid plughta'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if 'mechitzah' means wall, the Mishnah should say 'bonin oto' (build it), and if it means partition, it should say 'lachatzot' (to divide), and resolves that people colloquially say 'ta na'avid plughta' (let's make a division).

items.text: Question on the necessity of agreement
items.text_en: Question on the necessity of agreement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if hezek re'iyah is a damage, why does the Mishnah require agreement? Even without agreement, they should be compelled. Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: our Mishnah deals with a case where there is no din chalukah (legal obligation to divide), and only when they agree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if hezek re'iyah is a valid damage, why does the Mishnah condition the obligation on agreement; even without agreement they should be compelled.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: our Mishnah deals with a case where there is no din chalukah (legal obligation to divide), and only when they agree.

items.text: Clarification of the ruling's novelty
items.text_en: Clarification of the ruling's novelty
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Rabbi Yochanan's statement adds, since the Mishnah already says they divide when both agree. It explains that the novelty is about a wall (kotel), not just a boundary marker (mesifas). The seifa (about sacred scrolls) is necessary to teach that even when both agree, they may not divide sacred scrolls.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Rabbi Yochanan's statement adds, since the Mishnah already teaches that when both agree they divide.

The Gemara answers that the novelty is about a wall (כותל), not just a boundary marker (מסיפס), and the seifa about sacred scrolls is necessary to teach that even when both agree they may not divide sacred scrolls.

items.text: Alternative version and discussion of kinyan
items.text_en: Alternative version and discussion of kinyan
items.desc_en: An alternative version questions why agreement matters if they can retract. Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says it is when they made a kinyan (acquisition). The Gemara objects that a verbal kinyan is insufficient, and resolves that it is a kinyan with wind (kinyan sudar) or through chazakah (taking possession).

sub.desc_en: The alternative version questions why the agreement matters if they can retract.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that it refers to a case where they made a קִנְיָן (acquisition) from him.
The Gemara objects that a verbal קִנְיָן (acquisition) is insufficient.
The Gemara resolves that it is a קִנְיָן (acquisition) with wind (קִנְיַן סוּדָר).
Rav Ashi says it is a case where each one took possession (חֲזָקָה) within his own property.

items.text: Definitions of building materials
items.text_en: Definitions of building materials
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the building materials mentioned in the Mishnah: gvil (rough stones), gazit (smooth stones), kefisin (half-bricks), and levenin (bricks). A dispute arises about the purpose of the extra handbreadth: whether for the projection of the corners (mursha d'karnata) or for the interlocking of the beams (beinei urbei). The Gemara concludes that these definitions are received traditions (gemara).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines the four building materials from the Mishnah: גויל (rough stones), גזית (smooth stones), כפיסין (half-bricks), and לבנים (bricks).
Rabbah bar Rava questions Rav Ashi: perhaps the extra handbreadth is for interlocking beams (ביני אורבי), not for the projection of corners (מורשא דקרנתא).
Rabbah bar Rava argues that the definitions of כפיסין and לבנים already imply the extra handbreadth is for interlocking beams.
Rav Ashi responds that all these definitions are received traditions (גמרא), not derived from logical inference.

items.text: Practical implications and the Temple's amah traksin
items.text_en: Practical implications and the Temple's amah traksin
items.desc_en: Abaye derives that every interlocking (beinei urbei) requires a handbreadth, more for riccha (mortar) and less for tina (clay). The Gemara questions the stability of a wall of gazit, noting that the amah traksin (the wall of the Temple) stood at 30 cubits high with only 6 handbreadths width, but it stood because of the extra handbreadth. It then discusses why the Second Temple did not have an amah traksin, citing a dispute between Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar) about the verse 'Gadol yihyeh k'vod habayit hazeh ha'acharon min harishon'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye derives that every interlocking (beinei urbei) requires a handbreadth, with a dispute about whether more is needed for riccha (mortar) and less for tina (clay).
The Gemara questions the stability of a gazit wall, noting that the amah traksin (the wall of the Temple) stood at 30 cubits high with only 6 handbreadths width.
The Gemara answers that the wall stood because of the extra handbreadth, and then discusses why the Second Temple did not have an amah traksin.

The Gemara cites a dispute between Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar) about the verse 'Gadol yihyeh k'vod habayit hazeh ha'acharon min harishon' to explain why the Second Temple was taller.

items.text: Gemara's question about building materials for the Temple
items.text_en: Gemara's question about building materials for the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the thirty cubits of the Temple's height were achieved through actual building or through a curtain, and Abaye resolves that the entire structure must be either all building or all curtain, based on the Temple and Tabernacle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the thirty cubits of the Temple's height could not be partially built and partially a curtain, noting that even the built part stood on a ceiling and beams.
Abaye resolves that the entire structure must be either all building (from the Temple) or all curtain (from the Tabernacle), not a mixture.

items.text: Dispute about the thickness of the wall
items.text_en: Dispute about the thickness of the wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether the wall thickness includes the plaster or not, with Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak suggesting it includes the plaster, but the Gemara rejects this and concludes that the plaster is not included because it is less than a handbreadth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the wall thickness of a handbreadth include the plaster coating or not?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak argues that the thickness includes the plaster, reasoning that otherwise the Mishnah would have stated the measure explicitly.
The Gemara rejects Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's conclusion, asserting that the measure is without plaster, and since the plaster is less than a handbreadth, the Mishnah does not mention it.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states each neighbor gives a brick-and-a-half, implying a total of three handbreadths, which contradicts the idea that plaster is negligible.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to bricks suitable for plastering, so the plaster is already accounted for in the brick size.

items.text: Proof from the beam and brick measurements
items.text_en: Proof from the beam and brick measurements
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the Mishnah about the beam and brick, but deflects it by saying the brick referred to is a large one, as indicated by the mention of three handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the Mishnah about the beam and brick, citing that the beam must be wide enough to receive a brick, and the brick is half a brick of three handbreadths.
The Gemara deflects the proof by saying the brick referred to is a large one, as indicated by the mention of three handbreadths, implying there is a smaller brick.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on demolishing a synagogue
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on demolishing a synagogue
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that one should not demolish a synagogue until building another, with two reasons: due to negligence or due to prayer. The difference between them is when another synagogue already exists. Marimar and Mar Zutra acted by building summer and winter synagogues.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that one should not demolish a synagogue until building another one.
Two reasons are given for Rav Chisda's ruling: due to negligence (פשיעותא) or due to prayer (צלויי).
The gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two reasons.
The difference is when another synagogue already exists: the negligence reason would still forbid demolition, but the prayer reason would permit it.
Marimar and Mar Zutra acted by demolishing and building summer and winter synagogues, demonstrating the practical application of the ruling.

items.text: Questions about selling synagogue materials
items.text_en: Questions about selling synagogue materials
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about selling bricks and beams from a demolished synagogue, and Rav Ashi explains that they may be sold if the money is needed for redeeming captives, but the building itself is not sold because people do not sell their dwelling.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if they collected money and then lowered the price of the building materials, what is the law regarding selling them?
Rav Ashi answers that they may sell the materials because the money might be needed for redeeming captives.
Ravina asks further: what if they have already arranged the bricks and beams and then lowered the price?
Rav Ashi answers that even in that case they may sell, because the need for redeeming captives may arise.
Ravina objects: if so, even the building itself should be sellable for the same reason.
Rav Ashi resolves: people do not sell their dwelling place, so the building itself is not sold.

items.text: Exception for a dangerous synagogue
items.text_en: Exception for a dangerous synagogue
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the ruling applies only when there is no danger, but if the synagogue is dangerous, one may demolish and rebuild, as illustrated by Rav Ashi's action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the prohibition against demolishing a synagogue without rebuilding another applies only when there is no danger, but if the synagogue is dangerous, one may demolish and rebuild.
The Gemara cites Rav Ashi's action as a precedent: he saw danger in the synagogue of Mata Mechasya, demolished it, moved his bed there, and did not remove it until they fixed drainage spouts.

items.text: Narrative of Herod and Bava ben Buta
items.text_en: Narrative of Herod and Bava ben Buta
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Bava ben Buta advised Herod to demolish the Temple, given Rav Chisda's ruling, and answers that either the Temple was dangerous or the king is different. It then recounts the story of Herod's rise, his marriage to a Hasmonean princess, and his killing of the Sages except Bava ben Buta.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Bava ben Buta advised Herod to demolish the Temple, given Rav Chisda's ruling that one must not demolish a synagogue until building another.
The Gemara provides two answers: either the Temple had a structural flaw (תיווהא), or the king is different because a king does not retract his decree, citing Shmuel's principle.

The Gemara recounts the story of Herod, a slave of the Hasmonean house, who heard a heavenly voice, killed his masters, and attempted to marry the surviving princess, who then threw herself from the roof.

The Gemara digresses to describe how Herod preserved the princess's body in honey for seven years, with a dispute about whether he had relations with her, and explains the preservation as either to satisfy his desire or to claim he married a princess.
Herod, seeking to legitimize his kingship, killed all the Sages except Bava ben Buta, whom he spared to seek advice.

items.text: Bava ben Buta's advice to Herod
items.text_en: Bava ben Buta's advice to Herod
items.desc_en: Herod confesses to Bava ben Buta that he killed the Sages, and Bava advises him to rebuild the Temple as atonement. The Gemara presents two versions of Bava's advice, each using a metaphor of light or eyes.

sub.desc_en: Herod, disguised, tests Bava ben Buta's loyalty by complaining about a wicked servant, and Bava refuses to curse him, citing verses against cursing a king, a rich man, or a prince.
Herod reveals his identity and asks Bava ben Buta what atonement is available for him after killing the Sages.
Bava ben Buta advises Herod to rebuild the Temple, using the metaphor of extinguishing the light of the world (the Sages) and engaging with the light of the world (the Temple).
An alternative version presents Bava's advice using the metaphor of blinding the eye of the world (the Sages) and engaging with the eye of the world (the Temple).

items.text: Herod's fear of the kingdom and the response
items.text_en: Herod's fear of the kingdom and the response
items.desc_en: Herod expresses fear of the Roman authorities, and Bava advises a gradual rebuilding plan. The authorities send a threatening message, and the Gemara explains the meaning of the term 'רֵכָא'.

sub.desc_en: Herod expresses fear of the Roman authorities, and Bava advises a gradual rebuilding plan over three years.
The authorities send a threatening message, and the Gemara explains the meaning of the term 'רֵכָא'.
The Gemara resolves that 'רֵכָא' refers to the kingdom, citing verses from Chronicles and Genesis.

items.text: Description of Herod's building
items.text_en: Description of Herod's building
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the beauty of Herod's Temple construction, the materials used, and the Sages' advice to leave a layer of plaster to resemble sea waves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general praise of Herod's Temple construction, stating that one who has not seen it has never seen a beautiful building.
The Gemara asks what materials were used in the construction.
Rabbah answers that it was built with marble and alabaster stones.
An alternative tradition adds that the stones included black marble (כוחלא) as well.
The Gemara describes the construction technique of alternating protruding and recessed stone edges to hold plaster.
The Sages advised Herod not to cover the stones with gold, but to leave them bare so they would resemble sea waves, which is more beautiful.

items.text: Why Bava ben Buta was not punished like Daniel
items.text_en: Why Bava ben Buta was not punished like Daniel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Bava could advise a wicked king, given that Daniel was punished for advising Nebuchadnezzar. Two answers are given: a slave is obligated in mitzvot, and the Temple requires royal permission. The Gemara then discusses how Daniel was punished.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Bava ben Buta could advise Herod, given that Daniel was punished for advising Nebuchadnezzar.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the tradition that Daniel was punished for advising Nebuchadnezzar to perform charity, as recorded in the verses.
The Gemara offers the first answer: a slave (Herod) is obligated in מצוות (commandments), so advising him is permitted.
The Gemara offers the second answer: the Temple requires royal permission, so advising the king was necessary.
The Gemara asks how we know Daniel was punished, citing the verse about Esther calling Hatach.
Rav identifies Hatach as Daniel, indicating he was cut down from greatness.
The Gemara notes that this explanation works for one opinion, but questions what to say for the alternative opinion that Hatach means all royal matters were decided by him.
The Gemara resolves that Daniel was punished by being thrown into the lions' den.

items.text: Mishnah: 'All is according to regional custom'
items.text_en: Mishnah: 'All is according to regional custom'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'the all' includes places where they use mud and plaster. It then clarifies a case where a wall falls into one party's domain, teaching that the burden of proof is on the claimant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'the all' in the Mishnah comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes places where they use mud and plaster.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling that the place and stones are shared is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that even if the wall fell into one party's domain, the burden of proof is on the claimant, not the possessor.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah about gardens and fields
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah about gardens and fields
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies an apparent contradiction in the Mishnah regarding when one is obligated to build a fence. Abaye and Rava offer different resolutions to reconcile the statements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: regarding a garden, the Mishnah says one is obligated to build a fence only where it is customary, implying that by default (סְתָמָא) one is not obligated.

The Gemara then notes the opposite contradiction in the second clause: regarding a field, the Mishnah says one is not obligated where it is not customary, implying that by default one is obligated, which contradicts the default for a garden.

Abaye resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the Mishnah: the first clause refers to a default garden, and the second clause refers to a field where it is customary to build a fence, but Rava objects that this reading makes the word 'but' (אֲבָל) problematic.

Rava offers a different resolution: a default garden is treated as a place where it is customary to build a fence, so one is obligated, while a default field is treated as a place where it is not customary, so one is not obligated.

items.text: Definition of 'חזית' and the dispute about its direction
items.text_en: Definition of 'חזית' and the dispute about its direction
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the meaning of 'חזית' in the Mishnah. Rav Huna gives two versions of how to bend the corner, and the Gemara raises objections about the possibility of fraud. The section ends with Rabbi Yochanan's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'חזית' (the corner projection) means in the Mishnah.
Rav Huna answers: one bends the corner outward (toward the public domain).
The Gemara objects: why not bend it inward (into one's own property) instead?
The Gemara rejects the objection: if bent inward, the neighbor could also bend outward and claim the projection is partly his.
The Gemara objects: even with the outward bend, the neighbor could cut off the projection and claim it as his own.
The Gemara resolves: cutting (גיזוזא) is noticeable and thus prevents fraud, unlike the inward bend which is hidden.
An alternative version: Rav Huna says one bends the corner inward (into one's own property).
The Gemara objects: why not bend it outward instead?
The Gemara rejects: if bent outward, the neighbor could cut it off and claim it as his own.
The Gemara objects: even with the inward bend, the neighbor could wrap around it and claim it as his own.
The Gemara resolves: wrapping (ליפופא) is noticeable and prevents fraud.
The Gemara objects: the Mishnah explicitly says 'from the outside' (מבחוץ), contradicting the inward bend.
The Gemara declares the difficulty unresolved (קשיא).
The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yochanan's opinion on the matter.

items.text: Discussion of the הוצא (recessed area) and the concern of false claims
items.text_en: Discussion of the הוצא (recessed area) and the concern of false claims
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where a person builds a projection (הוצא) outside the wall. It raises the issue that the neighbor might later claim it is his own. Various solutions are proposed and rejected because of the possibility of the neighbor peeling off plaster and claiming ownership. The discussion cites Rav Nachman's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the projection (הוצא) is built outside the wall, suggesting it could be built inside to avoid the neighbor's claim of shared ownership.
The Gemara answers that if built inside, the neighbor could build outside and claim the entire projection as his own.
The Gemara objects that even with the current arrangement, the neighbor could peel off the plaster and claim ownership.
The Gemara resolves that peeling off plaster is a noticeable act (קילופא מידע ידיע), so the neighbor cannot easily fabricate a claim.

items.text: Abaye's ruling: הוצא only remedied by a document
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling: הוצא only remedied by a document
items.desc_en: Abaye states that the only remedy for the הוצא (projection) problem is to make a written document (שטרא) that records the agreement, thereby preventing future claims.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that the only remedy for a הוצא (projection) is a written document (שטרא) to establish ownership.
Abaye rules that the only remedy for the הוצא (projection) problem is a written document (שטרא).

items.text: Discussion of the Mishnah's phrase 'if they built with mutual consent' and the concern for tricksters
items.text_en: Discussion of the Mishnah's phrase 'if they built with mutual consent' and the concern for tricksters
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling about building with mutual consent is necessary, since it might teach a remedy for a trickster. Rabba bar Uzziel and Rav Ashi discuss. Ravina explains that the entire Mishnah deals with the הוצא case, countering Abaye's position that only a document works.

sub.text: Rava miParzika's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rava miParzika's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rava miParzika asks Rav Ashi: if they built with mutual consent, why would they need the Mishnah's ruling — wouldn't neither build?
Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah addresses a case where one built first and the other did not, so the first claims it is his alone.
The Gemara objects: does the Tanna teach a remedy for a trickster?
Rav Ashi retorts: isn't the first part of the Mishnah also a remedy for a trickster?
Ravina explains that the entire Mishnah deals with the הוצא (protrusion) case, countering Abaye's position that only a document works, and teaching that a visual inspection suffices.

items.text: Mishnah: One who surrounds his fellow on three sides and builds walls
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who surrounds his fellow on three sides and builds walls
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches: If someone surrounds his fellow on three sides and builds a wall on the first, second, and third sides, the fellow is not obligated to contribute. Rabbi Yose says: If the fellow then stands and builds the fourth wall, we compel him to pay for everything.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one surrounds his neighbor on three sides and fences them, the neighbor is not compelled to pay.
Rabbi Yose says that if the neighbor then fences the fourth side, he must pay for all the fencing.

items.text: Rav Yehuda said Shmuel's ruling: the law follows Rabbi Yose
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda said Shmuel's ruling: the law follows Rabbi Yose
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: The halakha follows Rabbi Yose, that if he stood and built the fourth wall, we compel him to pay for everything. This applies whether the one who built is the one who was surrounded (the neighbor) or the one who did the surrounding.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel rules the halacha follows Rabbi Yose, whether the fencer is the neighbor or the original surrounder.

items.text: Debate between Rav Huna and Chiya bar Rav: how to calculate the payment
items.text_en: Debate between Rav Huna and Chiya bar Rav: how to calculate the payment
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says the payment is according to what he actually built. Chiya bar Rav says it is according to the cheap price of reeds. The Gemara then analyzes the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yose, offering multiple possible explanations for their disagreement: whether the payment includes the value of guarding (אגר נטירא), whether it includes the first three walls, and whether it applies only when the surrounded one builds or also when the surrounding one builds.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Chiya bar Rav dispute the payment calculation: Rav Huna says it is according to what he actually built, while Chiya bar Rav says it is according to the cheap price of reeds.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah to frame the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yose.
According to Rav Huna, the difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yose is that the Tanna Kamma pays only according to cheap reeds, while Rabbi Yose pays according to what he actually built.
The Gemara asks: according to Chiya bar Rav, who says payment is only according to cheap reeds, what difference remains between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yose?
One answer: the difference is that the Tanna Kamma pays only the guarding fee (אגר נטירא) but not the cheap reeds, while Rabbi Yose pays the cheap reeds.
Another answer: the difference is that the Tanna Kamma pays only for the fourth wall, while Rabbi Yose also pays for the first three walls.

Another answer: the difference is that the Tanna Kamma applies the full payment only when the surrounded one (ניקף) built the fourth wall, but not when the surrounding one (מקיף) built it; Rabbi Yose applies it in both cases.

An alternative version reverses the positions: the Tanna Kamma requires payment even when the surrounding one built the fourth wall, while Rabbi Yose requires payment only when the surrounded one built it, indicating his consent.

items.text: Story of Runya and Ravina about fence payment
items.text_en: Story of Runya and Ravina about fence payment
items.desc_en: Runya built a fence around Ravina's property from four sides. Ravina refused to pay for the fence, the reeds, or the guarding. Later, when Ravina was fencing his palm trees, he told his tenant to take a bundle of dates from Runya, revealing that he benefited from the fence. Runya argued that even a goat needs guarding, and Ravina countered that a goat needs to eat, to which Runya replied that a man is needed to feed it.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces the story: Ravina surrounded Runya's field on all four sides and demanded payment for the fence, reeds, and guarding, but Runya refused.

The narrator describes a later incident: Ravina told his sharecropper to take a cluster of dates from Runya, leading to a dispute where Ravina argued that Runya benefited from the fence and demanded payment for a watchman.

items.text: Rava's ruling on the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on the dispute
items.desc_en: The case came before Rava, who instructed Runya to appease Ravina with whatever would satisfy him; otherwise, Rava would judge according to Rav Huna in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs Runya to appease Ravina with whatever would satisfy him; otherwise, Rava will judge according to Rav Huna in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Runya buys land adjacent to Ravina
items.text_en: Runya buys land adjacent to Ravina
items.desc_en: Runya bought land bordering Ravina's property. Ravina sought to evict him based on the law of bar metzra (adjacent owner's right of preemption). Rav Safra, son of Rav Yeiva, told Ravina that people say: four for a palm tree, four for a shadow (i.e., the buyer also needs the shade).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Ronya bought land adjacent to Ravina, and Ravina considered evicting him based on the law of בר מצרא (adjacent owner's right of preemption).
Rav Safra bar Rav Yeiva tells Ravina that people say: four for a palm tree, four for a shadow (i.e., the buyer also needs the shade), meaning Ronya also owns adjacent land and cannot be evicted.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of a fallen courtyard wall
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a fallen courtyard wall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If a courtyard wall falls, the neighbors are compelled to rebuild it up to four cubits. There is a presumption that payment has been given until proof otherwise. Above four cubits, they are not compelled. If another wall was attached, even without a roof, all costs are added. There is a presumption that payment has not been given until proof otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the law of a fallen courtyard wall: the court compels the neighbors to rebuild it up to four cubits, and there is a presumption that payment has been given until proof otherwise.

The Mishnah continues: above four cubits the court does not compel; but if the neighbor attached another wall, even without a roof, all costs are added, and there is a presumption that payment has not been given until proof otherwise.

items.text: Gemara: Repaying a loan within the term
items.text_en: Gemara: Repaying a loan within the term
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says: One who sets a time for repayment and claims to have paid within the term is not believed; it would be enough if he pays on time. Abaye and Rava both say that a person does pay within the term, as sometimes money comes to hand and he says, 'I'll go and repay him.'

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that a borrower who claims to have repaid within the term is not believed, as it is unlikely one pays early.
Abaye and Rava both disagree, asserting that a person does repay within the term when money comes to hand.

items.text: Reason for the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Reason for the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling that a borrower is presumed to have repaid a loan with a fixed term only after the term is to avoid burdening him with constant demands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling is to avoid burdening the borrower with constant demands (לִיטְרְדַן).

items.text: First Mishnah clause: presumed to have given
items.text_en: First Mishnah clause: presumed to have given
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's first clause: a borrower is presumed to have paid if he claims payment within the term. It suggests this is obvious if he says 'I paid you within my term,' but the Mishnah must refer to a case where he says 'I paid you within my term,' teaching that people do sometimes pay early. The Gemara deflects: here each installment has its own term.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's first clause: a borrower is presumed to have paid until the lender brings proof that he did not pay.
The Gemara asks: if the borrower says 'I paid you within my term,' the presumption is obvious, so what case does the Mishnah teach?
The Gemara suggests the Mishnah refers to a borrower who says 'I paid you within my term,' teaching that people sometimes pay early.
The Gemara deflects: here each installment has its own term, so paying early for one installment is still within its term.

items.text: Second Mishnah clause: presumed not to have given
items.text_en: Second Mishnah clause: presumed not to have given
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the second clause: a borrower is presumed not to have paid if he claims payment within the term. It suggests this is obvious if he says 'I paid you within my term,' but the Mishnah must refer to a case where he says 'I paid you within my term,' teaching that people do not pay early. The Gemara deflects: here the borrower says 'who says the court will obligate me?'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the second clause of the Mishnah: a borrower is presumed not to have paid until he brings proof that he paid.
The Gemara asks: what case is this? If the borrower says 'I paid you within my term,' why would he not be believed?
The Gemara answers: rather, the case is where the borrower says 'I paid you within my term,' teaching that people do not pay early.
The Gemara deflects: here it is different because the borrower says 'who says the court will obligate me?' — meaning he denies the debt entirely, so the presumption does not apply.

items.text: Dispute and halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Dispute and halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara records that Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua acted like Abaye and Rava (who follow the principle that people do not pay early), while Mar bar Rav Ashi acted like Resh Lakish (who does not rely on this principle). The halakha follows Resh Lakish, even against orphans, despite the rule that one who collects from orphans must swear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua acted in accordance with Abaye and Rava, who hold that people do not pay early.
The Gemara reports that Mar bar Rav Ashi acted in accordance with Resh Lakish, who holds that people do pay early.

The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Resh Lakish, even when collecting from orphans, despite the requirement that one who collects from orphans must swear, because the principle that a person does not pay within his term is a strong presumption (חזקה).

items.text: New inquiry: claim after the term
items.text_en: New inquiry: claim after the term
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new question: if the creditor demands payment after the term, and the debtor says 'I paid you within my term,' what is the law? Do we say that in the face of a presumption (that people do not pay early) we apply the principle 'what reason would he have to lie'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new inquiry: if the creditor demands payment after the term and the debtor claims 'I paid you within my term,' do we apply the principle of 'what reason would he have to lie' in the face of the presumption that people do not pay early?

items.text: First attempt to prove that מיגו applies even where there is a hazaka
items.text_en: First attempt to prove that מיגו applies even where there is a hazaka
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a possible proof from the Mishnah's rule about a lender who claims repayment within the loan period. The proof is rejected because in that case, every time period is its own time for repayment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether the principle of מיגו (what reason would I have to lie?) applies even where there is a hazaka (presumption) against the claim, and cites a Mishnah about a lender who is presumed to have received payment.

The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's case: if the lender claimed after the loan period, the borrower's claim of repayment within time is obvious; the proof must be about repayment within the loan period, but the Gemara rejects it because each time period is its own time for repayment, so the hazaka does not apply.

items.text: Second attempt to prove that מיגו does not apply where there is a hazaka
items.text_en: Second attempt to prove that מיגו does not apply where there is a hazaka
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another Mishnah about a wall that is four cubits high, where the neighbor is exempt from payment unless proof is brought. The Gemara analyzes the case and concludes that here, where there is a hazaka, we do not say מיגו, but the proof is rejected because the defendant can claim 'who says the Rabbis would obligate me?'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a Mishnah about a wall four cubits high where the neighbor is exempt from payment unless he brings proof that he paid.
The Gemara analyzes the case: if the neighbor claimed payment within the term, why would he be exempt? This is obvious.

The Gemara concludes that the case must be where he claimed payment within the term, proving that in a place of hazaka (presumption) we do not apply the principle of מיגו (what reason would I have to lie?).
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing the case because the defendant can claim 'who says the Rabbis would obligate me?' — meaning the hazaka is not strong enough to override the uncertainty.

items.text: Third attempt to prove that מיגו does not apply where there is a hazaka
items.text_en: Third attempt to prove that מיגו does not apply where there is a hazaka
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava brings a Mishnah about a loan where the borrower says 'I gave it to you' (within the time) and is exempt, versus 'I have nothing of yours' and is liable. The Gemara initially thinks this proves that where there is a hazaka we do not say מיגו, but rejects it by reinterpreting 'I have nothing of yours' as a denial of the loan itself, which is equivalent to a denial of repayment.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava brings a Mishnah about a loan where the borrower admits the loan but then claims repayment, distinguishing between saying 'I gave it to you' (exempt) and 'I have nothing of yours' (liable).

The Gemara infers that 'I gave it to you' refers to repayment within the loan period, and 'I have nothing of yours' refers to repayment after the period, concluding that where there is a hazaka (presumption of non-repayment within the period) we do not apply the principle of מיגו (since the borrower could have lied more plausibly).

The Gemara rejects the inference by reinterpreting 'I have nothing of yours' as a denial of the loan itself ('these things never happened'), citing the principle that one who says 'I never borrowed' is equivalent to one who says 'I never repaid' (and thus is liable).

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on the scope of hazaka when building a wall
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on the scope of hazaka when building a wall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one builds a wall adjacent to another's wall, we roll all the benefits onto him. Rav Huna and Rav Nachman dispute whether building a wall adjacent to part of the neighbor's wall establishes hazaka for the entire wall or only for the part adjacent. Both concede certain exceptions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that if one builds another wall adjacent, all benefits are rolled onto him.
Rav Huna states that if one builds a wall adjacent to part of the neighbor's wall, he acquires hazaka (presumptive ownership) over the entire wall.
Rav Nachman argues that the hazaka applies only to the part of the wall adjacent to which the new wall was built, not to the entire wall.
The Gemara records that Rav Huna concedes an exception for a corner or a loop, and Rav Nachman concedes an exception for a portico or a beam socket of arches.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on windows and hazaka
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on windows and hazaka
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that placing windows (בי כוי) does not establish a hazaka, even if one made a lintel, because the neighbor can claim he thought it was temporary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that placing windows (בי כוי) does not establish a hazaka, even if one made a lintel.
Rav Huna explains the reasoning: the neighbor can claim he thought the window was temporary, expecting compensation later.

items.text: Disputes between Rav Nachman and Rav Yosef about hazaka for different types of projections
items.text_en: Disputes between Rav Nachman and Rav Yosef about hazaka for different types of projections
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Yosef dispute whether establishing hazaka for one type of projection (e.g., הורדי, כשורי, נטפי, שפכי) establishes hazaka for another. Two versions of Rav Nachman's opinion are given, and Rav Yosef consistently takes a more expansive view. Rav Yosef even acted on his ruling regarding צריפא דאורבני.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that establishing hazaka (presumption of ownership) for one type of projection (הורדי) does not establish it for another (כשורי), but the reverse does.
Rav Yosef disagrees, asserting that hazaka for הורדי does establish hazaka for כשורי.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Nachman's opinion
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Nachman's opinion
sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Rav Nachman actually held that hazaka for either type establishes hazaka for the other.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's statement on נטפי and שפכי
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement on נטפי and שפכי
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that hazaka for נטפי (drip projections) establishes hazaka for שפכי (spout projections), but not vice versa.
Rav Yosef holds that even hazaka for שפכי establishes hazaka for נטפי.
An alternative version reports Rav Nachman's ruling on שפכי and נטפי, adding that hazaka for neither establishes hazaka for צריפא דאורבני (a reed hut).

sub.text: Rav Yosef's ruling on צריפא דאורבני
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling on צריפא דאורבני
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef holds that hazaka for any projection establishes hazaka even for צריפא דאורבני, and he acted on this ruling in practice.

items.text: Beginning of a new topic: renting a house
items.text_en: Beginning of a new topic: renting a house
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuh about a case where one rents a house to another, introducing a new subject that continues on the next daf.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuh introducing a new topic about one who rents a house to another.

items.text: Amoraic statements on hazakah in a large building and adjacent spaces
items.text_en: Amoraic statements on hazakah in a large building and adjacent spaces
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rava debate whether hazakah applies to a courtyard behind houses or a palace courtyard. Ravina adds that a sukka becomes a hazakah after thirty days, or immediately if plastered with mud.

sub.desc_en: The stam states the basic rule: in a large palace, one acquires hazakah by using its ledges and walls up to four cubits and in the thickness of the wall where customary, but not in a palace courtyard.
Rav Nachman extends hazakah even to a palace courtyard, but not to a space behind houses.
Rava further extends hazakah even to the space behind houses.
Ravina rules that a sukka becomes a hazakah after thirty days, or after seven days if it is a mitzvah sukka, or immediately if plastered with mud.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on two houses on opposite sides of a public domain
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on two houses on opposite sides of a public domain
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that each owner builds a parapet on half his roof, offset from the other, and adds a bit. The Gemara questions why this is needed only for a public domain.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that when two houses face each other across a public domain, each owner builds a parapet on half his roof, offset from the other, and adds a bit.

The Gemara questions why Abaye specifies a public domain, suggesting the same ruling would apply to a private domain, and proposes that the public domain case is needed to counter a potential claim that the neighbor could say 'you will eventually need to shield yourself from the public anyway'.
The Gemara resolves that Abaye teaches that the neighbor can respond: the public sees me only by day or when I stand or when they look, but you see me always, so your obligation to build is greater.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: why public domain is specified
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: why public domain is specified
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Abaye specifies a public domain, as a private domain would also apply. It explains that the case is needed to counter a potential claim that the neighbor can rely on passersby for privacy; the Gemara gives three distinctions between public and private viewing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Abaye specifies a public domain (רשות הרבים), as a private domain (רשות היחיד) would also apply.
The Gemara explains that the public domain is needed to counter a potential claim that the neighbor can rely on passersby for privacy.
The Gemara resolves that the case teaches three distinctions between public and private viewing: time of day, posture, and attention.

items.text: Gemara's question on the obviousness of Abaye's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the obviousness of Abaye's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Abaye's ruling is not obvious, and explains that it is needed when one built first; the other might claim he should build the entire parapet. Abaye teaches that each can say the other's wall would be weakened.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Abaye's ruling that each builds a parapet on half his roof is not obvious.
The Gemara explains the ruling is needed when one built first, teaching that each can claim the other's wall would be weakened.

items.text: Rav Nachman and Shmuel on a roof adjacent to a neighbor's courtyard
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Shmuel on a roof adjacent to a neighbor's courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel that one must build a four-cubit parapet for a roof next to a courtyard, but not between roofs. Rav Nachman himself says a ten-handbreadth partition suffices. The Gemara questions the purpose and concludes it is to prevent evasion of liability.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports Shmuel's ruling that a roof adjacent to a neighbor's courtyard requires a four-cubit parapet, but not between roofs.
Rav Nachman himself rules that a ten-handbreadth partition suffices instead of four cubits.
The Gemara questions the purpose of the ten-handbreadth partition, rejecting possible reasons of preventing visual harm, theft liability, or goat jumping.
The Gemara resolves that the ten-handbreadth partition is for theft liability, as a mere barrier allows evasion but a ten-handbreadth partition prevents it.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that if a courtyard is above a neighbor's roof, one is not obligated. It clarifies that this means not obligated for four cubits, but obligated for a ten-handbreadth partition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman's ruling by citing a baraita that says if a courtyard is above a neighbor's roof, one is not obligated to build a partition.
The Gemara infers that the baraita means no obligation at all, contradicting Rav Nachman's requirement of a ten-handbreadth partition.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita means no obligation for a four-cubit partition, but there is an obligation for a ten-handbreadth partition, aligning with Rav Nachman's view.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda on two courtyards one above the other
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda on two courtyards one above the other
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says the lower builds from his side upward and the upper builds from his side upward; Rav Chisda says the upper assists from below. A baraita supports Rav Chisda, and adds that if a courtyard is above a roof, no obligation applies.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda regarding two courtyards one above the other: Rav Huna says each builds from his own side upward.
Rav Chisda states that the upper courtyard owner assists from below in building the shared wall.
A baraita is cited in support of Rav Chisda, ruling that the upper owner must assist from below.
The baraita adds that if a courtyard is above a neighbor's roof, no obligation applies.

items.text: Story of two tenants and a collapsed lower floor
items.text_en: Story of two tenants and a collapsed lower floor
items.desc_en: A story is told of two tenants, one upper and one lower; the lower floor collapsed. The lower asked the upper to help rebuild, but the upper refused, saying he is fine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of two tenants, one upper and one lower; the lower floor collapsed, and the lower tenant asked the upper to help rebuild, but the upper refused, saying he is fine.

items.text: First case: building a wall that blocks light
items.text_en: First case: building a wall that blocks light
items.desc_en: A person wants to build a wall opposite his neighbor's windows, blocking the light. The neighbor objects, and the builder offers various compromises. Rav Chama rules that the neighbor can legally prevent the building if the wall is within ten handbreadths of the windows, but not if it is lower.

sub.desc_en: The neighbor objects to the wall blocking light, and the builder offers to demolish and rebuild, rent space, or have the neighbor duck in and out.
Rav Chama rules that the neighbor can legally prevent the building if the wall is within ten handbreadths of the windows, but not if it is lower.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling applies only when the walls are not adjacent; if they are adjacent, they demolish and rebuild together.

items.text: Measurement for building together
items.text_en: Measurement for building together
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much space is needed when neighbors build together. Rabbana cite Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Nachman that the height should be half the length and half the width. Rabba rejects this and quotes Rav Nachman's actual statement: the height should be as people normally dwell. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua gives a practical measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: when neighbors build together, what is the required height?

sub.text: Rabbana citing Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rabbana citing Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rabbana cite Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Nachman that the height should be half the length and half the width, as taught in a Mishnah.
Rabba rejects the attribution, saying not to hang empty statements on Rav Nachman.

sub.text: Rabba citing Rav Nachman's actual statement
sub.text_en: Rabba citing Rav Nachman's actual statement
sub.desc_en: Rabba states that Rav Nachman's actual ruling is that the height should be as people normally dwell.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's practical measure
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's practical measure
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua gives a practical measure: the height should be such that one can enter with the bundles of Mahoza.

items.text: Second case: building a wall behind windows
items.text_en: Second case: building a wall behind windows
items.desc_en: A man builds a wall behind his neighbor's windows, darkening them. The neighbor objects, and the builder offers to make new windows above. The neighbor argues the wall will not stand. The builder offers to rebuild the entire house, but the neighbor refuses due to inconvenience. Rav Chama rules the neighbor can legally prevent this.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where a man builds a wall behind his neighbor's windows, and the neighbor objects to the darkening and structural instability.
Rav Chama rules that the neighbor is legally justified in preventing the construction.

items.text: Clarification of the second case
items.text_en: Clarification of the second case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this case is repeated, and explains that it teaches that even if the neighbor only uses the space for straw and wood, the builder still cannot block the light.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the second case (segments 4-5) is repeated, since it seems identical to the first case (segments 0-1).
The Gemara answers that the second case teaches that even if the neighbor only uses the space for straw and wood (תִּיבְנָא וּבֵי צִיבֵי), the builder still cannot block the light.

items.text: Third case: brothers dividing property
items.text_en: Third case: brothers dividing property
items.desc_en: Two brothers divide property; one gets a portico (אספלידא) and the other gets a courtyard (תרביצא). The one with the courtyard builds a wall at the entrance of the portico, blocking light. The portico owner objects. Rav Chama rules the builder is within his rights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case of two brothers dividing property, where one receives a portico (אספלידא) and the other a courtyard (תרביצא), and the courtyard owner builds a wall at the portico's entrance.
The portico owner objects that the wall blocks his light.
The courtyard owner responds that he is building on his own property.
Rav Chama rules that the courtyard owner is within his rights.

items.text: Comparison with the case of a vineyard and a white field
items.text_en: Comparison with the case of a vineyard and a white field
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi why this case differs from the baraita where brothers divide a vineyard and a white field, and the vineyard owner gets four amot in the white field. Rav Ashi answers that there they valued the land together, but here they did not value the airspace. Ravina objects that they did value the land, but not the air.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi why this case differs from the baraita where brothers divide a vineyard and a white field, and the vineyard owner gets four amot in the white field.
Rav Ashi answers that there they valued the land together, but here they did not value the airspace.
Ravina objects that they did value the land, but not the air.
Rav Ashi clarifies that they valued the land and building materials together, but did not value the airspace together.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the name
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the name
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the portico owner could say he was given a portico but now gets a dark room. Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers that he was only given the name 'portico'. The Gemara supports this with a baraita about selling a 'beis kor' or 'pomegranate orchard' by name alone. It then distinguishes: there the seller can claim he sold only the name, but here the brothers intended to dwell as their ancestors did.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the portico owner could argue he was given a portico but now receives a dark room.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers that the brother was only given the name 'portico', not the actual structure.
The Gemara cites a baraita about selling a 'beis kor' or 'pomegranate orchard' by name alone to support the principle.
The Gemara distinguishes: there the seller can claim he sold only the name, but here the brothers intended to dwell as their ancestors did.

items.text: Conclusion of the discussion
items.text_en: Conclusion of the discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara records that the Sages said to him (presumably Rav Shimi bar Ashi) something that resolves the issue, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Sages tell Rav Shimi bar Ashi something that resolves the issue, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Dispute about brothers' rights after division
items.text_en: Dispute about brothers' rights after division
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rav Nachman citing Shmuel and Rava regarding whether brothers who divided an inheritance retain rights of way, windows, ladders, and water channels over each other's property. Rav Nachman says they do not, while Rava says they do.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story about Mar Yanoka and Mar Kashisha who brought a question to Rav Ashi, linking it to the Nehardeans' reasoning.
Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's ruling that brothers who divided an inheritance do not retain rights of way, windows, ladders, or water channels over each other's property.
Rava disputes Shmuel's ruling and holds that brothers do retain those rights after division.

items.text: Ruling on a torn promissory note of orphans
items.text_en: Ruling on a torn promissory note of orphans
items.desc_en: Rav Chama rules that a promissory note of orphans with a tear should not be collected nor torn, in case the orphans later bring proof of its validity. Rav Acha bar Rava asks Ravina for the halakha; Ravina rules like Rav Chama except for a tear, where witnesses are not assumed to be false. Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari also rules like Rav Chama, arguing that if the note were valid, it would have been presented during the father's lifetime.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chama rules that a torn promissory note of orphans should not be collected nor torn, in case the orphans later bring proof of its validity.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Ravina what the halakha is regarding the torn note.
Ravina rules like Rav Chama in all cases except for a tear, where witnesses are not assumed to be false.

sub.text: Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari's ruling
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari's ruling
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari also rules like Rav Chama, arguing that if the note were valid, it would have been presented during the father's lifetime.

items.text: Mishnah: Obligation to build gatehouse and wall
items.text_en: Mishnah: Obligation to build gatehouse and wall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that residents can compel each other to build a gatehouse and door for the courtyard, and a wall, doors, and bolt for the city. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees, saying not all courtyards or cities are suitable. It also discusses how long one must reside in a city to be considered a resident for tax purposes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the Tanna Kamma's ruling that residents can compel each other to build a gatehouse and door for the courtyard.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objects that not all courtyards are suitable for a gatehouse.
The Mishnah continues with the Tanna Kamma's ruling that residents can compel each other to build a wall, doors, and bolt for the city.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objects that not all cities are suitable for a wall.

The Mishnah concludes by resolving the residency requirement: one must live in the city for twelve months to be considered a resident for tax purposes, but purchasing a dwelling house grants immediate status.

items.text: Gemara: Resolving the apparent problem with a gatehouse
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolving the apparent problem with a gatehouse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a gatehouse is beneficial, citing a story of a pious man who built one and then Elijah stopped speaking to him. It resolves that a gatehouse on the inside is good, but on the outside is not. Further distinctions are made regarding whether it has a door or a wicket.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a gatehouse is beneficial, citing the story of a pious man who built one and then Elijah stopped speaking to him.
The Gemara resolves that a gatehouse on the inside (מגוואי) is good, but on the outside (מבראי) is not.
Alternatively, both cases are outside, but the distinction is whether the gatehouse has a door (דלת) or not.
Alternatively, both have a door, but the distinction is whether the gatehouse has a wicket (פותחת) or not.
Alternatively, both have a wicket, but the distinction is whether the wicket opens inward (מגוואי) or outward (מבראי).

items.text: Baraitot on gatehouse and wall
items.text_en: Baraitot on gatehouse and wall
items.desc_en: A baraita explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view: a courtyard near the public domain needs a gatehouse, but one not near does not; the Sages disagree because people might enter when crowded. Another baraita applies the same logic to a city wall: a city near the border needs a wall, but one not near does not; the Sages fear a military incursion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita elaborates Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position: only a courtyard near the public domain requires a gatehouse, while the Sages object that crowded people might enter.
A second baraita applies the same logic to a city wall: only a border city needs a wall, while the Sages fear a military incursion.

items.text: Dispute on how to collect for city improvements
items.text_en: Dispute on how to collect for city improvements
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yochanan whether funds for city walls are collected per capita or based on property value. Rabbi Yochanan answers: based on property value. In another version, the question is whether collection is based on proximity of houses or property value; Rabbi Yochanan answers: based on proximity of houses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yochanan whether funds for city walls are collected per capita or based on property value.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that collection is based on property value, and instructs Rabbi Elazar to fix this ruling with nails (i.e., make it permanent).

items.text: Exemption of Torah scholars from wall tax
items.text_en: Exemption of Torah scholars from wall tax
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia imposed a wall tax on the rabbis. Resh Lakish argues that rabbis do not need protection, citing a verse about the merit of righteous people being more protective than sand protects the sea. Rabbi Yochanan adds another verse, comparing Torah to a wall and breasts to towers.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia imposed a wall tax on the rabbis.
Resh Lakish argues that rabbis do not need protection, citing a verse that the merits of righteous people are more protective than sand protects the sea.
Rabbi Yochanan adds another verse comparing Torah to a wall and breasts to towers, as a stronger proof that rabbis are protected by their Torah study.

items.text: Resh Lakish's interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'I am a wall' as referring to the congregation of Israel, and 'my breasts are like towers' as referring to synagogues and study halls, establishing the importance of these institutions.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'I am a wall' as referring to the congregation of Israel and 'my breasts are like towers' as referring to synagogues and study halls, following Rava's earlier exposition.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's action and the proof from Torah, Prophets, and Writings
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's action and the proof from Torah, Prophets, and Writings
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda imposed a tax on the rabbis, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rebuked him, citing verses from Torah, Prophets, and Writings that show the importance of Torah scholars and their exemption from such burdens.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda imposed a tax on the rabbis, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rebuked him for violating Torah, Prophets, and Writings.

sub.text: Proof from Torah (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rav Yosef)
sub.text_en: Proof from Torah (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rav Yosef)
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse from the Torah (Deut 33:3) and Rav Yosef's interpretation that Torah scholars are God's treasured ones who wear themselves out traveling to learn Torah.

sub.text: Proof from Prophets (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Ulla)
sub.text_en: Proof from Prophets (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Ulla)
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse from the Prophets (Hosea 8:10) and Ulla's explanation that if the rabbis are gathered, they are exempt from the burden of king and ministers.

sub.text: Proof from Writings (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rav Yehuda)
sub.text_en: Proof from Writings (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, citing Rav Yehuda)
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse from the Writings (Ezra 7:24) and Rav Yehuda's interpretation that various taxes (מנדה, בלו, and הלך) cannot be imposed on those who serve God, i.e., Torah scholars.

items.text: Rav Pappa's action regarding orphans
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's action regarding orphans
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa built a new village for orphans, and when questioned whether it might not be profitable, he responded that he would take from them; if it profits, fine, and if not, he would return it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa builds a new village for orphans, and when Rav Shisha brei d'Rav Idi questions whether it might not be profitable, Rav Pappa responds that he will take from them; if it profits, fine, and if not, he will return it.
Rav Pappa explains that he will take the village from the orphans if it does not profit, and return it to them if it does.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on communal expenses
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on communal expenses
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that everyone must contribute to the city wall, even orphans, but rabbis are exempt because they do not need protection. Similarly, everyone must contribute to the deep ditch, even rabbis, unless they go out with the militia.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that everyone, even orphans, must contribute to the city wall, but rabbis are exempt because they do not need protection.
Rav Yehuda adds that everyone, including rabbis, must contribute to the deep ditch, unless the rabbis go out with the militia, in which case they are exempt.

items.text: Rabbi's storehouse and the incident with Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram
items.text_en: Rabbi's storehouse and the incident with Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram
items.desc_en: During a famine, Rabbi opened his storehouses only for Torah scholars, but Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram pushed in and asked for sustenance, claiming he had not studied. Rabbi initially regretted feeding an ignoramus, but discovered he was a scholar who never benefited from Torah honor, and then allowed everyone to enter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi opens his storehouses during a famine but restricts entry to Torah scholars, excluding the unlearned.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram pushes in and asks for sustenance, claiming he has not studied Torah, and requests to be fed like a dog or raven.
Rabbi provides him with food despite his lack of Torah study.
After Rabbi Yonatan leaves, Rabbi regrets having fed an ignoramus.
Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi suggests that the man might be Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram, a scholar who never benefited from the honor of Torah.
They investigate and confirm the identity; Rabbi then allows everyone to enter the storehouses.

items.text: Rabbi's principle and the story of the crown in Tiberias
items.text_en: Rabbi's principle and the story of the crown in Tiberias
items.desc_en: Rabbi held that punishment comes only for the ignoramuses, illustrated by a story where the townspeople of Tiberias tried to impose a tax on rabbis for a crown, and after the rabbis fled, the crown was thrown at a laundryman, leading to its destruction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's principle that punishment comes to the world only because of ignoramuses.
The Gemara begins the story of the crown tax in Tiberias: the townspeople ask Rabbi to include the Sages, he refuses, half flee, and the tax is halved.
The story continues: the remaining half also flee, leaving only a launderer, who also flees, and the crown tax is canceled.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi concludes from the story that punishment comes to the world only because of ignoramuses.

items.text: The Mishnah and the baraita on residency requirements
items.text_en: The Mishnah and the baraita on residency requirements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who lives in a city for twelve months is considered a resident. A contradiction is raised from a baraita about a caravan that stays less than thirty days, where the animals are stoned and property saved, but after thirty days they are killed by the sword and property lost. Rava resolves this by distinguishing between city residents and temporary settlers, and Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that the twelve-month rule applies only to city taxes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about a caravan that stays less than thirty days in an idolatrous city, where the members are stoned and their property saved.
The baraita states that after thirty days, the caravan members are killed by the sword and their property is destroyed, implying a thirty-day residency threshold.

Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between 'בני מתא' (members of the city, requiring twelve months) and 'יתובי מתא' (residents of the city, requiring thirty days), citing a baraita about vows.
The Gemara questions whether the twelve-month rule applies to all matters, citing a baraita with different time periods for various communal obligations.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
