sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that the twelve-month rule in the mishna applies only to 'פסי העיר' (city columns/taxes), not to other matters.

items.text: Rabbi Asi's ruling on city taxes and orphans
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's ruling on city taxes and orphans
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that everyone must contribute to city taxes, even orphans, but rabbis are exempt because they do not need protection. Rav Pappa adds that for walls, horsemen, and guards, even orphans must pay, but rabbis are exempt. The principle is that anything from which they benefit, even orphans must pay.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that everyone, even orphans, must contribute to city taxes (פסי העיר), but rabbis are exempt because they do not need protection.
Rav Pappa adds that for walls, horsemen, and guards, even orphans must pay, but rabbis are exempt, and the principle is that anything from which they benefit, even orphans must pay.

items.text: Rabbah's charity for orphans and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rabbah's charity for orphans and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbah imposed charity on the orphans of the house of Bar Maryon, and Abaye objected based on a teaching of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda that one may not impose charity on orphans even for redeeming captives. Rabbah responded that he was only doing so to enhance their reputation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah imposed charity on the orphans of the house of Bar Maryon.
Abaye objected, citing Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's teaching that one may not impose charity on orphans even for redeeming captives.
Rabbah responded that he was only doing so to enhance their reputation.

items.text: Ifra Hormiz's gift and Rav Yosef's deliberation
items.text_en: Ifra Hormiz's gift and Rav Yosef's deliberation
items.desc_en: Ifra Hormiz, the mother of King Shapur, sent a purse of dinars to Rav Yosef for a 'great mitzvah.' Rav Yosef deliberated what this meant, and Abaye suggested that since Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda taught that one may not impose charity on orphans even for redeeming captives, it must refer to something else.

sub.desc_en: Ifra Hormiz, mother of King Shapur, sends a purse of dinars to Rav Yosef for a 'great mitzvah' (מצוה רבה).
Rav Yosef deliberates what 'great mitzvah' (מצוה רבה) means, questioning the intended purpose of the gift.

Abaye answers that since Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda taught that one may not impose charity on orphans even for redeeming captives, the 'great mitzvah' must refer to something else, implying the gift is for a different purpose.

items.text: The greatness of redeeming captives and the hierarchy of suffering
items.text_en: The greatness of redeeming captives and the hierarchy of suffering
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabba bar Mari for the source of the rabbinic statement that redeeming captives is a great mitzvah. Rabba bar Mari cites a verse and Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation that the last item in the list (captivity) is the most severe. The Gemara then explains why each successive calamity is worse than the previous one, concluding that captivity includes all the others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the statement that redeeming captives is a great mitzvah.

sub.text: Rava's question to Rabba bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rava's question to Rabba bar Mari
sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabba bar Mari for the scriptural source of the rabbinic statement that redeeming captives is a great mitzvah.

sub.text: Rabba bar Mari's answer citing a verse and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Mari's answer citing a verse and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Mari cites the verse from Jeremiah listing four calamities (death, sword, famine, captivity) and Rabbi Yochanan's principle that each later item in the verse is more severe than the previous one.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation: sword is worse than death
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation: sword is worse than death
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the sword is worse than death, offering both a logical reason (the sword disfigures the body) and a scriptural proof (the verse 'precious in the eyes of God is the death of His pious ones').

sub.text: Gemara's explanation: famine is worse than sword
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation: famine is worse than sword
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why famine is worse than the sword, offering a logical reason (famine causes prolonged suffering) and a scriptural proof (the verse 'better were the slain of the sword than the slain of famine').

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion: captivity is worst of all
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion: captivity is worst of all
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that captivity is the most severe of all, because it includes all the other calamities (death, sword, and famine).

items.text: Laws of the charity fund (kuppah) and the soup kitchen (tamchui)
items.text_en: Laws of the charity fund (kuppah) and the soup kitchen (tamchui)
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the charity fund is collected by two people and distributed by three, while the soup kitchen is both collected and distributed by three. The soup kitchen is for daily needs and for all poor, while the fund is for weekly distribution and for local poor. Townspeople have authority to switch between them or change them as they wish, and to regulate measures, prices, and wages.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the charity fund (קופה) is collected by two people and distributed by three, explaining the reasons: no fewer than two for authority over the public, and three for monetary judgments.
The baraita contrasts the soup kitchen (תמחוי), which is both collected and distributed by three, and specifies that the soup kitchen operates daily while the fund distributes weekly.
The baraita explains that the soup kitchen serves all poor people while the fund serves only local poor, and that townspeople may switch between the two or change them as they wish.
The baraita concludes by granting townspeople authority to regulate measures, prices, wages, and to enforce penalties for violations.

items.text: Source for not appointing fewer than two leaders and the authority to compel charity
items.text_en: Source for not appointing fewer than two leaders and the authority to compel charity
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the rule that no fewer than two are appointed as leaders over the community. Rav Nachman cites a verse. This supports Rabbi Chanina's story that Rabbi appointed two brothers over the fund. The Gemara then discusses the meaning of 'leadership'—that they can seize collateral for charity, even on Shabbat eve. A contradiction is raised from a verse about oppressors, but resolved: it is only permitted when the person is wealthy and refusing to give. Rava forced Rav Nathan bar Ami to give four hundred zuz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Marr's statement that no fewer than two are appointed as leaders over the community.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this rule.
Rav Nachman cites a verse as the source for the rule of appointing two leaders.

sub.text: Gemara's inference and support for Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Gemara's inference and support for Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that while leadership is restricted, trustworthiness is not, and cites Rabbi Chanina's story that Rabbi appointed two brothers over the charity fund.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the nature of leadership
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the nature of leadership
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical meaning of this leadership.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the leadership involves the authority to seize collateral for charity, even on Shabbat eve.
The Gemara objects by citing a verse that God punishes oppressors, and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's statement that this includes even charity collectors.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a wealthy person who refuses to give (where coercion is permitted) and a poor person (where it is not).
The Gemara cites the case of Rava who forced Rav Nathan bar Ami to give four hundred zuz for charity, illustrating the permitted coercion.

items.text: Interpretation of verses about the righteous: judges, charity collectors, and teachers
items.text_en: Interpretation of verses about the righteous: judges, charity collectors, and teachers
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'And the wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament' as referring to a judge who judges truthfully, and 'those who lead many to righteousness' as charity collectors. A baraita adds that the first part also includes charity collectors, and the second part refers to teachers of children, like Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, whom Rav found in a garden and who explained his dedication. The Gemara then asks about the Sages themselves, and Ravina answers with another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'והמשכילים יזהירו כזוהר הרקיע' (the wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament) as referring to a judge who judges truthfully, and 'ומצדיקי הרבים ככוכבים לעולם ועד' (those who lead many to righteousness) as charity collectors.
A baraita adds that the first part of the verse also includes charity collectors, and the second part refers to teachers of children.

sub.text: Rav's story about Rav Shmuel bar Shilat
sub.text_en: Rav's story about Rav Shmuel bar Shilat
sub.desc_en: Rav identifies Rav Shmuel bar Shilat as an example of such a teacher, recounting how he found him in a garden and Rav Shmuel bar Shilat explained his dedication to his students.
The Gemara asks about the Sages themselves, who are not judges, charity collectors, or teachers.
Ravina answers with another verse: 'ואוהביו כצאת השמש בגבורתו' (and those who love Him shall be like the sun going forth in its might).

items.text: Rules for charity collectors regarding separation, found money, and handling funds
items.text_en: Rules for charity collectors regarding separation, found money, and handling funds
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that charity collectors may not separate from each other, but one may go to the gate and another to the shop. If one finds money in the market, he should not put it in his own pocket but in the charity purse, and later take it. Similarly, if someone repays a debt in the market, the collector should put it in the charity purse. Another baraita states that if collectors have no poor to distribute to, they may exchange coins with others but not with themselves. Money for charity should be counted one by one, not in pairs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that charity collectors may not separate from each other, but one may go to the gate and another to the shop; if one finds money in the market, he must put it in the charity purse, not his own pocket, and similarly for a debt repaid in the market.
A second baraita adds rules for when there are no poor to distribute to: collectors may exchange coins with others but not with themselves, and charity money must be counted one by one, not in pairs.

items.text: Abaye's practice regarding charity distribution
items.text_en: Abaye's practice regarding charity distribution
items.desc_en: Abaye relates that initially his master (Rabbah) would not sit at the entrance of the synagogue, but after hearing the baraita that townspeople may change the charity fund as they wish, he began to sit there. Abaye also says that initially his master would make two purses—one for the poor of the world and one for the poor of the town—but after hearing Shmuel's instruction to Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi to make one purse, he changed his practice.

sub.desc_en: Abaye reports that his master (Rabbah) initially would not sit at the synagogue entrance, but after hearing the baraita that townspeople may change the charity fund, he began to sit there.

Abaye further reports that his master initially made two purses—one for the poor of the world and one for the town's poor—but after hearing Shmuel's instruction to Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi to make one purse, he changed his practice.

items.text: Rav Ashi's exemption from a communal agreement
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's exemption from a communal agreement
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi claims he does not need to participate in a communal charity fund because all donors come on his account and he gives to whomever he wishes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi declares that he does not need to participate in the communal charity fund because all donors come on his account and he gives to whomever he wishes.

items.text: The butchers' agreement and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: The butchers' agreement and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: Two butchers made an agreement that each would work only on his designated day, with a penalty of tearing the hide of the violator. One violated the agreement, and Rava ruled that the others must compensate him. Rav Yemar bar Shelemia challenged Rava with a baraita about not enforcing penalties for violating a communal agreement, but Rava did not respond. Rav Pappa defended Rava, explaining that the baraita applies only where there is no important person, but here there was an important person (the violator).

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that two butchers made an agreement with a penalty of tearing the hide of a violator, and one violated it and his hide was torn.
The butchers came before Rava, and he ruled that the others must compensate the violator for the hide.
Rav Yemar bar Shelemia challenged Rava with a baraita about not enforcing penalties for violating a communal agreement, and Rava did not respond.
Rav Pappa defended Rava, explaining that the baraita applies only where there is no important person, but here there was an important person (the violator), so the agreement is not binding.

items.text: Trust in charity collectors and treasurers
items.text_en: Trust in charity collectors and treasurers
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one does not calculate precisely with charity collectors or with Temple treasurers, citing a verse about trustworthiness. Rabbi Elazar adds that even if one has a trusted treasurer at home, one should still count and seal the money, as the verse says 'they counted and sealed'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one does not calculate precisely with charity collectors or Temple treasurers, citing the verse about trustworthiness.
Rabbi Elazar adds that even with a trusted treasurer, one should still count and seal the money, citing the verse 'they counted and sealed'.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda on checking for food vs. clothing
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda on checking for food vs. clothing
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says we investigate the poor for food but not for clothing, offering both a logical reason (clothing causes embarrassment) and a scriptural support. Rav Yehuda argues the opposite: we investigate for clothing but not for food, with his own logic and verses. A baraita supports Rav Yehuda's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that we investigate the poor for food but not for clothing, offering both a logical reason (clothing causes embarrassment) and a scriptural support.
Rav Yehuda argues the opposite: we investigate for clothing but not for food, with his own logical reasoning and scriptural support.

items.text: The poor traveler and the one who goes door to door
items.text_en: The poor traveler and the one who goes door to door
items.desc_en: A mishnah details what is given to a poor person passing through: a loaf, lodging, and three meals for Shabbat. A baraita adds that if one goes door to door, we do not provide for him. Rav Pappa initially refuses to give to such a person, but Rav Sama bar Rav Yeiva argues that this would cause him to die. Rav Pappa clarifies that the baraita means we do not give a large gift, but we do give a small one.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the minimum provisions for a traveling poor person: a loaf, lodging, and three meals for Shabbat.
A baraita adds that if the poor person goes door to door, we do not provide for him.

sub.text: Rav Sama bar Rav Yeiva's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Yeiva's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Yeiva objects to Rav Pappa's refusal to give to a door-to-door beggar, arguing that if Rav Pappa does not give, no one else will, and the poor person will die.
Rav Pappa clarifies that the baraita means we do not give a large gift, but we do give a small one.

items.text: The greatness of charity and its rewards
items.text_en: The greatness of charity and its rewards
items.desc_en: Rav Asi teaches that one should never withhold a third of a shekel per year for charity, and that charity is equal to all other mitzvot. Rabbi Elazar says that one who causes others to give is greater than the giver. Rava instructs the people of Mehoza to give to each other for peace. Rabbi Elazar contrasts the Temple period with the present, where charity is still valuable even if taken by force. Rava relates a story from Ulla.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi teaches that one should never withhold giving a third of a shekel per year for charity, and that charity is equal to all other mitzvot.
Rabbi Elazar states that one who causes others to give charity is greater than the giver himself, citing a verse.
Rava instructs the people of Mehoza to give charity to each other for peace, and Rabbi Elazar contrasts the Temple period with the present, where charity is still valuable even if taken by force.
Rava relates a story from Ulla, serving as a brief digression.

items.text: Opening aggadic teaching on charity accumulating like armor or cloth
items.text_en: Opening aggadic teaching on charity accumulating like armor or cloth
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Ulla was called 'the one who confuses his mother's paths' by citing a teaching in the name of Rabbi Elazar: each small coin of charity joins together to form a great sum, just as each scale of armor joins to form a whole. Rabbi Chanina adds a similar analogy from a garment, where each thread joins to form a large cloth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Ulla was called 'the one who confuses his mother's paths' by citing Rabbi Elazar's teaching that each small coin of charity joins together to form a great sum, like scales of armor.
Rabbi Chanina adds a supporting analogy from a garment, where each thread joins to form a large cloth, to the same principle of charity accumulating.

items.text: The halakhic debate about a metzora during his counting days
items.text_en: The halakhic debate about a metzora during his counting days
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Ulla was called 'the one who confuses his mother's paths' by recounting a story: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asked Rav Sheshet for the source that a metzora during his counting days imparts impurity to a person. Rav Sheshet argued from the fact that he imparts impurity to garments, but Rav Achadvoi challenged this with the case of one who moves a carcass, which imparts impurity to garments but not to a person. Rav Sheshet then brought analogies from a sheretz and seminal emission, but Rav Achadvoi countered that those are explicitly written. Rav Sheshet became upset, and Rav Achadvoi's mother came to plead for her son's recovery, which was granted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Ulla was called 'the one who confuses his mother's paths'.
Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asked Rav Sheshet for the source that a metzora during his counting days imparts impurity to a person.
Rav Sheshet answered that since the metzora imparts impurity to garments, he also imparts impurity to a person.
Rav Achadvoi bar Ami objected that impurity in attached objects (טומאה בחיבורין) is different, as one who moves a carcass (הסיט נבילה) imparts impurity to garments but not to a person.
Rav Sheshet countered with analogies from a sheretz (creeping animal) and seminal emission, but Rav Achadvoi bar Ami rejected each because those are explicitly written in the Torah.
Rav Sheshet became upset, Rav Achadvoi bar Ami fell silent and his learning was honored, and after his mother's pleading, Rav Sheshet prayed for him and he was healed.

items.text: The source for the metzora's impurity to a person
items.text_en: The source for the metzora's impurity to a person
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides the actual source for the law that a metzora during his counting days imparts impurity to a person: a gezerah shavah from the word 'kibus begadim' (washing of garments) used both during the counting days and during the days of his isolation, just as in the latter he imparts impurity to a person, so too in the former.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: And the source we came to (the metzora's impurity to a person during counting days) — from where do we derive it?

The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says, a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'כיבוס בגדים' (washing of garments) used both during the counting days and during the isolation days teaches that just as in the latter the metzora imparts impurity to a person, so too in the former.

items.text: The greatness of secret charity vs. Moses and the dispute with Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: The greatness of secret charity vs. Moses and the dispute with Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that one who gives charity in secret is greater than Moses, as Moses feared anger, while charity in secret appeases anger. Rabbi Yitzchak disagrees, arguing that while charity appeases anger, it does not appease fierce wrath, as the verse says 'a gift in secret appeases anger, but a bribe in the bosom [brings] fierce wrath.' An alternative version has Rabbi Yitzchak saying that a judge who takes a bribe brings fierce wrath to the world.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar declares that one who gives charity in secret is greater than Moses, citing verses about Moses' fear of anger and the power of a secret gift to suppress anger.
Rabbi Yitzchak objects that while charity suppresses anger (אף), it does not suppress fierce wrath (חמה), as the verse continues 'and a bribe in the bosom brings fierce wrath.'
An alternative version reports Rabbi Yitzchak saying that any judge who takes a bribe brings fierce wrath to the world.

items.text: The blessings for giving charity and appeasing the poor
items.text_en: The blessings for giving charity and appeasing the poor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that one who gives a prutah to a poor person is blessed with six blessings, while one who appeases him with words is blessed with eleven blessings, as derived from verses in Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that one who gives a prutah to a poor person is blessed with six blessings.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites verses from Isaiah to support the six blessings for giving charity.
Rabbi Yitzchak adds that one who appeases a poor person with words is blessed with eleven blessings.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites a longer passage from Isaiah to support the eleven blessings for appeasing the poor with words.

items.text: The reward for pursuing charity and the prayer for worthy recipients
items.text_en: The reward for pursuing charity and the prayer for worthy recipients
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the verse 'one who pursues charity and kindness will find life, charity, and honor' means that God provides money for charity to those who pursue it. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that God provides worthy recipients so that the giver receives reward, contrasting with the prayer of Rabbah that the wicked should be given unworthy recipients so they receive no reward.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak questions the verse 'one who pursues charity and kindness will find life, charity, and honor' — why would pursuing charity lead to finding charity?
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the verse means God provides money to those who pursue charity, enabling them to perform it.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that God also provides worthy recipients for the charity, so the giver receives reward.
The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement excludes the opposite view of Rabbah.
Rabbah teaches that Jeremiah prayed for God to give wicked people unworthy recipients for their charity, so they receive no reward.

items.text: The reward for habitual charity: wise, wealthy, and aggadic children
items.text_en: The reward for habitual charity: wise, wealthy, and aggadic children
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who is accustomed to giving charity merits children who are wise, wealthy, and masters of aggadah, as derived from a verse (which is cut off at the end of the daf).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who is accustomed to giving charity merits children who are wise, wealthy, and masters of aggadah, citing a verse (which is cut off at the end of the daf).

items.text: Opening exposition on the verse 'ימצא חיים'
items.text_en: Opening exposition on the verse 'ימצא חיים'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'ימצא חיים' (Proverbs 21:21) as referring to charity (צדקה) and honor (כבוד), linking the latter to the honor of the wise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'ימצא חיים' (Proverbs 21:21) as referring to charity (צדקה) and honor (כבוד), linking the latter to the honor of the wise.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Akiva and Turnusrufus on charity
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Akiva and Turnusrufus on charity
items.desc_en: Turnusrufus asks why God, if He loves the poor, does not support them directly. Rabbi Akiva answers that charity allows Israel to be saved from Gehinnom. Turnusrufus counters with a parable of a king's slave, implying charity prolongs punishment. Rabbi Akiva responds with a parable of a king's son, showing charity is a gift. Turnusrufus then notes that Israel is called both sons and slaves, and when they do not do God's will they are slaves; Rabbi Akiva cites Isaiah 58:7 to show charity is commanded even now.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir presents a hypothetical challenge: if God loves the poor, why does He not sustain them directly?
Rabbi Meir answers that God leaves the poor in need so that we may be saved from Gehinnom through charity.
The Gemara introduces a historical parallel: the wicked Turnusrufus asked Rabbi Akiva the same question.
Turnusrufus asks Rabbi Akiva: if your God loves the poor, why does He not sustain them?
Rabbi Akiva answers that God leaves the poor in need so that we may be saved from Gehinnom through charity.
Turnusrufus objects with a parable of a king who imprisoned a slave: feeding the slave angers the king, and Israel are called 'slaves'.
Rabbi Akiva counters with a parable of a king who imprisoned his son: feeding the son earns a gift, and Israel are called 'sons'.
Turnusrufus objects that Israel are called both sons and slaves, and currently they are not doing God's will, so the slave parable applies.
Rabbi Akiva answers by citing the verse 'הלא פרוס לרעב לחמך' (Isaiah 58:7), which commands charity now, implying that even when Israel are not fully righteous, charity is still commanded.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Shalom on fixed sustenance and losses
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Shalom on fixed sustenance and losses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Shalom teaches that just as a person's sustenance is decreed on Rosh Hashanah, so too are his losses. If one merits, he gives bread to the hungry; if not, he brings the poor into his home (i.e., suffers loss).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shalom teaches that just as a person's sustenance is decreed on Rosh Hashanah, so too their losses are decreed; if one merits, they give charity, if not, they suffer the poor coming to them.
He explains that if one merits, he gives bread to the hungry; if not, he brings the poor into his home (i.e., suffers loss).

items.text: Story of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and his nephews
items.text_en: Story of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and his nephews
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai saw in a dream that his nephews would lose 700 dinars. He collected charity from them, leaving only 17 dinars. On Yom Kippur eve, the king's agents seized their money, but only 17 dinars were taken. When asked why he didn't tell them, he said he wanted them to perform the mitzvah for its own sake.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai saw in a dream that his nephews would lose 700 dinars, so he collected charity from them, leaving them only 17 dinars, and on Yom Kippur eve the king's agents seized the rest.

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai reassures his nephews that the 17 dinars were taken from them, explains he knew from the dream, and reveals he did not tell them earlier so they would perform the mitzvah for its own sake.

items.text: Rav Pappa's near fall and the sin of neglecting charity
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's near fall and the sin of neglecting charity
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa almost fell from a ladder and thought he was being punished like Sabbath desecrators or idolaters. Chiyya bar Rav Midifti suggested he might have neglected a poor person. A baraisa from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha equates ignoring charity to idolatry, based on a verbal analogy of 'בליעל'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa nearly falls from a ladder and fears he is being punished like Sabbath desecrators or idolaters.
Chiyya bar Rav Midifti suggests that Rav Pappa may have neglected a poor person who came to him.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: A baraita equates ignoring charity to idolatry via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'בליעל'.

items.text: Teachings on charity bringing peace and redeeming from death
items.text_en: Teachings on charity bringing peace and redeeming from death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei says charity and kindness create peace and advocates between Israel and God. Rabbi Yehuda says charity brings redemption and lists ten hard things, concluding that death is hardest, but charity saves from death, citing Proverbs 10:2.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei teaches that charity and kindness create peace and advocates between Israel and God, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yehuda says charity brings redemption and lists ten hard things, concluding that death is hardest but charity saves from death, citing Proverbs 10:2.

items.text: Charity enables seeing the Divine Presence
items.text_en: Charity enables seeing the Divine Presence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai contrasts human kings with God: giving a gift to a king may not be accepted, but giving a coin to a poor person merits seeing the Shechinah. Rabbi Elazar would give charity before praying, citing Psalm 17:15. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the verse refers to Torah scholars who deprive themselves of sleep in this world and are satiated with the Divine radiance in the next.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai contrasts human kings, where a gift may not be accepted and one may not see the king's face, with God, where giving a coin to a poor person merits seeing the Divine Presence, as per Psalm 17:15.
Rabbi Elazar would give a coin to a poor person before praying, citing the same verse from Psalms.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the verse 'I will be satisfied when I awake with Your likeness' refers to Torah scholars who deprive themselves of sleep in this world and are satiated with the Divine radiance in the next.

items.text: Charity as a loan to God and two types of salvation
items.text_en: Charity as a loan to God and two types of salvation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the verse 'מלוה ה' חונן דל' implies that one who gives to the poor is like a lender to God. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba notes a contradiction between two verses about charity saving from death: one saves from an unnatural death, the other from Gehinnom. The Gemara identifies the one with 'עברה' as saving from Gehinnom, and asks which saves from unnatural death.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains the verse 'מלוה ה' חונן דל' as implying that one who gives to the poor is like a lender to God.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yochanan raised a contradiction between two verses about charity saving from death, asking why two different formulations are needed.
The Gemara resolves that one verse refers to saving from an unnatural death and the other from the judgment of Gehinnom.
The Gemara asks which verse saves from Gehinnom and identifies it as the one containing 'עברה' (wrath), citing the verse 'יום עברה היום ההוא'.
The Gemara then asks which verse saves from an unnatural death, leaving the question open.

items.text: Anonymous charity and the solution of the charity fund
items.text_en: Anonymous charity and the solution of the charity fund
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case of giving or taking without knowing who is involved excludes the practices of Mar Ukva and Rabbi Abba. The solution is to give to a charity fund managed by a trustworthy person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's anonymous giving excludes Mar Ukva and Rabbi Abba, and recommends giving to a charity fund.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says one should not give to a charity fund unless supervised by a trustworthy person like Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's case is when such a supervisor is appointed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's leniency by citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov forbids giving to a charity fund unless supervised by a trustworthy person like Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's case is when a supervisor like Rabbi Chananya ben Teradyon is appointed over the fund.

items.text: Aggadic teachings on the power of charity
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings on the power of charity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu relates that Moses asked God how to elevate Israel, and God answered through the census (Ki Tisa). Then Rabbi Avahu reports that Solomon was asked about the power of charity, and he cited David's verse; Rabbi Abba adds another verse showing that charity leads to security.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports that Moses asked God how to elevate Israel, and God answered with the census (Ki Tisa).
Rabbi Avahu reports that Solomon was asked about the power of charity and cited David's verse that charity elevates one's horn.
Rabbi Abba adds a verse from Isaiah showing that charity leads to security and trustworthiness.

items.text: Who merits the World to Come and the martyrs of Lod
items.text_en: Who merits the World to Come and the martyrs of Lod
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports that Solomon was asked who merits the World to Come, and he answered: one who honors the elderly. A story about Yosef ben Rabbi Yehoshua's vision of the inverted world follows. The Gemara then discusses the special status of the martyrs of the kingdom, identifying them as the martyrs of Lod.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu reports a question to Solomon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu reports a question to Solomon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports that Solomon was asked who merits the World to Come, and he answered: one who honors the elderly.

sub.text: Story of Yosef ben Rabbi Yehoshua's vision
sub.text_en: Story of Yosef ben Rabbi Yehoshua's vision
sub.desc_en: A story is told about Yosef ben Rabbi Yehoshua who fell ill and had a vision of an inverted world, which his father interpreted as a clear world, illustrating the principle of honoring the elderly.
Yosef reports hearing that the martyrs of the kingdom have an exclusive place in the World to Come.
The Gemara asks who these martyrs are, suggesting Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues, but rejects this as obvious.
The Gemara concludes that the martyrs referred to are the martyrs of Lod.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of 'Tzedaka exalts a nation'
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of 'Tzedaka exalts a nation'
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asks his students about the verse. Rabbi Eliezer explains that 'tzedaka exalts a nation' refers to Israel, while the charity of other nations is a sin because they do it for self-aggrandizement. A challenge about a person giving charity for ulterior motives is resolved by distinguishing between Jews and non-Jews.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asks his students to interpret the verse 'צדקה תרומם גוי וחסד לאמים חטאת' (Proverbs 14:34).
Rabbi Eliezer explains that 'צדקה תרומם גוי' refers to Israel, while the charity of other nations is a sin because they do it only for self-aggrandizement, citing the verse from Ezra 6:10.

The Gemara objects: If one gives charity for ulterior motives, is it not considered complete charity? It cites a baraita that one who gives a coin for charity so his children will live or he will merit the World to Come is a complete righteous person.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the baraita about giving charity for ulterior motives applies to a Jew, while Rabbi Eliezer's statement about charity being a sin applies to a gentile.

items.text: Interpretations by Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabban Gamliel, and Rabbi Eliezer HaModai
items.text_en: Interpretations by Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabban Gamliel, and Rabbi Eliezer HaModai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua interprets the verse as referring to Israel and says non-Jews' charity is a sin because it is for political gain. Rabban Gamliel adds that it is for pride, which leads to Gehinnom. Rabbi Eliezer HaModai says it is to shame Israel, citing a verse about their sin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua interprets the verse 'צדקה תרומם גוי' as referring to Israel, and the charity of non-Jews as a sin done only for political gain.
Rabban Gamliel adds that non-Jews' charity is for pride, which leads to Gehinnom, citing a verse about 'עברה' (wrath) as Gehinnom.
Rabbi Eliezer HaModai says non-Jews' charity is to shame Israel, citing a verse about their sin leading to punishment.

items.text: Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana's interpretation and Rabban Yochanan's conclusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana's interpretation and Rabban Yochanan's conclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana interprets the verse as giving tzedaka and chesed to Israel and sin to the nations. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai endorses his view, adding that just as a sin-offering atones for Israel, so charity atones for the nations.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana interprets the verse 'צדקה תרומם גוי וחסד' as giving tzedaka and chesed to Israel, and sin to the nations.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai endorses Rabbi Nechunya's interpretation as superior to his own and the other disciples' views.
The gemara clarifies that Rabban Yochanan himself had a prior statement, citing a baraita where he taught that just as a sin-offering atones for Israel, so charity atones for the nations.

items.text: Accepting charity from non-Jews for the sake of peace
items.text_en: Accepting charity from non-Jews for the sake of peace
items.desc_en: Ifra Hormiz, mother of King Shapur, sent money to Rabbi Ami who refused, but Rava accepted for the sake of peace. Rabbi Ami was upset, citing a verse about shame. The Gemara explains that Rava gave it to non-Jewish poor, and Rabbi Ami could have done the same but was upset because he wanted to distribute it to Jewish poor.

sub.desc_en: Ifra Hormiz, mother of King Shapur, sent 400 dinars to Rabbi Ami who refused, then to Rava who accepted for the sake of peace (שלום מלכות).

Rabbi Ami became upset and cited the verse 'ביבוש קצירה תשברנה, נשים באות מאירות אותה' (When their harvest dries up, it is broken; women come and set it ablaze) to criticize accepting charity from non-Jews.
The Gemara explains that Rava accepted the money for the sake of peace (שלום מלכות).
The Gemara asks: Could Rabbi Ami also have accepted for the sake of peace (שלום מלכות)?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Ami could have distributed the money to non-Jewish poor for the sake of peace, but he was upset because he wanted to give it to Jewish poor.
The Gemara resolves that Rava also gave the money to non-Jewish poor, and Rabbi Ami's upset was because he wanted to give it to Jewish poor himself.

items.text: Story of Benjamin the Righteous and the charity fund
items.text_en: Story of Benjamin the Righteous and the charity fund
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story about Benjamin the Righteous, who was in charge of the charity fund. During a famine, a woman with seven children begged him for support; when the fund was empty, he gave from his own pocket. He later fell ill, and the ministering angels argued before God that he who saved a life should not die young; his decree was torn up and he was granted 22 more years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Benjamin the Righteous, noting that the previous discussion was not concluded before him.
A baraita relates the story of Benjamin the Righteous, who gave from his own pocket to support a woman and her seven children during a famine, and was rewarded with 22 additional years of life.

items.text: King Monbaz's defense of his charity
items.text_en: King Monbaz's defense of his charity
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how King Monbaz distributed his treasures and those of his ancestors during a famine. His family rebuked him, but he defended his actions with seven scriptural proofs: he stored treasures in heaven, in a place where no hand can reach, something that yields fruit, treasures of souls, for himself, and for the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the story of King Monbaz, who distributed his treasures during a famine, and his family's rebuke that his ancestors stored up wealth while he squanders it.
King Monbaz defends his charity by citing a verse: his ancestors stored treasures below, but he stored them above in heaven.
King Monbaz argues that his ancestors stored in a place where a hand can reach, but he stored in a place where no hand can reach, citing a verse about righteousness and justice.
King Monbaz argues that his ancestors stored something that does not yield fruit, but he stored something that yields fruit, citing a verse about the righteous eating the fruit of their deeds.
King Monbaz argues that his ancestors stored treasures of money, but he stored treasures of souls, citing a verse about the wise person who takes souls.
King Monbaz argues that his ancestors stored for others, but he stored for himself, citing a verse about righteousness being for oneself.
King Monbaz argues that his ancestors stored for this world, but he stored for the World to Come, citing a verse about righteousness going before one and God's glory gathering him.

items.text: Dispute about the Mishnah's ruling on purchasing a dwelling
items.text_en: Dispute about the Mishnah's ruling on purchasing a dwelling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one purchases a dwelling in a city, he is like the townspeople. The Gemara notes this contradicts Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says purchasing any land suffices. A baraita is cited where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires land fit for a dwelling, and the Gemara resolves that there are two Tannaitic versions of his opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one purchases a dwelling in a city, he is like the townspeople.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah contradicts Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says purchasing any land suffices.
A baraita is cited where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires land fit for a dwelling.
The Gemara resolves that there are two Tannaitic versions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion.

items.text: Mishnah: Minimum sizes for dividing a courtyard, field, garden, and other properties
items.text_en: Mishnah: Minimum sizes for dividing a courtyard, field, garden, and other properties
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum sizes required for forced division of a courtyard (4 amot each), a field (9 kav each, with Rabbi Yehuda requiring 9 half-kav), a garden (half-kav each, Rabbi Akiva says a beit rova). Other items like a hall, dovecote, bathhouse, etc. are divided only if each gets a viable portion. The general rule: if the item retains its name after division, it may be divided; if not, it cannot. When both parties agree, they may divide even smaller portions, except for sacred writings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum size for dividing a courtyard: four amot for each party.
The Mishnah gives the minimum for a field: nine kav for each party.
Rabbi Yehuda requires nine half-kav for each party instead of nine full kav.
The Mishnah gives the minimum for a garden: half a kav for each party.
Rabbi Akiva requires a beit rova (a quarter-kav area) for each party in a garden.
The Mishnah lists other items (hall, dovecote, bathhouse, etc.) and gives the general rule: if the item retains its name after division, it may be divided; if not, it cannot.
The Mishnah concludes that when both parties agree, they may divide even smaller portions, except for sacred writings which may never be divided.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the four amot for courtyard division
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the four amot for courtyard division
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan explains that the four amot mentioned in the Mishnah are exclusive of the space needed for doorways. A baraita supports this, requiring eight amot each, which is reconciled by understanding that the Mishnah's four amot are after deducting four amot for each doorway.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the four cubits mentioned in the Mishnah are exclusive of the space needed for doorways.
A baraita is cited that supports this interpretation, requiring eight cubits for each owner.
The Gemara questions the contradiction: the Mishnah states only four cubits for each, not eight.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by concluding that the baraita aligns with Rabbi Asi's explanation that the four cubits are exclusive of doorways.
Some present the contradiction explicitly: the Mishnah says four cubits, but the baraita says eight cubits.
Rabbi Asi again cites Rabbi Yochanan's explanation that the four cubits are exclusive of the space for doorways, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda on dividing the courtyard
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda on dividing the courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says the courtyard is divided according to its doorways, while Rav Chisda says each doorway gets four amot and the remainder is divided equally. A baraita supports Rav Chisda, detailing how one with one doorway gets four amot, one with two gets eight, and the rest is divided equally. For a wide doorway of eight amot, one takes eight amot opposite the doorway and four amot in the courtyard, which Abaye explains as eight amot in length and four in width.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a courtyard is divided according to its entrances.
Rav Chisda says each entrance gets four amot and the remainder is divided equally.
A baraita supports Rav Chisda, stating that entrances in a courtyard have four amot, and detailing the division for one or two entrances.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'four amot in the courtyard' for a wide entrance.
Abaye explains that for an eight-amah wide entrance, one takes eight amot in length and four amot in width of the courtyard.

items.text: Amemar's ruling on a protruding beam
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling on a protruding beam
items.desc_en: Amemar states that a protruding beam (פֵּירָא דְסוּפְלֵי) has four amot on each side, but only if it does not have a designated doorway.

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that a protruding beam (פֵּירָא דְסוּפְלֵי) has four amot on each side, but only if it does not have a designated doorway.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the portico (אכסדרה) and the four cubits
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the portico (אכסדרה) and the four cubits
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a portico does not have four cubits before its entrance because one can unload inside. Rav Sheishet objects with a baraita that includes porticoes, and the Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a specific type of portico (the Roman-style one).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one designates a doorway, he only gets four cubits before his entrance.
Rav Huna rules that a portico (אכסדרה) does not have four cubits because one can unload inside.
Rav Sheishet objects with a baraita that includes porticoes as having four cubits.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a Roman-style portico (אכסדרה רומייתא), not a standard one.

items.text: Baraita on gatehouse, portico, and balcony; Rabbi Yochanan's question about a chicken coop
items.text_en: Baraita on gatehouse, portico, and balcony; Rabbi Yochanan's question about a chicken coop
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a gatehouse, portico, and balcony have four cubits, but if five houses open onto a balcony, they share only four cubits. Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai whether a chicken coop has four cubits, and he answers that it does not, because chickens can climb up and down.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a gatehouse, portico, and balcony each have four cubits, but if five houses open onto a balcony, they share only four cubits.
Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai whether a chicken coop has the right to four cubits of space.
Rabbi Yannai answers that a chicken coop does not have four cubits, because chickens can climb up and down, so the rationale of unloading a burden does not apply.

items.text: Rava's question about a half-roofed house
items.text_en: Rava's question about a half-roofed house
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether a house that is half-roofed has four cubits. Rav Nachman rules it does not, because even if the roof is on the outside, one can enter the unroofed part to unload.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether a house that is half-roofed has the four cubits of space before its entrance.
Rav Nachman rules that the house does not have the four cubits, because even if the roof is on the outside, one can enter the unroofed part to unload.

items.text: Rav Huna's question about changing an entrance to another alley
items.text_en: Rav Huna's question about changing an entrance to another alley
items.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rabbi Ami whether one resident of an alley can change his entrance to another alley against the will of the other residents. Rabbi Ami rules that they can prevent him.

sub.text: Rav Huna's question to Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's question to Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rabbi Ami whether one resident of an alley can change his entrance to another alley against the will of the other residents.
Rabbi Ami rules that the other residents of the alley can prevent him from changing his entrance.

items.text: Division of the inn (אכסניא) and the dung heap
items.text_en: Division of the inn (אכסניא) and the dung heap
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether the inn is divided according to the number of people or the number of openings. The answer is by people, and a baraita supports this: dung in the courtyard is divided by openings, but the inn by people.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks whether the inn (אכסניא) is divided according to the number of people or the number of openings.
The answer is given that the inn is divided according to the number of people.
A baraita is cited to support the answer: dung in the courtyard is divided by openings, but the inn by people.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on blocking an entrance and the baraita about five courtyards
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on blocking an entrance and the baraita about five courtyards
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one resident cannot block his entrance because it increases the path for others. An objection is raised from a baraita about five courtyards opening into an alley, where the inner ones use the outer ones' space, implying that blocking is allowed. The Gemara notes that the baraita is a dispute between Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that residents of an alley can prevent one resident from blocking his entrance, because it increases their path.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about five courtyards opening into an alley, where inner courtyards use the outer ones' space, implying that blocking is allowed.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita reflects a dispute between Tannaim, citing Rabbi's position that reopening a sealed entrance is not blocked.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute and Rava's distinction about a sealed entrance
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute and Rava's distinction about a sealed entrance
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the baraita is a dispute: Rabbi permits reopening a sealed entrance, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar allows all to use the alley. Rava adds that if one broke the doorposts, the neighbors can prevent reopening. Abaye cites a supporting baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the baraita as a Tannaitic dispute, citing the first opinion of Rabbi who permits reopening a sealed entrance.
The Gemara corrects the baraita's text, explaining that Rabbi's statement originally referred to five courtyards, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar allows all to use the alley.
Rava distinguishes that the leniency applies only if one did not break the doorposts, but if he did, the neighbors can prevent reopening.
Abaye cites a supporting baraita to Rava's distinction.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Laws of a sealed house and a sealed grave
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Laws of a sealed house and a sealed grave
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sealed house has four cubits of space around it, but if its doorposts are broken, it loses that space. Similarly, a sealed grave does not transmit impurity to its surroundings, but if its doorposts are broken and then sealed, it does transmit impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sealed house has four cubits of space around it, but if its doorposts are broken, it loses that space.
The Mishnah adds that a sealed grave does not transmit impurity to its surroundings, but if its doorposts are broken and then sealed, it does transmit impurity.

items.text: Gemara: Alleys leading to another city
items.text_en: Gemara: Alleys leading to another city
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that if residents of a city want to seal alleys that lead to another city, the residents of that other city can prevent them, even if there is another path, due to the principle that a path established by many cannot be ruined.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that residents of a city can prevent sealing alleys leading to another city, even if there is an alternate path.

sub.text: Gemara citing Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Gemara citing Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the ruling by citing Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav that a boundary path established by many cannot be ruined.
Rav Giddel adds that when many have chosen a path for themselves, their choice is binding.

items.text: Gemara: Alleys leading to public domain
items.text_en: Gemara: Alleys leading to public domain
items.desc_en: Rav Anan in the name of Shmuel rules that if residents of alleys leading to the public domain want to install doors, the public can prevent them. The Gemara initially thinks this applies within four cubits of the public domain, but concludes that it is because the public sometimes needs to enter the alley.

sub.text: Rav Anan in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Anan in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Anan in the name of Shmuel rules that if residents of alleys leading to the public domain want to install doors, the public can prevent them.

The Gemara initially assumes that Shmuel's ruling applies only within four cubits of the public domain, citing Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Nachman that four cubits adjacent to the public domain are considered like the public domain.

The Gemara rejects this assumption, explaining that the earlier ruling about four cubits applies only to matters of ritual impurity (טומאה), but here the reason is that the public sometimes needs to enter the alley when crowded.

items.text: Mishnah: Field measurement and local custom
items.text_en: Mishnah: Field measurement and local custom
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses that a field must have nine kav of produce for each party. The Gemara notes that this is not disputed, as each follows local custom. In Babylonia, Rav Yosef says the measure is 'Be Radu Yoma'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a field is not divided unless it contains nine kav of produce for each party.
The Gemara resolves that the Tannaim do not dispute; each follows local custom.
The Gemara asks what the local custom is in Babylonia.
Rav Yosef answers that the measure in Babylonia is 'Be Radu Yoma' (a day's plowing).

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'Be Radu Yoma'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'Be Radu Yoma'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what 'Be Radu Yoma' means, suggesting it could be a day of plowing or a day of sowing. Two answers are given: one that it is a day of plowing (which includes teaching), and another that it is a day of sowing (which involves going around).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Be Radu Yoma' means, noting that if it is a day of sowing, it cannot also be a day of plowing, and vice versa.
One answer suggests it is a day of plowing (כְּרָבָא), which includes teaching (כָּרֵיב וְתָנֵי).
Another answer suggests it is a day of sowing (זַרְעָא), which involves going around (בְּהָדוֹרֵי).

items.text: Gemara: Measures for a vineyard and a garden
items.text_en: Gemara: Measures for a vineyard and a garden
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman defines 'Dawla' as a day of drawing water. The father of Shmuel defines 'Pardesa' as three kav. A baraisa supports this, stating that Somchos says a minimum of three kav for a vineyard, though Rabbi Yosei calls this prophecy. In Babylonia, Rava bar Kisna says it is three rows of twelve vines, enough for a man to hoe in a day.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman defines 'Dawla' as a day of drawing water.
The father of Shmuel defines 'Pardesa' as three kav.
A baraita supports the definition, citing Somchos who says a minimum of three kav for a vineyard.
Rabbi Yosei objects, calling Somchos' statement prophecy rather than halacha.
Rava bar Kisna defines the Babylonian measure as three rows of twelve vines, enough for a man to hoe in a day.

items.text: Gemara: Prophecy given to the wise
items.text_en: Gemara: Prophecy given to the wise
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa states that since the Temple's destruction, prophecy was taken from prophets and given to the wise. The Gemara questions this, and Amemar says a wise person is greater than a prophet. Abaye and Rava debate how to recognize this, with Rava suggesting that when a great person says something and it is also said by another great person, it shows they share the same mazal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa states that since the Temple's destruction, prophecy was taken from prophets and given to the wise.
The Gemara questions: Is a wise person not also a prophet?
The Gemara clarifies: Rabbi Avdimi meant that although prophecy was taken from prophets, it was not taken from the wise.
Amemar argues that a wise person is greater than a prophet, citing the verse 'ונביא לבב חכמה' (a prophet of the heart of wisdom) to show that wisdom is the greater thing upon which prophecy depends.
Abaye offers a practical sign: when a great person says something and it is also said in the name of another great person, this indicates shared wisdom.
Rava objects: perhaps both great people simply share the same mazal (astrological fortune), not necessarily wisdom.
Rava offers his own sign: when a great person says something and it is also said in the name of another great person, this indicates shared wisdom.

items.text: Rav Ashi's defense of Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's defense of Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions the difficulty raised against Rabbi Akiva, suggesting that a person's mazal (fortune) may be involved. He then proposes that when a great person says something that aligns with a halakha from Sinai, it is not mere coincidence, though the objection is raised that it could be like a blind person finding something through a window, lacking reason.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions the difficulty raised against Rabbi Akiva, suggesting that a person's mazal (fortune) may be involved.
Rav Ashi proposes that when a great person says something that aligns with a halakha from Sinai, it is not mere coincidence.
The Gemara objects that this could be like a blind person finding something through a window, lacking reason.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on prophecy given to fools and children
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on prophecy given to fools and children
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that since the Temple's destruction, prophecy has been given to fools and children. An example is given of a fool who predicted that the head of the academy in 'Mechasya' would be 'Tavyomi', which Mar bar Rav Ashi interpreted as referring to himself, leading to a series of events where he was appointed as head of the academy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by stating that since the Temple's destruction, prophecy has been given to fools and children.
The Gemara asks for an example of prophecy given to fools and introduces the story of a fool's prediction.

sub.text: Narrative of Mar bar Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Narrative of Mar bar Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: The fool predicts that the head of the academy in Mechasya will be signed 'Tavyomi', and Mar bar Rav Ashi interprets this as referring to himself and sets out.

The rabbis initially appoint Rav Acha as head, but upon hearing of Mar bar Rav Ashi's arrival, they send pairs to consult him, eventually assembling ten and appointing Mar bar Rav Ashi, who then opens and teaches.
Rav Acha applies to himself the principle that those who are troubled are not quickly benefited, and those who are benefited are not quickly troubled.

items.text: Example of prophecy through children
items.text_en: Example of prophecy through children
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides an example of prophecy through children: the daughter of Rav Chisda, when asked which of two sages she preferred, said both, leading Rava to conclude he would be the later one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for an example of prophecy through children.
The Gemara cites the story of Rav Chisda's daughter, who when asked which of two sages she preferred, said both, leading Rava to conclude he would be the later one.

items.text: Rabbi Avdimi and Rav Huna on the heart and wine
items.text_en: Rabbi Avdimi and Rav Huna on the heart and wine
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa teaches that before eating and drinking a person has two hearts (minds), but after only one, citing a verse. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that one accustomed to wine, even if his heart is sealed like a virgin, wine opens it, citing another verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa teaches that before eating and drinking a person has two hearts (minds), but after only one, citing a verse and its Aramaic translation.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that one accustomed to wine, even if his heart is sealed like a virgin, wine opens it, citing a verse.

items.text: Inheritance: portion of a firstborn and a yavam
items.text_en: Inheritance: portion of a firstborn and a yavam
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua asks whether a yavam (levirate heir) receives his portion from the same field as the other heirs. Abaye says yes, because the yavam is called 'firstborn' by the Torah. Rava argues that the verse 'and he shall be the firstborn' indicates his status is like a firstborn but his division is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua asks: it is clear that the portion of a firstborn and the regular portion are given together from one field; what is the law for a יבם (levirate heir) regarding the division of the fields?
Abaye answers that the yavam is treated like a firstborn because the Torah calls him 'firstborn' (בכור).
Rava objects that the verse 'וְהָיָה הַבְּכוֹר' (and he shall be the firstborn) indicates his status is like a firstborn but his division of fields is not like a firstborn.

items.text: Coercion against Sodomite behavior: buyer of land from wife's property
items.text_en: Coercion against Sodomite behavior: buyer of land from wife's property
items.desc_en: A man bought land from his wife's property. When dividing, he asked for his portion in that field. Rabbah rules that such a person is coerced against Sodomite behavior (i.e., the other heirs cannot refuse). Rav Yosef objects, saying the brothers can claim they are giving him an improvement like the property of Bar Marion. The halakha follows Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man bought land from his wife's property, and when the heirs divide the estate, he asks for his portion in that specific field.
Rabbah rules that such a person is coerced against Sodomite behavior (i.e., the other heirs cannot refuse his request).
Rav Yosef objects, arguing that the brothers can claim they are giving him an improvement like the property of Bar Marion (i.e., they can compensate him with a better portion elsewhere).
The gemara concludes that the halakha (binding law) follows Rav Yosef's objection.

items.text: Two fields on two furrows: coercion against Sodomite behavior
items.text_en: Two fields on two furrows: coercion against Sodomite behavior
items.desc_en: Regarding two fields on two furrows (adjacent strips), Rabbah rules that coercion against Sodomite behavior applies. Rav Yosef objects, noting that one field might be irrigated and the other not. The halakha follows Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that regarding two fields on two furrows, coercion against Sodomite behavior applies.
Rav Yosef objects that one field might be irrigated and the other not, making coercion inappropriate.
The halakha is ruled in accordance with Rav Yosef's position.

items.text: Two fields on one furrow: coercion against Sodomite behavior
items.text_en: Two fields on one furrow: coercion against Sodomite behavior
items.desc_en: Regarding two fields on one furrow, Rav Yosef rules that coercion against Sodomite behavior applies. Abaye objects, saying the other heir can claim he wants to increase the number of tenants. The halakha follows Rav Yosef, as increasing tenants is not a valid claim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that regarding two fields on one furrow, coercion against Sodomite behavior applies.
Abaye objects that the other heir can claim he wants to increase the number of tenants.
The halakha follows Rav Yosef, as increasing tenants is not a valid claim.

items.text: Mishnah: Dividing a house with one side a river and one side a path
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dividing a house with one side a river and one side a path
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a house has one side a river and one side a path, they divide it by the corner of the zol (a type of measurement). This sets up the context for the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a house has one side a river and one side a path, they divide it by the corner of the zol (a type of measurement).

items.text: Gemara's question and dispute about 'Gud or Agud'
items.text_en: Gemara's question and dispute about 'Gud or Agud'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the parts are insufficient for each partner, what is the law? Rav Yehuda says the principle of 'Gud or Agud' (cut or join) applies, while Rav Nachman says it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the parts are insufficient for each partner, what is the law?
Rav Yehuda says the principle of 'גוד או אגוד' (cut or join) applies.
Rav Nachman says the principle of 'גוד או אגוד' does not apply.

items.text: Rava's challenge to Rav Nachman regarding a slave and an unclean animal
items.text_en: Rava's challenge to Rav Nachman regarding a slave and an unclean animal
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman: according to your view that 'Gud or Agud' does not apply, how do a firstborn and a simple son divide a slave and an unclean animal left by their father? Rav Nachman answers that they work for one day for one and two days for the other.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman: according to your view that 'Gud or Agud' does not apply, how do a firstborn and a simple son divide a slave and an unclean animal left by their father?
Rav Nachman answers that they work for one day for one and two days for the other.

items.text: Objection from the case of a half-slave half-free person
items.text_en: Objection from the case of a half-slave half-free person
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah about a half-slave half-free person: Beit Hillel initially said he works for his master one day and for himself one day, but Beit Shammai objected that this doesn't solve his inability to marry. Beit Hillel later retracted, agreeing that the master is forced to free him and write a note for half his value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah about a half-slave half-free person, citing Beit Hillel's initial ruling and Beit Shammai's objection that the arrangement leaves the slave unable to marry.
Beit Shammai argues that the arrangement only helps the master but leaves the slave unable to marry, citing the verse that the world was created for procreation.
Beit Hillel retracts and agrees with Beit Shammai that the master is forced to free the slave and write a note for half his value.

items.text: Distinction: Here there is 'Agud' but not 'Gud'
items.text_en: Distinction: Here there is 'Agud' but not 'Gud'
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes: in the case of the half-slave, there is 'Agud' (joining) but not 'Gud' (cutting), so it does not apply to the dispute about 'Gud or Agud'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing: in the half-slave case there is 'אגוד' (joining) but not 'גוד' (cutting), so the dispute about 'גוד או אגוד' does not apply.

items.text: Further challenge from a case of two brothers with a bathhouse and olive press
items.text_en: Further challenge from a case of two brothers with a bathhouse and olive press
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another source: two brothers, one poor and one rich, inherit a bathhouse and olive press. If they rent them out, the income is shared; if they use them themselves, the rich brother can tell the poor brother something (the text is cut off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about two brothers inheriting a bathhouse and olive press, where the rich brother can tell the poor brother something (the text is cut off), as a challenge to the previous position.

items.text: Rejection of the proof from the slave and olive examples
items.text_en: Rejection of the proof from the slave and olive examples
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attempted proof from the cases of slaves and olives, arguing that those cases involve a form of "גוד" but not "אגוד" (the option to buy out).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attempted proof from the cases of slaves and olives, arguing that those cases involve a form of "גוד" but not "אגוד" (the option to buy out).

items.text: A new proof from the Mishnah and a tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: A new proof from the Mishnah and a tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah that states that if an item can be divided while retaining its name, it is divided; otherwise, it is valued in money. It then notes a tannaitic dispute about whether one can say "take the larger portion and I'll take the smaller" – the first Tanna allows it, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah as proof: any item that can be divided while retaining its name is divided; otherwise, it is valued in money.

sub.text: Gemara's identification of a tannaitic dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's identification of a tannaitic dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah reflects a tannaitic dispute: the first Tanna allows one to say 'take the larger portion and I'll take the smaller,' but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel does not allow it.

items.text: Analysis of the tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Analysis of the tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the nature of the dispute: if it is as stated, what is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning? It suggests that perhaps the Mishnah is missing a clause, and that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also rejects the principle of "גוד או אגוד".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances of the dispute? If it is as stated in the baraita, what is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning?

The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah is missing a clause: it originally stated that both 'take the larger and I the smaller' and 'גוד או אגוד' are accepted, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel comes to reject both.

items.text: Resolution of the tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Resolution of the tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the emendation and explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: the other party can claim he has no money to pay or that he hates gifts (based on Proverbs 15:27).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the emendation and explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: the other party can claim he has no money to pay or that he hates gifts (based on Proverbs 15:27).

items.text: Abaye's proof from Samuel's ruling on scrolls
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from Samuel's ruling on scrolls
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that Rav Yehuda's statement (that "גוד או אגוד" applies) is actually from Shmuel, based on a Mishnah about not dividing sacred scrolls. Shmuel says they may be divided only if they are in separate volumes, implying that in a single volume, the principle of "גוד או אגוד" does not apply.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asserts to Rav Yosef that Rav Yehuda's ruling about 'גוד או אגוד' actually originates from Shmuel.
Abaye cites the Mishnah that sacred scrolls may not be divided even if both partners agree.
Abaye cites Shmuel's ruling that the prohibition applies only to a single volume, but in separate volumes they may divide.
Abaye argues that if the principle of 'גוד או אגוד' did not exist, why would Shmuel distinguish between one volume and two?
Abaye objects that without the principle, even separate volumes should be indivisible.

items.text: Resolution of Abaye's proof
items.text_en: Resolution of Abaye's proof
items.desc_en: Rav Shalman explains that Shmuel's ruling applies only when both parties are willing to divide, so it does not contradict the principle of "גוד או אגוד".

sub.desc_en: Rav Shalman resolves the contradiction by explaining that Shmuel's ruling applies only when both parties are willing to divide, thus preserving the principle of "גוד או אגוד" (take or split).

items.text: Amemar's ruling and a counterexample from Rava
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling and a counterexample from Rava
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that the principle of "גוד או אגוד" applies. Rav Ashi asks about Rav Nachman's view, and Amemar says he is unaware of it. The Gemara brings a case where Rava ruled against the principle regarding two maidservants, but the Gemara distinguishes that case because each party needed both maidservants.

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that the principle of גוד או אגוד (the right to demand partition or joint ownership) is halachically recognized.
Rav Ashi asks Amemar about Rav Nachman's view on this principle.
Amemar says he has not heard of Rav Nachman's view, implying he does not accept it.
The Gemara objects by citing a case where Rava ruled against the principle of גוד או אגוד regarding two maidservants left by a father.

The Gemara distinguishes the case because each brother needed both maidservants, unlike the standard case of גוד או אגוד where each can take one, and notes that Rav Shalman's explanation about sacred scrolls applies only when both parties agree.

items.text: Baraita on binding biblical scrolls
items.text_en: Baraita on binding biblical scrolls
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the proper way to bind Torah, Prophets, and Writings: Rabbi Meir allows binding them together, Rabbi Yehuda says each should be separate, and the Sages say each book individually. A story is told about Bythos ben Zonin, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi approves of binding them together. Technical rules for spacing and rolling are given.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by presenting three positions: Rabbi Meir permits binding Torah, Prophets, and Writings together; Rabbi Yehuda says each section should be separate; the Sages say each individual book should be separate.
Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent: Baitos ben Zunin had eight Prophets bound together with the approval of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Others dispute the precedent, claiming that each book was actually a separate scroll.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reports that a scroll with Torah, Prophets, and Writings bound together was brought before him and he approved it, supporting Rabbi Meir's position.

The Gemara provides technical rules for spacing: four lines between books of the Torah and between Prophets, three lines within the Twelve Prophets, and the scribe may finish at the bottom of a column and start the next at the top.

A second baraita adds practical instructions: one who binds them together must leave space at the beginning for rolling around the pole and at the end for the circumference, and may finish at the bottom and start at the top.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's phrase 'if one wishes to cut, he may cut' as meaning that if one wants to cut the scroll into separate books, he is permitted to do so.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'if one wishes to cut, he may cut' means one is permitted to cut the scroll into separate books.

items.text: Contradiction regarding rolling the scroll and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding rolling the scroll and resolution
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised from a baraita about rolling a scroll from beginning to end versus to the middle. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the baraita refers to side margins, and Rav Ashi says it applies specifically to a Torah scroll, which is rolled to its middle with a column on each side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about rolling a scroll from beginning to end, questioning whether the required margin is for rolling a column or the circumference.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the baraita refers to the side margins, not the top and bottom.

Rav Ashi says the baraita applies specifically to a Torah scroll, which is rolled to its middle with a column on each side, citing a supporting baraita about how scribes in Jerusalem made their scrolls.

items.text: Dimensions of a Torah scroll and Rabbi's ruling
items.text_en: Dimensions of a Torah scroll and Rabbi's ruling
