items.desc_en: A baraita states that a Torah scroll's height should not exceed its circumference nor vice versa. When asked about the proper size, Rabbi says six handbreadths for gevil but is unsure for klaf.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule that a Torah scroll's height should not exceed its circumference nor vice versa.
The sages ask Rabbi about the proper size of a Torah scroll.
Rabbi answers that for gevil the scroll should be six handbreadths, but he does not know the measure for klaf.

items.text: Anecdotes about writing Torah scrolls and their accuracy
items.text_en: Anecdotes about writing Torah scrolls and their accuracy
items.desc_en: Stories are told about Rav Huna and Rav Acha bar Yaakov writing Torah scrolls, with the latter's scroll being accepted by the Sages but leading to his death. The Gemara then questions the claim that Rabbi Ami wrote 400 scrolls, suggesting he may have written only the verse 'Torah tzivah lanu Moshe'. Similarly, Rava questions a claim about Rabbi Yannai planting vineyards.

sub.desc_en: Two anecdotes are told: Rav Huna wrote seventy Torah scrolls but only one was accepted, while Rav Acha bar Yaakov wrote one on calfskin and it was accepted, but the Sages cast their eyes on him and he died.
The Sages ask Rav Hamnuna about the claim that Rabbi Ami wrote 400 Torah scrolls, implying a challenge to its plausibility.
Rav Hamnuna answers that perhaps Rabbi Ami only wrote the verse 'תורה צוה לנו משה' (Torah tzivah lanu Moshe) in each scroll, not the entire Torah.
Rava asks Rabbi Zeira about the claim that Rabbi Yannai planted 400 vineyards, similarly challenging its plausibility.
Rabbi Zeira answers that perhaps Rabbi Yannai planted vineyards in a pattern of two opposite two with one protruding like a tail, meaning a small number of vines counted as many vineyards.

items.text: Dimensions of the Ark and placement of the tablets and Torah scroll according to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Dimensions of the Ark and placement of the tablets and Torah scroll according to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the dimensions of the Ark made by Moses (2.5 cubits long, 1.5 wide, 1.5 high, with a cubit of 6 handbreadths). The tablets (6x6x3 handbreadths) are placed along the length, leaving space for the Torah scroll. Rabbi Meir explains that the scroll is placed in the remaining 2 handbreadths, and a verse is cited to show the scroll was in the Ark.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing the dimensions of the Ark made by Moses, measured in a cubit of six handbreadths.
The baraita calculates that the tablets (6x6x3 handbreadths) occupy 12 handbreadths along the Ark's length, leaving 2 handbreadths for the Torah scroll.
The baraita cites the verse 'אֵין בָּאָרוֹן רַק' (there was nothing in the Ark except) and interprets the double exclusion as including the Torah scroll placed inside the Ark.

The baraita calculates the width of the Ark: the tablets occupy 6 handbreadths, leaving 2 handbreadths of space so the Torah scroll is not inserted or removed with difficulty, according to Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view and the alternative placement of the Torah scroll
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's view and the alternative placement of the Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda uses a cubit of 5 handbreadths, leading to different calculations. He argues that the Torah scroll was placed alongside the Ark, not inside it, citing verses about the Philistine gift box and the command to place the scroll beside the Ark.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the cubit used for the Ark is based on a 5-handbreadth cubit, calculates the dimensions, and concludes that only a half-cubit remained in the length for the Torah scroll, with a minimal space of one finger on each side.

Rabbi Yehuda calculates the width of the Ark, showing that a handbreadth and a half remain on each side, leaving a full handbreadth in the center for the staves supporting the poles, citing the verse from Song of Songs about the king's palanquin.

Rabbi Yehuda cites the Philistine gift box placed beside the Ark and the verse commanding to place the Torah scroll beside the Ark, concluding that the scroll was placed alongside, not inside, the Ark.

items.text: Reconciliation of the verse 'There was nothing in the Ark except'
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the verse 'There was nothing in the Ark except'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to explain how the verse 'There was nothing in the Ark except' can be reconciled with the view that the Torah scroll was not inside, suggesting it comes to include something else.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to reconcile the verse 'There was nothing in the Ark except' with the view that the Torah scroll was outside, suggesting it must come to include something else.

items.text: Gemara's question on the scroll's rolling and Rav Acha's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the scroll's rolling and Rav Acha's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a Torah scroll with a circumference of six handbreadths can fit in the Ark alongside the tablets, given that a scroll with a three-handbreadth circumference has a width of one handbreadth. Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the scroll is rolled from its beginning, and Rav Ashi adds that it is rolled a bit and placed on top.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a Torah scroll with a circumference of six handbreadths can fit in the Ark alongside the tablets, given that a scroll with a three-handbreadth circumference has a width of one handbreadth, and the scroll is rolled from its middle, leaving only two handbreadths of space.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the Torah scroll is rolled from its beginning, not from its middle, so it takes up less space.
The Gemara objects that even with rolling from the beginning, two handbreadths of scroll still cannot fit in two handbreadths of space.
Rav Ashi resolves that the scroll is rolled a bit and placed on top of the tablets, not entirely within the space between them.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view on the scroll's placement before the Ark
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's view on the scroll's placement before the Ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, before the Ark was built, a board protruded from the Ark on which the Torah scroll rested. It also clarifies Rabbi Meir's interpretation of the verse 'from the side of the Ark' as meaning the scroll was placed on the side, not between the tablets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Torah scroll was placed before the Ark was built according to Rabbi Yehuda, and answers that a board protruded from the Ark on which the scroll rested.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir interprets the verse 'from the side of the Ark' to mean the scroll was placed on the side, not between the tablets, but still inside the Ark.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's sources for the pillars and broken tablets
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's sources for the pillars and broken tablets
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the pillars stood according to Rabbi Meir (outside the Ark) and how he knows the broken tablets were placed in the Ark. It cites Rav Huna's teaching that the verse 'who is called by the name of the Lord of Hosts, who sits upon the cherubim' implies that both the whole and broken tablets were in the Ark.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the pillars stood according to Rabbi Meir, given that he places the Torah scroll inside the Ark.
The Gemara answers that the pillars stood outside the Ark.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir derives that the broken tablets were placed in the Ark.
The Gemara cites Rav Huna's teaching that the verse 'who is called by the name of the Lord of Hosts, who sits upon the cherubim' implies that both the whole and broken tablets were placed in the Ark.

items.text: Alternative interpretations of the verses about the Ark
items.text_en: Alternative interpretations of the verses about the Ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that other sages use the verse for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that God's name and all its appellations were in the Ark, and for Resh Lakish's teaching that God praised Moses for breaking the tablets. It then asks how Rabbi Meir derives the broken tablets from another verse, citing a baraita of Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the other sages (who disagree with Rabbi Meir) interpret the verse that Rabbi Meir used to prove the broken tablets were in the Ark, and answers that they use it for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that God's name and all its appellations were in the Ark.
The Gemara objects that the other sages also need the verse for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching, and then concedes that this is indeed the case.
The Gemara asks again how the other sages derive that the broken tablets were in the Ark, since the verse is already used for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching.

The Gemara answers that the other sages derive the broken tablets from a baraita taught by Rav Yosef, who interprets the verse 'אֲשֶׁר שִׁבַּרְתָּ וְשַׂמְתָּם' (which you broke and you placed them) to teach that the tablets and broken tablets were placed in the Ark.

The Gemara notes that the other sages (who disagree with Rabbi Meir) use the verse from Rav Yosef's baraita for Resh Lakish's teaching that God praised Moses for breaking the tablets, saying 'יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ' (may your strength be straight for having broken them).

items.text: Order of the Prophets and the placement of Hosea and Isaiah
items.text_en: Order of the Prophets and the placement of Hosea and Isaiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the order of the prophetic books: Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and the Twelve. It questions why Hosea is placed last among the Twelve despite being earlier, and why Isaiah follows Jeremiah and Ezekiel despite being earlier. The answers involve Hosea's prophecy being grouped with later prophets and the thematic continuity of destruction and consolation.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the order of the prophetic books: Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and the Twelve.

The Gemara questions why Hosea, who prophesied earlier than the other Twelve, is placed last among them, citing the verse 'תְּחִלַּת דִּבֶּר ה' בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ' and Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Hosea was the first of four prophets in that era.

The Gemara answers that Hosea's prophecy is written together with Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who were the last prophets, so Hosea is grouped with them; and because his book is small, it is placed at the end to avoid being lost.
The Gemara questions why Isaiah, who prophesied earlier than Jeremiah and Ezekiel, is placed after them in the order.

The Gemara answers that Kings ends with destruction, Jeremiah is entirely destruction, Ezekiel begins with destruction and ends with consolation, and Isaiah is entirely consolation, so the books are arranged to juxtapose destruction with destruction and consolation with consolation.

items.text: Order of the Writings and the authorship of biblical books
items.text_en: Order of the Writings and the authorship of biblical books
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the order of the Writings: Ruth, Psalms, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Daniel, Esther, Ezra, and Chronicles. It explains why Job is not first (to avoid beginning with calamity) and why Ruth is not considered a calamity (it leads to David). It then details the authors: Moses wrote his book, the section of Balaam, and Job; Joshua wrote his book and the last eight verses of the Torah; Samuel wrote his book, Judges, and Ruth; David wrote Psalms through ten elders.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the order of the Writings (כתובים): Ruth, Psalms, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Daniel, Esther, Ezra, and Chronicles.
The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that Job lived in the time of Moses, why not place Job first in the order of the Writings?
The Gemara answers: we do not begin with calamity (פורענות), and Job's story is one of suffering.
The Gemara objects: Ruth's story also involves calamity (famine and death), yet it is placed first.
The Gemara resolves: Ruth's calamity has a positive outcome, as Rabbi Yochanan explains that she produced David, who filled God with songs and praises.
The Gemara shifts to ask: who wrote these books? It answers that Moses wrote his book (the Torah), the section of Balaam, and Job.

The Gemara continues listing authors: Joshua wrote his book and the last eight verses of the Torah; Samuel wrote his book, Judges, and Ruth; David wrote Psalms through ten elders including Adam, Melchizedek, Abraham, Moses, Heman, Jeduthun, and Asaph.

items.text: Opening list of biblical authors
items.text_en: Opening list of biblical authors
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the authors of various biblical books: Jeremiah wrote his book, Kings, and Lamentations; Hezekiah and his group wrote Isaiah, Proverbs, Song of Songs, and Ecclesiastes; the Men of the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel, the Twelve, Daniel, and Esther; Ezra wrote his book and the genealogy of Chronicles up to his time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists the authors of biblical books: Jeremiah wrote his book, Kings, and Lamentations; Hezekiah and his group wrote Isaiah, Proverbs, Song of Songs, and Ecclesiastes; the Men of the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel, the Twelve, Daniel, and Esther; Ezra wrote his book and the genealogy of Chronicles up to his time.

items.text: Support for Rav's statement about Ezra
items.text_en: Support for Rav's statement about Ezra
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this supports Rav, who said that Ezra did not ascend from Babylonia until he had established his genealogy, and Nehemiah completed it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita supports Rav's statement that Ezra did not ascend from Babylonia until he had established his genealogy, and Nehemiah completed it.

items.text: Debate on the last eight verses of the Torah
items.text_en: Debate on the last eight verses of the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses who wrote the last eight verses of the Torah describing Moses' death. Rabbi Yehuda says Joshua wrote them, while Rabbi Nehemya agrees. Rabbi Shimon objects that the Torah cannot be missing a letter, so Moses wrote them with tears, like Baruch wrote from Jeremiah's mouth.

sub.desc_en: Marei states that Joshua wrote his book and the last eight verses of the Torah.
A baraita supports the view that Joshua wrote the last eight verses, citing the difficulty of Moses writing about his own death, attributed to Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Nehemya.
Rabbi Shimon objects that the Torah cannot lack even one letter, so Moses must have written the last eight verses with tears, analogous to Baruch writing from Jeremiah's dictation.

items.text: Application of the debate to halakha
items.text_en: Application of the debate to halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the statement that one person reads the last eight verses aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view, and answers that even Rabbi Shimon would agree because the style changed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks with which Tanna the ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba (that one person reads the last eight verses of the Torah) aligns, suggesting it must be Rabbi Yehuda and not Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara answers that even Rabbi Shimon would agree to the ruling, because the style of these verses changed (from God speaking to Moses writing about Moses' death).

items.text: Authorship of Joshua and Samuel
items.text_en: Authorship of Joshua and Samuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Joshua wrote his book, but the account of his death was added by Eleazar, and Eleazar's death by Phinehas. Similarly, Samuel wrote his book, but his death was added by Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet.

sub.desc_en: Opens by stating that Joshua wrote his own book, then raises an objection from a verse about Joshua's death.
Answers that the account of Joshua's death was added by Eleazar, then raises a further objection from Eleazar's own death.
Answers that Eleazar's death was added by Phinehas.
States that Samuel wrote his book, then raises an objection from a verse about Samuel's death.
Answers that the account of Samuel's death was added by Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet.

items.text: Authorship of Psalms and identification of Ethan and Heman
items.text_en: Authorship of Psalms and identification of Ethan and Heman
items.desc_en: David wrote Psalms through ten elders, but Ethan the Ezrahite is identified as Abraham, and Heman is identified as Moses, though there were two Hemans.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that David wrote the Book of Psalms through ten elders.
The Gemara asks why Ethan the Ezrahite was not counted among the ten elders.
Rav identifies Ethan the Ezrahite as Abraham, based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of the word 'ממזרח' (from the east).
The Gemara notes a contradiction: Moses is listed among the ten elders, and Heman is also listed, but Rav said Heman is Moses.
The Gemara resolves that there were two different individuals named Heman.

items.text: Moses wrote Job, and the time of Job
items.text_en: Moses wrote Job, and the time of Job
items.desc_en: Moses wrote his book, the portion of Balaam, and Job. Rabbi Levi bar Lachma says Job was in Moses' time, based on the word 'efo'. The Gemara rejects suggestions that Job was in the times of Isaac, Jacob, or Joseph, because Moses is called 'mechokek' (lawgiver).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Moses wrote his book, the portion of Balaam, and the book of Job.

sub.text: Gemara's support for Rabbi Levi bar Lachma
sub.text_en: Gemara's support for Rabbi Levi bar Lachma
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this supports Rabbi Levi bar Lachma, who said Job lived in Moses' time, based on the shared word 'אפו' (efo) in Job and the Torah.
The Gemara objects that Job could have lived in the times of Isaac, Jacob, or Joseph, citing verses where the word 'אפו' appears.
The Gemara rejects these alternatives, arguing that Job's phrase 'וְיֻחָקוּ' (and be engraved) points to Moses, who is called 'מחוקק' (lawgiver) in the verse.

items.text: Rava's view: Job in the time of the spies
items.text_en: Rava's view: Job in the time of the spies
items.desc_en: Rava says Job was in the time of the spies, based on a wordplay between 'Utz' and 'etz' (tree), meaning a man whose years are long as a tree and who protects his generation.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that Job lived in the time of the spies, interpreting the name 'עוּץ' (Utz) as a reference to 'עֵץ' (tree), indicating a man of long years who protects his generation.

items.text: Debate: Was Job a real person or a parable?
items.text_en: Debate: Was Job a real person or a parable?
items.desc_en: One rabbi says Job never existed but was a parable. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani objects with the verse 'There was a man in the land of Utz, Job was his name.' The rabbi counters with the parable of the poor man's lamb, but the Gemara asks why his name and city are mentioned if it's a parable.

sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi sitting before Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani asserts that Job never existed but was a parable.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani objects, citing the verse 'There was a man in the land of Utz, Job was his name' to prove Job's existence.
The rabbi counters by citing the parable of the poor man's lamb from the book of Samuel, arguing that it too is a parable, so Job can be similarly understood.
The Gemara questions why Job's name and city are mentioned in the verse if it is merely a parable.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar: Job was from the returnees to Zion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar: Job was from the returnees to Zion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar say Job was among those who returned from the exile, and his study hall was in Tiberias. This is challenged by a baraita that says Job's years spanned from Israel's entry into Egypt until the exodus.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar assert that Job was among the returnees from the Babylonian exile and that his study hall was in Tiberias.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states Job's years spanned from the entry of Israel into Egypt until the exodus, contradicting the claim that he lived in the post-exilic period.

items.text: Initial proposal about Job's era
items.text_en: Initial proposal about Job's era
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Job lived from the time Israel entered Egypt until they left, based on a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Job lived from the time Israel entered Egypt until they left.

items.text: Challenge from the seven prophets to the nations
items.text_en: Challenge from the seven prophets to the nations
items.desc_en: A baraita lists seven prophets who prophesied to the nations, including Job. The Gemara resolves that Job was a prophet to the nations, not to Israel, and distinguishes between primary and secondary prophecy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that Job was a prophet to Israel by citing a baraita listing seven prophets who prophesied to the nations, including Job.
The Gemara answers that the baraita means these prophets primarily prophesied to the nations, but they could also be from Israel, as Elihu was; similarly, Job was a prophet to the nations.

items.text: Another baraita: Job was a gentile who blasphemed
items.text_en: Another baraita: Job was a gentile who blasphemed
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Job was a pious gentile who received suffering and blasphemed, and God doubled his reward in this world to drive him from the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that Job was a pious gentile who blasphemed under suffering, and God doubled his reward in this world to drive him from the World to Come.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about Job's era and his identity
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about Job's era and his identity
items.desc_en: Multiple Tannaim argue when Job lived: Rabbi Elazar says in the days of the Judges, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says in the days of Achashverosh, Rabbi Natan says in the days of the kingdom of Sheba, the Sages say in the days of the Chaldeans, and some say in the days of Jacob. All except the last hold Job was a Jew; the last opinion is rejected because the Shekhinah does not rest on gentiles after Moses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that Job lived in the days of the Judges, citing a verse about a generation of vanity.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha argues that Job lived in the days of Achashverosh, based on the beauty of Job's daughters, and rejects a possible objection that it could be the days of David.
Rabbi Natan says Job lived in the days of the kingdom of Sheba, and the Sages say in the days of the Chaldeans, each citing a verse.
Some say Job lived in the days of Jacob and married Dinah, based on a verbal analogy of the word 'נבלה' (folly).
The gemara notes that all the Tannaim except the last opinion hold that Job was a Jew.
The gemara rejects the minority opinion that Job was a gentile, arguing that after Moses the Shekhinah does not rest on gentiles, as Moses requested and was granted.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on the generation of Job and the Judges
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on the generation of Job and the Judges
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says Job's generation was steeped in licentiousness, and he explains the verse about the Judges as a generation that judges its judges, with mutual reproach.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by stating that Job's generation was steeped in licentiousness, citing verses about seeing and vanity.
The Gemara objects that the verse could refer to prophecy, but Rabbi Yochanan's proof is defended by noting the superfluous phrase 'why this vanity'.
Rabbi Yochanan explains the verse 'in the days when the judges judged' as a generation that judges its judges, with mutual reproach.

items.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: Queen of Sheba was a kingdom
items.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: Queen of Sheba was a kingdom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan says that anyone who says the Queen of Sheba was a woman is mistaken; it refers to the kingdom of Sheba.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan declares that anyone who says the Queen of Sheba was a woman is mistaken; it refers to the kingdom of Sheba.

items.text: Aggadic exposition of the beginning of Job
items.text_en: Aggadic exposition of the beginning of Job
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds verses from Job: the Satan's praise of Abraham, Rabbi Yochanan's comparison of Job to Abraham, Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel on Job's generosity, Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak on the blessing from Job's money, Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina on Job's livestock overpowering wolves, and Rabbi Yochanan on the first calamity.

sub.desc_en: The Satan reports to God that he found no one as faithful as Abraham, who did not complain even when he had to buy a burial plot for Sarah.

Rabbi Yochanan notes that the praise of Job exceeds that of Abraham, as Job is called 'תָּם וְיָשָׁר יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים' (perfect, upright, God-fearing) while Abraham is only called 'יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים' (God-fearing).

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel on Job's generosity
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel on Job's generosity
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel explains that Job was generous with his money, giving a half-prutah to a shopkeeper from his own pocket when others would only give a half-prutah.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak on the blessing from Job's money
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak on the blessing from Job's money
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak explains that anyone who takes a prutah from Job becomes blessed.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina on Job's livestock overpowering wolves
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina on Job's livestock overpowering wolves
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that Job's livestock broke the natural order: goats killed wolves instead of wolves killing goats.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan on the first calamity
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on the first calamity
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse 'the oxen were plowing and the donkeys grazing beside them' teaches that God gave Job a taste of the World to Come.

items.text: Opening: Job's initial response to calamity
items.text_en: Opening: Job's initial response to calamity
items.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the verses describing Job's reaction to the series of disasters that befell him, emphasizing that he did not sin or attribute folly to God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the verses describing Job's initial response to calamity, emphasizing that he did not sin or attribute folly to God.

items.text: The Satan's accusation and Rabbi Yochanan's comment
items.text_en: The Satan's accusation and Rabbi Yochanan's comment
items.desc_en: The Satan reports to God that he found no one like Abraham, who did not question God even when unable to bury Sarah. Rabbi Yochanan comments that the verse describing God as being incited by the Satan is anthropomorphic and difficult to say.

sub.desc_en: The Satan reports to God that he found no one like Abraham, who did not question God even when unable to bury Sarah.
God's response to the Satan is cited, showing that Job still holds to his integrity despite being incited against him.
Rabbi Yochanan comments that the verse describing God as being incited by the Satan is anthropomorphic and difficult to say.

items.text: Baraita on the Satan's actions
items.text_en: Baraita on the Satan's actions
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the Satan's role: he descends and leads astray, ascends and provokes, takes permission, and takes the soul.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes the Satan's four actions: descending and leading astray, ascending and provoking, taking permission, and taking the soul.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak and Resh Lakish on the Satan
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak and Resh Lakish on the Satan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says the Satan's suffering is greater than Job's, comparing him to a servant told to break a barrel but save the wine. Resh Lakish identifies the Satan as the evil inclination and the angel of death, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that the Satan's suffering is greater than Job's, using a parable of a servant told to break a barrel but save its wine.
Resh Lakish identifies the Satan as the evil inclination (יצר הרע) and the angel of death, citing verses to support each identification.

items.text: Rabbi Levi: Satan and Peninah acted for Heaven's sake
items.text_en: Rabbi Levi: Satan and Peninah acted for Heaven's sake
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi explains that both the Satan and Peninah (Elkanah's other wife) had good intentions: the Satan sought to prevent God's mercy from being forgotten, and Peninah provoked Hannah to pray.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi opens by stating that both the Satan and Peninah acted for the sake of Heaven.
Rabbi Levi explains that the Satan, seeing God's favor toward Job, feared that God's mercy toward Abraham would be forgotten.
Rabbi Levi explains that Peninah provoked Hannah to anger in order to drive her to prayer.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov taught this interpretation in Papponya.
The narrative concludes that the Satan came and kissed Rav Acha bar Yaakov's foot in approval of his teaching.

items.text: Rava and Abaye on Job's sin in his heart
items.text_en: Rava and Abaye on Job's sin in his heart
items.desc_en: Rava says Job sinned in his heart, not his lips, by questioning God's justice. Abaye counters that Job spoke only against the Satan. This is presented as a tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse that Job did not sin with his lips.
Rava explains that Job sinned in his heart, not his lips, by questioning God's justice.
Rava cites Job's statement 'The earth is given into the hand of the wicked' as evidence of his heart-sin.
Rava interprets Job's words as an attempt to overturn the divine order, accusing God of injustice.
Abaye objects that Job only spoke against the Satan, not against God.
The Gemara presents a tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer agrees with Rava that Job sought to overturn the order, while Rabbi Yehoshua agrees with Abaye that Job spoke only against the Satan.

items.text: Rava: Job sought to exempt the world from judgment
items.text_en: Rava: Job sought to exempt the world from judgment
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Job argued that since God created both righteous and wicked, no one can be held accountable. His friends responded that God created the evil inclination and the Torah as its antidote.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Job sought to exempt the entire world from judgment by arguing that God created all opposites, so no one can be held accountable.
Job's friends respond that God created the evil inclination and the Torah as its antidote, implying human accountability.

items.text: Rava on Job's righteousness in returning stolen fields
items.text_en: Rava on Job's righteousness in returning stolen fields
items.desc_en: Rava interprets Job's claim that he helped the orphan and widow: he would steal a field from orphans, improve it, and return it; he would publicize his name to enable a widow to remarry.

sub.desc_en: Rava interprets Job's claim about the 'blessing of the lost' as meaning he would steal a field from orphans, improve it, and return it.
Rava explains Job's second phrase: he would publicize his name over a widow so that others would marry her.

items.text: Rav and Rava criticize Job's words against God
items.text_en: Rav and Rava criticize Job's words against God
items.desc_en: Rav and Rava condemn Job's statements: Job's wish for a mediator is inappropriate for a servant to his master, and his claim of not looking at a virgin is contrasted with Abraham's greater modesty.

sub.desc_en: Rav condemns Job's wish for his suffering to be weighed, calling it inappropriate companionship against Heaven.
Rav condemns Job's wish for a mediator between him and God, arguing a servant does not rebuke his master.
Rava condemns Job's claim of not looking at a virgin, contrasting it with Abraham who did not even look at his own wife initially.

items.text: Rava and Rabbah on Job's denial of resurrection and his blasphemy
items.text_en: Rava and Rabbah on Job's denial of resurrection and his blasphemy
items.desc_en: Rava says Job denied the resurrection of the dead. Rabbah explains that Job blasphemed through a storm, suggesting God confused him with an enemy, and God answered him from the storm.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites Job's verse about the cloud vanishing and the descent to Sheol, and asserts that Job thereby denied the resurrection of the dead.
Rabbah explains that Job blasphemed through a storm, suggesting God confused him with an enemy, and God answered him from the storm, as the verse says 'וַיַּעַן ה׳ אֶת אִיּוֹב מִן הַסְּעָרָה'.

items.text: God's response: precision in creation refutes Job's claim
items.text_en: God's response: precision in creation refutes Job's claim
items.desc_en: God argues that if He did not confuse the hairs, raindrops, and thunderclaps in creation, He certainly did not confuse Job with an enemy. The Gemara explains the terms for the channels of rain.

sub.desc_en: God argues that if He did not confuse the hairs, each with its own follicle, He certainly did not confuse Job with an enemy.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the rain channels
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the rain channels
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the term 'תעלה' (channel) refers to a mold for raindrops, citing a verse from Kings to support this meaning.
God argues that if He did not confuse the thunderclaps, each with its own path, He certainly did not confuse Job with an enemy.

items.text: God's question about the wild goats and deer
items.text_en: God's question about the wild goats and deer
items.desc_en: The daf ends with God asking Job about the birth of the wild goats and deer, implying His control over nature.

sub.desc_en: God asks Job about the birth of wild goats and deer, emphasizing His control over nature and the paradox of the mother's cruelty.

items.text: God's precise timing in Job's suffering
items.text_en: God's precise timing in Job's suffering
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how God orchestrates events with perfect timing, using the examples of a deer giving birth and a woman in labor, to show that Job's confusion between 'Job' and 'enemy' is unfounded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes God's precise timing in the birth of a mountain goat, concluding that if God does not confuse moments, He would not confuse Job with an enemy.
The Gemara provides a second example of God's precise timing with a hind giving birth, reinforcing the same conclusion about Job.

items.text: Rava's principle: a person is not held accountable in distress
items.text_en: Rava's principle: a person is not held accountable in distress
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the verses that Job spoke without knowledge, but God later said he spoke correctly, teaching that a person is not judged during their time of suffering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites two contradictory verses: one says Job spoke without knowledge, and another says God praised Job's speech over his friends'.
Rava resolves the contradiction by stating that a person is not held accountable for what they say during their time of distress.

items.text: The arrival of Job's friends and their knowledge
items.text_en: The arrival of Job's friends and their knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Job's three friends came from distant places, each 300 parasangs apart, and how they knew of his suffering—either through crowns or trees that withered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the verse about Job's friends coming and asks what the phrase 'they met together' means; Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that they all entered through one gate.
A baraita adds that each friend lived 300 parasangs apart from the next.
The Gemara asks how the friends knew about Job's suffering and gives two answers: they had crowns that withered, or they had trees that withered.
Rava concludes that this proves the adage: either a friend like Job's friends, or death.

items.text: Dispute on 'increase' vs 'strife' and Job's daughters
items.text_en: Dispute on 'increase' vs 'strife' and Job's daughters
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish debate whether the verse 'when men began to multiply' refers to increase or strife. Reish Lakish questions why Job's daughters weren't doubled, and Rabbi Yochanan explains they were doubled in beauty, citing their names.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse about the increase of humanity and the birth of daughters.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse as indicating that increase (רבייה) came to the world.
Reish Lakish interprets the verse as indicating that strife (מריבה) came to the world.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan: if increase came to the world, why were Job's daughters not doubled in number?
Rabbi Yochanan responds that although their names were not doubled, their beauty was doubled.
Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse listing Job's three daughters by name to support his claim.

The gemara explains the names of Job's daughters: Yemimah (like the day), Ketziah (like cassia), and Keren HaPukh (like a horn of precious stone or safflower), with a brief digression about the interpretation of 'קרן הפוך'.

items.text: Bar Kappara's consolation about daughters
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's consolation about daughters
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Shimon's son was distressed over a daughter's birth, his father consoled him with 'increase', but Bar Kappara said it was vain comfort, citing that the world needs both genders but blessed is one with sons.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that a daughter was born to Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, and he was distressed.
Rabbi Shimon's father consoles him by saying that increase (רבייה) has come to the world.
Bar Kappara objects that the father's consolation is vain comfort.
A baraita is cited: the world cannot exist without both males and females, but blessed is one with sons and woe to one with daughters, analogous to the perfume and tanning trades.

items.text: Interpretations of 'bakol' regarding Abraham
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'bakol' regarding Abraham
items.desc_en: Tannaim debate what 'bakol' means: Rabbi Meir says he had no daughter, Rabbi Yehuda says he had a daughter, others say her name was Bakol. Rabbi Elazar HaModai says it refers to astrology, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai to a healing stone. The Gemara then discusses Esau's sins and the lentil stew.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'bakol' (in all) means in the verse about Abraham.
Rabbi Meir says 'bakol' means Abraham had no daughter.
Rabbi Yehuda says 'bakol' means Abraham had a daughter.
Acheirim say Abraham had a daughter named Bakol.
Rabbi Elazar HaModai says 'bakol' refers to Abraham's astrological wisdom (אצטגנינות) that drew all kings to his door.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says 'bakol' refers to a healing stone Abraham wore, which after his death was hung in the sun; Abaye adds a folk saying about the sun rising and healing.
Another interpretation: 'bakol' means that Esau did not rebel during Abraham's lifetime.
Another interpretation: 'bakol' means that Ishmael repented during Abraham's lifetime.
The Gemara proves that Esau did not rebel by citing the verse about Esau coming from the field exhausted on the day Abraham died, and a tradition that Jacob made lentil stew to comfort Isaac.
The Gemara asks why specifically lentil stew was used for mourning.
Rabba bar Mari explains that lentils have no mouth, symbolizing that a mourner has no mouth (should not speak much).
Another explanation: lentils are round and roll, symbolizing that mourning rolls and returns to all people.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations for lentils.
The difference is whether one may comfort with eggs (which also have no mouth) instead of lentils.

items.text: Esau's five sins on that day
items.text_en: Esau's five sins on that day
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists five sins Esau committed: betrothal, murder, denial of God, denial of resurrection, and despising the birthright, each supported by scriptural parallels.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by listing the five sins Esau committed on that day: betrothal, murder, denial of God, denial of resurrection, and despising the birthright.
The Gemara provides scriptural proof for each of the five sins, linking Esau's actions to verses from the Torah and Prophets.

items.text: Proof that Ishmael repented in his father's lifetime
items.text_en: Proof that Ishmael repented in his father's lifetime
items.desc_en: Ravina and Rav Chama bar Buzi discuss the term 'geviah' for righteous death, and Rava awakens to cite Rabbi Yochanan that Ishmael repented, proven by the order of names in Isaac's burial.

sub.text: Ravina's question to Rav Chama bar Buzi
sub.text_en: Ravina's question to Rav Chama bar Buzi
sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Chama bar Buzi whether every death described with the term 'גְּוִיעָה' (expiration) is the death of the righteous, and challenges with the generation of the flood.
Rav Chama bar Buzi clarifies that they require both 'גְּוִיעָה' (expiration) and 'אֲסִיפָה' (gathering) together to indicate a righteous death.
Ravina objects that Ishmael, who is not considered a righteous person, also has both 'גְּוִיעָה' and 'אֲסִיפָה' in his death account.
Rava awakens and cites Rabbi Yochanan that Ishmael repented in his father's lifetime, resolving the objection.
Rava cites the verse that Isaac and Ishmael buried Abraham together, implying Ishmael's repentance.
The gemara objects that perhaps the verse lists Ishmael first merely as a matter of respect for his age, not to indicate repentance.
The gemara rejects the objection by noting that in the burial of Isaac, Esau is listed before Jacob, yet no one claims Esau repented, so the order must be meaningful.
The gemara concludes that since Ishmael is listed before Isaac and the verse uses the term 'אַדְבּוֹרֵי' (he was brought to speak), it proves that Ishmael repented in his father's lifetime.

items.text: Introduction: three who tasted the World to Come
items.text_en: Introduction: three who tasted the World to Come
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new teaching about three individuals whom God allowed to taste the World to Come in this world.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces a teaching that three individuals were given a taste of the World to Come in this world.

items.text: Three who tasted the world to come and were not ruled by the evil inclination
items.text_en: Three who tasted the world to come and were not ruled by the evil inclination
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob each tasted the world to come, as indicated by the words 'bakol', 'mikol', and 'kol' in their respective blessings. It then adds that these three were not ruled by the evil inclination, citing the same verses. A dissenting opinion includes David, based on the verse 'my heart is pierced within me', but the Gemara explains that David was merely recalling his pain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob each tasted the world to come, citing the words 'bakol', 'mikol', and 'kol' in their respective blessings.
The Gemara adds that these three were not ruled by the evil inclination, citing the same verses.
A dissenting opinion includes David, based on the verse 'my heart is pierced within me'.
The Gemara rejects this, explaining that David was merely recalling his pain.

items.text: Six who were not ruled by the angel of death
items.text_en: Six who were not ruled by the angel of death
items.desc_en: A baraisa lists six people—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, and Miriam—over whom the angel of death had no power, citing the verses 'bakol', 'mikol', 'kol' for the patriarchs and 'al pi Hashem' for Moses and Aaron. The Gemara questions that Miriam's death is not described with 'al pi Hashem'. Rabbi Elazar answers that Miriam also died by a kiss, derived from a verbal analogy of 'sham' from Moses, but the phrase was omitted out of decency.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists six people over whom the Angel of Death had no power: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, citing verses for each.
The Gemara questions how Miriam is included, since the phrase 'by the mouth of the Lord' is not written about her.
Rabbi Elazar answers that Miriam also died by a divine kiss, derived via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of the word 'there' from Moses.
The Gemara explains that the phrase 'by the mouth of the Lord' was not stated regarding Miriam because it would be disgraceful to say so.

items.text: Seven who were not ruled by worms and maggots
items.text_en: Seven who were not ruled by worms and maggots
items.desc_en: A baraisa lists seven people—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Miriam, and Benjamin son of Jacob—over whom worms and maggots had no power, citing verses for each. A dissenting opinion adds David, based on 'my flesh dwells securely', but the Gemara explains that David was merely praying for security.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists seven people over whom worms and maggots had no power: the six from the previous baraita plus Benjamin son of Jacob, citing a verse for Benjamin.
A dissenting opinion includes David, citing the verse 'my flesh also shall rest in safety'.
The Gemara rejects this, explaining that David was merely requesting mercy.

items.text: Four who died due to the serpent's counsel
items.text_en: Four who died due to the serpent's counsel
items.desc_en: A baraisa lists four people—Benjamin son of Jacob, Amram father of Moses, Jesse father of David, and Chileab son of David—who died due to the serpent's counsel (i.e., without sin). The Gemara notes that all are derived from tradition except Jesse, whose death is hinted at in a verse that calls Abigail 'daughter of Nachash', interpreted as 'daughter of one who died due to the serpent'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists four people who died due to the serpent's counsel (i.e., without sin): Benjamin, Amram, Jesse, and Kilab, noting that all except Jesse are derived from tradition.
The Gemara cites a verse calling Abigail 'daughter of Nachash', questioning how she can be Jesse's daughter, and resolves that 'Nachash' refers to one who died due to the serpent.
The Gemara resolves that 'Nachash' means 'the daughter of one who died due to the serpent', i.e., Jesse.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter 'HaShutafin'
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter 'HaShutafin'
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter 'HaShutafin' with the phrase 'Hadran alach HaShutafin'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter 'HaShutafin' with the standard 'Hadran' formula.

items.text: Mishnah: Distancing excavations and hazards from a neighbor's wall
items.text_en: Mishnah: Distancing excavations and hazards from a neighbor's wall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new chapter, stating that one may not dig a pit, trench, cave, water channel, or washer's pool near a neighbor's wall unless he distances three handbreadths and plasters with lime. It further lists other items that must be distanced three handbreadths from a neighbor's wall: chaff, manure, salt, lime, and rocks; also seeds, a plow, and urine. Finally, it specifies distances for a millstone and an oven from the wall.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not dig a pit, trench, cave, water channel, or laundry basin near a neighbor's wall unless he distances three handbreadths and plasters with lime.

The Mishnah continues: one must distance dregs, manure, salt, lime, and rocks from a neighbor's wall by three handbreadths or plaster with lime; also seeds, plow, and urine must be distanced three handbreadths.
The Mishnah concludes: one must distance a millstone three handbreadths from the lower stone (four from the upper), and an oven three from the base (four from the rim).

items.text: Opening question and resolution about the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Opening question and resolution about the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah opens with 'bor' (pit) but ends with 'kotel' (wall), suggesting it should say 'from his neighbor's pit'. Abaye (or Rav Yehuda) answers that the Mishnah teaches 'from the wall of his pit', and this implies the wall is three handbreadths thick, which has practical implications for sales.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah opens with 'bor' (pit) but ends with 'kotel' (wall), and suggests it should say 'from his neighbor's pit'.
Abaye (or Rav Yehuda) answers that the Mishnah actually teaches 'from the wall of his pit'.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's wording teaches that the wall of a pit is three handbreadths thick, which has practical implications for sales.

items.text: First version of the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: First version of the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: one who wants to dig a pit next to his neighbor's boundary. In a field designated for pits, all agree it is forbidden. They disagree in a field not designated for pits: Abaye permits, Rava forbids because the neighbor might later decide to dig a pit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding one who wants to dig a pit adjacent to his neighbor's boundary, distinguishing between a field designated for pits and one not so designated.
Abaye permits digging immediately adjacent, reasoning that since the field is not designated for pits, the neighbor has no expectation to dig one.
Rava forbids digging immediately adjacent, arguing that the neighbor can claim that just as the digger changed his mind and dug, so too the neighbor might later decide to dig a pit.

items.text: Second version of the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Second version of the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: An alternative version: in a field not designated for pits, all agree one may dig. They disagree in a field designated for pits. Abaye permits, even according to the Rabbis who require distancing a tree from a pit, because here the pit does not yet exist. Rava forbids, even according to Rabbi Yosei who allows digging and planting in one's own property, because here the digging weakens the neighbor's land.

sub.desc_en: Introduces an alternative version of the dispute: in a field not designated for pits, all agree one may dig; the dispute is in a field designated for pits.
Abaye permits digging even in a field designated for pits, reasoning that since the pit does not yet exist, the rabbis' requirement to distance a tree from a pit does not apply.
Rava forbids digging even according to Rabbi Yosei, because each strike of the pickaxe weakens the neighbor's land.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and Rava's defense
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and Rava's defense
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: 'One may not dig a pit close to his neighbor's pit.' This implies that without a pit, one may dig. This supports the second version (where all agree in a non-pit field). But for the first version (where they disagree in a non-pit field), Rava's position is difficult. Rava responds by citing Abaye's earlier gloss that the Mishnah means 'from the wall of his pit'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that one may not dig a pit close to his neighbor's pit, implying that without a pit one may dig, which supports the second version but challenges Rava's position in the first version.
Rava responds by citing Abaye's earlier gloss that the Mishnah means 'from the wall of his pit', thereby resolving the challenge.

items.text: Alternative resolution and Abaye's defense
items.text_en: Alternative resolution and Abaye's defense
items.desc_en: Another version: the Mishnah is explained by Abaye's gloss. For the first version (where all agree in a pit-designated field), the Mishnah fits that case. But for the second version (where they disagree in a pit-designated field), Abaye's position is difficult. Abaye answers that the Mishnah refers to digging simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: Introduces an alternative version of the earlier dispute, citing Abaye's (or Rav Yehuda's) gloss that the Mishnah says 'from the wall of his pit'.

The Gemara notes that according to the first version of the dispute (where all agree in a pit-designated field), the Mishnah fits that case, but according to the second version (where they disagree in a pit-designated field), Abaye's position is difficult.
Abaye answers that the Mishnah refers to a case where both parties came to dig simultaneously (בבת אחת), thus resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Proof from a rock brought by hand
items.text_en: Proof from a rock brought by hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a rock is brought by hand, each person digs his pit and distances three handbreadths and plasters with lime. The Gemara distinguishes this case because the rock is brought by hand, and it teaches that even though it is brought by hand, one does not need extra space.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a rock brought by hand, where each person digs his pit, distances three handbreadths, and plasters with lime.
The Gemara distinguishes the case because the rock is brought by hand, and explains that the baraita teaches that even so, one does not need extra space.

items.text: Beginning of another baraita (incomplete)
items.text_en: Beginning of another baraita (incomplete)
items.desc_en: The Gemara starts to cite another baraita about distancing waste, manure, etc., but the segment is cut off.

sub.text: Gemara's attempt to cite a baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempt to cite a baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a baraita about distancing waste (גפת) and manure, but the citation is cut off.

items.text: First challenge: salt, lime, and stones from a wall
items.text_en: First challenge: salt, lime, and stones from a wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one must distance salt, lime, and stones three handbreadths from a neighbor's wall. It infers that without a wall, one may place them directly adjacent, but rejects this inference, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that these items damage the wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's requirement to distance salt, lime, and stones three handbreadths from a neighbor's wall that without a wall one may place them directly adjacent.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that even without a wall one may not place them adjacent, and the Mishnah merely teaches that these items damage a wall.

items.text: Second challenge: seeds, plow, and urine
items.text_en: Second challenge: seeds, plow, and urine
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah requiring distancing seeds, a plow, and urine three handbreadths from a wall. Again it infers that without a wall one may place them adjacent, but rejects this, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that these items are hard on the wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous rejection by citing a Mishnah that requires distancing seeds, a plow, and urine three handbreadths from a wall, inferring that without a wall one may place them adjacent.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that even without a wall one may not place them adjacent, and the Mishnah merely teaches that these items are hard on the wall.

items.text: Third challenge: millstones
items.text_en: Third challenge: millstones
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah requiring distancing millstones three handbreadths from the lower stone (four from the upper). Again it infers that without a wall one may place them adjacent, but rejects this, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that the vibration is hard on the wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah requiring distancing millstones three handbreadths from the lower stone (four from the upper) and infers that without a wall one may place them adjacent.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that even without a wall one may not place them adjacent, and the Mishnah teaches that the vibration (טיריא) is hard on the wall.

items.text: Fourth challenge: oven
items.text_en: Fourth challenge: oven
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah requiring distancing an oven three handbreadths from the kiln (four from the lip). Again it infers that without a wall one may place it adjacent, but rejects this, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that the heat is hard on the wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing a Mishnah that requires distancing an oven from a wall, inferring that without a wall one may place it adjacent.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that even without a wall one may not place the oven adjacent; the Mishnah merely teaches that the heat (הבלא) is hard on the wall.

items.text: Fifth challenge: bakery, dye-shop, and cattle shed under a storehouse
items.text_en: Fifth challenge: bakery, dye-shop, and cattle shed under a storehouse
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah that one may not open a bakery, dye-shop, or cattle shed under a neighbor's storehouse. It infers that without a storehouse one may do so, but distinguishes that a dwelling is different, as the Mishnah adds that if the cattle shed preceded the storehouse, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing a Mishnah that forbids opening a bakery, dye-shop, or cattle shed under a neighbor's storehouse, inferring that without a storehouse one may do so.
The Gemara distinguishes that a dwelling (דירה) is different from a storehouse, and proves this from the Mishnah's own ruling that if the cattle shed preceded the storehouse it is permitted.

items.text: Sixth challenge: tree near a field
items.text_en: Sixth challenge: tree near a field
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah requiring distancing a tree four cubits from a field for vineyard work. It infers that without this reason one may plant adjacent despite root damage, but resolves that the case involves a rock barrier. The Gemara then questions why roots still need to be cut three handbreadths deep, and explains that the barrier prevents lateral spread but not downward growth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah requiring a tree to be distanced four cubits from a field for vineyard work, implying that without this reason one may plant adjacent despite root damage.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a rock barrier (צונמא) that prevents root damage, so the distance is only for vineyard work.
The Gemara cites a baraita that when a fence separates, each may plant adjacent to the fence, supporting the presence of a barrier.
The Gemara objects that if a rock barrier exists, why must roots be cut three handbreadths deep to prevent plow obstruction?
The Gemara resolves that the ruling about cutting roots applies only when there is no rock barrier, as the barrier prevents lateral spread but not downward growth.

items.text: Seventh challenge: tree near a cistern
items.text_en: Seventh challenge: tree near a cistern
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah requiring distancing a tree twenty-five cubits from a cistern. It infers that without a cistern one may plant adjacent, but rejects this, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that roots damage a cistern up to that distance. The Gemara then questions the case where the tree preceded the cistern and one may not cut it, and resolves with Rav Pappa that it refers to a buyer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah requiring distancing a tree twenty-five cubits from a cistern, and infers that without a cistern one may plant adjacent.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that roots damage a cistern up to that distance, so even without a cistern one may not plant adjacent.
The Gemara objects: if the tree preceded the cistern, the Mishnah says one may not cut it down, but how can that be if planting adjacent is forbidden?
Rav Pappa resolves that the case refers to a buyer who purchased the tree after the cistern was dug, so the tree was planted permissibly.

items.text: Eighth challenge: soaking pit near vegetables, etc.
items.text_en: Eighth challenge: soaking pit near vegetables, etc.
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah requiring distancing a soaking pit from vegetables, leeks from onions, and mustard from bees. It infers that without the vegetables one may place the pit adjacent, but rejects this, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that these items harm each other. The Gemara then notes that Rabbi Yosei permits mustard because the beekeeper can be told to distance his bees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the general principle by citing a Mishnah that requires distancing a soaking pit from vegetables, implying that without vegetables one may place it adjacent.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that these items harm each other, not that one may place them adjacent in the absence of the other.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yosei permits planting mustard near bees because the beekeeper can be told to distance his bees, as they come and eat the mustard pods.

items.text: Rav Pappa's answer: the case of a buyer
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer: the case of a buyer
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa suggests that the Mishnah's case involves a buyer (לוקח) who purchased the field, not a neighbor. This raises the question of how the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei would rule in such a scenario.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah's case involves a buyer (לוקח) who purchased the field, not a neighbor.

items.text: Objection to Rav Pappa's answer
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Pappa's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if it is a buyer, what is the reasoning of the Rabbis? And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei? Even for soaking and vegetables, the same logic should apply!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Pappa's answer: if the case is a buyer, what is the reasoning of the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei? The same logic should apply even to soaking and vegetables.

items.text: Ravina's answer: the one who damages must distance himself
items.text_en: Ravina's answer: the one who damages must distance himself
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the Rabbis hold that the one who causes damage (המזיק) must distance himself, implying that the burden is on the damager.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that the Rabbis hold the principle that the one who causes damage (המזיק) must distance himself from the other's property.

items.text: Challenge: does Rabbi Yosei hold the opposite?
items.text_en: Challenge: does Rabbi Yosei hold the opposite?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: does this imply that Rabbi Yosei holds that the one who suffers damage (הניזק) must distance himself? If so, even for soaking and vegetables, the same would apply!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: does this imply that Rabbi Yosei holds that the one who suffers damage (הניזק) must distance himself? If so, even for soaking and vegetables, the same would apply!

items.text: First resolution: Rabbi Yosei also holds 'on the damager', but explains the difference
items.text_en: First resolution: Rabbi Yosei also holds 'on the damager', but explains the difference
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yosei also holds that the damager must distance himself. He argues to the Rabbis: regarding soaking and vegetables, only one damages the other, but mustard and bees both damage each other, so both must distance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei also holds the damager must distance himself, and explains his argument to the Rabbis: regarding soaking and vegetables only one damages the other, but mustard and bees both damage each other.
The Rabbis object that bees do not damage mustard: if the mustard is in the ground the bees cannot find it, and if it is in the leaves the bees return to the flowers.

items.text: Second resolution: Rabbi Yosei holds 'on the sufferer', speaking to the Rabbis' position
items.text_en: Second resolution: Rabbi Yosei holds 'on the sufferer', speaking to the Rabbis' position
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei says that if a pit precedes a tree, the tree owner need not cut it down, implying the sufferer must distance. It then resolves that Rabbi Yosei indeed holds 'on the sufferer', but he is speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning: for you who say 'on the damager', consider mustard and bees where both damage each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei rules that if a pit precedes a tree, the tree owner need not cut it down, implying that the sufferer must distance himself, contradicting the assumption that Rabbi Yosei holds 'on the damager'.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei indeed holds 'on the sufferer', but he is speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei's argument to the Rabbis
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's argument to the Rabbis
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states his own position that the sufferer must distance, then argues to the Rabbis that even according to their view that the damager must distance, the cases of mustard and bees are problematic because both damage each other.
The Rabbis reject Rabbi Yosei's argument, asserting that bees do not damage mustard, and if the mustard is in the stalk, the bees cannot find it, and if in the leaves, the branches regrow.

items.text: Distance for the washer's basin
items.text_en: Distance for the washer's basin
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between the Mishnah (three handbreadths) and a baraita (four cubits) by distinguishing between the basin's acidic water (three handbreadths) and its stagnant water (four cubits). Rav Nachman bar Rav Avuah's ruling is supported by a baraita and an alternative version of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah requires three handbreadths distance for the washer's basin, but a baraita requires four cubits.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Avuah's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Avuah's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Avuah resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah refers to the basin's acidic water (מחמצן), requiring three handbreadths, while the baraita refers to its stagnant water (נדיין), requiring four cubits.
A baraita is cited that explicitly states the washer's basin requires four cubits, supporting Rav Nachman's distinction.

The Gemara concludes that the contradiction is resolved in favor of Rav Nachman's distinction, as the Mishnah's three handbreadths applies to acidic water and the baraita's four cubits to stagnant water.

An alternative version of the Mishnah is presented, taught by Rav Chiyya bar Rav Avuah, which explicitly states 'three handbreadths from the edge of the acidic water to the wall,' confirming Rav Nachman's ruling.

items.text: Interpretation of 'and he plasters with lime'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'and he plasters with lime'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah says 'and he plasters with lime' (וְסָד בְּסִיד) or 'or he plasters with lime' (אוֹ סָד בְּסִיד). It initially assumes the former, but a proof from Rabbi Yehuda's statement is rejected because it might be necessary to teach a special case. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah means 'and he plasters with lime'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the Mishnah read 'and he plasters with lime' (וְסָד בְּסִיד) or 'or he plasters with lime' (אוֹ סָד בְּסִיד)?
The Gemara initially assumes it must be 'and he plasters with lime', because if it were 'or', the Mishnah could have combined the two cases into one clause.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the Mishnah separates them because the two types of damage (moisture damage and heat damage) are different, so they cannot be combined.

The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says that when a rock comes by hand, each neighbor must distance three handbreadths and plaster with lime, implying that without the rock coming by hand, plastering is not required.

The Gemara rejects the proof: even without the rock coming by hand, plastering is required; the case of 'coming by hand' was needed to teach that despite the need for more space, the distance remains three handbreadths.

items.text: Comparison of lists: geffen, manure, salt, stones vs. sand
items.text_en: Comparison of lists: geffen, manure, salt, stones vs. sand
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah here lists 'stones' but not 'sand', while in the chapter on insulating foods (Shabbat) it lists 'sand' but not 'stones'. Rav Yosef's answer (people don't insulate with stones) is rejected by Abaye. Abaye suggests each list implies the other, but Rava rejects this. Rava explains: there, sand is not listed because it heats up and cools down quickly; here, stones are not listed because they crack the pot. A baraita of Rabbi Oshaya is reconciled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's list of materials (geffen, manure, salt, stones) and contrasts it with the Mishnah in Shabbat about insulating foods, which lists sand but not stones.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah here lists stones but not sand, while the Mishnah there lists sand but not stones.
Rav Yosef answers that people do not typically insulate with stones.
Abaye objects that people do insulate with wool and purple cloth, as a baraita permits it, so Rav Yosef's reasoning is inconsistent.
Abaye suggests that each list implies the other: here stones are listed but sand is also included, and there sand is listed but stones are also included.
Rava rejects Abaye's suggestion, arguing that if one list implied the other, the Mishnah would have included both items in one place and stated the other as implied.
Rava explains that there (in Shabbat) stones are not listed because they crack the pot, and here (in Bava Batra) sand is not listed because it heats up and cools down quickly.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Oshaya's baraita includes sand in the list of materials for distancing, and asks why our Tanna does not list sand and explain it as referring to slow-cooking (מתונא).
The Gemara answers that our Tanna already listed the water channel (אמת המים) as a separate category, which covers the case of slow-cooking.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah also lists the washer's basin (ניברכת הכובסין), so why not list sand as well?
The Gemara explains that both the water channel and the washer's basin are necessary to teach distinct halachic principles, so sand is not needed.

items.text: Redundancy of 'seeds' and 'plow'
items.text_en: Redundancy of 'seeds' and 'plow'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists both 'seeds' and 'plow', as they seem to cause the same damage. It answers: 'seeds' refers to hand-sowing, and 'plow' refers to plowing for trees. It further asks why 'plow' is needed if water damage is already covered, and answers that the Mishnah speaks of the Land of Israel, which relies on rain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists both 'seeds' and 'plow', since the damage from seeds could be derived from the damage of plowing.
The Gemara answers that 'seeds' refers to hand-sowing (מפולת יד), which is a different type of damage than plowing.
The Gemara asks why 'plow' is listed separately, since its damage could be derived from 'seeds'.
The Gemara answers that 'plow' refers to plowing for trees, which is a distinct case from hand-sowing.
The Gemara asks why 'plow' is needed at all, since water damage (already covered in the Mishnah) would seem to include plowing's effect.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah speaks of the Land of Israel, which relies on rain (לִמְטַר הַשָּׁמַיִם תִּשְׁתֶּה מָּיִם), so water damage is not a concern there, and plowing is a separate category.

items.text: Opening challenge from the Mishnah on bending a vine
items.text_en: Opening challenge from the Mishnah on bending a vine
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling about roots spreading sideways, citing a Mishnah about bending a vine into the ground and the requirement of three handbreadths of earth. Rabbi Chaggai in the name of Rabbi Yosei explains that this is because the roots cause the ground to become loose and raise fine soil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier ruling about roots spreading sideways, citing a Mishnah that requires three handbreadths of earth over a bent vine before planting seed above it.
A baraita adds that one may plant on the sides, implying the roots spread sideways.

sub.text: Rabbi Chaggai in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chaggai in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chaggai explains that the three handbreadths are needed because the roots loosen the ground and raise fine soil, not because they spread sideways.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana's leniency on urinating near a wall and its refutation
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana's leniency on urinating near a wall and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana permits urinating near a neighbor's wall, citing a verse about Ahab. The Gemara objects from the Mishnah requiring three handbreadths for urine, and from a baraita that distinguishes between brick and stone walls. The conclusion is a refutation of Rabba bar bar Chana's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule requiring a three-handbreadth distance for urine from a wall.
Rabba bar bar Chana permits urinating near a neighbor's wall, citing the verse about Ahab's punishment.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly requires a three-handbreadth distance for urine.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's rule applies only to pouring water, not to direct urination.
The Gemara brings a baraita that prohibits pouring water near a wall without a three-handbreadth distance.
The Gemara again answers that the baraita also refers to pouring, not urinating.
The Gemara brings a baraita that explicitly prohibits urinating near a wall without a three-handbreadth distance.
The baraita distinguishes between brick walls (three handbreadths), stone walls (one handbreadth to prevent damage), and hard rock walls (permitted entirely).
The Gemara declares Rabba bar bar Chana's position refuted.

items.text: Defense of Rabba bar bar Chana's scriptural proof
items.text_en: Defense of Rabba bar bar Chana's scriptural proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara defends Rabba bar bar Chana by explaining that his proof from the verse was not about urine but about a dog, which naturally urinates on walls, and that he would not even allow that.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabba bar bar Chana was citing a verse, not speaking about urine, and explains that he was referring to a dog, which naturally urinates on walls.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a thin cake not reducing a window's size
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a thin cake not reducing a window's size
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tovi bar Kisna quotes Shmuel that a thin cake does not reduce the window's size for purposes of impurity. The Gemara questions why specifically a thin cake, and explains that Shmuel's statement includes even a thick cake, but he mentions the thin one to teach that even though it is repulsive, one does not nullify it.

sub.text: Rabbi Tovi bar Kisna quoting Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tovi bar Kisna quoting Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a thin cake does not reduce the window's size for impurity purposes.
The Gemara asks why Shmuel specifically mentions a thin cake; even a thick one should not reduce the window.
The Gemara explains that a thick cake is obviously not nullified since it is fit for eating, so Shmuel's statement is not needed for that case.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel specifically mentions a thin cake to teach that even though it becomes repulsive, one does not nullify it, so it does not reduce the window.
The Gemara objects that a thin cake is susceptible to impurity and therefore cannot serve as a barrier against impurity, so it should not reduce the window.
The Gemara resolves that the thin cake was kneaded with fruit juice, which does not render it susceptible to impurity, so it can serve as a barrier.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about a basket of straw and a barrel of figs
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about a basket of straw and a barrel of figs
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's ruling with a baraita stating that a basket of straw or a barrel of dried figs placed in a window can interpose if they can stand on their own. The Gemara resolves that the straw is moldy, the figs are dried up, and thus they are not fit for use, so they are nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: a basket of straw or a barrel of dried figs placed in a window can interpose if they can stand on their own, but why should they interpose if the straw is fit for animal feed?
The Gemara answers that the straw is rotted, then addresses further objections: it is not fit for bricks because it has thorns, not fit for kindling because it is wet, and a large fire is uncommon.
The Gemara asks about dried figs being fit for consumption, and Shmuel and Rabba bar Avuh answer that the case is where the figs became worm-infested, so they are not fit.

items.text: Question about the barrel's orientation
items.text_en: Question about the barrel's orientation
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze the case of the barrel, asking whether its opening faces outward or inward, which affects the ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the barrel's orientation, whether its opening faces outward or inward, to determine the applicable ruling.

items.text: Challenge to the Mishnah's ruling on clay vessel
items.text_en: Challenge to the Mishnah's ruling on clay vessel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a clay vessel should reduce the window, since it cannot become impure from its outside. It answers that the vessel's opening faces inward, or alternatively that the case involves a metal barrel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: the vessel itself should reduce the window, but a clay vessel cannot become impure from its outside, so why should it reduce?
The Gemara answers: the vessel's opening faces inward, so it can become impure from its inside.
Alternatively, the Gemara says: the case involves a metal barrel, which can become impure from its outside.

items.text: Baraita listing items that reduce or do not reduce the window
items.text_en: Baraita listing items that reduce or do not reduce the window
items.desc_en: A baraita enumerates items that reduce the window's size (e.g., detached herbs, patches, dangling flesh, a bird, a gentile, an eight-month-old infant, salt, clay vessel, Torah scroll) and those that do not (snow, hail, ice, frost, water).

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists items that reduce the window's size (detached herbs, patches, dangling flesh, a bird, a gentile, an eight-month-old infant, salt, clay vessel, Torah scroll) and those that do not (snow, hail, ice, frost, water).

items.text: Herbs: why they are not usable for animal feed
items.text_en: Herbs: why they are not usable for animal feed
