items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why herbs are not considered usable for animal feed, and answers that they are placed on a ledge (afrazta) where animals cannot reach them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why herbs are not considered usable for animal feed, given that they are fit for that purpose.
The Gemara answers that the herbs are placed on a ledge (אפרזתא) where animals cannot reach them.

items.text: Herbs that grew spontaneously: why they are not removed
items.text_en: Herbs that grew spontaneously: why they are not removed
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why herbs that grew on their own are not removed since they damage the wall. Rabba says the wall is a ruin; Rav Pappa says even in an inhabited wall, they are beyond three handbreadths from the window.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why herbs that grew spontaneously in the window are not removed, since they damage the wall.
Rabba answers that the case is in a ruined wall, where the herbs do not damage an inhabited structure.
Rav Pappa answers that even in an inhabited wall, the herbs are beyond three handbreadths from the window, so they do not reduce the window's size.

items.text: Patches: why they are not usable for clothing or craftsmen
items.text_en: Patches: why they are not usable for clothing or craftsmen
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why patches are not usable for tearing into clothing strips or for a craftsman. It answers that they are small scraps (s'michta) or rags (riska). The Gemara then notes that if they are rags, the baraita should say 'less than four by four' rather than 'three by three', and resolves that they are like rags.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why patches (מטלוניות) are not usable for tearing into clothing strips.
The Gemara answers that they are small scraps (סמיכתא) and thus not usable for clothing.
The Gemara asks why patches are not usable for a craftsman.
The Gemara answers that they are rags (ריסקא) and thus not usable for a craftsman.
The Gemara objects that if they are rags, the baraita should say 'less than four by four' rather than 'three by three'.
The Gemara resolves that they are like rags (כעין ריסקא), explaining the measure of three by three.

items.text: Dangling flesh: why it is not removed or used
items.text_en: Dangling flesh: why it is not removed or used
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the dangling flesh is not removed since it will tear off. It answers that it is tied. Further questions: why not slaughter the animal (if kosher), sell to a gentile, or throw to dogs? Answers: the animal is non-kosher, lean, or one cannot cause pain to animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the dangling flesh will tear off and fall, so why does the baraita list it as a valid partition reducer?
The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with flesh that is tied securely so it does not fall.
The Gemara asks why one cannot simply kill the animal, thereby detaching the flesh intentionally.
The Gemara answers that the animal is a non-kosher species (טְמֵאָה), so slaughtering it is pointless.
The Gemara asks why one cannot sell the animal to a gentile for consumption, thereby circumventing the prohibition of eating non-kosher meat.
The Gemara answers that the animal is emaciated (כְּחוּשָׁה) and therefore unsellable.
The Gemara asks why one cannot cut off the flesh and throw it to dogs for disposal, as it is permitted to feed non-kosher material to dogs.
The Gemara answers that one may not cause unnecessary pain to a living animal (צַעַר בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים), so cutting the flesh while the animal is alive is forbidden.

items.text: Bird that nested: why it is not removed or used
items.text_en: Bird that nested: why it is not removed or used
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the bird is not removed since it will fly away. It answers that it is tied. Further questions: why not slaughter it (if kosher), sell to a gentile, or give to a child? Answers: it is non-kosher, a kalanita (a type of bird), or it scratches. The Gemara notes that a kalanita does not scratch, so it is like a kalanita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a bird that nested in a window is not removed, since it will fly away.
The Gemara answers that the bird is tied, so it cannot fly away.
The Gemara asks why one cannot slaughter the bird if it is kosher.
The Gemara answers that the bird is non-kosher (טמא), so slaughter is irrelevant.
The Gemara asks why one cannot sell the bird to a gentile.
The Gemara answers that the bird is a קלניתא (a type of bird that is not desirable for sale).
The Gemara asks why one cannot give the bird to a child.
The Gemara answers that the bird scratches (מסרט), making it unsuitable for a child.
The Gemara objects that a קלניתא does not scratch, contradicting the previous answer.
The Gemara resolves that the bird is like a קלניתא (similar but not identical), so it scratches.

items.text: Gentile who sat: why he does not leave
items.text_en: Gentile who sat: why he does not leave
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the gentile does not get up and leave. It answers that he is bound. If a friend comes to release him, the Gemara says he is a leper. If a leper's friend comes, the Gemara concludes it is a royal prisoner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the gentile who sat in the window is not considered likely to leave, since he could just get up and go.
The gemara answers that the gentile is bound (כפות) and therefore cannot leave.
The gemara objects: if a friend comes to untie him, he can leave; so the gemara revises the answer that the gentile is a leper (מצורע) who is forbidden to enter the city.
The gemara concludes that the gentile is a royal prisoner (חבשי מלכות), who cannot be released by anyone.

items.text: Eight-month-old infant: why the mother does not take him
items.text_en: Eight-month-old infant: why the mother does not take him
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mother does not take the infant. It answers that it is Shabbat, and an eight-month-old is like a stone, forbidden to move, though the mother may bend over to nurse due to danger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mother does not simply take the eight-month-old infant from the window.
The Gemara answers that it is Shabbat, and an eight-month-old infant is like a stone, forbidden to move (לטלטל).
A baraita is cited: an eight-month-old is like a stone, forbidden to move on Shabbat, but his mother may bend over to nurse him due to danger.

items.text: Salt: why it is not usable or removed
items.text_en: Salt: why it is not usable or removed
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why salt is not usable. It answers that it is bitter salt (mirirta) or used for hides with thorns. The Gemara then asks why it is not removed since it damages the wall, and answers that it sits on a potsherd. The Gemara then questions why the potsherd itself does not reduce, implying it is not considered a vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why salt is not considered usable, noting that salt is usable for seasoning food.
The Gemara gives a first answer: the salt in question is bitter salt (מלוח מרירא), fit only for hides and not for human consumption.
An alternative answer: the salt is used for treating hides that have thorns, so despite being bitter it is still usable.
The Gemara asks: since the salt damages the wall, why not remove it (it would reduce the aperture by its own removal)?
The Gemara answers that the salt sits on a potsherd (חַסְפָּא), so it does not directly contact the wall and is not removed.
The Gemara then asks why the potsherd itself does not reduce the aperture (since it is a vessel and itself reduces).

items.text: Salt as a partition material
items.text_en: Salt as a partition material
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the use of salt for partitions, citing Rav and Shmuel's dispute about whether salt can be used. Rav Pappa reconciles their views by distinguishing between Sodomite salt and Istrokanite salt. Rabba adds that if a beam is placed on two piles of salt, even Istrokanite salt is effective because the beam holds the salt in place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a baraita about the minimum size of a potsherd for a partition, then extends the discussion to other items like a clay vessel and a Torah scroll.
The Gemara questions the use of a clay vessel for a partition, noting it is usable, and similarly questions a Torah scroll, resolving that it can be stored there.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether salt can be used for a partition; Rav Pappa reconciles them by distinguishing between Sodomite salt and Istrokanite salt.
Rabba adds that if a beam is placed on two piles of salt, even Istrokanite salt is effective because the beam holds the salt in place, resolving the dispute.

items.text: Reason for distancing millstones
items.text_en: Reason for distancing millstones
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why millstones must be distanced from a neighbor's wall. The Mishnah states the distance is three handbreadths from the lower stone (שכב) or four from the upper stone (רכב). The Gemara initially suggests it is due to vibration (טיריא), but notes a baraita about a donkey mill that also requires distancing, where vibration is not a factor. It concludes the reason is noise (קלא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the reason is for the Mishnah's requirement to distance millstones from a neighbor's wall.
The Gemara initially answers that the reason is vibration (טיריא) from the millstones.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita about a donkey mill that also requires distancing, where vibration is not a factor.
The Gemara resolves that the actual reason is noise (קלא), not vibration.

items.text: Distance for an oven and Abaye's deduction
items.text_en: Distance for an oven and Abaye's deduction
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an oven must be distanced three handbreadths from the kiln (כיליא) or four from the lip (שפה). Abaye deduces that the kiln of an oven is one handbreadth thick, which has practical implications for buying and selling.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the required distance for an oven: three handbreadths from the kiln (כיליא) or four from the lip (שפה).
Abaye deduces from the Mishnah's measurements that the kiln (כיליא) of an oven is one handbreadth thick.
The gemara notes that this deduction has practical implications for buying and selling ovens.

items.text: Mishnah: Placing an oven in a house
items.text_en: Mishnah: Placing an oven in a house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not place an oven in a house unless there is a ceiling height of four cubits above it. If placed in an upper story, there must be a plaster floor (מעזיבה) of three handbreadths, or one handbreadth for a kiln (כירה). If damage occurs, the one who caused it pays. Rabbi Shimon says these measurements are only to exempt from payment if damage occurs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one may not place an oven in a house unless there is a ceiling height of four cubits above it; if in an upper story, a plaster floor (מעזיבה) of three handbreadths is required, or one handbreadth for a kiln (כירה).
The Mishnah rules that if damage occurs, the one who caused it pays.
Rabbi Shimon says these measurements are only to exempt from payment if damage occurs.

items.text: Mishnah: Opening a bakery or stable under a storehouse
items.text_en: Mishnah: Opening a bakery or stable under a storehouse
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not open a baker's shop or a dyer's shop under a neighbor's storehouse, nor a cattle stable. However, for wine, it is permitted because it improves the wine, but not a cattle stable because it spoils it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not open a bakery, dye shop, or cattle stable under a neighbor's storehouse, but permits a wine shop because wine improves the storehouse's air.

items.text: Gemara: Discrepancy in oven distances
items.text_en: Gemara: Discrepancy in oven distances
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says an oven requires three handbreadths from the kiln, but a baraita says four. Abaye resolves this by explaining that the baraita refers to a baker's oven, which is larger; our oven (a regular one) is like a baker's kiln.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that an oven requires four handbreadths distance and a kiln three, while the Mishnah implies three for an oven.
Abaye resolves the discrepancy by explaining that the baraita refers to a baker's oven, which is larger, while our regular oven is comparable to a baker's kiln.

items.text: Gemara: Questions about precedence and modifications
items.text_en: Gemara: Questions about precedence and modifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's rule about not opening a shop under a storehouse. A baraita teaches that if the stable preceded the storehouse, it is permitted. Abaye raises several unresolved questions (תיקו): if one cleaned and prepared the area for a storehouse, if one added windows, if there was a portico under the storehouse, or if one built an upper story over his house. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua asks about dates and pomegranates, also left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that clarifies the Mishnah's rule: if a stable preceded the storehouse, it is permitted.
Abaye raises an unresolved question: if one cleaned and prepared the area for a storehouse, what is the law?
Abaye raises further unresolved questions: if one added windows, if there was a portico under the storehouse, or if one built an upper story over his house.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua asks about dates and pomegranates, also left unresolved.

items.text: Gemara: Wine and stable, and additional comments
items.text_en: Gemara: Wine and stable, and additional comments
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's exception for wine: it improves the wine, while a stable spoils it. Rav Yosef comments that our wine (in Babylonia) is even harmed by the smoke of a lamp. Rav Sheshet says that a cesspool (אספסתא) is like a cattle stable in terms of damage.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna's baraita explains the Mishnah's exception: wine is permitted because it improves the stored produce, while a cattle stable is forbidden because it spoils it.
Rav Yosef adds that in Babylonia, even the smoke of a lamp harms the wine, making it even more sensitive than the Mishnah's case.
Rav Sheshet rules that a cesspool (אספסתא) is legally equivalent to a cattle stable in terms of the damage it causes to stored produce.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Shop in a courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Shop in a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a resident of a courtyard can prevent a neighbor from opening a shop there due to the noise of people coming and going. However, one cannot prevent a craftsman from making tools and selling them in the market, nor object to the noise of a hammer, mill, or children. The Gemara asks why the first clause is strict and the latter lenient. Abaye says the latter case refers to a different courtyard. Rava objects that if so, the Mishnah should explicitly say 'another courtyard,' and offers an alternative explanation (cut off in the text).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: a resident can prevent a shop in the courtyard due to noise of people, but cannot prevent a craftsman from making tools and selling in the market, nor object to noise of hammer, mill, or children.
The Gemara asks why the first clause is strict and the latter lenient.
Abaye says the latter case refers to a different courtyard.
Rava objects that if so, the Mishnah should explicitly say 'another courtyard' is permitted.
Rava begins to offer an alternative explanation, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Historical background of Yehoshua ben Gamla's ordinance
items.text_en: Historical background of Yehoshua ben Gamla's ordinance
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the progression of Torah education: initially only children with fathers learned; then teachers were placed in Jerusalem; then in each district; finally Yehoshua ben Gamla established teachers in every town and city, admitting children from age six or seven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of children's education and the ordinance of Yehoshua ben Gamla.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav praises Yehoshua ben Gamla, noting that initially only children with fathers learned Torah.
The Gemara describes the intermediate stages: teachers were placed in Jerusalem, then in each district, with children entering at age sixteen or seventeen.
Yehoshua ben Gamla established teachers in every town and city, admitting children from age six or seven.

items.text: Rav's instructions to Rav Shmuel bar Shilat
items.text_en: Rav's instructions to Rav Shmuel bar Shilat
items.desc_en: Rav instructs Rav Shmuel bar Shilat not to accept students under six, but from that age onward to accept them and feed them like an ox. He also advises that when hitting a child, use only a shoelace, and that a student who reads should be with a friend who does not.

sub.text: Rav's instruction to Rav Shmuel bar Shilat
sub.text_en: Rav's instruction to Rav Shmuel bar Shilat
sub.desc_en: Rav instructs Rav Shmuel bar Shilat not to accept students under six years old, but from that age onward to accept them and feed them like an ox.
Rav advises Rav Shmuel bar Shilat that when hitting a child, use only a shoelace, and that a student who reads should be with a friend who does not.

items.text: Objections from neighbors regarding teachers
items.text_en: Objections from neighbors regarding teachers
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises objections from baraitot that neighbors can prevent a resident from becoming a teacher of children. The answers distinguish between Jewish children (permitted) and gentile children (restricted), and between a local scribe and others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that neighbors can prevent a resident from becoming a teacher of children, implying a restriction on teaching.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to teaching gentile children, which is restricted, not Jewish children.
The Gemara brings another baraita that two neighbors can prevent each other from becoming a teacher, again challenging the permissibility.
The Gemara answers that this baraita also refers to teaching gentile children.
The Gemara brings a third baraita that one may not rent a house in a shared courtyard to a Jewish scribe or an Aramean scribe, implying a restriction on teaching.
The Gemara answers that this baraita refers to a town scribe (סופר מתא), who deals with public documents and causes noise, not a teacher of children.

items.text: Rava's rulings on moving students
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on moving students
items.desc_en: Rava rules that after Yehoshua ben Gamla's ordinance, a child is not moved from one town to another, but may be moved from one synagogue to another. If a river separates, he is not moved; if there is a bridge, he is moved; if there is a camel, he is not moved.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens with a ruling that since Yehoshua ben Gamla's ordinance, a child is not moved from one town to another.
Rava adds that a child may be moved from one synagogue to another within the same town.
Rava rules that if a river separates the synagogues, the child is not moved.
Rava rules that if there is a bridge over the river, the child is moved.
Rava rules that if a camel (a dangerous obstacle) is present, the child is not moved.

items.text: Rava's ruling on class size
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on class size
items.desc_en: Rava states that the maximum number of students per teacher is twenty-five. If there are fifty, two teachers are appointed; if forty, an assistant is appointed from the town.

sub.desc_en: Rava states the maximum number of students per teacher is twenty-five.
Rava rules that if there are fifty students, two teachers are appointed.
Rava rules that if there are forty students, an assistant is appointed from the town.

items.text: Dispute on replacing a teacher with a better one
items.text_en: Dispute on replacing a teacher with a better one
items.desc_en: Rava says a teacher who is competent should not be replaced by a more competent one, lest the first become negligent. Rav Dimi from Neharde'a argues that jealousy among scribes increases wisdom.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a competent teacher should not be replaced by a more competent one, lest the first become negligent.
Rav Dimi from Neharde'a argues that replacing with a better teacher is beneficial, because jealousy among scribes increases wisdom.

items.text: Dispute on choosing between a fluent and a precise teacher
items.text_en: Dispute on choosing between a fluent and a precise teacher
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one teacher is fluent but not precise, and another is precise but not fluent, the fluent one is preferred because errors will correct themselves. Rav Dimi from Neharde'a argues for the precise one, citing a verse about Joab's campaign.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that when choosing between two teachers, one fluent but imprecise and the other precise but not fluent, the fluent one is appointed because errors will correct themselves.
Rav Dimi from Neharde'a argues for the precise teacher, citing the verse about Joab's campaign in Edom to support that once an error enters, it is difficult to remove.

items.text: Story of the teacher who misread 'זכר'
items.text_en: Story of the teacher who misread 'זכר'
items.desc_en: A teacher is questioned for teaching 'זְכַר' instead of 'זֵכֶר' in the verse about Amalek. He justifies himself with a verse, but his student nearly kills him with an axe, citing another verse. The story ends with a dispute whether the student actually killed him.

sub.desc_en: The student asks the teacher why he taught the verse as 'זְכַר' instead of 'זֵכֶר', and the teacher explains he was taught that way.
The student consults the teacher's own master, who confirms the correct reading is 'זֵכֶר'.
The student takes an axe to kill the teacher, citing the verse 'אָרוּר עֹשֶׂה מְלֶאכֶת ה׳ רְמִיָּה' and then 'וְאָרוּר מֹנֵעַ חַרְבּוֹ מִדָּם' when the teacher protests.
The gemara records a dispute about whether the student actually killed the teacher.

items.text: Rava's ruling on those who are like warned and standing
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on those who are like warned and standing
items.desc_en: Rava states that a teacher of children, a planter, a butcher, a craftsman, and a town scribe are all considered as if they are warned and standing (i.e., they cannot be easily dismissed). The general principle is that any loss that cannot be recovered is considered as if the person is warned and standing.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a teacher of children, a planter, a butcher, a craftsman, and a town scribe are all considered as if they are warned and standing, and the general principle is that any loss that cannot be recovered is treated as such.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a miller blocking an alley
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a miller blocking an alley
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if a resident of an alley sets up a mill, and another resident comes to set up a mill next to him, the first can prevent it because it cuts off his livelihood. The Gemara attempts to support this from a mishna about fish traps, but rejects it because fish give a scent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a resident of an alley who sets up a mill can prevent another resident from setting up a competing mill next to him, because it cuts off his livelihood.
The Gemara attempts to support Rav Huna from a mishna requiring distance between fish traps, as cited by Rabbah bar Rav Huna.
The Gemara rejects the support, distinguishing fish because they give off a scent that attracts other fish, unlike mills.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling compared to Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling compared to Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages
items.desc_en: Ravina asks if Rav Huna's ruling aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who prohibits a storekeeper from giving nuts to children. The Gemara answers that even the Sages, who permit that, would agree here because the miller cuts off the other's livelihood entirely.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava whether Rav Huna's ruling that a resident can block a competitor from setting up a mill in the same alley aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's position that a storekeeper may not distribute nuts to children because it habituates them to his store.

Rava answers that even the Sages, who permit the storekeeper's distribution, would agree with Rav Huna here because the miller cuts off the other's livelihood entirely, unlike the storekeeper who merely gives away nuts.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution with Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution with Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita that allows one to open a store next to another's store. The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute among Tannaim: one baraita allows it, while another baraita (with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) says neighbors can prevent certain trades.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that explicitly permits opening a store or bathhouse next to a neighbor's, because each may do as they please on their own property.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by identifying a Tannaitic dispute: the first baraita reflects the Tanna Kamma who allows it, while another baraita records Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position that neighbors can prevent certain trades.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's distinctions and the question of a resident from another alley
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's distinctions and the question of a resident from another alley
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua clarifies that a resident of one town can prevent a resident of another town, but not if he pays taxes there. A resident of the same alley cannot prevent another. He then raises a question about a resident of one alley against a resident of another alley, which remains unresolved. Rav Yosef adds that one cannot prevent a teacher of children, citing Ezra's enactment.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's opening statement
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's opening statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua states three clear cases: a resident of one town can block a resident of another town unless he pays taxes there, and a resident of an alley cannot block another resident of the same alley.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua raises an unresolved question about whether a resident of one alley can block a resident of a different alley.
Rav Yosef adds that Rav Huna concedes one cannot block a teacher of children, because Ezra enacted that scribes be placed next to each other.
The gemara objects: why not worry that the children will become neglectful (due to multiple teachers)?

items.text: Opening maxim
items.text_en: Opening maxim
items.desc_en: The daf opens with the maxim that jealousy among scribes increases wisdom, setting a thematic backdrop for the ensuing discussions.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with the maxim that jealousy among scribes increases wisdom.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's ruling on peddlers and Torah scholars
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's ruling on peddlers and Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that Rav Huna bar Yehoshua agrees that peddlers who travel from town to town cannot be blocked, as Ezra instituted this for the availability of jewelry. However, this applies only to traveling, not to settling permanently, unless the peddler is a Torah scholar, who may settle to avoid distraction from study.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that Rav Huna bar Yehoshua agrees that peddlers traveling between towns cannot be blocked, citing Mar's tradition that Ezra instituted this practice so that jewelry would be available for Jewish women.

The Gemara qualifies that this leniency applies only to traveling peddlers, not to permanent settlement, but a Torah scholar may settle permanently, as illustrated by Rava permitting Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Ovadya to settle to avoid distraction from their studies.

items.text: Case of date-palm sellers in Babylonia
items.text_en: Case of date-palm sellers in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Date-palm sellers brought dates to Babylonia, and local townspeople tried to block them. Ravina ruled that since they came from elsewhere, they may sell to all, but only on market day and only in the market, not by going door-to-door.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where date-palm sellers brought dates to Babylonia and local townspeople tried to block them.
Ravina rules that since the sellers came from elsewhere, they may sell to all.
The Gemara qualifies Ravina's ruling: selling is permitted only on market day and only in the market, not by going door-to-door.

items.text: Case of wool merchants at the mouth of the canal
items.text_en: Case of wool merchants at the mouth of the canal
items.desc_en: Wool merchants brought wool to the mouth of the canal, and locals blocked them. Rav Kahana ruled that the locals are justified, but the merchants may sell enough for their livelihood until they remove their permits and leave.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: wool merchants brought wool to the mouth of the canal, and local townspeople blocked them.
Rav Kahana rules that the locals are justified in blocking the merchants.
The merchants object that they have permits (אשרי) allowing them to sell.
Rav Kahana compromises: the merchants may sell enough for their livelihood until they remove their permits and leave.

items.text: The tragic story of Rav Adda bar Abba
items.text_en: The tragic story of Rav Adda bar Abba
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi brought dried figs by boat; the Exilarch asked Rava to check if he was a Torah scholar to secure market priority. Rava sent Rav Adda bar Abba, who tested Rav Dimi with a difficult question, leading to a dispute. Rav Adda was delayed and missed Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's lecture, resulting in his death. Several rabbis claimed responsibility for his punishment.

sub.desc_en: The story opens: Rav Dimi brings dried figs by boat; the Exilarch asks Rava to check if he is a Torah scholar to grant market priority, and Rava sends Rav Adda bar Abba to test him.
Rav Adda bar Abba asks Rav Dimi a difficult halachic question about an elephant that swallowed a Egyptian basket and excreted it, which Rav Dimi cannot answer.
Rav Dimi retorts, questioning Rav Adda bar Abba's authority, and Rav Adda bar Abba slaps him with a sandal, asserting that he is Rav Dimi's teacher and Rava is his teacher's teacher.

Rav Dimi is not granted market priority, his figs spoil; he complains to Rav Yosef, who rebukes him by citing a verse about the king of Edom, implying that one who delays a royal ship will not be delayed.

sub.text: Narrative conclusion: Rav Adda bar Abba's death
sub.text_en: Narrative conclusion: Rav Adda bar Abba's death
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Abba dies, and several rabbis (Rav Yosef, Rav Dimi, Abaye, Rava) each claim responsibility for his punishment, citing different reasons.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's claim and the final incident
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's claim and the final incident
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak claims responsibility, explaining that Rav Adda bar Abba was delayed from his lecture by Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua, and as a result missed the session, leading to his death; the gemara concludes that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak likely punished him.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara on wall distancing
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara on wall distancing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who builds a wall next to a neighbor's wall must distance it four cubits. The Gemara begins by questioning how the first wall was built, with Rav Yehuda explaining the Mishnah's meaning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who builds a wall next to a neighbor's wall must distance it four cubits, and similarly for windows.
The Gemara questions how the first wall was built, since the Mishnah only addresses the second wall.
Rav Yehuda explains the Mishnah's meaning, implying that the first wall was already built by the neighbor.

items.text: Rava's correction of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's correction of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the Mishnah's wording, arguing that it should read: 'One whose wall was close to his fellow's wall at a distance of four cubits, and it fell, he should not lean another wall against it unless he distances four cubits.' The reason is that the trampling of the ground here benefits the ground there.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the Mishnah's wording, arguing it should read 'One whose wall was close to his fellow's wall' rather than 'One who comes to lean.'

Rava corrects the Mishnah: one whose wall was close to his fellow's wall at four cubits and fell may not lean another wall unless he distances four cubits, because the trampling of the ground here benefits the ground there.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Oshaya
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Oshaya
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the Mishnah's distancing requirement applies only to a garden wall, but for a courtyard wall one may lean. Rabbi Oshaya disagrees, saying both require distancing. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina reconciles them: one refers to an old city, the other to a new city.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the Mishnah's distancing requirement applies only to a garden wall (כותל גינה), but for a courtyard wall (כותל חצר) one may lean without distancing.
Rabbi Oshaya disagrees, asserting that both a garden wall and a courtyard wall require distancing; one may not lean.
Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina reconciles the dispute: one ruling applies to an old city (עיר ישנה) where walls are thick, the other to a new city (עיר חדשה) where walls are thin.

items.text: Gemara's question about windows and trampling
items.text_en: Gemara's question about windows and trampling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about windows requiring four cubits distance for various reasons, and notes that the reason given is to prevent darkening, not trampling. It answers that the case is when the window is on the side, not directly opposite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita about windows gives the reason of preventing darkening (האפלה) rather than trampling (דוושא), implying a contradiction.
The Gemara answers that the case is when the window is on the side (מן הצד), not directly opposite, so trampling is not relevant.

items.text: Measurement for side window and Rav Zevid's resolution
items.text_en: Measurement for side window and Rav Zevid's resolution
items.desc_en: Yeiva quotes Rav that the distance for a side window is the width of the window. The Gemara objects that one could still see, and Rav Zevid answers that the wall is plastered. Another objection from the Mishnah's four cubits is resolved by distinguishing one side versus two sides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the measurement for a side window, and Yeiva quotes Rav that it is the width of the window.
The Gemara objects that one could still see through the window despite the distance.
Rav Zevid answers that the case is where the wall is plastered, preventing a direct line of sight.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah requires a distance of four cubits, not just the window's width.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a window on one side (requiring only the window's width) and windows on two sides (requiring four cubits).

items.text: Gemara's question about the gutter and trampling
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the gutter and trampling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah requires distancing the wall from the gutter only for ladder access, not for trampling. It answers that the gutter is sloped, so trampling is not an issue as one can walk underneath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's ruling about distancing the wall from the gutter, arguing that the stated reason (ladder access) implies that trampling (דוושא) is not a concern.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a sloped gutter (מזחילה משופעת), under which one can walk, so trampling is not an issue.

items.text: Mishnah on ladder and dovecote, and the principle of gerama
items.text_en: Mishnah on ladder and dovecote, and the principle of gerama
items.desc_en: The Mishnah requires distancing a ladder from a dovecote to prevent the weasel from jumping. The Gemara questions if this aligns with Rabbi Yosi, who allows indirect damage. Rav Ashi says Rabbi Yosi admits in his own 'arrows' (direct damage). Rav Tovi bar Masna concludes that indirect damage (gerama) is prohibited in cases of damage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a ladder must be distanced four cubits from a dovecote to prevent the weasel from jumping, and a wall from a gutter to allow ladder placement.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Yosi, who permits indirect damage (גרמא) when each acts within his own property.
Rav Ashi resolves that even Rabbi Yosi would agree here because the weasel may be in the hole when the ladder is placed, making it direct damage (גירי דידיה).
The Gemara objects that this is still indirect damage (גרמא), not direct.
Rav Tovi bar Masna concludes that this teaches that indirect damage (גרמא) is prohibited in cases of damage.

items.text: Story of Rav Yosef's palm trees
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yosef's palm trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rav Yosef who had certain palm trees, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rav Yosef who had certain palm trees, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's opening story about gerama
items.text_en: Gemara's opening story about gerama
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef orders the removal of a dovecote because birds cause damage. Abaye objects that this is only indirect damage (gerama), but Rav Yosef cites Rav Tovi bar Masna that gerama is forbidden in cases of damage. The Gemara questions the validity of the chazakah (presumption) and resolves it with Rav Nachman's principle that there is no chazakah for damages, and Rav Mari and Rav Zevid's distinction regarding a chimney or latrine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes a situation where workers sat under a dovecote, crows ate blood, climbed onto date palms, and damaged dates.
Rav Yosef orders the removal of the dovecote to prevent damage.
Abaye objects that the damage is only indirect (גרמא) and therefore not actionable.
Rav Yosef cites Rav Tovi bar Masna that indirect damage (גרמא) is forbidden in cases of damage.
The Gemara questions the validity of the chazakah (presumption) that the dovecote owners had established.
The Gemara answers with Rav Nachman's principle that there is no chazakah for damages.
The Gemara objects that Rav Nachman's statement was limited to a chimney or latrine, not general damages.
Rav Yosef resolves that for him, the dovecote is like a chimney or latrine because he is sensitive.

items.text: Mishnah: Distancing a dovecote
items.text_en: Mishnah: Distancing a dovecote
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a dovecote must be distanced fifty cubits from a city, and one may only build a dovecote in his own property if he has fifty cubits in every direction. Rabbi Yehuda requires a field of four kor. If one purchased it, even a beit rova is in his presumptive ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a dovecote must be distanced fifty cubits from a city, and one may only build a dovecote on his own property if he has fifty cubits in every direction; Rabbi Yehuda requires a field of four kor, but if one purchased even a beit rova, it remains in his presumptive ownership.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and resolution regarding distance
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and resolution regarding distance
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah requires only fifty cubits, citing a baraita that requires thirty ris for nets. Abaye explains that pigeons fly far but fill their crops within fifty cubits. The Gemara then questions the thirty ris limit, citing another baraita that in a settled area even one hundred mil is forbidden. Rav Yosef and Rava offer different resolutions: Rav Yosef says it refers to a vineyard settlement, Rava says it refers to a dovecote settlement. The Gemara then addresses why the owner's own dovecote is not a problem, offering three possibilities: it is his own, a gentile's, or ownerless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah requires only fifty cubits, citing a baraita that requires thirty ris from settlement for nets.
Abaye explains that pigeons fly far but fill their crops within fifty cubits, resolving the contradiction.
The Gemara questions the thirty ris limit, citing a baraita that in a settled area even one hundred mil is forbidden.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by saying the baraita refers to a vineyard settlement.
Rava offers an alternative resolution, saying the baraita refers to a dovecote settlement.
The Gemara objects that the owner's own dovecote should also be a problem.
The Gemara resolves the objection by offering three possibilities: the dovecote is his own, a gentile's, or ownerless.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and the principle of claiming for a purchaser and heir
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and the principle of claiming for a purchaser and heir
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa or Rav Zevid derives from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that we make claims for a purchaser and an heir. The Gemara notes that an heir is already known from a Mishnah, so the novelty is for a purchaser. It then explains why both cases are necessary: in the case of a public domain one might think the owner is encroaching or the public waived, but here with an individual one might think he waived; conversely, with an individual one might think he was appeased, but with the public one might think no one can appease or waive.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa or Rav Zevid derives from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that we make claims for a purchaser and an heir.
The Gemara objects that the case of an heir is already known from a Mishnah, so the novelty is only for a purchaser.
The Gemara further objects that even the case of a purchaser is already taught in a Mishnah about a courtyard with ledges.

The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: in the public domain one might think the owner is encroaching or the public waived, but here with an individual one might think he waived; conversely, with an individual one might think he was appeased, but with the public one might think no one can appease or waive.

items.text: Challenge to the Mishnah's 'in his presumptive ownership'
items.text_en: Challenge to the Mishnah's 'in his presumptive ownership'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that the purchased dovecote is in his presumptive ownership, citing Rav Nachman's principle that there is no chazakah for damages. It then cites Rav Mari and Rav Zevid's distinction regarding a chimney or latrine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's ruling that the purchased dovecote is in his presumptive ownership (חזקה), citing Rav Nachman's principle that there is no presumptive ownership (חזקה) for damages.

sub.text: Rav Mari and Rav Zevid's distinction
sub.text_en: Rav Mari and Rav Zevid's distinction
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari and Rav Zevid resolve the challenge by limiting Rav Nachman's principle to cases of a chimney (קוטרא) or a latrine (בית הכסא), implying that a dovecote is not classified as a direct damage.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a fledgling found within fifty cubits of a dovecote belongs to the dovecote owner; beyond fifty cubits, to the finder. If between two dovecotes, it belongs to the nearer one; if equidistant, they divide it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a fledgling found within fifty cubits of a dovecote belongs to the dovecote owner; beyond fifty cubits, to the finder; if between two dovecotes, to the nearer one; if equidistant, they divide it.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's principle: majority overrides proximity
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's principle: majority overrides proximity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that even though both majority and proximity are Torah principles, majority takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that even though both majority (רוב) and proximity (קרוב) are Torah principles, majority takes precedence.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection from the Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection from the Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges Rabbi Chanina from the verse about the heifer whose neck is broken, which follows the nearest city even if another city has a larger population. The Gemara answers that the verse speaks when there is no other city, and the majority of the world is not considered because the city is situated among mountains.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects to Rabbi Chanina's principle that majority overrides proximity, citing the verse about the heifer whose neck is broken (עגלה ערופה) which follows the nearest city even when another city has a larger population.
The Gemara answers that the verse speaks when there is no other city, so proximity alone applies.
The Gemara objects: even if no other city is nearby, why not follow the majority of the world's population to determine the city of origin?
The Gemara answers that the city is situated among mountains, so the majority of the world is irrelevant because the body could not have come from elsewhere.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chanina from the Mishnah itself: within fifty cubits, the fledgling belongs to the dovecote owner even if there is a larger dovecote elsewhere. The answer is that there is no other dovecote. The Gemara then asks about the case beyond fifty cubits, and resolves that the fledgling is hopping, and a hopping bird does not go beyond fifty cubits, as stated by Rav Ukva bar Chama.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chanina from the Mishnah: within fifty cubits the fledgling belongs to the dovecote owner even if there is a larger dovecote elsewhere.
The Gemara answers that there is no other dovecote.
The Gemara asks about the case beyond fifty cubits: if there is no other dovecote, the fledgling must have fallen from that one.
The Gemara resolves that the fledgling is hopping, and a hopping bird does not go beyond fifty cubits, as stated by Rav Ukva bar Chama.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question and expulsion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question and expulsion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a fledgling with one foot within fifty cubits and one foot outside. For this question, he was expelled from the study hall.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a fledgling with one foot within fifty cubits and one foot outside, and for this question he was expelled from the study hall.

items.text: Challenge from the case of two dovecotes
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of two dovecotes
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chanina from the Mishnah's case of two dovecotes: the fledgling goes to the nearer one even if one is larger. The answer is that both are equal in size. The Gemara then asks why not follow the majority of the world, and the answer is that the case is where both dovecotes are equal and there is no other dovecote.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chanina from the Mishnah's case of two dovecotes: the fledgling goes to the nearer one even if one is larger.
The answer is that both dovecotes are equal in size.
The Gemara then asks why not follow the majority of the world.
The answer is that the case is where both dovecotes are equal and there is no other dovecote.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the vineyard path
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the vineyard path
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if a bird came from afar, it would not be able to find its nest because it would wander off; only a bird from nearby would return.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a bird from afar would not return to its nest because it would wander off, while a nearby bird would.

items.text: Abaye's proof and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's proof and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a proof from a mishna about blood found in a hallway, which is deemed impure due to its source, even though there is an upper room nearby. Rava objects that Abaye is conflating a majority with a common occurrence, and no one holds that a common occurrence is like a majority.

sub.desc_en: Abaye brings a proof from a mishna about blood found in a hallway, which is deemed impure due to its source, even though there is an upper room nearby.
Rava objects that Abaye is conflating a majority with a common occurrence, and no one holds that a common occurrence is like a majority.

items.text: Rava's deduction from Rabbi Ḥiyya's baraita
items.text_en: Rava's deduction from Rabbi Ḥiyya's baraita
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita of Rabbi Ḥiyya about blood found in a hallway, from which he derives three principles: follow the majority over the proximate, majority is a Torah law, and Rabbi Zeira's statement applies even when the city gates are locked. He illustrates with the case of a woman who is like locked gates, yet we follow the majority.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita of Rabbi Ḥiyya stating that blood found in a hallway renders one liable for entering the Temple and requires burning תרומה (priestly portion).
Rava derives three principles from the baraita: follow the majority over the proximate, majority is a Torah law, and Rabbi Zeira's statement applies even when city gates are locked.
Rabbi Zeira states that the principle applies even when the city gates are locked.
Rava illustrates with a woman who is like locked gates, yet we follow the majority.

items.text: Rava's retraction
items.text_en: Rava's retraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava previously said there is no one who holds the principle of majority and common occurrence, so he must have retracted that view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava previously stated there is no one who holds the principle of majority and common occurrence, so he must have retracted that view.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel about a barrel in a river
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel about a barrel in a river
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue about a barrel found floating in a river: Rav permits it if opposite a Jewish-majority city, but Shmuel forbids it even then, suspecting it came from a nearby gentile. The Gemara suggests they disagree about Rabbi Ḥanina's principle, but concludes they both accept it; they differ on whether the barrel would have been damaged if it came from the nearby city.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rav permits a barrel found floating in a river if opposite a Jewish-majority city, while Shmuel forbids it even then, suspecting it came from a nearby gentile city.
The Gemara suggests that Rav and Shmuel disagree about Rabbi Ḥanina's principle regarding following the majority.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion and concludes that both accept Rabbi Ḥanina's principle; they differ on whether the barrel would have been damaged if it came from the nearby city.

items.text: Case of a jug of wine in an orlah orchard
items.text_en: Case of a jug of wine in an orlah orchard
items.desc_en: Ravina permitted a jug of wine found in an orchard of orlah, and the Gemara questions whether he follows Rabbi Ḥanina's principle. It distinguishes: if stolen, the thief would not hide it there; but this applies only to wine, not to grapes, which would be hidden.

sub.desc_en: Ravina permitted a jug of wine found in an orchard of orlah.
The Gemara asks whether Ravina's ruling follows Rabbi Ḥanina's principle that proximity is overridden by majority.
The Gemara distinguishes: the case is different because a thief would not hide a stolen jug in the orchard, but this reasoning applies only to wine, not to grapes, which would be hidden.

items.text: Case of wine skins found among gentiles
items.text_en: Case of wine skins found among gentiles
items.desc_en: Rava permitted wine skins found among gentile porters, and the Gemara questions whether he rejects Rabbi Ḥanina's principle. The segment is cut off, but the answer likely involves a majority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where wine skins were found among gentile porters and Rava permitted them.
The Gemara questions whether Rava's ruling contradicts Rabbi Ḥanina's principle.
The Gemara distinguishes the case because a majority (רוב) of the porters are gentiles, so the wine is permitted by the principle of following the majority.

items.text: Clarification on the previous daf's ruling about found animals
items.text_en: Clarification on the previous daf's ruling about found animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the previous ruling about found animals applies to large animals, but small ones might have fallen from travelers. If large animals are found with them, they were likely placed there by shepherds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the previous ruling about found animals applies to large animals, but small ones might have fallen from travelers; if large animals are found with them, they were likely placed there by shepherds.

items.text: Mishnah: Distance of trees from the city
items.text_en: Mishnah: Distance of trees from the city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a tree must be distanced 25 amot from the city, and for a carob or sycamore, 50 amot. Abba Shaul says any barren tree requires 50 amot. If the city preceded the tree, it is cut down without compensation; if the tree preceded, it is cut down with compensation; in case of doubt, it is cut down without compensation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a tree must be distanced 25 amot from the city, with carob and sycamore requiring 50 amot; Abba Shaul says any barren tree requires 50 amot; if the city preceded the tree, the tree is cut down without compensation; if the tree preceded, compensation is given; in case of doubt, it is cut down without compensation.

items.text: Gemara's question on the reason for the distance
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the reason for the distance
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why trees must be distanced from the city. Ulla says it is for the city's beauty. The Gemara objects that one cannot turn a field into a city's open space (migrash) or vice versa. The Gemara resolves that this applies according to Rabbi Elazar, who permits such conversion, but here it is prohibited due to city aesthetics. Even for the Rabbis who prohibit conversion, it applies to crops but not trees; here, trees are also prohibited for aesthetics.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why trees must be distanced from the city, and Ulla answers that it is for the city's beauty.
The Gemara objects that one cannot turn a field into a city's open space (מגרש) or vice versa, which would seem to contradict the allowance of planting trees near the city.
The Gemara resolves that this applies according to Rabbi Elazar, who permits converting a field into a city's open space, but here it is prohibited due to city aesthetics.
Even for the Rabbis who prohibit conversion, the prohibition applies to crops but not trees; here, trees are also prohibited for aesthetics.

items.text: Proof that trees differ from crops
items.text_en: Proof that trees differ from crops
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita to prove that trees are treated differently from crops regarding the laws of a courtyard (karpaf). If most of a karpaf larger than two beit se'ah is sown, it is considered a garden and prohibited for dwelling; if most is planted with trees, it is considered a courtyard and permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita to prove the distinction between grains and trees: a karpaf (enclosed area) larger than two beit se'ah that was mostly sown is treated as a garden and forbidden, but if mostly planted with trees it is treated as a courtyard and permitted.
The Gemara asks for the source that distinguishes between crops and trees regarding the laws of a karpaf.
The Gemara cites a baraita that rules: if most of a karpaf larger than two beit se'ah is sown, it is prohibited as a garden; if most is planted with trees, it is permitted as a courtyard.

items.text: Discussion on compensation when cutting trees
items.text_en: Discussion on compensation when cutting trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the difference between the Mishnah here and the case of a pit (bor), where compensation is given. Rav Kahana says 'a pot of partners is neither hot nor cold.' The Gemara initially objects that the difference might be between public and private damage. It then reinterprets Rav Kahana's statement as referring to the case where the tree preceded: one might demand payment before cutting, but Rav Kahana says no. For a doubt, the Gemara explains that since the tree is definitely to be cut, we tell the owner to bring proof and take compensation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah rules differently regarding compensation for cutting trees near a city compared to the case of a pit (בור).
Rav Kahana responds with a proverb: 'a pot of partners is neither hot nor cold,' implying the question is unresolved.
The Gemara objects that the difference might simply be between damage to the public (רבים) and damage to an individual (יחיד).
The Gemara reinterprets Rav Kahana's statement as referring to the case where the tree preceded: one might demand payment before cutting, but Rav Kahana says no.
The Gemara asks why in a case of doubt the tree is cut without compensation, unlike the pit where one does not cut.
The Gemara explains that since the tree is definitely to be cut, we tell the owner to bring proof and take compensation.

items.text: Mishnah: Distance of a permanent threshing floor from the city
items.text_en: Mishnah: Distance of a permanent threshing floor from the city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a permanent threshing floor must be distanced 50 amot from the city. A person may not establish a permanent threshing floor within his own property unless he has 50 amot on each side. He must distance it from his neighbor's plantings and plowed field to prevent damage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a permanent threshing floor must be distanced 50 amot from the city; one may not establish a permanent threshing floor on his own property unless he has 50 amot on each side; and one must distance it from a neighbor's plantings and plowed field to prevent damage.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the threshing floor Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the threshing floor Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first clause (distance from city) differs from the latter clause (distance from neighbor's property). Abaye says the latter clause refers to a non-permanent threshing floor. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina defines a non-permanent one as where winnowing is not done with a shovel. Rav Ashi says the Mishnah explains the reason: the distance is to prevent damage. A baraita supports Rav Ashi by listing distances from melons, cucumbers, plantings, and plowed fields. The Gemara questions why plowed fields are included, and Rabbi Abba bar Zavda explains it is because of the chaff that damages the plowed soil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first clause (distance from city) differs from the latter clause (distance from neighbor's property).
Abaye answers that the latter clause refers to a non-permanent threshing floor.
The Gemara asks for a definition of a non-permanent threshing floor.
Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina defines a non-permanent threshing floor as one where winnowing is not done with a shovel.
Rav Ashi says the Mishnah explains the reason: the distance is to prevent damage.
A baraita supports Rav Ashi by listing distances from melons, cucumbers, plantings, and plowed fields.
The Gemara objects that the baraita supports Rav Ashi but is difficult for Abaye.
The Gemara questions why plowed fields are included in the baraita's list.
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda explains it is because of the chaff that damages the plowed soil.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that carcasses, graves, and tanneries must be distanced fifty amot from the city. A tannery may only be placed to the east of the city; Rabbi Akiva permits any direction except the west, requiring a fifty-amah distance. Additional restrictions are given for soaking flax near vegetables, leeks near onions, and mustard near bees, with Rabbi Yosei permitting mustard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that carcasses, graves, and tanneries must be distanced fifty amot from the city.
The Mishnah states that a tannery may only be placed to the east of the city.
Rabbi Akiva permits a tannery in any direction except the west, requiring a fifty-amah distance.
The Mishnah lists additional restrictions: distancing flax soaking from vegetables, leeks from onions, and mustard from bees.
Rabbi Yosei permits mustard near bees.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's intent
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Akiva mean that one may build a tannery in any direction as long as he distances it fifty amot, except for the west where he must also distance it fifty amot? Or does he mean that one may build in any direction with a fifty-amah distance, except for the west where he may not build at all? A baraita is cited to resolve the question: Rabbi Akiva explicitly says that in the west one may not build at all because it is 'frequent' (תְּדִירָא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Akiva mean one may build a tannery in any direction with a fifty-amah distance except the west where he must also distance fifty amah, or except the west where he may not build at all?
A baraita is cited to resolve the question: Rabbi Akiva explicitly says that in the west one may not build at all because it is 'frequent' (תְּדִירָא).

items.text: Rava's question on 'frequent' and the winds
items.text_en: Rava's question on 'frequent' and the winds
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: what does 'frequent' (תְּדִירָא) mean? If it means frequent in winds, that is problematic because Rav Chanan bar Abba said in the name of Rav that all four winds blow daily, with the north wind accompanying all of them, and the south wind is the harshest, restrained only by the 'ben netz' bird. This suggests the west wind is not uniquely frequent.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: what does 'frequent' (תְּדִירָא) mean in this context?

Rava objects: if 'frequent' refers to winds, Rav Chanan bar Abba citing Rav stated that all four winds blow daily, with the north wind accompanying all, and the south wind is the harshest, so the west wind is not uniquely frequent.

items.text: Answer: 'frequent' refers to the Shekhinah
items.text_en: Answer: 'frequent' refers to the Shekhinah
items.desc_en: Rava answers that 'frequent' refers to the frequent presence of the Shekhinah (Divine Presence) in the west. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says we should thank our ancestors for revealing the place of prayer, as it is written: 'And the host of heaven bows down to You.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers: 'frequent' refers to the frequent presence of the Divine Presence (שכינה) in the west, as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said we should thank our ancestors for revealing the place of prayer.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says we should thank our ancestors for revealing the place of prayer, citing the verse 'And the host of heaven bows down to You' (וּצְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם לְךָ מִשְׁתַּחֲוִים).

items.text: Objection by Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.text_en: Objection by Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects: perhaps the verse describes a servant who takes a gift from his master and then steps backward to bow, implying the Shekhinah is not necessarily in the west. The objection remains unresolved (קַשְׁיָא).

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects: perhaps the prayer direction is like a slave who takes a gift from his master and then steps backward to bow, not indicating the Divine Presence's location.

items.text: Support for Shekhinah in all places
items.text_en: Support for Shekhinah in all places
items.desc_en: Three amoraim argue that the Shekhinah is everywhere. Rabbi Oshaya derives from a verse that God's messengers return from where they are sent, showing the Shekhinah is omnipresent. Rabbi Yishmael's school learns from a verse about angels meeting each other. Rav Sheshet instructs his attendant to face any direction except east, not because the Shekhinah is absent there, but because heretics (minim) are there.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya asserts that the Shekhinah is everywhere, deriving it from a verse about God's messengers returning from where they are sent.
Rabbi Yishmael's school learns from a verse about angels meeting each other that the Shekhinah is everywhere.
Rav Sheshet instructs his attendant to face any direction except east, not because the Shekhinah is absent there, but because heretics (מִינֵי) are there.

items.text: Shekhinah in the west and the four winds
items.text_en: Shekhinah in the west and the four winds
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that the Shekhinah is in the west, interpreting 'Oryah' as 'air of God'. Rav Yehudah expounds a verse to identify each wind: the west wind comes from the 'back of the world', the north wind 'distills gold', the east wind 'storms the world like a goat', and the south wind 'brings dew and grows grass'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that the Shekhinah is in the west, interpreting 'Oryah' as 'air of God'.
Rav Yehudah expounds a verse to identify the west wind as coming from the 'back of the world'.
Rav Yehudah identifies the north wind as the one that 'distills gold', citing a supporting verse.
Rav Yehudah identifies the east wind as storming the world like a goat and the south wind as bringing dew and growing grass.

items.text: Beginning of Rabbi Eliezer's statement on the world
items.text_en: Beginning of Rabbi Eliezer's statement on the world
items.desc_en: A baraita begins with Rabbi Eliezer's opinion about the world, but the segment is cut off mid-sentence, leaving the argument incomplete.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer begins a statement about the world.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on the nature of the world and the wind
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on the nature of the world and the wind
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer compares the world to a porch, with the north wind not circulating, while Rabbi Yehoshua compares it to a tent, with the north wind circulating. Rabbi Yehoshua supports his view with a verse from Ecclesiastes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that the world is like a porch (אכסדרה), with the north wind not circulating, and describes the sun's path.
Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the world is like a tent (קובה), with the north wind circulating, and the sun goes behind the dome.
Rabbi Yehoshua cites Ecclesiastes 1:6 to support his view, interpreting the verse as describing the sun's daily and nightly circuits.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's identification of the four winds from verses
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's identification of the four winds from verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer cites verses from Job to identify the south, north, west, and east winds.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer cites four verses from Job to identify the south, north, west, and east winds.

items.text: Reconciliation of a contradiction about the south wind
items.text_en: Reconciliation of a contradiction about the south wind
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the south wind is said to bring dew and grow herbs, but also brings storms. It resolves that one refers to gentle rain and the other to heavy downpour.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Master previously said the south wind brings dew and grows herbs, but here it is associated with storms.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one refers to gentle rain and the other to a heavy downpour.

items.text: Rav Chisda on the north wind refining gold
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on the north wind refining gold
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the verse 'From the north comes gold' refers to the north wind that refines gold, citing another verse as support.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the verse 'From the north comes gold' refers to the north wind that refines gold, citing another verse as support.

items.text: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda on the cessation of beneficial winds and rains after the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda on the cessation of beneficial winds and rains after the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa reports that since the Temple's destruction, the south wind has not brought beneficial rain, and rains no longer come from the 'good storehouse', as per the verse in Deuteronomy.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa reports in the name of Rav Chisda that since the Temple's destruction, the south wind has not brought beneficial rain, citing verses from Isaiah and Psalms.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa adds that since the Temple's destruction, rains no longer come from the 'good storehouse' (אוצר טוב), as per Deuteronomy 28:12, conditional on Israel's presence on their land.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on the direction for wisdom and wealth, and the Shekhinah's location
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on the direction for wisdom and wealth, and the Shekhinah's location
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak advises facing south for wisdom and north for wealth, with a mnemonic from the Temple. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says one should always face south, as wisdom leads to wealth, but also states the Shekhinah is in the west. The Gemara reconciles this by saying one should face slightly south. Rabbi Chanina advises Rabbi Ashi, who sits in the north of Israel, to face south.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that one who wants wisdom should face south, and one who wants wealth should face north, with a mnemonic from the Temple arrangement.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi argues that one should always face south, because wisdom leads to wealth, citing the verse that the Torah's right hand holds length of days and its left hand wealth and honor.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi himself said the Shekhinah (Divine Presence) is in the west, contradicting his advice to face south.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi meant one should face slightly south (to the side), not directly south, thus accommodating both the Shekhinah's location in the west and the benefit of wisdom from the south.
Rabbi Chanina instructs Rabbi Ashi, who sits in the north of Eretz Yisrael, to face south, providing practical application of the principle.
The Gemara proves that Babylonia is north of Eretz Yisrael by citing the verse 'From the north evil will open upon all the inhabitants of the land,' referring to Babylonia.

items.text: Tosefta on Rabbi Yosei permitting mustard near bees
items.text_en: Tosefta on Rabbi Yosei permitting mustard near bees
items.desc_en: A Tosefta states that Rabbi Yosei permits planting mustard near bees, as the beekeeper can be told to move his bees instead, since they eat the mustard pods.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited stating that Rabbi Yosei permits planting mustard near bees, because the beekeeper can be told to move his bees since they eat the mustard pods.

items.text: Mishnah on distancing a tree from a pit
items.text_en: Mishnah on distancing a tree from a pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a tree must be distanced 25 amot from a pit, and 50 for a carob or sycamore. If the pit preceded the tree, the tree is cut down and compensation given; if the tree preceded, it is not cut. In case of doubt, it is not cut. Rabbi Yosei says even if the pit preceded, it is not cut, as each acts within their own property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule: one must distance a tree 25 amot from a pit, and 50 for a carob or sycamore.
The Mishnah clarifies that the distance applies whether the tree is above or to the side of the pit.
The Mishnah rules: if the pit preceded the tree, the tree is cut down with compensation; if the tree preceded, it is not cut; in case of doubt, it is not cut.
Rabbi Yosei states that even if the pit preceded the tree, it is not cut, because each acts within their own property.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling for a pit above and tree below
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling for a pit above and tree below
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah applies whether the pit is below and tree above (roots damage the pit) or the pit is above and tree below, because roots harden the ground and crack the pit's floor, as taught by Rabbi Chaggai in the name of Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that the Mishnah's ruling applies whether the pit is below and the tree above, or the pit is above and the tree below.
The Gemara questions why the ruling applies when the pit is above and the tree below, since roots would not directly reach the pit.

sub.text: Rabbi Chaggai in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chaggai in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chaggai explains in the name of Rabbi Yosei that roots harden the ground and crack the pit's floor, causing damage even when the pit is above.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on the halakha like Rabbi Yosei, and the case of Papi Yona'ah
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on the halakha like Rabbi Yosei, and the case of Papi Yona'ah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Ashi notes that in the school of Rav Kahana they said Rabbi Yosei admits in the case of his own 'arrows' (i.e., when his property causes direct damage). The Gemara then recounts a case of Papi Yona'ah, who built a mansion near olive pressers whose vibrations damaged it, and Rav Ashi applied the same principle.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yosei's position that even if the pit preceded the tree, the tree owner need not cut it down, since each acts within his own property.
Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yosei's lenient position.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's report from the school of Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's report from the school of Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi notes that in the school of Rav Kahana they said Rabbi Yosei admits in the case of his own 'arrows' (direct damage from his property).

The Gemara recounts the case of Papi Yona'ah, who built a mansion near olive pressers whose vibrations damaged it, and Rav Ashi applied the same principle that Rabbi Yosei admits in cases of direct damage.
The Gemara asks: And how much distance must be maintained in such a case?

items.text: Gemara's discussion of indirect damage from flax processing
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion of indirect damage from flax processing
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where flax chaff from the house of Bar Marion flew and injured people. Ravina distinguishes between damage caused directly by one's force (giri didei) and damage carried by wind (zika). Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges this, comparing it to a winnower aided by wind, and Marimar agrees with the comparison. Ravina then distinguishes from a spark from a hammer, where the owner benefits from the spark's travel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case from the house of Bar Marion where flax chaff flew and injured people.
Ravina rules that Rabbi Yosei's principle of liability for direct force (גירי דיליה) does not apply here because the chaff was carried by wind (זיקא), not by the owner's direct force.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects by comparing the case to a winnower aided by wind, where the winnower is liable.
Marimar agrees with Mar bar Rav Ashi, stating that this case is indeed like a winnower aided by wind.
The Gemara asks Ravina why this case differs from a spark from a hammer, where the owner is liable for damage.
Ravina distinguishes that in the spark case the owner benefits from the spark's travel, but here the flax processor does not benefit from the chaff's travel.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of planting trees near a neighbor's field
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of planting trees near a neighbor's field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not plant a tree within four cubits of a neighbor's field, whether vines or any other tree. If there is a fence between them, each may plant up to the fence. If roots extend into the neighbor's field, the neighbor may dig down three handbreadths to remove them. If digging a pit, cistern, or cave, one may cut roots as needed, and the wood belongs to the root owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of planting trees at a distance of four cubits from a neighbor's field, the rule for a fence between them, and the rights to cut roots extending into the neighbor's property.

items.text: Gemara: Distance requirement for planting in Babylonia vs. Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Gemara: Distance requirement for planting in Babylonia vs. Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the four cubits are for vineyard work. Shmuel says this applies only in Eretz Yisrael; in Babylonia, the requirement is two cubits. A baraita supports Shmuel, stating two cubits. Another version presents a contradiction between the Mishnah (four cubits) and the baraita (two cubits), resolved by Shmuel's distinction.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explains that the four cubits distance mentioned in the Mishnah is for vineyard work.
Shmuel rules that the four-cubit distance applies only in Eretz Yisrael, but in Babylonia the requirement is two cubits.
A baraita supports Shmuel, stating that the required distance is two cubits.
The Gemara questions the contradiction: the Mishnah requires four cubits, not two.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita must align with Shmuel's distinction, concluding that the two-cubit rule applies in Babylonia.
An alternative version explicitly raises the contradiction between the Mishnah (four cubits) and the baraita (two cubits).
Shmuel resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Babylonia (two cubits) and Eretz Yisrael (four cubits).

items.text: Case of Rava bar Rav Chanan's date palms near Rav Yosef's vineyard
items.text_en: Case of Rava bar Rav Chanan's date palms near Rav Yosef's vineyard
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan had date palms on the border of Rav Yosef's vineyard. Birds would sit in the palms and damage the vineyard. Rav Yosef demanded he cut them down, but Rava argued he had distanced them properly. Rav Yosef replied that the distance requirement is greater for trees near vines.
