Rava cited Rav's ruling that a fruit-bearing tree may not be cut down, and Rabbi Chanina's statement about the fate of one who cuts a fig tree prematurely, leaving the decision to Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the case: Rava bar Rav Chanan had date palms on the border of Rav Yosef's vineyard, and birds would sit in the palms and damage the vineyard.
Rav Yosef demands that Rava bar Rav Chanan cut down the date palms.
Rava bar Rav Chanan objects that he has already distanced the palms properly according to the Mishnah's requirement.
Rav Yosef responds that the Mishnah's distance applies to trees near trees, but trees near vines require greater distance.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Chanan's objection from the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's objection from the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan objects by citing the Mishnah which states that the same distance applies to both vines and all trees.
Rav Yosef clarifies that the Mishnah's rule applies to tree near tree or vine near vine, but tree near vine requires greater distance.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Chanan's final statement
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's final statement
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan refuses to cut the palms himself, citing Rav's ruling that a fruit-bearing tree may not be cut and Rabbi Chanina's statement about the fate of one who cuts a fig tree prematurely, and leaves the decision to Rav Yosef.

items.text: Case of Rav Papa's date palms and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's digging
items.text_en: Case of Rav Papa's date palms and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's digging
items.desc_en: Rav Papa found Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua digging and cutting roots from Rav Papa's date palms. Rav Huna cited the Mishnah allowing digging three handbreadths to remove roots. Rav Papa objected that he was digging deeper. Rav Huna replied he was digging pits and caves, which permits cutting roots entirely, with the wood belonging to the root owner. Rav Papa admitted he could not refute him.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Rav Papa had date palms on the boundary of Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's field, and found Rav Huna digging and cutting their roots.
Rav Papa asks Rav Huna what he is doing.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua cites the Mishnah that permits digging three handbreadths deep to remove encroaching roots so as not to impede the plow.
Rav Papa objects that the Mishnah only permits three handbreadths, but Rav Huna is digging deeper.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's rejoinder
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's rejoinder
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua responds that he is digging pits, trenches, and caves, which according to the Mishnah permits cutting roots entirely, with the wood belonging to the root owner.
The narrator concludes that Rav Papa admitted he could not refute Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's argument.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling and the Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling and the Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara recalls that Rav Yehuda said a boundary that many have used is forbidden to damage. After the discussion, the Gemara wonders why it didn't answer with the distinction between within and beyond sixteen cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recalls that Rav Yehuda ruled that a boundary (מצר) that many have used is forbidden to damage.
After leaving, the Gemara wonders why it did not answer with the distinction between within and beyond sixteen cubits.

items.text: Ya'akov the Dyer's question to Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Ya'akov the Dyer's question to Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: Ya'akov the Dyer asks Rav Chisda: to whom do the cut wood belong when digging a pit?

sub.desc_en: Ya'akov the Dyer asks Rav Chisda: to whom do the cut wood belong when digging a pit?

items.text: Rav Chisda's answer from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's answer from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a baraita about roots of a private tree in consecrated ground: one may not benefit but is not liable for misuse, implying roots follow the tree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a baraita about roots of a private tree in consecrated ground: one may not benefit but is not liable for misuse, implying roots follow the tree.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita: if roots follow the tree, why no misuse? If they follow the ground, why no misuse? It resolves that the baraita deals with later growths, where there is no misuse of consecrated growths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita: if roots follow the tree, why no misuse in the first case? If they follow the ground, why no misuse in the second case?
The Gemara raises the opposite possibility: if roots follow the tree, why no misuse in the second case?
The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with later growths, where there is no misuse of consecrated growths.

items.text: Ravina's resolution
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution
items.desc_en: Ravina says there is no difficulty: within sixteen cubits the roots follow the tree, beyond that they follow the ground.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between roots within sixteen cubits (which follow the tree) and beyond sixteen cubits (which follow the ground).

items.text: Ulla's ruling
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling
items.desc_en: Ulla rules that a tree within sixteen cubits of a boundary is a robber, and one may not bring first fruits from it.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules that a tree within sixteen cubits of a boundary is a robber, and one may not bring first fruits from it.

items.text: Source for Ulla's ruling
items.text_en: Source for Ulla's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for Ulla's ruling. It first considers a mishna about ten saplings, but the calculation does not match. Then it considers a mishna about three trees belonging to three people, which allows plowing the entire area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where does Ulla derive his ruling about a tree within sixteen cubits of the boundary?

sub.text: First answer (from mishna about ten saplings)
sub.text_en: First answer (from mishna about ten saplings)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers the mishna about ten saplings scattered within a בית סאה (a seah's area), but calculates that each sapling gets only 250 cubits, not the 256 cubits implied by Ulla's ruling, so this source is rejected.

sub.text: Second answer (from mishna about three trees)
sub.text_en: Second answer (from mishna about three trees)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara alternatively considers the mishna about three trees belonging to three people, which allows plowing the entire area, as a possible source for Ulla's ruling.

items.text: Refining the calculation for Ulla's tree
items.text_en: Refining the calculation for Ulla's tree
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Ulla's earlier calculation of 16⅔ amot per tree was imprecise, but objects that imprecision is only allowed leniently, not stringently. It resolves by explaining the calculation was for a circle, not a square, and the remaining half-amah is the imprecision, which is acceptable for a leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Ulla's calculation by noting that a בית סאה (a se'ah's area) is 2500 square amot, which would give each tree only 833⅓ amot, less than Ulla's 16⅔ amot per tree, concluding that Ulla was imprecise (לא דק).
The Gemara objects that imprecision (לא דק) is only allowed for leniencies (לקולא), not for stringencies (לחומרא), yet Ulla's imprecision would be stringent.
The Gemara answers that Ulla's calculation was for a circle (בעיגולא), not a square (בריבועא), so the area per tree is different.

The Gemara resolves that even after accounting for the circle-to-square ratio (a quarter less), a half-amah remains, which is the imprecision (לא דק) acceptable for a leniency (לקולא), not a stringency (לחומרא).

items.text: Proof from the law of one tree
items.text_en: Proof from the law of one tree
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who buys a tree with its land brings bikurim and recites the declaration. It asks whether this implies any amount of land suffices, but answers that it requires sixteen amot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who buys a tree with its land brings bikurim and recites the declaration.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita implies that any amount of land suffices.
The Gemara answers that the baraita requires sixteen amot of land, not any amount.

items.text: Proof from two trees vs. three trees
items.text_en: Proof from two trees vs. three trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita: one who buys two trees on another's land brings bikurim but does not recite, implying three trees require recitation. It asks if this means any amount of land, but answers that here too it is sixteen amot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who buys two trees on another's land brings bikurim but does not recite the declaration, implying that three trees would require recitation.
The Gemara infers that three trees require recitation and asks whether this implies any amount of land suffices.
The Gemara answers that here too the required land is sixteen amot, not any amount.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's opinion on minimal land
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's opinion on minimal land
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite Rabbi Akiva's statement that any amount of land obligates in pe'ah and bikurim and allows writing a prozbul, but the segment is cut off, leaving the argument incomplete.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Akiva's statement that any amount of land (קרקע כל שהוא) obligates in pe'ah (פאה) and bikurim (ביכורים) and allows writing a prozbul (פרוזבול), but the argument is cut off before completion.

items.text: Gemara's question about acquiring land with a tree
items.text_en: Gemara's question about acquiring land with a tree
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a tree can acquire land without אחריות, and resolves that it refers to wheat. It notes that the Mishnah's phrase 'כל שהוא' supports this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a tree can acquire land without אחריות (liability), and resolves that the Mishnah refers to wheat.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's phrase 'כל שהוא' (any amount) supports the interpretation that it refers to wheat.

items.text: Dispute about a tree partly in Israel and outside
items.text_en: Dispute about a tree partly in Israel and outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagree about a tree with roots in both Israel and outside: Rabbi says it is mixed, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says each part follows its own status. The Gemara explains they argue about ברירה, but agree that what grows outside is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a tree partly in Israel and outside, presenting Rabbi's position that it is mixed.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that each part of the tree follows its own status regarding tithes.
The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hinges on whether ברירה (retroactive designation) applies.
The Gemara concludes that all agree that what grows outside Israel is exempt from tithes.

items.text: Resolution of the dispute with a rock barrier
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute with a rock barrier
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case involves a rock barrier (צונמא) separating the roots. Rabbi holds that the roots re-intertwine, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the air space separates them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the scenario: a rock barrier (צונמא) separates the roots.
The Gemara asks: if there is a rock barrier, why does Rabbi hold that the roots re-intertwine?
The Gemara answers: because the roots re-intertwine above the rock barrier.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: Rabbi holds that the air space (אוירא) reconnects the roots, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that each root stands independently.

items.text: Question about the sixteen amah distance
items.text_en: Question about the sixteen amah distance
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies sixteen amah for a tree's roots, given another Mishnah requires twenty-five amah from a pit. Abaye explains that roots spread far but only damage up to sixteen amah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies only sixteen amot for tree roots, citing a Mishnah that requires twenty-five amot distance from a pit.
Abaye answers that roots extend far but only drain the soil's strength up to sixteen amot; beyond that they do not weaken the soil.

items.text: Dispute about a tree near the border
items.text_en: Dispute about a tree near the border
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan about a tree within sixteen amah of the border; Rabbi Yochanan says it is a robber and its fruits cannot be brought as firstfruits. Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan later ruled that one brings and recites, because Joshua allocated the land with that condition.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan about a tree planted within sixteen amot of a neighbor's border, and Rabbi Yochanan rules it is a robber and one may not bring first fruits from it.
Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan rules both a tree near the border and an overhanging tree may bring first fruits and recite the declaration, because Joshua stipulated this when dividing the land.

sub.text: Ravin's report of Rabbi Yochanan's revised ruling
sub.text_en: Ravin's report of Rabbi Yochanan's revised ruling
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan later ruled that one brings and recites, because Joshua allocated the land with that condition.

items.text: Mishnah: Cutting a tree that overhangs a neighbor's field
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cutting a tree that overhangs a neighbor's field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a tree overhanging a neighbor's field must be cut back to the plow handle's length, with special rules for carob and sycamore trees, irrigated fields, and Abba Shaul's opinion that all barren trees are cut to the plumb line.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that for a tree overhanging a neighbor's field, one cuts branches up to the height of a plow; for a carob or sycamore, up to a plumb line; for an irrigated field, the entire tree is cut to the plumb line; Abba Shaul says any barren tree is cut to the plumb line.

items.text: Gemara: Abba Shaul's position clarified
items.text_en: Gemara: Abba Shaul's position clarified
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Abba Shaul's opinion applies to the first clause (irrigated fields) or the last clause (all trees). A baraita shows he refers to irrigated fields, and Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's wording that he refers to the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Abba Shaul's statement refers to the first clause (irrigated field) or the last clause (barren tree).
The Gemara asks whether Abba Shaul's statement in the Mishnah refers to the first clause (irrigated fields) or the last clause (all trees).
The Gemara brings a baraita where Abba Shaul explicitly says 'for an irrigated field, the entire tree is cut to the plumb line because shade harms it,' proving he refers to the first clause.
A baraita is cited showing that Abba Shaul explicitly applies his ruling to irrigated fields (בית השלחין), indicating he refers to the first clause.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that Abba Shaul refers to the first clause (irrigated fields).
Rav Ashi supports this from the Mishnah's wording 'כל אילן סרק' (any barren tree), which would be redundant if Abba Shaul referred to the last clause.

items.text: Mishnah: Tree overhanging public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Tree overhanging public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a tree overhanging public domain must be cut to allow a camel with its rider to pass. Rabbi Yehuda requires space for a camel loaded with flax, and Rabbi Shimon requires cutting to the plumb line due to impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that for a tree overhanging public domain, one cuts enough for a camel with its rider to pass; Rabbi Yehuda says a camel loaded with flax or vine branches; Rabbi Shimon says the entire tree to the plumb line due to impurity.
The Mishnah opens with the ruling that a tree overhanging the public domain must be cut to allow a camel with its rider to pass.
Rabbi Yehuda requires space for a camel loaded with flax or bundles of branches.
Rabbi Shimon requires cutting the entire tree to the plumb line due to טומאה (ritual impurity) concerns.

items.text: Gemara: Who holds that damages follow current state?
items.text_en: Gemara: Who holds that damages follow current state?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that damages are assessed by the current state. Reish Lakish says it is the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer, who allows a pit under public domain if a wagon can pass. Rabbi Yochanan says even the Rabbis agree here because the owner cuts gradually.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who follows current assessment in damages.
Reish Lakish answers that it is taught in a dispute and follows Rabbi Eliezer, who permits making pits under public domain as long as a loaded wagon can pass.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that even the Rabbis agree here, because in the pit case the damage may go unnoticed, but here the owner cuts branches gradually and is aware.

items.text: Question about Rabbi Yehuda's measurement
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi Yehuda's measurement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's measurement is larger or smaller than the Rabbis'. It concludes that the Rabbis' measurement is larger, and Rabbi Yehuda's is smaller, as a camel can bend and pass under.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda's measure (loaded camel) is larger or smaller than the Rabbis' measure (camel with rider).
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis' measure is obviously larger, since Rabbi Yehuda's measure could be accommodated by a camel bending under the branches.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a Tanna explains Rabbi Shimon's reason is due to impurity from a tent. It clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'because of impurity' might have been misunderstood as a raven bringing impurity, but the Tanna teaches it is about a tent of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a baraita specifies 'because of אוהל הטומאה (tent of impurity)' when the Mishnah already says 'because of הטומאה (impurity).'

The Gemara answers that without the baraita, one might think the concern is a raven bringing impurity, requiring only a minimal gap; the baraita teaches it is about אוהל הטומאה (tent impurity), requiring full clearance.

The Gemara explains that without the Tanna, one might have thought the impurity comes from a raven bringing impurity there, requiring only a minimal barrier; the Tanna teaches it is about the laws of a tent of impurity (אוהל הטומאה).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Items requiring three-year chazakah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Items requiring three-year chazakah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists properties (houses, pits, caves, dovecotes, bathhouses, olive-presses, irrigated fields, slaves, and anything that produces fruit continuously) whose chazakah is three years from day to day. For a rain-fed field, the chazakah is three years but not from day to day. Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva debate the calculation for rain-fed fields, and Rabbi Yishmael distinguishes between a white field (grain) and a tree field.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing properties (houses, pits, caves, dovecotes, bathhouses, olive-presses, irrigated fields, slaves, and anything that produces fruit continuously) whose chazakah (presumption of ownership) is three years from day to day.
The Mishnah states that for a rain-fed field (שדה בעל), the chazakah is three years but not counted from day to day.
Rabbi Yishmael gives his calculation for a rain-fed field: three months in the first year, three in the last, and twelve in the middle, totaling eighteen months.
Rabbi Akiva gives his calculation: one month in the first year, one in the last, and twelve in the middle, totaling fourteen months.
Rabbi Yishmael clarifies that his calculation applies only to a white field (שדה לבן, grain field), but for a tree field (שדה אילן), the chazakah is three full years based on harvest cycles.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of three-year chazakah from the forewarned ox
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of three-year chazakah from the forewarned ox
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports that he heard from the people of Usha that the source for a three-year chazakah is the law of the forewarned ox (shor ha-mu'ad). Just as an ox that gores three times leaves the status of tam and becomes mu'ad, so too one who consumes a field for three years leaves the seller's domain and enters the buyer's domain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports that he heard from the people of Usha that the source for a three-year chazakah is the law of the forewarned ox (שור המועד).

Rabbi Yochanan draws an analogy: just as an ox that gores three times leaves the status of תם (innocuous) and becomes מועד (forewarned), so too one who consumes a field for three years leaves the seller's domain and enters the buyer's domain.

items.text: Objection: Why not wait until the fourth year?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not wait until the fourth year?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: with the forewarned ox, liability only begins after the fourth goring; similarly, shouldn't the buyer's ownership only be established after the fourth year? The Gemara rejects this: in the case of the ox, after three gorings it becomes mu'ad, but the liability for the fourth goring is immediate; the analogy is not exact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: just as the forewarned ox is not liable until the fourth goring, so too should the buyer's ownership not be established until the fourth year.
The Gemara rejects the analogy: in the ox case, after three gorings it becomes mu'ad, and liability for the fourth goring is immediate, so the parallel is inexact.

items.text: Answer to the previous objection about the three-year requirement
items.text_en: Answer to the previous objection about the three-year requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the three-year requirement for hazakah is analogous to the three goring incidents needed for a mu'ad ox, because after three years the land is established in the possessor's domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers the previous objection by analogizing the three-year requirement for hazakah to the three goring incidents needed for a mu'ad ox, because after three years the land is established in the possessor's domain.

items.text: Objection: What about hazakah without a claim?
items.text_en: Objection: What about hazakah without a claim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the analogy holds, then a hazakah without a claim should be valid, but the Mishnah explicitly says it is not. The reason is that we cannot make a claim for the possessor if he does not make one himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the analogy to a goring ox holds, then a hazakah without a claim should be valid, but the Mishnah explicitly rules it is not.
The Gemara answers that the reason is we cannot make a claim for the possessor if he does not make one himself.

items.text: Rav Avira's challenge: Protest not in the presence of the possessor
items.text_en: Rav Avira's challenge: Protest not in the presence of the possessor
items.desc_en: Rav Avira challenges the analogy: if hazakah is like a mu'ad ox, then a protest not in the possessor's presence should not be valid, but the Gemara distinguishes: for an ox, the Torah requires warning in the owner's presence, but for hazakah, the protest is conveyed through friends.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avira challenges the analogy: if hazakah is like a mu'ad ox, then a protest not in the possessor's presence should not be valid, just as warning an ox requires the owner's presence.

The Gemara distinguishes: for an ox, the Torah requires warning in the owner's presence (וְהוּעַד בִּבְעָלָיו), but for hazakah, the protest is conveyed through friends, so it need not be in the possessor's presence.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's view: Eating three fruits in one day
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's view: Eating three fruits in one day
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Rabbi Meir's opinion that if an ox gored three times in one day it is liable, so by analogy, if one eats three fruits from a tree in one day (like a fig tree), it should establish a hazakah. However, the Gemara rejects this because the analogy requires that each goring be a separate incident, and here the fruits are from the same season.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: according to Rabbi Meir, who says that if an ox gored with gaps between gorings it is still liable, then by analogy, if one ate three fruits from a tree in one day (like a fig tree), should that establish a hazakah (presumption of ownership)?
The Gemara rejects the analogy: just as a mu'ad ox requires that each goring be a separate incident (not all in one day), so too the fruits must come from separate seasons, not all from the same day.

items.text: Eating three fruits in three days (e.g., a caper bush)
items.text_en: Eating three fruits in three days (e.g., a caper bush)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if eating three fruits in three days (like a caper bush) establishes a hazakah, but rejects it because the fruit still exists and is just ripening gradually.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether eating three fruits over three days, as with a caper bush (צָלָף), should establish a hazakah.
The Gemara rejects the proposal because the fruit still exists on the tree and is merely ripening gradually, so the consumption is not complete.

items.text: Eating three fruits in thirty days (e.g., asparagus)
items.text_en: Eating three fruits in thirty days (e.g., asparagus)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if eating three fruits in thirty days (like asparagus) establishes a hazakah, but rejects it because the possessor is only plucking and eating, not demonstrating continuous use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether eating three fruits in thirty days, like asparagus (אספסתא), should establish a hazakah (presumption of ownership).
The Gemara rejects the question, explaining that the possessor is merely plucking and eating (שָׁמֵיט וְאָכֵיל), not demonstrating continuous use.

items.text: Eating three fruits in three months (asparagus) and Rabbi Yishmael's view
items.text_en: Eating three fruits in three months (asparagus) and Rabbi Yishmael's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if eating three fruits in three months (asparagus) establishes a hazakah, and cites Rabbi Yishmael who holds that for a field of trees, gathering the produce, harvesting olives, and collecting summer fruit constitute three years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether eating three fruits in three months, such as asparagus, establishes a hazakah (presumption of ownership).

The Gemara cites Rabbi Yishmael's view that for a field of trees, gathering the produce, harvesting olives, and collecting summer fruit constitute three years, implying that eating three fruits in three months does not establish a hazakah.

items.text: The Rabbis' view and Rav Yosef's scriptural support
items.text_en: The Rabbis' view and Rav Yosef's scriptural support
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis (who disagree with Rabbi Yishmael) hold. Rav Yosef cites a verse from Jeremiah about buying fields and writing deeds, indicating that even during the siege, the prophet encouraged buying land, implying that hazakah requires three years. Abaye objects that this may just be good advice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis (who disagree with Rabbi Yishmael) hold regarding the required duration of hazakah.

Rav Yosef cites a verse from Jeremiah (32:44) about buying fields and writing deeds, arguing that even during the siege, the prophet encouraged buying land, implying that hazakah requires three years.
Abaye objects that the verse may merely be offering good advice (עצה טובה) rather than establishing a halachic requirement of three years.

items.text: Rejection of the first explanation (advice) and support from Jeremiah
items.text_en: Rejection of the first explanation (advice) and support from Jeremiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that the three-year period is merely good advice, citing a parallel verse from Jeremiah where advice is given. It argues that just as there the advice is for preservation, here too the three years are for practical reasons, not a legal requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that the three-year period is a legal requirement, arguing that just as Jeremiah's advice to build and plant was for preservation, so too the three years are merely good advice.

items.text: Rava's first explanation: forbearance for three years
items.text_en: Rava's first explanation: forbearance for three years
items.desc_en: Rava proposes that a person is willing to forgo protest for the first two years but not the third, establishing the three-year hazakah period. This is a standalone statement without immediate challenge.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that a person is willing to forgo protest for two years but not the third, establishing the three-year hazakah period.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rava's first explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rava's first explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava: if forbearance is the reason, then when the land is returned after three years, the fruits should also be returned, contradicting Rav Nachman's ruling that fruits are not returned. This objection undermines the forbearance theory.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's forbearance theory: if forbearance is the reason, then when the land is returned after three years, the fruits should also be returned, contradicting Rav Nachman's ruling that fruits are not returned.

items.text: Rava's second explanation: indifference for three years
items.text_en: Rava's second explanation: indifference for three years
items.desc_en: Rava revises his explanation: a person is not particular about the first two years but becomes particular in the third, leading to protest. This shifts from forbearance to indifference.

sub.desc_en: Rava revises his explanation: a person is not particular about the first two years but becomes particular in the third, shifting the basis from forbearance to indifference.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rava's second explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rava's second explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: if the standard is based on being particular, then for people like the house of Bar Elyashiv who are particular even about passersby, hazakah would be immediate, which is absurd. This would make the law dependent on individual temperament.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the standard is based on being particular (קפדן), then for people like the house of Bar Elyashiv who are particular even about passersby, hazakah would be immediate, which is absurd, making the law dependent on individual temperament.

items.text: Rava's third explanation: document preservation
items.text_en: Rava's third explanation: document preservation
items.desc_en: Rava offers a final explanation: a person is careful with their document for the first three years, but after that they may lose it, so the three-year period allows the possessor to claim hazakah. This becomes the accepted rationale.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the sugya by stating that a person is careful with their document for the first three years, but beyond that they are not careful, establishing the three-year period for hazakah.

items.text: Abaye's objection to the third explanation regarding protest not in his presence
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to the third explanation regarding protest not in his presence
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges: if the reason is document preservation, then a protest not made in the owner's presence should be invalid, because the owner could claim he would have preserved his document if he had known. The Gemara responds with the principle that news travels through friends, so the owner is deemed to know.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the reason for the three-year period is document preservation, then a protest not made in the owner's presence should be invalid, because the owner could claim he would have preserved his document if he had known.
The Gemara responds that the owner is deemed to know of the protest because news travels through a network of friends, so he cannot claim ignorance.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling: three years must be consecutive
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling: three years must be consecutive
items.desc_en: Rav Huna clarifies that the three years of hazakah must be consecutive (רצופות), not scattered. The Gemara notes that this is already implied by 'from day to day' in the Mishnah, but Rav Huna emphasizes that even if the years are not exactly to the day, they must be uninterrupted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the three years of hazakah must be consecutive (רצופות), not scattered.
The Gemara questions what Rav Huna adds, since the Mishnah already states 'from day to day' implying consecutiveness.
The Gemara explains that Rav Huna's statement clarifies that 'from day to day' excludes scattered years, not just interrupted ones.

items.text: Rav Chama's qualification: fields that are fallow
items.text_en: Rav Chama's qualification: fields that are fallow
items.desc_en: Rav Chama states that Rav Huna conceds in places where fields are left fallow (מוברי באגי). The Gemara explains that this applies when some fields are fallow and others are not, and the possessor worked the fallow field. The owner cannot claim he would have planted it, as the possessor can argue that a single field in a large area is hard to guard, or that leaving it fallow is beneficial for the land.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chama states that Rav Huna concedes in places where fields are left fallow (מוברי באגי).
The Gemara questions the novelty, noting that the case involves a mixed area where some fields are fallow and others are not, and the possessor worked the fallow one.

The Gemara explains that without Rav Chama's statement, one might think the owner could argue the possessor should have planted it; but the possessor can respond that a single field in a large area is hard to guard.
Alternatively, the possessor can claim that leaving the field fallow is beneficial for the land, as it improves its yield.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah: hazakah for houses
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah: hazakah for houses
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the Mishnah states that hazakah applies to houses, but houses are occupied day and night, so how can three years be established? The challenge is that witnesses may not know about nighttime occupancy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's rule that hazakah applies to houses, arguing that since houses are occupied day and night, witnesses cannot testify about nighttime occupancy, undermining the three-year hazakah period.

items.text: Abaye's answer: neighbors testify
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: neighbors testify
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that neighbors, who are the witnesses for houses, know about both day and night occupancy because they live nearby and observe the comings and goings.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that neighbors (שיבובי) testify about houses because they observe both day and night occupancy.

items.text: Rava's answer: witnesses who rented
items.text_en: Rava's answer: witnesses who rented
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the witnesses are two people who rented the house from the possessor and lived there for three years day and night, thus providing direct testimony.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the witnesses are two people who rented the house from the possessor and lived there for three years day and night, thus providing direct testimony.

items.text: Objection: witnesses are interested parties, and resolution
items.text_en: Objection: witnesses are interested parties, and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yeimar objects that such witnesses are interested parties because if they don't testify, they would have to pay rent. Rav Ashi resolves that the case is where they hold the rent money and ask whom to give it to, so they have no personal stake.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yeimar objects to Rav Ashi that the witnesses are interested parties (נוגעין בעדותן), because if they do not testify, the court would tell them to pay rent to the claimant.
Rav Ashi resolves that the case involves low-level judges who hold the rent money and ask whom to give it to, so the witnesses have no personal stake.

items.text: Mar Zutra's ruling: if the claimant demands witnesses
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's ruling: if the claimant demands witnesses
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that if the claimant demands two witnesses to testify that the possessor lived there for three years day and night, his claim is valid and must be addressed.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that if the claimant demands two witnesses to testify that the possessor lived there for three years day and night, his claim is valid and must be addressed.

items.text: Mar Zutra and Rav Huna's concessions
items.text_en: Mar Zutra and Rav Huna's concessions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Mar Zutra concedes regarding peddlers who return to towns, that even if the claimant did not argue, we argue for him. Rav Huna concedes regarding the shops of Mehoza, which are used only by day, not by night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Mar Zutra concedes regarding peddlers who return to towns, that even if the claimant did not argue, we argue for him.
The Gemara states that Rav Huna concedes regarding the shops of Mehoza, which are used only by day, not by night.

items.text: Rami bar Hama and Rav Ukva bar Hama's alternating use
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama and Rav Ukva bar Hama's alternating use
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama and Rav Ukva bar Hama bought a maidservant together, using her on alternating days. When a third party claimed ownership, they came before Rava, who ruled that their alternating use prevented hazakah for themselves and for the world.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the case: Rami bar Hama and Rav Ukva bar Hama jointly bought a maidservant and used her on alternating days, until a third party claimed ownership.
Rava rules that their alternating use, intended to prevent hazakah (presumption of ownership) between themselves, also prevents hazakah against the world.

items.text: Exception for a written document
items.text_en: Exception for a written document
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds that this ruling applies only if there is no written document, but if there is a written document, it has publicity and can establish hazakah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara limits the previous ruling: the exemption from hazakah applies only when there is no written document, but if a document exists, it generates publicity and can establish hazakah.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a field with a small uncultivated patch
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a field with a small uncultivated patch
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one consumed an entire field except for a beit rova, he acquires the entire field except for that patch. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that this applies only if the patch is suitable for sowing, but if not, it is acquired along with the land.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one consumed an entire field except for a beit rova (a small uncultivated patch), he acquires the entire field except for that patch.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that this ruling applies only if the patch is suitable for sowing, but if not, it is acquired along with the land.

items.text: Rav Bivi bar Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rav Bivi bar Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Bivi bar Abaye objects: if the patch is not suitable for sowing, how does one acquire it? He answers that one must place animals or spread fruit there, and similarly here one should have done so.

sub.desc_en: Rav Bivi bar Abaye objects that if the patch is not suitable for sowing, one must acquire it by placing animals or spreading fruit there, and similarly here one should have done so.

items.text: Dispute about a house with a claim of tenancy
items.text_en: Dispute about a house with a claim of tenancy
items.desc_en: A man claimed he bought a house from another and used it for the hazakah period. The seller responded that he was an inner tenant. They came before Rav Nachman, who told the buyer to clarify his consumption. Rava objected, citing the principle that the burden of proof is on the claimant.

sub.desc_en: A man confronts another about occupying a house; the occupant claims he bought it and used it for the hazakah period, while the seller responds that he was an inner tenant.
Rav Nachman tells the buyer to clarify his consumption (i.e., bring proof of his hazakah).
Rava objects to Rav Nachman's instruction, citing the principle that the burden of proof is on the claimant (המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה).

items.text: Contradictions in Rava and Rav Nachman's rulings
items.text_en: Contradictions in Rava and Rav Nachman's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes apparent contradictions in Rava's and Rav Nachman's own rulings, beginning to cite another case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rava's own rulings and between Rav Nachman's own rulings, beginning to cite another case.

items.text: Case of the Bar Sisim field
items.text_en: Case of the Bar Sisim field
items.desc_en: A seller sells 'all the property of Bar Sisim' but the land is only called by that name. Rav Nachman rules for the buyer, and Rava objects, citing the principle that the burden of proof is on the claimant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a seller sells 'all the property of Bar Sisim' but the land is only called by that name, not actually owned by Bar Sisim.
Rav Nachman rules in favor of the buyer, placing the field in his possession.
Rava objects to Rav Nachman's ruling, invoking the principle that the burden of proof is on the claimant (המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה).

items.text: Gemara notes contradictions
items.text_en: Gemara notes contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara observes that Rava's objection contradicts another ruling of Rava, and similarly Rav Nachman's ruling contradicts another ruling of his.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava's objection contradicts another ruling of Rava, and similarly Rav Nachman's ruling contradicts another ruling of his.

items.text: Resolution of Rava's contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of Rava's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rava's contradiction: in the other case the seller is in possession, here the buyer is in possession, so the burden of proof differs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rava's contradiction by distinguishing the two cases: there the seller is in possession, here the buyer is in possession, so the burden of proof differs.

items.text: Resolution of Rav Nachman's contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of Rav Nachman's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rav Nachman's contradiction: since the seller called it 'Bar Sisim' and it is known as such, the seller must prove otherwise, analogous to requiring a deed holder to validate his document.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rav Nachman's contradiction: since the seller called it 'Bar Sisim' and it is known as such, the seller must prove otherwise, analogous to requiring a deed holder to validate his document.

items.text: Case of the house and the traveling seller
items.text_en: Case of the house and the traveling seller
items.desc_en: A buyer claims he purchased a house and held it for the chazaka period; the seller claims he was away in distant markets. Rava rules that a person is typically busy in the market for thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a buyer claims he purchased a house and held it for the chazaka period.
The seller objects that he was away in distant markets during the chazaka period.
The buyer counters that witnesses testify the seller was present for thirty days each year.
The seller rejects the testimony, claiming he was busy in his own market during those thirty days.
Rava rules that a person is typically busy in the market for thirty days, so the seller's claim is plausible.

items.text: Case of the land bought from a third party
items.text_en: Case of the land bought from a third party
items.desc_en: A buyer claims he bought land from someone who said he bought it from the original owner; the original owner does not admit this. The case is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a buyer claims he bought land from someone who said he bought it from the original owner.
The original owner responds that the buyer himself admits he did not buy directly from him, leaving the case unresolved.

items.text: First case: Claimant says 'I didn't sell to you'
items.text_en: First case: Claimant says 'I didn't sell to you'
items.desc_en: A claimant tells the possessor that the land is his and he never sold it. Rava rules that this is a valid legal claim.

sub.desc_en: The claimant asserts that the land is his and that the possessor never bought it from him, declaring the possessor has no standing.
Rava rules that the claimant's statement is a valid legal claim.

items.text: Second case: Possessor consulted claimant before buying
items.text_en: Second case: Possessor consulted claimant before buying
items.desc_en: The possessor claims he bought from a thief and consulted the claimant, who told him to buy. The claimant responds that the second (consultation) is easy for him, but the first (theft) is difficult. Rava rules this is a valid legal claim.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where a possessor is asked why he occupies the land and responds that he bought it from a certain person and held it for the years of hazakah.
The claimant objects that the seller was a thief, undermining the possessor's claim.
The possessor counters that he consulted the claimant before buying, and the claimant told him to go ahead and purchase.
The claimant argues that the second matter (the consultation) is easy for him to accept, but the first (the theft) is difficult to overcome.
Rava rules that the claimant's argument is a valid legal claim.

items.text: Comparison with Admon's ruling
items.text_en: Comparison with Admon's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares this case to a Mishnah where Admon says the second is easy and the first is difficult, while the Sages say he loses his right. The Gemara explains that even according to the Sages, here the claimant only spoke, not acted, so he can claim he was merely reading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rava's ruling aligns with Admon's position in the Mishnah.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Admon rules that the second claimant is easy and the first is difficult, while the Sages disagree.
The Gemara resolves that even according to the Sages, here the claimant only spoke (דיבורא) and did not act, so he can claim he was merely reading.

items.text: Third case: Claimant says he intended to buy his lawsuit
items.text_en: Third case: Claimant says he intended to buy his lawsuit
items.desc_en: The possessor says he bought from a thief and the claimant told him to buy it. The claimant responds that he meant to buy his lawsuit (i.e., to settle the claim). Rava rules that people do sell their lawsuits.

sub.desc_en: A case is presented where the possessor claims he bought the land from a thief, and the claimant responds that he meant to buy his lawsuit (i.e., to settle the claim).
Rava rules that people do sell their lawsuits, meaning the claimant's statement is valid and the possessor's claim is accepted.

items.text: Fourth case: Claimant has a bill of sale from four years ago
items.text_en: Fourth case: Claimant has a bill of sale from four years ago
items.desc_en: The claimant holds a bill of sale from four years ago, and the possessor claims he ate the land for 'years of chazakah'. The Gemara explains that 'years of chazakah' can mean many years, not necessarily three. Rava rules that people call many years 'years of chazakah'.

sub.desc_en: The claimant challenges the possessor, stating he holds a bill of sale from four years ago, implying the possessor cannot claim three years of chazakah.
The possessor clarifies that 'years of chazakah' does not necessarily mean three years; he meant many years.
Rava rules that people commonly call many years 'years of chazakah', so the possessor's claim is valid.

items.text: Clarification: Only if he ate for seven years
items.text_en: Clarification: Only if he ate for seven years
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that this ruling applies only if he ate for seven years, because then his chazakah precedes the other's bill of sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the ruling applies only if he ate for seven years, because then his chazakah (presumption of ownership) precedes the other's bill of sale.

items.text: Opening statement: Six years of cultivation is the strongest protest
items.text_en: Opening statement: Six years of cultivation is the strongest protest
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that cultivating a field for six years constitutes the strongest possible protest against a previous owner's claim, establishing a baseline for hazakah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that cultivating a field for six years constitutes the strongest possible protest against a previous owner's claim.

items.text: The case of two claimants and the principle of 'what reason to lie'
items.text_en: The case of two claimants and the principle of 'what reason to lie'
items.desc_en: When one claimant brings witnesses that the field is his father's and the other brings witnesses of three years of cultivation, Rabbah argues the latter could have claimed he bought it, so his testimony is credible. Abaye objects that 'what reason to lie' does not apply in the presence of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: one claimant brings witnesses that the field is his father's, and the other brings witnesses of three years of cultivation (חזקה).
Rabbah argues that the second claimant could have claimed he bought the field, so the principle of 'מה לו לשקר' (what reason to lie) makes his testimony credible.
Abaye objects that the principle of 'מה לי לשקר' (what reason to lie) does not apply in the presence of witnesses (במקום עדים).

items.text: Rabbah's retraction: Admitting the field is the other's but claiming purchase
items.text_en: Rabbah's retraction: Admitting the field is the other's but claiming purchase
items.desc_en: Rabbah revises his position, suggesting the claimant can admit the field belongs to the other's father but claim he bought it, and his earlier statement was merely a claim of reliance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah retracts his earlier position and now admits the field belongs to the other's father but claims he bought it, explaining his earlier statement was merely a claim of reliance.

items.text: The dispute between Ulla and Nehardeans on 'claim and retract'
items.text_en: The dispute between Ulla and Nehardeans on 'claim and retract'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether a litigant can change his claim in court. Ulla says he may retract and re-claim, while the Nehardeans say he cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a litigant who has made a claim may retract it and make a different claim.
Ulla rules that a litigant may retract and re-claim.
The Nehardeans rule that a litigant may not retract and re-claim.

items.text: Ulla's concessions: When retraction is not allowed
items.text_en: Ulla's concessions: When retraction is not allowed
items.desc_en: Ulla concedes that if the claimant initially said 'my father's and not your father's', he cannot retract. Similarly, if he was in court and did not claim, then later claimed outside, he cannot retract because his claim was finalized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Ulla concedes: if the claimant initially said 'my father's and not your father's', he cannot retract and change his claim.
The Gemara adds that Ulla also concedes: if he was in court and did not claim, then later claimed outside, he cannot retract.
The Gemara explains the reason: his claim was finalized (טַעְנְתֵיהּ אַגְמְרֵיהּ), so he cannot retract.

items.text: Nehardeans' concessions: When retraction is allowed
items.text_en: Nehardeans' concessions: When retraction is allowed
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans concede that if the claimant says 'my father's, purchased from your fathers', he may retract. Also, if he spoke outside court without claiming, then later claims in court, he may retract because people do not reveal their claims outside court.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans concede that if the claimant says 'my father's, purchased from your fathers', he may retract his claim.
The Nehardeans also concede that if someone spoke outside court without claiming, then later claims in court, he may retract because people do not reveal their claims outside court.

items.text: Amemar's ruling: Halakha follows 'claim and retract'
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling: Halakha follows 'claim and retract'
items.desc_en: Amemar, identifying as a Nehardean, rules that the halakha is that one may claim and retract.

sub.desc_en: Amemar declares himself a Nehardean and rules that the halakha follows the principle that one may claim and retract.

items.text: Case of contradictory testimonies: Rav Nachman and Rava's dispute
items.text_en: Case of contradictory testimonies: Rav Nachman and Rava's dispute
items.desc_en: When one claimant brings witnesses that the field is his father's and that he cultivated for three years, and the other brings witnesses of three years of cultivation, Rav Nachman says to set the cultivation testimonies against each other and leave the field in the possession of the fathers. Rava objects that the testimonies are contradictory, but Rav Nachman argues that only the cultivation testimonies are contradicted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one claimant brings witnesses that the field is his father's and that he cultivated for three years, and the other brings only witnesses of three years of cultivation.
Rav Nachman rules to set the cultivation testimonies against each other and leave the field in the possession of the fathers.
Rava objects that the testimonies are contradictory.
Rav Nachman rejects the objection, arguing that only the cultivation testimonies are contradicted, not the ownership testimonies.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Can one contradict his own witnesses about his father? This sets up the core question of the sugya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Can one contradict his own witnesses regarding his father?

items.text: Attributing Rav Nachman and Rava to a prior dispute
items.text_en: Attributing Rav Nachman and Rava to a prior dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Nachman and Rava's disagreement aligns with the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda about two sets of conflicting witnesses. It then refines the attribution, noting that Rava would only agree with Rav Chisda regarding a different testimony, not the same one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rava and Rav Nachman aligns with the earlier dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda regarding two sets of conflicting witnesses.
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda about two conflicting sets of witnesses, and proposes that Rav Nachman follows Rav Huna and Rava follows Rav Chisda.

The Gemara refines the attribution: everyone agrees with Rav Chisda; the dispute is only according to Rav Huna, and Rava would only agree with Rav Huna regarding a different testimony, not the same one.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the court will both remove and restore the litigant's status, disregarding the degradation of the court. This shows his practical approach despite the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the court will both remove and restore the claimant's possession, disregarding the court's embarrassment.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about conflicting witnesses
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about conflicting witnesses
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Zeira) raises an objection from a baraita where two witnesses say a woman's husband died and two say he didn't; the woman may not remarry, but if she does, she does not leave. Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei distinguishes based on the timing of the witnesses' arrival.

sub.text: Rava (or Rabbi Zeira) raises an objection
sub.text_en: Rava (or Rabbi Zeira) raises an objection
sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Zeira) objects by citing a baraita where conflicting witnesses about a husband's death or divorce leave the woman in a state of ספק (doubt): she may not remarry, but if she does, she does not leave.
Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei distinguishes: the woman leaves only if the witnesses came before she remarried, but if she remarried and then the witnesses came, she does not leave.

items.text: Rav Nachman's response to the objection
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's response to the objection
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman admits that he intended to act but now, due to the objections from Rava and Rav Hamnuna, he will not rule practically in this case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman concedes that he would have acted but now refrains due to the objections from Rava and Rav Hamnuna.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Nachman's actual ruling
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Nachman's actual ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Nachman did in fact rule, but observers thought it was an error. It was actually based on a tannaitic dispute about elevating someone to kehunah on the testimony of a single witness, where Rabbi Elazar and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel differ regarding the presence of a single challenger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Nachman went out and ruled, and observers thought it was an error.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dispute whether one may elevate someone to kehunah (priesthood) on the testimony of a single witness.

The Gemara resolves that the difference between Rabbi Elazar and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is only regarding the presence of a single challenger (ערער חד), and Rav Nachman's ruling was based on this dispute.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a challenge requires two witnesses, but Rabbi Yochanan stated that everyone agrees a challenge requires at least two. This creates a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires two witnesses for a challenge, yet Rabbi Yochanan stated that everyone agrees a challenge requires at least two, creating a contradiction.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: the case involves sequential witnesses and court dignity
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: the case involves sequential witnesses and court dignity
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case involves a priest whose status was repeatedly challenged and restored by alternating single witnesses and pairs. The dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is about whether the court should be concerned for its own dignity when reversing its ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by describing a scenario where a priest's status is repeatedly challenged and restored by alternating single witnesses and pairs, establishing the context for the dispute.
The Gemara notes that all parties agree that the testimonies of the single witnesses and pairs combine to form valid evidence.

The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is about whether the court should be concerned for its own dignity when reversing its ruling: Rabbi Elazar holds that once the court has demoted the priest, it cannot reinstate him due to concern for the court's dignity, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the court can both demote and reinstate without concern for its dignity.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and reframing as a tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and reframing as a tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that if the concern is court dignity, the same issue would arise with two witnesses. He instead explains that the dispute is about whether testimony can be combined when witnesses testify sequentially, and cites a tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Natan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that if the concern were court dignity, the same problem would arise even with two witnesses, not just one.
Rav Ashi reframes the dispute: all agree court dignity is not a concern; the disagreement is about whether testimony can be combined when witnesses testify sequentially.

Rav Ashi cites a tannaitic dispute: the Tanna Kamma requires simultaneous testimony, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha allows sequential testimony, and Rabbi Natan allows hearing each witness on separate days.

items.text: Introduction of a new case: a land claim with a document
items.text_en: Introduction of a new case: a land claim with a document
items.desc_en: The Gemara transitions to a new scenario where one person challenges another's possession of land, and the defendant claims to have purchased it with a deed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new case: one person challenges another's possession of land, and the defendant claims to have purchased it and presents a deed.

items.text: First case: Creditor admits document is forged but claims he had a valid one
items.text_en: First case: Creditor admits document is forged but claims he had a valid one
items.desc_en: A creditor presents a document for payment, and the debtor claims it is forged. The creditor whispers to Rabbah that it is indeed forged but he had a valid document that was lost. Rabbah trusts him because he could have simply claimed the document is valid, but Rav Yosef objects that the document is worthless.

sub.desc_en: The creditor whispers to Rabbah that the document is forged but he had a valid one that was lost.
Rabbah trusts the creditor because he could have simply claimed the document is valid.
Rav Yosef objects that the document is worthless and cannot be relied upon.

items.text: Second case: Similar scenario with Rava
items.text_en: Second case: Similar scenario with Rava
items.desc_en: A similar case occurs where a creditor presents a document, the debtor claims it is forged, and the creditor whispers to Rava that it is forged but he had a valid one. Rava trusts him, but Rav Yosef again objects that the document is worthless.

sub.desc_en: A creditor demands repayment from a debtor, presenting a document; the debtor claims it is forged, and the creditor whispers to Rava that it is indeed forged but he had a valid one that was lost.
Rava reasons that the creditor has no motive to lie (מה לו לשקר), since he could have simply claimed the document was valid.
Rav Yosef objects that the document is worthless (חספא בעלמא) and Rava should not rely on it.

items.text: Rav Idi bar Avin's ruling: Distinction between land and money
items.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's ruling: Distinction between land and money
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin rules that the halakha follows Rabbah regarding land (the land remains in the creditor's possession) and follows Rav Yosef regarding money (the money remains where it is).

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin rules that the halakha follows Rabbah regarding land (the land remains where it is) and follows Rav Yosef regarding money (the money remains where it is).

items.text: Case of a guarantor and Abaye's response
items.text_en: Case of a guarantor and Abaye's response
items.desc_en: A guarantor claims he paid the creditor and presents a document, but the debtor says he already repaid the guarantor. Rav Idi bar Avin asks Abaye about this case, and Abaye applies the earlier ruling: the money remains where it is.

sub.desc_en: The narrator presents a case: a guarantor claims he paid the creditor and shows a document, but the debtor denies having repaid the guarantor.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin sends this case to Abaye, asking what the ruling is in such a scenario.
Abaye responds by applying the earlier ruling: the money remains where it is, as per the principle of Rav Yosef regarding movable property.

items.text: Exception: If the debtor says he returned the money due to poor quality
items.text_en: Exception: If the debtor says he returned the money due to poor quality
items.desc_en: Abaye adds that if the debtor says he returned the money because the coins were defective, the document's lien still applies, as the return does not cancel the debt.

sub.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes: if the debtor claims he returned the money as a new loan, the lien is void; but if he claims he returned it because the coins were defective (שייפי וסומקי), the original lien still applies.

items.text: Case of Rava bar Sharshum and land of orphans
items.text_en: Case of Rava bar Sharshum and land of orphans
items.desc_en: A rumor spread that Rava bar Sharshum was consuming land of orphans. Abaye asks him for the facts, and he explains that he held the land as a mortgage from the orphans' father.

sub.desc_en: A rumor spread that Rava bar Sharshum was consuming land belonging to orphans.
Abaye asks Rava bar Sharshum to explain the actual facts of the case.
Rava bar Sharshum explains that he held the land as a mortgage from the orphans' father.

items.text: Creditor's plan to recover debt from orphans
items.text_en: Creditor's plan to recover debt from orphans
items.desc_en: A creditor holds a mortgage on land belonging to orphans. He considers that if he returns the land and claims the debt, he would need to swear an oath. Instead, he decides to suppress the mortgage document and claim the land as a purchase, relying on the principle that one who could claim ownership by purchase is believed to also claim a debt.

sub.desc_en: The creditor notes that he has additional money owed to him from the orphans' father and has held the land as a mortgage for two years.
The creditor considers that if he returns the land to the orphans and claims the debt, the rabbis require an oath before collecting from orphans' property.

The creditor decides to suppress the mortgage document and claim the land as a purchase, relying on the principle that one who could claim ownership by purchase (מיגו) is believed to also claim a debt.

items.text: Response: the claim is invalid due to public knowledge
items.text_en: Response: the claim is invalid due to public knowledge
items.desc_en: The creditor is told that he cannot claim the land as purchased because there is public knowledge (קָלָא) that it belongs to the orphans. Instead, he should return the land and sue the orphans when they come of age.

sub.desc_en: The advisor tells the creditor that he cannot claim the land as purchased (לְקוּחָה בְּיָדִי) because there is public knowledge (קָלָא) that it belongs to the orphans; instead, he should return the land and sue the orphans when they come of age.

items.text: Dispute over a date tree between relatives
items.text_en: Dispute over a date tree between relatives
items.desc_en: A relative of Rav Idi bar Avin died, leaving a date tree. Rav Idi bar Avin and another man both claimed to be closer relatives. The other man eventually admitted Rav Idi was closer, and Rav Chisda awarded the tree to Rav Idi.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a relative of Rav Idi bar Avin died, leaving a date tree.
Rav Idi bar Avin claims he is the closer relative.
Another man also claims to be the closer relative.
The other man eventually admits Rav Idi is closer, and Rav Chisda awards the tree to Rav Idi.

items.text: Demand for produce and rejection of Rav Chisda's ruling
items.text_en: Demand for produce and rejection of Rav Chisda's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin demands that the other man return the produce he consumed from the tree. The other man questions Rav Idi's greatness, arguing that Rav Idi himself claimed to be the closer relative. Abaye and Rava reject Rav Chisda's ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin demands that the other man return the produce he consumed from the tree from that day until now.
The other man questions Rav Idi's greatness, arguing that Rav Idi himself claimed to be the closer relative, so why should he rely on Rav Chisda's ruling?
Abaye and Rava reject Rav Chisda's ruling, indicating they do not accept it as binding law.

items.text: Opening principle: admission stands
items.text_en: Opening principle: admission stands
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that once a litigant admits something, it is binding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes the principle that once a litigant admits something, the admission is binding.

items.text: Dispute over inheritance and hazakah
items.text_en: Dispute over inheritance and hazakah
items.desc_en: Two claimants each say the land is from their fathers; one brings witnesses that it is his father's, the other brings witnesses of hazakah for two years. Rav Chisda argues the latter could have claimed he bought it, so why would he lie? Abaye and Rava reject this principle in the presence of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where two claimants each say the land is from their fathers; one brings witnesses that it is his father's, the other brings witnesses of hazakah for two years.
Rav Chisda argues that the latter claimant could have claimed he bought it, so the principle of 'why would he lie?' applies.
Abaye and Rava reject Rav Chisda's principle, stating that 'why would he lie?' is not invoked in the presence of witnesses.

items.text: Case of buyer with two years of hazakah
items.text_en: Case of buyer with two years of hazakah
items.desc_en: A man claims he bought land and had hazakah for two years; he brings witnesses only for two years. Rav Nachman rules the land and its produce are returned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one man asks another why he is occupying his land, and the occupant claims he bought it and held hazakah for two years.
The occupant brings witnesses that he consumed the produce for two years, and Rav Nachman rules that both the land and its produce are returned to the original owner.

items.text: Claim of entering for produce and the distinction from land
items.text_en: Claim of entering for produce and the distinction from land
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid says if the defendant claims he entered only for the produce, he is believed, analogizing to Rav Yehuda's principle that one does not dare cut another's palm tree. The Gemara objects that the same should apply to land, but distinguishes: for land, one can demand a deed; for produce, people do not make deeds.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid rules that if the defendant claims he entered the land only for the produce, he is believed.

sub.text: Rav Zevid's analogy to Rav Yehuda's principle
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid's analogy to Rav Yehuda's principle
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid supports his ruling by analogizing to Rav Yehuda's principle that one does not dare cut another's palm tree, so here too one does not dare eat another's produce.
The Gemara objects that the same reasoning should apply to land itself, not just produce.
The Gemara answers that for land one can demand a deed, but for produce people do not make deeds, so the distinction stands.

items.text: Case with one witness and the precedent of Rabbi Abba's snatch
items.text_en: Case with one witness and the precedent of Rabbi Abba's snatch
items.desc_en: A man claims he bought land and had hazakah for three years; he brings one witness. The rabbis before Abaye consider this similar to the case of Rabbi Abba's snatch, where a man snatched a wine libation, one witness testified, and the defendant admitted but claimed it was his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a man claims he bought land and had hazakah for three years, and brings one witness to support his claim.
The rabbis before Abaye consider this case similar to the precedent of Rabbi Abba's snatch (חטיפה) of a wine libation.
The Gemara recounts the precedent: a man snatched a wine libation, one witness testified, and the defendant admitted but claimed it was his own, leading to Rabbi Ammi's ruling.

items.text: Gemara's question on adjudicating the case
items.text_en: Gemara's question on adjudicating the case
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the dilemma: how should judges rule when there is one witness but the defendant admits to seizing the field, making him a robber?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the dilemma: how should judges rule when there is one witness but the defendant admits to seizing the field, making him a robber?

items.text: Rabbi Abba's ruling: obligated to pay
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's ruling: obligated to pay
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba responds that this is a case of one who is obligated to take an oath but cannot, and therefore must pay.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that the defendant is a case of one who is obligated to take an oath but cannot, and therefore must pay.

items.text: Abaye's objection: witness comes to assist, not challenge
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: witness comes to assist, not challenge
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the cases are not analogous: there the witness comes to challenge the defendant, but here the witness comes to assist the plaintiff, so the ruling differs.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the cases are not analogous: there the witness comes to challenge the defendant, but here the witness comes to assist the plaintiff, so the ruling differs.

items.text: Alternative comparison: one witness and two years of produce
items.text_en: Alternative comparison: one witness and two years of produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Abba's case is actually comparable to a case of one witness and two years of produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Abba's case is comparable to a case of one witness and two years of produce, rather than the standard case of two witnesses.

items.text: The case of the disputed boat and the initial dispute
items.text_en: The case of the disputed boat and the initial dispute
items.desc_en: Two people are fighting over a boat; each claims it is his. One litigant comes to court and asks the court to seize the boat until he brings witnesses. The Gemara presents the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda: Rav Huna says we seize it, Rav Yehuda says we do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: two people are fighting over a boat, each claiming it is his.
One litigant comes to court and asks the court to seize the boat until he brings witnesses; the Gemara asks whether we seize it or not.
Rav Huna rules that we do seize the boat.
Rav Yehuda rules that we do not seize the boat.

items.text: The litigant fails to bring witnesses and asks for release
items.text_en: The litigant fails to bring witnesses and asks for release
items.desc_en: The litigant went but did not find witnesses. He then asks the court to release the boat, saying 'whoever is stronger will prevail.' The Gemara presents the dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Pappa: Rav Yehuda says we do not release it, Rav Pappa says we do. The halakha is concluded: we do not seize it initially, but if it was seized, we do not release it.

sub.desc_en: The litigant fails to find witnesses and asks the court to release the boat; the Gemara asks whether we release it.
Rav Yehuda rules that we do not release the boat.
Rav Pappa rules that we do release the boat.
The halakha is concluded: we do not seize it initially, but if it was seized, we do not release it.

items.text: The case of ancestral property and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: The case of ancestral property and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: A new case: each litigant says 'it is my ancestral property.' Rav Nachman rules: whoever is stronger prevails. The Gemara then asks: what is the difference between this case and the case of two deeds that emerge on the same day?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a new case where each litigant claims the property is their ancestral inheritance.
Rav Nachman rules that whoever is stronger prevails in this case.
The Gemara asks what distinguishes this case from the case of two deeds that emerge on the same day.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav and Shmuel disagree about dividing a field (Rav says divide, Shmuel says the court decides) in a case where the facts can be determined, unlike the earlier case where they cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav and Shmuel disagree about dividing a field (Rav says divide, Shmuel says the court decides) in a case where the facts can be determined, unlike the earlier case where they cannot.

items.text: Comparison to the Mishna about a cow or slave
items.text_en: Comparison to the Mishna about a cow or slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishna where a cow or slave gives birth during a sale, and the buyer and seller dispute the timing; there the ruling is that they divide the offspring, seemingly contradicting Shmuel's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shmuel's ruling differs from the Mishna about a cow or slave, where the buyer and seller divide the offspring.

items.text: Gemara's answer distinguishing the cases
items.text_en: Gemara's answer distinguishing the cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that in the Mishna's case, there is no way to ascertain the truth, so they divide; but here, there is a way to ascertain the truth, so the court decides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that in the Mishna's case there is no way to ascertain the truth, so they divide, but here there is a way, so the court decides.

items.text: The dispute about 'gazlan shel rabbim'
items.text_en: The dispute about 'gazlan shel rabbim'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether a robber of the public is considered a robber. Neharde'i rules that if someone from the market takes possession of such land, we do not remove it from his hands, citing Rabbi Chiya's teaching that a robber of the public is not called a robber. Rav Ashi argues that he is still called a robber, but the phrase means that he is not required to make restitution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets up the problem: a disputed field has monetary value for each claimant, but neither can prove ownership.
