Neharde'i rules that if someone from the market takes possession of such land, we do not remove it, citing Rabbi Chiya's teaching that a robber of the public (גזלן של רבים) is not called a robber.
Rav Ashi argues that a robber of the public is still called a robber, but the phrase means he is not required to make restitution (שבועה).

items.text: Rabbi Abba's ruling on immediate hazakah
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's ruling on immediate hazakah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba states that if the owner himself lifts a basket of fruit from the land, it immediately establishes a hazakah (presumption of ownership). Rav Zevid adds that if the claimant says 'I appointed him for the fruit,' he is believed, but only within three years, not after.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that the hazakah (presumption of ownership) requires three years from day to day.
Rabbi Abba rules that if the owner himself lifts a basket of fruit from the land, it immediately establishes a hazakah (presumption of ownership).
Rav Zevid adds that if the claimant says 'I appointed him for the fruit,' he is believed.
Rav Zevid qualifies that this belief applies only within three years, but not after three years.

items.text: Rav Ashi's question and the analogy to mortgages
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question and the analogy to mortgages
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana: if the owner appointed him for fruit, what should he have done? The answer is that he should have protested. This is proven by analogy to mortgages in Sura, where if the creditor claims the land is purchased, he must have protested; otherwise, the rabbis would not have instituted a rule leading to loss.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana: if the owner appointed him for fruit, what should he have done?
Rav Kahana answers that he should have protested.

The Gemara proves the answer by analogy to mortgages in Sura, where if the creditor claims the land is purchased, he must have protested; otherwise, the rabbis would not have instituted a rule leading to loss.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on an Israelite from a gentile
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on an Israelite from a gentile
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: an Israelite who comes to claim land from a gentile is like a gentile; just as a gentile has no hazakah without a deed, so too this Israelite has no hazakah without a deed. Rava adds a condition: if the Israelite says something (the continuation is on the next daf).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that an Israelite who comes to claim land from a gentile is like a gentile, having no hazakah without a deed.
Rava adds a condition: if the Israelite says something (the continuation is on the next daf).

items.text: Testimony of a Jew about a purchase from a gentile
items.text_en: Testimony of a Jew about a purchase from a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a Jew can be believed when he says a gentile told him he bought the field from the original owner, since the gentile himself would not be believed. Rava resolves that the Jew is believed because he could have simply claimed he bought it directly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a Jew can be believed when he testifies that a gentile told him he bought the field from the original owner, since the gentile himself would not be believed.
Rava resolves that the Jew is believed because he could have simply claimed he bought the field directly from the original owner.

items.text: Cutting a palm tree as evidence of ownership
items.text_en: Cutting a palm tree as evidence of ownership
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that if someone is seen carrying a sickle and basket and says he is going to cut so-and-so's palm tree because he bought it, he is believed, as no one would dare cut a tree that isn't his.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a person seen carrying a sickle and basket who says he is going to cut someone else's palm tree because he bought it is believed, since no one would dare cut a tree that is not his.

items.text: Possession from the outer side of a fence
items.text_en: Possession from the outer side of a fence
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that if one establishes possession from the outer side of a fence of arudi (a type of thorn), it is not valid possession, because the owner can claim that the arudi ate any crops planted there.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that possession from the outer side of an arudi fence is not valid.
Rav Yehuda explains the reason: the owner can claim that the arudi ate any crops planted there.

items.text: Eating orlah, shemittah, or kilayim does not establish possession
items.text_en: Eating orlah, shemittah, or kilayim does not establish possession
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that if one eats produce that is orlah, shemittah, or kilayim, it does not establish possession. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that eating produce that is ערלה (orlah, fruit from a tree in its first three years) does not establish a חזקה (presumption of ownership).

A baraita supports Rav Yehuda's ruling, adding that eating produce of שביעית (shemittah, the sabbatical year) or כלאים (kilayim, forbidden mixtures) also does not establish a presumption of ownership.

items.text: Eating shachat and the exception in Mahoza
items.text_en: Eating shachat and the exception in Mahoza
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says that if one eats shachat (a type of grass), it is not valid possession. Rava adds that if it is in the neck of Mahoza, it is valid possession.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that eating שחת (a type of grass) does not constitute valid possession (חזקה).
Rava adds an exception: if the grass is in the neck of Mahoza (a place where such grass is valuable), eating it does constitute valid possession.

items.text: Tafticha and the house of the Exilarch
items.text_en: Tafticha and the house of the Exilarch
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that tafticha (a type of plant) does not establish possession, nor does bringing in and taking out a kor of produce. Additionally, the house of the Exilarch does not establish possession against others, nor do others against them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that tafticha (a type of plant) does not establish possession (חזקה).
Rav Nachman adds that bringing in and taking out a kor of produce does not establish possession.
The house of the Exilarch does not establish possession against others, nor do others establish possession against them.

items.text: Possession of slaves and a minor in a cradle
items.text_en: Possession of slaves and a minor in a cradle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether slaves have possession, citing Resh Lakish that grazing animals have no immediate possession. Rava explains that slaves have no possession immediately but do after three years. Rava adds that a minor in a cradle has immediate possession, even if he has a mother, as a mother does not forget her child.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether slaves have possession (חזקה), given that Resh Lakish said grazing animals have no possession.
The Gemara cites Resh Lakish's ruling that grazing animals (הגדרות) have no possession, implying slaves also lack it.
Rava resolves the contradiction: slaves have no immediate possession (חזקה לאלתר) but do after three years.
Rava adds that a minor in a cradle has immediate possession (חזקה לאלתר).
The Gemara objects that this ruling is obvious.
Rava explains the novelty: even if the minor has a mother, we do not suspect she brought him there, because a mother does not forget her child.

items.text: Goats eating shoots in Nehardea
items.text_en: Goats eating shoots in Nehardea
items.desc_en: A case of goats that ate shoots in Nehardea: the owner seized them and claimed their value. The father of Shmuel rules he can claim up to their value because he could say they are purchased. The Gemara resolves the contradiction with Resh Lakish by noting that goats are different as they are entrusted to a shepherd, and in Nehardea, Arabs are common and they hand them over from hand to hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case in Nehardea where goats ate shoots and the owner seized them, claiming their full value.
The father of Shmuel rules that the owner can claim up to the goats' value because he could say they are purchased (לְקוּחוֹת הֵן בְּיָדִי).
The Gemara objects that Resh Lakish ruled that goats (הַגּוֹדְרוֹת) have no presumption of ownership (חזקה).
The Gemara resolves that goats are different because they are entrusted to a shepherd, and in Nehardea, Arabs are common and hand them from hand to hand, so the owner's claim is credible.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about plowing
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about plowing
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael (who requires three months) and Rabbi Akiva (who requires three years) is about whether plowing (ניר) establishes possession. The Gemara rejects this, asking: according to Rabbi Akiva, why mention a month?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael (three months) and Rabbi Akiva (three years) revolves around whether plowing (ניר) constitutes a valid act of possession (חזקה).
The Gemara rejects the suggestion, asking: according to Rabbi Akiva, why mention a month at all (if the dispute is about plowing)?

items.text: Opening question on plowing as chazakah
items.text_en: Opening question on plowing as chazakah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether even one day of plowing could establish chazakah, and clarifies that generally plowing is not considered chazakah, but here there is a distinction between major and minor produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does even one day of plowing establish chazakah?
The Gemara resolves that generally plowing is not a chazakah, but here the distinction is between major and minor produce.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on plowing
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on plowing
items.desc_en: A baraisa records a dispute: the first opinion holds that plowing is not chazakah, while 'Yesh Omrim' says it is. Rav Chisda identifies 'Yesh Omrim' as Rabbi Acha, citing a related Tannaitic source.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa opens with a dispute: the first opinion holds that plowing (ניר) is not a valid chazakah, while 'Yesh Omrim' says it is.
The Gemara asks who the anonymous 'Yesh Omrim' refers to.
Rav Chisda identifies 'Yesh Omrim' as Rabbi Acha.
A supporting baraita is cited: if one plowed for one year and sowed for two, or plowed for two and sowed for one, it is not a chazakah; Rabbi Acha says it is a chazakah.

items.text: Amoraic support and reasoning
items.text_en: Amoraic support and reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that all the great sages of the generation say plowing is chazakah. Rav Bibi asks Rav Nachman for the reasoning behind both positions: one who claims it is chazakah argues that a person would not remain silent while his land is plowed; the other argues that the plower can claim he was just using the land for temporary grazing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he asked all the great sages of the generation and they said plowing (ניר) constitutes a chazakah (חזקה).

sub.text: Rav Bibi's question to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi's question to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi asks Rav Nachman for the reasoning behind the position that plowing is a chazakah, and explains that a person would not remain silent while his land is plowed.

sub.text: Rav Bibi's second question (reasoning for the opposing view)
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi's second question (reasoning for the opposing view)
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi asks for the reasoning behind the opposing view that plowing is not a chazakah, explaining that the plower can claim he was just bringing in every bundle of straw.

items.text: Inquiry from Pum Nahara
items.text_en: Inquiry from Pum Nahara
items.desc_en: The people of Pum Nahara send a query to Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda asking whether plowing is chazakah. He responds that Rabbi Acha and all the great sages say it is chazakah.

sub.desc_en: The people of Pum Nahara send a query to Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda asking whether plowing (ניר) constitutes a chazakah (presumption of ownership).

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's response
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's response
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda responds that Rabbi Acha and all the great sages of the generation say that plowing (ניר) is indeed a chazakah.

items.text: Objection citing great authorities
items.text_en: Objection citing great authorities
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects: is it proper to count personalities? Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia, and Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva in Eretz Yisrael, all say plowing is not chazakah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects to counting personalities, citing that Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia, and Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva in Eretz Yisrael, all rule that plowing (ניר) is not a valid chazakah (חזקה).

items.text: Sources for Rav and Shmuel's positions
items.text_en: Sources for Rav and Shmuel's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the sources: Rav's view is from a statement by Rav Yehuda citing Rav that the requirement of three years from day to day excludes plowing; Shmuel's view is from a statement by Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that chazakah requires three harvests, with Abaye explaining the practical difference between them regarding a date palm that produces three times a year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the source for Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is the Mishnah itself; what is the source for Rav's position?
Rav Yehuda cites Rav that the phrase 'three years from day to day' in the Mishnah excludes plowing (ניר) from constituting a chazakah.
The Gemara asks: what is the source for Shmuel's position?
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that chazakah requires three harvests (grape-gathering, olive-picking, or fig-gathering).
The Gemara asks: what is the practical difference between Rav's requirement of three years from day to day and Shmuel's requirement of three harvests?
Abaye explains that the difference is a date palm (דקל נערה) that produces three times a year: according to Rav, one year suffices; according to Shmuel, three harvests are needed.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's distinction and Abaye's inference
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's distinction and Abaye's inference
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael states that the previous rules apply only to a white field (grain field). Abaye infers from this that according to the Rabbis, if one had thirty trees planted ten per beit se'ah and ate ten each year for three years, it constitutes chazakah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael states that the previous rules apply only to a white field (grain field).
Abaye infers from Rabbi Yishmael's statement that according to the Rabbis, if one had thirty trees planted ten per beit se'ah and ate ten each year for three years, it constitutes chazakah.

items.text: Gemara's analogy to Rabbi Yishmael's ruling on chazakah for multiple trees
items.text_en: Gemara's analogy to Rabbi Yishmael's ruling on chazakah for multiple trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara draws an analogy from Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that one fruit establishes chazakah for all fruits, applying it here: consuming fruit from one tree establishes chazakah for that tree, and from another for that other. However, this only applies if the fruit was brought out of the field; if it was brought out but not eaten, there is no chazakah, and only if the branches were broken off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that one fruit establishes chazakah for all fruits applies here, so that consuming fruit from one tree establishes chazakah for that tree and from another for that other.
The Gemara answers that this applies only if the fruit was brought out of the field, but if brought out and not eaten there is no chazakah, and only if the branches were broken off.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa on land acquisition with trees
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa on land acquisition with trees
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid rules that if one person acquired trees through chazakah and another acquired the land, the tree owner owns only the trees and no land. Rav Pappa objects, arguing that the landowner could then tell the tree owner to uproot his trees and leave. Rav Pappa instead rules that the tree owner acquires the trees and half the land, and the other person acquires the other half of the land.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where one person acquired trees through chazakah and another acquired the land.
Rav Zevid rules that the tree owner acquires only the trees and the other person acquires the land.
Rav Pappa objects that under Rav Zevid's ruling, the landowner could tell the tree owner to uproot his trees and leave.
Rav Pappa rules instead that the tree owner acquires the trees and half the land, and the other person acquires the other half of the land.

items.text: Clarification: seller who retains trees retains land even according to Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Clarification: seller who retains trees retains land even according to Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is obvious: if one sold land but retained the trees for himself, he retains land (for the trees' needs). Even according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a seller sells generously, this applies only to a cistern or dovecote, which do not deplete the land, but trees do deplete the land, so the seller retains land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is obvious: if one sold land but retained the trees for himself, he retains land (for the trees' needs).
The Gemara clarifies that even according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a seller sells generously (בעין יפה), this applies only to a cistern or dovecote, which do not deplete the land.
The Gemara concludes that trees do deplete the land, so the seller retains land for them.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case involves trees that weaken the land, so the seller retains some land; otherwise, the buyer could demand the seller uproot the trees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case involves trees that weaken the land, so the seller retains some land; otherwise, the buyer could demand the seller uproot the trees.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis on land retention
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis on land retention
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: according to Rabbi Akiva, who says a seller sells generously, the seller retains land; according to the Rabbis, he does not. It then qualifies the positions with the views of Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa regarding two buyers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis regarding whether the seller retains land when he sells trees and leaves land before him.

sub.text: Gemara's qualification for Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's qualification for Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara qualifies that even according to Rav Zevid, who denies the seller's retention in the case of two buyers, here the seller retains because the seller sells with a generous eye.

sub.text: Gemara's qualification for the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's qualification for the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara qualifies that even according to Rav Pappa, who grants the seller's retention in the case of two buyers, here the seller does not retain because the seller sells with a grudging eye.

items.text: Nehardeans' ruling on contiguous trees and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Nehardeans' ruling on contiguous trees and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that if one ate fruits from trees planted contiguously, he has no presumption of ownership. Rava objects, asking how one acquires a row of trees, and instead rules that selling them contiguously means the buyer acquires no land.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans state that if one ate fruits from trees planted consecutively (רצופין), he does not acquire a chazakah (presumption of ownership) on the land.
Rava objects: if so, how does one acquire a strip of land (מישרא דאספסתא) that is planted consecutively?
Rava resolves: if one sold trees planted consecutively (מכרן רצופין), the buyer does not acquire the land.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's comparison to Tannaitic dispute on a vineyard
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's comparison to Tannaitic dispute on a vineyard
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira compares the case to a Tannaitic dispute: a vineyard planted less than four cubits apart—Rabbi Shimon says it is not a vineyard, while the Sages say it is, viewing the middle trees as if they do not exist.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's citation of Tannaitic dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's citation of Tannaitic dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a Tannaitic dispute about a vineyard planted less than four cubits apart: Rabbi Shimon says it is not a vineyard, while the Sages say it is a vineyard and the middle vines are considered as if they do not exist.

The baraita presents the Tannaitic dispute: a vineyard planted less than four cubits apart—Rabbi Shimon says it is not a vineyard, while the Sages say it is, viewing the middle trees as if they do not exist.

items.text: Nehardeans' ruling on buying a palm tree
items.text_en: Nehardeans' ruling on buying a palm tree
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that one who buys a palm tree from another acquires it from its base to the depths of the earth.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans state that one who sells a palm tree to another acquires it from its base (שיפולי) down to the depths (תהומא).

items.text: Rava's objection and the necessity of protest
items.text_en: Rava's objection and the necessity of protest
items.desc_en: Rava objects that if someone sold saffron, the buyer could be told to uproot it and leave, so the case must involve a claim of ownership. Mar Kashisha then argues that even if it were a sale, the buyer should have protested; he compares this to mortgages in Sura where failure to protest would lead to loss, concluding that protest is required.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that if the land were sold with saffron, the buyer could be told to uproot the saffron and leave, so the case must involve a claim of ownership.
Rava resolves that the case involves a claimant who comes with a specific claim of ownership, not a mere sale.
Mar Kashisha asks: even if it were a sale of saffron, what could the buyer have done to prevent the loss?
Mar Kashisha answers that the buyer should have protested (מחאה) to preserve his claim.

sub.text: Supporting argument from mortgages in Sura
sub.text_en: Supporting argument from mortgages in Sura
sub.desc_en: The gemara supports the need for protest by comparing to mortgages in Sura, where failure to protest would lead to loss, concluding that protest is required here as well.

items.text: Mishnah: Three lands for hazakah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three lands for hazakah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for hazakah (presumptive ownership), the land is divided into three regions: Judea, Transjordan, and Galilee. If one was in Judea and claimed hazakah in Galilee, or vice versa, it is not valid unless the claimant was in the same province. Rabbi Yehuda adds that the three-year period accounts for time to travel and inform the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that for hazakah (presumptive ownership), the land is divided into three regions: Judea, Transjordan, and Galilee, and hazakah is invalid if the claimant was not in the same province.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that the three-year period accounts for time to travel and inform the owner, specifying that the owner must be in Aspamya (a distant location) for the hazakah to be valid.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Tanna Kamma's view
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Tanna Kamma's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does the Tanna Kamma hold? If protest not in the presence of the claimant is valid, then even Judea and Galilee should be valid; if not, even Judea and Judea should be invalid. Rabbi Abba bar Memel answers in the name of Rav that the Tanna Kamma holds protest not in the presence is valid, but the Mishnah was taught during a time of danger (חירום), and the mention of Judea and Galilee teaches that even in such times, one must be in the same province.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does the Tanna Kamma hold? If protest not in the presence of the claimant is valid (מחאה שלא בפניו הויא מחאה), then even Judea and Galilee should be valid; if not, even Judea and Judea should be invalid.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel answers in the name of Rav that the Tanna Kamma holds protest not in the presence is valid (מחאה שלא בפניו הויא מחאה), but the Mishnah was taught during a time of danger (חירום), and the mention of Judea and Galilee teaches that even in such times, one must be in the same province.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah teaches us that even during a time of danger, the requirement of being in the same province applies.

items.text: Opening statement: the status of Judea and Galilee
items.text_en: Opening statement: the status of Judea and Galilee
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general statement that Judea and Galilee are considered like a time of war, setting the context for the discussion of fugitives' property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general statement that Judea and Galilee are considered like a time of war, setting the context for the discussion of fugitives' property.

items.text: First version: Rav says no hazakah for fugitive's property
items.text_en: First version: Rav says no hazakah for fugitive's property
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah reports in Rav's name that one does not acquire fugitive property by hazakah. Shmuel objects, arguing that the owner cannot protest. The Gemara explains that Rav is merely explaining the Tanna's view, not his own.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah reports in Rav's name that one does not acquire fugitive property by hazakah (presumptive ownership).
Shmuel objects: why would the fugitive need to protest in person if he is unavailable?
The Gemara asks: what new point is Rav teaching us?
The Gemara explains that Rav is merely explaining the Tanna's reasoning, not stating his own view.

items.text: Second version: Rav says hazakah is valid for fugitive's property
items.text_en: Second version: Rav says hazakah is valid for fugitive's property
items.desc_en: An alternative version has Rav stating that one does acquire fugitive property by hazakah. Shmuel considers this obvious)Skip. The Gemara questions why Rav repeats himself, and explains that he teaches that a protest before two people who cannot inform the occupant is still valid. Rav Anan reports Shmuel's distinction between witnesses who can and cannot inform the occupant.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports Rav Yehudah citing Rav that one does acquire fugitive property by hazakah.
Shmuel objects that Rav's statement is obvious, since the fugitive cannot protest in person.
The Gemara questions what Rav is teaching, since he already stated that a protest not in the owner's presence is valid.
The Gemara explains that Rav teaches that even a protest before two witnesses who cannot inform the occupant is still valid.

Rav Anan reports Shmuel's distinction: a protest before witnesses who can inform the occupant is valid, but before those who cannot inform is not, and Rav holds that one's friend has a friend who can pass the message.

items.text: Rava's ruling: distinction between types of fugitives
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: distinction between types of fugitives
items.desc_en: Rava rules that one does not acquire fugitive property by hazakah, yet a protest not in the owner's presence is valid. He resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between a fugitive from financial matters and one from fear of persecution.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one cannot acquire fugitives' property by hazakah, and protest not in the owner's presence is valid.
The Gemara objects that Rava's two statements seem contradictory.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a fugitive from financial matters and a fugitive from persecution.

items.text: Definition of a valid protest
items.text_en: Definition of a valid protest
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid explains what constitutes a valid protest: saying 'So-and-so is a robber' is insufficient; one must specify that he holds the land through robbery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes a valid protest.
Rav Zevid answers that saying 'So-and-so is a robber' is not a valid protest, but specifying 'he holds my land by robbery' is.

items.text: Opening statement: A protest made with the phrase 'tomorrow I will sue him' is valid
items.text_en: Opening statement: A protest made with the phrase 'tomorrow I will sue him' is valid
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one says 'tomorrow I will sue him' in the context of a protest, it constitutes a valid protest (מחאה). This sets the stage for the discussion of what constitutes a valid protest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a protest made with the phrase 'tomorrow I will sue him' constitutes a valid protest (מחאה).

items.text: Dispute about the meaning of 'do not tell him' and similar phrases
items.text_en: Dispute about the meaning of 'do not tell him' and similar phrases
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa debate whether saying 'do not tell him' constitutes a valid protest. Rav Zevid holds it is a protest, while Rav Pappa argues it means only not to tell him directly, but others may be told, thus it is not a protest. Similar debates arise for 'we will not tell him' and 'do not go out to the market'. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that anything not on one's mind is said without intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether saying 'do not tell him' constitutes a valid protest.
Rav Zevid holds that saying 'do not tell him' is indeed a valid protest.
Rav Pappa argues that 'do not tell him' means only not to tell him directly, but others may be told, so it is not a valid protest.
The Gemara asks whether saying 'we will not tell him' constitutes a valid protest.
Rav Zevid holds that saying 'we will not tell him' is a valid protest.
Rav Pappa argues that 'we will not tell him' means only not to tell him directly, but others may be told, so it is not a valid protest.
The Gemara asks whether saying 'do not go out to the market' constitutes a valid protest.
Rav Zevid holds that saying 'do not go out to the market' is a valid protest.
The Gemara asks whether saying 'we will not go out to the market' constitutes a valid protest.
Rav Pappa holds that saying 'we will not go out to the market' is a valid protest.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds a general principle: anything not on one's mind is said without intent, explaining why such phrases may not constitute a valid protest.

items.text: Rava and Rav Nachman: Protest not in the presence of the possessor is valid, with an objection
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Nachman: Protest not in the presence of the possessor is valid, with an objection
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that a protest not made in the presence of the possessor is valid. Rava objects from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that the three-year period for hazakah includes time for the possessor to be in Spain and be informed, implying that protest must be in his presence. The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda merely teaches good advice to come and take land and produce.

sub.desc_en: Rava states in the name of Rav Nachman that a protest made not in the presence of the possessor (מחאה שלא בפניו) is a valid protest.

Rava raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says the three-year period for hazakah (חזקה) is calculated to allow time for the owner to be in Spain, for the possessor to hold for a year, for people to go inform the owner for a year, and for the owner to return for another year.
Rava argues: if a protest not in the possessor's presence is valid, why would the owner need to return? He could just sit there and protest.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita merely teaches good advice: that the owner should come and take the land and its produce, rather than relying on a protest alone.

items.text: Rava's change of opinion on protest not in the presence of the possessor
items.text_en: Rava's change of opinion on protest not in the presence of the possessor
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava initially objected to Rav Nachman's ruling, implying he did not accept it, but later Rava himself stated the same ruling. The Gemara explains that after hearing it from Rav Nachman, he accepted it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rava's objection that he initially did not accept that a protest not in the possessor's presence is valid.
The Gemara notes the contradiction: but Rava himself later stated that a protest not in the possessor's presence is valid.
The Gemara resolves that after Rava heard this ruling from Rav Nachman, he accepted it.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Avahu about the number of witnesses needed for a protest
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Avahu about the number of witnesses needed for a protest
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina asks Rabbi Yochanan's students about the number of witnesses required for a protest. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a protest requires two witnesses, while Rabbi Avahu says it requires three. The Gemara suggests they may be arguing about the principle of Rabba bar Rav Huna, who said that any matter said in front of three is not subject to false claims.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina asks Rabbi Yochanan's students how many witnesses Rabbi Yochanan required for a protest.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a protest requires two witnesses.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a protest requires three witnesses.

The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Avahu may be based on the principle of Rabba bar Rav Huna, that any matter stated before three people is not subject to false claims.

items.text: Debate on the number of witnesses needed for protest
items.text_en: Debate on the number of witnesses needed for protest
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers two possible explanations for the dispute between those who require protest before two witnesses and those who require three. One explanation is that they disagree about Rabba bar Rav Huna's principle; the other is that they disagree about whether protest must be in the presence of the squatter or whether testimony is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute about the number of witnesses needed for protest (מחאה) stems from disagreement over Rabba bar Rav Huna's principle.
The first answer rejects the question and explains that all agree on Rabba bar Rav Huna's principle, but they dispute whether protest must be in the squatter's presence.

The second answer offers an alternative explanation: all agree protest need not be in the squatter's presence, but they dispute whether testimony (סהדותא) or mere disclosure (גלויי מילתא) is required.

items.text: Story of Giddel bar Minyomei's protest
items.text_en: Story of Giddel bar Minyomei's protest
items.desc_en: Giddel bar Minyomei came to protest before Rav Huna, Chiyya bar Rav, and Rav Chilkiya bar Tovi. They told him that after the first protest, he need not protest again, citing Rav's ruling. An alternative version attributes this ruling to Chiyya bar Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Giddel bar Minyomei had protests to make and found Rav Huna, Chiyya bar Rav, and Rav Chilkiya bar Tovi sitting together, and he protested before them.

sub.text: Rav Huna, Chiyya bar Rav, and Rav Chilkiya bar Tovi
sub.text_en: Rav Huna, Chiyya bar Rav, and Rav Chilkiya bar Tovi
sub.desc_en: When Giddel returned the following year to protest again, they told him he need not, citing Rav's ruling that once he protested the first year, he need not protest again.
An alternative version attributes the ruling directly to Chiyya bar Rav, who told Giddel that after the first protest, he need not protest again.

items.text: Reish Lakish's ruling and Rabbi Yochanan's objection
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's ruling and Rabbi Yochanan's objection
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Bar Kappara rules that one must protest at the end of every three years. Rabbi Yochanan questions this, arguing that a robber cannot acquire through hazakah, but then clarifies that the case is like a robber (כגזלן).

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Bar Kappara rules that one must protest at the end of every three years.
Rabbi Yochanan objects: can a robber (גזלן) acquire through hazakah (חזקה)?
The gemara clarifies that the case is not a literal robber but one who is like a robber (כגזלן), and such a person does have hazakah.

items.text: Rava's ruling and Bar Kappara's baraitha
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and Bar Kappara's baraitha
items.desc_en: Rava rules that one must protest at the end of every three years. Bar Kappara's baraitha states that if a person repeatedly protests based on the same claim, the squatter does not acquire hazakah; otherwise, he does.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one must protest at the end of every three-year period to prevent hazakah.
Bar Kappara's baraitha teaches that if a person repeatedly protests based on the same claim, the squatter does not acquire hazakah; otherwise, he does.

items.text: Rava's citation of Rav Nachman on protest before two
items.text_en: Rava's citation of Rav Nachman on protest before two
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that a protest must be before two witnesses, beginning a new discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites Rav Nachman that a protest (מחאה) must be made before two witnesses.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rules for moda'a, hoda'a, kinyan, and validation of documents
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rules for moda'a, hoda'a, kinyan, and validation of documents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a moda'a requires two witnesses but does not require them to say 'write'; a hoda'a requires two witnesses and requires them to say 'write'; a kinyan requires two witnesses and does not require them to say 'write'; validation of documents requires three judges.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists four legal procedures: moda'a (declaration of duress) requires two witnesses but not the phrase 'write'; hoda'a (admission) requires two witnesses and the phrase 'write'; kinyan (acquisition) requires two witnesses but not the phrase 'write'; validation of documents requires three judges.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic) for the Mishnah
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic) for the Mishnah
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign 'ממה״ק' is provided to remember the order of the Mishnah's topics.

sub.desc_en: The gemara provides a mnemonic sign 'ממה״ק' to remember the order of the Mishnah's topics.

items.text: Rava's question and resolution about the kinyan
items.text_en: Rava's question and resolution about the kinyan
items.desc_en: Rava questions the nature of a kinyan: if it is like a court proceeding, it should require three judges; if not, why does it not require saying 'write'? He then resolves that a kinyan is not like a court proceeding, and the reason it does not require saying 'write' is because a standard kinyan is intended for writing.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions the nature of a kinyan: if it is like a court proceeding (מעשה בית דין), it should require three judges; if not, why does it not require saying 'write'?
Rava resolves that a kinyan is not like a court proceeding, and the reason it does not require saying 'write' is because a standard kinyan is intended for writing (סתם קנין לכתיבה עומד).

items.text: Dispute about writing a moda'a
items.text_en: Dispute about writing a moda'a
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef say a moda'a is only written for one who does not obey the court; Abaye and Rava say even for 'me and you' (i.e., even for a judge). The Nehardeans add a statement about moda'a.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that a moda'a (protest) is only written for one who does not obey the court.
Abaye and Rava argue that a moda'a is written even for 'me and you' (i.e., even for a judge).
The Nehardeans add a general statement about moda'a, likely supporting the broader application.

items.text: Opening statement on moda'a without mention of coercion
items.text_en: Opening statement on moda'a without mention of coercion
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a moda'a does not specify that the person was coerced, it is not a valid moda'a.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a moda'a (prior protest) that does not explicitly mention coercion is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's question and objection regarding moda'a
items.text_en: Gemara's question and objection regarding moda'a
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of a moda'a: for a get or gift it is merely revealing a matter, and for a sale, Rava said we do not write a moda'a for sales.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of document a moda'a is for: if for a get or gift, it is merely revealing a matter (and thus unnecessary).
The Gemara objects that if the moda'a is for a sale, Rava explicitly stated that we do not write a moda'a for sales.

items.text: Resolution: Rava's exception for coercion
items.text_en: Resolution: Rava's exception for coercion
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it refers to a sale where there is coercion, like the case of the orchard, where a moda'a is written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that Rava concedes a moda'a is written for sales involving coercion, as in the orchard case.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on a hidden gift
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on a hidden gift
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that a hidden gift (matana temirta) cannot be collected. Rav Yosef defines it as when the donor tells witnesses to hide and write, or alternatively, not to sit publicly. The difference between the two definitions is a case of stam (unspecified).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a hidden gift (מתנתא טמירתא) cannot be collected.
The Gemara asks what constitutes a hidden gift.
Rav Yosef defines a hidden gift as one where the donor tells witnesses to hide and write the document.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's definition
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's definition
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yosef defines a hidden gift as when the donor does not tell witnesses to sit publicly in the marketplace and write.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two definitions.
The Gemara resolves that the difference lies in a case of stam (unspecified) — where the donor merely says 'write' without further instructions.

items.text: Rava's statement on moda'a for another transaction
items.text_en: Rava's statement on moda'a for another transaction
items.desc_en: Rava says that a moda'a for one transaction serves as a moda'a for another. Rav Pappa notes that this was not stated explicitly but inferred from a case.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a moda'a (prior declaration of duress) for one transaction serves as a moda'a for another related transaction.
Rav Pappa notes that Rava's statement was not stated explicitly but was inferred from a case.

items.text: The case of the man who wrote all his property to his wife
items.text_en: The case of the man who wrote all his property to his wife
items.desc_en: A man wrote all his property to his wife under coercion, then told witnesses to hide and write for his son. Rava ruled that neither the wife nor the son acquired the property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a man, pressured by his prospective wife to write all his property to her, secretly instructs witnesses to hide and write a gift to his son.
The parties come before Rava, who rules that neither the wife nor the son acquired the property.

items.text: Distinguishing the case from Rava's principle
items.text_en: Distinguishing the case from Rava's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that observers might think the ruling was due to moda'a for another, but actually the wife's gift was coerced, while the son's gift was not, so the principle does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by explaining that in the wife's case the gift was clearly coerced, unlike the son's case, so Rava's principle does not apply.

items.text: A dilemma is raised
items.text_en: A dilemma is raised
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new unresolved question (iba'ya lehu) for discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new unresolved dilemma (אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ) for discussion.

items.text: Stam's question and ruling on chazakah
items.text_en: Stam's question and ruling on chazakah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether we are concerned about a potential claim (chazakah) without explicit assertion. Ravina and Rav Ashi debate, and the halakhah follows Rav Ashi that we are concerned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a claim without explicit assertion (סְתָמָא) is considered a valid chazakah.
Ravina rules that we are not concerned about a potential claim without explicit assertion.
Rav Ashi rules that we are concerned about a potential claim without explicit assertion.
The halakhah is decided in accordance with Rav Ashi that we are concerned.

items.text: Mishnah: Chazakah requires a claim
items.text_en: Mishnah: Chazakah requires a claim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any chazakah without a claim is invalid. Examples are given: a claim of 'no one ever objected' is insufficient, while claims of purchase, gift, or inheritance establish a chazakah. One who inherits needs no claim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that any chazakah (presumption of ownership) without a claim is invalid.
The Mishnah gives an example: if the occupant merely says 'no one ever objected,' the chazakah is invalid.
The Mishnah lists valid claims (purchase, gift, inheritance from father) that establish a chazakah.
The Mishnah concludes that one who inherits does not need a claim.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling is not obvious. It explains that one might think a person who claims 'no one ever objected' actually had a lost deed and is afraid to mention it, so the Mishnah teaches that we do not open his mouth for him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling is obvious (פשיטא).
The Gemara explains that one might think the claimant had a lost deed and is afraid to mention it, so the Mishnah teaches that we do not open his mouth for him (פתח פיך לאלם).

items.text: Siman (mnemonic)
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic)
items.desc_en: A mnemonic word 'עֵנָב' is given to mark the following stories.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a mnemonic word 'עֵנָב' to mark the following series of stories.

items.text: Story of Rav Anan and the fence
items.text_en: Story of Rav Anan and the fence
items.desc_en: Rav Anan built a fence on his neighbor's land. Rav Nachman ruled he must remove it. When Rav Anan claimed chazakah, Rav Nachman rejected it, citing that the halakhah does not follow Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael that immediate chazakah applies. When Rav Anan argued that the neighbor helped, Rav Nachman said it was a mistaken waiver.

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan built a fence on his neighbor's land; Rav Nachman ruled he must remove it.
Rav Anan claims he has a chazakah (presumption of ownership) over the land.
Rav Nachman rejects the claim, stating the halakhah does not follow Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael that immediate chazakah applies.
Rav Anan argues that the neighbor helped build the fence, implying a waiver of rights.
Rav Nachman explains that the waiver was mistaken, as neither party knew the land belonged to the neighbor.

items.text: Beginning of Rav Kahana's story
items.text_en: Beginning of Rav Kahana's story
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana took a palm branch in his field and built a fence on land not his own, setting up a similar case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana took a palm branch from his own field and built a fence on land not his own, setting up a case parallel to Rav Anan's.

items.text: Case of conflicting witnesses and Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Case of conflicting witnesses and Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: A person comes before Rav Yehuda with two witnesses who disagree on the number of measures (two or three). Rav Yehuda rules that the defendant must pay two out of three. The litigant questions this ruling, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on two sets of witnesses but disagree on one set. Rav Yehuda responds that he will consider a letter from the West that says the halakha is not like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

sub.desc_en: A person comes before Rav Yehuda with two witnesses who disagree on the number of measures (two or three), and Rav Yehuda rules that the defendant must pay two out of three.

The litigant questions Rav Yehuda's ruling, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on two sets of witnesses but disagree on one set, implying the ruling follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Rav Yehuda responds that he will consider a letter from the West that says the halakha is not like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and tells the litigant to wait for it.

items.text: Case of a squatter and Rabbi Chiyya's ruling
items.text_en: Case of a squatter and Rabbi Chiyya's ruling
items.desc_en: A man lived in an upper chamber for four years. The owner found him and the squatter claimed he bought it from someone who bought it from the owner. Rabbi Chiyya rules that if the squatter has witnesses that the seller lived there even one day, the court establishes the property in his hands; otherwise not.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a man lived in an upper chamber for four years, the owner found him, and the squatter claimed he bought it from someone who bought it from the owner.
Rabbi Chiyya rules that if the squatter has witnesses that the seller lived there even one day, the court establishes the property in his hands; otherwise not.

items.text: Rav's opinion on the squatter's claim
items.text_en: Rav's opinion on the squatter's claim
items.desc_en: Rav recounts sitting before his teacher and arguing that a person might buy and sell at night. He concludes that if the squatter says 'I bought it from you in front of me (the seller)', he is believed because he could have simply said 'I bought it from you'.

sub.desc_en: Rav recounts sitting before his teacher and arguing that a person might buy and sell at night.
Rav concludes that if the squatter says 'I bought it from you in front of me (the seller)', he is believed because he could have simply said 'I bought it from you'.

items.text: Rava's support for Rabbi Chiyya and the need for proof
items.text_en: Rava's support for Rabbi Chiyya and the need for proof
items.desc_en: Rava says the reasoning of Rabbi Chiyya is correct, citing a mishnah that one who comes through inheritance does not need a claim but does need proof. The Gemara questions whether proof is needed, and offers an alternative: a purchaser is different because he would not throw away his money for nothing.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Chiyya's reasoning is correct, citing a mishnah that one who comes through inheritance does not need a claim but does need proof.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the mishnah means neither proof nor claim is needed.
The Gemara offers an alternative: a purchaser is different because he would not throw away his money for nothing.

items.text: Dispute about 'appeared in it' (nir'ah bo)
items.text_en: Dispute about 'appeared in it' (nir'ah bo)
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if the seller was seen on the land (nir'ah bo), what is the law? Abaye says it is the same (as living there). Rava says a person might walk his land and not sell it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if the seller was seen on the land (נִרְאָה בּוֹ), what is the law regarding a claim of hazakah?
Abaye rules that being seen on the land is the same as living there for establishing hazakah.
Rava argues that a person might walk his land without intending to sell it, so being seen does not establish hazakah.

items.text: Three purchasers combine and Rav's view on documents
items.text_en: Three purchasers combine and Rav's view on documents
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that three purchasers combine (for hazakah). Rav says all require a document. The Gemara questions whether Rav holds that a document has publicity (kala) but witnesses do not, citing a contradiction from Rav's own ruling that a sale by witnesses allows collection from liened property. The Gemara distinguishes: there, purchasers (are different).

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that three purchasers combine (for hazakah).
Rav rules that all three purchasers require a document (שטר) for their hazakah to combine.
The Gemara questions whether Rav holds that a document has publicity (קלא) but witnesses do not.
The Gemara objects by citing Rav's own ruling that a sale by witnesses allows collection from liened property, implying witnesses do have publicity.
The Gemara distinguishes: there, purchasers (are different, so the case of witnesses suffices).

items.text: Conclusion of previous argument
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the buyers (the purchasers) caused their own loss by not protesting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the buyers caused their own loss by not protesting.

items.text: Distinction between loan and sale regarding publicity
items.text_en: Distinction between loan and sale regarding publicity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's statement by citing a Mishnah that a loan with witnesses only collects from unencumbered property, implying no publicity. It then distinguishes: a loan is done discreetly to avoid devaluing assets, while a sale is done publicly to generate a reputation (קלא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's statement by citing a Mishnah that a loan with witnesses collects only from unencumbered property, implying no publicity.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rav is a Tanna disputing the Mishnah, citing that both Rav and Shmuel agree an oral loan does not collect from heirs or buyers.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: a loan is done discreetly (בצנעא) to avoid devaluing assets, while a sale is done publicly (בפרהסיא) to generate a reputation (קלא).

items.text: Baraita on cumulative possession and contradiction
items.text_en: Baraita on cumulative possession and contradiction
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught: if the father, son, and buyer each possessed the land for a year, it constitutes a chazakah. The Gemara objects: if a buyer has publicity (קלא), then the owner's silence is the greatest protest, so why is this a valid chazakah?

sub.desc_en: A baraita (תנו רבנן) teaches that cumulative possession by father, son, and buyer over three years constitutes a valid chazakah (חזקה).
The Gemara objects: if a buyer has publicity (קלא), then the owner's silence is the greatest protest, so why is this a valid chazakah?

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction: the baraita refers to a case where the seller sold his fields without specification (סתם), so the buyer does not have full publicity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by stating that the baraita refers to a case where the seller sold his fields without specification (סתם), so the buyer does not have full publicity.

items.text: Mishnah: Those who cannot establish a chazakah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who cannot establish a chazakah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists categories of people who cannot establish a chazakah: craftsmen, partners, sharecroppers, guardians, a husband in his wife's property, a wife in her husband's, a father in his son's, and a son in his father's. However, for gifts, divided brothers, and a possessor of a convert's property, any minimal act establishes a chazakah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists categories of people who cannot establish a chazakah (חזקה, presumptive ownership) through possession: craftsmen, partners, sharecroppers, guardians, a husband in his wife's property, a wife in her husband's, a father in his son's, and a son in his father's.

The Mishnah adds an exception: for gifts, divided brothers, and a possessor of a convert's property, any minimal act such as locking, fencing, or breaching establishes a chazakah (חזקה, presumptive ownership).

items.text: Opening dispute: partner's chazakah
items.text_en: Opening dispute: partner's chazakah
items.desc_en: The father of Shmuel and Levi teach that a partner has no chazakah, and certainly a craftsman. Shmuel teaches that a craftsman has no chazakah, but a partner does have chazakah, consistent with his view that partners can establish chazakah against each other, testify for each other, and become paid watchmen for each other.

sub.text: Tannaic teaching (Father of Shmuel and Levi)
sub.text_en: Tannaic teaching (Father of Shmuel and Levi)
sub.desc_en: The father of Shmuel and Levi teach that a partner has no chazakah (presumption of ownership), and certainly a craftsman has none.
Shmuel teaches that a craftsman has no chazakah, but a partner does have chazakah.
The gemara notes that Shmuel's ruling is consistent with his general view that partners can establish chazakah against each other, testify for each other, and become paid watchmen for each other.

items.text: Gemara's question and first resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and first resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba raises a contradiction to Rav Yehuda: Shmuel said a partner has chazakah, but also said a partner is like one who descends with permission, implying no chazakah. The Gemara resolves: the latter refers to one who entered the entire field, the former to one who entered half.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba raises a contradiction to Rav Yehuda: Shmuel said a partner has chazakah, but also said a partner is like one who descends with permission, implying no chazakah.
The Gemara resolves: the latter refers to one who entered the entire field, the former to one who entered half.

items.text: Alternative attribution of the resolution
items.text_en: Alternative attribution of the resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the resolution is attributed to one side or the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the resolution is alternatively attributed to one side or the other.

items.text: Ravina's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Ravina says both cases are where he entered the entire field, but the distinction is whether the field is subject to division (דין חלוקה) or not.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by asserting that both cases involve entering the entire field, but the distinction lies in whether the field is subject to division (דין חלוקה) or not.

items.text: Gemara's question on Shmuel's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Shmuel's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Shmuel said a partner is like one who descends with permission – what does this teach? If it means a partner has no chazakah, why not just say that directly?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's statement that a partner is like one who descends with permission, asking why he did not simply state directly that a partner has no chazakah.

items.text: Rav Nachman's answer: taking the increase
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer: taking the increase
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh explains: Shmuel's statement teaches that a partner takes the increase that reaches the shoulders, in a field not planted but treated as if planted.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh explains that Shmuel's statement teaches that a partner takes the increase that reaches the shoulders, in a field not planted but treated as if planted.

items.text: Continuation: partners testify for each other
items.text_en: Continuation: partners testify for each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds that partners can testify for each other, as part of Shmuel's earlier statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara appends that partners may testify for each other, completing Shmuel's earlier ruling.

items.text: Opening question: Why can the seller testify?
items.text_en: Opening question: Why can the seller testify?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the seller is allowed to testify about the field, since he might be biased (a witness with personal interest is disqualified).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the seller is allowed to testify about the field, since he might be biased (a witness with personal interest is disqualified).

items.text: First answer: He waived all claims
items.text_en: First answer: He waived all claims
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the seller wrote a document stating he has no claims on the field, but a baraita rules such a statement is ineffective unless formal acquisition (kinyan) is made.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the seller wrote a document waiving all claims, but a baraita rules such a statement is ineffective without formal acquisition (קִנְיָן).

items.text: Second answer: With kinyan, but still problematic
items.text_en: Second answer: With kinyan, but still problematic
items.desc_en: The Gemara says the case involves a kinyan, but even then the seller might still be interested because he could be sued by a creditor, as per Ravin bar Shmuel's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case involves a formal kinyan (acquisition) from the seller.
The Gemara objects that even with a kinyan, the seller might still be interested because he could be sued by a creditor, citing Ravin bar Shmuel's ruling in Shmuel's name.

items.text: Third answer: Seller accepted responsibility
items.text_en: Third answer: Seller accepted responsibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the seller accepted responsibility (achrayut) for claims arising from his own actions, which removes his interest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the case involves a seller who accepted responsibility (אחריות) only for claims arising from his own actions, thereby removing his disqualifying interest.

items.text: Objection: Even with self-removal, interest remains?
items.text_en: Objection: Even with self-removal, interest remains?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita about a stolen Torah scroll: even if two people recuse themselves, they cannot judge, because the Torah is for public benefit. The Gemara distinguishes the case of a Torah scroll due to its public nature.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the judge recuses himself, he remains a stakeholder, citing a baraita about a stolen Torah scroll where recusal does not help because the Torah is for public benefit.
The Gemara distinguishes the case of a Torah scroll because it is designated for public reading, so recusal does not remove the public interest.

items.text: Second objection: Case of 'give a maneh to my townspeople'
items.text_en: Second objection: Case of 'give a maneh to my townspeople'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita where townspeople cannot judge, and the answer is again that it involves a Torah scroll.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita about a man who says 'give a maneh to my townspeople,' where the townspeople cannot judge or testify, challenging the earlier resolution.
The Gemara answers that here too the case involves a Torah scroll, which is why the townspeople are disqualified.

items.text: Third objection: Case of 'give a maneh to the poor of my city'
items.text_en: Third objection: Case of 'give a maneh to the poor of my city'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about poor people, corrects the text to refer to poor judges, and answers that it also involves a Torah scroll, as everyone is 'poor' relative to Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about one who says 'give a maneh to the poor of my city' and notes that the judges and witnesses of that city are disqualified, raising the objection that they could simply recuse themselves.

The Gemara objects that the baraita cannot be about poor recipients disqualifying judges, since the poor are the recipients not the judges, and corrects the text to refer to 'poor judges' of that city.
The Gemara asks why the poor judges cannot simply recuse themselves from the case and then judge.
The Gemara answers that the case also involves a Torah scroll, and the judges are called 'poor' because everyone is considered poor relative to the Torah.

items.text: Alternative answer: Real poor with fixed allowance
items.text_en: Alternative answer: Real poor with fixed allowance
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the poor are real, but they have a fixed allowance; if they recuse themselves, they lose nothing, so they can judge. If the allowance is not fixed, they cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative: the poor are real poor, but they have a fixed allowance (קיץ) from the charity fund.
The Gemara questions: if the allowance is fixed, why can't two of them recuse themselves by giving up their allowance and then judge?
The Gemara answers: the case is where the allowance is not fixed, so they cannot recuse themselves without losing their livelihood.
The Gemara offers another resolution: even if the allowance is fixed, the poor are satisfied with it, so once they recuse themselves they lose nothing and can judge.

items.text: Conclusion: They become paid guards for each other
items.text_en: Conclusion: They become paid guards for each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the seller and buyer become paid guards for each other, which resolves the conflict of interest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the seller and buyer become paid guards (שומרי שכר) for each other, resolving the conflict of interest.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a seller cannot testify about a field he sold, given that his responsibility for it makes him a partial owner. Rav Pappa explains that the seller might have said 'Guard for me today and I will guard for you tomorrow,' creating a reciprocal obligation that disqualifies him as a witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a seller cannot testify about a field he sold, given that his responsibility for it makes him a partial owner (שְׁמִירָה בִּבְעָלִים).
Rav Pappa explains that the seller might have said 'Guard for me today and I will guard for you tomorrow,' creating a reciprocal obligation that disqualifies him as a witness.

items.text: Baraita contrasting land and movable property
items.text_en: Baraita contrasting land and movable property
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one sells a house or field, he cannot testify about it because he bears responsibility for it; but if he sells an ox or garment, he can testify. The Gemara asks what distinguishes the two cases.

sub.desc_en: A baraita (תנו רבנן) rules that one who sold a house or field cannot testify about it because he bears responsibility (אחריות), but one who sold an ox or garment can testify because he bears no responsibility.
The Gemara asks what distinguishes the first case (land) from the second case (movable property) to justify the different rule.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's first explanation: stolen field scenario
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's first explanation: stolen field scenario
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the case involves Reuven who stole a field from Shimon and sold it to Levi, and then Yehuda challenges Levi's ownership. Shimon cannot testify for Levi because he prefers the field to return to him (the original owner) rather than remain with Levi. The Gemara objects that if Shimon testifies that Levi owns it, how can he later take it from him? The answer is that Shimon claims 'the second (Yehuda) is preferable to me; the first (Levi) is more difficult for me.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the first clause involves Reuven who stole a field from Shimon and sold it to Levi, and Yehuda challenges; Shimon cannot testify for Levi because he prefers the field to return to him.
The Gemara objects: if Shimon testifies that the field belongs to Levi, how can he later take it from him? The same testimony that removes it from Levi should also remove it from Yehuda.

The Gemara answers that Shimon claims 'the second (Yehuda) is preferable to me; the first (Levi) is more difficult for me,' meaning he prefers the field to go to Yehuda rather than remain with the thief Levi.

items.text: Alternative explanation: equal witnesses
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: equal witnesses
items.desc_en: Alternatively, the case is where each party has witnesses, and the Sages rule that the land remains where it is (i.e., the status quo is maintained).

sub.desc_en: The gemara offers an alternative explanation: each party has witnesses, so the Sages rule that the land remains in its current status quo (הֵיכָא דְּקַיְימָא – תֵּיקוּם).

items.text: Gemara's question: Why specifically a robber?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why specifically a robber?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a robber (גזלן) rather than a thief, implying a need to justify the choice of case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a robber (גזלן) rather than a thief, implying a need to justify the choice of case.

items.text: Answer: Because of the seifa's implication
items.text_en: Answer: Because of the seifa's implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah uses a robber because the seifa (later clause) distinguishes between sale (which involves יאוש ושינוי רשות) and no sale (where the item returns), so the reisha also discusses sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah uses a robber because the seifa (later clause) distinguishes between sale (which involves יאוש ושינוי רשות) and no sale (where the item returns), so the reisha also discusses sale.

items.text: Objection: What about the proceeds?
items.text_en: Objection: What about the proceeds?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the robber despairs of the object itself, he does not despair of its monetary value, so the Mishnah's case is still problematic; it resolves by citing a Mishnah about a robber who dies and leaves the stolen item to his children, who are exempt from payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the robber despairs of the object itself (גּוּפַיהּ), he does not despair of its monetary value (דְּמֶיהָ), so the Mishnah's case remains problematic.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to a case where the robber died, citing a Mishnah that if a robber feeds his children the stolen item and leaves it to them, they are exempt from payment.

items.text: Alternative: Why not an heir?
items.text_en: Alternative: Why not an heir?
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case could be about an heir (יורש) rather than a robber, but notes this works only for the opinion that an heir's possession is not like a buyer's; for the opposing opinion, the question remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative: why not interpret the Mishnah's case as involving an heir (יורש) rather than a robber?

The Gemara explains that this works only for the opinion that an heir's possession (רשות יורש) is not like a buyer's possession; for the opposing opinion that it is like a buyer's, the question remains unresolved.

items.text: Abaye's difficulty with the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Abaye's difficulty with the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Abaye questions why the Mishnah uses the phrase 'because his responsibility is upon him' and 'his responsibility is not upon him' instead of 'because it returns to him' and 'it does not return to him', pointing to a textual inconsistency.

sub.desc_en: Abaye questions why the Mishnah uses the phrase 'because his responsibility is upon him' and 'his responsibility is not upon him' instead of 'because it returns to him' and 'it does not return to him', pointing to a textual inconsistency.

items.text: Resolution via Ravin bar Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Resolution via Ravin bar Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the issue by citing Ravin bar Shmuel in the name of Shmuel: one who sells a field without responsibility cannot testify about it because the seller can place it before his creditor; this applies only to land, not to movable property like a cow or cloak.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Ravin bar Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Ravin bar Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the issue by citing Ravin bar Shmuel in the name of Shmuel: one who sells a field without אחריות (responsibility) cannot testify about it because the seller can place it before his creditor.
The Gemara clarifies that this ruling applies specifically to land (בית or שדה), but not to movable property like a cow or cloak.

items.text: Gemara's question on movables and Rava's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's question on movables and Rava's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why movables are not subject to a lien even if specified in the contract, and cites Rava's distinction: a slave made an apotheke (collateral) and sold is recoverable by the creditor, but an ox or donkey is not, because the latter lacks publicity (קלא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why movables are not subject to a lien even if specified in the contract, and explains that this applies only when the movables are still in existence, but not when they are gone.
The Gemara objects that even if the debtor made the movables explicit collateral (אפותיקי), the creditor still cannot recover them, and asks for the reason.
Rava answers that a slave made explicit collateral and sold is recoverable by the creditor because it has publicity (קלא), but an ox or donkey lacks such publicity and is not recoverable.

items.text: Concern about acquisition via land and Rabba's ruling
items.text_en: Concern about acquisition via land and Rabba's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the seller might have acquired the movables together with land, citing Rabba's rule that acquiring land with movables transfers the movables, and Rav Chisda's condition that the document must state it is not an asmachta or a standard form.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the seller might have transferred the movables to the creditor via acquisition together with land (אגב מקרקעי), citing Rabba's rule that acquiring land with movables transfers the movables.
Rav Chisda adds that Rabba's rule applies only if the document explicitly states it is not an asmachta (a sham transaction) and not a standard form.

items.text: Resolution: case of immediate resale
items.text_en: Resolution: case of immediate resale
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the concern by stating that the case involves a buyer who purchased and immediately resold the land, so there was no opportunity to acquire movables with it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the concern by stating that the case involves a buyer who purchased and immediately resold the land, so there was no opportunity to acquire movables with it.

items.text: Further concern about prior acquisition and witness testimony
items.text_en: Further concern about prior acquisition and witness testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the seller might have acquired the movables earlier (דאיקני) and then sold the land, and answers that witnesses testify the seller never owned land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the seller might have acquired the movables after the loan (דאיקני) and then sold the land, questioning whether such property is not subject to the lien.
The Gemara answers that the case is where witnesses testify that the seller never owned land at all, so the concern about דאיקני (future acquisition) is irrelevant.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling on selling without warranty and Rav Zevid's dispute
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling on selling without warranty and Rav Zevid's dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that if a field sold without warranty is seized by a creditor, the seller is not liable, but if the field is found not to be his, the seller is liable. Rav Zevid disagrees, arguing that selling without warranty exempts the seller even in that case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Pappa's ruling that selling a field without warranty exempts the seller from liability if a creditor seizes it, but if the field is found not to be the seller's, the seller is liable.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a seller who recognizes the field as one that was previously his donkey's burden (i.e., he knows it was stolen from him).
Rav Zevid objects, arguing that even if the field is found not to be the seller's, selling without warranty exempts the seller, as the buyer was told 'I sold you without warranty.'

items.text: Ravin bar Shmuel's statement on witnesses for a field sold without warranty
items.text_en: Ravin bar Shmuel's statement on witnesses for a field sold without warranty
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Shmuel quotes Shmuel: one who sells a field without warranty cannot testify about it because he would be protecting it from his own creditor. The Gemara then asks for clarification of the scenario.

sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Shmuel cites Shmuel's ruling: one who sells a field without warranty cannot testify about it, because he would be protecting it from his own creditor.
The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances of this case?

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the seller's liability
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the seller's liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling: if the seller has other land, the buyer can collect from it; if not, what does the buyer gain? It answers that even without other land, the seller avoids being called a 'wicked borrower who does not pay' by selling without responsibility.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling: if the seller has other land, the buyer can collect from it; if not, what does the buyer gain from the sale?
