The Gemara answers that even without other land, the seller avoids being called a 'wicked borrower who does not pay' by selling without responsibility.

items.text: Rava's (or Rav Pappa's) ruling on a donkey seized by a gentile
items.text_en: Rava's (or Rav Pappa's) ruling on a donkey seized by a gentile
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Pappa) announces a ruling: if a Jew buys a donkey from a fellow Jew and a gentile seizes it, the seller must compensate the buyer. This applies only if the buyer does not recognize the donkey as the seller's, and if the gentile did not also seize the seller's own property. Amemar adds that even without these conditions, the seller is liable because a gentile is presumed to be a robber.

sub.text: Rava (or Rav Pappa) announces a ruling
sub.text_en: Rava (or Rav Pappa) announces a ruling
sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Pappa) announces that if a Jew buys a donkey from a fellow Jew and a gentile seizes it, the seller must compensate the buyer.
The Gemara qualifies the ruling: it applies only if the buyer does not recognize the donkey as the seller's, and if the gentile did not also seize the seller's own property.
Amemar adds that even without these conditions, the seller is liable because a gentile is presumed to be a robber, as the verse says 'their right hand is a right hand of falsehood'.

items.text: Rabba and Abaye debate the craftsman's presumptive ownership
items.text_en: Rabba and Abaye debate the craftsman's presumptive ownership
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the Mishnah's rule that a craftsman has no presumptive ownership (חזקה). Rabba says this applies only if the owner gave the item to the craftsman in front of witnesses; otherwise, the craftsman can claim he bought it. Abaye objects: even with witnesses, the craftsman could claim he returned it. Rabba begins to respond.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that a craftsman has no presumptive ownership (חזקה).

Rabba explains that the Mishnah's rule applies only when the owner gave the item to the craftsman in front of witnesses (בעדים); without witnesses, the craftsman can claim he bought it because he could otherwise deny the transaction entirely.
Abaye objects that even with witnesses, the craftsman could claim he returned the item, so he should still be believed to claim he bought it.
Rabba begins to respond to Abaye's objection, but the Gemara cuts off his statement.

items.text: Gemara's initial question about returning a deposit
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question about returning a deposit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one deposits an item with another in front of witnesses, must it be returned in front of witnesses? It rejects the possibility that it does not require witnesses, concluding that it does require witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one who deposits an item with another in front of witnesses must return it in front of witnesses.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that witnesses are not required and concludes that return must be in front of witnesses.

items.text: Abaye's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita: if one sees his slave with a craftsman or his garment with a launderer, and the craftsman claims he bought it or received it as a gift, his words are meaningless. But if the craftsman says 'In my presence you told him to sell or give it to me,' his words stand.

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises an objection from a baraita: if one sees his slave with a craftsman or his garment with a launderer, the craftsman's claim of purchase or gift is meaningless unless he says 'In my presence you told him to sell or give it to me,' in which case his words stand.

items.text: Gemara's question on the baraita's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the baraita's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the difference between the first case (where the craftsman's claim is rejected) and the second case (where it is accepted)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the first case of the baraita (where the craftsman's claim is rejected) from the second case (where it is accepted).

items.text: Rabbah's answer: the principle of migo
items.text_en: Rabbah's answer: the principle of migo
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains: the second case involves an item that came from another person's possession, and the craftsman says 'In my presence you told him to sell it.' Since the craftsman could have claimed 'I bought it from you' (and would be believed due to possession), he is also believed when he says 'In my presence you told him to sell it' — this is the principle of migo.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the second case involves an item that came from another person's possession, and the craftsman says 'In my presence you told him to sell it'; since the craftsman could have claimed 'I bought it from you' (and would be believed due to possession), he is also believed when he says 'In my presence you told him to sell it' — this is the principle of מיגו (a claim that is credible because a stronger claim would also have been credible).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the first case: witnesses or not?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the first case: witnesses or not?
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the first case of the baraita: 'He saw.' If there are witnesses, why mention seeing? Let him bring witnesses! Rather, it must be that there are no witnesses, and seeing alone gives him a claim of possession.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the first case of the baraita: if there are witnesses, why mention seeing? Let him bring witnesses and take the object.
The Gemara answers that there are no witnesses, and seeing alone gives him a claim of possession.

items.text: Refutation and retraction
items.text_en: Refutation and retraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: no, it always means there are witnesses, and he saw them. But you yourself said that a deposit with witnesses requires return with witnesses! The interlocutor responds: I retract that statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case always involves witnesses and the owner saw them, but then challenges: you yourself said that a deposit with witnesses requires return with witnesses.
The interlocutor retracts his earlier statement, conceding the objection.

items.text: Rava's support for Rabbah from a baraita on a craftsman
items.text_en: Rava's support for Rabbah from a baraita on a craftsman
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita to support Rabbah: one who gives his garment to a craftsman, and the craftsman claims he cut two (lengths) while the owner says only one. While the garment is in the craftsman's hand, the burden of proof is on the owner. After it is returned, if within the time, the craftsman swears and takes; if time passed, the burden is on the claimant. The Gemara asks: if there are witnesses, let them testify!

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita to support Rabbah: a craftsman who claims he cut two lengths while the owner says only one; while the garment is in the craftsman's hand the burden is on the owner, after return within the time the craftsman swears and takes, after time the burden is on the claimant.
The Gemara asks: if there are witnesses, let them testify — what do they say?

items.text: Defense of Rava's position
items.text_en: Defense of Rava's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara defends Rava's earlier ruling that an artisan is believed about his fee when there are no witnesses, but only if the artisan did not see the owner using the item. This resolves the previous challenge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's position by inferring that the baraita must be discussing a case without witnesses, yet the artisan is believed about his fee due to the מיגו (coherent claim) that he could have claimed the item was purchased.
The Gemara defends Rava by clarifying that the baraita indeed deals with a case without witnesses, but the artisan's credibility is limited to when he did not see the owner using the item.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita: an artisan has no presumptive ownership
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita: an artisan has no presumptive ownership
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita stating that an artisan has no presumptive ownership (חזקה) over an item, implying others do. The Gemara analyzes the case: if there are witnesses, why would others have a claim? It concludes that the baraita contradicts Rava, and declares the challenge a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita that an artisan has no presumptive ownership (חזקה), implying others do, to challenge Rava's position.
The Gemara questions the baraita's scenario: if there are witnesses, why would another person have presumptive ownership?
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must refer to a case without witnesses, and thus it refutes Rava's position.

items.text: Baraita on swapped vessels in different settings
items.text_en: Baraita on swapped vessels in different settings
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught: if vessels were swapped in an artisan's house, the artisan may use them until the owner comes; but in a house of mourning or a wedding feast, he may not. The Gemara asks why the ruling differs between the two cases.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if vessels were swapped in an artisan's house, the artisan may use them until the owner comes; but in a house of mourning or a wedding feast, he may not.
The Gemara asks why the ruling differs between the artisan's house and the house of mourning or wedding feast.

items.text: Rav's explanation: the artisan is assumed to have bought the item
items.text_en: Rav's explanation: the artisan is assumed to have bought the item
items.desc_en: Rav reports that his teacher (Chabibi) explained the distinction: in the artisan's house, the owner might have told the artisan to sell the item for him, so the artisan is believed; but in a house of mourning or wedding, people do not give such instructions.

sub.desc_en: Rav reports that his teacher Chabibi explained the distinction in the baraita: an owner is likely to tell an artisan 'sell my cloak for me,' so the artisan is believed, but this does not apply in a house of mourning or wedding.

items.text: Limitation: only the artisan, and only when unspecified
items.text_en: Limitation: only the artisan, and only when unspecified
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Nachman limits the ruling: only the artisan himself, not his wife or children, may use the swapped item; and only if the owner said 'a cloak' (סתם), not 'your cloak' (טליתְךָ), which would indicate the artisan's own cloak.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Nachman limits the ruling to the artisan himself, excluding his wife and children.
Rav Chiyya bar Rav Nachman further limits the ruling: only when the owner said 'a cloak' (סתם), not 'your cloak' (טליתְךָ), which would indicate the artisan's own cloak.

items.text: Abaye's story of the Pumbeditan tricksters and Rava's approval
items.text_en: Abaye's story of the Pumbeditan tricksters and Rava's approval
items.desc_en: Abaye tells Rava about a Pumbeditan debtor who, when asked for a garment, denies ever having it, then claims that witnesses saw a different garment, and refuses to produce it. Rava approves the debtor's response as valid.

sub.desc_en: Abaye invites Rava to observe the deceptive tactics of the Pumbeditan tricksters.
The debtor first denies ever having the garment when asked for it.
When confronted with witnesses who saw a garment in his possession, the debtor claims it was a different garment.
When asked to produce the garment for inspection, the debtor refuses to bring it out.
Rava approves the debtor's response as valid, concluding the story.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation of the Mishnah's term 'ra'ah'
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of the Mishnah's term 'ra'ah'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that if the claimant is clever, he can use the term 'ra'ah' (saw) to argue that the possessor must have seen the property and thus has a claim. Rav Acha bar Rav Avya objects that the possessor can refuse the valuation, saying earlier courts already valued it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah's term 'רָאָה' (saw) as the basis for discussion.
Rav Ashi explains that a clever claimant can use the term 'רָאָה' to argue that the possessor must have seen the property and thus has a claim, proposing a mutual valuation.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya objects that the possessor can refuse the valuation, claiming earlier courts already valued it.

items.text: The rule that an aris has no hazakah
items.text_en: The rule that an aris has no hazakah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an aris (sharecropper) has no hazakah. The Gemara questions why, since he now possesses the entire field whereas before he only had a share. Rabbi Yochanan answers that this applies to arisim of ancestral homes (where the aris is a family member).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an aris (sharecropper) has no hazakah (presumption of ownership).
The Gemara questions why the aris has no hazakah, given that he now possesses the entire field whereas before he only had a share.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Mishnah's rule applies specifically to arisim of ancestral homes (בתי אבות), where the aris is a family member and thus his possession is not considered a hazakah.

items.text: Rav Nachman: An aris who appoints other arisim has hazakah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman: An aris who appoints other arisim has hazakah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that if an aris brings in other arisim under him, he does have hazakah, because a person would not remain silent while others work his land without protest.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that an aris who brings in other arisim under him does have hazakah.
Rav Nachman explains the reason: a person would not remain silent while others work his land without protest.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: An aris who divides the field among arisim has no hazakah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: An aris who divides the field among arisim has no hazakah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that if an aris divides the field among other arisim, he has no hazakah, because it is presumed that he merely appointed them as managers (harmanya).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that an aris who divides the field among other arisim has no hazakah.
The Gemara explains the reason: it is presumed that the aris merely appointed them as managers (הרמניא).

items.text: The question of whether an aris can testify
items.text_en: The question of whether an aris can testify
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda asks Rav Nachman bar Yaakov whether an aris can testify. Rav Yosef reports Shmuel's ruling that an aris may testify, but a baraisa states he cannot. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if there is fruit in the field, he is disqualified due to interest; if not, he may testify.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's question
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda sends a query to Rav Nachman bar Yaakov asking whether an aris (sharecropper) may testify.
Rav Yosef, sitting before Rav Nachman bar Yaakov, reports that Shmuel ruled an aris may testify.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraisa that states an aris may not testify.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if there is fruit in the field, the aris is disqualified due to interest; if not, he may testify.

items.text: Testimony of a guarantor, lender, and first buyer
items.text_en: Testimony of a guarantor, lender, and first buyer
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that a guarantor may testify for the borrower, a lender for the borrower, and a first buyer for a second buyer, provided each has other land (so they are not suspected of lying to protect their own interest).

sub.desc_en: The baraisa opens by stating that a guarantor may testify for the borrower, provided the guarantor has other land.
The baraisa continues that a lender may testify for the borrower, provided the lender has other land.
The baraisa concludes that a first buyer may testify for a second buyer, provided the first buyer has other land.

items.text: Dispute about a קבלן's testimony
items.text_en: Dispute about a קבלן's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute about whether a קבלן (a contractor who collects debts) can testify. One view compares him to a guarantor (ערב) who can testify, while the other argues he cannot because he benefits from having both the debtor and the property in his hands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute about whether a קבלן (contractor who collects debts) can testify, with two opinions: one says he may testify, the other says he may not.
The first opinion compares the קבלן to a guarantor (ערב), who is permitted to testify.
The second opinion argues the קבלן cannot testify because he benefits from having both the debtor and the property in his hands, so he can take whatever he wants when the creditor comes.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on chazakah for craftsman, tenant, and robber
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on chazakah for craftsman, tenant, and robber
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a craftsman (אומן) and a tenant farmer (אריס) have no chazakah, but their sons do. A robber (גזלן) and his son have no chazakah, but the robber's grandson does.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a craftsman (אומן) and a tenant farmer (אריס) have no chazakah, but their sons do; a robber (גזלן) and his son have no chazakah, but the robber's grandson does.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution regarding the distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution regarding the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the distinction: if descendants claim based on their father's right, even the grandson should not have chazakah; if they claim independently, even the son of a robber should. It resolves that the case involves witnesses saying the robber admitted in their presence, but the robber's admission is not trusted due to Rabbi Kahana's principle that he would admit to avoid a greater loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the distinction: if descendants claim based on their father's right, even the grandson should not have chazakah; if they claim independently, even the son of a robber should.

The Gemara resolves that the case involves witnesses saying the robber admitted in their presence, but the robber's admission is not trusted due to Rabbi Kahana's principle that he would admit to avoid a greater loss.

items.text: Rava's qualification: even the grandson may lack chazakah
items.text_en: Rava's qualification: even the grandson may lack chazakah
items.desc_en: Rava adds that sometimes even the robber's grandson has no chazakah, specifically when he claims based on his grandfather's right (the robber).

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces a qualification: even the robber's grandson may lack chazakah when he claims based on his grandfather's right.

items.text: Definitions of a robber (גזלן)
items.text_en: Definitions of a robber (גזלן)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines a robber as one who has been established as having robbed this specific field. Rav Chisda defines him as one from a household that kills people over money matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What are the circumstances that define a robber (גזלן) for the purpose of the rule that a robber has no presumptive ownership (חזקה)?
Rabbi Yochanan defines a robber as one who has been established by witnesses as having robbed this specific field.
Rav Chisda defines a robber as a member of a household known to kill people over money matters, even if not proven to have robbed this specific field.

items.text: Baraita on craftsman, tenant, son who divided, and divorced woman
items.text_en: Baraita on craftsman, tenant, son who divided, and divorced woman
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a craftsman and tenant have no chazakah, but if they leave their profession, they do. A son who divided property and a divorced woman are like any other person. The Gemara explains the necessity of the baraita for the son who divided (lest one think he waived his rights) and questions why the divorced woman is mentioned, concluding it is needed for a case where she was divorced and remarried.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that a craftsman and tenant have no chazakah (presumption of ownership) while in their profession, but if they leave it they do, and a son who divided property or a divorced woman are like any other person.
The Gemara explains why the case of a son who divided property is necessary in the baraita, as one might have thought he waived his rights, but the baraita teaches that he did not.
The Gemara questions why a divorced woman is mentioned in the baraita, since it seems obvious, and concludes it is necessary for a specific case.

items.text: Opening reference to the case of a doubtfully divorced woman
items.text_en: Opening reference to the case of a doubtfully divorced woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept of a woman who is 'divorced and not divorced,' citing Rabbi Zeira's statement that in such cases the husband is liable for her sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of a woman who is 'divorced and not divorced' (מגורשת ואינה מגורשת), citing Rabbi Zeira's tradition from Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Shmuel that in all such cases the husband is liable for her sustenance.

items.text: Rav Nachman's distinction between a robber and other litigants
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's distinction between a robber and other litigants
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in the name of Huna that all litigants who bring evidence have their evidence accepted and the field is placed in their hands, but a robber who brings evidence does not have his evidence accepted and the field is not placed in his hands.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in the name of Huna that all litigants who bring evidence have their evidence accepted and the field is placed in their hands, but a robber who brings evidence does not have his evidence accepted and the field is not placed in his hands.

items.text: Clarifying the novelty of Rav Nachman's ruling against Rav and in accordance with Shmuel
items.text_en: Clarifying the novelty of Rav Nachman's ruling against Rav and in accordance with Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Rav Nachman is teaching, noting that a Mishnah already states that a purchase from a sikarikon is void. It explains that Rav Nachman's ruling excludes Rav's opinion that a bill of sale without a guarantee clause is effective, and instead follows Shmuel's view that even with a bill of sale, one does not acquire until a guarantee of property is written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novelty Rav Nachman is teaching, given that a Mishnah already rules that a purchase from a sikarikon is void.
The Gemara explains that Rav Nachman's ruling excludes Rav's opinion that a bill of sale without a guarantee clause is effective.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Nachman follows Shmuel's view that even with a bill of sale, one does not acquire until a guarantee of property is written.

items.text: Rav Bibi's addition regarding the robber's liability for money
items.text_en: Rav Bibi's addition regarding the robber's liability for money
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi concludes in the name of Rav Nachman that the robber does not acquire the land, but he does have money (compensation). This applies only when witnesses say 'he counted money in our presence,' but not when they say 'he admitted in our presence,' as per Rav Kahana's reasoning that without admission, the robber would have harmed the claimant.

sub.text: Rav Bibi's conclusion in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi's conclusion in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi concludes in the name of Rav Nachman that the robber does not acquire the land, but he does have money (compensation).
Rav Bibi qualifies that the robber's liability for money applies only when witnesses say 'he counted money in our presence,' but not when they say 'he admitted in our presence.'

Rav Kahana explains that without the admission, the robber would have harmed the claimant (by causing him to lose his donkey and himself to the pit), so the admission is not a reliable basis for liability.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a sale under duress
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a sale under duress
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if one was hung (tortured) and sold, his sale is valid. The Gemara explains the reasoning: any person who sells, if not coerced, would not sell, yet even so the sale is valid. It then questions whether coercion of oneself differs from coercion by others, and introduces a baraita to resolve this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one was hung (tortured) and sold, his sale is valid.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Huna's reasoning: any person who sells, if not coerced, would not sell, yet even so the sale is valid.
The Gemara objects: perhaps coercion of oneself differs from coercion by others.
The Gemara introduces a baraita to resolve the objection.

items.text: Establishing the principle of coerced consent from the sacrifice verse
items.text_en: Establishing the principle of coerced consent from the sacrifice verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'yakriv oto' that a person is forced to bring a sacrifice, but 'lirtzono' teaches it must be with consent; the resolution is that coercion continues until he says 'I want.' The Gemara questions whether this is unique to sacrifice (where atonement is desired) and then to divorce (where obeying the Sages is a mitzvah), but concludes that the underlying logic is that under duress, one ultimately agrees (agav unseih gamer umakneh).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'יַקְרִיב אֹתוֹ' that one is coerced to bring a sacrifice, but 'לִרְצוֹנוֹ' teaches it must be with consent, resolved by coercion until he says 'I want.'
The Gemara objects that the sacrifice case is unique because atonement is desirable, and then cites the parallel of divorce where coercion is also applied until consent.
The Gemara rejects the objection for divorce (since obeying Sages is a mitzvah) and concludes that the underlying logic is that under duress one ultimately agrees (אגב אונסיה גמר ומקנה).

items.text: Challenge from a forced divorce by a gentile (Rav Yehuda)
items.text_en: Challenge from a forced divorce by a gentile (Rav Yehuda)
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites a baraita: a forced get by a Jew is valid, but by a gentile it is invalid; yet the gentile is beaten until he does what the Jew says. The Gemara asks: why not apply the principle 'agav unseih gamer umegaresh' here? Rav Mesharshiya answers that by Torah law even a gentile's forced get is valid, but the Sages invalidated it to prevent women from colluding with a gentile to escape their husbands.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites a baraita that a forced get (גט מעושה) by a Jew is valid but by a gentile is invalid, yet the gentile is beaten until he complies, and challenges: why not apply the principle 'agav unseih gamer umegaresh' (אגב אונסיה גמר ומגרש) here as well?
Rav Mesharshiya answers that by Torah law even a gentile's forced get is valid, but the Sages invalidated it as a decree to prevent women from colluding with a gentile to escape their husbands.

items.text: Challenge from a forced sale by a Sikarikon (Rav Hamnuna)
items.text_en: Challenge from a forced sale by a Sikarikon (Rav Hamnuna)
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna cites a mishna: if one buys from a Sikarikon (a robber who seized land) and then from the original owner, the purchase is void. The Gemara asks: why not apply 'agav unseih gamer umakneh'? Rav answers that this applies only when the seller said 'go, take possession and acquire' (lech chazek ukni), but with a document (shtar) the sale is valid. Shmuel disagrees, but concedes if money was paid. Rav Bibi's version from Rav Nachman adds that the land is not acquired but the money is returned; the Gemara notes this is a separate statement not accepted by Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges the principle of 'agav unseih gamer umakneh' by citing a mishna where a purchase from a Sikarikon (robber) and then from the original owner is void, asking why the principle should not apply here.
Rav answers that the mishna's ruling applies only when the seller said 'lech chazek ukni' (go, take possession and acquire), but with a document (shtar) the sale is valid.
The Gemara objects that Shmuel disagrees even with a document, and resolves that Shmuel concedes when money was paid.

sub.text: Rav Bibi's version from Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi's version from Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes Rav Bibi's version from Rav Nachman that the land is not acquired but the money is returned, and clarifies that this is a separate statement not accepted by Rav Huna.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a sale under threat of execution
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a sale under threat of execution
items.desc_en: Rava states the halakha: if a person was hanged (threatened with execution) and then sold property, the sale is valid. He adds a qualification that this applies only in certain circumstances, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava states the halakha (הלכה) that if a person was hanged (threatened with execution) and then sold property, the sale is valid, but he begins a qualification that is cut off.

items.text: Distinction between a general field and a specific field
items.text_en: Distinction between a general field and a specific field
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier ruling about a sale being valid applies only to a general field (שדה סתם), not a specific field (שדה זו). However, even for a specific field, if the seller accepted money, the sale is not valid. Additionally, if the seller had a way to avoid the sale, the sale is not valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by distinguishing that the earlier ruling about a sale being valid applies only to a general field (שדה סתם), not to a specific field (שדה זו).
The Gemara qualifies that even for a specific field, if the seller accepted money (ארצי זוזי), the sale is not valid.
The Gemara further qualifies that if the seller had a way to avoid the sale (הוה ליה לאשתוטי), the sale is not valid.

items.text: Halakha: All such sales are valid, even for a specific field
items.text_en: Halakha: All such sales are valid, even for a specific field
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha that in all these cases the sale is valid, even for a specific field, because a woman is analogous to a specific field, and Ameimar said that if one hung a woman and betrothed her, the betrothal is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that in all these cases the sale is valid, even for a specific field.
The Gemara supports the ruling by citing Ameimar's analogy: a woman is like a specific field, and if one hung a woman and betrothed her, the betrothal is valid.

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi disputes: Betrothal is not valid
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi disputes: Betrothal is not valid
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi argues that in the case of a woman, the betrothal is certainly not valid; since he acted improperly, the Sages treated him improperly and voided the betrothal.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi rules that in the case of a woman, the betrothal is certainly not valid; since he acted improperly, the Sages treated him improperly and voided the betrothal.

items.text: Ravina's question about betrothal through intercourse
items.text_en: Ravina's question about betrothal through intercourse
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the betrothal was with money, that is understandable, but if he betrothed through intercourse, what is the ruling? Rav Ashi answers that the Sages rendered his intercourse as an act of licentiousness.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the betrothal was with money, that is understandable, but if he betrothed through intercourse, what is the ruling?
Rav Ashi answers that the Sages rendered his intercourse as an act of licentiousness, invalidating the betrothal.

items.text: Case of conflicting documents and Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Case of conflicting documents and Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: Tavi hung a document on a palm tree and sold it. Rabbah bar bar Chanah signed a moda'a (declaration of duress) and a receipt (ashkalta). Rav Huna says that whoever signed the moda'a did well, and whoever signed the receipt did well. The Gemara questions this, and explains that Rav Huna means: if not for the moda'a, the one who signed the receipt did well, consistent with Rav Huna's own view that if one hung and sold, the sale is valid.

sub.desc_en: Tavi hung a document on a palm tree and sold the property; Rabbah bar bar Chanah signed both a moda'a (declaration of duress) and an ashkalta (receipt).
Rav Huna rules that whoever signed the moda'a did well, and whoever signed the receipt also did well.
The Gemara objects: the two documents contradict each other — if the sale was under duress (moda'a), the receipt is invalid, and vice versa.
The Gemara resolves: Rav Huna meant that if not for the moda'a, the one who signed the receipt did well, consistent with Rav Huna's own view that if one hung and sold, the sale is valid.
The Gemara cites Rav Huna's own principle: if one hung and sold, the sale is valid, which supports his ruling on the receipt.

items.text: Rav Nachman's statement about witnesses retracting
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement about witnesses retracting
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion with Rav Nachman's statement: witnesses who said 'our words were a loan' (i.e., they were not actually witnesses to the transaction) – the continuation is presumably about the validity of their testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Rav Nachman's statement that witnesses who say 'our words were a loan' (i.e., they were not actual witnesses) are not believed, implying a contradiction with the previous discussion.

items.text: Gemara's initial clarification of the mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's initial clarification of the mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah's statement that claims of 'אמנה' or 'מודעא' are not believed applies only when the claim is oral, because an oral claim cannot invalidate a written deed. But if the claim is also in writing, one deed can invalidate another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the mishnah's ruling that claims of 'אמנה' or 'מודעא' are not believed, and implicitly questions how this can be consistent.
The Gemara explains that the mishnah's ruling applies only to an oral claim, because an oral claim cannot invalidate a written deed, but a written claim can.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Mar bar Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Mar bar Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that both claims of 'אמנה' and 'מודעא' are not believed. Mar bar Rav Ashi disagrees: 'אמנה' is not believed, but 'מודעא' is believed, because a protest (מודעא) is meant to be written down, while a prior agreement (אמנה) is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that both a claim of 'אמנה' (prior agreement) and 'מודעא' (protest) are not believed against a written deed.
Mar bar Rav Ashi distinguishes: a claim of 'אמנה' is not believed, but a claim of 'מודעא' is believed, because a protest (מודעא) is meant to be written down while a prior agreement (אמנה) is not.

items.text: Gemara's question on the mishnah's ruling about a husband's lack of presumptive ownership
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the mishnah's ruling about a husband's lack of presumptive ownership
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: It is obvious that a husband has no presumptive ownership of his wife's property, since he merely eats the produce – that is not an act of ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah's ruling that a husband has no presumptive ownership of his wife's property is not obvious, since he only eats the produce.

items.text: Gemara's answer: the case where the husband wrote a waiver
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: the case where the husband wrote a waiver
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah is necessary for a case where the husband wrote to his wife 'I have no claim or legal right to your property' – even then, he might still claim ownership, so the mishnah teaches that he does not acquire presumptive ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah is necessary for a case where the husband wrote to his wife a waiver of claims on her property.

items.text: Objection: such a waiver is legally meaningless
items.text_en: Objection: such a waiver is legally meaningless
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Even if he wrote such a waiver, what does it matter? A baraita teaches that if someone says 'I have no claim or legal right to this field' or 'I have no business with it' or 'my hands are removed from it', he has said nothing – the statement is ineffective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if a husband writes a waiver of rights to his wife's property, it is legally meaningless, citing a baraita that such a declaration is ineffective.

items.text: Resolution: the case is when he wrote it while she was still betrothed
items.text_en: Resolution: the case is when he wrote it while she was still betrothed
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing the school of Rabbi Yannai: the mishnah deals with a case where the husband wrote the waiver while she was still betrothed, consistent with a statement of Rav Kahana.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai resolves the objection by explaining that the mishnah deals with a case where the husband wrote the waiver while she was still betrothed, consistent with a statement of Rav Kahana.

items.text: Opening principle and Rava's rule
items.text_en: Opening principle and Rava's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a person can stipulate not to inherit property that comes from another source, citing Rava's principle that one who says 'I do not want this rabbinic enactment' is listened to.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the principle that a person can stipulate not to inherit property that comes from another source.
The Gemara cites Rava's rule that one who says 'I do not want this rabbinic enactment' is listened to, supporting the opening principle.

items.text: Clarification of 'such as this' with Rav Huna's example
items.text_en: Clarification of 'such as this' with Rav Huna's example
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what 'such as this' means, citing Rav Huna quoting Rav that a wife can say to her husband 'I will not be supported and I will not work.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'such as this' refers to in the context of Rava's ruling.
Rav Huna citing Rav provides an example: a wife can say to her husband 'I will not be supported and I will not work.'

items.text: Objection from the Mishna about a wife's sale
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishna about a wife's sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: in a Mishna, when a husband buys a field from a seller and then the wife buys it back, the sale is void because the wife can claim she acted to please her husband. This seems to contradict the idea that a wife can opt out of the rabbinic enactment, as she might similarly claim she acted to please her husband here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: is there a proof? The wife can claim she acted to please her husband, so the sale should be void.
The Gemara cites a Mishna: if a man buys from a husband and then from the wife, the sale is void because the wife can claim she acted to please her husband, and applies the same reasoning here.

items.text: Resolution by Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Resolution by Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who said that the Mishna's ruling was only necessary for the three specific fields that a husband writes in his wife's ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna resolves the objection by stating that the Mishna's ruling was only necessary for the three specific fields that a husband writes in his wife's ketubah.

items.text: Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three types of property a wife brings into marriage, including melog property, which the husband cannot sell.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three types of property a wife brings into marriage, including melog property, which the husband cannot sell.

items.text: Gemara's question on the exclusion
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah excludes, suggesting it cannot be other property because that would cause enmity, as the husband would suspect she wants divorce or his death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah excludes, suggesting it cannot be other property because that would cause enmity, as the husband would suspect she wants divorce or his death.

items.text: Amemar's ruling on melog property
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling on melog property
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the exclusion is melog property, citing Amemar that a husband and wife who sell melog property have done nothing. It then qualifies that Amemar's ruling applies only when one spouse sells and dies, allowing the other to retrieve it, but if both sell or the wife sells to the husband, the sale is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the exclusion is for melog property (נִכְסֵי מְלוֹג), citing Amemar's ruling that a husband and wife who sell such property have done nothing.

The Gemara qualifies that Amemar's ruling applies only when one spouse sells and dies, allowing the other to retrieve it, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's enactment in Usha (אוּשָׁא) that a wife who sells melog property and dies allows the husband to recover it from buyers.
The Gemara concludes that if both spouses sell together or the wife sells to the husband, the sale is valid (זְבִינַהּ זְבִינֵי).

items.text: Alternative explanation via Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Alternative explanation via Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Amemar's ruling aligns with Rabbi Elazar, who holds that a seller who stipulates continued service for thirty days creates a situation where the first buyer is considered under the seller's authority. The baraita cites Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei debating whether the buyer of a slave who stipulated thirty days of service is subject to the law of 'day or two' (Exodus 21:21), based on whether acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: Amemar's ruling aligns with Rabbi Elazar's position.
A baraita is cited about selling a slave with a stipulation of continued service for thirty days.
Rabbi Meir rules that the first owner is subject to the law of 'day or two days' because the slave is under him, but the second is not.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir holds that a קניין פירות (right to usufruct) is equivalent to קניין הגוף (ownership of the body).
Rabbi Yehuda rules that the second owner is subject to the law because the slave is his money, but the first is not, holding that קניין פירות is not equivalent to קניין הגוף.
Rabbi Yosei's position is introduced but not elaborated in the given text.

items.text: Opening dispute: both parties in the law of day or two days
items.text_en: Opening dispute: both parties in the law of day or two days
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a safek (doubt) whether the husband's acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body, and therefore both the husband and the creditor are considered "under him" and "his money" respectively, leading to a leniency in capital cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a safek (doubt) whether the husband's acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body, and therefore both the husband and the creditor are considered "under him" and "his money" respectively, leading to a leniency in capital cases.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's opposing view and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's opposing view and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar argues that neither party is subject to the law of day or two days, because the husband is not "under him" and the creditor's money is not "his money." Rava explains the scriptural basis: the verse says "his money" meaning money specifically designated to him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that neither party is subject to the law of day or two days, because the husband is not 'under him' and the creditor's money is not 'his money'.
Rava explains Rabbi Elazar's scriptural basis: the verse says 'כי כספו הוא' (for it is his money), meaning money specifically designated to him.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's statement about a husband's hazakah
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's statement about a husband's hazakah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's rule that a husband has no hazakah in his wife's property, citing Rav's statement that a married woman must protest. It asks whether this refers to a third party or the husband, concluding it must be the husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the statement that a husband has no chazakah (presumption of ownership) in his wife's property, citing Rav's rule that a married woman must protest encroachment, and asks whether this refers to the husband.

items.text: Rava's answer: digging pits, and the principle of no hazakah for damages
items.text_en: Rava's answer: digging pits, and the principle of no hazakah for damages
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the case is indeed about a husband who dug pits, but Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuah says there is no hazakah for damages. The Gemara corrects this to mean there is no "din hazakah" (legal presumption) for damages.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the case is indeed about a husband, and specifically one who dug pits, cisterns, and caves in his wife's property.
The Gemara objects that Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuah stated there is no hazakah (presumption of ownership) for damages, which would contradict Rava's explanation.
The Gemara corrects the statement to mean there is no 'din hazakah' (legal presumption) for damages, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Alternative resolution: the case of a smoke outlet or latrine
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: the case of a smoke outlet or latrine
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the statement about no hazakah for damages was said regarding a smoke outlet (Kutra) or a latrine, not the husband's digging.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: Rav Mari says it refers to a smoke-hole, and Rav Zevid says it refers to a latrine.

items.text: Rav Yosef's answer: partial hazakah during husband's life and after death
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer: partial hazakah during husband's life and after death
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the case involves a third party who consumed the land partially during the husband's life and for three years after his death, allowing the claim of purchase due to migo.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves that it always refers to a third party, in a case where the third party consumed the property partially during the husband's lifetime and for three years after his death, and is believed due to the principle of מיגו (since he could claim he bought it from her).

items.text: Return to the main statement: Rav's rule
items.text_en: Return to the main statement: Rav's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rav's original statement that there is no hazakah in the property of a married woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav's original statement that one cannot acquire a chazakah (presumption of ownership) in the property of a married woman.

items.text: Rav's ruling and retraction
items.text_en: Rav's ruling and retraction
items.desc_en: Rav rules like the Diaspora judges that a wife can acquire her husband's field through hazakah. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask if he retracted his earlier view; Rav says he only stated his opinion in accordance with Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Diaspora judges rule that a wife can acquire her husband's field through hazakah.
Rav rules that the law follows the Diaspora judges.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav whether he has retracted his earlier position.
Rav explains that he only stated his opinion in accordance with Rav Yosef, not as a retraction.

items.text: The wife's acquisition and the concern of revealing money
items.text_en: The wife's acquisition and the concern of revealing money
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a wife needs hazakah if she already eats from the husband's property, and answers that he designated other land for her support. It then asks whether the wife's claim of purchase is merely to reveal hidden money, and distinguishes between a sale and a gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a wife needs a hazakah (presumption of ownership) since she already eats from her husband's property for her support.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the husband designated other land specifically for her support, so she does not eat from this land.
The Gemara asks whether the wife's claim of purchase is merely to reveal hidden money (i.e., to collect a debt from her husband).
The Gemara answers that the case of a sale to one's wife is not about revealing money; rather, the proof is from a gift document (שטר מתנה), where no money is involved.

items.text: Rav Nachman and Rav Huna discuss the ruling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Huna discuss the ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman tells Rav Huna that he missed a good teaching: that a husband who sells a field to his wife acquires it, and we do not suspect it is to reveal money.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman tells Rav Huna that he missed a good teaching: that a husband who sells a field to his wife acquires it, and we do not suspect it is to reveal money.

items.text: The debate on acquisition by deed and the resolution
items.text_en: The debate on acquisition by deed and the resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna argues that the wife acquires by deed alone, citing the Mishnah. Rav Nachman counters with Shmuel's distinction between a gift deed and a sale deed, and resolves the contradiction by explaining the case is selling due to poor land or a gift disguised as a sale to enhance the recipient's power.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna challenges Rav Nachman, arguing that the wife acquires the field by deed alone, citing the Mishnah that properties with liens are acquired by money, deed, or possession.

Rav Nachman counters with Shmuel's ruling that the Mishnah's acquisition by deed applies only to a gift deed, not a sale deed, and cites Rav Hamnuna's objection from a baraita that a sale deed alone suffices.
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to a case where one sells his field because it is poor, so the deed alone suffices.

sub.text: Rav Bibi and Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi and Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi concludes in Rav Nachman's name, and Rav Ashi adds, that the transaction was intended as a gift, but the deed was written in sale language to enhance the recipient's power (ייפוי כח).

items.text: Challenge from a loan to a slave or wife
items.text_en: Challenge from a loan to a slave or wife
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one borrows from a slave or wife and then frees or divorces them, they have no claim, implying it was a sham to reveal money. The Gemara distinguishes because the borrower does not want to become a 'borrower slave to a lender'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if one borrows from a slave or wife and then frees or divorces them, they have no claim, implying the transaction was a sham to reveal hidden money.
The Gemara distinguishes: there the borrower does not want to make himself a 'עבד לוה לאיש מלוה (a borrower slave to a lender)', so the loan is genuine, not a sham.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin sends a ruling: one who sells a field to his wife acquires it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin sends a ruling that one who sells a field to his wife acquires it.

items.text: Opening statement: husband eats the produce
items.text_en: Opening statement: husband eats the produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that according to Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Avahu, and other greats, the transaction was intended as a gift, but written as a sale to enhance her rights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the principle that the husband eats the produce of the field.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Avahu, and the greats of the generation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Avahu, and the greats of the generation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Avahu, and the greats explain that the transaction was intended as a gift but written as a sale to enhance her rights.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about loans
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about loans
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if one borrowed from a slave and freed him, or from a woman and divorced her, they have no claim. The Gemara questions whether this is because the loan was a pretext, and answers that the case is different to avoid making the borrower a slave to the lender.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita: if one borrowed from a slave and freed him, or from a woman and divorced her, they have no claim, suggesting the loan was a pretext (גילוי זוזי).
The Gemara answers that the case is different, because the ruling there is to prevent the borrower from becoming a 'עבד לוה לאיש מלוה' (a slave to the lender).

items.text: Rav and Rabbi Elazar's dispute
items.text_en: Rav and Rabbi Elazar's dispute
items.desc_en: Rav rules: if a man sells a field to his wife, she acquires it and the husband eats the produce; if he gives it as a gift, she acquires it and the husband does not eat the produce. Rabbi Elazar rules: in both cases she acquires it and the husband does not eat the produce.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that if a man sells a field to his wife, she acquires it and the husband eats the produce; if he gives it as a gift, she acquires it and the husband does not eat the produce.
Rabbi Elazar rules that in both cases (sale and gift) she acquires it and the husband does not eat the produce.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling and the challenge
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling and the challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda ruled like Rabbi Elazar. Rabban Ukva and Rabban Nechemya, grandsons of Rav, challenged him for abandoning the greats (Rav) for the lesser (Rabbi Elazar). Rav Chisda defended himself, citing Rabbi Yochanan who also ruled like Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Chisda ruled practically like Rabbi Elazar.

sub.text: Rabban Ukva and Rabban Nechemya's challenge
sub.text_en: Rabban Ukva and Rabban Nechemya's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rabban Ukva and Rabban Nechemya, grandsons of Rav, challenge Rav Chisda for abandoning the greats (Rav) and ruling like the lesser (Rabbi Elazar).
Rav Chisda defends himself by citing Rabbi Yochanan, who also ruled like Rabbi Elazar, thus aligning himself with a great authority.

items.text: Rava's halakha and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's halakha and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava states the halakha: if a man sells a field to his wife, she does not acquire it and the husband eats the produce; if he gives it as a gift, she acquires it and the husband does not eat the produce. The Gemara questions the contradiction, and resolves it by distinguishing between hidden money (she does not acquire) and non-hidden money (she acquires), citing Rav Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Rava states the halakha: selling a field to one's wife does not transfer ownership, but gifting it does, and the husband does not eat the produce of a gift.
The Gemara objects that Rava's ruling appears self-contradictory: why does a sale fail but a gift succeed?
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing hidden money (sale fails) from non-hidden money (sale succeeds), citing Rav Yehuda's principle.

items.text: Baraita on accepting deposits from women, slaves, and minors
items.text_en: Baraita on accepting deposits from women, slaves, and minors
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one should not accept deposits from women, slaves, or minors. If one accepted from a woman, he returns it to her; if she dies, to her husband. If from a slave, to him; if he dies, to his master.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one should not accept deposits from women, slaves, or minors, and specifies the return procedure upon their death.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Guardian's responsibility and deathbed declarations
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Guardian's responsibility and deathbed declarations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a guardian receives property from a minor, he must set aside a 'segulah' for him; if the minor dies, he returns it to his heirs. If a dying person says 'these belong to so-and-so', the guardian must follow their words; otherwise, he interprets their intent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a guardian who receives property from a minor must set aside a segulah for him, and if the minor dies, returns it to his heirs; if a dying person designates property, the guardian follows their words or interprets their intent.

items.text: Gemara: Case of Rabba bar bar Chanah's wife
items.text_en: Gemara: Case of Rabba bar bar Chanah's wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where Rabba bar bar Chanah's wife, on her deathbed, designated certain items. He came before Rav, who told him: if you trust her, follow her words; if not, interpret her intent. A second version says: if you are certain, follow her words; if not, interpret.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabba bar bar Chanah's wife, on her deathbed, designated certain items for her daughter and her daughter's children.
Rav instructs Rabba bar bar Chanah: if you trust her, follow her words; if not, interpret her intent.

items.text: Gemara: Meaning of 'segulah'
items.text_en: Gemara: Meaning of 'segulah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'segulah' means. Rav Chisda says it is a Torah scroll. Rabba bar Rav Huna says it is a date palm that produces dates for him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'סגולה' (segulah) means in the Mishnah's instruction to make a segulah for a minor.
Rav Chisda answers that 'סגולה' (segulah) means a Torah scroll (ספר תורה).
Rabba bar Rav Huna answers that 'סגולה' (segulah) means a date palm from which he eats dates.

items.text: Gemara: The son's status after dividing property
items.text_en: Gemara: The son's status after dividing property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a son does not inherit from his father's property after dividing. Rav Yosef says even if they divided, the rule applies. Rava says if they divided, it does not. Rav Pappi ruled like Rava, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reported a tradition supporting Rava. A baraisa confirms that a son who divided is like any other person.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a father does not inherit from the son's property, nor does a son inherit from the father's property after division.
Rav Yosef asserts that even if the son divided the property, the rule still applies.
Rava counters that if they divided, the rule does not apply.
Rav Pappi ruled in practice according to Rava's position that division nullifies the rule.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reports a chain of tradition from Rav Nachman bar Yaakov that division nullifies the rule.
The Gemara concludes that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rava: if they divided, the rule does not apply.
A baraita (תוספתא) supports Rava: a son who divided and a wife who divorced are treated like any other person.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel about an heir's claim
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel about an heir's claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one brother managed the household and documents were in his name; he claims they fell to him from his maternal grandfather. Rav says he must bring proof. Shmuel says the brothers must bring proof. Shmuel adds that Abba (Rav) agrees that if he died, the brothers must bring proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one brother managed the household and documents were in his name, and he claims they fell to him from his maternal grandfather.
Rav rules that the brother who claims the documents must bring proof that they are his.
Shmuel rules that the other brothers must bring proof that the documents belong to the estate.
Shmuel adds that Rav agrees that if the brother died, the other brothers must bring proof.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Pappa's objection and Rava's precedent
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Pappa's objection and Rava's precedent
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: do we claim for orphans what their father did not claim? Rava once took a cloak and a book of aggadah from orphans without proof, in cases of items typically lent or rented.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: do we claim for orphans what their father did not claim?
Rav Pappa cites a precedent: Rava once took a cloak and a book of aggadah from orphans without proof, in cases of items typically lent or rented.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling and the difficulty
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling and the difficulty
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin sent a ruling: for items that are typically lent or rented, if someone claims they are his purchases, he is not believed. This raises a difficulty with the earlier mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin sends a ruling: for items typically lent or rented, a claimant who says they are his purchases is not believed.
The gemara notes a difficulty: this ruling contradicts the earlier mishnah.

items.text: Rav Chisda's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the difficulty: the mishnah's leniency applies only when the brothers are not divided in their dough (i.e., they share expenses), but if they are divided, the claimant is believed because he may have saved from his own portion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the difficulty: the mishnah's leniency applies only when the brothers are not divided in their dough (i.e., they share expenses), but if they are divided, the claimant is believed because he may have saved from his own portion.

items.text: Dispute about the required proof
items.text_en: Dispute about the required proof
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Sheishes disagree on what constitutes valid proof: Rabbah says witnesses, Rav Sheishes says verification of the document.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What constitutes the required proof (ראיה) in this context?
Rabbah answers: The proof must be through witnesses (עדים).
Rav Sheishes answers: The proof must be through verification of the document (קיום השטר).

items.text: Rava's question to Rav Nachman and the baraita
items.text_en: Rava's question to Rav Nachman and the baraita
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman which opinion he follows. Rav Nachman cites a baraita: if one brother was managing the household and documents emerge in his name, he must bring proof that they are his inheritance. The baraita continues with a similar case for a woman managing the household.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman which opinion he follows among the earlier disputes (Rav vs. Shmuel, Rabbah vs. Rav Sheshet).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's answer citing a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds by citing a baraita: if one brother was managing the household and documents emerge in his name claiming they are his inheritance, he must bring proof.
The baraita adds a parallel case: a woman managing the household who claims documents are her inheritance must also bring proof.

items.text: Explanation of 'vechen' regarding the woman
items.text_en: Explanation of 'vechen' regarding the woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the baraita adds 'and similarly' for the woman: one might think she is trusted because she works for the orphans, so the baraita teaches that she too must bring proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita adds 'and similarly' regarding the woman, suggesting one might think she is trusted because she works for the orphans and would not steal from them.
The Gemara answers that the baraita teaches that even the woman must bring proof, countering the mistaken assumption.

items.text: Clarification of hazakah with and without a claim
items.text_en: Clarification of hazakah with and without a claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction: the mishnah distinguishes between a possessor and a gift recipient, but all are possessors. It resolves by saying the mishnah is missing a clause: the distinction is between hazakah with a claim (e.g., seller says 'I didn't sell', buyer says 'I bought') and hazakah without a claim (e.g., gift, division, or property of a convert). In the latter, any minimal act like locking or fencing in the owner's presence constitutes hazakah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's distinction between a possessor and a gift recipient, noting that all are possessors.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah is missing a clause: the distinction is between hazakah with a claim (e.g., seller says 'I didn't sell', buyer says 'I bought').
The Gemara explains that for hazakah without a claim (gift, division, or property of a convert), any minimal act like locking or fencing in the owner's presence constitutes hazakah.

items.text: Rav Hoshaya's baraita and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Hoshaya's baraita and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya taught in the school of Levi: locking, fencing, or breaching any amount in the owner's presence constitutes hazakah. The Gemara questions whether 'in his presence' is required. Rava explains: 'in his presence' means he does not need to say 'go take possession and acquire'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya teaches in the school of Levi that locking, fencing, or breaching any amount in the owner's presence constitutes hazakah.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita implies that only in his presence, but not outside his presence, is hazakah effective.
Rava explains that 'in his presence' means the owner does not need to explicitly say 'go take possession and acquire'.

items.text: Rav's question about gift and Shmuel's response
items.text_en: Rav's question about gift and Shmuel's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for a sale not conducted in the seller's presence, the seller must say 'Go, take possession and acquire.' Rav asks whether the same applies to a gift. Shmuel argues that if a sale requires such a declaration, a gift certainly does, but Rav holds that a giver gives with a generous eye, implying less formality.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule that for a sale not conducted in the seller's presence, the seller must say 'Go, take possession and acquire.'
Rav asks whether the same requirement of a verbal declaration applies to a gift.
Shmuel argues that if a sale requires such a declaration, a gift certainly does, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.
Rav holds that a giver gives with a generous eye (עין יפה), implying less formality and thus no need for a verbal declaration.

items.text: Definition of minimal improvement: Shmuel's example of a fence and breach
items.text_en: Definition of minimal improvement: Shmuel's example of a fence and breach
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much improvement constitutes a chazakah, citing Shmuel's example: building a fence to complete a height of ten handbreadths, or widening a breach to allow entry and exit. It then analyzes the fence and breach cases, concluding that the improvement must be meaningful—e.g., making access easier from spacious to cramped, or vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much improvement constitutes a chazakah, and answers by citing Shmuel's example.
Shmuel states that building a fence to complete a height of ten handbreadths, or widening a breach to allow entry and exit, constitutes a chazakah.
The Gemara analyzes the fence and breach cases, concluding that the improvement must be meaningful—e.g., making access easier from spacious to cramped, or vice versa.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on placing or removing a stone
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on placing or removing a stone
items.desc_en: Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: placing a stone that benefits the field or removing a stone that benefits it constitutes a chazakah. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to damming water to irrigate or draining water to dry the field, not merely preventing damage (which would be like repelling a lion from another's property).

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that placing or removing a stone that benefits the field constitutes a chazakah, and the Gemara asks what these actions mean.
The Gemara objects that if the stone was placed to block water or removed to drain water, it would merely be repelling a lion from another's property, not a valid chazakah.
The Gemara resolves that the stone was placed to dam water to irrigate the field or removed to drain water to dry it, which directly benefits the field.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on two fields with a common border
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on two fields with a common border
items.desc_en: Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: if one has two adjacent fields and performs a chazakah on one to acquire it, he acquires only that field, not the other.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if one has two adjacent fields with a common border and performs a chazakah (presumptive acquisition) on one field to acquire it, he acquires only that field, not the other.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: acquiring one field and its neighbor
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: acquiring one field and its neighbor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one intends to acquire a field and its neighbor, only the intended field is acquired; if one intends only the neighbor, neither is acquired.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for acquiring a field and its neighbor: if one intends both, only the intended field is acquired; if one intends only the neighbor, neither is acquired.

items.text: Two unresolved queries about the boundary strip
items.text_en: Two unresolved queries about the boundary strip
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about taking possession of one field to acquire it, the boundary strip, and the other field; Rabbi Elazar asks about taking possession of the boundary strip to acquire both fields. Both queries end with 'teiku' (undecided).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether taking possession of one field with intent to acquire it, the boundary strip (מֶצֶר), and the other field is effective, and the query remains unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).
Rabbi Elazar asks whether taking possession of the boundary strip (מֶצֶר) alone suffices to acquire both fields, and the query remains unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on two houses, one inside the other
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on two houses, one inside the other
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh rules that if one takes possession of the outer house to acquire it, he acquires it; to acquire both, only the outer is acquired; to acquire the inner, neither is acquired. For the inner house, taking possession to acquire it alone works; to acquire both, both are acquired; to acquire the outer, neither is acquired.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh rules that if one takes possession of the outer house to acquire it, he acquires it; to acquire both, only the outer is acquired; to acquire the inner, neither is acquired.
Rav Nachman bar Avuh completes the ruling: for the inner house, taking possession to acquire it alone works; to acquire both, both are acquired; to acquire the outer, neither is acquired.

items.text: Building large halls in a convert's property and adding doors
items.text_en: Building large halls in a convert's property and adding doors
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh rules that if one builds large halls in a convert's property and another adds doors, the latter acquires it, because the first merely turned over bricks.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha states: one who builds large halls on property of a convert (who died without heirs) and another comes and installs doors for them acquires the halls.
The Gemara explains the reason: the first builder merely turned over stones (a non-acquisitive act), so the second who installed doors performed a significant act of acquisition.

items.text: Finding halls and plastering or whitewashing them
items.text_en: Finding halls and plastering or whitewashing them
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Elazar rules that if one finds halls in a convert's property and plasters or whitewashes a certain amount, he acquires them. Rav Yosef specifies the amount as one cubit, and Rav Chisda adds that it must be opposite the entrance.

sub.text: Rav Dimi bar Yosef citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Elazar states: one who finds halls on property of a convert and plasters them with one plaster or paints them with one painting acquires them.
The Gemara asks: how much plaster is needed? Rav Yosef answers: one amah (cubit).
Rav Chisda adds: and it must be opposite the entrance.

items.text: Spreading beds in a convert's property and the baraita on hazakah
items.text_en: Spreading beds in a convert's property and the baraita on hazakah
items.desc_en: Rav Amram reports that Rav Sheshet taught that spreading beds in a convert's property acquires it, and he illuminated this from a baraita listing acts of hazakah like locking, carrying items, and lifting. The Gemara explains that the baraita means if a slave lifts his master, he acquires him, but not vice versa, and Rabbi Shimon comments that lifting is not a greater hazakah than lifting itself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram reports in the name of Rav Sheshet: one who spreads bedding on property of a convert acquires it.
The Gemara asks: what is the baraita that illuminated their eyes?
The Gemara cites a baraita listing acts of chazakah (presumptive acquisition) for a slave: locking his shoe, carrying his belongings, bathing him, anointing him, and lifting him — all acquire him.
Rabbi Shimon states: no chazakah is greater than הגבהה (lifting), which acquires in every place.

items.text: Rav Yirmiyah Bira'ah's statement on hazakah
items.text_en: Rav Yirmiyah Bira'ah's statement on hazakah
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmiyah Bira'ah quoting Rav Yehudah begins a statement about a person who... (the text is cut off).

sub.text_en: Rav Yirmiyah Bira'ah citing Rav Yehudah

items.text: Opening ruling: planting turnips in furrows does not establish hazakah
items.text_en: Opening ruling: planting turnips in furrows does not establish hazakah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one plants turnips in the furrows of a gentile's field, it does not constitute a hazakah (presumptive ownership). The reason is that at the time of planting, there is no improvement, and the subsequent growth occurs naturally, not through the planter's effort.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that planting turnips in a gentile's furrows does not establish hazakah, because the planting provides no improvement and the growth is spontaneous.

items.text: Four rulings of Shmuel on hazakah through specific acts
items.text_en: Four rulings of Shmuel on hazakah through specific acts
items.desc_en: Shmuel presents four cases where an action may or may not establish hazakah depending on the intent: (1) cutting a palm tree – if cut from both sides, intent is for the tree (acquires); if from one side, intent is for the branches (does not acquire). (2) clearing thorns – if large and small are removed, intent is for the land; if only large are removed, intent is for firewood. (3) removing stones – if large stones are taken and placed in a marsh, intent is for the land; if large with large and marsh with marsh, intent is for a storehouse. (4) opening water channels – if two openings (inlet and outlet) are made, intent is for fish; if one opening, intent is for the land.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that cutting a palm tree establishes hazakah if done from both sides (intent for the tree), but not if from one side (intent for branches).
Shmuel rules that clearing thorns establishes hazakah if large and small are removed (intent for land), but not if only large are removed (intent for firewood).
Shmuel rules that removing stones establishes hazakah if large stones are placed in a marsh (intent for land), but not if large with large and marsh with marsh (intent for a storehouse).
Shmuel rules that opening water channels establishes hazakah if two openings (inlet and outlet) are made (intent for fish), but not if one opening (intent for land).

items.text: Case of a woman who ate from a palm tree for thirteen years
items.text_en: Case of a woman who ate from a palm tree for thirteen years
items.desc_en: A woman consumed dates from a palm tree for thirteen years by climbing it. When a man came and dug a little under it, the court (Levi or Mar Ukva) awarded possession to the man. The woman cried out, but the court told her she did not establish hazakah in the manner that people typically do (i.e., by improving the land itself).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of a woman who ate from a palm tree for thirteen years by climbing it.
A man came and dug a little under the tree.
The case came before Levi (or Mar Ukva), and the court awarded possession of the tree to the man.
The woman cried out, and the court told her she did not establish hazakah (presumption of ownership) in the manner that people typically do.

items.text: Rav's ruling: drawing a figure on a gentile's property acquires it
items.text_en: Rav's ruling: drawing a figure on a gentile's property acquires it
items.desc_en: Rav states that if one draws a figure (a form) on the property of a gentile, he acquires it. This is illustrated by the fact that Rav himself only acquired the garden of the house of Rav through drawing a figure (i.e., a symbolic act of ownership).

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that drawing a figure on a gentile's property acquires it.
The gemara notes that Rav himself only acquired the garden of the house of Rav through drawing a figure, illustrating the ruling.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on acquiring a bounded field through one hoe-strike
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on acquiring a bounded field through one hoe-strike
