items.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute regarding a field whose boundaries are marked: Rav Huna citing Rav says that once one strikes it once with a hoe, he acquires the entire field. Shmuel argues that he acquires only the spot of the hoe-strike.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about a field whose boundaries are marked.
Rav Huna in the name of Rav rules that one who strikes the field once with a hoe acquires the entire field.
Shmuel argues that the acquirer acquires only the spot of the hoe-strike, not the entire field.

items.text: Definition of an unmarked field boundary
items.text_en: Definition of an unmarked field boundary
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa defines how far one must go to mark a field's boundaries for the purpose of hazakah (presumption of ownership).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For a field that is not marked by its boundaries, how far must one go to mark it for the purpose of hazakah (presumption of ownership)?
Rav Pappa answers: One must go as far as a plowman goes and returns (i.e., the length of a plowing circuit).

items.text: Shmuel's principle: gentile property is like a desert
items.text_en: Shmuel's principle: gentile property is like a desert
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel stating that gentile property is ownerless because the gentile loses ownership upon receiving payment, while the Jewish buyer does not acquire until the deed reaches his hand. Therefore, anyone who takes possession acquires it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel stating that gentile property is like a desert, and anyone who takes possession acquires it.

items.text: Abaye's challenge from the law of the kingdom
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge from the law of the kingdom
items.desc_en: Abaye questions Shmuel's ruling because Shmuel also said that the law of the kingdom is binding, and the kingdom requires a deed for land acquisition. Rav Yosef responds with a case from the generation of persecution where a second Jew who worked the land was awarded it by Rav Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef by pointing out a contradiction: Shmuel said that the law of the kingdom is binding (דינא דמלכותא דינא), yet the kingdom requires a deed (איגרתא) for land acquisition, which seems to conflict with Shmuel's ruling that a gentile's land is like a desert and anyone who takes possession acquires it.

Rav Yosef admits he does not know the answer but cites a precedent from the generation of persecution (דורא דרעוותא) where a second Jew who worked the land was awarded it by Rav Yehuda, supporting Shmuel's ruling.

items.text: Distinction: the case of tax evaders
items.text_en: Distinction: the case of tax evaders
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the case involved tax evaders (bagi mitmari) who did not pay the king's tax, so the king declared that whoever pays the tax may eat the land. This is a special case, not a general rule.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the case involved tax evaders (באגי מטמרי) who did not pay the king's tax, so the king declared that whoever pays the tax may eat the land, making it a special case rather than a general rule.

items.text: Rav Huna's case and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Huna's case and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bought land from a gentile, and another Jew worked it. Rav Nachman awarded the land to the second Jew, citing Shmuel's principle. This shows that the principle applies even when the first Jew paid money.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: Rav Huna bought land from a gentile, and another Jew worked it slightly.
Rav Nachman awarded the land to the second Jew who worked it.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's rhetorical question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's rhetorical question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rav Huna what he thought, citing Shmuel's principle that gentile property is like a desert.
The gemara completes the citation of Shmuel's principle that whoever takes possession of gentile property acquires it.

items.text: Dispute about acquisition through one strike of the pickaxe
items.text_en: Dispute about acquisition through one strike of the pickaxe
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the earlier ruling follows Shmuel's view that one only acquires the place of the pickaxe, but the master (Rav) holds that one strike acquires the entire field. Rav Huna citing Rav asserts that one strike of the pickaxe acquires the whole field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the master does not follow Shmuel's view that one only acquires the place of the pickaxe.
The master answers that he follows his own tradition, citing Rav Huna in the name of Rav that one strike of the pickaxe acquires the entire field.

items.text: Ruling on an Israelite who purchases land from a gentile
items.text_en: Ruling on an Israelite who purchases land from a gentile
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin sends a ruling: if an Israelite buys a field from a gentile and another Israelite takes possession, the second does not have to return it. Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Ila'a, and all the rabbis agree on this matter.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin sends a ruling: if an Israelite buys a field from a gentile and another Israelite takes possession, the second does not have to return it.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Ila'a, and all the rabbis
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Ila'a, and all the rabbis
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Ila'a, and all the rabbis agree on this ruling.

items.text: Three principles from Shmuel via Uqvan bar Nechemyah
items.text_en: Three principles from Shmuel via Uqvan bar Nechemyah
items.desc_en: Rabbah reports three statements from Shmuel: the law of the land is law, Persian tenancy lasts up to forty years, and those who buy land for taska (land tax) have a valid sale.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah reports three statements from Shmuel via Uqvan bar Nechemyah: the law of the land is law, Persian tenancy lasts up to forty years, and those who buy land for taska (land tax) have a valid sale.

items.text: Distinction between taska and karga
items.text_en: Distinction between taska and karga
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the ruling about buying land for tax applies only to taska (land tax), not karga (poll tax), because karga is a head tax. Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua adds that even the hairs of a jug are subject to karga.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the ruling about buying land for tax applies only to taska (land tax), not karga (poll tax), because karga is a head tax levied on the person.
Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua adds that even the hairs of a jug are subject to karga, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the poll tax.

items.text: Objection regarding the firstborn's inheritance
items.text_en: Objection regarding the firstborn's inheritance
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports Huna bar Natan's objection: if karga applies to all property, it would nullify the firstborn's inheritance because the property becomes 'reuy' (not yet in possession). The Gemara counters that the same applies to taska if the debtor dies after paying the tax.

sub.text: Huna bar Natan's objection via Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Huna bar Natan's objection via Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Huna bar Natan objects that if karga (a head tax) applies to all property, it would nullify the firstborn's inheritance because the property becomes 'reuy' (not yet in possession), and a firstborn does not take in reuy as in muchzak.
The Gemara counters that the same objection would apply to taska (land tax) if the debtor dies after paying the tax, so the objection is resolved by noting that the tax is paid before death.

items.text: Halachic ruling on karga
items.text_en: Halachic ruling on karga
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he asked the scribes of Rava and they said the halacha follows Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua, but notes that this was said only to support his position.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that Huna bar Natan asked the scribes of Rava and they ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua.
The gemara qualifies that this ruling was only said to support Rav Ashi's own position, not as a definitive הלכה (binding law).

items.text: Distinction between pardakhta and andiskei
items.text_en: Distinction between pardakhta and andiskei
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that a pardakhta (a type of official) assists the city, but this applies only if the city appointed him; an andiskei (a royal appointee) is considered heavenly assistance.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi distinguishes between a pardakhta (city-appointed official) who assists the city, and an andiskei (royal appointee) who is considered heavenly assistance.

items.text: Dispute about metzer and chatav interrupting for pe'ah and tumah
items.text_en: Dispute about metzer and chatav interrupting for pe'ah and tumah
items.desc_en: Rav Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan says that a metzer (boundary marker) and chatav (a type of partition) interrupt for the property of a convert, but not for pe'ah and tumah. Ravin citing Rabbi Yochanan says they even interrupt for pe'ah and tumah. The Gemara then cites a Mishnah about what interrupts for pe'ah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a metzer (boundary marker) and chatav (a type of partition) interrupt for the property of a convert, but not for pe'ah (corner of the field) and tum'ah (ritual impurity).
Ravin, upon arrival, cites Rabbi Yochanan's opposing view that the metzer and chatav even interrupt for pe'ah and tum'ah.

sub.text: Gemara's question and citation of Mishnah
sub.text_en: Gemara's question and citation of Mishnah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the case of pe'ah is, and cites a Mishnah listing what interrupts for pe'ah: a stream (נחל) and a shlulit (a type of water channel).

items.text: Definition of a fixed path
items.text_en: Definition of a fixed path
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists types of paths, including a private path that is fixed for use in both summer and winter, implying that a path not fixed for both seasons is not considered a permanent path.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a private path as one fixed for use in both summer and winter, implying that a path not fixed for both seasons is not considered a permanent path.

items.text: Gemara's question and the dispute about uncertainty of entering a contaminated area
items.text_en: Gemara's question and the dispute about uncertainty of entering a contaminated area
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the halakhic status of impurity (טומאה) in such a case, citing a Mishnah where one is unsure if they entered a contaminated field. Rabbi Eliezer rules that uncertainty about entering is pure, while uncertainty about touching impurity is impure; the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the halakhic status of טומאה (ritual impurity) is in this context, citing a Mishnah about one who entered a valley during the rainy season and is uncertain whether he entered a field known to be contaminated.

The Mishnah records the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer rules that uncertainty about entering (ספק ביאה) is pure, while uncertainty about touching impurity (ספק מגע טומאה) is impure; the Sages disagree and deem the person impure in both cases.

items.text: Limitation to impurity, not Shabbat
items.text_en: Limitation to impurity, not Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this leniency of Rabbi Eliezer applies only to impurity, but not to Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Eliezer's leniency of ספק ביאה (doubtful entry) applies only to טומאה (ritual impurity), but not to Shabbat.

items.text: Rava's objection and the baraita about Shabbat
items.text_en: Rava's objection and the baraita about Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the same principle applies even to Shabbat, citing a baraita where one who carries out half a fig twice in one lapse is liable, but in two lapses is exempt. Rabbi Yosei adds a condition about a single lapse.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that the same principle of uncertainty applies even to Shabbat, and introduces a supporting baraita.
The baraita states that one who carries out half a fig twice in a single lapse of awareness is liable, but in two separate lapses is exempt.
Rabbi Yosei adds a condition that the exemption applies only when the two acts occur in a single lapse of awareness.

items.text: Dispute about domains on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about domains on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that carrying within one domain is liable, but between two domains is exempt. Rabba qualifies this, requiring a domain where a sin-offering is due, excluding karmelit. Abaye extends it to karmelit but not pisla, while Rava includes even pisla, aligning with his view that Shabbat domains are like divorce domains.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: carrying within one domain is liable, but between two domains is exempt.
Rabba qualifies the Mishnah: the rule applies only where a sin-offering is due, excluding a karmelit (a neutral domain).
Abaye extends the rule to include a karmelit, but excludes a pisla (a small platform).
Rava includes even a pisla, aligning with his broader view of Shabbat domains.

items.text: Definition of a named field
items.text_en: Definition of a named field
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a field without borders or stone markers. Rabbi Marinus says it is considered named if it is called by someone's name, and Rav Pappa explains that it is called 'Be Garguta of so-and-so'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a field has no border markers or stone markers, what is its legal status regarding hazakah (presumption of ownership)?
Rabbi Marinus answers in his own name: any field that is called by someone's name is considered a named field.
Rav Pappa clarifies the practical example: a field called 'Be Garguta of so-and-so' is considered named.

items.text: Stone marker interrupts a convert's property
items.text_en: Stone marker interrupts a convert's property
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya states in the name of Rabbi Asi bar Chanina that a stone marker (chatzuva) interrupts the inheritance of a convert's property. Rav Yehuda explains that this marker is the one with which Joshua divided the land for Israel.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Avya citing Rabbi Asi bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avya citing Rabbi Asi bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya states in the name of Rabbi Asi bar Chanina that a stone marker (חצובא) interrupts the inheritance of a convert's property.
Rav Yehuda explains in the name of Rav that the stone marker is the one with which Joshua divided the land for Israel.

items.text: Joshua only counted border cities
items.text_en: Joshua only counted border cities
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that Joshua only enumerated the cities that stood on the borders.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that Joshua only enumerated the cities that stood on the borders.

items.text: Land shown to Moses is tithed
items.text_en: Land shown to Moses is tithed
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that all land shown to Moses is obligated in tithes, excluding the lands of the Kenites, Kenizzites, and Kadmonites. A baraita records disputes among Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon about the specific boundaries.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that all land shown by God to Moses is obligated in tithes.
The Gemara asks what lands are excluded from this obligation.
The Gemara answers that the lands of the Kenites, Kenizzites, and Kadmonites are excluded.
A baraita records disputes among Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon about the specific boundaries of the land obligated in tithes.

items.text: Mishnah: False witnesses in a chazakah case
items.text_en: Mishnah: False witnesses in a chazakah case
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if two witnesses testify that someone consumed a field for three years and are found to be conspiring, they pay the full value. If two testify for each year separately, the ruling is introduced but cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of two witnesses testifying that someone consumed a field for three years; if found to be conspiring, they pay the full value.
The Mishnah introduces a second scenario where two witnesses testify for each year separately, but the ruling is cut off mid-sentence.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that three brothers and one additional witness constitute three testimonies, but they are considered one testimony for the purpose of hazamah (disqualification as conspiring witnesses).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that three brothers and one additional witness constitute three testimonies for monetary division, but they are considered one testimony for the purpose of hazamah (disqualification as conspiring witnesses).

items.text: Gemara's identification of the Mishnah's position
items.text_en: Gemara's identification of the Mishnah's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Akiva, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei recounts a discussion between Abba Chalfta and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri about a case of eating produce over three years with different pairs of witnesses each year. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules it is a valid hazakah, but notes that Rabbi Akiva disagrees, holding that 'davar' excludes 'chatzi davar' (half a matter).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Akiva's position.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei recounts a discussion between Abba Chalfta and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri about a case of eating produce over three years with different pairs of witnesses each year, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules it is a valid hazakah.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri agrees with the ruling but notes that Rabbi Akiva disagrees, holding that the verse's word 'דבר' (matter) excludes 'חצי דבר' (half a matter).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Sages' interpretation
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Sages' interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Sages interpret the verse 'davar' to exclude 'chatzi davar'. It rejects the possibility that it excludes one witness saying 'one in its back' and another saying 'one in its belly', as that is half a matter and half testimony. Instead, it concludes that it excludes two witnesses saying 'one in its back' and two saying 'one in its belly'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Sages interpret the verse 'דבר' (matter) to exclude 'חצי דבר' (half a matter).
The Gemara suggests that the exclusion applies to one witness saying 'one in its back' and another saying 'one in its belly'.
The Gemara rejects this, arguing that this is half a matter and half testimony, not a case of 'חצי דבר'.
The Gemara concludes that the exclusion applies to two witnesses saying 'one in its back' and two saying 'one in its belly'.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Yehudah and Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Yehudah and Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah rules that if one witness says the claimant ate wheat and another says barley, it is a valid hazakah. Rav Nachman objects, arguing that if one witness says the claimant ate in odd years and another in even years, that would not be valid. Rav Yehudah distinguishes: in Rav Nachman's case, each witness testifies about different years, but in his case, both testify about the same year, and the difference between wheat and barley is not significant to people's awareness.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah rules that if one witness says the claimant ate wheat and another says barley, it constitutes a valid hazakah (presumption of ownership).
Rav Nachman objects: if one witness says the claimant ate in odd years and another in even years, would that also constitute a hazakah?

Rav Yehudah distinguishes: in Rav Nachman's case each witness testifies about different years, but here both testify about the same year, and the difference between wheat and barley is not significant to people's awareness.

items.text: Repetition of Mishnah
items.text_en: Repetition of Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's ruling is repeated verbatim: three brothers and one additional witness constitute three testimonies, but they are considered one testimony for hazamah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah's ruling is repeated verbatim: three brothers and one additional witness constitute three testimonies, but they are considered one testimony for hazamah.

items.text: Case of a signed document and Ravina's comparison
items.text_en: Case of a signed document and Ravina's comparison
items.desc_en: A document signed by two witnesses, one of whom died. The brother of the living witness and another person come to testify about the deceased witness's signature. Ravina compares this to the Mishnah's case of three brothers and one additional witness, but Rav Ashi rejects the comparison because here money is taken from the brothers' share.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a document signed by two witnesses, one of whom died; the brother of the living witness and another person come to testify about the deceased witness's signature.
Ravina sought to compare this case to the Mishnah's case of three brothers and one additional witness, implying the testimony is valid.
Rav Ashi rejects the comparison: in the Mishnah's case no money is taken from the brothers' share, but here money is taken from the brothers' share via their testimony.

items.text: Mishnah: Actions that do and do not establish hazakah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Actions that do and do not establish hazakah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists actions in a courtyard that do not establish hazakah (e.g., placing an animal, oven, millstones, stove, raising chickens, or putting manure), and contrasts them with actions that do establish hazakah (e.g., building a partition ten handbreadths high, bringing chickens indoors, or making a place for manure three handbreadths deep or high).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing actions in a courtyard that do not establish hazakah (חזקה, presumptive ownership), such as placing an animal, oven, millstones, stove, raising chickens, or putting manure.

The Mishnah contrasts with actions that do establish hazakah (חזקה), such as building a partition ten handbreadths high, bringing chickens indoors, or making a place for manure three handbreadths deep or high.

items.text: Gemara's question and Ulla's principle
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Ulla's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the first set of actions from the second. Ulla answers with a general rule: any action that would acquire property in the case of a convert's ownerless property also establishes hazakah in a neighbor's property; otherwise, it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the first set of actions (which do not establish hazakah) from the second set (which do).
Ulla states a general principle: any action that would acquire property in the case of a convert's ownerless property also establishes hazakah in a neighbor's property; otherwise, it does not.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection to Ulla's rule
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection to Ulla's rule
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Ulla's rule with counterexamples: plowing (nir) acquires for a convert but not for a neighbor, while eating fruit (achilat peirot) acquires for a neighbor but not for a convert, showing the rule is not absolute.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Ulla's rule by citing counterexamples: plowing (ניר) acquires for a convert but not for a neighbor, while eating fruit (אכילת פירות) acquires for a neighbor but not for a convert, showing the rule is not absolute.

items.text: Rav Nachman's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, begins to offer a different explanation for the Mishnah's distinction, though the segment cuts off mid-statement.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuha, begins to offer an alternative explanation for the Mishnah's distinction, though the statement is cut off mid-sentence.

items.text: Initial distinction between standing and partition in a shared courtyard
items.text_en: Initial distinction between standing and partition in a shared courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that in a shared courtyard, partners are particular about a partition but not about standing (being seen).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially distinguishes that in a shared courtyard, partners are particular about a partition but not about standing (being seen).

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah about mutual vows
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah about mutual vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if partners are not particular about standing, how can they be forbidden to enter the courtyard when they have vowed not to benefit from each other?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Are they not particular about standing? But the Mishnah teaches that partners who vowed mutual benefit are forbidden to enter the courtyard.

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution: the alley behind houses
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution: the alley behind houses
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Abba explains that the case is about an alley behind houses, where standing is not a concern, but a partition is.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha answers that the case is about an alley behind houses, where partners are not particular about standing but are particular about a partition.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction: some are particular, some are not
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction: some are particular, some are not
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says that both cases are in a shared courtyard, but some are particular and some are not; regarding monetary matters we are lenient, regarding prohibitions we are stringent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that both cases are in a shared courtyard, but some are particular and some are not; regarding monetary matters we rule leniently, and regarding prohibitions we rule stringently.

items.text: Ravina's alternative: always not particular, following Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative: always not particular, following Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Ravina says that partners are never particular about standing, and the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer, who forbids even a trivial benefit to one who is under a vow of benefit.

sub.desc_en: Ravina answers that in truth they are not particular, and the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that even a trivial benefit is forbidden to one who is vowed from benefit.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: partners may prevent each other from everything except laundry
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: partners may prevent each other from everything except laundry
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah states that partners can prevent each other from doing anything in the shared courtyard except laundry, because Jewish women should not be degraded by doing laundry in public.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Bena'ah states that partners may prevent each other from everything except laundry, because Jewish women should not be degraded over laundry.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse and the obligation to avert one's eyes
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse and the obligation to avert one's eyes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba explains that 'closing his eyes from seeing evil' refers to one who does not look at women doing laundry. The Gemara questions: if there is another path, he is wicked; if not, he is compelled. It concludes that even if there is no other path, he must force himself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba interprets the verse 'closing his eyes from seeing evil' as referring to one who does not look at women when they are doing laundry.
The Gemara questions the scenario: if there is another path, the one who looks is wicked; if there is no other path, he is compelled and not liable.
The Gemara resolves that even when there is no other path, one must force himself to avert his eyes.

items.text: The attire and table of a Torah scholar, and the placement of his ring
items.text_en: The attire and table of a Torah scholar, and the placement of his ring
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Bena'ah about the proper garments and table of a Torah scholar. The Gemara then discusses a contradiction regarding whether the ring is worn on the outside or inside, resolving it based on the presence of a child, a servant, or day versus night.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question to Rabbi Bena'ah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question to Rabbi Bena'ah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Bena'ah about the proper attire, table, and ring placement of a Torah scholar, receiving a series of definitions.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says the ring is worn on the inside, contradicting Rabbi Bena'ah's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when a child is present (ring inside) and when not (ring outside).
An alternative resolution distinguishes between when a servant is present (ring inside) and when not (ring outside), even without a child.
A third resolution distinguishes between day (ring outside) and night (ring inside), even when a servant is present.
The Gemara notes that the ring of an ignoramus (עם הארץ) is similar in placement to that of a Torah scholar.

items.text: The beds of Torah scholars and ignoramuses
items.text_en: The beds of Torah scholars and ignoramuses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the bed of a Torah scholar as one that has only sandals under it in summer and shoes in winter, while the bed of an ignoramus resembles a chaotic storehouse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the bed of a Torah scholar as one that has only sandals under it in summer and shoes in winter.
The Mishnah contrasts the bed of an ignoramus, which resembles a chaotic storehouse.

items.text: Rabbi Bena'ah at the cave of Abraham
items.text_en: Rabbi Bena'ah at the cave of Abraham
items.desc_en: Rabbi Bena'ah, while marking caves, encounters Eliezer at the entrance of Abraham's cave. Eliezer tells him Abraham is sleeping in Sarah's lap, and when Rabbi Bena'ah asks to enter, Eliezer says there is no yetzer hara in this world, so he enters, measures, and leaves.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Bena'ah, while marking caves, arrives at the cave of Abraham and finds Eliezer standing at the entrance.
Rabbi Bena'ah asks Eliezer what Abraham is doing.
Eliezer replies that Abraham is sleeping in Sarah's lap and she is looking at his head.
Rabbi Bena'ah tells Eliezer to inform Abraham that Bena'ah is at the entrance.
Eliezer says that Abraham can enter because there is no evil inclination (יצר הרע) in the World to Come.
Rabbi Bena'ah enters, measures the cave, and leaves.

items.text: Rabbi Bena'ah at the cave of Adam and the beauty hierarchy
items.text_en: Rabbi Bena'ah at the cave of Adam and the beauty hierarchy
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Bena'ah reaches Adam's cave, a bat kol warns him not to look at Adam's likeness. He is told the inner cave is proportional to the outer. He then describes Adam's heels as like two suns, and compares the beauty of Sarah, Eve, and Adam relative to each other and the Shekhinah.

sub.desc_en: When Rabbi Bena'ah reaches the cave of Adam, a bat kol (heavenly voice) warns him not to look at Adam's likeness.
Rabbi Bena'ah objects that he needs to measure the cave for marking boundaries.
The bat kol instructs him that the inner cave is proportional to the outer, or the upper to the lower.
Rabbi Bena'ah reports that he saw Adam's heels, which were like two suns.

Rabbi Bena'ah establishes a beauty hierarchy: all people compared to Sarah are like a monkey before a human, Sarah compared to Eve is like a monkey, Eve compared to Adam is like a monkey, and Adam compared to the Shekhinah (Divine Presence) is like a monkey.

items.text: Chain of beauty from Rav Kahana to Adam
items.text_en: Chain of beauty from Rav Kahana to Adam
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the beauty of Rav Kahana was akin to that of Rav, Rav's to Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Abbahu's to Jacob, and Jacob's to Adam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a chain of diminishing beauty from Rav Kahana back to Adam, each link being a reflection of the next.

items.text: The magus who grabbed Rav Tovi bar Mattena's beard
items.text_en: The magus who grabbed Rav Tovi bar Mattena's beard
items.desc_en: A magus who was measuring graves grabbed Rav Tovi bar Mattena by the beard. Abaye asked him to let go, but the next year he did it again, and Abaye had his beard shaved off.

sub.desc_en: The narrator recounts that a magus measuring graves grabbed Rav Tovi bar Mattena by the beard; Abaye intervened the first year, and the second year Abaye had the magus's beard shaved off.

items.text: The case of the three jars: earth, bones, and chaff
items.text_en: The case of the three jars: earth, bones, and chaff
items.desc_en: Someone left a will with three jars: one of earth, one of bones, and one of chaff. The heirs did not understand, so they came to Rabbi Bena'ah, who explained that it meant they had land, livestock, and clothing, and that the deceased was referring to these.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces a man who left a will with three jars (earth, bones, chaff) to three sons, and the heirs did not understand the meaning.
The heirs came before Rabbi Bena'ah, who began to question them about their assets.
After the heirs confirmed they had land, livestock, and clothing, Rabbi Bena'ah explained that the jars were a riddle referring to these assets.

items.text: The case of the man who left all to one son
items.text_en: The case of the man who left all to one son
items.desc_en: A man heard his wife say she had only one son from him, so he left all his property to one son. The heirs did not know which son, so Rabbi Bena'ah told them to strike their father's grave until he reveals. Only the true son refused, and Rabbi Bena'ah identified him. The others informed the king, and Rabbi Bena'ah was imprisoned.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces a man who overheard his wife telling her daughter that she has ten sons but only one from him.
The narrator relates that when the man died, he left all his property to one son, without specifying which.
The narrator states that the heirs did not know which son was the designated heir.
Rabbi Bena'ah instructs the heirs to strike their father's grave until he reveals which son was designated.
All the sons except the true son went to strike the grave, and Rabbi Bena'ah identified the true son as the one who refused.
The other sons informed the king that Rabbi Bena'ah extracts money without witnesses, and he was imprisoned.

items.text: The case of the slave's skin used as a waterskin
items.text_en: The case of the slave's skin used as a waterskin
items.desc_en: A woman complained that her slave was killed, his skin used as a waterskin, and she received no payment. The officials did not understand, so they brought Rabbi Bena'ah, who explained she meant a waterskin (zarnuka). They then appointed him as a judge.

sub.desc_en: A woman complains to the officials that her slave was killed, his skin used as a waterskin, and she received no payment.

sub.text: The officials' confusion and Rabbi Bena'ah's explanation
sub.text_en: The officials' confusion and Rabbi Bena'ah's explanation
sub.desc_en: The officials do not understand the woman's words, so they bring Rabbi Bena'ah, who explains she meant a waterskin (זרנוקא), and they appoint him as a judge.

items.text: Rabbi Bena'ah's reluctance to judge
items.text_en: Rabbi Bena'ah's reluctance to judge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Bena'ah saw an inscription on the gate saying that any judge who is called to judge is not a judge. He questioned this, implying he was reluctant to take the position.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Bena'ah sees an inscription on the gate stating that any judge who is called to judge is not a judge, and he questions this, implying reluctance to take the position.

items.text: Inscription about judges
items.text_en: Inscription about judges
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses an inscription found in a cemetery that states a judge who is called to judgment and has money taken from him by judgment is not called a judge. The elders of Judah confirm this saying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a judge who is summoned to judgment and has money taken from him is thereby disqualified.
The Gemara explains that the inscription means any judge who is called to judgment and has money taken from him by judgment is not called a judge.
The elders of Judah confirm this saying in their own inscription.

items.text: Inscription about blood and wine
items.text_en: Inscription about blood and wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines another inscription that says 'I am blood at the head of all death, I am wine at the head of all life.' It questions the logic and corrects it to 'I am blood at the head of all illnesses, I am wine at the head of all cures,' with an addition about spices where wine is unavailable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports seeing an inscription that claims 'I am blood at the head of all death, I am wine at the head of all life.'
The Gemara objects: if blood causes all death, then why do people die from falls, and if wine cures all, why do people die despite drinking wine?
The Gemara corrects the inscription: it should read 'I am blood at the head of all illnesses, I am wine at the head of all cures.'
The Elders of Judah confirm the corrected version and add that where wine is unavailable, spices are sought instead.

items.text: Inscription on the gate of Kapotkia
items.text_en: Inscription on the gate of Kapotkia
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an inscription on the gate of Kapotkia with three words: 'Anpak, Anbag, Antal,' and identifies 'Antal' as the Torah's quarter-log measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports an inscription on the gate of Kapotkia containing three words: 'Anpak, Anbag, Antal.'
The Gemara identifies 'Antal' as the Torah's quarter-log measure (רביעית).

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of presumptive ownership for gutters, ladders, and windows
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of presumptive ownership for gutters, ladders, and windows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a gutter (מרזב) does not acquire presumptive ownership (חזקה) but its place does; a drainpipe (מזחילה) does acquire. An Egyptian ladder has no presumptive ownership, but a Tyrian one does. An Egyptian window has no presumptive ownership, but a Tyrian one does. Rabbi Yehuda adds that if a window has a frame, even if a person's head cannot enter, it acquires presumptive ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a gutter (מרזב) does not acquire presumptive ownership (חזקה) but its place does, and a drainpipe (מזחילה) does acquire.
The Mishnah continues: an Egyptian ladder has no presumptive ownership, but a Tyrian one does.

The Mishnah concludes: an Egyptian window has no presumptive ownership, but a Tyrian one does; Rabbi Yehuda adds that if a window has a frame (מלבן), even if a person's head cannot enter, it acquires presumptive ownership.

items.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: Gutter from one side vs. two sides
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: Gutter from one side vs. two sides
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains the Mishnah: a gutter has no presumptive ownership from one direction (i.e., the neighbor cannot prevent the owner from shortening it), but its place has presumptive ownership from two directions (i.e., the neighbor cannot remove it entirely).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by saying a gutter has no presumptive ownership but its place does.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains: the gutter has no presumptive ownership from one direction (the neighbor cannot prevent shortening), but its place has presumptive ownership from two directions (the neighbor cannot remove it entirely).

items.text: Rabbi Chanina: Gutter can be shortened, place cannot be removed
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina: Gutter can be shortened, place cannot be removed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains: a gutter has no presumptive ownership because if it is long, the neighbor can shorten it; but its place has presumptive ownership because if one wants to remove it entirely, he cannot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains that a gutter (מרזב) has no presumptive ownership (חזקה) because if it is long the neighbor can shorten it, but its place has presumptive ownership because one cannot remove it entirely.

items.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba: Building under the gutter, but cannot remove it
items.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba: Building under the gutter, but cannot remove it
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba explains: a gutter has no presumptive ownership because if one wants to build underneath it, he may; but its place has presumptive ownership because if one wants to remove it, he cannot.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba explains that a gutter has no presumptive ownership (חזקה) because one may build under it, but its place has presumptive ownership because one cannot remove it.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on a waterspout
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on a waterspout
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that a waterspout has a presumption of ownership. It explains that the Mishnah refers to a built waterspout, where the neighbor can claim that the water flow damages his wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a waterspout has a presumption of ownership, noting it works well for the opinion that the two presumptions (for the waterspout and the window) are distinct.
The Gemara questions: according to the opinion that one may build beneath a neighbor's projection, what practical difference does the waterspout's presumption make?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with a built waterspout, where the neighbor can object that the water flow will damage his wall.

items.text: Dispute about a pipe that spills water into a neighbor's courtyard
items.text_en: Dispute about a pipe that spills water into a neighbor's courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a roof owner cannot block a pipe that spills water into a neighbor's courtyard, because the courtyard owner benefits from the water. A dispute follows between Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Chama, with Rabbi Beisa ruling that the courtyard owner can block it.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that the roof owner cannot block a pipe spilling water into the neighbor's courtyard, because the courtyard owner benefits from the water.

The gemara reports a dispute: Rabbi Oshaya says the courtyard owner can block the pipe, Rabbi Chama says he cannot; Rabbi Beisa rules in favor of blocking, and Rami bar Chama applies a verse praising Rabbi Oshaya as a third-generation scholar.

items.text: Definition of an Egyptian ladder and the structure of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Definition of an Egyptian ladder and the structure of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines an Egyptian ladder as one with fewer than four rungs. It then explains why the Mishnah specifies the size for a window but not for a ladder: to allow for Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting opinion in the latter clause.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an Egyptian ladder does not establish a presumptive right (חזקה).
The Gemara asks: what is the definition of an Egyptian ladder?
Beit Rabbi Yannai defines an Egyptian ladder as one with fewer than four rungs.
The Gemara asks: why does the Mishnah specify the size for an Egyptian window but not for an Egyptian ladder?
The Gemara answers: because the Mishnah needs to allow for Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting opinion in the latter clause regarding the window.

items.text: Dispute about a window's height and the right to object
items.text_en: Dispute about a window's height and the right to object
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira rules that a window below four cubits has a presumption and the neighbor can object, while above four cubits there is no presumption and no right to object. Rabbi Ila argues that even above four cubits there is no presumption but the neighbor can still object. The Gemara explains the dispute is not about coercion (כופין על מדת סדום) but about the neighbor's claim of privacy. The halakha follows Rabbi Ila.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira rules that a window below four cubits has a presumption (חזקה) and the neighbor can object, while above four cubits there is no presumption and no right to object.
Rabbi Ila argues that even above four cubits there is no presumption but the neighbor can still object.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute is about the principle of coercion regarding the measure of Sodom (כופין על מדת סדום).
The Gemara rejects that explanation, stating that all agree on coercion, but the dispute is about the neighbor's claim of privacy — he might place a bench and stand to look through the window.

sub.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abba bar Memel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Abba bar Memel
sub.desc_en: A case came before Rabbi Ami, who sent it to Rabbi Abba bar Memel, who ruled in accordance with Rabbi Ila.

items.text: Ruling on a skylight and beginning of the Mishnah on a projection
items.text_en: Ruling on a skylight and beginning of the Mishnah on a projection
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a skylight (אורה) has a presumption even if it is any size. The Mishnah then begins discussing a projection (זיז): if it is up to a handbreadth, it has a presumption.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a skylight (אורה) has a presumption (חזקה) even if it is any size.
The Mishnah begins discussing a projection (זיז): if it is up to a handbreadth, it has a presumption.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a protrusion of a handbreadth or more grants hazakah and the right to protest, while less than a handbreadth does not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a protrusion of a handbreadth or more grants hazakah and the right to protest, while less than a handbreadth does not.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Mani, or alternatively Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Mani, states that holding a handbreadth in length of four handbreadths grants hazakah for a width of four. Abaye explains the statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Mani that holding a handbreadth grants possession of four, and asks what this means.
Abaye explains that holding a handbreadth in width over a length of four handbreadths grants possession of a width of four handbreadths.
Abaye explains that the statement means: holding a width of one handbreadth over a length of four handbreadths grants hazakah for a width of four.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Huna limits the Mishnah's rule to the roof owner against the courtyard owner, but the courtyard owner can protest. Rav Yehuda says even the courtyard owner cannot protest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara restates the Mishnah's rule that less than a handbreadth grants no hazakah and no right to protest.
Rav Huna limits the Mishnah's leniency to cases where the roof owner protests against the courtyard owner, but not vice versa.
Rav Yehuda rules that even the courtyard owner cannot protest against the roof owner.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether hezek re'iyah (damage by seeing) is considered damage, but rejects this. It explains that all agree it is damage, but the courtyard owner can say the protrusion is useless for him, while the other says sometimes he might need it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda is about whether hezek re'iyah (damage by seeing) is considered legal damage.

The Gemara rejects the proposal, stating that all agree hezek re'iyah is damage, but the courtyard owner can argue the protrusion is useless for him except for hanging things, which he can avoid by turning his face away.
The second opinion (Rav Yehuda) responds that sometimes the courtyard owner might be startled and need the protrusion for support, so he cannot be forced to remove it.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Opening windows into a shared courtyard
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Opening windows into a shared courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits opening windows into a shared courtyard, even if one buys a house in another courtyard or builds an upper story, unless one builds an inner room and opens the window into one's own house.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not open windows into a shared courtyard, and if one builds an upper story, he must open it into his own house.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a shared courtyard; even a private courtyard should be prohibited. It answers that the Mishnah uses a 'not necessary' style: it is obvious for a private courtyard, but for a shared courtyard one might think it is permitted because the other partner already sees him in the courtyard; the Mishnah teaches that the partner can say now he also wants privacy in the house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifically mentions a shared courtyard (חצר השותפין); even a private courtyard should also be forbidden.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah uses a 'not necessary' style: it is obvious for a private courtyard, but for a shared courtyard one might think it is permitted because the partner already sees him in the courtyard; the Mishnah teaches that the partner can say now he also wants privacy in the house.

items.text: Story with Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Chiyya, and Rav Nachman's statement
items.text_en: Story with Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Chiyya, and Rav Nachman's statement
items.desc_en: A story is told of a man who opened windows into a shared courtyard; Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosi said he had established hazakah, but Rabbi Chiyya said he must close them. Rav Nachman begins to speak, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces a story of a man who opened his windows into a shared courtyard.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosi rules that the man has established חֲזָקָה (presumptive right) to keep the windows open.
Rabbi Chiyya gives the opposite ruling: since the man opened the windows with effort, he must exert himself to close them.
Rav Nachman begins to speak, but the text cuts off before his statement is recorded.

items.text: Opening statement: blocking a window
items.text_en: Opening statement: blocking a window
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one blocks a window, the presumption of ownership is immediate because a person does not silently allow his light to be blocked.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that blocking a window establishes an immediate presumption (חזקה) because a person does not silently allow his light to be blocked.

items.text: Gemara's question on opening a door to a shared courtyard
items.text_en: Gemara's question on opening a door to a shared courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one who buys a house in another courtyard cannot open a door to the shared courtyard because it increases traffic. It then cites a contradiction from the Mishnah itself, and Rav Huna resolves it by reinterpreting the terms.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who buys a house in another courtyard may not open a door to the shared courtyard because it increases traffic.
The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah's own continuation, which permits building a room or upper story, which also increases traffic.
Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting 'room' as a partition within the existing house and 'upper story' as a porch (אפתאי), which do not increase traffic.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition of facing openings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition of facing openings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not open a door or window directly opposite another's in a shared courtyard, and may not enlarge or multiply openings. However, one may do so facing the public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not open a door or window directly opposite another's in a shared courtyard, and may not enlarge or multiply openings, but may do so facing the public domain.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the prohibition
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the prohibition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives the prohibition from Balaam's blessing, where he saw that the Israelites' tent openings were not aligned, indicating divine presence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the prohibition of opening a door opposite a door) derived?
Rabbi Yochanan answers by citing a verse about Balaam, who saw that the Israelites' tent openings were not aligned, indicating divine presence, thus deriving the prohibition from modesty.

items.text: Gemara: Enlarging a small opening
items.text_en: Gemara: Enlarging a small opening
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama thought that enlarging a small opening is permitted if it doesn't increase the total width, but Rava objects that the neighbor can claim he could hide from a small opening but not a large one.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not enlarge a small opening into a courtyard.
Rami bar Chama thought that enlarging a small opening is only prohibited if it increases the total width (e.g., from 4 to 8 handbreadths), but enlarging from 2 to 4 handbreadths is permitted.
Rava objects that the neighbor can claim: with a small opening I could hide from you, but with a large opening I cannot.

items.text: Gemara: Multiplying openings
items.text_en: Gemara: Multiplying openings
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama thought that splitting one opening into two is permitted if the total width remains the same, but Rava objects that the neighbor can hide from one opening but not from two.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not turn a single opening into two.
Rami bar Chama thought that splitting a large opening into two smaller ones of equal total width should be permitted, since the total area taken from the courtyard remains the same.
Rava objects that the neighbor can say: from one opening I can hide, but from two I cannot hide.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for allowing openings to public domain
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for allowing openings to public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one may open a door opposite another facing the public domain because the neighbor can say he must hide from the public anyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that one may open a door opposite another facing the public domain because the neighbor can claim he must hide from the public anyway.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Excavations under public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Excavations under public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits making cavities under public domain, but Rabbi Eliezer permits it if a loaded wagon can pass. The Gemara notes that the Rabbis are concerned about collapse without the owner's knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition against making cavities under public domain, with Rabbi Eliezer's leniency, and additional rules about protruding ledges.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis prohibit cavities under public domain because the ground might collapse without the owner's knowledge.

items.text: Stories about projections and trees in public domain
items.text_en: Stories about projections and trees in public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts two stories: Rabbi Ami tells a man with a projection into public domain to cut it down, explaining that the public does not forgive. Similarly, Rabbi Yannai deals with a man whose tree overhangs public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not extend projections or balconies into the public domain unless he withdraws into his own property and then extends.
The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Ami had a projection extending into an alley, and when a man with a projection into the public domain came before him, Rabbi Ami told him to cut it down.

The man objects that Rabbi Ami himself has a projection, and Rabbi Ami explains that his own projection is into an alley where neighbors can forgive, but the man's projection is into the public domain where no one can forgive.
The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Yannai had a tree overhanging the public domain, and when a man with a similar tree came before him, Rabbi Yannai addressed him.

items.text: The story of the tree and the principle of self-correction
items.text_en: The story of the tree and the principle of self-correction
items.desc_en: A story about a man who cut his own tree after seeing that the public benefited from its shade, but then delayed cutting the neighbor's tree to teach a lesson. The Gemara explains the initial and final reasoning, and invokes Reish Lakish's principle that one must correct oneself before correcting others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara tells a story of a man who was told to cut his tree tomorrow, but cut his own tree at night, and then instructed the neighbor to check if his own tree was cut before cutting the neighbor's.
The Gemara asks what the man initially thought and what he ultimately thought about the public's benefit from the tree's shade.
The Gemara explains that initially the man thought the public enjoyed the shade, but when he saw they were delaying, he cut his own tree.
The Gemara objects: why didn't the man simply tell the neighbor to cut his tree first, and then he would cut his own?
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Reish Lakish's principle that one must correct oneself before correcting others.

items.text: Dispute about retracting walls after encroachment
items.text_en: Dispute about retracting walls after encroachment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one wishes, he may bring his projection back into his property and then extend it out. The Gemara raises a question: if he brought it in but did not yet extend it, may he still extend? Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute this, with Rabbi Yaakov clarifying that the dispute is actually about whether he may restore the walls to their original place. Rabbi Yochanan prohibits restoration due to the principle that a path established by the public may not be disturbed, while Reish Lakish permits it because there remains space for the public.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one wishes, he may bring his projection back into his property and then extend it out.
The Gemara raises a question: if he brought the projection in but did not yet extend it, may he still extend?
Rabbi Yochanan rules that if he brought it in, he may still extend it.
Reish Lakish rules that if he brought it in, he may not extend it.
Rabbi Yaakov clarifies to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Tachlifa that the dispute is not about extending but about restoring the walls to their original place.
The positions are reversed: Rabbi Yochanan prohibits restoring the walls, while Reish Lakish permits it.
Rabbi Yochanan prohibits restoration because of Rav Yehuda's principle that a path established by the public may not be disturbed.
Reish Lakish permits restoration because the public still has space to pass, unlike the case where the path is blocked.

items.text: The law of a purchased courtyard with projections and the exception of prohibition
items.text_en: The law of a purchased courtyard with projections and the exception of prohibition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one buys a courtyard with existing projections and balconies, it retains its presumptive status. Rav Huna adds that if they fall, he may rebuild them. An objection is raised from a baraita about the prohibition of plastering, whitewashing, and painting in the present era, which states that if one buys a courtyard that was already treated, it retains its status, but if it falls, he may not rebuild. The Gemara resolves that the case of prohibition (issura) is different.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one buys a courtyard with existing projections and balconies, it retains its presumptive status.
Rav Huna adds that if the projections fall, the buyer may rebuild them.

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about the prohibition of plastering, whitewashing, and painting in the present era, which states that if one buys a courtyard that was already treated, it retains its status, but if it falls, he may not rebuild.
The Gemara resolves that the case of prohibition (איסורא) is different from the case of monetary law, so the baraita does not contradict Rav Huna.

items.text: Baraita on plastering with lime and the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Baraita on plastering with lime and the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one should not plaster his house with lime, but if he mixed in sand or straw, it is permitted. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: if he mixed sand, it becomes traksid (a type of plaster) and is forbidden; if straw, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: one should not plaster his house with lime, but if he mixed in sand or straw it is permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: mixing sand creates טרכסיד (a type of plaster) which is forbidden, but mixing straw is permitted.

items.text: The debate about mourning practices after the destruction and the compromise
items.text_en: The debate about mourning practices after the destruction and the compromise
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that after the Second Temple's destruction, many ascetics refrained from meat and wine. Rabbi Yehoshua engaged them, arguing that if they go to extremes, they would also have to abstain from bread, fruits, and water. He then taught that complete mourning is impossible, but excessive mourning is also not feasible. Instead, the Sages prescribed moderate practices: one should plaster his house but leave a small amount unfinished, specifically an amah by an amah opposite the door.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing that after the Second Temple's destruction, many ascetics (פרושים) in Israel refrained from eating meat and drinking wine, and Rabbi Yehoshua engaged them, asking why they do so; they replied that since meat and wine were used in Temple offerings which are now nullified, they abstain.

Rabbi Yehoshua argues reductively that if they follow this logic, they would also have to abstain from bread (since meal-offerings ceased), fruits (since first-fruits ceased), and water (since the water-libation ceased), leaving them silent.

Rabbi Yehoshua teaches that complete abstention from mourning is impossible because the decree has already been decreed, but excessive mourning is also impossible because a decree is not imposed on the community unless the majority can endure it, citing the verse 'במארה אתם נארים' (Malachi 3:9).

The Sages prescribed a moderate mourning practice: one should plaster his house with lime but leave a small unfinished area, and Rav Yosef specifies it as an amah by an amah, while Rav Chisda adds that it should be opposite the door.

items.text: Additional mourning practices: meal, jewelry, and the ash on the groom's head
items.text_en: Additional mourning practices: meal, jewelry, and the ash on the groom's head
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues with other mourning practices: one should prepare all needs for a meal but leave a small item (a cup of harasana); a woman should wear all her jewelry but leave one item (a bat tzida). The verse about remembering Jerusalem is cited. Rav Yitzchak explains that 'the head of my joy' refers to the ash of the kiln placed on the heads of grooms, and Rav Pappa tells Abaye that it is placed where tefillin are worn, as per the verse. One who mourns for Jerusalem will merit to see her joy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one should prepare all needs for a meal but leave out a small item as a sign of mourning.
Rav Pappa answers that the small item left out is a cup of harasana (a type of dish).
The Gemara states that a woman should wear all her jewelry but leave out one item as a sign of mourning.
Rav answers that the item left out is a bat tzida (a type of head ornament).
The Gemara cites the verse 'If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget; let my tongue cleave to my palate' to support the practice of remembering Jerusalem.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'the head of my joy' from the verse.
Rav Yitzchak explains that 'the head of my joy' refers to the ash of the kiln placed on the heads of grooms as a sign of mourning.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye where the ash is placed on the head.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's answer (or Abaye's implied answer)
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer (or Abaye's implied answer)
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that it is placed where tefillin are worn, citing the verse 'to give them beauty (פאר) instead of ash'.
The Gemara concludes that one who mourns for Jerusalem will merit to see her joy, citing the verse 'Rejoice with Jerusalem'.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's principle: let Israel be unwitting rather than deliberate
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's principle: let Israel be unwitting rather than deliberate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha teaches that since the Temple's destruction, it would be fitting to decree against meat and wine, but the community cannot bear it. Similarly, since the wicked kingdom's decrees, it would be fitting to decree against marriage and procreation, but it is better to let Israel be unwitting rather than deliberate sinners.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha states that since the Temple's destruction, it would be fitting to decree against meat and wine, but the community cannot bear such a decree.
Rabbi Yishmael adds that since the wicked kingdom's decrees, it would be fitting to decree against marriage and procreation, but the community cannot bear that either.
Rabbi Yishmael concludes that it is better to let Israel be unwitting rather than deliberate sinners.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items not sold with a house: an alcove (יציע), an inner room (חדר), and a roof with a parapet ten handbreadths high. Rabbi Yehuda adds that a roof with a doorway-shaped entrance is not sold even if the parapet is lower.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing items not sold with a house: an alcove (יציע), an inner room (חדר), and a roof with a parapet ten handbreadths high; Rabbi Yehuda adds that a roof with a doorway-shaped entrance is not sold even if the parapet is lower.

items.text: Gemara's definition of 'יציע'
items.text_en: Gemara's definition of 'יציע'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'יציע' means. In the West they translate it as 'אפתא' (a side chamber), while Rav Yosef says it is 'בדקא חלילה' (a recess). Rav Yosef then teaches that 'יציע' has three names: 'יציע', 'צלע', and 'תא', citing biblical verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'יציע' (side chamber) means.
In the West they translate 'יציע' as 'אפתא' (a side chamber).
Rav Yosef says 'יציע' means 'בדקא חלילה' (a recess).
The Gemara analyzes the practical halachic difference between the two definitions regarding whether the side chamber is included in the sale of the house.
Rav Yosef teaches a baraita that 'יציע' has three names — 'יציע', 'צלע', and 'תא' — and cites biblical verses for each.

items.text: Size requirement for 'יציע'
items.text_en: Size requirement for 'יציע'
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra states that the 'יציע' is not sold only if it is four cubits wide. Ravina challenges him by comparing to a cistern (בור) which is never sold even if large. The Gemara distinguishes: a cistern is a separate use, while an alcove is part of the house; only if it is four cubits is it significant enough to be excluded.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra states that the 'יציע' (alcove) is excluded from the sale only if it is four cubits wide.
Ravina challenges Mar Zutra by comparing to a cistern (בור), which is never sold even if large, questioning why size should matter for the 'יציע'.
The Gemara distinguishes: a cistern is a separate use, while an alcove is part of the house; only if it is four cubits is it significant enough to be excluded.

items.text: Question on 'חדר'
items.text_en: Question on 'חדר'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that even an 'יציע' (alcove) is not sold, is it necessary to mention that a 'חדר' (inner room) is not sold? The implication is that a 'חדר' is more obviously excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to mention the inner room (חדר) separately, since if even the alcove (יציע) is not sold, certainly the more significant inner room is not sold.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on selling a house in a large complex
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on selling a house in a large complex
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even when the seller delineates outer boundaries, he does not sell the entire complex, following Rav Nachman's principle that boundaries are given only to clarify the property. The Gemara clarifies the case: the house is commonly called 'house' and the complex 'complex', but some call the complex 'house'; the seller's failure to write 'I have not retained anything' indicates he reserved the rest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that even when the seller delineates outer boundaries, it does not sell the entire complex, following Rav Nachman's principle that boundaries are only to expand the property.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Rabbah bar Avuha's ruling that a seller of a house in a large complex, even when marking outer boundaries, only expands the boundaries but does not sell the entire complex.
The Gemara questions the case: if the house is called 'house' and the complex 'complex', it is obvious only the house is sold; if the complex is also called 'house', the entire complex would be sold.

The Gemara resolves that the case is where most call the house 'house' and the complex 'complex', but some call the complex 'house'; the seller's failure to write 'I have not retained anything' indicates he reserved the rest.

items.text: Rav Nachman's parallel ruling on selling a field in a large valley
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's parallel ruling on selling a field in a large valley
items.desc_en: The same principle applies to a field in a large valley: outer boundaries do not convey the entire valley. The Gemara again clarifies that the field is commonly called 'field' and the valley 'valley', but some call the valley 'field'; the absence of a clause stating no reservation indicates a reservation.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Rabbah bar Avuha's ruling that selling a field in a large valley with outer boundaries does not convey the entire valley.
The Gemara asks about the case: if the field is commonly called 'field' and the valley 'valley', the ruling is obvious; if the valley is also called 'field', the entire valley is sold.

The Gemara resolves that the case is where most call the field 'field' and the valley 'valley', but some call the valley 'field'; the absence of a clause stating no reservation indicates a reservation.

items.text: Why both cases are necessary
items.text_en: Why both cases are necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both rulings are needed: the case of a house might suggest the seller reserves nothing because the uses are distinct, while the case of a field might suggest the opposite because the use is uniform; each ruling teaches the principle in its own context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that both cases are necessary, explaining that if only the house case were taught, one might think the seller reserves nothing in a field because the field's use is uniform.

The Gemara completes the explanation by noting that if only the field case were taught, one might think the seller reserves nothing in a house because he had the opportunity to delineate boundaries and did not; therefore both rulings are necessary.

items.text: Rav Mari's statement in support of Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rav Mari's statement in support of Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel quotes Abaye that a seller must write 'I have not retained anything' in the deed, and this aligns with Rav Nachman's ruling.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel citing Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel citing Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel cites Abaye's rule that a seller must write 'I have not retained anything' in the deed, establishing a general requirement.
The Gemara concludes that Abaye's rule aligns with Rav Nachman's ruling cited by Rabbah bar Avuha, confirming that the seller's failure to write the standard clause indicates he retained something.

items.text: Case of ambiguous property names and the rule of 'ar'ata'
items.text_en: Case of ambiguous property names and the rule of 'ar'ata'
items.desc_en: A case is presented where someone said 'I am selling you the land of Bei Chiyya' and had two such lands; Rav Ashi rules he meant only one. The Gemara then discusses the implications of using plural 'ar'ata' (lands) and 'kol ar'ata' (all lands), excluding gardens and orchards, while 'zihara' includes even gardens and orchards but excludes houses and slaves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a seller said 'I am selling you the land of Bei Chiyya' and had two lands called Bei Chiyya.
Rav Ashi rules that the seller meant only one of the two lands, not both.
The Gemara states that if one says 'ar'ata' (lands) in the plural, the minimum is two.
If one says 'kol ar'ata' (all lands), it includes all his lands except gardens and orchards.
If one says 'zihara' (bright/choice), it includes even gardens and orchards but excludes houses and slaves.

items.text: General rule: 'Nikhsei' includes houses and slaves
items.text_en: General rule: 'Nikhsei' includes houses and slaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one says 'nikhsei' (my property), it includes even houses and slaves, establishing a broad interpretation of the term.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the term 'נִכְסֵי' (my property) includes even houses and slaves, establishing a broad interpretation.

items.text: Rav's ruling on long and short boundaries
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on long and short boundaries
items.desc_en: Rav rules that if one boundary is long and the other short, the buyer acquires only the area opposite the short boundary. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object, arguing the buyer should acquire opposite the 'rosh tor' (the entire field), but Rav remains silent.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that if one boundary is long and the other short, the buyer acquires only the area opposite the short boundary.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object, arguing the buyer should acquire opposite the 'rosh tor' (the entire field).
Rav remains silent, indicating he has no response to the objection.

items.text: Rav's concession: boundaries from different sides
items.text_en: Rav's concession: boundaries from different sides
items.desc_en: Rav concedes that when boundaries are from different sides (e.g., Reuven and Shimon on one side, Levi and Yehuda on the other), the buyer acquires opposite the 'rosh tor', because the seller would have written the specific alignments if not intended.

sub.desc_en: Rav concedes that when boundaries are from different sides (e.g., Reuven and Shimon on one side, Levi and Yehuda on the other), the buyer acquires opposite the 'rosh tor', because the seller would have written the specific alignments if not intended.

items.text: Requirement for specifying directions
items.text_en: Requirement for specifying directions
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if boundaries are on different sides (e.g., Reuven east-west, Shimon north-south), the deed must specify each boundary's directions explicitly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that when boundaries are on different sides (e.g., Reuven east-west, Shimon north-south), the deed must specify each boundary's directions explicitly.

items.text: Unresolved questions: corners and L-shaped fields
items.text_en: Unresolved questions: corners and L-shaped fields
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises two unresolved questions: what if the seller marked the corners (siyeim et hakarnot), and what if the field is L-shaped (kemin gam)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question: if the seller marked the corners (siyeim et hakarnot) of the field, what is the halacha regarding the buyer's acquisition?
The Gemara raises a second unresolved question: if the field is L-shaped (kemin gam), what is the halacha regarding the buyer's acquisition?

items.text: Unresolved question about serugin
items.text_en: Unresolved question about serugin
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a sale made in installments (serugin) and leaves it unresolved with 'teiku'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question about a sale made in installments (serugin) and leaves it with 'teiku'.

items.text: Dispute over omitted boundary
items.text_en: Dispute over omitted boundary
items.desc_en: When a seller lists three boundaries but omits a fourth, Rav says the buyer acquires everything except that omitted boundary, Shmuel says even that boundary is acquired, and Rav Asi says only a single furrow is acquired. The Gemara explains Rav Asi's reasoning as consistent with Rav's view that the seller retained something.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the case where a seller lists three boundaries but omits the fourth.
Rav rules that the buyer acquires everything except the omitted fourth boundary.
Shmuel rules that even the omitted fourth boundary is acquired by the buyer.
Rav Asi rules that the buyer acquires only a single furrow across the entire field.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Asi's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Asi's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Asi agrees with Rav that the seller retained something, and since he retained in the boundary, he also retained in the entire field.

items.text: Rava's first version of the ruling
items.text_en: Rava's first version of the ruling
