items.desc_en: Rava rules that the buyer acquires everything except the fourth boundary, but only if that boundary is not swallowed up (mubla) and has a date-grove ridge of nine kavs; otherwise, the buyer acquires it.

sub.text: Rava's first version of the ruling
sub.text_en: Rava's first version of the ruling
sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the buyer acquires everything except the fourth boundary, but only if the boundary is not absorbed and has a date-palm ridge of nine kav; if absorbed, or without the ridge, the buyer acquires even the fourth boundary.
Rava adds that even when not swallowed up, the buyer acquires the fourth boundary if there is no date-grove ridge of nine kavs on it.

items.text: Rava's second version of the ruling
items.text_en: Rava's second version of the ruling
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rava rules the buyer acquires everything including the fourth boundary, but only if it is swallowed up and has no date-grove ridge of nine kavs; otherwise, he does not acquire it.

sub.text: Rava's second version of the ruling
sub.text_en: Rava's second version of the ruling
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rava rules the buyer acquires everything including the fourth boundary, but only if the boundary is absorbed and lacks a date-palm ridge of nine kav; otherwise, the buyer does not acquire it.

sub.text: Gemara's clarification of the alternative version
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the alternative version
sub.desc_en: The gemara adds that even when swallowed up, the buyer does not acquire if there is a date-grove ridge of nine kavs; otherwise, he does not acquire.

items.text: Consensus from both versions
items.text_en: Consensus from both versions
items.desc_en: From both versions of Rava's ruling, we learn that in a field the seller retains nothing, and the decisive factors are whether the boundary is swallowed up and whether there is a date-grove ridge of nine kavs. The case where both conditions are present or both absent is left as a dispute among judges.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes from both versions of Rava's ruling that in a field the seller retains nothing, and that when the boundary is swallowed up and there is no date-grove ridge of nine kavs the buyer acquires, but when the boundary is not swallowed up and there is such a ridge the buyer does not acquire.
The Gemara notes that the case where both conditions are present or both absent is left as a dispute among judges (שודא דדייני).

items.text: Rabbah's interpretation of 'half' in a deed
items.text_en: Rabbah's interpretation of 'half' in a deed
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that if one writes 'half that I have in the land' he sells half, but if he writes 'half in the land that I have' he sells a quarter. Abaye questions the distinction, and Rabbah is silent. Abaye initially thinks the silence indicates acceptance, but later sees deeds from Rabbah's house confirming the distinction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah distinguishes between 'half that I have in the land' (half) and 'half in the land that I have' (quarter), and remains silent when Abaye asks for the reason.
Abaye asks Rabbah what is the difference between the two formulations, and Rabbah remains silent.
Abaye initially thought Rabbah's silence indicated acceptance, but later saw deeds from Rabbah's house confirming the distinction.

items.text: Rabbah on 'boundary from which half'
items.text_en: Rabbah on 'boundary from which half'
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one writes 'boundary of the land from which half' he sells half, but if he writes 'boundary of the land from which it is cut off' he sells nine kavs. Abaye questions the distinction, Rabbah is silent, and the Gemara initially assumes both mean half.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one writes 'boundary of the land from which half' he sells half, but if he writes 'boundary of the land from which it is cut off' he sells nine kavs.
Abaye questions the distinction between the two formulations, and Rabbah remains silent.
The Gemara initially assumes that both phrases mean half, resolving the distinction in favor of a uniform interpretation.

items.text: Distinction between two boundary clauses
items.text_en: Distinction between two boundary clauses
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya reports a clarification from Abaye: whether the seller says 'from this boundary it is divided' or 'from this boundary it is cut off', if he says 'these are its boundaries' the buyer gets half; if not, only nine kav.

sub.text: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya citing Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya citing Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya reports from Abaye that whether the seller says 'from this boundary it is divided' or 'from this boundary it is cut off', if he says 'these are its boundaries' the buyer gets half; if not, only nine kav.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'give a portion'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'give a portion'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one says 'let so-and-so take a portion in my property', he gets half; but if he says 'give a portion to so-and-so in my property', what is the law?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one says 'let so-and-so take a portion in my property', he gets half; but if he says 'give a portion to so-and-so in my property', what is the law?

items.text: Answer from a baraita on 'give a portion' in vessels
items.text_en: Answer from a baraita on 'give a portion' in vessels
items.desc_en: Ravina bar Kisi brings a baraita: if one says 'give a portion to so-and-so in a cistern', Sumchos says no less than a quarter; for a barrel, an eighth; for a pot, a twelfth; for a pitcher, a sixteenth. This implies 'give a portion' grants a minimum, not half.

sub.desc_en: Ravina bar Kisi cites a baraita where Sumchos rules that 'give a portion' in vessels sets a minimum measure, not half.

items.text: Baraita: Levite selling field with condition on tithe
items.text_en: Baraita: Levite selling field with condition on tithe
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: a Levite who sold a field to an Israelite and said 'on condition that the first tithe is mine' – the tithe is his. If he said 'for me and my sons', after his death he gives it to his sons. If he said 'as long as this field is in your hand', and the buyer sold it and bought it back, the Levite has no claim.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the case of a Levite selling a field to an Israelite on condition that the first tithe (מעשר ראשון) belongs to the Levite, and rules that the tithe is indeed his.
The baraita adds that if the Levite specified 'for me and my sons,' after his death the tithe is given to his sons.
The baraita concludes with a third condition: if the Levite said 'as long as this field is in your hand,' and the buyer later sold and repurchased the field, the Levite has no claim to the tithe.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why is the tithe his? One cannot acquire something not yet in the world! It answers: since he said 'on condition that the first tithe is mine', he reserved the place of the tithe for himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why is the tithe his? One cannot acquire something not yet in the world!
The Gemara answers: since he said 'on condition that the first tithe is mine', he reserved the place of the tithe for himself.

items.text: Resh Lakish's principle: selling a house with an upper room
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's principle: selling a house with an upper room
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says: this teaches that one who sells a house to another and says 'on condition that the upper room is mine' – the upper room is his.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish derives from the previous baraita that one who sells a house and stipulates that the upper room (דיוטא העליונה) remains his — the upper room is indeed his.

items.text: Two interpretations of the Mishnah's implication
items.text_en: Two interpretations of the Mishnah's implication
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa offer competing explanations for the practical halakhah derived from the Mishnah's phrase 'this teaches'. Rav Zevid says it permits extending beams from the wall, while Rav Pappa says it permits building an upper story on top of the house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halakhah (הלכה) is derived from the Mishnah's phrase 'this teaches'.
Rav Zevid says the Mishnah teaches that if one wishes to extend beams (זיזין) from the wall, he may do so.
Rav Pappa says the Mishnah teaches that if one wishes to build an upper story (עלייה) on top of the house, he may build it.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Pappa's interpretation
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Pappa's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Zevid's explanation fits the Mishnah's wording 'this teaches', but Rav Pappa's does not, leaving a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Zevid's explanation fits the Mishnah's wording 'this teaches'.
The Gemara objects that Rav Pappa's explanation does not align with the Mishnah's phrase 'this teaches', leaving a difficulty.

items.text: Rav Dimi's ruling on selling a house
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's ruling on selling a house
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi from Neharde'a states that when selling a house, even if the seller writes 'depth and height' in the deed, he must also write 'acquire from the depth of the earth to the height of the sky'. The reason is that 'depth and height' alone do not grant ownership of pits, cisterns, and caves, whereas the fuller phrase does.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi rules that when selling a house, the seller must write 'acquire from the depth of the earth to the height of the sky' to convey pits, cisterns, and caves, because writing only 'depth and height' does not suffice.

items.text: Supporting evidence from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Supporting evidence from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Dimi from the Mishnah's statement that a seller does not sell the pit or cistern even if he wrote 'depth and height'. The Gemara initially challenges this, but resolves that the Mishnah means even if he did not write 'depth and height', it is as if he wrote it for acquiring depth and height, but for pits and cisterns, only if he wrote 'depth and height' does he acquire them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to support Rav Dimi from the Mishnah's statement that a seller does not sell the pit or cistern even if he wrote 'depth and height'.
The Gemara objects: if one normally acquires depth and height without explicit mention, then writing 'depth and height' should suffice to acquire pits and cisterns, but the Mishnah says it does not.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah means 'even if he did not write', as if he wrote for acquiring depth and height, but for pits and cisterns, only if he wrote 'depth and height' does he acquire them.

items.text: New evidence from the Mishnah's ruling on a roof
items.text_en: New evidence from the Mishnah's ruling on a roof
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a new source: the Mishnah's statement that a seller does not sell the roof when it has a parapet ten handbreadths high, to further clarify the law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah as supporting evidence: a seller does not sell the roof when it has a parapet ten handbreadths high.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption about implicit acquisition of depth and height
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption about implicit acquisition of depth and height
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether selling a field implicitly includes its depth and height, and argues that if it does, a ten-handbreadth protrusion would be considered significant and thus not included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether selling a field implicitly includes its depth and height, arguing that a ten-handbreadth protrusion would be considered significant and thus not included.

items.text: Ravina's proof from Reish Lakish's statement
items.text_en: Ravina's proof from Reish Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: Ravina cites Reish Lakish's ruling that if one sells a house and stipulates that the upper story remains his, he retains rights to project beams or build an upper story. The Gemara argues that if the seller did not implicitly acquire depth and height, the stipulation would be unnecessary; rather, it serves to allow rebuilding if it collapses.

sub.desc_en: Ravina cites Reish Lakish's ruling that if one sells a house and stipulates the upper story remains his, he retains rights to project beams or build an upper story.
The Gemara questions why the stipulation 'on condition' is needed if the seller does not acquire depth and height by default.
The Gemara answers that the stipulation serves to allow the seller to rebuild the upper story if it collapses.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling a field excluding pits and cisterns
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling a field excluding pits and cisterns
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when one sells a field, the sale does not include its pits or cisterns, even if the seller wrote 'depth and height' in the contract. Rabbi Akiva requires the seller to purchase a right of way, while the Sages disagree. Rabbi Akiva concedes that if the seller explicitly excluded them, no right of way is needed. If the seller sold the pits to another, Rabbi Akiva says no right of way is needed, but the Sages require it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that selling a field does not include its pits or cisterns, and Rabbi Akiva requires the buyer to purchase a right of way.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Akiva and rule that no right of way is needed.
Rabbi Akiva concedes that if the seller explicitly excluded the pits, no right of way is needed.
If the seller sold the pits to another person, Rabbi Akiva says no right of way is needed, but the Sages require it.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the terms 'bor' and 'dut'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the terms 'bor' and 'dut'
items.desc_en: Ravina and Rav Ashi each question the difference between 'bor' and 'dut', and are answered by Rava Tosfa'ah and Mar Kashisha respectively, citing a baraita that both are in the ground, but a 'bor' is dug and a 'dut' is built.

sub.desc_en: Ravina questions why the Mishnah lists both 'bor' and 'dut' if they seem synonymous.
Rava Tosfa'ah answers Ravina by citing a baraita that distinguishes them: a 'bor' is dug into the ground, while a 'dut' is built above ground.
Rav Ashi independently raises the same question about the distinction between 'bor' and 'dut'.
Mar Kashisha answers Rav Ashi by citing the same baraita that distinguishes a 'bor' as dug and a 'dut' as built.

items.text: Gemara's inference about the dispute over right of way
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about the dispute over right of way
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages regarding the need for a right of way, suggesting that they disagree about whether the seller implicitly retains a right of way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages over the right of way hinges on whether the seller implicitly retains a right of way.

items.text: Initial claim: proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Initial claim: proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis in the Mishnah proves that Rabbi Akiva holds מוכר בעין יפה and the Rabbis hold מוכר בעין רעה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that the Mishnah proves Rabbi Akiva holds מוכר בעין יפה (the seller sells generously) and the Rabbis hold מוכר בעין רעה (the seller sells stingily).

items.text: First objection: alternative explanation
items.text_en: First objection: alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis disagree about whether a buyer minds being trampled or a seller minds his money floating away, not about מוכר בעין יפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis might be about whether a buyer minds being trampled or a seller minds his money floating away, not about the principle of מוכר בעין יפה (the seller sells generously).

items.text: Second attempt: proof from the Mishnah's continuation
items.text_en: Second attempt: proof from the Mishnah's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the case of selling to another that Rabbi Akiva holds מוכר בעין יפה, but objects that perhaps they disagree about following the buyer's or seller's intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a proof from the Mishnah's continuation: when selling to another, Rabbi Akiva says the buyer need not purchase a path, implying מוכר בעין יפה (the seller gives generously).
The Gemara objects that perhaps the dispute is about whether we follow the buyer's intent (Rabbi Akiva) or the seller's intent (Sages), not about מוכר בעין יפה.

items.text: Third attempt: proof from the Mishnah about a pit and dovecote
items.text_en: Third attempt: proof from the Mishnah about a pit and dovecote
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva requires a path for a pit, dovecote, etc., and the Rabbis do not, and argues this proves the principle of מוכר בעין יפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about a pit, winepress, and dovecote, where Rabbi Akiva requires the seller to provide a path and the Rabbis do not, as a potential proof for the principle of מוכר בעין יפה (the seller sells generously).
The Gemara asks rhetorically why this Mishnah is needed, implying it must teach the principle of מוכר בעין יפה (generous sale) versus מוכר בעין רעה (stingy sale).

items.text: Rejection: perhaps the Mishnah teaches a new case
items.text_en: Rejection: perhaps the Mishnah teaches a new case
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah might be necessary to teach both a house and a field, as each has its own reason (privacy vs. trampling), so it does not prove the principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by suggesting the Mishnah teaches both a house and a field because each has its own distinct reason (privacy vs. trampling), so it does not prove the principle of מוכר בעין יפה מוכר (the seller sells generously).

items.text: Final proof: from the Mishnah's continuation about selling to another
items.text_en: Final proof: from the Mishnah's continuation about selling to another
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the case of selling to another, noting that it is redundant unless it teaches the principle of מוכר בעין יפה, and concludes that this is indeed the proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the final proof from the Mishnah's continuation about selling to another, citing the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages.
The Gemara asks why this case is needed, noting it seems redundant with the earlier Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that the redundancy teaches the principle of מוכר בעין יפה (the seller sells generously), and concludes that this is the definitive proof.

items.text: Transition: Rav Huna's statement
items.text_en: Transition: Rav Huna's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new statement by Rav Huna citing Rav, beginning a new discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new statement by Rav Huna citing Rav, beginning a new discussion.

items.text: Dispute about the halakha between Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav Huna
items.text_en: Dispute about the halakha between Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that Shmuel ruled like Rabbi Akiva, but Rav Huna challenges him, leading to the revelation that Rav Yirmeya had taught the Mishnah in reverse order, explaining why Rav did not respond.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that the halakha follows the Sages.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that Shmuel ruled like Rabbi Akiva, contrary to the Mishnah.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba challenges Rav Huna, noting that he had stated Shmuel's ruling before Rav many times without objection.
Rav Huna asks how Rav Yirmeya taught the Mishnah, and upon learning he taught it in reverse order, explains that this is why Rav did not respond.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rav and Shmuel's positions on brothers dividing property
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rav and Shmuel's positions on brothers dividing property
items.desc_en: Ravina suggests to Rav Ashi that Rav and Shmuel follow their own reasoning, citing a dispute about whether brothers who divide property have rights of way, ladders, windows, or water channels. The Gemara explains why both rulings are necessary, showing that each might concede in the other case.

sub.desc_en: Ravina suggests to Rav Ashi that Rav and Shmuel follow their own reasoning in their dispute about brothers dividing property.

sub.text: Citation of Rav Nachman's report of Shmuel's ruling
sub.text_en: Citation of Rav Nachman's report of Shmuel's ruling
sub.desc_en: Ravina cites the dispute: Shmuel rules that brothers who divide property retain no rights of way, ladders, windows, or water channels, while Rav rules they do retain them.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of why both rulings are necessary
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of why both rulings are necessary
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both rulings are necessary, as each case might have led to the opposite conclusion, showing that Rav and Shmuel each might concede in the other's case.

items.text: Rav Nachman asks Rav Huna about the halakha
items.text_en: Rav Nachman asks Rav Huna about the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rav Huna whether the halakha follows their view or his, and Rav Huna rules in favor of Rav Nachman because they are close to the Exilarch's court where judges are frequent.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rav Huna whether the halakha follows their view or Rav Huna's view.
Rav Huna rules in favor of Rav Nachman because they are close to the Exilarch's court where judges are frequent.

items.text: Case of two houses one inside the other: sale vs. gift
items.text_en: Case of two houses one inside the other: sale vs. gift
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case of two houses, one inside the other, where both are sold or both given as gifts, or one is a gift and the other a sale. It initially suggests that even when the outer is sold and the inner is a gift, there is no right of way, but then rejects this, arguing that a giver gives with a generous eye, so the inner house retains a right of way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the case of two houses one inside the other, and rules that when both are sold or both given as gifts, or the outer is a gift and the inner a sale, they have no right of way over each other.
The Gemara initially assumes that even when the outer house is sold and the inner is a gift, they have no right of way over each other.
The Gemara rejects the initial assumption, citing the principle that a giver gives with a generous eye (בְּעַיִן יָפָה יָהֵיב), so the inner house retains a right of way.

items.text: Mishnah: What is included when selling a house
items.text_en: Mishnah: What is included when selling a house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are or are not included in the sale of a house, such as the door but not the key, the fixed millstone but not the portable one, and the oven and stove are not included unless specified.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items included or excluded when selling a house, such as the door but not the key, the fixed millstone but not the portable one, and the oven and stove are not included unless specified.

items.text: Mishnah conclusion
items.text_en: Mishnah conclusion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sells a house, all these items (door, bolt, lock) are sold, but not the key.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes that all these items (door, bolt, lock) are sold with the house, but not the key.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Meir, who holds that selling a vineyard includes its accessories. It then attempts to reconcile with Rabbi Meir by distinguishing between fixed and non-fixed items, but concludes that the Mishnah indeed does not follow Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Meir, who holds that selling a vineyard includes its accessories.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Meir, because Rabbi Meir holds that selling a vineyard includes its accessories.
The Gemara attempts to reconcile the Mishnah with Rabbi Meir by distinguishing between fixed items (there) and non-fixed items (here).

The Gemara rejects the initial suggestion, arguing that even Rabbi Meir would agree here because the key is not fixed like the door, but then concludes that the Mishnah indeed does not follow Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's pairing of key with door implies the key is also fixed, undermining the distinction.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah indeed does not follow Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Baraita on what is sold with a house
items.text_en: Baraita on what is sold with a house
items.desc_en: A baraita lists items sold with a house (door, bolt, lock) and those not sold (key, mortar, oven, etc.). Rabbi Eliezer rules that anything attached to the ground is considered like the ground. The baraita adds that if the seller says 'it and everything within it,' all are sold, but a cistern, pit, or gallery are not sold.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists items sold with a house (door, bolt, lock) and not sold (key, etc.), and Rabbi Eliezer rules that anything attached to the ground is like the ground.

The baraita lists items sold with a house (door, bolt, lock) and those not sold (key, mortar, oven, etc.), with Rabbi Eliezer's rule that anything attached to the ground is like the ground, and adds that if the seller says 'it and everything within it,' all are sold except a cistern, pit, or gallery.
The baraita adds that if the seller says 'it and everything in it,' all are sold, but still not the cistern, pit, or gallery.

items.text: Baraita on a pipe and the mikveh
items.text_en: Baraita on a pipe and the mikveh
items.desc_en: Another baraita discusses a pipe: if carved and then fixed, it invalidates a mikveh; if fixed and then carved, it does not. The Gemara notes that this baraita does not align with either Rabbi Eliezer or the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: A baraita discusses a pipe that is hollowed and then fixed (invalidates a mikveh) versus fixed and then hollowed (does not invalidate), and the Gemara notes it follows neither Rabbi Eliezer nor the Sages.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this baraita follows, noting it aligns with neither Rabbi Eliezer nor the Rabbis.

items.text: Rejecting Rabbi Eliezer of the house
items.text_en: Rejecting Rabbi Eliezer of the house
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that the baraita refers to Rabbi Eliezer of the house, because his reasoning there is about a seller selling generously, not about attachment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Rabbi Eliezer is meant, and proposes it might be Rabbi Eliezer of the house (from the baraita about selling a house).
The Gemara rejects this identification, because Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning there is about a seller selling generously (בעין יפה), not about the principle of attachment to the ground.

items.text: Considering Rabbi Eliezer of the beehive
items.text_en: Considering Rabbi Eliezer of the beehive
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita might align with Rabbi Eliezer's view on a beehive, where he considers it like land for the purpose of a prozbul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita might align with Rabbi Eliezer's view on a beehive, where he considers it like land for the purpose of a prozbul.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on beehive status
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on beehive status
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a beehive: Rabbi Eliezer considers it like ground (not susceptible to impurity, liable for Sabbath extraction), while the Sages disagree (susceptible to impurity, exempt on Sabbath).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Eliezer's position: a beehive is like ground — not susceptible to impurity in its place, and one who extracts honey from it on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering.
The Mishnah presents the Sages' opposing view: the beehive is not like ground — it is susceptible to impurity in its place, and one who extracts honey on Shabbat is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar's explanation for Rabbi Eliezer's view: a beehive is compared to a forest, as both involve extracting something from a growing source, making one liable on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Elazar's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: a beehive is compared to a forest (יַעַר) via the verse 'וַיִּטְבֹּל אוֹתָהּ בְּיַעְרַת הַדְּבָשׁ' — just as one who plucks from a forest on Shabbat is liable, so too one who extracts honey from a beehive is liable.
Rabbi Elazar draws an analogy: just as one who plucks from a forest on Shabbat is liable for a חטאת (sin-offering), so too one who extracts honey from a beehive on Shabbat is liable.

items.text: Transition to a parallel case: baker's shelf
items.text_en: Transition to a parallel case: baker's shelf
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a different dispute of Rabbi Eliezer regarding a baker's shelf fixed to a wall, where he declares it pure (not susceptible to impurity) and the Sages declare it impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara shifts to a related Mishnah about a baker's board (דַּף שֶׁל נַחְתּוֹמִין) fixed to the wall, where Rabbi Eliezer declares it pure and the Sages declare it susceptible to impurity.

items.text: Gemara's question on the shelf dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the shelf dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which opinion is at play: if it's Rabbi Eliezer, even if he hollowed it out and then fixed it, he would be consistent; if it's the Rabbis, even if he fixed it and then hollowed it, they would be consistent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the attribution of the baker's board Mishnah: if it follows Rabbi Eliezer, even if he hollowed it out and then fixed it, it should be pure; if it follows the Sages, even if he fixed it and then hollowed it out, it should be impure — yet the Mishnah distinguishes between cases.

items.text: Answer: Distinction based on rabbinic impurity
items.text_en: Answer: Distinction based on rabbinic impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the shelf dispute is indeed Rabbi Eliezer's view, but it differs because the impurity of simple wooden vessels is rabbinic, not biblical. This leads to a question about whether the beehive's impurity is biblical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the shelf dispute is indeed Rabbi Eliezer's view, but the distinction is that simple wooden vessels have only rabbinic impurity (טומאה דרבנן), not biblical.
The Gemara questions whether this implies that the impurity of the beehive itself is biblical (דאורייתא), challenging the consistency of the answer.

items.text: Objection to the previous resolution
items.text_en: Objection to the previous resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's ruling is according to the Rabbis, and further cites Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Chanina who says the dispute is specifically about a metal sheet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's ruling is according to the Rabbis, and further cites Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Chanina who says the dispute is specifically about a metal sheet.

items.text: Gemara's resolution and further challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution and further challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it is indeed the Rabbis, but the case of drawing water is different because it is rabbinic. A challenge is raised that even if one hollowed it out and then attached it, it should be similar, but the Gemara distinguishes because when detached it had the form of a vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah follows the Rabbis, but the case of drawing water is different because it is a rabbinic prohibition.
The Gemara challenges that even if one hollowed out a vessel and then attached it to the ground, it should be similar to the case of drawing water.
The Gemara distinguishes that when the vessel was hollowed out while detached, it retains the form of a vessel, unlike the case of drawing water.

items.text: Rav Yosef's question about rainwater for seeds
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's question about rainwater for seeds
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether rainwater designated for washing a latrine is considered prepared for seeds. The Gemara clarifies that the question is only according to the Rabbis, who say attached is not like ground, and concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether rainwater that one designated for washing a latrine is considered prepared (מוכן) for seeds.
The Gemara clarifies that the question is only according to the Rabbis, who hold that attached is not like ground, and leaves it unresolved with 'תיקו' (let it stand).

items.text: Beginning of a new narrative
items.text_en: Beginning of a new narrative
items.desc_en: Rav Nechemya, son of Rav Yosef, sends a message to Rabba, son of Rav Huna Zuti, to Nehardea, regarding a woman who comes before him, beginning a new legal case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nechemya, son of Rav Yosef, sends a message to Rabba, son of Rav Huna Zuti, in Nehardea, instructing him regarding a woman who comes before him.

items.text: Opening statement on collecting from millstones
items.text_en: Opening statement on collecting from millstones
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that in the school of Rav Kahana, they would collect even from the labor of houses, extending the principle of collecting from millstones.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when collecting a debt, one may collect even from millstones, which are movable property attached to the ground.
Rav Ashi reports that in the school of Rav Kahana, they would collect even from the labor of houses, extending the principle of collecting from millstones.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling a courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling a courtyard includes houses, pits, and caves, but not movable items. If the seller says 'it and everything in it,' all are sold. However, a bathhouse and olive press are not included. Rabbi Eliezer says only the airspace of the courtyard is sold.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling a courtyard includes houses, pits, and caves, but not movable items; if the seller says 'it and everything in it,' all are sold; however, a bathhouse and olive press are not included, and Rabbi Eliezer says only the airspace of the courtyard is sold.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on courtyard sale details
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on courtyard sale details
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates: selling a courtyard includes outer and inner houses, and a 'beit hacholsiot.' Shops open to the courtyard are included; those not open are not. If open to both sides, they are included. Rabbi Eliezer says only the 'milusah' (fill) of the courtyard is sold.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, detailing that selling a courtyard includes outer and inner houses and a 'beit hacholsiot,' with shops included or excluded based on their openings, and Rabbi Eliezer limits the sale to the 'milusah' (fill) of the courtyard.

items.text: Resolution of a contradiction regarding shops open to both sides
items.text_en: Resolution of a contradiction regarding shops open to both sides
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the baraita and a teaching of Rabbi Chiyya regarding shops open to both sides. It resolves that if most of their use is inward, they are included; if outward, they are not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's ruling that shops open to both sides are sold with the courtyard.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a teaching of Rabbi Chiyya that such shops are not sold with the courtyard.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between shops whose primary use is inward (included) and those whose primary use is outward (not included).

items.text: Rabba's explanation of the dispute: 'darta' vs. 'chatzer'
items.text_en: Rabba's explanation of the dispute: 'darta' vs. 'chatzer'
items.desc_en: Rabba explains that if the seller said 'darta' (dwelling), all agree it includes houses. The dispute is when he said 'darta' (courtyard) – one holds it means a courtyard (open space), the other holds it means houses.

sub.desc_en: Rabba states that if the seller said 'דירתא' (dwelling), all agree it includes houses.
Rabba resolves the dispute: when the seller said 'דרתא' (courtyard), one opinion holds it means a courtyard (open space), the other holds it means houses.

items.text: Alternative version of Rabba's explanation: 'darta' vs. 'chatzer'
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rabba's explanation: 'darta' vs. 'chatzer'
items.desc_en: An alternative version: if the seller said 'darta', all agree it includes houses. The dispute is when he said 'chatzer' – one holds it means airspace, the other compares it to the courtyard of the Tabernacle (which includes structures).

sub.desc_en: Introduces an alternative version of Rabba's statement: if the seller said 'דרתא' (darta), all agree it includes houses.
States the dispute is when the seller said 'חצר' (chatzer): one opinion holds it means airspace, the other compares it to the courtyard of the Tabernacle (which includes structures).

items.text: Rabba and Rav Nachman on acquisition of adjacent properties
items.text_en: Rabba and Rav Nachman on acquisition of adjacent properties
items.desc_en: Rabba quotes Rav Nachman: if one sells a 'cholsit' (a type of house) and a 'metzulah' (a pit), taking possession of one does not acquire the other. This is contrasted with Shmuel's ruling that taking possession of one of ten fields in ten provinces acquires all, because they are a single landmass and use. Here, each has a distinct use.

sub.desc_en: Rabba reports Rav Nachman's ruling that taking possession of a 'cholsit' (house) does not acquire a 'metzulah' (pit), and vice versa.
The Gemara objects by citing Shmuel's ruling that taking possession of one of ten fields in ten provinces acquires all, implying a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's case involves a single landmass and uniform use, whereas here each property has a distinct use, so possession of one does not acquire the other.

items.text: Alternative version of the previous statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of the previous statement
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the previous teaching is introduced, though the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version of the previous teaching is introduced, though the text is cut off.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on חולסית and מצולה
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on חולסית and מצולה
items.desc_en: Rabbah quotes Rav Nachman: if one takes possession of the slope (חולסית), he acquires the deep pit (מצולה). The Gemara initially finds this obvious based on Shmuel's ruling about selling ten fields, but suggests a possible distinction that the slope and pit are separate uses, which the statement rejects.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah quotes Rav Nachman's ruling that taking possession of the slope (חולסית) acquires the deep pit (מצולה).
The Gemara questions why this ruling is not obvious, citing Shmuel's principle about selling ten fields.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary to reject a possible distinction that the slope and pit are separate uses, teaching that they are considered one unit.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling a בית הבד
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling a בית הבד
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items sold with a בית הבד (olive press): the ים (vat), ממל (beam), and בתולות (supports), but not the עבירים (rollers), גלגל (wheel), or קורה (beam). If the seller says 'it and all within it', all are included. Rabbi Eliezer adds that the קורה is sold.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing items sold with a בית הבד (olive press): the ים (vat), ממל (beam), and בתולות (supports).
The Mishnah states that the עבירים (rollers), גלגל (wheel), and קורה (beam) are not sold.
The Mishnah adds that if the seller says 'it and all within it', all items are included.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that the קורה (beam) is sold with the olive press.

items.text: Gemara: Definitions of Mishnah terms
items.text_en: Gemara: Definitions of Mishnah terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the terms from the Mishnah: ים is a vat, ממל is a press, בתולות are cedar poles supporting the beam, עבירים are rollers, גלגל is a wheel, and קורה is a beam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by defining the Mishnah term ים (vat) as טְלָפְחָא (a vat).
Rabbi Abba bar Memel defines ממל (the press) as מַפְרַכְתָּא (a crushing stone).
Rabbi Yochanan defines בתולות (virgins) as cedar poles (כְּלוֹנְסוֹת שֶׁל אֶרֶז) that support the beam.
The Gemara defines עבירים (rollers) as כִּבְשֵׁי (rollers).
The Gemara defines גלגל (wheel) as חוּמַרְתָּא (a wheel).
The Gemara defines קורה (beam) as קוֹרָה (a beam).

items.text: Baraita: Additional details on selling a בית הבד
items.text_en: Baraita: Additional details on selling a בית הבד
items.desc_en: A Baraita adds that selling a בית הבד includes the boards, vats, presses, and lower millstones, but not the upper millstone. With 'it and all within it', all are included. In any case, the rollers, sacks, and hammers are not sold.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita lists items included and excluded when selling a בית הבד (olive press), with the rule that specifying 'it and all within it' includes everything, but rollers, sacks, and hammers are never sold.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning on the קורה
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning on the קורה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer explains that the קורה is sold because the place is called a בית הבד only on account of the beam (קורה).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that one who sells a בית הבד (olive press) has sold the קורה (beam) as well, because the place is called a בית הבד only on account of the beam.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling a מרחץ
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling a מרחץ
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling a מרחץ (bathhouse) does not include the boards, basins, or bath attendants. With 'it and all within it', all are included. In any case, the water reservoirs and wood stores are not sold.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling a bathhouse does not include the boards, basins, or bath attendants, but with 'it and all within it' all are included, while water reservoirs and wood stores are never sold.

items.text: Baraita: Details on selling a מרחץ
items.text_en: Baraita: Details on selling a מרחץ
items.desc_en: A Baraita elaborates: selling a bathhouse includes the rooms for boards, for towels, for basins, and for curtains, but not the boards, towels, basins, or curtains themselves. With 'it and all within it', all are included. In any case, the water pools that supply it are not sold.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita lists what is included and excluded when selling a bathhouse, with the water pools that supply it never included.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt on selling a bathhouse
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt on selling a bathhouse
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when one sells a bathhouse, certain attached structures are included, but not the wood storage room. However, if the seller says 'the bathhouse and all its appurtenances', everything is sold.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when one sells a bathhouse, certain attached structures are included, but not the wood storage room; however, if the seller says 'the bathhouse and all its appurtenances', everything is sold.

items.text: Gemara's case and resolution on selling an olive press
items.text_en: Gemara's case and resolution on selling an olive press
items.desc_en: A case is brought where one sold 'the olive press and all its appurtenances', and there were outer shops used for drying sesame. Rav Yosef initially rules based on the Mishnah that they are included, but Abaye objects with a beraita of Rabbi Chiya that they are not. Rav Ashi resolves that if the seller specified the boundaries, they are included; otherwise not.

sub.desc_en: A case is introduced where one sold 'the olive press and all its appurtenances' and there were outer shops used for drying sesame.
Rav Yosef rules based on the Mishnah that if one says 'the bathhouse and all its appurtenances', all are sold, implying the shops are included.
Abaye objects with a beraita of Rabbi Chiya that not all are sold.
Rav Ashi resolves that if the seller specified the boundaries, the shops are included; otherwise not.

items.text: Mishnah on selling a city
items.text_en: Mishnah on selling a city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists what is included when selling a city: houses, cisterns, pits, caves, bathhouses, dovecotes, olive presses, and irrigated fields, but not movable property. If the seller says 'it and all that is in it', even animals and slaves are included. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that the 'santer' is included.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the immovable properties included when selling a city, excluding movable property.
The Mishnah states that if the seller says 'it and all that is in it', even animals and slaves are included.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that the 'santer' (the city's steward or governor) is included in the sale.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of slaves as movable or land
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of slaves as movable or land
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi whether the Mishnah implies slaves are considered movable property, since they are not automatically sold with the city. The Gemara concludes that even if slaves are like land, there is a distinction between movable land (slaves) and immovable land.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Avya asks Rav Ashi whether the Mishnah implies that slaves are considered movable property (מטלטלין), since if they were like land they would be sold with the city, and questions the meaning of 'even' in the Mishnah.

The Gemara resolves the question by distinguishing between movable land (slaves) and immovable land, explaining that even if slaves are like land, they are not sold with the city because they are movable.

items.text: Interpretation of 'santer'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'santer'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the term 'santer' in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement. In the West they translate it as 'bar makhvonita' (a bathhouse attendant), while Shimon ben Avtulmos says it is 'bagei' (a garden). The Gemara notes the logical relationship between these interpretations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'santer' means in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement.
The Gemara reports that in the West they translate 'santer' as 'bar makhvonita' (a bathhouse attendant).
Shimon ben Avtulmos says 'santer' means 'bagei' (a garden).
The Gemara explains the logical relationship: one who says 'bar makhvonita' certainly includes 'bagei', but one who says 'bagei' excludes 'bar makhvonita' from the sale.

items.text: First version of the dispute over 'shlahin'
items.text_en: First version of the dispute over 'shlahin'
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes 'shlahin' in the Mishnah means 'bagei' (gardens). It explains that according to the one who says 'santer' is 'bar makhvonita', the Tanna Kamma includes gardens but not bathhouse attendants, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds attendants. But according to the one who says 'santer' is 'bagei', the Tanna Kamma already includes gardens, so what does Rabban Shimon add? The Gemara then reinterprets 'shlahin' as 'ginunyata' (orchards), so that gardens are not included by the Tanna Kamma, and Rabban Shimon adds them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah and initially assumes that 'שלחין' (shlahin) means 'באגי' (gardens), citing a verse about sending water.

The Gemara explains that according to the one who says 'סנטר' (santer) is 'בר מחווניתא' (bathhouse attendant), the Tanna Kamma includes gardens but not attendants, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds attendants.
The Gemara objects that according to the one who says 'סנטר' (santer) is 'באגי' (gardens), the Tanna Kamma already includes gardens, so what does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel add?
The Gemara resolves by reinterpreting 'שלחין' (shlahin) as 'גינוניאתא' (orchards), so that gardens are not included by the Tanna Kamma, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds them.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute over 'shlahin'
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute over 'shlahin'
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that initially 'shlahin' was understood as 'ginunyata' (orchards). According to the one who says 'santer' is 'bagei', the Tanna Kamma includes orchards but not gardens, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds gardens.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that initially 'shlahin' was understood as 'ginunyata' (orchards), and then explains the positions of the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel according to the one who interprets 'santer' as 'bagei' (gardens).

items.text: Clarifying the dispute about בר מחווניתא
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute about בר מחווניתא
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's positions regarding the term שלחין. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues that even בר מחווניתא is sold with the city.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that according to the Tanna Kamma, the term שלחין refers to gardens (גינונייתא), not to בר מחווניתא (the area outside the city gates).
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel responds that the Tanna Kamma is mistaken: שלחין means 'בגי' (irrigation channels), not gardens, and therefore בר מחווניתא is not sold with the city.
The Gemara concludes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel comes to say that even בר מחווניתא is sold with the city, disagreeing with the Tanna Kamma.

items.text: Attempt to prove from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Attempt to prove from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove that סנטר and אנקולמוס are both people, but rejects the inference, noting they are different types.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that both סנטר (santer) and אנקולמוס (ankulmus) are people, since the latter is a person.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that each term refers to a different type of entity (one is a person, the other is not).

items.text: Proof from the baraisa's continuation
items.text_en: Proof from the baraisa's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraisa that lists items not sold with the city, including שייריה (בזלי) which are pieces of בגדי, implying that בגדי themselves are sold. This supports the earlier interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous interpretation by asking how one can maintain it given the baraisa's continuation.
The Gemara cites the baraisa's continuation listing items not sold with the city, including its 'שייריה' (remnants) and 'בנותיה' (suburbs), and enclosures for animals, birds, and fish.
The Gemara asks what 'שייריה' refers to, and then what 'ביזלי' means.
Rabbi Abba explains that 'ביזלי' are pieces of בגדי (fine garments).
The Gemara concludes that only pieces of בגדי are not sold, but the בגדי themselves are sold, supporting the earlier interpretation that 'שלחין' refers to בגדי.

items.text: Proposal to reverse Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Proposal to reverse Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests reversing Rabbi Yehuda's statement: סנטר is sold, אנקולמוס is not sold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes reversing Rabbi Yehuda's statement: סנטר (the chin) is sold, אנקולמוס (the neck) is not sold.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda cannot agree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda cannot agree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda cannot hold like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since the baraisa shows Rabbi Yehuda does not sell בנותיה, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda cannot hold like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since the baraisa shows Rabbi Yehuda does not sell בנותיה (subsidiary towns), while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel does.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Yehuda agrees in one matter but disagrees in another
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Yehuda agrees in one matter but disagrees in another
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on one point (סנטר/אנקולמוס) but disagrees on another (בנותיה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on one matter (סנטר/אנקולמוס) but disagrees on another (בנותיה).

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding ביברים
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding ביברים
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the mishnah (which says ביברים are not sold) and a baraisa (which says they are sold). It resolves by distinguishing between ביברים that open inward (sold) and those that open outward (not sold). It also emends the text regarding חורשין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the mishnah states that ביברים (animal enclosures) are not sold with the city, but a baraisa states that they are sold with it.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between ביברים that open inward (sold) and those that open outward (not sold), and emends the mishnah's text from 'המוקצין לה' to 'המוקצין הימנה'.

items.text: Mishnah: What is sold with a field
items.text_en: Mishnah: What is sold with a field
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists items that are and are not sold with a field, including stones, reeds, produce, a reed-thicket, a watchman's booth, a carob tree, and a sycamore tree, with conditions.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists items sold with a field: stones needed for it, reeds in the vineyard, attached produce, a reed-thicket less than a בית רובע (quarter-kav area), a watchman's booth not made with clay, a non-grafted carob tree, and a young sycamore tree.

The mishnah lists items not sold with the field: stones not needed for it, reeds not needed for the vineyard, detached produce, a reed-thicket of a בית רובע, a watchman's booth made with clay, a grafted carob tree, and a sycamore stump.

items.text: Clarifying the stones sold with the field
items.text_en: Clarifying the stones sold with the field
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'stones that are for its needs' means. The local tradition says they are stones for a dam (אבני דאכפא). Ulla says they are stones arranged for a fence. A baraita of Rabbi Chiyya uses the term 'piled stones' (צבורות), so the Mishnah must be emended to 'arranged' (סדורות). The Gemara then explains the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding whether the stones need to be placed or arranged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'stones that are for its needs'.
The local tradition explains that these are stones for a dam (אבני דאכפא).
Ulla says they are stones arranged for a fence.
The Gemara objects that a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya uses the term 'piled stones' (צבורות), not 'arranged'.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah should be emended to read 'arranged' (סדורות).
The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding whether the stones need to be placed or arranged.
The Gemara explains the dispute according to Ulla's interpretation: Rabbi Meir requires them to be placed even if not arranged, while the Rabbis require them to be arranged.

items.text: Clarifying the reeds sold with the vineyard
items.text_en: Clarifying the reeds sold with the vineyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what reeds are for their needs. The school of Rabbi Yannai says they are split reeds placed under vines. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis is whether they need to be smoothed or actually placed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what function the reeds mentioned in the Mishnah serve.
The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that these are split reeds placed under the vines to support them.
The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Meir, the reeds are included if they are smoothed, even if not yet placed under the vines.
The Gemara explains that according to the Rabbis, the reeds are included only if they are actually placed under the vines.

items.text: Items sold even when detached or weak
items.text_en: Items sold even when detached or weak
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items sold with the field even if they are ready to be harvested (produce attached to the ground), a reed fence less than a beit rova (even if strong), a watchman's booth not made with clay (even if not fixed in the ground), and a carob not grafted and a sycamore sapling (even if strong).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items sold with the field: produce attached to the ground even if ready to harvest, a reed fence less than a beit rova even if strong, a watchman's booth not made with clay even if not fixed, and a carob not grafted and a sycamore sapling even if strong.

items.text: Items not sold with the field
items.text_en: Items not sold with the field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items not sold: stones not for its needs, reeds not for its needs, and detached produce. The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding the condition of the stones and reeds.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that stones not needed for the field are not sold with it.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for Rabbi Meir and Rabbis
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for Rabbi Meir and Rabbis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Meir, stones not sold are those not prepared (not smoothed), and according to the Rabbis, those not placed (not set in the ground).
Ulla explains that according to his view, Rabbi Meir excludes stones not arranged (not smoothed), and the Rabbis exclude those not set in order (not arranged in a row).
The Mishnah continues listing items not sold: reeds not needed for the vineyard and detached produce, even if needed for the land.

items.text: Exception for a named garden bed
items.text_en: Exception for a named garden bed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that even a small bed of spices with its own name is not sold with the field. Rav Papa adds that this applies only if it is called 'so-and-so's rose garden'.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that even a small bed of spices with its own name is not sold with the field.
Rav Papa adds that this applies only if the bed is called 'so-and-so's rose garden'.

items.text: More items not sold
items.text_en: More items not sold
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: a watchman's booth made with clay (even if attached to the ground), a grafted carob, and a sycamore stump (even if small).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional items not included in the sale: a watchman's booth made of clay, a grafted carob tree, and a sycamore stump, even if they are small.

items.text: Unresolved queries about frames
items.text_en: Unresolved queries about frames
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks about door frames (מלבנות של פתחים) that are held by pegs but not attached with clay; Rabbi Zeira asks about window frames; Rabbi Yirmeya asks about bed leg frames that are not movable. All remain unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether door frames (מלבנות של פתחים) held by pegs but not attached with clay are sold with the house; the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
Rabbi Zeira asks whether window frames (מלבנות של חלונות) are considered mere decoration or are attached enough to be sold with the house; the question remains unresolved (תיקו).
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether bed leg frames (מלבנות של כרעי המטה) that are not movable are sold with the bed; the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Repetition of Mishnah clause
items.text_en: Repetition of Mishnah clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the Mishnah's final clause about the grafted carob and sycamore stump, likely as a transition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the Mishnah's final clause about the grafted carob and sycamore stump, likely as a transition.

items.text: Source for boundaries from the Torah
items.text_en: Source for boundaries from the Torah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav derives from the verse about the field of Ephron that one must include boundaries in a sale, excluding items that do not require boundaries. Rav Mesharshiya adds that this shows boundaries are from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that boundaries are included in a sale) derived?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites the verse about Ephron's field to show that only items needing boundaries are included, excluding those that do not.
Rav Mesharshiya infers from this that the requirement to include boundaries (מצרים) in a sale is from the Torah.

items.text: Standard phrasing in a deed
items.text_en: Standard phrasing in a deed
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that when selling land, one should write in the deed 'acquire for yourself date palms, trees, reeds, and branches' even though the sale is valid without it, as it enhances the document.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that when selling land, one should write in the deed 'acquire for yourself date palms, trees, reeds, and branches' even though the sale is valid without it, as it enhances the document.

items.text: Sale of land with date palms
items.text_en: Sale of land with date palms
items.desc_en: If one sells 'land and date palms', we examine the situation: if he has date palms, he gives two; if not, he buys two; if they are encumbered, he redeems two.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the rule: if one sells 'land and date palms', we examine the situation — if he has date palms he gives two, if not he buys two, if they are encumbered he redeems two.

items.text: Sale of land with date palms or in a date-palm area
items.text_en: Sale of land with date palms or in a date-palm area
items.desc_en: If one sells 'land with date palms', we examine: if it has date palms, he gives them; if not, it is a mistaken transaction. If one sells 'land of date palms', he has no date palms, meaning he refers to land suitable for date palms. If he says 'except for a certain date palm', we examine: if it is a good date palm, it is excluded; if it is a bad one, all the more so the others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if one sells 'land with date palms' (אַרְעָא בְּדִיקְלֵי), we examine the land: if it has date palms, he gives them; if not, the transaction is mistaken.
The Gemara explains that if one sells 'land of date palms' (אַרְעָא בֵּי דִיקְלֵי), he does not receive date palms, as the seller refers to land suitable for date palms.
The Gemara rules that if the seller says 'except for a certain date palm', we examine: if it is a good date palm, it is excluded; if it is a bad one, all the more so the others are included.

items.text: Exceptions for trees, date palms, and vines
items.text_en: Exceptions for trees, date palms, and vines
items.desc_en: If one says 'except for trees', and he has trees, they are excluded; if he has date palms, they are excluded; if he has vines, they are excluded. Further cases: if he has trees and vines, except for trees; trees and date palms, except for trees; vines and date palms, except for vines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule: if one says 'except for trees' and he has trees, date palms, or vines, they are excluded.
The Gemara extends the rule: when one has mixed types, the exclusion applies to the specified type.

items.text: Rav's rule on what constitutes a reservation
items.text_en: Rav's rule on what constitutes a reservation
items.desc_en: Rav states: anything that one can climb with a rope is considered a reservation; anything that one cannot climb with a rope is not a reservation.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that anything one can climb with a rope is considered a reservation (שיור), and anything one cannot climb with a rope is not a reservation.

items.text: Introduction of the dispute between Babylonian and Exilic judges
items.text_en: Introduction of the dispute between Babylonian and Exilic judges
items.desc_en: The Babylonian and Exilic judges disagree about what constitutes a retained item (שיור) in a field sale: anything the yoke presses down is not a שיור, but what the yoke does not press down is a שיור. They do not actually disagree, as one refers to palm trees and the other to other trees.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the dispute between the Babylonian and Exilic judges regarding what constitutes a retained item (שיור) in a field sale, and resolves that they do not actually disagree.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Huna's question about excluding a specific carob or sycamore
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Huna's question about excluding a specific carob or sycamore
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna asks Rav Sheshet whether saying 'except for such-and-such carob' or 'except for such-and-such sycamore' means only that tree is not acquired, but others are, or even others are not acquired. Rav Sheshet answers that he does not acquire any. An objection is raised from a baraita that seems to imply only the named tree is excluded, but Rav Sheshet explains that even other trees are not acquired, analogizing to a field sold except for another field.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna asks Rav Sheshet whether excluding a specific carob or sycamore tree from a sale means only that tree is not acquired, or even other trees of the same type are not acquired.
Rav Sheshet answers that the buyer does not acquire any trees, including other carob or sycamore trees.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that seems to imply only the named tree is excluded, while other trees are acquired.
Rav Sheshet explains that even other trees are not acquired, analogizing to a field sold except for another field, where the buyer does not acquire any other field either.

items.text: Alternative version: excluding half a carob or sycamore
items.text_en: Alternative version: excluding half a carob or sycamore
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the question: if one says 'except for half of such-and-such carob' or 'half of such-and-such sycamore', does the buyer acquire the remaining half of that tree? Rav Sheshet answers he does not. An objection is raised from a baraita that seems to imply only other trees are not acquired, but the retained half is acquired; Rav Sheshet explains that even the retained half is not acquired, again analogizing to a field sold except for half another field.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Huna's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Huna's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna asks Rav Sheshet whether, when one sells a field except for half a specific carob or sycamore, the buyer acquires the remaining half of that tree.
Rav Sheshet answers that the buyer does not acquire the remaining half of that tree.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states 'except for half a carob' or 'half a sycamore' — other carobs are not acquired, implying that the retained half of that tree is acquired.
Rav Sheshet explains that even the retained half of that tree is not acquired, analogizing to a field sold except for half another field, where the buyer does not acquire the other field.

items.text: Rav Amram's question about a bailee claiming return while holding the receipt
items.text_en: Rav Amram's question about a bailee claiming return while holding the receipt
items.desc_en: Rav Amram asks Rav Chisda: if someone deposits an item with a receipt and the bailee says 'I returned them to you', is he believed? The question is whether we apply the principle of migo (since he could have claimed they were lost, he is believed) or the claimant can say 'why is your receipt still in my hand?' Rav Chisda answers he is believed. The Gemara challenges: why not say 'why is your receipt in my hand'? Rav Chisda retorts: according to your reasoning, if he claimed 'they were lost', could the claimant not also say that?

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram asks Rav Chisda: if a bailee with a receipt claims he returned the deposit, do we believe him via migo (since he could have claimed loss), or does the depositor retort 'why is your receipt in my hand'?
Rav Chisda answers that the bailee is deemed credible.
Rav Amram objects: but let the depositor say 'why is your receipt in my hand'?
Rav Chisda rejects the objection: according to your reasoning, if the bailee claimed loss, could the depositor not also say 'why is your receipt in my hand'?

items.text: Gemara's question on the meaning of 'ne'eman'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the meaning of 'ne'eman'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement that a bailee is 'ne'eman' (believed) when claiming return of a deposit, clarifying that this belief is only with an oath, similar to the case of 'ne'ensu' (they were forced) which requires an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement that a bailee is 'ne'eman' (believed) when claiming return of a deposit, clarifying that this belief is only with an oath, similar to the case of 'ne'ensu' (they were forced) which requires an oath.

items.text: Dispute between Dayanei Golah and Dayanei Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Dispute between Dayanei Golah and Dayanei Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute regarding a business contract (shtar kis) that comes against orphans: Dayanei Golah say the creditor swears and collects the full amount, while Dayanei Eretz Yisrael say he swears and collects half. The Gemara initially suggests the dispute is about whether the debtor can say 'why is your document in my hands' (indicating payment), but then rejects this and explains it as a dispute about whether the debtor would have mentioned payment if it occurred, or if the Angel of Death forced him to forget.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Dayanei Golah and Dayanei Eretz Yisrael regarding a שטר כיס (business contract) that comes against orphans: one says the creditor swears and collects the full amount, the other says he swears and collects half.
The Gemara notes that everyone agrees with the Neharde'i principle that a business contract (עיסקא) is half a loan and half a deposit.
The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether the debtor can say 'שטרך בידי מאי בעי' (why is your document in my hands), indicating payment.
The Gemara rejects the initial suggestion and explains that the dispute is about whether the debtor would have mentioned payment if it occurred, or if the Angel of Death forced him to forget.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin rules that one who deposits with a friend via a document and says 'I returned it to you' is believed, and for a business contract against orphans, the creditor swears and collects the full amount. The Gemara notes the apparent contradiction (two rulings) and resolves it by distinguishing the cases: in the deposit case, if he had paid, he would have said so; in the business contract case, the debtor might have been forced by the Angel of Death.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin sends a ruling: one who deposits with a friend via a document and says 'I returned it to you' is believed, and for a business contract against orphans, the creditor swears and collects the full amount.
The Gemara objects that Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling contains two contradictory positions.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the cases: in the deposit case, if the debtor had paid, he would have said so; in the business contract case, the debtor might have been forced by the Angel of Death.

items.text: Final halachic rulings by Rava and Mar Zutra
items.text_en: Final halachic rulings by Rava and Mar Zutra
items.desc_en: Rava rules that the creditor swears and collects half, while Mar Zutra rules like Dayanei Golah (full amount). Ravina challenges Mar Zutra with Rava's ruling, and Mar Zutra responds that they (his court) follow Dayanei Golah.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the creditor swears and collects half the amount.
Mar Zutra rules that the law follows Dayanei Golah, allowing the creditor to swear and collect the full amount.
Ravina challenges Mar Zutra by citing Rava's ruling that the creditor swears and collects only half.
Mar Zutra responds that his court follows the practice of Dayanei Golah, thereby justifying his ruling.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and related Tannaitic statements
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and related Tannaitic statements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages about whether a seller who excludes a pit, winepress, or dovecote from a field sale must purchase a right of way. It then lists cases where the entire field is transferred: gift, inheritance, possession of a convert's property, and consecration, with Rabbi Shimon's exception for grafted carob and sycamore stumps.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the Mishnah is taught in a reversed version.
The Mishnah states the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages regarding a seller who excludes a pit, winepress, or dovecote from a field sale, and whether he must purchase a right of way.
The Mishnah adds that Rabbi Akiva concedes when the seller says 'except these,' and presents the reverse dispute when the seller sells the excluded items to another.
The Mishnah states that the dispute applies only to a seller, but a gift, inheritance, or possession of a convert's property transfers the entire field.
The Mishnah concludes that consecration transfers the entire field, except that Rabbi Shimon excludes grafted carob and sycamore stumps.

items.text: Gemara's question on the sale-gift distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the sale-gift distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a gift transfers everything but a sale does not. Yehuda ben Nekosa answers that the seller specified the exclusion, but the Gemara objects that both parties did not specify. It then refines: the seller had reason to specify, while the giver did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a sale does not transfer everything but a gift does.
Yehuda ben Nekosa answers before Rabbi: in the sale case the seller specified the exclusion, while in the gift case the giver did not specify.
The Gemara objects that in both cases neither party specified the exclusion, so the distinction is invalid.
The Gemara refines: the seller had reason to specify the exclusion, while the giver did not have reason to specify.

items.text: Supporting case and Rav Ashi's proof
items.text_en: Supporting case and Rav Ashi's proof
items.desc_en: A case is brought where someone said to give a house that holds 100 barrels, but it held 120. Mar Zutra says only 100 is given. Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's gift clause that a giver gives generously, so here too the giver intended the larger house.

sub.desc_en: A case is presented where someone instructed to give a house that holds 100 barrels, but it was found to hold 120; Mar Zutra rules that only 100 is given.
Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's gift clause that a giver gives generously (בעין יפה), so here too the giver intended the larger house.

items.text: Rav Huna's extension to consecration and trees
items.text_en: Rav Huna's extension to consecration and trees
items.desc_en: Rav Huna notes that even though buying two trees does not acquire land, selling land while retaining two trees does grant land. He argues that even Rabbi Akiva, who says a seller gives generously, would agree regarding trees because they weaken the land, unlike a pit or dovecote.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna opens by stating that although the Sages ruled that buying two trees does not acquire land, selling land while retaining two trees does grant land.
Rav Huna argues that even Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a seller gives generously, would agree regarding trees because they weaken the land, unlike a pit or dovecote.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the seller had not retained rights to the trees, the buyer could simply tell him to uproot and take his trees, implying that the seller must have retained rights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the seller had not retained rights to the trees, the buyer could simply tell him to uproot and take his trees.

items.text: Mishnah citation: Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Mishnah citation: Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon says that one who consecrates a field only consecrates the grafted carob and the sycamore stump, because they draw nourishment from the consecrated field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that one who consecrates a field consecrates only a grafted carob and a sycamore stump, because they draw nourishment from the consecrated field.

items.text: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the seller had retained rights to the trees, then when they draw nourishment they draw from their own (the seller's) portion, not from the buyer's field, contradicting Rabbi Shimon's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the seller had retained rights to the trees, then when they draw nourishment they would be drawing from his own property, contradicting Rabbi Shimon's reasoning.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon's view aligns with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that one who sells a field does not retain rights to the trees, while Rav Huna's view aligns with the Rabbis who hold that he does retain rights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon's position follows Rabbi Akiva, while Rav Huna's position follows the Rabbis.
The Gemara objects that aligning Rav Huna with the Rabbis is obvious, and explains the practical ramification: if the trees fall, the seller may replant them.

items.text: Practical difference between the views
items.text_en: Practical difference between the views
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the practical difference between Rav Huna's view (following the Rabbis) and the Rabbis is whether, if the trees fall, the seller may replant them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the ruling according to the Rabbis is obvious, and the practical difference is whether if the trees fall, the seller may replant them.
The Gemara answers: The practical difference is that if the trees fall, the seller may replant them.

items.text: Baraita on consecrating three trees
items.text_en: Baraita on consecrating three trees
