items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between consecrating three trees within a ten-per-seah planting (which consecrates the land between them) and fewer or more trees, or consecrating them one after another (which does not consecrate the land).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon's position can be aligned with Rabbi Akiva's.

The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between consecrating three trees within a ten-per-seah planting (which consecrates the land between them) and fewer or more trees, or consecrating them one after another (which does not consecrate the land).

items.text: Analysis of the baraita's author
items.text_en: Analysis of the baraita's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes who authored the baraita, ruling out Rabbi Akiva (who holds a seller gives generously, all the more so a consecrator) and the Rabbis (who hold a seller gives stingily but a consecrator gives generously), concluding it must be Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the baraita, and rules out Rabbi Akiva because he holds that a seller gives generously (בעין יפה), and all the more so a consecrator.
The Gemara also rules out the Rabbis, who hold that a seller gives stingily (בעין רעה) but a consecrator gives generously (בעין יפה).
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must be Rabbi Shimon's position.

items.text: Determining Rabbi Shimon's alignment
items.text_en: Determining Rabbi Shimon's alignment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority Rabbi Shimon follows, ruling out Rabbi Akiva (who holds a seller gives generously) and concluding that Rabbi Shimon follows the Rabbis, holding that just as a seller gives stingily, so too a consecrator gives stingily and leaves land unconsecrated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority Rabbi Shimon follows in the baraita.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Akiva, because Rabbi Akiva holds that a seller gives generously, and all the more so a consecrator.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon follows the Rabbis, holding that just as a seller gives stingily, so too a consecrator gives stingily and leaves land unconsecrated.

items.text: Resolution of Rabbi Shimon's contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of Rabbi Shimon's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier difficulty by explaining that Rabbi Shimon was speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning. For himself, he holds that one consecrates with a grudging eye and retains some rights, but for the Rabbis, he concedes that only the grafted carob and sycamore trunk are not consecrated. The Rabbis respond that there is no difference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the earlier explanation fails because the consecrated field's produce nourishes the trees.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon was speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning, conceding that only the grafted carob and sycamore trunk are not consecrated, but the Rabbis reject the distinction.

items.text: Challenge from the mishnah's continuation
items.text_en: Challenge from the mishnah's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the interpretation that the mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon by citing the continuation: if one consecrated trees and then the land, when redeeming, he redeems the trees at their value and the land at the fixed rate. If it were Rabbi Shimon, he would follow the time of redemption and allow the trees to be redeemed with the land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the interpretation that the mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon by citing the continuation: if one consecrated trees and then the land, when redeeming, he redeems the trees at their value and the land at the fixed rate.
The Gemara objects that if the mishnah followed Rabbi Shimon, he would follow the time of redemption and allow the trees to be redeemed with the land.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Shimon follows the time of redemption
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Shimon follows the time of redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon derive that a field purchased from one's father and then consecrated, after the father dies, is considered an ancestral field, showing they follow the time of redemption. Rabbi Meir disagrees. The Gemara infers that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon require a verse only when consecration preceded death, implying they follow redemption.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon deriving from a verse that a field purchased from one's father and consecrated before the father's death is treated as an ancestral field.
Rabbi Meir requires a verse only when the father died before consecration, implying he follows the time of consecration.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon only need a verse when consecration preceded death, not when death preceded consecration.
The Gemara asks: from where do they derive this distinction? If from the same verse, it would only support Rabbi Meir; therefore, it must be because they follow the time of redemption.

items.text: Rejection: they do not follow redemption
items.text_en: Rejection: they do not follow redemption
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the proof: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon do not generally follow the time of redemption; here they derived from the verse's extra wording that a field not fit to be an ancestral field is excluded, and this field is fit. Thus the verse itself, not the principle of following redemption, is the source.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the proof that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon follow the time of redemption, explaining that they derived their ruling from the verse's extra wording excluding a field not fit to be an ancestral field.

items.text: Rav Huna's dual status rulings
items.text_en: Rav Huna's dual status rulings
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a grafted carob and sycamore trunk have both the status of a tree and of land: as a tree, it has land when selling two trees; as land, it is not sold with the land. He also rules that a sheaf containing two se'ah has both the status of a sheaf and a stack: as a sheaf, two sheaves are forgotten but not one; as a stack, it is not subject to the law of forgotten sheaves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna opens with a dual-status ruling: a grafted carob and a sycamore trunk have both the status of a tree and of land.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's first ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's first ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical halachic implications of Rav Huna's first ruling: as a tree, it has land when selling two trees; as land, it is not sold with the land.

Rav Huna adds a second dual-status ruling: a sheaf containing two se'ah has both the status of a sheaf and a stack, with the Gemara explaining that as a sheaf, two sheaves are forgotten but not one, and as a stack, it is not subject to the law of forgotten sheaves.

items.text: Resh Lakish's dispute attribution
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's dispute attribution
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quotes Resh Lakish that the status of a grafted carob and sycamore trunk is a matter of dispute between Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei and the Rabbis.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports Resh Lakish's statement that the status of a grafted carob and a sycamore trunk is subject to the dispute between Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei and the Rabbis.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis is referenced to show that Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei holds like Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah does not simply state the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah teaches that Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei holds like Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Hadran (concluding formula)
items.text_en: Hadran (concluding formula)
items.desc_en: The standard formula marking the end of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The standard Hadran formula marks the end of the previous chapter.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Sale of a ship
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Sale of a ship
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items included in the sale of a ship (mast, flag, anchors, oars) and those not included (slaves, hides, cargo), with a caveat for a blanket sale.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items included in the sale of a ship (mast, flag, anchors, oars) and those not included (slaves, hides, cargo), with a caveat for a blanket sale.

items.text: Gemara: Definitions of ship components
items.text_en: Gemara: Definitions of ship components
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the terms from the Mishnah: תּוֹרֶן (mast), נֵס (sail), עוֹגִין (anchors), and מַנְהִיגִין (oars), citing biblical verses and a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by defining the term תּוֹרֶן (mast) as אִיסְקַרְיָא, citing a biblical verse from Ezekiel.
The Gemara defines נֵס (sail) as אַדְרָא, citing a verse from Ezekiel.
Rabbi Chiyya teaches that עוֹגִין are the ship's anchors, citing a verse from Ruth.
Rabbi Abba defines מַנְהִיגִין as the ship's oars, citing a verse from Ezekiel.
An alternative proof for the definition of oars is offered from a verse in Ezekiel.

items.text: Baraita: Additional items sold with a ship
items.text_en: Baraita: Additional items sold with a ship
items.desc_en: A baraita lists additional items sold with a ship: the gangplank and water cistern. Rabbi Natan adds the בִּיצִּית (small boat), and Somkhos adds the דּוּגִית (fishing boat).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that selling a ship includes the gangplank and the water cistern within it.
Rabbi Natan adds that the sale includes the בִּיצִּית (small boat).
Somkhos adds that the sale includes the דּוּגִית (fishing boat).

items.text: Rava: Identifying the small boat
items.text_en: Rava: Identifying the small boat
items.desc_en: Rava explains that בִּיצִּית and דּוּגִית refer to the same small boat, with Rabbi Natan using the Babylonian term and Somkhos the Palestinian term, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rava identifies that בִּיצִּית and דּוּגִית refer to the same small boat.
Rava explains that Rabbi Natan, being a Babylonian, uses the term בּוּצִּית as in the common phrase 'boats of Meishan'.
Rava explains that Somkhos, being from Eretz Yisrael, uses the term דּוּגִית, citing the verse 'and your end in boats of דּוּגָה'.

items.text: Aggadic tales of the sea
items.text_en: Aggadic tales of the sea
items.desc_en: Rabbah recounts stories from sailors about a destructive wave that appears like a white flame, the distance between waves, and a dialogue between waves about God's boundary of sand.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah reports from sailors that a destructive wave appears with a white flame-like crest and is subdued by striking it with an inscribed staff bearing God's names.
Rabbah recounts the vast distance between waves (300 parasangs) and how a wave once lifted them close to a small star, nearly scorching them from its heat.
A wave calls to another asking if anything remains unflooded, and the other responds by pointing to God's boundary of sand that the sea cannot cross, citing the verse from Jeremiah.

items.text: Tale of the demon Hurmin bar Lilith
items.text_en: Tale of the demon Hurmin bar Lilith
items.desc_en: Rabbah relates seeing the demon Hurmin bar Lilith running on the wall of Mehoza, outpacing a horseman, and being bound with two mules.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah relates seeing the demon Hurmin bar Lilith running on the wall of Mehoza, outpacing a horseman, and being bound with two mules.

items.text: The fish of the Gishrei of Rogneg
items.text_en: The fish of the Gishrei of Rogneg
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah describes a giant fish that was used as a bridge between two rivers, with a man carrying two jugs of wine crossing back and forth without spilling a drop, despite a stormy day. The fish was eventually killed by the kingdom.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah describes a giant fish used as a bridge between two rivers, where a man crossed with two jugs of wine without spilling, until the kingdom killed the fish.

items.text: The giant bird Urzila
items.text_en: The giant bird Urzila
items.desc_en: Rabbah describes seeing a one-day-old bird as large as Mount Tabor (which is four parsa), with a neck of three parsa and a head-rest of one and a half parsa. It threw a clod and blocked the Jordan River.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah testifies that he personally saw the one-day-old bird Urzila, which was as large as Mount Tabor (four parsa), with a neck of three parsa and a head-rest of one and a half parsa, and it threw a clod that blocked the Jordan River.

items.text: The frog, snake, and scorpion
items.text_en: The frog, snake, and scorpion
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah saw a frog as large as the fortress of Hagronia (sixty houses). A snake swallowed the frog, then a scorpion swallowed the snake and sat in a tree. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel says he would not have believed it if he hadn't been there.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports seeing a frog as large as the fortress of Hagronia, which was sixty houses in size.
He then describes how a snake swallowed the frog, and a scorpion swallowed the snake and sat in a tree.
He exclaims about the great strength of the tree that supported the scorpion.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel states that if he had not been there himself, he would not have believed the story.

items.text: The giant fish that destroyed sixty cities
items.text_en: The giant fish that destroyed sixty cities
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah saw a fish that had sand on its back, was washed ashore, and destroyed sixty cities, was eaten by sixty cities, and was salted for sixty cities. One eye socket filled three hundred barrels of oil. After twelve months, they saw carpenters sawing its bones to rebuild those cities.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah recounts seeing a giant fish with sand on its back that was washed ashore and destroyed sixty cities.
He adds that sixty cities ate from the fish and sixty cities salted it.
He reports that one eye socket of the fish filled three hundred barrels of oil.
After twelve months, he saw carpenters sawing the fish's bones to rebuild the destroyed cities.

items.text: The fish mistaken for land
items.text_en: The fish mistaken for land
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah saw a fish with sand on its back and reeds growing on it; they thought it was dry land, went up, baked and cooked on it. When its back got hot, it turned over, and they nearly drowned.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah recounts seeing a fish with sand on its back and reeds growing on it.
They mistakenly thought the fish was dry land, so they went up and baked and cooked on its back.
When the fish's back got hot, it turned over, and they nearly drowned.

items.text: The fish with two fins
items.text_en: The fish with two fins
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's ship sailed between the fins of a fish for three days and nights, with the fish upright and them below. Rav Dimi says a ship travels sixty parsa in the time it takes to heat a kettle, and an arrow shot by a horseman is outpaced. Rav Ashi identifies this as a גילדנא דימא (sea-monster) with two fins.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah recounts that their ship sailed between the fins of a fish for three days and nights, with the fish upright and them below.
The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the ship did not travel far, implying the fish might not be enormous.
Rav Dimi answers that a ship travels sixty parsa in the time it takes to heat a kettle, and an arrow shot by a horseman is outpaced, showing the fish is indeed enormous.
Rav Ashi resolves the matter by identifying the creature as a גילדנא דימא (sea-monster) that has two fins.

items.text: The bird Ziz Sadai
items.text_en: The bird Ziz Sadai
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah saw a bird standing ankle-deep in water with its head in the sky; they thought the water was shallow and wanted to cool off, but a heavenly voice warned them not to descend, as a carpenter's axe had fallen there seven years ago and had not yet reached the ground. Rav Ashi identifies this as Ziz Sadai.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah recounts seeing a bird standing ankle-deep in water with its head in the sky, and a heavenly voice warns them not to descend because a carpenter's axe fell there seven years ago and has not yet reached the ground.
Rav Ashi identifies the bird as Ziz Sadai, citing the verse 'וְזִיז שָׂדַי עִמָּדִי' (and Ziz Sadai is with me).

items.text: The fat geese and the question of the World to Come
items.text_en: The fat geese and the question of the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah saw geese so fat that their wings fell off, and rivers of oil flowed from under them. He asked if Israel has a share in the World to Come from them; one lifted a wing, another a thigh. When he came before Rabbi Elazar, he said that Israel will have to give an accounting for them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah recounts seeing geese so fat their wings fell off and rivers of oil flowed beneath them.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah asks the geese whether Israel has a share in the World to Come from them.
One goose lifts a wing and another lifts a thigh, indicating a share in the World to Come.
Rabbi Elazar tells Rabbah bar bar Chanah that Israel will have to give an accounting for these geese.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic)
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic)
items.desc_en: A mnemonic phrase for the following stories: 'Like the dust of blue wool, a scorpion struck his basket.'

sub.desc_en: The gemara provides a mnemonic phrase 'Like the dust of blue wool, a scorpion struck his basket' to organize the following stories.

items.text: The Arab guide who smelled the ground
items.text_en: The Arab guide who smelled the ground
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah traveled with an Arab who could smell earth and tell the way. He asked how far from water they were; the Arab asked for dirt, smelled it, and said eight parsa. They tested him and he said three parsa. Rabbah could not outsmart him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah recounts traveling in the desert with an Arab guide who could smell earth to determine the path.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah and his companions
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah and his companions
sub.desc_en: They ask the Arab how far they are from water, and he requests earth to smell.
The Arab smells the earth and reports they are eight parsa from water; after they test him by giving earth from a different spot, he says three parsa.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah admits he could not outsmart the Arab guide.

items.text: The dead of the desert
items.text_en: The dead of the desert
items.desc_en: The Arab offered to show Rabbah bar bar Chanah the dead of the desert. He saw them lying as if intoxicated.

sub.desc_en: The Arab invites Rabbah bar bar Chanah to see the dead of the desert, and Rabbah sees them lying as if intoxicated.

items.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's encounter with the giant frog
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's encounter with the giant frog
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah describes seeing a giant frog whose leg was so tall that a caravan could pass under it, and a thread of blue wool was broken, causing them to lose their way until he returned it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah describes a giant frog whose leg was so tall that a caravan passed under it, and how he returned a broken thread of blue wool to restore their ability to travel.

items.text: Rabbis criticize Rabbah bar bar Chanah's action
items.text_en: Rabbis criticize Rabbah bar bar Chanah's action
items.desc_en: When Rabbah bar bar Chanah came before the rabbis, they rebuked him for taking the thread, saying that all 'Abba' are fools and all 'Bar bar Chanah' are confused; they told him he should have counted threads and links instead.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis rebuke Rabbah bar bar Chanah for taking the thread, calling all 'Abba' fools and all 'Bar bar Chanah' confused, and telling him he should have counted threads and links instead.

items.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah at Mount Sinai and the Bat Kol
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah at Mount Sinai and the Bat Kol
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah shows Mount Sinai, surrounded by scorpions like white donkeys, and hears a Bat Kol lamenting an oath. The rabbis criticize him for not saying 'Mufar lach', but he thought it was the oath of the Flood; the rabbis counter that if so, why 'oy li'?

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah invites the Gemara to see Mount Sinai, where he observes scorpions standing like white donkeys.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah hears a Bat Kol (heavenly voice) lamenting an oath and asking who can annul it.
The rabbis criticize Rabbah bar bar Chanah, saying he should have responded to the Bat Kol with 'Mufar lach' (it is annulled for you).
Rabbah bar bar Chanah thought the oath was the oath of the Flood, which cannot be annulled.
The rabbis reject his reasoning, arguing that if it were the Flood oath, the Bat Kol would not have said 'oy li' (woe is me).

items.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah at the pit of Korach
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah at the pit of Korach
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah shows the pit of Korach, where smoke emerges and voices declare that Moses and his Torah are true, while they are liars; Gehenna turns them every thirty days like meat in a pot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah invites his companion to see the pit of Korach, and they observe smoke emerging from two holes, testing it with a water-soaked wool plug on a spear.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's report of the voices
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's report of the voices
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports hearing voices from the pit declaring that Moses and his Torah are true, while they (Korach's assembly) are liars.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's concluding explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's concluding explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah explains that every thirty days Gehenna returns them to that spot like meat in a pot, and they repeat the declaration that Moses and his Torah are true.

items.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah at the place where heaven and earth meet
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah at the place where heaven and earth meet
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah shows where heaven and earth kiss; he places his basket in a window of heaven, but after praying it disappears; he is told it was taken by the revolving sphere of heaven and will be found tomorrow.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah invites the narrator to see where heaven and earth meet, and the narrator places his basket in a window of heaven.
After praying, the narrator cannot find his basket and asks if there are thieves there.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah explains that the revolving sphere of heaven took the basket and tells the narrator to wait until tomorrow to find it.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Safra's sea creature sightings
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Safra's sea creature sightings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan recounts seeing a fish with eyes like two moons that spouted water like two rivers of Sura; Rav Safra recounts seeing a fish with horns inscribed 'I am a minor creature of the sea', and Rav Ashi identifies it as a sea-goat that is voracious and has horns.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan recounts seeing a fish whose eyes were like two moons and which spouted water like two rivers of Sura.
Rav Safra recounts seeing a fish with horns inscribed 'I am a minor creature of the sea', and they traveled three hundred parasangs to the mouth of the Leviathan.
Rav Ashi identifies the creature as a sea-goat (עיזא דימא) that is voracious and has horns.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's story of the basket of precious stones
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's story of the basket of precious stones
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan recounts seeing a basket set with precious stones and pearls, surrounded by fish called karsha; he descended to retrieve it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan recounts seeing a basket set with precious stones and pearls, surrounded by fish called karsha, and descending to retrieve it.

items.text: Stories of the precious stone and the tannin
items.text_en: Stories of the precious stone and the tannin
items.desc_en: Two stories are told: one about a precious stone guarded by a tannin (sea monster) that a bar amora'i retrieves, and another about a similar stone where a bird kills the monster. The stone is taken and birds fly off with it.

sub.desc_en: Bar Amora'i attempts to retrieve a precious stone guarded by a tannin (sea monster), but a heavenly voice intervenes, declaring the stone belongs to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's wife for the righteous in the World to Come.
Rav Yehuda Hindva'a recounts a similar incident where a bird decapitates the tannin guarding a precious stone, the stone is taken aboard, and birds fly off with it.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua see the Leviathan's eyes
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua see the Leviathan's eyes
items.desc_en: The Sages relate a story of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on a ship. Rabbi Yehoshua sees a great light in the sea, and Rabbi Eliezer suggests it might be the eyes of the Leviathan, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Sages relate a story of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua traveling on a ship.
Rabbi Eliezer wakes and asks Rabbi Yehoshua why he was startled.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers that he saw a great light in the sea.
Rabbi Eliezer suggests that the light was the eyes of the Leviathan, citing the verse 'עֵינָיו כְּעַפְעַפֵּי שָׁחַר' (his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn).

items.text: Story of the meat that revived and the coals
items.text_en: Story of the meat that revived and the coals
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports a story from Huna bar Natan about a piece of meat that revived after being placed on grass, and coals that still hissed after a year. Amemar explains the grass was samteri and the coals were from broom-plant.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports a story from Huna bar Natan about a piece of meat that revived after being placed on grass.
Huna bar Natan adds that after twelve months, they saw the coals still hissing.
Amemar explains that the grass was samteri and the coals were from broom-plant.

items.text: Interpretation of 'the great tanninim'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'the great tanninim'
items.desc_en: The verse 'And God created the great tanninim' is interpreted: in the West they say it refers to sea monsters, while Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to the Leviathan the straight serpent and the Leviathan the crooked serpent.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse and reports that in the West they interpret 'the great tanninim' as sea monsters (אורזילי דימא).
Rabbi Yochanan offers an alternative interpretation: the great tanninim refer to the Leviathan the straight serpent and the Leviathan the crooked serpent, citing a supporting verse.

items.text: God created Leviathan and Behemoth male and female, then neutered them
items.text_en: God created Leviathan and Behemoth male and female, then neutered them
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said Rav taught that God created the Leviathan and Behemoth male and female, but to prevent them from destroying the world, He neutered the male and killed/salted the female for the righteous. The Gemara questions why the same method wasn't used for both, and answers that fish are better salted, while meat is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that God created the Leviathan male and female, then neutered the male and killed and salted the female for the righteous.
The same pattern is applied to Behemoth: God created it male and female, neutered the male, and cooled the female to preserve it for the righteous.
The Gemara asks why the same method of neutering the male and cooling the female was not used for the Leviathan as well.
The first answer explains that fish (like the Leviathan) are prolific breeders, so cooling alone would not suffice.
The Gemara asks why the opposite was not done: kill the male and salt it, and neuter the female.
The second answer states that a female fish is better salted, and additionally, it would be improper for the Leviathan to play with a female.
The Gemara asks why the same salting method was not applied to the female Behemoth.
The Gemara resolves that salted fish is good, but salted meat is not, so the Behemoth could not be salted.

items.text: The prince of the sea named Rahab
items.text_en: The prince of the sea named Rahab
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said Rav taught that when God wanted to create the world, He told the prince of the sea to swallow all the waters, but he refused and was killed. Rabbi Yitzchak deduces that the prince's name is Rahab, and that without water covering him, no creature could withstand his smell.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that God commanded the prince of the sea to swallow all the waters, but the prince refused, claiming his own waters were sufficient, so God killed him.
Rabbi Yitzchak deduces that the prince's name is Rahab and that without water covering him, no creature could withstand his smell, citing a verse with a homiletic reading.

items.text: The Jordan River's source and its flow into the Leviathan's mouth
items.text_en: The Jordan River's source and its flow into the Leviathan's mouth
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said Rav taught that the Jordan River emerges from the Cave of Pamyas. A baraita confirms this and adds that it flows into the Great Sea and eventually into the mouth of the Leviathan. Rava bar Ulla objects that the verse refers to Behemoth, and explains that Behemoth is confident when the Jordan flows into the Leviathan's mouth.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that the Jordan River originates from the Cave of Pamyas.

A baraita confirms the Jordan's origin and adds that it flows through the Sea of Sibkhi and the Sea of Tiberias, eventually reaching the mouth of the Leviathan, citing the verse 'יִבְטַח כִּי יָגִיחַ יַרְדֵּן אֶל פִּיהוּ' (he trusts that the Jordan will surge into his mouth).
Rava bar Ulla objects that the verse 'יִבְטַח כִּי יָגִיחַ יַרְדֵּן אֶל פִּיהוּ' actually refers to Behemoth, not the Leviathan.
Rava bar Ulla resolves the objection by explaining that Behemoth is confident specifically when the Jordan surges into the Leviathan's mouth, thus harmonizing the verse with the baraita.

items.text: The seven seas and four rivers surrounding Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: The seven seas and four rivers surrounding Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi said Rabbi Yochanan taught that the verse 'For He founded it upon the seas' refers to the seven seas and four rivers that surround Eretz Yisrael, listing them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan identified the seven seas and four rivers surrounding Eretz Yisrael, as implied by the verse about God founding the earth on seas and rivers.

items.text: Gabriel will hunt the Leviathan
items.text_en: Gabriel will hunt the Leviathan
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi said Rabbi Yonatan taught that in the future, Gabriel will hunt the Leviathan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Yonatan that in the future, Gabriel will hunt the Leviathan.

items.text: The Leviathan's hunger and thirst
items.text_en: The Leviathan's hunger and thirst
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the Leviathan's power: when hungry, it boils the deep; when thirsty, it creates furrows in the sea, which take seventy years to heal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Leviathan's struggle with God, citing verses to show God's help.
Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan's description of the Leviathan's hunger: it boils the deep with its breath, and only entering the Garden of Eden prevents its stench from overwhelming creation.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds that when the Leviathan is thirsty, it creates furrows in the sea that take seventy years to heal, as derived from the verse.

items.text: The feast of Leviathan's flesh
items.text_en: The feast of Leviathan's flesh
items.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will make a feast for the righteous from the Leviathan's flesh, and the remainder will be traded in Jerusalem's markets.

sub.text: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will make a feast for the righteous from the Leviathan's flesh, citing verses to interpret 'חברים' as Torah scholars.

sub.text: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan (continued)
sub.text_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan (continued)
sub.desc_en: Rabba adds that the remainder of the Leviathan's flesh will be traded in Jerusalem's markets, citing verses to interpret 'כנענים' as merchants.

items.text: The sukkah from Leviathan's skin
items.text_en: The sukkah from Leviathan's skin
items.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will make a sukkah for the righteous from the Leviathan's skin, with varying rewards based on merit, and the remainder will adorn Jerusalem's walls.

sub.text: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will make a sukkah for the righteous from the Leviathan's skin, with a graded reward: one who merits gets a sukkah, one who does not gets a צלצל (a clasp or ornament).
The teaching continues with further gradations: one who merits a צלצל gets a ענק (necklace), and one who merits a ענק gets a קמיע (amulet), each supported by a verse.
The remainder of the skin God will spread over Jerusalem's walls, and its radiance will shine from one end of the world to the other, as per the verse.

items.text: The precious stones for Jerusalem's gates
items.text_en: The precious stones for Jerusalem's gates
items.desc_en: A dispute between angels and amoraim about the identity of the stones (shoham or yashfeh). Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will bring huge precious stones for the gates; a student mocks him, but later sees angels cutting such stones and repents, but is punished for his mockery.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports a dispute between angels Gabriel and Michael (or amoraim Judah and Chizkiyah) about whether the precious stones for Jerusalem's gates are שׁוֹהַם (shoham) or יָשְׁפֵה (yashfeh), and God says both.
Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will bring huge precious stones (30x30 cubits) for Jerusalem's gates, and a student mocks him, doubting such stones exist.
The student later sees angels cutting such stones, repents to Rabbi Yochanan, but Rabbi Yochanan rebukes him for mocking the sages and causes his death.

items.text: The height of the righteous in the future
items.text_en: The height of the righteous in the future
items.desc_en: A baraita cites a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about the height of the righteous in the future (200 vs. 100 cubits). The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's earlier statement refers to the height of the doorways.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, with Rabbi Meir interpreting the verse 'וָאוֹלֵךְ אֶתְכֶם קוֹמְמִיּוּת' to mean the righteous will be 200 cubits tall, like the double height of Adam.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that the height is 100 cubits, corresponding to the Temple and its walls, citing the verse about children like cornerstones.

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by explaining that Rabbi Yochanan's earlier statement about 100 cubits referred specifically to the height of the doorways (כַּוֵּוי דְּבֵי זִיקָא), not the height of the righteous.

items.text: Seven wedding canopies for each righteous person
items.text_en: Seven wedding canopies for each righteous person
items.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will make seven wedding canopies for each righteous person. Rabbi Chanina explains the purpose of smoke and fire in the canopies, and a parallel is drawn to Moses and Joshua.

sub.text: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will make seven wedding canopies for each righteous person, citing a verse.
The gemara asks why there is smoke in the canopy.
Rabbi Chanina explains that smoke is for those who were stingy with their eyes toward Torah scholars in this world.
The gemara asks why there is fire in the canopy.
Rabbi Chanina explains that fire teaches each person is singed by their fellow's canopy, expressing shame.

items.text: The number of canopies for Adam and the interpretation of a verse
items.text_en: The number of canopies for Adam and the interpretation of a verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says God made ten canopies for Adam; Mar Zutra says eleven. Rabbi Yochanan notes that gold is the least valuable among them. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets a verse about Hiram, king of Tyre.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that God made ten canopies (חופות) for Adam in the Garden of Eden, citing a verse.
Mar Zutra argues that there were eleven canopies, based on the phrase 'כׇּל אֶבֶן יְקָרָה' (every precious stone).
Rabbi Yochanan notes that gold is the least valuable among the precious stones listed, as it appears last in the verse.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'מְלֶאכֶת תֻּפֶּיךָ וּנְקָבֶיךָ בָּךְ' (the work of your tambourines and your perforations were in you).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that God told Hiram, king of Tyre, 'I looked at you and created perforations in man,' interpreting the verse.

items.text: Opening verse and transition to Gemara
items.text_en: Opening verse and transition to Gemara
items.desc_en: The Gemara quotes a verse about God imposing death on Adam, then immediately asks about the meaning of a phrase from the previous Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes a verse about God imposing death on Adam.

items.text: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan on the future Jerusalem
items.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan on the future Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan explains that the Jerusalem of the world to come is unlike the present one: anyone may ascend now, but only those invited may ascend in the future.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'ועל מקראה' from the Mishnah.
Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that unlike the earthly Jerusalem, the future Jerusalem is only entered by those invited.

items.text: Three entities called by God's name
items.text_en: Three entities called by God's name
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani teach that the righteous, the Messiah, and Jerusalem are called by God's name, citing verses. Rabbi Elazar adds that the righteous will be called 'holy' like God.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan citing Rabbi Yohanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan citing Rabbi Yohanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Yohanan teaches that the righteous will be called by God's name, citing the verse 'כֹּל הַנִּקְרָא בִשְׁמִי וְלִכְבוֹדִי בְּרָאתִיו, יְצַרְתִּיו אַף עֲשִׂיתִיו'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani citing Rabbi Yohanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani citing Rabbi Yohanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani in the name of Rabbi Yohanan adds that three entities are called by God's name: the righteous, the Messiah, and Jerusalem.

The gemara cites prooftexts for each entity: the righteous from the earlier verse, the Messiah from 'וְזֶה שְּׁמוֹ אֲשֶׁר יִקְרְאוֹ ה׳ צִדְקֵנוּ', and Jerusalem from 'וְשֵׁם הָעִיר מִיּוֹם ה׳ שָׁמָּה' with a homiletic reading.
Rabbi Elazar adds that the righteous will be called 'holy' like God, citing the verse 'וְהָיָה הַנִּשְׁאָר בְּצִיּוֹן וְהַנּוֹתָר בִּירוּשָׁלִַם, קָדוֹשׁ יֵאָמֶר לוֹ'.

items.text: Jerusalem elevated three parasangs
items.text_en: Jerusalem elevated three parasangs
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan says God will raise Jerusalem three parasangs, citing a verse and a tradition from an elder. Rav Pappa infers that a cloud rises three parasangs.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan states that the Holy One will elevate Jerusalem three parasangs, citing the verse 'וְרָאֲמָה וְיָשְׁבָה תַחְתֶּיהָ' and interpreting 'תַּחְתֶּיהָ' as 'like its lower part'.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan citing an elder
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan citing an elder
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Yohanan supports the measure by citing an elder who personally saw the original Jerusalem and confirmed it was three parasangs.
Rav Pappa infers from the verse 'מִי אֵלֶּה כָּעָב תְּעוּפֶינָה' that a cloud rises three parasangs, resolving the concern about the effort of ascent.

items.text: Angels protest measuring Jerusalem
items.text_en: Angels protest measuring Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa recounts that God initially wanted to measure Jerusalem, but the ministering angels protested, arguing that other cities are not measured. God then promised Jerusalem would be unwalled due to its population.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa says God wanted to measure Jerusalem, citing a verse.
The ministering angels object to measuring Jerusalem, arguing that other cities are not measured.
God responds by saying Jerusalem will be unwalled due to its multitude.

items.text: Future expansion of Jerusalem
items.text_en: Future expansion of Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish describes God adding thousands of gardens, towers, and fortresses to Jerusalem, each as large as Tzippori in its tranquility. Rabbi Yosei testifies that he saw Tzippori with 180,000 markets.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish declares that God will add thousands of gardens, towers, and fortresses to Jerusalem, each as large as Tzippori in its tranquility.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei testifying that he saw Tzippori in its tranquility with 180,000 markets of spice sellers.

items.text: Interpretation of 'three and thirty times'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'three and thirty times'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin explains a verse about Jerusalem's chambers: if there are three Jerusalems, each has thirty levels; if thirty, each has three levels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of 'three and thirty times' in the verse about Jerusalem's chambers.

sub.text: Rabbi Levi citing Rav Papei in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin
sub.text_en: Rabbi Levi citing Rav Papei in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi explains that if there are three Jerusalems, each has thirty levels; if thirty Jerusalems, each has three levels.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on acquiring a boat
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on acquiring a boat
items.desc_en: Rav holds that pulling a boat any amount acquires it; Shmuel requires pulling the entire boat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about the acquisition of a ship by pulling (משיכה).
Rav rules that pulling any part of the ship acquires it.
Shmuel rules that one does not acquire the ship until pulling its entirety.

items.text: Tannaitic sources on acquisition by pulling
items.text_en: Tannaitic sources on acquisition by pulling
items.desc_en: A baraita describes acquisition by pulling for animals: lifting a foot or leg suffices, but Rabbi Aha requires walking a full body length.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel aligns with a Tannaitic dispute.
The baraita describes acquisition by delivery (מסירה) for an animal.
The baraita describes acquisition by pulling (משיכה) for an animal: once it lifts a foreleg and hindleg, it is acquired.
Rabbi Achai (or Rabbi Acha) requires the animal to walk its full height for acquisition.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel align with tannaitic views
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel align with tannaitic views
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Rav follows the first Tanna and Shmuel follows Rabbi Aha, but each explains that their ruling applies specifically to boats, not animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rav's position aligns with the first Tanna and Shmuel's with Rabbi Aha.
Rav explains that even Rabbi Aha would agree with him regarding boats, since a boat moves entirely when any part is pulled, unlike animals.
Shmuel explains that even the first Tanna would agree with him regarding boats, since only pulling the entire boat effects acquisition, unlike animals where a partial movement suffices.

items.text: Another tannaitic dispute on boat acquisition
items.text_en: Another tannaitic dispute on boat acquisition
items.desc_en: A baraita states a boat is acquired by pulling; Rabbi Natan adds that a boat and letters are acquired by pulling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests another Tannaitic source for the dispute.
A baraita states that a ship is acquired by pulling.
Rabbi Natan adds that a ship and documents are acquired by pulling.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial correction
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial correction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a textual issue in the Mishnah: the word 'and by a document' (וּבִשְׁטָר) seems misplaced. It suggests the Mishnah should be read as: 'A ship is acquired by pulling, and documents by delivery. Rabbi Natan says: A ship and documents are acquired by pulling and by a document.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions 'and by a document' (וּבִשְׁטָר) in the context of documents, asking who mentioned documents.

The Gemara resolves the issue by asserting that the Mishnah is missing words and should be read as: 'A ship is acquired by pulling, and documents by delivery. Rabbi Natan says: A ship and documents are acquired by pulling and by a document.'

items.text: Question on the need for a document for a ship
items.text_en: Question on the need for a document for a ship
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a document would be needed for a ship, since it is movable property. It proposes an alternative reading of Rabbi Natan's statement: 'A ship by pulling, and documents by a document.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a document would be needed for a ship, since it is movable property, and proposes an alternative reading of Rabbi Natan's statement: 'A ship by pulling, and documents by a document.'

items.text: Resolution of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that if Rabbi Natan agrees with the first Tanna on the ship, the dispute is only about documents. It explains that all agree on the ship, and the disagreement is only about documents: Rabbi Natan requires a document for documents, while the first Tanna does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Natan agrees with the first Tanna on the ship, the dispute between Rav and Shmuel is not present.
The Gemara explains that all agree on the ship, and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel is irrelevant here.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is only about documents: Rabbi Natan requires a document for documents, while the first Tanna does not.

items.text: Tannaitic support for the dispute
items.text_en: Tannaitic support for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita where Rabbi holds that documents are acquired by delivery, while the Sages require both writing and delivery. This supports the earlier analysis of the dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita where Rabbi holds that documents are acquired by delivery, while the Sages require both writing and delivery, supporting the earlier analysis of the dispute.

items.text: Challenge: If the Mishnah follows Rabbi, why not acquire the ship by delivery?
items.text_en: Challenge: If the Mishnah follows Rabbi, why not acquire the ship by delivery?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If the Mishnah is interpreted according to Rabbi, then a ship should also be acquirable by delivery, as a Baraita states that Rabbi says a ship is acquired by delivery, while the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If the Mishnah is interpreted according to Rabbi, then a ship should also be acquirable by delivery, as a Baraita states that Rabbi says a ship is acquired by delivery, while the Sages disagree.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction between the Mishnah and the Baraita
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction between the Mishnah and the Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction between the Mishnah's requirement of pulling or renting the place and a Baraita. It resolves this by distinguishing between a public domain (reshut harabim) and a side street (simta).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah requires pulling or renting the place, but a Baraita implies a different rule.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a public domain (רשות הרבים) and a side street (סימטא).

items.text: Challenging the resolution and reinterpreting the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenging the resolution and reinterpreting the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution by questioning how pulling can acquire in a public domain and cites Abaye and Rava's principle about modes of acquisition. It then reinterprets the Mishnah to mean pulling from the public domain into a simta, or renting the place if it is the owner's property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution by asking how the Mishnah's case could be in a public domain (רשות הרבים), since the buyer would have no one from whom to rent the place.

The Gemara objects that pulling (משיכה) does not effect acquisition in a public domain, citing the principle of Abaye and Rava that only delivery (מסירה) acquires in a public domain, pulling in a simta (סימטא), and lifting (הגבהה) anywhere.

The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: 'until he pulls it' means pulling from the public domain into a simta (סימטא), and 'until he rents its place' applies when the place belongs to the owner, so the buyer must rent it.

items.text: Questioning whether Abaye and Rava follow Rabbi
items.text_en: Questioning whether Abaye and Rava follow Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Abaye and Rava's ruling that meshikhah acquires in a simta aligns with Rabbi's opinion in the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Abaye and Rava's ruling that meshikhah acquires in a simta aligns with Rabbi's opinion in the Mishnah.

items.text: Rav Ashi's distinction and the dispute about intent
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's distinction and the dispute about intent
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi distinguishes between a case where the seller said 'go, take possession and acquire' (where meshikhah is not needed) and where he said 'go, pull and acquire' (where meshikhah is required). The dispute between Rabbi and the Sages is about whether the seller is particular about the mode of acquisition or merely showing the place.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi distinguishes between two cases: if the seller said 'go, take possession and acquire', meshikhah is not needed; but here we deal with a case where he said 'go, pull and acquire'.
The gemara explains that one authority (Rabbi) holds the seller is particular about the mode of acquisition, while the other (the Sages) holds he is merely showing the place.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling on transferring a document with its lien
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling on transferring a document with its lien
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that when selling a document, one must write 'acquire it and all its lien'. Rav Ashi questions whether without this phrase the buyer does not acquire the lien, and Rav Kahana responds that it is necessary to seal the deal tightly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that when selling a document, one must write 'acquire it and all its lien'.
Rav Ashi questions Rav Kahana whether without this phrase the buyer does not acquire the lien.
Rav Kahana responds that the phrase is necessary to seal the deal tightly, like sealing a flask.

items.text: Amemar's ruling and Rav Ashi's question
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling and Rav Ashi's question
items.desc_en: Amemar states the halakha that letters are acquired by delivery, consistent with Rabbi. Rav Ashi asks whether this is from tradition or logic, and Amemar says it is tradition. Rav Ashi then argues that logic also supports it because letters are mere words, and words cannot be acquired by words.

sub.desc_en: Amemar states the halakha that letters are acquired by delivery, consistent with Rabbi.

items.text: Rabbah bar Yitzchak's two-document case
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Yitzchak's two-document case
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi's logic by citing Rabbah bar Yitzchak's ruling about two types of documents: if one says 'Acquire the field for so-and-so and write him the document,' the seller can retract the document but not the field; if one says 'On condition that you write him the document,' the seller can retract both.

items.text: Rav Chiya bar Avin's three-document case
items.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin's three-document case
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin cites Rav Huna, who adds a third type of document: if the seller wrote the document first, the ruling differs from the previous cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that logic also supports it because letters are mere words, and words cannot be acquired by words.
Rav Ashi asks Amemar: is this a gemara (tradition) or a sevara (logical reasoning)?
Amemar answers: it is a gemara.
Rav Ashi objects: it is also sevara — letters are words, and words are not acquired by words (i.e., a verbal agreement does not transfer ownership).

Rav Ashi cites a supporting baraita from Rabbah bar Yitzchak quoting Rav: there are two types of documents — 'Acquire the field for so-and-so and write him the document' — the seller retracts from the document but not from the field.
Rav Ashi cites a second baraita: 'On condition that you write him the document' — the seller retracts from both the document and the field.
Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Rav Huna: there are three types of documents; two are the ones we already discussed, and the third is if the seller wrote the document first.

items.text: Acquisition of coins agav land
items.text_en: Acquisition of coins agav land
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that movable property can be acquired together with land through the principle of agav, citing the Mishnah about writing a deed for a seller. It distinguishes coins from other movables, noting that coins are not acquired through halipin but can be acquired agav land, and illustrates with the story of Rav Pappa acquiring coins for Rav Shmuel bar Acha agav his doorstep.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah rule that movable property is acquired together with land (agav) through money, deed, or hazakah.
The Gemara explains that coins are different: they are not acquired through halipin (exchange) but can be acquired agav land.

sub.text: Story of Rav Pappa and Rav Shmuel bar Acha
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Pappa and Rav Shmuel bar Acha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara illustrates the principle with the story of Rav Pappa acquiring twelve thousand zuz for Rav Shmuel bar Acha agav his doorstep.

items.text: Definition of 'antikei'
items.text_en: Definition of 'antikei'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when selling a courtyard, one does not sell slaves, mortars, or 'antikei'. Rav Pappa explains that 'antikei' refers to the merchandise within the courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when selling a courtyard, one does not sell slaves, mortars, or 'antikei'.
The Gemara asks what the term 'antikei' means.
Rav Pappa explains that 'antikei' refers to the merchandise within the courtyard.

items.text: Mishnah: Sale of wagon, mules, yoke, and oxen
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sale of wagon, mules, yoke, and oxen
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that selling a wagon does not include the mules, and vice versa; selling a yoke does not include the oxen, and vice versa. Rabbi Yehuda says the price indicates intent, giving an example where a yoke sold for 200 zuz clearly does not include the oxen. The Sages disagree, saying price is not evidence.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: selling a wagon does not include the mules, and selling a yoke does not include the oxen.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that the price indicates intent, giving the example of a yoke sold for 200 zuz, which clearly does not include the oxen.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda, asserting that price is not evidence of intent.

items.text: Gemara's question on wagon and mules
items.text_en: Gemara's question on wagon and mules
items.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva taught before Rabbi Avahu that selling a wagon includes the mules, contradicting the Mishnah. Rabbi Avahu challenges him, and Rav Tachlifa explains that the Mishnah refers to mules that are not attached (adukin bo).

sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva teaches before Rabbi Avahu that selling a wagon includes the mules, contradicting the Mishnah.
Rabbi Avahu objects that the Mishnah explicitly states 'did not sell' the mules.
Rabbi Avahu asks if Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva is confused about the Mishnah.
Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva answers that the Mishnah refers to mules that are not attached (אדוקין בו) to the wagon.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of yoke and oxen dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of yoke and oxen dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of selling a yoke without oxen, considering whether the terms are distinct or ambiguous. It concludes that the dispute applies where both terms are used, but some also call oxen 'yoke'. Rabbi Yehuda holds that price indicates intent, while the Sages say price is not evidence, leading to a question about whether the sale is void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks under what circumstances the Mishnah's dispute applies, rejecting the simple case where the terms are distinct.
The Gemara considers the alternative where oxen are also called 'yoke', which would make the sale include everything.
The Gemara explains that the dispute applies in a place where both terms are used, with Rabbi Yehuda holding that price indicates intent and the Sages holding that price is not evidence.
The Gemara objects that if the Sages hold price is not evidence, the sale should be void due to uncertainty.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about bitul mekach
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about bitul mekach
items.desc_en: The Gemara first challenges the assumption that rabbinic law does not recognize bitul mekach, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda lists items without ona'ah and the Sages object. It then offers two resolutions: either the cited case itself involves bitul mekach, or the principle of bitul mekach applies only when the price error is within the range of common mistake, not when it is so extreme that the buyer must have intended a gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that rabbinic law does not recognize ביטול מקח (annulment of sale), citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda lists items without אונאה (overcharge) and the Sages object.
The Gemara offers the first resolution: the cited case itself involves ביטול מקח (annulment of sale), meaning the principle is acknowledged.

The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the principle of אונאה (overcharge) and ביטול מקח (annulment) applies only when the error is within the range of common mistake, but when the error is so extreme that the buyer must have intended a gift, it does not apply.

items.text: Mishnah: Sale of a donkey does not include its vessels
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sale of a donkey does not include its vessels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling a donkey does not include its vessels, with Nachum HaMadi arguing they are included. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: if the buyer said 'sell me this donkey of yours' the vessels are included, but if he said 'your donkey' they are not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule: one who sells a donkey does not sell its vessels.
Nachum HaMadi disputes the Tanna Kamma and rules that the vessels are included in the sale.
Rabbi Yehuda introduces a distinction: sometimes the vessels are sold, sometimes not, depending on the buyer's phrasing.

items.text: Ulla's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Ulla's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Nachum HaMadi is limited to sacks and saddlebags, because the Tanna Kamma assumes a donkey is typically for riding, while Nachum HaMadi assumes it is for carrying loads. However, all agree that items like a saddle, blanket, and girth are included in the sale.

sub.desc_en: Ulla explains that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Nachum HaMadi is limited to sacks and saddlebags, while items like a saddle, blanket, and girth are universally included in the sale.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that seems to contradict Ulla: it states that only when the seller explicitly says 'donkey and its vessels' are the saddle and blanket sold, implying that without such specification they are not sold. The Gemara resolves that the baraita's intent is to teach that even when saying 'donkey and its vessels', sacks and saddlebags are not included, but the saddle and blanket are sold even without that specification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states only when the seller explicitly says 'donkey and its vessels' are the saddle and blanket sold, implying that without such specification they are not sold, contradicting Ulla's ruling.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita's intent is to teach that even when saying 'donkey and its vessels', sacks and saddlebags are not included, but the saddle and blanket are sold even without that specification.

items.text: Definition of 'kumnei'
items.text_en: Definition of 'kumnei'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel explains that 'kumnei' refers to a woman's saddle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'kumnei' means.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel answers that 'kumnei' refers to a woman's saddle.

items.text: Clarifying the scope of the dispute: whether vessels are on the donkey
items.text_en: Clarifying the scope of the dispute: whether vessels are on the donkey
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the dispute apply only when the vessels are on the donkey, or only when they are not? It attempts to resolve this from the baraita's clause 'when he said 'it and all that is on it' all are sold', but the answer is inconclusive. The Gemara then considers whether Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the Mishnah refers to the Tanna Kamma's position, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Nachum HaMadi apply only when the vessels are on the donkey, or only when they are not on the donkey?
The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing the baraita's clause that when the buyer said 'it and all that is on it' all are sold.

The Gemara analyzes the baraita: if the dispute is when vessels are on the donkey, the baraita aligns with the Rabbis; if the dispute is when vessels are not on the donkey, the baraita's ruling that all are sold when on the donkey is unanimous, leaving the baraita's author unidentified.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is when the vessels are not on the donkey, and the baraita's phrase 'it and all that is on it' is interpreted as 'it and all that is fit to be on it'.
The Gemara attempts another proof from Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the Mishnah, asking whether Rabbi Yehuda is referring to the Tanna Kamma's position.
The Gemara rejects the proof, stating that Rabbi Yehuda's statement is not referring to the Tanna Kamma's position, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction about selling a wagon with its mules
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction about selling a wagon with its mules
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi with a contradiction between the Mishnah (which says selling a wagon does not include its mules) and a baraita (which says it does). Rabbi Avahu resolves the baraita by explaining it refers to mules yoked to the wagon. The Gemara then questions whether the Mishnah's other clauses also require specific conditions, concluding that the Tanna teaches separate cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Tanna is speaking of a separate matter.
Ravina challenges Rav Ashi by citing a contradiction between the Mishnah and a baraita taught by Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva before Rabbi Avahu.
Rabbi Avahu resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to mules yoked to the wagon.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's first clause is about unyoked mules, then the later clause about other items must also be about items not currently on the wagon.
The Gemara resolves by citing Rav Pappa's explanation of 'אנתיקי' (goods) and concluding that the Tanna teaches separate cases (מילי מילי קתני).

items.text: Abaye's list of Tannaim who hold that selling an item includes its accessories
items.text_en: Abaye's list of Tannaim who hold that selling an item includes its accessories
items.desc_en: Abaye lists five Tannaim (Rabbi Eliezer, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Natan, Sumchos, and Nachum HaMadi) who all hold the principle that when a person sells an item, they sell it with all its accessories. The Gemara provides prooftexts for each.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by listing six Tannaim who all hold the principle that when a person sells an item, they sell it with all its accessories.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that selling a בית הבד (olive press) includes the beam (קורה).

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that selling a city includes the סנטר (the city's market or main street).
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that selling a vineyard includes its accessories (תשמישי הכרם).

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Natan and Sumchos
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Natan and Sumchos
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Natan and Sumchos rule that selling a boat includes its accessories (ביצית – a small boat, and דוגית – a fishing boat).
The Gemara notes that Nachum HaMadi's position is the one already mentioned (referring to a previously cited baraita).

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the difference between 'your donkey' and 'this donkey'
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the difference between 'your donkey' and 'this donkey'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the Mishnah's distinction between 'your donkey' and 'this donkey' in the context of selling a donkey with its accessories. Rava explains that 'this donkey' implies the buyer knows the donkey is his, and the seller specifies the accessories; 'your donkey' implies the buyer does not know the donkey is his, and the seller is asking to sell it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the difference between the Mishnah's phrases 'your donkey this' and 'your donkey it'.

Rava explains that 'your donkey this' indicates the buyer already knows the donkey is his and the seller specifies the accessories, while 'your donkey it' indicates the buyer does not know and the seller is asking to sell it.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on selling a donkey with its foal vs. a cow with its calf
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on selling a donkey with its foal vs. a cow with its calf
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that selling a donkey includes its foal, but selling a cow does not include its calf. The Gemara questions the distinction, and Rav Pappa explains that the seller specifies 'a nursing donkey' and 'a nursing cow'; for a cow, the buyer might want it for milk, but for a donkey, the only reason to specify 'nursing' is to include the foal. The foal is called a 'syach' because it follows a beautiful mare.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases: selling a donkey includes its foal, but selling a cow does not include its calf; selling an ashpit includes its manure, a cistern its water, a beehive its bees, a dovecote its pigeons.
The Gemara questions the distinction: if the seller said 'it and its young,' even a cow's calf would be included; if not, even a donkey's foal would not be included.

Rav Pappa explains: the seller specified 'a nursing donkey' and 'a nursing cow'; for a cow, the buyer might want it for milk, but for a donkey, the only reason to specify 'nursing' is to include the foal, and the foal is called a 'syach' because it follows a beautiful mare.

items.text: Homiletical interpretation of the verse 'Therefore the poets say, Come to Heshbon'
items.text_en: Homiletical interpretation of the verse 'Therefore the poets say, Come to Heshbon'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets the biblical verse allegorically: 'the poets' are those who master their evil inclination; 'Come to Heshbon' means to calculate the world's accounting; 'built and established' refers to this world and the next; 'city of Sichon' is one who follows his inclination like a foal; the fire from Heshbon consumes those who do not calculate; and 'we shot them' refers to the wicked who deny God's greatness.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan introduces a homiletical interpretation of the verse 'עַל כֵּן יֹאמְרוּ הַמֹּשְׁלִים' (Therefore the poets say).

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Interprets 'the poets' as those who master their evil inclination, and 'Come to Heshbon' as a call to calculate the world's accounting — the loss of a מצוה (commandment) against its reward, and the reward of a transgression against its loss.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Interprets 'built and established' as building in this world and being established in the World to Come; 'city of Sichon' as one who follows his inclination like a foal; and the fire from Heshbon as consuming those who do not calculate.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Interprets 'flame from the city of Sichon' as from the city of righteous ones called 'שִׂיחִין'; 'consumed Ar of Moab' as one who follows his inclination; and 'lords of the high places of Arnon' as the arrogant who fall into Gehinnom.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Interprets 'we shot them' as the wicked saying there is no Most High; 'Heshbon is lost' as the world's accounting is lost; and God says to wait until judgment comes.

items.text: Aggadic opening: punishment for abandoning Torah
items.text_en: Aggadic opening: punishment for abandoning Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the biblical place names 'Nofah' and 'Medeva' as allegories for divine punishment. Rav Yehuda citing Rav and Rabbi Yonatan teach that one who separates from Torah study will be consumed by fire or fall into Gehinnom, citing verses from Ezekiel and Proverbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the place names 'Nofah' and 'Medeva' as allegories for divine punishment: fire that needs no fanning and a place that causes the soul to despair.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav teaches that one who separates from Torah study will be consumed by fire, citing a verse from Ezekiel.
Rabbi Yonatan teaches that one who separates from Torah study falls into Gehinnom, citing a verse from Proverbs.

items.text: Mishnah and Tosefta: consecrated items and their contents
items.text_en: Mishnah and Tosefta: consecrated items and their contents
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta from Me'ilah discussing the principle of me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property) for items like a pit, dung heap, dovecote, field, or tree. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between items consecrated when full (me'ilah applies to both container and contents) and those consecrated empty and later filled (me'ilah applies only to the container). Rabbi Yosei argues that for a field or tree, me'ilah applies to their growths because they are 'growths of consecration'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Tosefta from Me'ilah stating the general rule that me'ilah applies to consecrated items and their contents.
The Tosefta gives examples of items consecrated when full (pit, dung heap, dovecote, field, tree) where me'ilah applies to both container and contents.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that if items were consecrated empty and later filled, me'ilah applies only to the container, not the contents.
Rabbi Yosei argues that for a field or tree consecrated empty, me'ilah applies to their growths because they are 'growths of consecration'.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a baraita where Rabbi says: 'The words of Rabbi Yehuda appear correct for a pit and dovecote, and the words of Rabbi Yosei appear correct for a field and tree.' The Gemara questions whether this implies Rabbi Yosei disagrees regarding a pit and dovecote, which seems contradictory since Rabbi Yosei only mentioned field and tree. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi means Rabbi Yehuda's view is accepted by Rabbi Yosei for pit and dovecote, as Rabbi Yosei only disputes regarding field and tree.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi states that Rabbi Yehuda's words appear correct for a pit and dovecote, and Rabbi Yosei's words appear correct for a field and tree.

The Gemara questions the implication of Rabbi's statement: if Rabbi Yosei's words appear correct for field and tree, does that mean he disagrees regarding pit and dovecote, even though he only mentioned field and tree?

The Gemara objects to a possible interpretation that Rabbi Yosei was speaking to Rabbi Yehuda's position, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei explicitly says he does not see Rabbi Yehuda's words regarding field and tree, implying he does see them regarding pit and dovecote.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi's statement means Rabbi Yehuda's words appear correct to Rabbi Yosei regarding pit and dovecote, as Rabbi Yosei only disputes regarding field and tree but agrees regarding pit and dovecote.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one consecrated items when empty and they later filled, me'ilah applies to the container but not the contents. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says me'ilah applies even to the contents. Rabba explains that the dispute is only regarding a field and tree (Tanna Kamma follows Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Yosei), but for a pit and dovecote, all agree me'ilah applies only to the container. Abaye challenges this with another baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon reverses the ruling for full items.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if one consecrated containers when empty and they later filled, me'ilah applies to the container but not the contents; Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says me'ilah applies even to the contents.

Rabba explains that the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon is limited to a field and tree, where Tanna Kamma follows Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Yosei; but for a pit and dovecote, all agree me'ilah applies only to the container.
Abaye challenges Rabba by citing another baraita where, for full items, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon reverses the ruling, contradicting Rabba's explanation.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbah asserts that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon is specifically about a pit and a dovecote, but regarding a field and a tree, all agree that one acquires them and their contents.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah would present a dispute about exchanging a field and a tree if all agree on the acquisition.
Rabbah resolves that the dispute is specifically about a pit and a dovecote, but regarding a field and a tree, all agree that one acquires them and their contents.

items.text: Empty pit and dovecote: dispute over acquiring future objects
items.text_en: Empty pit and dovecote: dispute over acquiring future objects
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the basis of the dispute in empty cases, and explains that the Tanna Kamma follows the Rabbis who hold that one cannot acquire something not yet in existence, while Rabbi Elazar bar Simon follows Rabbi Meir who holds that one can.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute in the Mishnah about empty pits and dovecotes is based on, and also what the dispute about full ones is based on.
The Gemara explains that the dispute about empty pits and dovecotes is based on the disagreement between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding whether one can acquire something not yet in existence.

items.text: Objection and Rava's resolution for empty cases
items.text_en: Objection and Rava's resolution for empty cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Meir's principle applies only to items that will certainly come, but water and doves are not guaranteed. Rava answers that the case involves water that flows through his courtyard and doves that come through his dovecote, which are certain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Meir's principle of acquiring something not yet in the world applies only to items that will certainly come, but water and doves are not guaranteed to arrive.
Rava answers that the case involves water that flows through his courtyard into the pit and doves that come through his dovecote to the dovecote, which are certain to arrive.

items.text: Full pit and dovecote: dispute over divine vs. human law
items.text_en: Full pit and dovecote: dispute over divine vs. human law
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the dispute in full cases. Rava explains that it involves a case where one consecrated a pit without specifying the water. Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon follows his father's view that one can derive divine law from human law, so just as in human law one can sell a pit without its water, so too in consecration the water is not consecrated. The Tanna Kamma holds that one cannot derive divine law from human law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In the case of full pits and dovecotes, what is the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon?
