sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the storekeeper is a seller of flasks, the latter clause where the Sages exempt him contradicts the view of Rabbah and Rav Yosef that the child was sent only to inform.

sub.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin resolve the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a different scenario, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Objection to Rabba's analogy
items.text_en: Objection to Rabba's analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabba's ruling about a live animal that kicked and caused injury may not apply to an inanimate object like a scale pan. The objection distinguishes between living creatures, which naturally resist, and objects, which do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabba's ruling about a live animal that kicked does not apply to an inanimate scale pan, since living creatures naturally resist but objects do not.

items.text: Rava's resolution and the dispute about borrowing without knowledge
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and the dispute about borrowing without knowledge
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the case involves taking the scale pan to measure for others, and the dispute is about whether one who borrows without the owner's knowledge is considered a borrower or a thief. The two opinions are presented.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by stating that he and the lion of the group (Rabbi Zeira) interpreted the case as involving taking the scale pan to measure for others.
The Gemara clarifies that the case involves one who took the scale pan to measure for others.
The Gemara explains that the dispute between the two sages (Mar) is about whether one who borrows without the owner's knowledge is considered a borrower (שואל) or a thief (גזלן).

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on taking a vessel to inspect it
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on taking a vessel to inspect it
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who takes a vessel from a craftsman to inspect it is liable for an accident, provided the price is fixed. This is a standalone statement.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who takes a vessel from a craftsman to inspect it is liable for an accident, provided the price is fixed.

items.text: Case of the meat piece taken from a butcher
items.text_en: Case of the meat piece taken from a butcher
items.desc_en: A man lifted a piece of meat in a butcher shop, and a horseman snatched it. Rav Yemar ruled he must pay its value, provided the price was fixed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts a case where a man lifted a piece of meat in a butcher shop and a horseman snatched it from him.
Rav Yemar ruled that the man must pay the value of the meat.
The gemara qualifies that this ruling applies only when the meat's price was fixed.

items.text: Case of the gourds and the attempted consecration
items.text_en: Case of the gourds and the attempted consecration
items.desc_en: A man brought gourds to the riverbank; people took them. He declared them consecrated. Rav Kahana ruled that one cannot consecrate what is not his, but if the price is not fixed, the items are still in the owners' possession and the consecration is valid.

sub.desc_en: A man brought gourds to the riverbank; people took them, and he declared them consecrated.
Rav Kahana ruled that one cannot consecrate what is not his, but if the price is not fixed, the items are still in the owners' possession and the consecration is valid.

items.text: Baraita on buying vegetables and the principle of intent
items.text_en: Baraita on buying vegetables and the principle of intent
items.desc_en: The baraita discusses one who buys vegetables and selects them; he does not acquire them until he decides to buy. Rav Hoshaya explains that this applies to a God-fearing person like Rav Safra, who fulfills 'speaks truth in his heart'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who buys vegetables and selects them without deciding to buy does not acquire them and is not liable for מעשר (tithe).
The baraita continues that if one resolved in his heart to buy, he acquires and becomes liable for מעשר (tithe), and provides a remedy for the dilemma of returning or tithing the produce.
The gemara questions how mere mental resolve can effect acquisition and liability for מעשר (tithe).
Rav Hoshaya answers that the baraita deals with a God-fearing person like Rav Safra, who fulfills 'speaks truth in his heart' and thus his mental resolve is halachically binding.

items.text: Mishnah: Cleaning measures and scales
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cleaning measures and scales
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a wholesaler cleans his measures every thirty days, a homeowner every twelve months; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reverses the ruling. A shopkeeper cleans his measures twice a week and wipes his weights once a week, and cleans the scales after each weighing; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel limits this to moist items.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a wholesaler cleans his measures every thirty days, a homeowner every twelve months, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reverses the ruling.

The Mishnah continues with the rule for a shopkeeper: cleans measures twice a week, wipes weights once a week, and cleans scales after each weighing; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel limits this to moist items.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one must give a handbreadth of extra weight when weighing, and if weighing eye-to-eye, one must add gerumin. It also discusses local customs regarding measuring and heaping.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one must give a handbreadth of extra weight when weighing, and if weighing eye-to-eye, one must add gerumin.
The Mishnah specifies the ratio of gerumin: one per ten for liquids and one per twenty for dry goods.
The Mishnah rules that one must follow local custom regarding measuring with fine or coarse measures, and regarding heaping or leveling.

items.text: Gemara's question and Reish Lakish's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Reish Lakish's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the requirement to give extra weight. Reish Lakish cites the verse 'even shleimah vatzedek' – 'tzedek mish'elkha v'ten lo'. The Gemara then questions how one can weigh eye-to-eye if the extra weight is biblical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the requirement to give extra weight (הכרעה).
Reish Lakish cites the verse 'אֶבֶן שְׁלֵמָה וָצֶדֶק' (a perfect and just stone) to derive that one must add extra weight from one's own.
The Gemara objects: if the extra weight is biblical (דאורייתא), how can the mishnah allow weighing eye-to-eye and then adding a small extra (גירומין)?

items.text: Resolution and definition of gerumin
items.text_en: Resolution and definition of gerumin
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the first part of the Mishnah refers to a place where it is customary to give extra weight, and Reish Lakish's statement was actually said about the latter part. Rabbi Abba bar Memel defines gerumin as one-tenth of a litra for wet goods.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the first part of the Mishnah as referring to a place where it is customary to give extra weight, and reassigns Reish Lakish's statement to the latter part.
Reish Lakish derives from the verse 'וָצֶדֶק' (and righteousness) that one must add extra weight from one's own when weighing eye-to-eye.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel defines gerumin as one-tenth of a litra for wet goods, i.e., one extra unit per ten litras.

items.text: Unresolved question about the Mishnah's statement
items.text_en: Unresolved question about the Mishnah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the Mishnah's phrase 'one for ten in wet, one for twenty in dry' – whether it means one-tenth for ten of wet and one-twentieth for twenty of dry, or one-tenth for both ten of wet and twenty of dry. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question about whether the Mishnah's phrase 'one for ten in wet, one for twenty in dry' means one-tenth for ten of wet and one-twentieth for twenty of dry, or one-tenth for both ten of wet and twenty of dry.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Levi: Severity of dishonest measures
items.text_en: Rabbi Levi: Severity of dishonest measures
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi states that the punishment for dishonest measures is greater than that for illicit sexual relations, as the former uses the term 'El' (strong) while the latter uses 'Elle' (these). The Gemara clarifies that 'Elle' in the context of illicit relations is to exclude measures from karet, and the advantage of measures is that repentance is impossible for them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi opens by asserting that the punishment for dishonest measures is greater than that for illicit sexual relations, citing the use of 'אל' (strong) for measures versus 'אלה' (these) for illicit relations, and proving 'אל' denotes severity from the verse 'וְאֶת אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ לָקָח' (and the strong of the land he took).
The Gemara objects that regarding illicit relations, the term 'אלה' is also written, questioning the distinction.
The Gemara answers that the term 'אלה' in the context of illicit relations serves to exclude dishonest measures from the punishment of כרת (karet).

The Gemara resolves the comparison by explaining that the greater severity of dishonest measures lies in the fact that repentance (תשובה) is possible for illicit relations but impossible for dishonest measures.

items.text: Rabbi Levi: Theft from an individual vs. theft from God
items.text_en: Rabbi Levi: Theft from an individual vs. theft from God
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi states that theft from an individual is more severe than theft from God, as in the former the Torah mentions 'chet' (sin) before 'me'ilah' (trespass), while in the latter it mentions 'me'ilah' before 'chet'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi states that theft from an individual is more severe than theft from God, as in the former the Torah mentions 'chet' (sin) before 'me'ilah' (trespass), while in the latter it mentions 'me'ilah' before 'chet'.

items.text: Rabbi Levi: God's blessings and curses vs. Moses'
items.text_en: Rabbi Levi: God's blessings and curses vs. Moses'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi notes that God blessed Israel with 22 blessings and cursed them with 8, while Moses blessed them with 8 and cursed them with 22. The specific verses are cited.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi opens by contrasting God's and Moses' blessings and curses, noting that God blessed Israel with 22 blessings from 'אם בחקותי' to 'קוממיות'.
Rabbi Levi specifies that God cursed Israel with eight curses from 'ואם בחקתי תמאסו' to 'ואת חקתי געלה נפשם'.
Rabbi Levi contrasts Moses, who blessed Israel with only eight blessings and cursed them with twenty-two.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Local measuring customs
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Local measuring customs
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one must follow local custom regarding whether to heap or level measures, and that one may not deviate from the local practice even if the buyer or seller agrees to adjust the price.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that one must follow local custom regarding heaping or leveling measures, and that deviation from local practice is forbidden even if the buyer or seller agrees to adjust the price.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from 'eifah shleimah'
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from 'eifah shleimah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'eifah shleimah' that one may not level where heaping is customary, nor heap where leveling is customary. It further derives that if one proposes to deviate and adjust the price, we do not listen to him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by deriving from the verse 'אֵיפָה שְׁלֵמָה' (a complete ephah) that one may not level where heaping is customary, nor heap where leveling is customary.

The baraita further derives from the verse 'אֵיפָה שְׁלֵמָה וָצֶדֶק' (a complete and righteous ephah) that if one proposes to deviate from local practice and adjust the price accordingly, we do not listen to him.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from 'even shleimah'
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from 'even shleimah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara similarly derives from the verse 'even shleimah' that one may not use a plumb line where weighing is customary, nor weigh where a plumb line is used. If one proposes to deviate and adjust the price, we do not listen to him.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'אֶבֶן שְׁלֵמָה' (a complete stone) that one may not use a plumb line where weighing is customary, nor weigh where a plumb line is used.

The baraita further derives from the verse 'אֶבֶן שְׁלֵמָה וָצֶדֶק' (a complete and righteous stone) that if one proposes to deviate from the local practice and adjust the price accordingly, we do not listen to him.

items.text: Rav Yehuda from Sura: Reason for the prohibitions
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda from Sura: Reason for the prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda from Sura explains that the verse 'lo yihyeh lecha beveitecha' refers to having two different eifah measures, and 'lo yihyeh lecha bechisecha' refers to having two different stone weights, while the positive command is to have 'even shleimah' and 'eifah shleimah'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda from Sura asks what the verse 'לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ בְּבֵיתְךָ' teaches, and answers that it prohibits having two different eifah measures.
Rav Yehuda from Sura explains that the verse 'לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ בְּכִיסְךָ' prohibits having two different stone weights, while the positive command requires 'אֶבֶן שְׁלֵמָה' and 'אֵיפָה שְׁלֵמָה'.

items.text: Appointing agardemin for measures and prices
items.text_en: Appointing agardemin for measures and prices
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that agardemin (market inspectors) are appointed for measures but not for prices. However, the house of the Nasi appointed them for both. Shmuel told Karna to teach that they are appointed only for measures, but Karna taught the opposite, leading to a curse that blinded him. Rami bar Chama in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak explains that they are appointed for both due to deceivers.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that market inspectors (אגרדמין) are appointed for measures but not for prices.
The house of the Nasi deviated from the baraita and appointed inspectors for both measures and prices.
Shmuel instructed Karna to teach the public that inspectors are appointed only for measures, not prices.
Karna went out and taught the opposite of Shmuel's instruction, that inspectors are appointed for both measures and prices.
Shmuel cursed Karna by name, and Karna's eye was blinded as a result.
The gemara explains that Karna followed the opinion of Rami bar Chama citing Rabbi Yitzchak, who ruled that inspectors are appointed for both measures and prices due to deceivers (רמָאִין).

items.text: Laws of weighing: standard weights and heaping
items.text_en: Laws of weighing: standard weights and heaping
items.desc_en: Three baraisos teach: (1) one must have standard weights for a litra, half-litra, and quarter-litra; (2) when asked for three-quarters of a litra, one should weigh a full litra and leave a quarter with the meat rather than weigh three separate quarters; (3) when asked for ten litrin, one should weigh them all at once with a single heaping rather than each individually.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita teaches that one must have standard weights for a litra, half-litra, and quarter-litra, and the gemara clarifies that this establishes the requirement to prepare weights down to that measure.

The second baraita teaches that when a customer asks for three-quarters of a litra, the seller should weigh a full litra and leave a quarter-litra with the meat rather than weighing three separate quarter-litras.
The third baraita teaches that when a customer asks for ten litrin, the seller should weigh them all at once with a single heaping rather than weighing each individually.

items.text: Dimensions of scales for different trades
items.text_en: Dimensions of scales for different trades
items.desc_en: A baraisa specifies the dimensions of scales for different trades: for wool dealers and glassmakers, the scale hangs three handbreadths in the air and is three high, with a twelve-handbreadth beam; for grocers and householders, one handbreadth each, with a six-handbreadth beam; for butchers, three fingerbreadths each, with an unknown beam length. The Gemara questions the need for the earlier dimensions.

sub.desc_en: The baraita specifies the dimensions of scales for wool dealers and glassmakers: the scale hangs three handbreadths in the air, is three handbreadths high, and has a twelve-handbreadth beam; for others, two handbreadths each and a nine-handbreadth beam.
The baraita continues with dimensions for grocers and householders (one handbreadth each, six-handbreadth beam) and for butchers (three fingerbreadths each, beam length unknown).
The Gemara asks: if the baraita already gave dimensions for the first group (wool dealers and glassmakers), what purpose do those earlier dimensions serve?

items.text: Rav Pappa's statement and its clarification
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's statement and its clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces the term 'digaromei' (a type of weight). Rabbi Mani bar Pattish explains that the same rules apply to their impurity as to their prohibition. The Gemara questions what novelty this teaches, noting that the Mishnah already states the width of a storekeeper's scale beam is a handbreadth, but the rule about the beam's rod and its covering was not taught.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces the term 'digaromei' (a type of weight).
Rabbi Mani bar Pattish explains that the same rules apply to their impurity as to their prohibition.
The Gemara questions what novelty Rav Pappa's statement teaches.

The Gemara notes that the Mishnah already states the width of a storekeeper's scale beam is a handbreadth, but the rule about the beam's rod and its covering was not taught, so Rav Pappa's statement is needed.

items.text: Baraitot on materials for weights and scrapers
items.text_en: Baraitot on materials for weights and scrapers
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one forbids making weights from certain metals but permits stone and glass; the other forbids making a scraper (for leveling a measure) from gourd or metal, but permits olive wood, nut wood, sycamore, and boxwood.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita forbids making weights from certain metals but permits stone and glass.
The second baraita forbids making a scraper from gourd or metal, but permits olive wood, nut wood, sycamore, and boxwood.

items.text: Baraita on the scraper's shape and method
items.text_en: Baraita on the scraper's shape and method
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a scraper should not be made with one thick side and one thin side. One should not scrape all at once (bad for seller) nor little by little (bad for buyer).

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a scraper must not be made with one thick side and one thin side, and prohibits both scraping all at once (bad for seller) and scraping little by little (bad for buyer).

items.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's dilemma and resolution
items.text_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's dilemma and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai expresses a dilemma about whether to reveal certain details of trade practices, fearing it might teach swindlers or lead them to claim sages are ignorant. The Gemara asks whether he revealed it, and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that he did, citing a verse about the righteous walking and the wicked stumbling.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai expresses a dilemma: if he reveals trade details, swindlers might learn; if he does not, they might claim sages are ignorant of practical matters.
The Gemara asks whether Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai actually revealed the information or not.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that he did reveal it, citing the verse 'For the ways of the Lord are straight; the righteous walk in them, and the wicked stumble in them.'

items.text: Exegesis of the verse on injustice in measures
items.text_en: Exegesis of the verse on injustice in measures
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'Do not commit injustice in judgment, in measure, in weight, or in volume,' explaining each term. It then derives a kal vachomer: if the Torah is strict about a small measure (one thirty-sixth of a log), how much more so for larger measures like hin, half-hin, etc.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'Do not commit injustice in judgment, in measure, in weight, or in volume' and explains each term: 'measure' refers to land measurement, 'weight' forbids salting weights, and 'volume' forbids causing foam.

The gemara derives a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if the Torah is strict about a small measure (one thirty-sixth of a log), how much more so for larger measures like hin, half-hin, third-hin, quarter-hin, log, half-log, quarter-log, half-tomen, and ukhla.

items.text: Prohibition of keeping inaccurate measures and exceptions
items.text_en: Prohibition of keeping inaccurate measures and exceptions
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav forbids keeping an inaccurate measure even for a chamber pot. Rav Pappa limits this to places without seals or where measures are not standardized. The Gemara adds a concern about twilight confusion, and a supporting baraita is cited, which also lists permitted measures (se'ah, tarkav, etc.).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that it is forbidden for a person to keep an inaccurate measure in his house, even for use as a chamber pot.
Rav Pappa limits the prohibition: it applies only where measures are not sealed or where they are not standardized by surveyors.
The Gemara objects that even with seals, one might mistakenly take the measure at twilight when the seal is not visible.
A baraita is cited that supports the prohibition, but lists permitted standard measures such as a se'ah, tarkav, and half-tomen.

items.text: Definition of an ukhla
items.text_en: Definition of an ukhla
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines an ukhla as one-fifth of a revi'it, and lists the measures for liquids: hin, half-hin, third-hin, quarter-hin, log, half-log, quarter-log, eighth-log, and one-eighth of an eighth, which is a kortov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines an ukhla as one-fifth of a revi'it and lists the liquid measures from hin down to a kortov.

items.text: Gemara's question about making kav measures
items.text_en: Gemara's question about making kav measures
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not make kav measures, and answers that it would be confused with a tarkav. It then questions why not make a half-tarkav, and explains that a kav would be confused with a half-tarkav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not include a kav measure (two kavim) among the dry measures.
The Gemara answers that a kav measure would be confused with a tarkav (three-kav measure).
The Gemara objects that if people err by a third, then even a single kav should not be made, as it would be confused with a half-tarkav.
The Gemara resolves that the reason for not making a kav measure is specifically that it would be confused with a half-tarkav.

items.text: Objection about half-tomen and ukhla
items.text_en: Objection about half-tomen and ukhla
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if people err by a quarter, then half-tomen and ukhla should also not be made. Rav Papa answers that people are familiar with small measures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if people err by a quarter, then half-tomen and ukhla should also not be made.
Rav Papa answers that people are familiar with small measures, so no confusion arises.

items.text: Question about third-hin and quarter-hin
items.text_en: Question about third-hin and quarter-hin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not make third-hin and quarter-hin measures, and answers that since they were used in the Temple, the Sages did not decree against them. It then questions why not decree in the Temple, and answers that priests are vigilant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages did not prohibit making measures of שלישית ההין (third-hin) and רביעית ההין (quarter-hin) to prevent confusion.
The Gemara answers that since these measures were used in the Temple (מקדש), the Sages did not decree against them outside.
The Gemara objects that even in the Temple, the Sages should have decreed against these measures to prevent error.
The Gemara answers that priests are vigilant (זריזין) and will not err, so no decree is needed in the Temple.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on adding a sixth
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on adding a sixth
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that one may not add more than a sixth to measures, coins, or profit. The Gemara questions the reason for not adding more than a sixth to measures, suggesting it might be to prevent breaking the door, but then objects that even a sixth would be problematic.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that one may not add more than a sixth to measures, coins, or profit.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Shmuel's ruling.
The Gemara suggests the reason might be to prevent breaking the door, but objects that even a sixth would be problematic.

items.text: Alternative reason: ona'ah
items.text_en: Alternative reason: ona'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the reason is to prevent ona'ah (overcharging) that would void the sale, but objects that Rava said for anything measured, weighed, or counted, even less than the amount of ona'ah, the sale is void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the reason for the limit is to prevent אונאה (overcharging) that would void the sale, but objects by citing Rava's rule that for anything measured, weighed, or counted, even less than the amount of אונאה, the sale is void.

items.text: Reason: preventing loss to the merchant
items.text_en: Reason: preventing loss to the merchant
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the reason is to prevent loss to the merchant. It then objects that if only loss is prevented, what about profit? The Gemara answers that one who buys and sells is called a merchant, implying profit is expected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the reason for the limit on adding to measures is to prevent loss to the merchant.
The Gemara objects that if the concern is only preventing loss, why not also allow profit?
The Gemara answers that one who buys and sells is called a merchant, implying profit is expected and thus not a separate concern.

items.text: Rav Chisda's scriptural source for Shmuel
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's scriptural source for Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says Shmuel found a verse and expounded it: 'And the shekel shall be twenty gerahs; twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, fifteen shekels shall be your maneh.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that Shmuel's ruling is derived from a scriptural verse about the maneh.

items.text: Conclusion from the previous sugya: three inferences from the maneh of the sanctuary
items.text_en: Conclusion from the previous sugya: three inferences from the maneh of the sanctuary
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers three halakhot from the fact that a maneh of the sanctuary was doubled: that one may add up to a sixth to measures, and that the sixth is added externally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by inferring three halakhot from the doubled maneh of the sanctuary: that measures may be increased, only up to a sixth, and the sixth is added externally.

items.text: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel's measure and its acceptance
items.text_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel's measure and its acceptance
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel instituted a measure of three kav, but was challenged because Shmuel said one may not add more than a sixth. He responded that it was a new measure. It was sent to Pumbedita and rejected, but accepted in Papunya, where it was called 'Ruz Pappa'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel instituted a measure of three kav.
The sages objected that Shmuel ruled one may not add more than a sixth to a measure.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel responded that he instituted a new measure, not an addition to an existing one.
The measure was sent to Pumbedita and rejected, but accepted in Papunya, where it was called 'Ruz Pappa'.

items.text: Siman for the following baraitot
items.text_en: Siman for the following baraitot
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided for the topics that follow: hoarders of produce, lenders with interest, etc.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided listing the topics: hoarders of produce, lenders with interest, etc.

items.text: Baraita on hoarders and the verse of Amos
items.text_en: Baraita on hoarders and the verse of Amos
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: hoarders of produce, lenders with interest, those who reduce the ephah, and those who raise prices – about them the verse says 'When will the new moon pass...' and God swears not to forget their deeds. Rabbi Yochanan identifies an example of a hoarder: Shabtai the produce hoarder.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists four categories of sinners (hoarders, lenders with interest, those who reduce the ephah, and those who raise prices) and cites the verse from Amos where God swears not to forget their deeds.
The gemara asks for a concrete example of a produce hoarder.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies Shabtai the produce hoarder as an example of a hoarder.

items.text: The practice of Shmuel's father and Shmuel regarding produce
items.text_en: The practice of Shmuel's father and Shmuel regarding produce
items.desc_en: Shmuel's father sold produce at the cheap price, while Shmuel waited and sold at the expensive price. They sent from there: 'The good of Abba is better than that of the son' because a cheap market is beneficial.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Shmuel's father sold produce at the cheap market price.
The Gemara contrasts that Shmuel, his son, waited and sold at the expensive price.
The academy sent a message that the good of Abba (Shmuel's father) is better than that of the son, because a cheap market benefits the public.

items.text: Laws of hoarding produce: exceptions and time limits
items.text_en: Laws of hoarding produce: exceptions and time limits
items.desc_en: Rav says one may make his storehouse a storage for produce. A baraita states: one may not hoard essential goods like wines, oils, and flours, but spices are permitted. This applies when buying from the market, but if bringing from one's own field it is permitted. One may hoard in Eretz Yisrael for three years: before the Sabbatical year, during, and after. In a famine year, even a kav of carobs may not be hoarded. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina instructed his attendant to hoard for him for three years.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that a person may turn his storehouse into a storage facility for produce.

A baraita supports Rav: one may not hoard essential goods like wines, oils, and flours, but spices are permitted; this applies when buying from the market, but if bringing from one's own field it is permitted.
The baraita specifies that one may hoard produce in Eretz Yisrael for three years: before the Sabbatical year, during, and after.

sub.text: Famine exception and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's instruction
sub.text_en: Famine exception and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's instruction
sub.desc_en: In a famine year, even a kav of carobs may not be hoarded; Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina instructed his attendant to hoard for him for three years.

items.text: Baraita on exporting produce from Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Baraita on exporting produce from Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: one may not export essential goods from Eretz Yisrael. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira permits wine because it reduces idolatry. Just as one may not export to outside the land, so too one may not export to Syria. Rabbi permits... (the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the general prohibition against exporting essential goods (wine, oil, flour) from Eretz Yisrael.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira permits exporting wine specifically, because it reduces idolatry (תיפלה).
The baraita extends the prohibition: just as one may not export from Eretz Yisrael to outside the land, so too one may not export from Eretz Yisrael to Syria.
Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) permits something (the text cuts off, likely permitting export of certain items).

items.text: Restriction on profiteering from essential goods and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's practice
items.text_en: Restriction on profiteering from essential goods and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's practice
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one may not profiteer from essential goods like wine, oil, and flour in Eretz Yisrael. It then notes that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya did profiteer from wine and oil, explaining that he followed Rabbi Yehuda's lenient view on wine, and in his region oil was abundant.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one may not profiteer from essential goods like wine, oil, and flour in Eretz Yisrael.

sub.text: Baraita's report about Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.text_en: Baraita's report about Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.desc_en: The baraita reports that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya profiteered from wine and oil, explaining that he followed Rabbi Yehuda's lenient view on wine and that oil was abundant in his region.

items.text: Dispute about profiteering from eggs
items.text_en: Dispute about profiteering from eggs
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may not profiteer twice from eggs. Mari bar Mari reports a dispute between Rav and Shmuel: one says the profit margin is limited to 100%, the other says it applies only to a wholesaler selling to another wholesaler.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that one may not profiteer twice from eggs.

sub.text: Mari bar Mari reporting a dispute
sub.text_en: Mari bar Mari reporting a dispute
sub.desc_en: Mari bar Mari reports that Rav and Shmuel dispute the baraita's meaning: one says the profit margin is limited to 100%, the other says it applies only to a wholesaler selling to another wholesaler.

items.text: Public prayer for price drops and Rabbi Yochanan's examples
items.text_en: Public prayer for price drops and Rabbi Yochanan's examples
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may sound trumpets for public prayer over commodity prices, even on Shabbat. Rabbi Yochanan specifies this applies to linen garments in Babylonia and wine and oil in Eretz Yisrael. Rav Yosef adds that this is only when the price drops from ten to six units.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one may sound trumpets for public prayer over commodity prices, even on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yochanan specifies that this applies to linen garments in Babylonia and wine and oil in Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Yosef adds that this is only when the price drops from ten to six units.

items.text: Leaving Eretz Yisrael due to famine and the lesson from Elimelech
items.text_en: Leaving Eretz Yisrael due to famine and the lesson from Elimelech
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may leave Eretz Yisrael only when two se'ah of grain cost a sela. Rabbi Shimon qualifies this: if one cannot find grain to buy, even at a higher price one may leave; but if one can find grain, one should not leave even at a lower price. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai then teaches that Elimelech, Machlon, and Chilyon were great leaders who were punished for leaving the land, as the townspeople remarked about Naomi's fate.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: one may not leave Eretz Yisrael unless two se'ah of grain cost a sela.
Rabbi Shimon qualifies the baraita: one may leave only when one cannot find grain to buy, but if grain is available, one should not leave even at a lower price.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches that Elimelech, Machlon, and Chilyon were great leaders who were punished specifically for leaving Eretz Yisrael.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains the townspeople's rhetorical question about Naomi: they pointed out that leaving Eretz Yisrael brought her misfortune.

items.text: Boaz's family and his sons' deaths
items.text_en: Boaz's family and his sons' deaths
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak relates that on the day Ruth arrived in Eretz Yisrael, Boaz's wife died, illustrating the proverb that a man's wife dies when he is about to marry another. Rabbah bar Rav Huna identifies Ibtzan as Boaz, who made 120 wedding feasts for his children, but all died in his lifetime because he did not invite Manoach, thinking him childless. A baraita confirms all his children died in his lifetime.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that on the day Ruth arrived in Eretz Yisrael, Boaz's wife died, illustrating the folk saying that a man's wife dies when he is about to marry another.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav identifies Ibtzan (from the book of Judges) as Boaz, and explains that Boaz made 120 wedding feasts for his children, as derived from the verse about Ibtzan's thirty sons and thirty daughters.

The gemara elaborates that Boaz made two feasts for each child, one at his own house and one at the in-laws', but he did not invite Manoach (Samson's father) because Manoach was childless at the time, and Boaz thought he could not repay the favor.

A baraita confirms that all of Boaz's children died during his lifetime, and the gemara cites a folk saying that one should focus on raising a single capable child rather than many who will not survive.

items.text: The lineage of Elimelech and the lesson of ancestral merit
items.text_en: The lineage of Elimelech and the lesson of ancestral merit
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava reports that Elimelech, Salmon, Ploni Almoni, and Naomi's father were all descendants of Nachshon ben Aminadav. This teaches that even one with ancestral merit cannot rely on it when leaving Eretz Yisrael.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava reports in Rav's name that Elimelech, Salmon, Ploni Almoni, and Naomi's father were all descendants of Nachshon ben Aminadav.
The gemara infers the lesson: even one with ancestral merit (זְכוּת אָבוֹת) cannot rely on it when leaving Eretz Yisrael.

items.text: Mothers of biblical figures and Abraham's imprisonment
items.text_en: Mothers of biblical figures and Abraham's imprisonment
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava reports the names of the mothers of Abraham, Haman, David, and Samson, noting the mnemonic that the impure are paired with the impure and the pure with the pure. He also reports that Abraham was imprisoned for ten years, three in Kuta and seven in Kardu, with a dispute about the order. Rav Chisda identifies the small district of Kuta as Ur Kasdim. Finally, he describes the mourning of the nations at Abraham's death.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava reports the names of the mothers of Abraham and Haman, with a mnemonic that the impure are paired with the impure and the pure with the pure.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava continues, naming the mothers of David and Samson, and notes that this information is useful for responding to heretics.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava reports that Abraham was imprisoned for ten years, three in Kuta and seven in Kardu.
Rav Dimi from Nehardea transmits the tradition in the opposite order, reversing the years in Kuta and Kardu.
Rav Chisda identifies the small district of Kuta as Ur Kasdim.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava describes how all the great nations of the world stood in a row and mourned at Abraham's death.

items.text: Opening aphorism on leadership
items.text_en: Opening aphorism on leadership
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a metaphor: a ship without a captain is doomed. Rav Chanan bar Rava quotes Rav that even a minor leader is appointed by heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a metaphor: a ship without a captain is doomed.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava quotes Rav that even a minor leader is appointed from heaven.

items.text: Why the generation of the flood was punished
items.text_en: Why the generation of the flood was punished
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: the generation of the flood was not punished for robbery of bran, but for failing to pray for their generation.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: the generation of the flood was not punished for robbery of bran, but for failing to pray for their generation, as per the verse 'בְּזַעֲקֵךְ יַצִּילֻךְ קִבּוּצַיִךְ' (in your cry, your gatherings will save you).

items.text: Conditions for leaving due to famine
items.text_en: Conditions for leaving due to famine
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan: the ruling that one may leave a famine-stricken city applies only when money is cheap and produce expensive; but if money is expensive, even if four se'ah cost a sela, they may leave.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah introduces Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the leniency to leave a famine-stricken city applies only when money is cheap and produce expensive.
Rabbi Yochanan states the exception: if money is expensive, even when four se'ah cost a sela, people may leave.

items.text: Memories of past famines and abundance
items.text_en: Memories of past famines and abundance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar recall times of severe famine and great abundance, including the sweetness of carob and the purity of youth. The Gemara notes that in those days, the study hall taught that one who admits to the Sages falls into their hands, and one who relies on them, his property becomes theirs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan recalls a time when four se'ah of grain cost a sela, yet there was severe famine in Tiberias due to lack of coinage.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls that laborers would not hire themselves out to the east of the city because they would die from the smell of bread.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls a time when a child would break a carob and honey would flow over both his arms.
Rabbi Elazar recalls a time when a raven would take meat and oil would drip from the top of the wall to the ground.
Rabbi Yochanan recalls a time when boys and girls of sixteen and seventeen would stroll in the market without sinning.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's fifth memory (study hall saying)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's fifth memory (study hall saying)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan recalls that in the study hall they used to say: one who admits to the Sages falls into their hands, and one who relies on them, his property becomes theirs.

items.text: Dispute over the names of Mahlon and Chilion
items.text_en: Dispute over the names of Mahlon and Chilion
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether Mahlon and Chilion were their real names or nicknames. One says their real names were Mahlon and Chilion, and they were called Yoash and Saraf because they despaired of redemption and were liable for burning. The other says their real names were Yoash and Saraf, and they were called Mahlon and Chilion because they made their bodies profane and were liable for destruction. A baraisa supports the first opinion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes a contradiction between two verses, one calling them Mahlon and Chilion and the other Yoash and Saraf, and introduces the dispute between Rav and Shmuel.
One opinion (Rav) says Mahlon and Chilion were their real names, and they were called Yoash and Saraf because they despaired of redemption and were liable for burning.
The other opinion (Shmuel) says Yoash and Saraf were their real names, and they were called Mahlon and Chilion because they made their bodies profane and were liable for destruction.
A baraita supports the first opinion (Rav) by citing a verse that identifies Yoash and Saraf as Mahlon and Chilion, explaining the nicknames similarly.

items.text: Exegesis of the verses about Mahlon, Chilion, and Ruth
items.text_en: Exegesis of the verses about Mahlon, Chilion, and Ruth
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verses in Chronicles: 'Yokim' refers to Joshua who established the oath to the Gibeonites; 'Men of Cozeba' are the Gibeonites who deceived Joshua; 'Yoash and Saraf' are Mahlon and Chilion. 'Yashuvi Lechem' is Ruth who returned to Bethlehem. 'These are ancient things' means the Ancient of Days said them. Further verses are expounded: 'The potters' are the sons of Jonadab; 'Dwellers of plantations' is Solomon; 'Fence' is the Sanhedrin; 'With the king in his work' is Ruth who saw the kingdom of Solomon her descendant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the discrepancy between the names Mahlon and Chilion in Ruth and Yoash and Saraf in Chronicles, and asks why they are called by two sets of names.

One of the two sages (Rav or Shmuel) explains that Mahlon and Chilion are their original names, while Yoash and Saraf are epithets: Yoash because they despaired of redemption, Saraf because they were liable for burning by Heaven.

The other of the two sages (Rav or Shmuel) argues that Yoash and Saraf are their original names, while Mahlon and Chilion are epithets: Mahlon because they made their bodies profane (חולין), Chilion because they were liable for destruction by Heaven.

A baraita is cited that supports the first opinion (Mahlon and Chilion are their original names), by expounding the verses in Chronicles: 'Yokim' is Joshua, 'Men of Cozeba' are the Gibeonites, 'Yoash and Saraf' are Mahlon and Chilion, with the same epithets.

The baraita continues: 'Who married Moabite women' refers to their marriage to Moabite women; 'Yashuvi Lechem' is Ruth who returned to Bethlehem; 'These are ancient things' means the Ancient of Days (God) said them, as proven by verses about David and his daughters.
The baraita expounds: 'The potters' are the sons of Jonadab ben Rechab, who preserved their father's oath.

The baraita concludes: 'Dwellers of plantations' is Solomon; 'Fence' is the Sanhedrin; 'With the king in his work' is Ruth, who saw the kingdom of Solomon her descendant, as Rabbi Elazar says: 'to the mother of the kingdom.'

items.text: The meaning of 'without salmantun' in the blessing of old produce
items.text_en: The meaning of 'without salmantun' in the blessing of old produce
items.desc_en: The Sages taught the verse 'You shall eat old produce' without salmantun. Rav Nachman explains it as without rot, Rav Sheshet as without mold. Two baraisos support each opinion: one says the old produce was so abundant that they did not need new until it came naturally; the other says the old produce was so good that they did not desire new until it came naturally.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught the verse 'You shall eat old produce' without salmantun, introducing the term to be explained.
The gemara asks what 'without salmantun' means.
Rav Nachman explains 'without salmantun' as without rot (בלא רצינתא).
Rav Sheshet explains 'without salmantun' as without mold (בלא שדיפא).
A baraita is cited in support of Rav Sheshet's interpretation.
A baraita is cited in support of Rav Nachman's interpretation.
The baraita supporting Rav Nachman teaches that the old produce was so abundant that they did not need new until it came naturally.
The baraita supporting Rav Sheshet teaches that the old produce was so good that they did not desire new until it came naturally.

items.text: The virtue of aged items and the exception
items.text_en: The virtue of aged items and the exception
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that 'old and aged' produce teaches that older items are better than newer ones, and this applies even to items not typically aged. The verse 'You shall bring out old from before new' describes a time when granaries were full of old and new, and Israel wondered how to remove one for the other. Rav Pappa concludes: all aged items are good except for dates, beer, and a certain vegetable.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the verse 'וַאֲכַלְתֶּם יָשָׁן נוֹשָׁן' implies that anything aged is better than its counterpart.
The baraita extends the principle to items not typically aged, using the double expression 'יָשָׁן נוֹשָׁן' to include all cases.
The baraita describes a scenario where granaries were full of old and new, and Israel wondered how to remove one for the other.
Rav Pappa concludes that all aged items are good except for dates, beer, and a certain vegetable (הרסנא).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sells produce to another, and the buyer plants it but it does not sprout, is not liable for the failure, even for flax seed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that for garden seeds that are not eaten, the seller is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ruling that one who sells produce to another, and the buyer plants it but it does not sprout, is not liable for the failure, even for flax seed.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that for garden seeds that are not eaten, the seller is liable.

items.text: Gemara's dispute: Rav vs. Shmuel on a goring ox
items.text_en: Gemara's dispute: Rav vs. Shmuel on a goring ox
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: if one sells an ox to another and it is found to be a gorer, Rav says it is a mistaken transaction (the buyer can void it), while Shmuel says the seller can claim he sold it for slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: if one sells an ox to another and it is found to be a gorer, Rav says it is a mistaken transaction (the buyer can void it), while Shmuel says the seller can claim he sold it for slaughter.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why not infer from the buyer's usual practice?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why not infer from the buyer's usual practice?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not look at the buyer? If he usually buys for sacrifice, he buys for sacrifice; if for plowing, for plowing. The answer: the buyer purchases for both purposes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not look at the buyer's usual practice — if he usually buys for sacrifice, he buys for sacrifice; if for plowing, for plowing?
The Gemara answers: the case is where the buyer purchases for both purposes (sacrifice and plowing), so his usual practice does not resolve the doubt.

items.text: Gemara's further analysis: price and practical difference
items.text_en: Gemara's further analysis: price and practical difference
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not look at the price? It answers: the case is where meat became expensive and reached the price of a plowing ox. Then it asks: what is the practical difference? The answer: it matters for the trouble (of finding a buyer for slaughter).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not examine the price to determine the intended use?
The Gemara answers: the case is where meat became expensive and reached the price of a plowing ox, so price alone does not indicate intent.
The Gemara asks: if so, what practical difference does the dispute make?
The Gemara answers: the practical difference is the trouble (of finding a buyer for slaughter).

items.text: Gemara's clarifying question
items.text_en: Gemara's clarifying question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? (to further clarify the dispute).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the circumstances of the dispute to clarify its application.

items.text: Clarification of the previous objection
items.text_en: Clarification of the previous objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the previous objection assumed there was no way for the buyer to recoup his loss from the seller, but if there is such a way, the sale is not void. This sets up the distinction between cases where the buyer can seek compensation and where he cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if there is no way for the buyer to recoup his loss from the seller, why should the sale not be void? The buyer should simply keep the ox and his money, as people say: from your creditor, collect your debt.
The Gemara answers: the objection is unnecessary, because the case is one where the buyer can recoup his loss from the seller.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's positions on following the majority in monetary matters
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's positions on following the majority in monetary matters
items.desc_en: Rav holds that this is a mistaken transaction because we follow the majority, and most people buy oxen for plowing. Shmuel counters that we follow the majority only in matters of prohibition, not in monetary matters.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that this is a mistaken transaction because we follow the majority, and most people buy oxen for plowing.
Shmuel counters that we follow the majority only in matters of איסורא (prohibition), not in monetary matters.

items.text: Siman for the following baraitot
items.text_en: Siman for the following baraitot
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign is given for the upcoming baraitot: woman, slave, ox, oxen, and produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic sign (סִימָן) listing the topics of the upcoming baraitot: woman, slave, ox, oxen, and produce.

items.text: First challenge: the case of the woman claiming to be a virgin
items.text_en: First challenge: the case of the woman claiming to be a virgin
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a woman who claims she was married as a virgin, and the husband disputes it. The baraita says that only if there are witnesses that she went out with her head uncovered does she get 200 zuz. The Gemara challenges Shmuel: why not follow the majority of women who marry as virgins? Ravina answers that although most women marry as virgins, most virgins have a public reputation (kol), and since this woman lacks that reputation, the majority is weakened. The Gemara then refines the explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a woman claiming virginity whose ketubah is 200 zuz only if there are witnesses that she went out with her head uncovered.
The Gemara challenges Shmuel: why not follow the majority of women who marry as virgins, so that even without witnesses she should get 200 zuz?
Ravina answers that although most women marry as virgins, most virgins have a public reputation (קול), and since this woman lacks that reputation, the majority is weakened.
The Gemara objects: if all virgins have a public reputation, then even when there are witnesses, they would be false witnesses, undermining the baraita's logic.
The Gemara refines: most virgins have a public reputation, not all, so the lack of reputation weakens the majority without invalidating the witnesses.

items.text: Second challenge: the case of the slave found to be a thief
items.text_en: Second challenge: the case of the slave found to be a thief
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite another baraita about a slave sold who turns out to be a thief or gambler, where the sale stands, but if he is a highwayman or liable to royal punishment, the buyer can return him. The Gemara starts analyzing the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a slave sold who turns out to be a thief or gambler, where the sale stands, but if he is a highwayman or liable to royal punishment, the buyer can return him.
The Gemara begins to analyze the first clause of the baraita, indicating a question or objection is forthcoming.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and answer about the majority
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and answer about the majority
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the reason for the earlier ruling is because we follow the majority (רוב), and answers that it is because all such cases are that way, not specifically due to majority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the reason for the earlier ruling is because we follow the majority (רוב).
The Gemara answers that it is because all such cases are that way, not specifically due to majority.

items.text: Challenge from the case of a goring ox and a pregnant cow
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of a goring ox and a pregnant cow
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where an ox gored a cow and the calf was found dead; the owner pays half damages for the cow and quarter for the calf, even though most cows give birth after being impregnated. The Gemara explains that this is because there is a doubt whether the calf was born before the goring or miscarried due to it, making it money in doubt, which is divided.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about an ox that gored a cow and the calf was found dead; the owner pays half damages for the cow and quarter for the calf, presenting a case where doubt about the cause of death leads to divided payment.

The Gemara asks why we do not follow the רוב (majority) of cows that become pregnant and give birth, which would indicate the calf was born before the goring, and instead assume the cow miscarried due to the goring.

The Gemara answers that there is a doubt whether the ox came from the front and the cow miscarried from fright, or from behind and gored her causing miscarriage, so it is money in doubt (ממון המוטל בספק) which is divided.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about presumption and majority
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about presumption and majority
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: the first Tanna says that if a goring ox is found near a dead ox, we do not assume it was the one that gored it, while Rabbi Acha says that if a camel is found among other camels, we assume it killed the dead camel. This sets up the debate between following a presumption (חזקה) versus a majority (רוב).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel about following a majority (רוב) versus a presumption (חזקה) corresponds to a Tannaitic dispute in a baraita about a goring ox and a camel found among camels.

items.text: Attributing Rav and Shmuel's positions to the Tannaim
items.text_en: Attributing Rav and Shmuel's positions to the Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav and Shmuel's dispute about whether to follow a majority aligns with the Tannaitic dispute: Rav follows Rabbi Acha (who follows a presumption), and Shmuel follows the first Tanna (who does not).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav and Shmuel's dispute about whether to follow a majority aligns with the Tannaitic dispute: Rav follows Rabbi Acha (who follows a presumption), and Shmuel follows the first Tanna (who does not).
Rav defends his position, arguing that even the first Tanna would agree to follow a majority, as his objection was only against following a presumption.
Shmuel defends his position, arguing that even Rabbi Acha would not follow a majority, as his ruling was based on a presumption of the ox's own status, not on a general majority.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel reject the attribution
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel reject the attribution
items.desc_en: Rav explains that he could even agree with the first Tanna, who only rejects a presumption but would follow a majority. Shmuel explains that he could even agree with Rabbi Acha, who only follows a presumption about the animal itself but would not follow a general majority.

sub.desc_en: Rav explains that he could agree even with the first Tanna, who only rejects a presumption (חזקה) but would follow a majority (רוב).
Shmuel explains that he could agree even with Rabbi Acha, who only follows a presumption (חזקה) about the animal itself but would not follow a general majority (רוב).

items.text: Challenge from the case of selling seeds
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of selling seeds
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where a seller of seeds is not liable if they do not sprout, even for flax seeds, which are usually bought for planting. The Gemara asks: does this show we do not follow the majority?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita (תָּא שְׁמַע) about a seller of seeds who is not liable if they do not sprout, even for flax seeds, which are typically bought for planting.
The Gemara asks: does the word 'אפילו' (even) imply that even for flax seeds, which most people buy for planting, we do not follow the majority (רוב)?

items.text: Resolution: the case is a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Resolution: the case is a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is a Tannaitic dispute: one Tanna holds the seller liable for garden seeds that are not eaten, while another holds that flax seeds are not liable. Rabbi Yosei offers a different view, indicating that the ruling depends on the specific Tanna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is a Tannaitic dispute, citing a baraita where the first Tanna distinguishes between garden seeds (liable) and flax seeds (exempt), and Rabbi Yosei offers a different view.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt and initial dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt and initial dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the seller gives only the value of the seed. The Sages object that many buyers purchase seeds for other purposes, implying a different measure of liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the seller gives only the value of the seed (דְּמֵי זֶרַע).
The Sages object that many buyers purchase seeds for other purposes, implying a different measure of liability.

items.text: Identifying the tannaitic disputants
items.text_en: Identifying the tannaitic disputants
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tannaim are behind the Mishnah's statement and the Sages' objection. It first suggests Rabbi Yossi and the Sages, but notes both follow the majority—one follows the majority of people, the other the majority of planting. It then reconsiders, proposing the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yossi, or the Tanna Kamma and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tannaim are the disputants behind the Mishnah's statement and the Sages' objection.
The Gemara suggests Rabbi Yossi and the Sages, but notes both follow the majority—one follows the majority of people, the other the majority of planting.
The Gemara reconsiders, proposing the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yossi, or the Tanna Kamma and the Sages.

items.text: Baraita on compensation and identification of 'Yesh Omrim'
items.text_en: Baraita on compensation and identification of 'Yesh Omrim'
items.desc_en: A Baraita clarifies that 'he gives him' means the value of the seed, not expenses; but some say even expenses. Rav Chisda identifies this 'Yesh Omrim' as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: A Baraita is cited: 'What does he give him? The value of the seed, but not expenses; and some say: even expenses.'
Rav Chisda identifies the anonymous 'Yesh Omrim' as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Attempt to identify Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
items.text_en: Attempt to identify Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to match Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel from the Mishnah in Bava Batra, but finds the Tanna Kamma there agrees with him. It then suggests the dispute is about expenses: one holds seed value only, the other includes expenses. The Gemara supports this by noting that the later Tanna always adds something.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is meant, citing the Mishnah in Bava Batra where he holds a seller liable for non-edible garden seeds.
The Gemara objects that the Tanna Kamma in that Mishnah already says the same thing as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, so the identification fails.
The Gemara answers that the dispute is about expenses: one holds only seed value, the other includes expenses.
The Gemara supports this by noting that the later Tanna always adds something, so the identification is consistent.

items.text: Alternative: entire Baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Alternative: entire Baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers that the entire Baraita might be Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, with a missing clause, but this is rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the entire Baraita might be attributed to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, with a missing clause, but this is rejected.

items.text: Another Baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on liability
items.text_en: Another Baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on liability
items.desc_en: A different Baraita presents Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that one who damages another's property pays for embarrassment, and describes a custom in Jerusalem regarding hospitality.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a different Baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding liability for damage to entrusted goods.
The Baraita lists cases where a bailee is liable because he is considered a paid bailee (נושא שכר).
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that one who damages another's property pays for the owner's embarrassment and the embarrassment of his guests.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel describes a custom in Jerusalem: one who spoils a meal for a friend pays for the embarrassment of the host and his guests.
The Baraita adds another Jerusalem custom: a cloth over the door signals that guests may enter; when removed, guests may not enter.

items.text: Mishnah on acceptable defects in produce
items.text_en: Mishnah on acceptable defects in produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the amount of spoilage a seller must accept for various products: a quarter of a kav of waste per se'ah for grain, ten wormy figs per hundred, ten sour barrels per hundred for wine, and ten defective jugs per hundred for jars from Sharon.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the acceptable spoilage rates a seller must tolerate for grain, figs, wine, and Sharon jars.

items.text: Gemara on the measure of waste
items.text_en: Gemara on the measure of waste
items.desc_en: Rav Katina teaches that the quarter refers to a quarter of legumes per se'ah. The Gemara questions whether dust is not included, citing Rabba bar Chiya Katosfa'ah in the name of Rabba about removing a pebble from a friend's granary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Katina teaches a baraita that the quarter-kav measure refers specifically to legume waste, not general dust.
The Gemara objects: does the seller not also accept dusty waste?

sub.text: Citation (Rabba bar Chiya Ktospa'a in the name of Rabba)
sub.text_en: Citation (Rabba bar Chiya Ktospa'a in the name of Rabba)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabba bar Chiya Ktospa'a in Rabba's name that one must pick out a pebble from a friend's granary, implying dust is also included.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a seller delivers wheat, he must accept a quarter-kav of admixture per se'ah; for lentils, a quarter-kav of dust; for inferior produce, less than a quarter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a seller of wheat must accept a quarter-kav of admixture per se'ah; for lentils, a quarter-kav of dust; for inferior produce, less than a quarter.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding lentils
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding lentils
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why lentils allow a quarter of dust, citing a baraita that permits a quarter of dust for lentils but not for wheat or barley. It resolves that lentils are uprooted entirely, so the allowance is specific; the baraita teaches that even for lentils, one does not accept more than a quarter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's allowance of a quarter of dust for lentils, citing a baraita that permits a quarter of dust for lentils but not for wheat or barley.
The Gemara initially suggests that the baraita applies equally to wheat and barley, but distinguishes lentils because they are uprooted entirely, so the allowance is specific.
The Gemara objects that if the allowance is only for lentils, then wheat and barley would not accept any dust, contradicting the Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that wheat and barley do accept dust, and the baraita specifically teaches that even for lentils, one does not accept more than a quarter.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on sifting
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on sifting
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if a buyer demands sifting, the seller must sift the entire batch. Two explanations are given: one says it is a matter of law because the buyer pays for fine produce and once he bothers, he bothers for all; the other says it is a penalty because a quarter is common but more is rare, and since the seller mixed it, the Sages penalized him fully.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if a buyer demands sifting, the seller must sift the entire batch, with two explanations given for this ruling.
The first explanation holds that it is a matter of law (דינא): the buyer pays for fine produce, and once he bothers to sift out the excess, he bothers for the entire batch.
The second explanation holds that it is a penalty (קנסא): a quarter-kav of impurity is common but more is rare, and since the seller mixed it in, the Sages penalized him to sift the entire batch.

items.text: Objection from kilayim and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from kilayim and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about kilayim, which requires reducing a se'ah containing a quarter of another species. Initially thought to contradict Rav Huna, it is resolved that the quarter for kilayim is equivalent to the quarter here, but the reduction is due to the stringency of kilayim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about kilayim (mixed seeds), which requires reducing a se'ah containing a quarter of another species, initially thought to contradict Rav Huna's ruling.
The Gemara initially assumes the quarter for kilayim is like 'more than a quarter' here, but then rejects this and equates the quarter for kilayim to the quarter here.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the reduction is required due to the stringency of kilayim (חוּמְרָא דְכִלְאַיִם), not because the quarter is larger.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yosei's position on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yosei's position on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei is based on whether the excess is considered like more than a quarter of waste (and thus penalized) or like exactly a quarter (and thus not penalized). It concludes that Rabbi Yosei's reasoning is that the mixture appears as if one is intentionally maintaining kilayim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's continuation where Rabbi Yosei says 'he should select out' (יָבוֹר), and then poses a dilemma: if the excess is considered like more than a quarter waste, the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei makes sense (Tanna Kamma does not penalize, Rabbi Yosei does); but if it is considered like exactly a quarter, why would Rabbi Yosei require selection?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei's reasoning is not about penalizing excess but because the mixture appears as if one is intentionally maintaining kilayim (forbidden mixed seeds).

items.text: First attempted proof from a deposit case
items.text_en: First attempted proof from a deposit case
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a case where two people deposited money with a third, each claiming the larger amount. The ruling is that each receives a smaller amount and the remainder is left until Elijah. The Gemara rejects this proof because in that case each claimant definitely has a right to the smaller amount, whereas here it is uncertain whether the mixture is entirely mixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about two depositors, one with 100 and one with 200, where each claims 200; the ruling is to give each 100 and leave the remainder until Elijah comes.
The Gemara rejects the comparison: there, each definitely has 100, but here, who says the entire mixture is not fully intermingled?

items.text: Second attempted proof from the deposit case's continuation
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from the deposit case's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei's statement in the same case that all the money should be left until Elijah, to penalize the liar. The Gemara rejects this because there is definitely a liar, whereas here it is uncertain whether the mixture is entirely mixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the continuation of the baraita where Rabbi Yosei argues that if the deceiver loses nothing, all should be left until Elijah comes.
The Gemara rejects: there, there is definitely a deceiver, but here, who says the mixture is intermingled?

items.text: Third attempted proof from a usurious document
items.text_en: Third attempted proof from a usurious document
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a case where a document contains interest, and Rabbi Meir penalizes by not collecting even the principal. The Gemara rejects this because there the document was written with a fixed sum, whereas here it is uncertain whether the mixture is entirely mixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a promissory note containing usury: Rabbi Meir says it is penalized and one cannot collect either principal or interest.
The Gemara rejects: there, the penalty applies from the time of writing, but here, who says the mixture is intermingled?

items.text: Fourth attempted proof from the usurious document's continuation
items.text_en: Fourth attempted proof from the usurious document's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Sages' opinion that the principal is collected but not the interest. The Gemara rejects this because there the principal is definitely permitted, whereas here it is uncertain whether the entire mixture is mixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the continuation of the baraita where the Sages say one collects the principal but not the interest.
The Gemara rejects: there, the principal is definitely permitted, but here, who says the entire mixture is not intermingled?

items.text: Fifth attempted proof from Ravin bar Rav Nachman's teaching
items.text_en: Fifth attempted proof from Ravin bar Rav Nachman's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching that one must return all the quarters, not just the excess, implying that when one must return, he returns everything. The Gemara rejects this proof as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita taught by Ravin bar Rav Nachman: one returns not only the excess but all the quarters, indicating that where return is required, one returns everything.
The Gemara rejects this as well with the standard dismissal 'Is that so?!'

items.text: Analogy from land sale: a quarter-kav is insignificant
items.text_en: Analogy from land sale: a quarter-kav is insignificant
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the case of land, a deficiency of a quarter-kav is not considered significant, but more than a quarter-kav is, because it can combine with other land to form a significant area. Therefore, the entire sale is void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that in the land sale case, a deficiency of a quarter-kav is insignificant, but more than that is significant because it can combine with other land to form a significant area, voiding the sale.

items.text: Challenge from the law of ona'ah (overcharge)
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of ona'ah (overcharge)
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about ona'ah: less than a sixth is a valid sale, more than a sixth voids it, exactly a sixth requires returning the overcharge. The Gemara questions why the entire sale is not void for less than a sixth, concluding that one can return the entire item if desired.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about the law of ona'ah (overcharge): less than a sixth is a valid sale, more than a sixth voids it, exactly a sixth requires returning the overcharge.
The Gemara questions why the entire sale is not void for less than a sixth, since the buyer could return the item.
The Gemara concludes that one can return the entire item if desired, explaining the baraita's ruling.

items.text: Rejection of the analogy: ona'ah is different
items.text_en: Rejection of the analogy: ona'ah is different
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy, explaining that in ona'ah, the initial transaction was for equal value, and less than a sixth is not noticeable in a large sum, so people forgive it; a sixth is noticeable and not forgiven; more than a sixth is a mistaken transaction and void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy from ona'ah, explaining that in ona'ah the initial transaction was for equal value, so less than a sixth is forgiven, a sixth is noticeable and not forgiven, and more than a sixth renders the transaction void.

items.text: Challenge from the law of a field for planting
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of a field for planting
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: one who accepts a field to plant must accept ten defective vines per hundred; more than that, the entire burden is shifted to the planter. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that any excess is treated as if he started planting anew.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about one who accepts a field for planting, which sets a threshold of ten defective vines per hundred, beyond which the planter bears full responsibility.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that any excess beyond the threshold is treated as if the planter started planting anew, shifting the entire burden.

items.text: Analysis of the wine cellar case
items.text_en: Analysis of the wine cellar case
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's case of a wine cellar, distinguishing between selling a 'wine cellar' unspecified, 'this wine cellar', and 'this cellar'. A baraita clarifies the different obligations for each type of sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to understand the Mishnah's case of a wine cellar, noting that whether the seller said 'wine cellar' unspecified, 'this wine cellar', or 'this cellar', each formulation presents a difficulty.

A baraita is cited clarifying the three formulations: 'wine cellar' unspecified obligates the seller to provide all good wine; 'this wine cellar' obligates wine sold in a shop; 'this cellar' obligates even if it is all vinegar.

items.text: Resolution: the baraita refers to a specific case
items.text_en: Resolution: the baraita refers to a specific case
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a case where the seller said 'wine cellar' unspecified, and the buyer accepts ten defective barrels per hundred. It then addresses an objection from Rabbi Chiya's baraita about a barrel of wine, distinguishing between a barrel (all the same wine) and a cellar (mixed wines). Finally, it cites Rav Zevid's baraita that even for a 'wine cellar' unspecified, the seller gives good wine but the buyer accepts ten defective barrels.
