sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a case where the seller said 'wine cellar' unspecified, and the buyer accepts ten defective barrels per hundred.
The Gemara objects that in an unspecified case, the buyer should not accept defective barrels, citing Rabbi Chiya's baraita that a seller of a barrel of wine gives all good wine.
The Gemara distinguishes between a barrel (all the same wine) and a cellar (mixed wines), explaining why the baraita about a barrel does not apply.
The Gemara cites Rav Zevid's baraita that even for a 'wine cellar' unspecified, the seller gives good wine but the buyer accepts ten defective barrels.

items.text: Introduction of the contradiction
items.text_en: Introduction of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah's 'treasury' (אוצר) is the same as the one taught in the baraita, but then points out a contradiction between the mishnah and the baraita regarding the term 'this' (זה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the 'treasury' (אוצר) in the mishnah as the same one taught in the baraita.
The Gemara notes that the mishnah also uses the term 'this' (זה), raising a contradiction.
The Gemara explicitly states the contradiction between the 'this' (זה) in the mishnah and the 'this' (זה) in the baraita.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases where the seller said 'for casking' (למיקפה) and where he did not, attributing the mishnah to Rav Zevid's case and the baraita to the other.

The Gemara summarizes the halachic conclusions: for 'a cellar of wine' with 'for casking' (למיקפה) gives good wine; 'this cellar of wine' with 'for casking' gives good wine but accepts ten barrels per hundred; 'this cellar of wine' without 'for casking' gives wine sold in a shop.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the seller said 'for fermentation' (למיקפה). Rav Zevid's statement applies when he said 'for fermentation', while the baraita applies when he did not say 'for fermentation'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially states that the Mishnah also deals with a case where the seller said 'this' (זה), but then notes a contradiction between two uses of 'this'.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the seller said 'for fermentation' (למיקפה): Rav Zevid's statement applies when he said 'for fermentation', while the baraita applies when he did not say 'for fermentation'.

items.text: Halachic conclusions based on the distinction
items.text_en: Halachic conclusions based on the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara summarizes the halakhah: for a 'wine cellar' without 'this', if he said 'for fermentation', he gives all good wine; for 'this wine cellar' with 'for fermentation', he accepts ten bad barrels per hundred; for 'this wine cellar' without 'for fermentation', he gives wine sold in a shop.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara summarizes the halachic conclusions for three cases of selling a wine cellar, distinguishing between the presence or absence of 'this' and the phrase 'for fermentation'.

items.text: Debate about 'wine cellar' without 'for fermentation'
items.text_en: Debate about 'wine cellar' without 'for fermentation'
items.desc_en: A question is raised about a 'wine cellar' without 'this' and without 'for fermentation'. Rav Acha and Ravina disagree: one says he accepts ten bad barrels, the other says he does not. Each deduces his position from Rav Zevid or the baraita, and the Gemara resolves the apparent contradictions by emending the sources.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the case of 'a wine cellar' without specifying 'this' and without saying 'for fermentation'.
Rav Acha and Ravina disagree: one says the buyer accepts ten bad barrels, the other says he does not.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the first position
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the first position
sub.desc_en: The one who says he accepts deduces this from Rav Zevid's ruling, implying that without 'for fermentation' the buyer accepts bad barrels.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the second position
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the second position
sub.desc_en: The one who says he does not accept deduces this from the baraita, which implies that without 'for fermentation' the buyer does not accept bad barrels.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the first position
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the first position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita contradicts the first position, and resolves by emending the baraita to include the condition 'for fermentation'.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the second position
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the second position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Zevid's ruling contradicts the second position, since it implies that without 'for fermentation' the buyer accepts bad barrels.
The Gemara resolves that even without 'for fermentation' the buyer does not accept bad barrels, and the earlier emendation was only to resolve the contradiction between the two uses of 'this'.

items.text: Blessing on wine sold in a shop
items.text_en: Blessing on wine sold in a shop
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says that wine sold in a shop requires the blessing 'Borei Pri HaGefen', while Rav Chisda questions this for wine that has turned sour. A baraita is brought that says one recites 'Shehakol' over wine that has turned sour. Rav Zevid clarifies that Rav Yehuda agrees regarding wine sold at the corners (פורצמא דמיזדבן אקרנתא).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that wine sold in a shop requires the blessing 'Borei Pri HaGefen'.
Rav Chisda questions Rav Yehuda's ruling regarding wine that has turned sour.
A baraita is cited that over wine that has turned sour one recites 'Shehakol', contradicting Rav Yehuda's ruling.
Rav Zevid resolves the contradiction by stating that Rav Yehuda concedes regarding wine sold at the corners (פורצמא דמיזדבן אקרנתא), which is of inferior quality.

items.text: Abaye's question to Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Abaye's question to Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef which opinion he follows, and Rav Yosef responds that he knows the mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef: which opinion does the master (מר) follow — Rav Yehudah's or Rav Chisda's?
Rav Yosef replies: I know a mishnah (מתניתא ידענא) — implying he relies on the mishnah's ruling.

items.text: Opening baraita
items.text_en: Opening baraita
items.desc_en: The baraita states that one who checks a barrel to separate terumah from it, and later it is found to be vinegar: within three days it is certain (wine), thereafter it is uncertain.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who checks a barrel to separate תרומה (priestly portion) from it, and later it is found to be vinegar: within three days it is certain (wine), thereafter it is uncertain.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the baraita means the first three days are certainly wine, thereafter uncertain. The reason is that wine begins to turn from the top, and if it has been tasted and not turned, it is still wine; even if after tasting it turns, the smell is vinegar but taste is wine, and such is wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the baraita means the first three days are certainly wine, thereafter uncertain.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the last three days are certainly vinegar, thereafter uncertain. The reason is that wine turns from the bottom, and perhaps it turned without one's knowledge; even if it turned from the top after tasting, the smell is vinegar and taste is wine, and such is vinegar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that the last three days are certainly vinegar, thereafter uncertain.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains his reasoning: wine turns from the bottom, so it may have turned without one's knowledge; even if it turned from the top after tasting, the smell is vinegar and taste is wine, and such is vinegar.

items.text: The Daroma'i tradition and resolution
items.text_en: The Daroma'i tradition and resolution
items.desc_en: The Daroma'i teach in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: first days certainly wine, last days certainly vinegar, middle days uncertain. The Gemara notes a contradiction: first days certain wine implies smell vinegar taste wine is wine, but last days certain vinegar implies the opposite. The resolution is when a vinegar flask is found, for if it had not turned for three days, a vinegar flask would not be found.

sub.desc_en: The Daroma'i teach in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the first days are certainly wine, the last days are certainly vinegar, and the middle days are uncertain.
The Gemara points out a contradiction: the first days being certainly wine implies that smell vinegar taste wine is wine, but the last days being certainly vinegar implies the opposite.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case is where a vinegar flask is found, for if the wine had not turned for three days, a vinegar flask would not be found.

items.text: Dispute over the resolution's authority
items.text_en: Dispute over the resolution's authority
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the resolution follows, and Rav Mari and Rav Zevid dispute: one says like Rabbi Yochanan, the other says like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks according to whose opinion the practical ruling is resolved.
Rav Mari and Rav Zevid disagree: one says the ruling follows Rabbi Yochanan, the other says it follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

items.text: Rav's ruling on seller liability
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on seller liability
items.desc_en: It was stated: One who sells a barrel of wine to another and it turns sour – Rav says: the first three days are in the seller's domain, thereafter in the buyer's domain.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that if one sells a barrel of wine to another and it turns to vinegar, the first three days are at the seller's risk, thereafter at the buyer's risk.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on beer and wine liability
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on beer and wine liability
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree on the liability for beer and wine; Rav holds the seller is liable for beer, Shmuel holds the buyer is liable for wine. Rav Yosef acts according to both, and the halacha follows Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that wine liability rests on the buyer (the wine is placed on the buyer's shoulder).
Rav Yosef acts according to Rav's view for beer and Shmuel's view for wine, and the halacha (הלכה) follows Shmuel.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on blessings for beer and wine sediment
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on blessings for beer and wine sediment
items.desc_en: The Tannaim debate the blessing for beer and wine sediment: the first Tanna says 'Shehakol', while Acheirim say if sediment has wine taste, one says 'Borei Pri HaGefen'. Rabba and Rav Yosef rule the halacha is not like Acheirim.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that for beer from dates, beer from barley, and wine sediment, the blessing is 'Shehakol'.
Acheirim (the other sages) state that if wine sediment retains the taste of wine, one recites 'Borei Pri HaGefen'.
Rabba and Rav Yosef both rule that the halacha does not follow Acheirim.

items.text: Rava's principle: three parts water to one part wine
items.text_en: Rava's principle: three parts water to one part wine
items.desc_en: Rava states that if one mixes three parts water and four parts wine, it is still wine. This aligns with his view that wine that cannot bear three parts water is not wine.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that if one mixes three parts water and four parts wine, the mixture is still considered wine.
The Gemara explains that Rava's statement follows his own consistent principle: any wine that cannot bear three parts water is not considered wine.

items.text: Dispute on diluted wine: three parts water and three and a half parts wine
items.text_en: Dispute on diluted wine: three parts water and three and a half parts wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one mixes three parts water and three and a half parts wine. The Rabbis hold that only half remains, which is negligible in six parts water, so it is not wine. Acheirim hold that two and a half parts emerge, leaving a jug of wine that is good.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one mixes three parts water and three parts wine, the result is negligible (not wine).
The Gemara clarifies that the dispute arises when one mixes three parts water and three and a half parts wine.
The Rabbis hold that three parts water enter and three parts wine emerge, leaving only half a part of wine, which is negligible in six parts water, so it is not wine.
Acheirim hold that three parts water enter and two and a half parts wine emerge, leaving a jug of wine that is good (מעליא).

items.text: Question on more than its measure
items.text_en: Question on more than its measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute applies to cases where the mixture exceeds the wine's measure, citing a Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute applies even when the mixture exceeds the wine's measure, and cites a Mishnah as evidence.

items.text: Dispute about measuring wine with added water
items.text_en: Dispute about measuring wine with added water
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a winepress worker added water and found the expected volume, he is exempt from liability, but Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable. The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is only about the exact measure, but for more than the measure they agree. Alternatively, the dispute extends even to more than the measure, and the Mishnah's phrasing highlights Rabbi Yehuda's stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a winepress worker added water and found the expected volume, he is exempt, but Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is only about the exact measure, but for more than the measure they agree.
Alternatively, the dispute extends even to more than the measure, and the Mishnah's phrasing highlights Rabbi Yehuda's stringency.

items.text: Inquiry about wine lees with wine taste
items.text_en: Inquiry about wine lees with wine taste
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rav Chiyya bar Avin about the status of wine lees that still have a wine taste. Rav Chiyya responds that it is not considered wine but merely a preservative (kiyuha).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rav Chiyya bar Avin about the status of wine lees that still have a wine taste.
Rav Chiyya bar Avin responds that the lees are not considered wine but merely a preservative (קיוהא).

items.text: Baraita on lees of terumah, maaser, and hekdesh
items.text_en: Baraita on lees of terumah, maaser, and hekdesh
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that lees of terumah are forbidden in the first and second pressings but permitted in the third; Rabbi Meir says the third is also forbidden based on taste. For maaser, the first pressing is forbidden, the second permitted; Rabbi Meir says the second is forbidden based on taste. For hekdesh, the third is forbidden, the fourth permitted; Rabbi Meir says the fourth is forbidden based on taste.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule for lees of תרומה (priestly portion): the first and second pressings are forbidden, the third is permitted.
Rabbi Meir adds that even the third pressing is forbidden if it imparts taste.
The baraita continues with lees of מעשר (tithe): the first pressing is forbidden, the second permitted.
Rabbi Meir adds that even the second pressing of מעשר is forbidden if it imparts taste.
The baraita concludes with lees of הקדש (sanctified property): the third pressing is forbidden, the fourth permitted.
Rabbi Meir adds that even the fourth pressing of הקדש is forbidden if it imparts taste.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution for hekdesh and maaser lees
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution for hekdesh and maaser lees
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: another source states that hekdesh lees are always forbidden and maaser lees always permitted. It resolves that for hekdesh, one case involves sanctity of the body (kedushat haguf) and the other sanctity of value (kedushat damim). For maaser, one case is definite maaser (vadai) and the other is doubtful maaser (demai).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: another source states that hekdesh lees are always forbidden and maaser lees always permitted, challenging the earlier baraita.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: for hekdesh, one case involves sanctity of the body (קדושת הגוף) and the other sanctity of value (קדושת דמים); for maaser, one case is definite maaser (ודאי) and the other is doubtful maaser (דמאי).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement on lees and susceptibility to impurity
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement on lees and susceptibility to impurity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak that the same rules apply for susceptibility to impurity (hechsher) as for prohibition. The Gemara questions what susceptibility applies to: if water, it already makes things susceptible; if wine, it also does. It explains that the case is when the lees were pressed with rainwater, but since the worker handles them, they become susceptible. The Gemara counters that the liquid flows out immediately, so it is already susceptible. Rav Papa resolves that it refers to a cow drinking the liquid drop by drop.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak that the same rules governing the prohibition of lees apply to their susceptibility to impurity (הכשר).
The Gemara asks what susceptibility to impurity (הכשר) applies to: if the liquid is water or wine, it already makes the lees susceptible.
The Gemara explains that the case is when the lees were pressed with rainwater, which does not inherently make them susceptible.
The Gemara objects that since the worker handles the lees, they become susceptible to impurity (הכשר) through his intentional handling.
The Gemara rejects the objection by saying the case is where the lees were pressed by themselves, without human handling.
The Gemara objects further that since the liquid flows out drop by drop, each drop becomes susceptible as it exits.
Rav Papa resolves that the case is where a cow drinks the liquid drop by drop, so the drops never accumulate to become susceptible.

items.text: Kiddush requires wine fit for the altar
items.text_en: Kiddush requires wine fit for the altar
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya says in the name of Rav that kiddush may only be recited over wine fit for libation on the altar. The Gemara asks what this excludes, suggesting wine from the press (yayin migito). But a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya states that such wine is valid if brought, so even initially it should be permitted. The Gemara implies that the exclusion is for wine that is unfit for the altar, such as wine that has become unfit.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya states in the name of Rav that kiddush may only be recited over wine fit for libation on the altar.
The Gemara asks what wine is excluded by this rule.

The Gemara suggests the exclusion is wine from the press (יין מגתו), but objects that since a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya rules such wine is valid if brought, it should be permitted even לכתחילה (a priori).

items.text: Rava's statement on squeezing grapes for Kiddush
items.text_en: Rava's statement on squeezing grapes for Kiddush
items.desc_en: Rava asserts that one may squeeze a cluster of grapes and recite Kiddush over the juice, implying that such wine is considered fit for sacred use.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that one may squeeze a cluster of grapes and recite Kiddush over the juice, implying such wine is fit for sacred use.

items.text: Refining the disqualifications: three categories
items.text_en: Refining the disqualifications: three categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines three possible exclusions from the Mishnah's rule: wine from the mouth and sediment (which is valid if brought), inferior wines like Kushite or raisin wine (valid if brought), and wine that is sour, diluted, uncovered, from lees, or foul-smelling (invalid even if brought).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's exclusion applies to wine from the mouth and sediment of the vat.
Rabbi Chiyya's baraita teaches that wine from the mouth and sediment is valid if brought, so the Mishnah cannot be excluding it.
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah excludes inferior wines like Kushite wine, sparkling wine, Heliston, cellar wine, or raisin wine.
A baraita states that all these wines are valid if brought, so the Mishnah cannot be excluding them either.
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah excludes sour wine, diluted wine, uncovered wine, wine from lees, or foul-smelling wine.
A baraita teaches that for these wines, if brought they are invalid, confirming the Mishnah's exclusion.

items.text: Analyzing each disqualification
items.text_en: Analyzing each disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara systematically analyzes each type of wine: sour wine is a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi; diluted wine is permitted for the cup of blessing per Rabbi Yosi; uncovered wine is a danger; wine from lees depends on the ratio; and foul-smelling wine is the intended exclusion, with an alternative answer that uncovered wine is invalid even if strained, citing Rabbi Nechemya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which disqualification the Mishnah intends to exclude, noting that sour wine (קוֹסֵס) is already disputed between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
The Gemara suggests diluted wine (מָזוּג) is excluded, citing Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer that the cup of blessing requires added water.
The Gemara rejects uncovered wine (מְגוּלֶּה) as the exclusion because it is a danger (סכנה), not a halachic disqualification.

The Gemara asks about wine from lees (שֶׁל שְׁמָרִים), analyzing the ratio: if three parts water yield four parts wine it is fine, but if three yield three and a half it is disputed between the Rabbis and Others.

The Gemara concludes that foul-smelling wine (שֶׁרֵיחוֹ רַע) is the intended exclusion, or alternatively, uncovered wine is excluded even if strained, following Rabbi Nechemya's view that it remains unfit for the altar.

items.text: Inquiry about white wine
items.text_en: Inquiry about white wine
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rava about white wine (chamar chivuryan) for libations, and Rava responds with a verse emphasizing the redness of wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rava whether white wine (חמר חוורין) is valid for libations.
Rava answers by citing the verse 'אל תרא יין כי יתאדם' (Do not look at wine when it is red), implying that wine must be red, disqualifying white wine.

items.text: Baraita on sealed jugs
items.text_en: Baraita on sealed jugs
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited regarding the Mishnah's mention of jugs in Sharon, describing them as beautiful and sealed with pitch.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited to explain the Mishnah's mention of jugs in Sharon, describing them as beautiful and sealed with pitch.

items.text: Mishnah: seller of wine that soured
items.text_en: Mishnah: seller of wine that soured
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one sells wine to another and it sours, the seller is not liable unless it was known that the wine tends to sour, in which case it is a mistaken transaction; if the seller explicitly guaranteed the wine, it is a sale that can be retracted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a seller of wine that soured is not liable for its quality.
The Mishnah adds that if the wine was known to sour, the sale is a mistaken transaction.
The Mishnah begins the third clause, stating that if the seller explicitly guaranteed the wine, the sale can be retracted.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a seller says 'I am selling you perfumed wine,' he must provide wine that stays fresh until Shavuot. 'Old' wine is from last year, and 'very old' is from three years ago.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the terms for selling perfumed wine, old wine, and very old wine.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina limits the Mishnah to cases where the buyer owns the jars, but Rava argues that the Mishnah itself implies the buyer told the seller to wait, based on the clause about known souring wine.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina limits the Mishnah to cases where the buyer owns the jars; if the seller owns them, the seller can say 'here is your wine and here are your jars'.
The Gemara objects: even if the seller owns the jars, the buyer could have taken the wine immediately, so why is the seller liable?
The Gemara answers that the case is where the buyer told the seller to wait (למיקפה), so the seller is responsible for storage.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina was forced to interpret the Mishnah as involving buyer-owned jars and a request to wait, rather than seller-owned jars without such a request.
Rava resolves that the Mishnah itself forced Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's interpretation, because the clause about known souring wine implies the buyer told the seller to wait (למיקפה).

items.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's alternative view and related aggadah
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's alternative view and related aggadah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef attributes wine souring to the owner's arrogance, citing a verse. Rabbi Mari and Rav Yehuda elaborate on the punishment for the arrogant, linking it to exclusion from God's presence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef disputes the previous ruling, attributing wine souring to the owner's arrogance, citing the verse 'גבר יהיר' (a haughty man).
Rabbi Mari adds that an arrogant person is not accepted even by his household, interpreting the verse 'ולא ינוה' as 'in his own dwelling.'

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that one who arrogantly wears a scholar's cloak without being a scholar is not admitted into God's presence, linking the verse 'ולא ינוה' to 'אל נוה קדשך' (the abode of Your holiness).

items.text: Rava's rulings on returning soured wine
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on returning soured wine
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if a buyer purchased a barrel of wine for retail and it soured partially, the seller must accept it back, with exceptions for when the buyer changed the seal or market day has passed. Similarly, if wine was accepted for transport to a port and soured en route, the seller must accept it.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a buyer purchased a barrel of wine for retail and it soured partially, the seller must accept it back.
Rava qualifies that the seller must accept the wine back only if the buyer did not change the seal (ברזא); if he changed it, the seller need not accept it.
Rava further qualifies that the seller must accept the wine back only if the market day has not yet passed; if it has passed, the seller need not accept it.
Rava rules that if wine was accepted for transport to the port of 'וול שפט' and it soured en route, the seller must accept it back.

items.text: Debate on vinegar as a separate case
items.text_en: Debate on vinegar as a separate case
items.desc_en: A question arises whether the same rule applies if the wine turned into vinegar. Rav Hillel reports that Rav Kahana said vinegar is not accepted, disagreeing with Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina. An alternative version says even vinegar is accepted, aligning with Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the wine turned into vinegar (חלא), what is the ruling — does the buyer have recourse?
Rav Hillel reports to Rav Ashi that Rav Kahana taught: vinegar (חלא) is not accepted — the buyer has no recourse, disagreeing with Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina.
An alternative version states that even vinegar (חלא) is accepted, aligning with Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's lenient position.

items.text: Return to Mishnah text
items.text_en: Return to Mishnah text
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the Mishnah's definition of 'old' wine as from last year, resuming the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's definition of 'old' wine as from last year, resuming the discussion.

items.text: Mishnah: Dimensions for a wedding house and general building sizes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dimensions for a wedding house and general building sizes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sells a place for a son-in-law's wedding house or a daughter's widow's house builds four by six amot, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yishmael says this is a cattle shed. It then lists standard dimensions for a small house, large house, and hall, with height half the length and width, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's proof from the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna introduces a general statement about extending the time until the festival.
The Mishnah states that one who sells a place for a wedding house builds four by six amot according to Rabbi Akiva, while Rabbi Yishmael says this is a cattle shed.
The Mishnah adds that one who wants to make a cattle shed builds four by six amot.
The Mishnah lists standard dimensions for a small house, large house, and hall, with height half the length and width, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's proof from the Temple.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrasing and a proverb
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrasing and a proverb
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'wedding house for his son' and 'widow's house for his daughter' instead of a general formulation. It explains that the Mishnah teaches incidentally that it is not customary for a son-in-law to live with his in-laws, citing Ben Sira's proverb about the lightness of a son-in-law living with his father-in-law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'wedding house for his son' and 'widow's house for his daughter' instead of using a general formulation that would apply to both genders.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah incidentally teaches that it is not customary for a son-in-law to live with his father-in-law.
The Gemara cites a proverb from Ben Sira that ranks a son-in-law living with his father-in-law as the lightest thing, even lighter than bran, to support the claim that it is not customary.

items.text: Debate on who teaches the cattle shed statement
items.text_en: Debate on who teaches the cattle shed statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's statement 'Rabbi Yishmael says: This is a cattle shed! One who wants to make a cattle shed builds four by six.' It presents two interpretations: one says Rabbi Akiva teaches it, meaning even a cattle shed can be a dwelling; another says Rabbi Yishmael teaches it, meaning the dimensions are for a cattle shed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement of Rabbi Yishmael about the cattle shed and the dimensions for one who wants to build it.
The Gemara asks who teaches the cattle shed statement in the Mishnah.
One opinion says Rabbi Yishmael himself teaches the statement, meaning the dimensions are for a cattle shed.
Another opinion says Rabbi Akiva teaches the statement, meaning even a cattle shed can serve as a dwelling, and the dimensions are for a dwelling.

items.text: Explanation of 'traklin' and 'kanteir'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'traklin' and 'kanteir'
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'traklin' as a vaulted room (קוּבְּתָא בֵּי וַורְדֵי) and cites a baraita that 'kanteir' is twelve by twelve, explaining it as a large hall (תַּרְבֵּץ אַפַּדְנֵי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'traklin' means.
The Gemara answers that 'traklin' is a vaulted room (קוּבְּתָא בֵּי וַורְדֵי).
A baraita is cited stating that 'kanteir' is twelve by twelve, and the Gemara explains it as a large hall (תַּרְבֵּץ אַפַּדְנֵי).

items.text: Debate on the proof for the height rule
items.text_en: Debate on the proof for the height rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses who teaches the proof for the height rule. One view says Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches it, meaning the proof is from the Temple. Another view says the first Tanna teaches it, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is astonished, questioning whether everyone builds like the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who teaches the phrase 'ראיה לדבר' (a proof for the matter) in the Mishnah.
One view holds that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel himself teaches the phrase, meaning he provides the proof from the Temple structure.
Another view holds that the first Tanna (תנא קמא) teaches the phrase, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel expresses astonishment, questioning whether everyone builds like the Temple.

items.text: Alternative opinion on height and resolution
items.text_en: Alternative opinion on height and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that 'others' say the height is like its beams. The Gemara questions why not say height equals width, and offers two answers: either the house is wider at the top, or because of recesses (בֵּי כַוֵּוי).

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Acherim who state that the height of a house is like its beams (i.e., the length of the beams determines the height).
The Gemara questions why Acherim did not simply say the height equals the width, which would be a simpler rule.
The Gemara offers a first answer: the house is wider at the top (so the width at the top is like the beams, not the floor width).
The Gemara offers a second answer: the height is like the beams because of recesses (בֵּי כַוֵּוי) that protrude and affect the measurement.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina resolves a contradiction in Temple measurements
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina resolves a contradiction in Temple measurements
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina went to a village and was asked about a contradiction: one verse says the Temple was 60 by 20 by 30, another says the Debir was 20 by 20 by 20. He answered that the measurement is from the lip of the cherubim upward. The Gemara asks what this teaches.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina went to a village and was presented with a contradiction between two verses describing the Temple's dimensions.
The villagers cited the second verse that describes the Debir as 20 by 20 by 20, creating the contradiction.
Rabbi Chanina resolved the contradiction by explaining that the measurement is taken from the lip of the cherubim upward.
The Gemara asks what principle Rabbi Chanina's answer teaches us.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches a principle: just as above (in the Holy of Holies) the cherubim do not occupy measurable space, so too below (in the Tabernacle) they do not occupy space. This supports Rabbi Levi's tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that the principle of 'below as above' teaches that the cherubim do not occupy measurable space.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Levi's tradition
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Levi's tradition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi, or alternatively Rabbi Yochanan, states that it is a tradition from the fathers that the place of the Ark and the cherubim is not included in the measurement. A baraita confirms that the Ark had ten cubits of space on each side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Levi's tradition that the place of the Ark and cherubim is not included in the measurement, and a baraita supports this with the detail that the Ark had ten cubits of space on each side.
A baraita confirms that the Ark made by Moses had ten cubits of space on each side, supporting the tradition.

items.text: Ravnai's statement: Cherubim stood miraculously
items.text_en: Ravnai's statement: Cherubim stood miraculously
items.desc_en: Ravnai said in the name of Shmuel that the cherubim stood miraculously, as the verse describes their wings spanning ten cubits, but their bodies would require additional space, implying a miracle.

sub.desc_en: Ravnai in the name of Shmuel states that the cherubim stood miraculously, as the verse describes their wings spanning ten cubits, implying their bodies were not within the measured space.

items.text: Objections to the miracle claim
items.text_en: Objections to the miracle claim
items.desc_en: Abaye, Rava, Rav Acha bar Yaakov, Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi each raise alternative explanations for how the cherubim could fit, such as protruding like roosters, not being aligned, standing diagonally, the room being wider above, their wings being bent, or their wings overlapping.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the cherubim might have been protruding like roosters, not standing miraculously.
Rava objects that the cherubim might have been standing not directly opposite each other.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that the cherubim might have been standing diagonally.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua objects that the room might have been wider above.
Rav Pappa objects that the cherubim's wings might have been bent.
Rav Ashi objects that the cherubim's wings might have been overlapping.

items.text: Dispute about the cherubim's orientation
items.text_en: Dispute about the cherubim's orientation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree: one says the cherubim faced each other, the other says they faced the Temple. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction in verses by explaining that when Israel does God's will, they face each other; when not, they face the Temple. Onkelos the convert adds that they were slightly turned, like a student taking leave of his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the cherubim stood, and presents the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar: one says they faced each other, the other says they faced the Temple.

The Gemara objects to the view that they faced each other, citing the verse 'and their faces were toward the house', and resolves that when Israel does God's will they face each other, when not they face the Temple.

The Gemara objects to the view that they faced the Temple, citing the verse 'and their faces were one toward his brother', and resolves that they were slightly turned, as Onkelos the convert taught, like a student taking leave of his teacher.

items.text: Mishnah: Cistern inside another's courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cistern inside another's courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a person has a cistern inside another's courtyard, he may enter and exit only at normal times, cannot water his animal inside, and each party may make a lock for the cistern.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the laws of a person whose cistern is inside another's courtyard, including entry times and the requirement for each to make a lock.

items.text: Gemara: Purpose of the lock
items.text_en: Gemara: Purpose of the lock
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks: to where is the lock? He answers that both locks are for the cistern. The cistern owner needs to protect his water, but the courtyard owner's need is questioned. Rabbi Elazar begins to explain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: to where does the lock open?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that both locks open toward the cistern.
The Gemara questions why the homeowner needs a lock, since the cistern owner needs one to guard his water.
Rabbi Elazar begins to answer, but the text cuts off; the answer is presumably that the homeowner needs a lock to prevent the cistern owner from entering his property at will.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion by explaining that the earlier ruling was due to suspicion regarding one's wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the earlier ruling was due to suspicion regarding one's wife.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of entering a neighbor's garden
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of entering a neighbor's garden
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who has a garden within another's garden may enter and exit only at times when people normally do, cannot bring merchants, and cannot pass through to another field. The outer owner may sow the path. If they agree on a side path, the inner owner may enter and exit at will and bring merchants, but neither may sow the path.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the default rule: one whose garden lies within another's may enter and exit only at normal times, may not bring merchants in, and may not pass through to another field; the outer owner sows the path.
The Mishnah presents the alternative: if both parties agree to a side path, the inner owner may enter and exit freely and bring merchants, but neither may sow the path.

items.text: Gemara: Selling a strip of land for irrigation
items.text_en: Gemara: Selling a strip of land for irrigation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that if one sells an 'amma of irrigated field', he gives two amot inside and one amah on each side for borders. For a 'amma of dry field', he gives one amah inside and half an amah on each side. A dispute arises between Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman regarding who plants the borders: Rav Yehuda says the field owner sows, Rav Nachman says he plants trees, with the Gemara clarifying the logical implications.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that selling an 'amma of irrigated field' requires giving two amot inside and one amah on each side for borders, while for a dry field one gives one amah inside and half an amah on each side.
The Gemara asks who plants those borders.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that the field owner sows them.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel answers that the field owner plants trees there.
The Gemara clarifies that the one who says sowing certainly allows planting, but the one who says planting forbids sowing because roots would undermine the borders.

items.text: Gemara: Repairing a water channel
items.text_en: Gemara: Repairing a water channel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that if a water channel's banks have eroded, the owner may repair them using soil from the same field. Rav Pappa objects, arguing the other party could claim the water damaged his land, but resolves that the field owner accepted this condition.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that if a water channel's banks have eroded, the owner may repair them using soil from that same field, provided it is known that the erosion only affected that field.
Rav Pappa objects, arguing that the other party could claim the water damaged his land, so taking soil from that field is unfair.
Rav Pappa resolves the objection by stating that the field owner accepted this condition from the outset, so the repair is permitted.

items.text: Mishnah: Public path and measurements
items.text_en: Mishnah: Public path and measurements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a public path passes through one's field and he gives them a side path instead, the gift is valid but he does not acquire the vacated path. It then lists standard widths: private path 4 amot, public path 16 amot, king's path and burial path have no fixed measure, and the standing place for eulogies is 4 kav according to the judges of Tzippori.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a public path through one's field: if he gives them a side path instead, the gift is valid but he does not acquire the vacated path.

The Mishnah lists standard widths: private path 4 amot, public path 16 amot, king's path and burial path have no fixed measure, and the standing place for eulogies is 4 kav according to the judges of Tzippori.

items.text: Gemara: Why the vacated path is not acquired
items.text_en: Gemara: Why the vacated path is not acquired
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the owner does not acquire the vacated path; he could simply take it by force. It concludes that one may not take the law into their own hands even in a case of loss. Rav Zevid and Rav Mesharshiya offer alternative explanations involving a crooked path.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the owner does not acquire the vacated path, suggesting he could simply take it by force.
The Gemara objects that this would imply one may not take the law into their own hands even in a case of loss.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava explains that the concern is a decree lest the owner give them a crooked path.

sub.text: Rav Mesharshiya in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya in the name of Rava offers an alternative explanation that the case involves one who actually gave them a crooked path.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah's case of a path on the side of a field is considered a winding path, close to one and far from another, justifying the ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah's case of a path on the side of a field is considered a winding path (דרך עקלתון), close to one and far from another.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah's author and resolving contradictions
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah's author and resolving contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah doesn't simply say 'take yours and give me mine,' and identifies it as following Rabbi Eliezer. Rav Giddel explains that the case is where the path was lost, and Rav Huna's ruling against Rabbi Eliezer is reconciled by noting different versions of the tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's litigants cannot simply say 'take yours and give me mine' to resolve the dispute.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that once many have chosen a path, their choice is binding.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Eliezer, the many would be considered robbers for taking a path without the owner's consent.
Rav Giddel in the name of Rav explains that the case is where the many lost their path in that field, so they are not robbers.
The Gemara objects that if so, why did Rabbah bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav rule that the הלכה (binding law) does not follow Rabbi Eliezer?
The Gemara resolves that the two traditions (the Mishnah and Rav's ruling) come from different teachers, so they do not conflict.

items.text: Reason for the ruling: Rav Yehuda's principle
items.text_en: Reason for the ruling: Rav Yehuda's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the underlying reason: Rav Yehuda stated that a boundary that many have taken possession of cannot be disturbed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the reason for the ruling?
Rav Yehuda explains: a boundary (מצר) that the public has taken possession of may not be damaged.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's view on acquisition by walking
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's view on acquisition by walking
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds that walking (hilukha) acquires a path, citing a verse about Abraham. The Sages disagree, saying walking alone is insufficient until formal possession (hazakah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Eliezer, by what act do the many acquire the path? It answers: by walking (הילוך).
A baraita is cited: if one walks the length and breadth of a path, he acquires the place of his walking, according to Rabbi Eliezer.
The Sages object: walking alone is ineffective; formal possession (חזקה) is required.
Rabbi Elazar explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: the verse 'קום התהלך בארץ' (Arise, walk through the land) shows that walking acquires.
The Sages reject the proof: that verse was said to Abraham out of affection, to make the land easy to conquer for his children, not as a halachic acquisition method.

items.text: Sages' concession for vineyard paths and practical ruling
items.text_en: Sages' concession for vineyard paths and practical ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding a vineyard path, as it is made for walking. Rav Yitzchak bar Ami rules that the path is acquired by carrying a load of branches and returning, with details about boundary markers.

items.text: Width of a private path
items.text_en: Width of a private path
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a private path is four cubits wide. Others say enough for a donkey with its load, and the Diaspora judges say two and a half cubits. Rav Huna rules both are the same measure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a private path is four cubits wide.
A baraita teaches: Acheirim say it is enough for a donkey with its load to pass.
Rav Huna rules: the halacha is like Acheirim.
Another baraita teaches: the judges of the exile say two and a half cubits.
Rav Huna also rules: the halacha is like the judges of the exile.
The Gemara asks: but Rav Huna said the halacha is like Acheirim!
The Gemara resolves: both are the same measure.

items.text: Width of a public path and additional measures
items.text_en: Width of a public path and additional measures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a public path is sixteen cubits. A baraita adds that a path from city to city is eight cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a public path is sixteen cubits wide.
The Rabbis taught: a private path is four cubits; a path from city to city is eight cubits.

items.text: Dimensions of paths and roads
items.text_en: Dimensions of paths and roads
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the width of a public road (16 amot) and a city of refuge road (32 amot). Rav Huna cites a verse for the latter. The Gemara adds that a king's road has no fixed measure, and a funeral path has no measure due to the honor of the deceased.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the width of a public road (16 amot) and a city of refuge road (32 amot).
Rav Huna cites a verse (Deuteronomy 19:3) to derive the 32-amah measure for the city of refuge road via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the doubled word 'דרך'.
The Gemara adds that a king's road has no fixed measure, as the king may break down fences to make a path without objection.
The Gemara adds that a funeral path has no fixed measure due to the honor of the deceased.

items.text: Ma'amad and the sale of a burial plot
items.text_en: Ma'amad and the sale of a burial plot
items.desc_en: The Tanna of Tzippori defines the ma'amad (standing place) as four kav. The Sages teach that if one sells his grave, path, ma'amad, or eulogy house, the family may bury him there against his will due to family disgrace.

sub.desc_en: The Dayanei Tzippori define the ma'amad (standing place) as a space of four kav.
The Sages teach in a baraita that if one sells his grave, path, ma'amad, or eulogy house, the family may bury him there against his will due to family disgrace (פגם משפחה).

items.text: Seven ma'amadot u'moshavot
items.text_en: Seven ma'amadot u'moshavot
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that one must not reduce from seven ma'amadot u'moshavot for the deceased, corresponding to the verse 'Hevel havalim...'. Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi how this is done, and Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Yehuda's description of the practice in Judea, with the phrases 'Imdu yekarim imdu' and 'Shevu yekarim shevu'. The Sages object that if so, it would be permitted on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one must not reduce from seven ma'amadot u'moshavot (standing and sitting stations) for the deceased, corresponding to the verse 'Hevel havalim...'.
Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi how the practice of ma'amadot u'moshavot is performed.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's answer citing Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer citing Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers by citing Rabbi Yehuda's description of the practice in Judea, where the mourners would say 'Imdu yekarim imdu' and 'Shevu yekarim shevu'.
The Sages object that if the practice is as described, it would be permitted on Shabbat, which is problematic.

items.text: Rav Avya's mistaken practice
items.text_en: Rav Avya's mistaken practice
items.desc_en: Rav Avya made a ma'amad u'moshav for his wife, the sister of Rami bar Pappa. Rav Yosef says he erred in two ways: he did it for distant relatives (only close relatives are appropriate) and on the second day (only the first day is appropriate). Abaye adds a third error: he did it in the city (only in the cemetery). Rava adds a fourth: he did it where it was not customary.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rav Avya made a ma'amad u'moshav (standing and sitting ceremony) for his wife, the sister of Rami bar Pappa, after her death.
Rav Yosef objects that Rav Avya erred in two ways: the ceremony is only for close relatives, not distant ones, and only on the first day of burial, not the second.
Abaye adds a third error: the ceremony should be performed only in the cemetery, but Rav Avya did it in the city.
Rava adds a fourth error: the ceremony is only performed where it is customary, but in that place it was not customary.

items.text: Objection from the Sages' statement
items.text_en: Objection from the Sages' statement
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from the Sages' earlier statement that if so, it would be permitted on Shabbat. If the practice is only in the cemetery and on the first day, why would they mention Shabbat? The Gemara answers: it refers to a city adjacent to the cemetery, where the body was brought between sunset and nightfall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Sages' statement that if the practice is only in the cemetery and on the first day, why would they mention Shabbat, since people do not go to the cemetery on Shabbat.
The Gemara answers that the case refers to a city adjacent to the cemetery, where the body was brought between sunset and nightfall, so the practice could occur on Shabbat.

items.text: Mishnah: Dimensions of a burial cave
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dimensions of a burial cave
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who sells a place for a burial cave, or accepts such a contract, must make the cave's interior 4 amot by 6 amot, and open into it eight niches: three on each side and two opposite. The length of each niche is 4 amot, and its height is 7 tefachim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dimensions of a burial cave and the arrangement of niches within it.

items.text: Mishnah: Dimensions of the cave and courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dimensions of the cave and courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Shimon's view on the dimensions of a burial cave (six by eight cubits) and the arrangement of thirteen niches, as well as the courtyard (six by six cubits) and the number of caves opening into it. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that everything depends on the rock.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Shimon's view that the interior of the cave is six by eight cubits, with thirteen niches arranged around it.
The Mishnah adds that a courtyard of six by six cubits is made at the cave's entrance, sufficient for the bier and its bearers.

sub.text: Mishnah: Caves opening into the courtyard
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Caves opening into the courtyard
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that two caves open into the courtyard, one on each side, while Rabbi Shimon says there are four caves, one on each side.

sub.text: Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's qualification
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's qualification
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies that all dimensions depend on the hardness of the rock.

items.text: Gemara's question: Where are the two extra niches placed?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Where are the two extra niches placed?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the two additional niches (beyond the standard arrangement) are placed, noting that if they are outside, they would be in the courtyard which is tahor. It cites the Mishnah that the courtyard of a grave is tahor for one standing in it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the two additional niches (beyond the standard arrangement) are placed, noting that if they are outside, they would be in the courtyard which is טהור (ritually pure) according to the Mishnah.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers that the two extra niches are made like a kind of bolt (נגר), i.e., they are placed in the courtyard but in a way that does not render the courtyard impure.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement, which will challenge the proposed solution.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers that the two extra niches are made like a bolt (i.e., perpendicular to the wall, projecting inward).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers that the two extra niches are made like a bolt (i.e., perpendicular to the wall, projecting inward).

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to raise an objection based on a statement of Rabbi Yochanan, which will be elaborated in the following segments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to raise an objection based on a statement of Rabbi Yochanan, which will be elaborated in the following segments.

items.text: Objection to Rabbi Yochanan's arrangement
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbi Yochanan's arrangement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's arrangement of four caves in a corner results in the niches touching each other, which is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's arrangement of four caves in a corner results in the niches touching each other, which is invalid.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan places the caves in a corner, which is the source of the problem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan places the caves in a corner, which is the source of the problem.

items.text: Reiteration of the objection
items.text_en: Reiteration of the objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the objection that the niches touch each other in this arrangement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the niches would touch each other in this arrangement.

items.text: Rav Ashi's answer: digging deeper
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer: digging deeper
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the niches are dug deeper into the rock, so they do not touch each other. He supports this by noting that Rabbi Shimon's four caves would also require this solution.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the niches are dug deeper into the rock, so they do not touch each other.
Rav Ashi supports his answer by noting that Rabbi Shimon's four caves would also require this solution, otherwise the niches would touch each other.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's alternative arrangement
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's alternative arrangement
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua proposes that Rabbi Shimon's four caves are arranged like a 'charuta' (a type of diagonal layout) to avoid the niches touching.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua proposes that Rabbi Shimon's four caves are arranged like a 'charuta' (a diagonal layout) to avoid the niches touching.

items.text: Rejection of Rav Huna's view as mistaken
items.text_en: Rejection of Rav Huna's view as mistaken
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that the diagonal length of a square amah is 1.4 amot, and shows that Rav Huna's arrangement cannot accommodate eight niches within the available space, concluding his view is erroneous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that the diagonal of a square amah is 1.4 amot, and demonstrates that Rav Huna's arrangement cannot fit eight niches within the available space, concluding that his view is mistaken.

items.text: Alternative answer: using niches
items.text_en: Alternative answer: using niches
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative solution, citing Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi, that the niches are arranged in 'niflei' (recesses or alcoves) to avoid contact.

sub.text: Gemara's alternative answer citing Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi
sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative answer citing Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative solution, citing Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi, that the niches are arranged in 'niflei' (recesses or alcoves) to avoid contact.

items.text: Introduction of a new Mishnah
items.text_en: Introduction of a new Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic by citing a Mishnah about one who finds a corpse lying in its natural position, and the laws of taking it along with its surrounding earth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that one who finds a corpse lying in its natural position takes it along with its surrounding earth, and for two corpses, takes them with their surrounding earth.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one finds three corpses with between four and eight cubits between them, it is a burial cave, and one must check twenty cubits further. If one finds a single corpse at the end of twenty cubits, one checks another twenty cubits, because there is a presumption of a cave.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for finding three corpses spaced between four and eight cubits apart, indicating a burial cave, and the requirement to check twenty cubits further, with a presumption of a cave if a single corpse is found at the end.

items.text: Gemara's question on the measurement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the measurement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah follows: the Rabbis (who require four by six cubits) or Rabbi Shimon (who requires six by eight cubits). The Mishnah's range of four to eight cubits does not match either precisely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah follows, noting that the Rabbis require four by six cubits and Rabbi Shimon requires six by eight cubits, while the Mishnah's range of four to eight cubits matches neither precisely.

items.text: First answer: It is Rabbi Shimon, citing a baraita
items.text_en: First answer: It is Rabbi Shimon, citing a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, as taught in a baraita: if corpses are found contiguous with less than four cubits between them, they have תפוסה but not a burial cave. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon says to view the middle ones as if they do not exist, and the rest combine to four to eight cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, and this is the Tanna cited in the baraita.
The Gemara cites a baraita: if corpses are found contiguous with less than four cubits between them, they have תפוסה but not a burial cave.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda citing Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda citing Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon says to view the middle corpses as if they do not exist, and the rest combine to four to eight cubits.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah's twenty cubits
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah's twenty cubits
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, the required check should be twenty-two cubits (six plus eight plus eight), not twenty. If it follows the Rabbis, it should be eighteen cubits (four plus six plus six plus two).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's measurement of twenty cubits does not match either Rabbi Shimon's calculation (twenty-two) or the Rabbis' calculation (eighteen).

items.text: Second answer: It is the Rabbis, measured diagonally
items.text_en: Second answer: It is the Rabbis, measured diagonally
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah actually follows the Rabbis, and the twenty cubits are measured diagonally (אלכסונא), which yields the correct measurement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, and the twenty cubits are measured diagonally (באלכסונא).

items.text: Refinement: Only one diagonal measurement
items.text_en: Refinement: Only one diagonal measurement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if this is diagonal, it should be twenty-two cubits (since the diagonal of a six-by-eight rectangle is ten). The Gemara resolves: we say one diagonal measurement, but we do not say two diagonal measurements (i.e., only the initial cave is measured diagonally, not the subsequent check).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if the initial measurement is diagonal, then the subsequent check should also be diagonal, yielding twenty-two cubits, not twenty.
The Gemara resolves: we apply one diagonal measurement (for the initial cave) but not two diagonal measurements (for the subsequent check).

items.text: Rav Shisha's resolution of the contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Rav Shisha's resolution of the contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that the earlier dispute is about a burial cave with niches (ניפלי), not about a standard cave. He argues that only one niche is considered part of the cave, not two, thus resolving the numerical discrepancy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi opens by asserting that the earlier dispute is about a burial cave with niches (ניפלי), not a standard cave.
He resolves the numerical discrepancy by explaining that only one niche is considered part of the cave, not two.

items.text: Introduction of new contradictions between the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Introduction of new contradictions between the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises contradictions within the views of the Rabbis and within Rabbi Shimon's own statements, based on a baraita about a vineyard planted on less than four amot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that it will raise contradictions within the views of the Rabbis and within Rabbi Shimon's own statements.

items.text: Citation of the baraita and statement of the contradictions
items.text_en: Citation of the baraita and statement of the contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that a vineyard planted on less than four amot is not a vineyard, while the Rabbis consider it a vineyard and view the middle vines as nonexistent. This creates apparent contradictions with their earlier positions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that a vineyard planted on less than four amot is not a vineyard, while the Sages consider it a vineyard and view the middle vines as nonexistent.
The Gemara raises contradictions: the Sages' position here contradicts their earlier position, and Rabbi Shimon's position here contradicts his earlier position.

items.text: Resolution of Rabbi Shimon's contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of Rabbi Shimon's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rabbi Shimon's contradiction by distinguishing between the cases: in the vineyard, people do not plant with the intention to uproot, so it is not a vineyard; in the burial cave, sometimes a corpse is placed at twilight and then removed, so it is considered a grave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rabbi Shimon's contradiction by distinguishing between the vineyard case, where people do not plant with intent to uproot, and the burial cave case, where a corpse may be placed at twilight and then removed, so it is considered a grave.

items.text: Resolution of the Rabbis' contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the Rabbis' contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the Rabbis' contradiction by explaining that in the burial cave, since the niche is repulsive (מנול), it is not called a grave; in the vineyard, the Rabbis assume that the owner thinks: whichever vines are good are good, and the bad ones will be used for firewood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the Rabbis' positions by explaining that in the burial cave, the niche is repulsive (מנול) and thus not called a grave, while in the vineyard, the Rabbis assume the owner considers any good vines acceptable and the bad ones as firewood.

items.text: New Mishnah: selling land by volume
items.text_en: New Mishnah: selling land by volume
items.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a new chapter: if one sells a beit kor of earth, deep pits or high rocks of ten handbreadths are not measured with it, but less than that are. If he says 'like a beit kor of earth,' even larger pits or rocks are included.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a new chapter: if one sells a beit kor of earth, deep pits or high rocks of ten handbreadths are not measured with it.
The Mishnah states that pits or rocks less than ten handbreadths are measured with the land.
The Mishnah concludes that if the seller says 'like a beit kor of earth,' even larger pits or rocks are included in the measurement.

items.text: Gemara's citation of a parallel Mishnah from Arachin
items.text_en: Gemara's citation of a parallel Mishnah from Arachin
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins its analysis by citing a Mishnah from tractate Arachin about one who consecrates his field during the Jubilee period, where similar rules apply regarding pits and rocks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah from tractate Arachin about one who consecrates his field during the Jubilee period, where similar rules apply regarding pits and rocks.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that pits (or rocky areas) of a certain size are not measured with the field, while smaller ones are.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that pits of a certain size are not measured with the field, while smaller ones are.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Ukva bar Chama's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Ukva bar Chama's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why larger pits are not measured, suggesting they could be consecrated separately. It cites a baraita that includes various measures for consecration. Rav Ukva bar Chama answers that the Mishnah deals with pits filled with water, which are not arable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why larger pits are not measured with the field, suggesting they could be consecrated separately, and anticipates the objection that less than a בית כור (a field of a kor's area) cannot be consecrated.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the word 'שדה' (field) that even smaller measures like a לתך (half-kor), סאה (seah), or תרקב (three seahs) can be consecrated, contradicting the assumption that only a full בית כור qualifies.
Rav Ukva bar Chama answers that the Mishnah deals with pits filled with water, which are not arable, and notes that the Mishnah's comparison to rocks supports this.

items.text: Objection and resolution
items.text_en: Objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even smaller pits should be excluded if filled with water, but resolves that such pits are called 'furrows' or 'ridges' of the land, not pits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the pits are water-filled, even small ones should not be measured, but they are called 'נגאני דארעא' (hollows of the land) or 'שדרי דארעא' (ridges of the land).
The Gemara resolves that such small water-filled pits are called 'furrows of the land' or 'ridges of the land', not pits, so they are not excluded.

items.text: Rav Papa's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Papa's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that even if the pits are not filled with water, they are not measured because a person does not want to give money for one area that appears as multiple places.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that even when not water-filled, large pits are not measured because a person does not want his money to appear as multiple separate places.
Rav Papa answers that even if the pits are not filled with water, they are not measured because a person does not want to give money for one area that appears as multiple places.

items.text: Ravina's objection
items.text_en: Ravina's objection
items.desc_en: Ravina objects that the Mishnah compares pits to rocks, implying they are not arable, and clarifies that the comparison applies only to smaller pits.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects that the Mishnah's parallel to rocks indicates only non-arable land is excluded, and that the parallel applies only to smaller pits.

items.text: Definitions of 'trashim' and their measurement
items.text_en: Definitions of 'trashim' and their measurement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak defines 'trashim' (rocky areas) as those of four kav. Rav Ukva bar Chama and Rabbi Yochanan add conditions about their absorption within the field.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that the rocky patches referred to are of four kav in size.
Rav Ukva bar Chama qualifies that this applies only when they are absorbed within five kav.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's qualification via Rav Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's qualification via Rav Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, transmitted by Rav Chiya bar Abba, qualifies that they must be absorbed in the majority of the field.

items.text: Unresolved queries
items.text_en: Unresolved queries
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yirmeya pose unresolved questions about the distribution of rocks within the field, left as 'teiku'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Abba asks about the status of rocks when the majority are in a small area and the minority in a large area, left unresolved as 'teiku'.
Rabbi Yirmeya poses an unresolved question, but the text cuts off before stating its content.

items.text: Unresolved queries about irregular features and adjacent rock
items.text_en: Unresolved queries about irregular features and adjacent rock
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved questions (teiku) about whether a kishir, keshurah, or amphitheater is measured with the field, and about a winding path. A baraita states that a solitary rock or one adjacent to the boundary is not measured with the field. Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi ask further questions about intervening earth or layers of earth and rock, all left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved queries (תיקו) about whether a kishir (a row of vines), keshurah (a tied bundle), amphitheater, or winding path is measured with the field.
A baraita teaches that a solitary rock or one adjacent to the boundary is not measured with the field.
Rav Pappa asks whether earth intervening between the rock and the field changes the ruling, left unresolved.
Rav Ashi asks about layers of earth and rock in different orders, all left unresolved.

items.text: Mishnah: Selling a beit kor by measure with allowances
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling a beit kor by measure with allowances
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sells a beit kor of earth by rope-measure, any deficiency or excess is adjusted: deficiency is deducted, excess is returned. If the seller says 'more or less', a deviation of up to a quarter-kav per se'ah is acceptable; beyond that, an accounting is made. The buyer returns money, but if the excess is at least a certain area (beit tis'ah kabbin for a field, beit chatzi kav for a garden, or beit rova according to Rabbi Akiva), the land itself is returned, including all the excess.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of selling a beit kor of earth by rope-measure, stating that any deficiency is deducted and any excess is returned.
The Mishnah adds that if the seller says 'more or less', a deviation of up to a quarter-kav per se'ah is acceptable; beyond that, an accounting is made.

The Mishnah explains that the buyer normally returns money, but if the excess is at least a certain area (beit tis'ah kabbin for a field, beit chatzi kav for a garden, or beit rova according to Rabbi Akiva), the land itself is returned.
The Mishnah concludes that the buyer returns not only the excess area but all the surplus land.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Default meaning of 'beit kor'
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Default meaning of 'beit kor'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If one simply says 'beit kor' without specifying 'by rope-measure', what is the law? It attempts to resolve this from the Mishnah's wording, which says 'beit kor of earth I am selling to you – by rope-measure', implying that without that specification, the sale might be different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If one simply says 'beit kor' without specifying 'by rope-measure', what is the law? It attempts to resolve this from the Mishnah's wording, which says 'beit kor of earth I am selling to you – by rope-measure', implying that without that specification, the sale might be different.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the first clause of the Mishnah (if the field is less or more by any amount, the seller deducts or the buyer returns) implies that an unspecified sale is like one with the condition 'either deficient or surplus'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's first clause that an unspecified sale is treated like one with the condition 'either deficient or surplus'.

items.text: Contradiction from the Mishnah's second clause
items.text_en: Contradiction from the Mishnah's second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out that the second clause (if he said 'either deficient or surplus', even a quarter-kav per se'ah deviation is acceptable) suggests that an unspecified sale is like a precise measurement. It concludes that no inference can be drawn from this Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing the Mishnah's second clause, which seems to imply that an unspecified sale is like a sale by precise measure, and then concludes that no inference can be drawn from the Mishnah.
The Gemara concludes that no inference can be drawn from this Mishnah, as the contradiction remains unresolved.

items.text: Attempted proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Attempted proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that lists three formulations for selling a beit kor of earth, including 'either deficient or surplus', and states that even a quarter-kav per se'ah deviation is acceptable.
