This seems to prove that an unspecified sale is like 'either deficient or surplus', but the Gemara deflects by saying the baraita is merely explaining what 'beit kor that is like a beit kor' means.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that lists three sale formulas, all of which allow a quarter-kav per se'ah deviation, and then rejects the proof by explaining that the baraita is merely defining what 'like a beit kor' means.

The Gemara deflects the proof by explaining that the baraita is merely clarifying what 'beit kor that is like a beit kor' means, i.e., it refers to a case where the seller explicitly said 'either deficient or surplus'.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and conclusion
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that if the baraita is merely explanatory, why does it repeat 'I am selling to you'? He concludes that the baraita indeed proves that an unspecified sale is like 'either deficient or surplus'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that if the baraita were merely explanatory, the repetition of 'I am selling to you' would be superfluous, and concludes that an unspecified sale is indeed like 'either deficient or surplus'.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita indeed proves that an unspecified sale is like 'either deficient or surplus'.

items.text: Question about the method of refund
items.text_en: Question about the method of refund
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states that the seller returns money (when the field is larger) but does not say that the buyer returns money (when the field is smaller) to favor the seller.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says the buyer returns money, implying the seller's power is enhanced, and asks why the buyer's power is not similarly enhanced.

items.text: Baraita about forced sale
items.text_en: Baraita about forced sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that if the deviation is up to seven and a half kav per kor, it is acceptable; beyond that, the court forces both seller and buyer to complete the transaction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that states for deviations up to seven and a half kav per kor the sale stands, and beyond that both parties are compelled to complete the sale.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction between the Mishnah and the baraita
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction between the Mishnah and the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita deals with a case where the land was expensive initially and cheap now, so the buyer can demand the current cheap price. Another baraita is cited where the land was cheap initially and expensive now, and the seller gives the refund at the original price.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita deals with a case where the land was expensive initially and cheap now, so the buyer can demand the current cheap price.
A baraita is cited where the land was cheap initially and expensive now, and the seller gives the refund at the original price.
The Gemara explains that the baraita refers to a case where the land was cheap initially and expensive now, so the refund is at the original price.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman about the minimum remaining area
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman about the minimum remaining area
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the seller left a plot of nine kav in the field, the sale is valid. Rav Huna says this applies even in a large valley, while Rav Nachman says the seller must leave seven and a half kav per kor.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the Mishnah's minimum of nine kav applies even in a large valley.
Rav Nachman counters that the seller must leave seven and a half kav per kor of the field's total area.

items.text: Rule about extra land returning
items.text_en: Rule about extra land returning
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if there is extra land amounting to nine kav, the seller must return it to the buyer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if there is extra land amounting to nine kav, the seller must return it to the buyer.

items.text: Rava's objection to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman by citing a baraita about selling a field of two kor or a garden of two se'ah, where the seller retains a small remainder. Rav Nachman clarifies that the baraita refers to selling one kor or one se'ah, not two.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman by citing a baraita about selling a field of two kor, implying the seller retains a small remainder.
Rav Nachman clarifies that the baraita refers to selling one kor, not two.
Rava continues his objection, citing the baraita's clause about a garden of two se'ah.
Rav Nachman clarifies that the baraita refers to selling one se'ah, not two.
Rava objects further, citing the baraita's reference to Rabbi Akiva's opinion about a rova, implying a sale of one se'ah.
Rav Nachman clarifies that the baraita refers to selling half a se'ah, not a full se'ah.

items.text: Rav Ashi's query about field becoming garden
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's query about field becoming garden
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks what the law is if a field becomes a garden or a garden becomes a field, and the Gemara leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks what the law is if a field becomes a garden or a garden becomes a field, and the Gemara leaves it unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Tanna's ruling on adjacent land
items.text_en: Tanna's ruling on adjacent land
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if the extra land is adjacent to the buyer's own field, even a tiny amount must be returned as land.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if the extra land is adjacent to the buyer's own field, even a tiny amount must be returned as land.

items.text: Rav Ashi's queries about interruptions
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's queries about interruptions
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether a cistern, water channel, public road, or palm row interrupts the contiguous area, and the Gemara leaves all unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether a cistern, water channel, public road, or palm row interrupts the contiguous area for the purpose of returning land.
The Gemara leaves all of Rav Ashi's queries unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Returning all the quarter-kavs
items.text_en: Returning all the quarter-kavs
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that not only the remainder of a quarter-kav is returned, but all the quarter-kavs are returned, as taught by Ravin bar Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that not only the quarter-kav remainder is returned, but all the surplus.
The Gemara asks whether this is obvious, given the previous ruling.
Ravin bar Rav Nachman teaches that not only the surplus is returned, but all the quarter-kavs are returned.

items.text: Mishnah: Contradictory terms in sale
items.text_en: Mishnah: Contradictory terms in sale
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where the seller says 'I am selling you a measure by rope, whether short or over,' and the phrase 'whether short or over' nullifies 'measure by rope,' but if reversed, the latter phrase prevails.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a seller says 'I am selling you a measure by rope, whether short or over,' the phrase 'whether short or over' nullifies 'measure by rope,' meaning the sale is valid even if the measured area deviates.
The Mishnah adds that if the order is reversed — 'whether short or over, measure by rope' — the latter phrase 'measure by rope' prevails, requiring precise measurement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a tenant says 'I cancel the rental by measure or by excess or deficiency' (i.e., retracts), the rental is void; this is the opinion of Ben Nannas.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a tenant cancels the rental by saying 'measure with a rope' or 'whether deficient or excessive', the rental is void according to Ben Nannas.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav's teaching
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav's teaching
items.desc_en: Rav, via Rabbi Abba bar Memel, states that Ben Nannas's colleagues disagree with him. The Gemara questions what Rav adds, since a similar case in Tzippori already shows that the Sages rule to divide the month. Rav's teaching clarifies that in the Tzippori case, the tenant might have been merely explaining, not retracting, so the ruling there is not conclusive; here, where retraction is certain, one might think the Sages would disagree, but Rav teaches that they still agree with Ben Nannas.

sub.text: Gemara's question via Rabbi Abba bar Memel quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Gemara's question via Rabbi Abba bar Memel quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav, via Rabbi Abba bar Memel, asserts that Ben Nannas's colleagues disagree with him, and the Gemara asks what novel point Rav is teaching.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav, transmitted by Rabbi Abba bar Memel, states that Ben Nannas's colleagues disagree with him.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of a supporting baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of a supporting baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a bathhouse rental in Tzippori where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yosei ruled that the parties split the intercalated month.
The Gemara questions what Rav adds by stating this, since the Tzippori case already shows the Sages' position.

The Gemara explains that Rav's teaching is necessary: in the Tzippori case, the tenant might have been merely explaining, not retracting, so the ruling is not conclusive; here, where retraction is certain, one might think the Sages would disagree, but Rav teaches that they still agree with Ben Nannas.
The Gemara explains that without Rav's statement, one might have distinguished the baraita as a case of ambiguous retraction, but Rav teaches that even in a clear retraction the colleagues disagree.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: Shmuel, via Rav Yehuda, says that Ben Nannas's ruling is his individual opinion, but the Sages say: follow the lesser of the two expressions (i.e., the tenant's retraction is not automatically accepted).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling that Ben Nannas's position is his individual opinion.
The Sages rule that one follows the lesser of the two expressions, meaning the tenant's retraction is not automatically accepted.

items.text: Contradiction from Rav and Shmuel's own ruling
items.text_en: Contradiction from Rav and Shmuel's own ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rav and Shmuel both rule that in a sale of a kor for thirty, the seller can retract even on the last se'ah, implying that retraction is allowed. But Shmuel here seems to reject Ben Nannas's view. The Gemara resolves that Shmuel actually accepts Ben Nannas's view, as shown by his ruling in the sale case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Shmuel can say 'this is Ben Nannas's view' (implying he disagrees) when both Rav and Shmuel rule that in a sale of a kor for thirty, the seller can retract even on the last se'ah, which aligns with Ben Nannas's position.

The Gemara resolves that Shmuel actually accepts Ben Nannas's view, as shown by his ruling that in a sale of a kor for thirty at a se'ah per sela, each se'ah is acquired immediately, which parallels Ben Nannas's principle.

items.text: Further contradiction from Shmuel's rental ruling
items.text_en: Further contradiction from Shmuel's rental ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction: Shmuel rules that if a tenant enters in the middle of the month, the rental is divided; but if at the beginning, it's all for the landlord; if at the end, all for the tenant. This seems to contradict his acceptance of Ben Nannas's view that retraction voids the rental. The Gemara leaves this unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's acceptance of Ben Nannas's view by citing Shmuel's own ruling that a tenant entering at the beginning or end of the month gets no division, which seems to contradict Ben Nannas's principle.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about seizure
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about seizure
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the earlier case (where the buyer seizes) is different because there the buyer actually seized the property, whereas here the seller seized the money. Thus the principle of 'tefisah' applies consistently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by asserting that the earlier case involves seizure of property by the buyer, while here the seller seized the money, so the principle of תפיסה (seizure) applies consistently.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on ambiguous language
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on ambiguous language
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if someone says 'an istira, one hundred ma'ah' the amount is one hundred ma'ah, but if he says 'one hundred ma'ah, an istira' the amount is an istira, following the last expression.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that in a statement with two conflicting amounts, the last expression determines the obligation.

items.text: Gemara's question: redundancy with Rav's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question: redundancy with Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Huna's ruling is necessary, since Rav already stated that the last expression is followed. The Gemara cites Rav's earlier statement about giving the entire amount to the renter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Huna's ruling is necessary, since Rav already stated that the last expression is followed, and cites Rav's earlier statement about giving the entire amount to the renter.

items.text: Answer: Rav Huna clarifies that Rav did not retract
items.text_en: Answer: Rav Huna clarifies that Rav did not retract
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that without Rav Huna's statement, one might think Rav retracted his earlier ruling. But here, Rav Huna teaches that Rav was merely explaining the principle, not retracting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without Rav Huna's statement, one would think Rav retracted, but Rav Huna teaches that Rav was merely explaining the principle, not retracting.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a field is sold with its boundaries and the actual size differs, a discrepancy of less than one-sixth is considered acceptable (the sale stands), while exactly one-sixth requires a deduction.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a field is sold with its boundaries and the actual size differs, a discrepancy of less than one-sixth is considered acceptable (the sale stands), while exactly one-sixth requires a deduction.

items.text: Amoraic dispute on the status of one-sixth
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute on the status of one-sixth
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah argue whether the Mishnah's 'up to one-sixth' includes or excludes the exact one-sixth. Rav Huna holds that one-sixth is like less than one-sixth (sale stands), while Rav Yehudah holds it is like more than one-sixth (deduction applies). Each explains the Mishnah accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav Huna says that a discrepancy of exactly one-sixth is treated like less than one-sixth (the sale stands), while Rav Yehuda says it is treated like more than one-sixth (a deduction is made).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Huna's view: the Mishnah means that less than one-sixth, and one-sixth included, the sale stands; more than one-sixth requires a deduction.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Yehuda's view: the Mishnah means that less than one-sixth the sale stands, but up to and including one-sixth requires a deduction.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that seems to contradict Rav Huna: it says that if the discrepancy is exactly one-sixth, the sale stands, and it compares this to the valuation of judges (shum hadayanin) where one-sixth is considered more than one-sixth (voiding the sale). Rav Huna responds that the baraita is not entirely like shum hadayanin: it is like it regarding the one-sixth threshold, but unlike it because there the sale is void, while here the sale stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if a field sold with its boundaries is short or over by one-sixth, it is like the valuation of judges (שׁוּם הַדַּיָּינִין) and the sale stands, but in the case of judges' valuation, one-sixth is treated as more than one-sixth (voiding the sale), so the baraita contradicts Rav Huna.

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if the discrepancy is exactly one-sixth, it is like the valuation of judges (shum hadayanin), where one-sixth is considered more than one-sixth (voiding the sale). This contradicts Rav Huna.

Rav Huna responds: according to your reasoning, the baraita itself says 'the sale stands' (הִגִּיעוֹ), so it must be interpreted as similar to but not identical to judges' valuation — like judges' valuation regarding the one-sixth threshold, but unlike it because there the sale is void, while here the sale stands.

items.text: Story of Rav Pappa's purchase
items.text_en: Story of Rav Pappa's purchase
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a narrative about Rav Pappa who bought land from a certain man, which will likely illustrate the halakhic principles discussed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rav Pappa buying land from a certain man, which will serve as a practical illustration of the halachic dispute.

items.text: Case of a land sale with a mistaken measure
items.text_en: Case of a land sale with a mistaken measure
items.desc_en: A buyer claims the seller promised 20 se'ah but only got 15. Abaye rules that since the buyer was aware of the land's size and accepted, he cannot deduct. The seller's claim of 20 is explained as referring to land that yields as if it were 20.

sub.desc_en: The buyer claims the seller promised 20 se'ah of land but measurement revealed only 15.
Abaye rules that since the buyer was aware of the land's size and accepted, he cannot deduct.
The gemara objects citing the Mishnah that for a deficiency up to one-sixth the buyer deducts.
Abaye distinguishes: the Mishnah applies only when the buyer was unaware of the land, but here he was aware and accepted.
The buyer objects that the seller explicitly said '20'.
Abaye explains that the seller meant land that yields produce as if it were 20 se'ah.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei on division by lot among brothers
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei on division by lot among brothers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that when brothers divide property, once the lot falls for one, all acquire their portions. Rabbi Elazar compares this to the original division of Eretz Yisrael by lot. Rav Ashi explains that the mutual benefit of accepting the lot creates a kinyan.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei's ruling that when brothers divide an inheritance, once the lot falls to one, all acquire their portions.
Rabbi Elazar explains the reason: just as the initial division of Eretz Yisrael was by lot, so too here the division is by lot.
The gemara objects: if we compare to the original division, shouldn't it require a lottery box and Urim veTummim?
Rav Ashi resolves: the brothers acquire through the mutual benefit of listening to each other, not through a formal lottery.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a returning brother
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a returning brother
items.desc_en: If two brothers divided and a third returns from overseas, Rav says the division is void, while Shmuel says they take from each brother's share. Rava questions Rav's position by comparing to a case where two of three judges divide property, but Rav Nachman distinguishes because here they never relied on a third party.

sub.desc_en: An amoraic dispute: if two brothers divided and a third brother arrives from overseas, Rav says the division is void, Shmuel says they deduct from each.
Rava asks Rav Nachman: according to Rav that the division is void, would the same apply if two of three judges left and divided?
Rav Nachman distinguishes: in the court case they initially relied on three judges, but the brothers did not initially rely on a third brother.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question on Shmuel's position
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question on Shmuel's position
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if Shmuel holds that the division stands (and they compensate), does that mean the sale is final? He cites a case where Rav and Shmuel agree that in a sale of a kor for thirty, the seller can retract until the last se'ah, but if sold by the se'ah, each se'ah is acquired immediately.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: according to Shmuel that they deduct, does that mean the original division stands?

sub.text: Rav Pappa's objection from a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection from a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects citing a baraita where both Rav and Shmuel agree that in a sale of a kor for thirty, the seller can retract even on the last se'ah, but if sold per se'ah, each se'ah is acquired immediately.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the previous ruling was made to benefit both seller and buyer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the rabbis enacted the previous ruling to benefit both seller and buyer.

items.text: Dispute about brothers who divided and a creditor seizes one's share
items.text_en: Dispute about brothers who divided and a creditor seizes one's share
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Asi debate whether the division is voided, the brother forfeits, or he takes a quarter in land and a quarter in money. The Gemara explains their reasoning based on whether brothers are considered heirs or purchasers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute among Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Asi regarding brothers who divided an inheritance and a creditor seized one brother's share.
Rav rules that the division is nullified, reasoning that brothers who divide an inheritance are considered heirs, not purchasers.
Shmuel rules that the brother forfeits his share, reasoning that brothers who divide are considered purchasers and like a purchaser without אחריות (guarantee).
Rav Asi is uncertain whether they are heirs or purchasers, so he rules that the creditor takes a quarter in land and a quarter in money.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Amemar rule on the halakha
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Amemar rule on the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says that in all these rulings we 'fold' (compromise), but Amemar rules that the division is voided, and the halakha follows Amemar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that in all these rulings one compresses, and Amemar rules that the division is nullified, and the halakha follows that.
Amemar rules that the division is voided.
The gemara concludes that the halakha follows Amemar: the division is voided.

items.text: Baraita about three appraisers who disagree
items.text_en: Baraita about three appraisers who disagree
items.desc_en: The baraita presents cases where one appraiser values at one amount and two at another, or where three give different valuations. Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok and others offer opinions on how to resolve the disagreement.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that when three appraisers disagree, the minority opinion is nullified.
The baraita continues with cases of three differing appraisals and the opinions of Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok and Acherim.
Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok offers an alternative opinion: the value is set at 90.
Acherim (others) rule that the appraisers average their valuations and divide the difference.

items.text: Gemara explains the opinions in the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara explains the opinions in the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to explain the reasoning behind the opinions, stating that the one who says 'judged at a maneh' holds the middle value, and Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok holds that the land is...

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who says 'judged at a maneh' holds the middle value, while Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok says 'judged at ninety' because he considers the land's value.
The Gemara states that Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok holds the land is judged at ninety, because he considers the land itself to be the primary factor.

items.text: Debate over the value of the field and the division method
items.text_en: Debate over the value of the field and the division method
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute about the actual value of the field based on the offers. One view holds the field is worth 90, with the 20-offer being 10 too low and the 100-offer being 10 too high. Another view counters that it is worth 110, with the 100-offer being 10 too low and the 30-offer being 10 too high. The Gemara then introduces the opinion of Acheirim, who calculate the value as 93⅓ and divide accordingly, but a counter-argument suggests the value is 113⅓, leading to a conclusion that the first two buyers are not removed from the transaction.

sub.desc_en: The first view contends that the field is worth 90; the 20 offer is 10 too low and the 100 offer is 10 too high.
The Gemara objects: on the contrary, the field is worth 110; the 100 offer is 10 too low and the 30 offer is 10 too high, concluding that the first two buyers are not removed from the transaction.

Acheirim assess the field at 93⅓, calculating that the 20-offer falls 13⅓ short and the 100-offer overshoots by 13⅓, with the high bidder not adding more because he is content to gain so much over his fellow.
The Gemara objects: on the contrary, the field is worth 113⅓; the 100-offer is 13⅓ too low and the 30-offer overshoots by 13⅓, yet the first two buyers are still not removed from the transaction.

items.text: Ruling on the law according to Acheirim and Dayanei Golah
items.text_en: Ruling on the law according to Acheirim and Dayanei Golah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the law follows Acheirim. Rav Ashi questions this, noting that since we do not know the reasoning of Acheirim, how can we rule like them? The Gemara then cites that the Dayanei Golah also rule that they make an appraisal and divide. Rav Huna rules like the Dayanei Golah, but Rav Ashi again questions this due to lack of knowledge of their reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the law follows Acheirim.
Rav Ashi objects that since we do not know the reasoning of Acheirim, how can we rule like them?
The Gemara cites that the Dayanei Golah also rule that they make an appraisal and divide.
Rav Huna rules that the law follows the Dayanei Golah.
Rav Ashi again objects that since we do not know the reasoning of the Dayanei Golah, how can we rule like them?

items.text: Mishnah: Selling half a field
items.text_en: Mishnah: Selling half a field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where one says to another 'I am selling you half of my field.' They appraise the field and the buyer takes half. If the seller specifies 'half of it in the south,' they appraise and the buyer takes half in the south. The buyer also accepts responsibility for the place of the fence, the ditch, and the bank of the ditch, with specific measurements given.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of selling half a field, specifying the appraisal process, the buyer's right to half in the south if specified, and the buyer's acceptance of responsibility for the fence, ditch, and bank of the ditch with their measurements.

items.text: Gemara: The buyer takes the inferior part
items.text_en: Gemara: The buyer takes the inferior part
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the buyer takes the inferior part of the field. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba objects from the Mishnah which says 'they appraise between them.' Rabbi Yochanan responds by explaining that the Mishnah's phrase 'they appraise' refers to the value, not the division of land, as seen from the latter clause where the buyer specifies a location, yet they still appraise for value.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Abba reports Rav Yochanan's ruling that in a sale of half a field without specification, the buyer receives the inferior part.
Rav Chiyya bar Abba objects to Rav Yochanan from the Mishnah which states 'they appraise between them', implying a fair division rather than the buyer taking the inferior part.

Rav Yochanan rebuts by citing the latter clause of the Mishnah where the buyer specifies a location, and yet it still says 'they appraise', proving that the appraisal is for value (דמי) not for land division.

items.text: Explanation of the ditch and bank
items.text_en: Explanation of the ditch and bank
items.desc_en: A baraisa explains the placement: the ditch is outside the fence and the bank of the ditch is inside. Both are behind the fence.

sub.desc_en: A baraita clarifies the placement of the ditch (חָרִיץ) outside the fence and the bank of the ditch (בֶן חָרִיץ) inside, both behind the fence.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter's discussion on ditches
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter's discussion on ditches
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a practical problem about preventing animals from jumping over a ditch by distinguishing between a חָרִיץ (ditch) and a בֶּן חָרִיץ (smaller ditch), concluding that the difference between them is a tefach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not just make a ditch (חָרִיץ) without a smaller ditch (בֶּן חָרִיץ), and answers that the animal would stand inside the wide ditch and jump.
The Gemara then asks why not make only the smaller ditch, and answers that the animal would stand on its edge and jump.
The Gemara concludes that the difference in depth between a ditch (חָרִיץ) and a smaller ditch (בֶּן חָרִיץ) is one tefach.

items.text: Closing formula of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Closing formula of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing phrase 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ' marks the end of the previous chapter (בֵּית כּוֹר).

sub.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ' marks the end of the previous chapter (בֵּית כּוֹר).

items.text: Opening Mishnah on inheritance: four categories
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah on inheritance: four categories
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents four categories of people regarding inheritance: those who inherit and transmit, those who inherit but do not transmit, those who transmit but do not inherit, and those who neither inherit nor transmit. It then lists examples for each category.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces four categories of relatives regarding inheritance: those who inherit and bequeath, those who inherit but do not bequeath, those who bequeath but do not inherit, and those who neither inherit nor bequeath.

The Mishnah lists specific examples for each category: father and sons and paternal brothers inherit and bequeath; a man to his mother, wife, and nephews inherit but do not bequeath; a woman to her sons, husband, and maternal uncles bequeath but do not inherit; maternal brothers neither inherit nor bequeath.

items.text: Gemara's question on the order of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the order of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah begins with 'the father inherits from the sons' rather than 'the sons inherit from the father', and answers that one does not begin a teaching with a calamity (since a father inheriting from his son is a misfortune).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah begins with 'the father inherits from the sons' rather than 'the sons inherit from the father'.
The Gemara answers that one does not begin a teaching with a calamity, since a father inheriting from his son is a misfortune.

items.text: Gemara's observation on the verse's placement
items.text_en: Gemara's observation on the verse's placement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse 'If a man dies and has no son' is written, and the tanna, because the derivation comes from a midrash, holds it dear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the verse 'If a man dies and has no son' is cited, and the tanna holds it dear because the derivation comes from a midrash.

items.text: The baraita's derivation of father's precedence
items.text_en: The baraita's derivation of father's precedence
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the midrash: 'she'ero' refers to the father, teaching that the father precedes brothers. One might think he precedes the son, but the verse says 'the closest' – the closer relative takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what midrashic derivation the Tanna used, introducing the baraita.
The baraita interprets 'she'ero' as the father, teaching that the father precedes the brothers.
The baraita raises the possibility that the father might precede the son, but rejects it by citing 'the closest' – the closer relative takes precedence.

items.text: Challenge: brother vs. son based on levirate marriage
items.text_en: Challenge: brother vs. son based on levirate marriage
items.desc_en: The baraita asks why the son is included and the brother excluded, answering that the son stands in the father's place for ייעוד and ancestral field. The Gemara objects: the brother stands in the brother's place for יבום. The Gemara counters that יבום only applies where there is no son, so where there is a son, there is no יבום.

sub.desc_en: The baraita asks why the son is included in inheritance and the brother excluded, given the general principle that closer relatives take precedence.
The baraita answers that the son is preferred because he stands in the father's place for ייעוד (designation of a Hebrew maidservant) and for the ancestral field (שדה אחוזה).
An objection is raised: on the contrary, the brother should be preferred because he stands in the brother's place for יבום (levirate marriage).
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that יבום applies only where there is no son, so where there is a son, the brother's יבום status is irrelevant.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion on the necessity of the refutation
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion on the necessity of the refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that were it not for this refutation, one might have thought the brother is preferred; but the refutation shows otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the refutation is necessary to prevent the mistaken assumption that the brother takes precedence over the son.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous argument is inconsistent: in one case there are two reasons, in another only one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous argument is inconsistent: in one case there are two reasons, in another only one.

items.text: Explanation of the Tanna's reasoning
items.text_en: Explanation of the Tanna's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Tanna's logic: the field of inheritance is based on the principle that there is no levirate marriage where there is a son, so a son and daughter are equal in inheritance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna's ruling about the field of inheritance (שדה אחוזה) is based on the principle that levirate marriage (ייבום) only applies where there is no son, so where there is a son, there is no levirate marriage, and thus a son and daughter are equal in inheritance.

items.text: Derivation that father precedes daughter
items.text_en: Derivation that father precedes daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse 'his flesh' teaches that the father precedes the daughter, but not the son, as the word 'the near one' indicates that the closer relative takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the verse 'שארו' (his flesh) refers to the father, teaching that the father precedes the daughter in inheritance.
The Gemara asks whether one might think the father also precedes the son.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'הקרוב' (the near one) teaches that the closer relative takes precedence, so the son, being closer than the father, precedes the father.

items.text: Refutation: son and daughter are equal
items.text_en: Refutation: son and daughter are equal
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the suggestion, arguing that since for levirate marriage a son and daughter are equivalent, for inheritance they are also equivalent, so the father does not precede the son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the suggestion that the father precedes the son, arguing that since for יבום (levirate marriage) a son and daughter are equivalent, for inheritance they are also equivalent, so the father does not precede the son.

items.text: Alternative derivation: father precedes father's brothers
items.text_en: Alternative derivation: father precedes father's brothers
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the verse teaches that the father precedes the father's brothers, but not the deceased's own brothers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative derivation: the verse 'שארו' (his close relative) teaches that the father precedes the father's brothers, but the phrase 'הקרוב' (the close one) indicates that closer relatives take precedence, so the father does not precede the deceased's own brothers.

items.text: Objection: father's brothers don't need a verse
items.text_en: Objection: father's brothers don't need a verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the father's brothers inherit only through the father, so if the father is alive, they cannot inherit; thus no verse is needed to exclude them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the father's brothers do not need a verse to exclude them from inheritance, because they inherit only through the father; if the father is alive, they cannot inherit at all.

items.text: Resolution: verses are written out of order
items.text_en: Resolution: verses are written out of order
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verses are not written in their logical order, so the derivation is valid despite the objection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by stating that the verses are not written in their logical order, so the derivation is valid despite the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's derivation
items.desc_en: The Tanna derives from the verse that in the place of a daughter, you transfer inheritance from the father, but you do not transfer inheritance from the father in the place of brothers. The Gemara then questions whether this applies to transferring from the brothers as well.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei's derivation from the verse 'איש כי ימות ובן אין לו' that inheritance is transferred from the father in the place of a daughter but not in the place of brothers.
The Gemara questions whether the verse could be interpreted to mean that inheritance is transferred from the brothers in the place of a daughter, rather than from the father.

items.text: Gemara's question on the necessity of 'והעברתם'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the necessity of 'והעברתם'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah needed the word 'והעברתם' (and you shall transfer) regarding the daughter's inheritance, since the father cannot transfer inheritance even in the daughter's place. It implies that without this word, one might think otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah needed the word 'והעברתם' (and you shall transfer) regarding the daughter's inheritance, since the father cannot transfer inheritance even in the daughter's place, implying that without this word one might think otherwise.

items.text: Interpretation of 'שארו' for the one who derives from 'והעברתם'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'שארו' for the one who derives from 'והעברתם'
items.desc_en: For the one who derives the daughter's inheritance from 'והעברתם', the Gemara asks what he does with the word 'שארו'. It answers that 'שארו' refers to his wife, teaching that a husband inherits his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the one who derives the husband's inheritance from 'והעברתם', what does he do with the word 'שארו' (his flesh)? It answers that it teaches that the husband inherits his wife.
The Gemara answers that 'שארו' is needed for the teaching that a husband inherits his wife.

items.text: Interpretation of 'והעברתם' for the one who derives from 'שארו'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'והעברתם' for the one who derives from 'שארו'
items.desc_en: For the one who derives the husband's inheritance from 'שארו', the Gemara asks what he does with 'והעברתם'. Rabbi says that in all other inheritances the term 'נתינה' (giving) is used, but here 'העברה' (transfer) is used because only a daughter transfers inheritance from tribe to tribe, since her son and husband inherit her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the one who derives the husband's inheritance from 'שארו', what does he do with 'והעברתם'? It answers that it teaches that only a daughter transfers inheritance from tribe to tribe, since her son and husband inherit her.
Rabbi answers that the term 'העברה' (transfer) is used specifically for a daughter, because she transfers inheritance from tribe to tribe since her son and husband inherit her.

items.text: Challenge: 'שארו' might refer to the mother
items.text_en: Challenge: 'שארו' might refer to the mother
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that 'שארו' refers to the father, citing verses where 'שאר' is used for the mother. It suggests that 'שארו' could mean the mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the proof that 'שארו' refers to the father, suggesting it could refer to the mother, citing the verse 'שאר אמך היא' (she is the flesh of your mother).

items.text: Rava's proof that 'שארו' refers to the father
items.text_en: Rava's proof that 'שארו' refers to the father
items.desc_en: Rava proves that 'שארו' refers to the father by citing the verse 'ממשפחתו וירש אותה', showing that only the father's family is called 'משפחה', as written 'למשפחתם לבית אבותם'. The mother's family is not called 'משפחה'.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the father is intended, because the verse 'ממשפחתו' (from his family) refers only to the father's family, as it is written 'למשפחותם לבית אבותם' (to their families, to their fathers' houses).

items.text: Challenge: Mother's family called 'משפחה' in Scripture
items.text_en: Challenge: Mother's family called 'משפחה' in Scripture
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's proof by citing a verse that calls the mother's family 'משפחת יהודה', indicating that the mother's family is also called 'משפחה'. The verse describes a Levite from the family of Judah, implying his mother was from Judah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mother's family is also called 'משפחה' (family), citing the verse about the Levite from Bethlehem who was from the family of Judah, implying a mixed lineage.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Chanan's resolution: 'Levi' is a personal name
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's resolution: 'Levi' is a personal name
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'Levi' in the verse is not a tribal name but a personal name of a man. The Gemara questions this based on another verse where 'the Levite' is mentioned, and he confirms it was a man named Levi.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan answers that the man named Levi was actually a person named Levi, not a Levite, and the coincidence explains the verse.
The Gemara questions Rava bar Rav Chanan's explanation by citing a verse from Micah where 'the Levite' appears to refer to a tribal Levite, not a personal name.
Rava bar Rav Chanan confirms that in Micah's verse as well, 'the Levite' refers to a man named Levi who happened to be appointed as priest.

items.text: Challenge: The man's name was Yehonatan, not Levi
items.text_en: Challenge: The man's name was Yehonatan, not Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the man's name was not Levi but Yehonatan, as stated in another verse. The Gemara then counters that if so, he was not the son of Menashe but of Moshe, as written. This leads to a resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the man's name was not Levi but Yehonatan, and further questions why he is called 'ben Menashe' when he was actually a descendant of Moses.
The Gemara counters that if so, he was not the son of Menashe but of Moshe, as written.

items.text: Resolution: Scripture attributes a blemish to the blemished
items.text_en: Resolution: Scripture attributes a blemish to the blemished
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that because Yehonatan acted like Menashe (a wicked king), Scripture attributed him to Menashe. Similarly, because the Levite came from Judah (through his mother), Scripture attributed him to Judah, explaining the use of 'משפחת יהודה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that because he acted like Menashe, the verse attributed him to Menashe; similarly, because he came from Judah but acted like Menashe, the verse attributed him to Judah.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: Principle of attributing a blemish to the blemished
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: Principle of attributing a blemish to the blemished
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that from here we learn that Scripture attributes a blemish to the blemished. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds a proof from Adoniyahu being attributed to Avshalom because he rebelled against the kingdom.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai states that the principle is to attribute a flaw to the flawed person, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina supports this with the example of Adoniyahu being attributed to Avshalom.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds a proof from Adoniyahu being attributed to Avshalom because he rebelled against the kingdom, and applies the same principle to the earlier case of Menashe.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: Always cleave to the good
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: Always cleave to the good
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that one should always cleave to the good, as Moshe who married the daughter of Yitro produced Yehonatan (a righteous priest), while Aharon who married the daughter of Aminadav produced Pinchas.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that one should always attach oneself to good people, citing Moses and Aaron as examples who produced righteous descendants.

items.text: Challenge: Pinchas descended from Yitro?
items.text_en: Challenge: Pinchas descended from Yitro?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Pinchas also descended from Yitro, as the verse says Elazar took a wife from the daughters of Putiel, implying from Yitro who fattened calves for idolatry. The Gemara answers that it means from Yosef who controlled his passion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Pinchas also descended from Yitro, who fattened calves for idolatry, but answers that he also descended from Joseph, who controlled his desire.
The Gemara answers that 'Putiel' refers to Yosef, who controlled his passion, not Yitro.

items.text: The tribes' insult: 'Ben Puti' as a disgrace
items.text_en: The tribes' insult: 'Ben Puti' as a disgrace
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the tribes would insult Pinchas, calling him 'ben Puti' – the son of one whose maternal grandfather fattened calves for idolatry, yet he killed a prince of Israel. This highlights the tension in his lineage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that the tribes mocked Pinchas, calling him 'ben Puti' (son of the one who fattened calves for idolatry), questioning how such a person could kill a prince of Israel.

items.text: Lineage of Putiel's daughters
items.text_en: Lineage of Putiel's daughters
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the ambiguity of 'Putiel' by explaining that one of his daughters married a descendant of Yosef and the other married a descendant of Yitro, as implied by the dual meaning of 'Putiel'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the ambiguity of 'Putiel' by explaining that one of his daughters married a descendant of Yosef and the other married a descendant of Yitro, as implied by the dual meaning of 'Putiel'.

items.text: Rava's teaching on checking brothers
items.text_en: Rava's teaching on checking brothers
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse about Aharon marrying Elisheva that a man must investigate the brothers of the woman he intends to marry, because most children resemble their maternal uncles.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that a man who marries a woman must investigate her brothers.
Rava cites the verse about Aharon marrying Elisheva and argues that the extra phrase 'sister of Nachshon' teaches that one must check the brothers.
A baraita (תנא) provides the rationale: most children resemble their maternal uncles.

items.text: Yonatan ben Gershom's encounter with David's messengers
items.text_en: Yonatan ben Gershom's encounter with David's messengers
items.desc_en: David's messengers question Yonatan ben Gershom about his presence, implying he is a descendant of Moshe. Yonatan explains his tradition that it is better to serve idolatry than to be dependent on others, but the Gemara clarifies that 'idolatry' here means any despised work, as Rav advised Rav Kahana.

sub.desc_en: The verse describes David's messengers arriving and questioning Yonatan ben Gershom with three rhetorical questions.
The messengers infer that Yonatan is a descendant of Moshe based on verbal parallels to Moshe's encounters, and demand that he become a priest for idolatry.
Yonatan explains his family tradition that it is better to hire oneself out to idolatry than to be dependent on others.
The Gemara clarifies that Yonatan understood 'idolatry' literally, but the term actually means any despised work, citing Rav's advice to Rav Kahana to take any menial job rather than rely on charity.

items.text: David appoints Yonatan over the treasuries
items.text_en: David appoints Yonatan over the treasuries
items.desc_en: David saw that Yonatan valued money greatly, so he appointed him over the treasuries. Rabbi Yochanan explains that his name Shebuel indicates he returned to God with all his heart.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that David appointed Yonatan over the treasuries because he valued money greatly.
The Gemara questions why the verse calls him Shebuel when his real name is Yonatan.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the name Shebuel indicates he returned (שב) to God (אל) with all his heart.

items.text: Inheritance priority of son over daughter
items.text_en: Inheritance priority of son over daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that a son precedes a daughter in inheritance. Rav Pappa challenges Abaye with a hypothetical: if there is a son and a daughter, neither should inherit, but the Gemara rejects this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a son precedes a daughter in inheritance? It answers from the verse 'אִישׁ כִּי יָמוּת' — if there is no son, the daughter inherits, implying that if there is a son, he precedes.

Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: if the verse implies that a son inherits when there is a son, and a daughter inherits when there is a daughter, then when both exist, neither should inherit — a logical absurdity.
The Gemara rejects Rav Pappa's objection with the word 'וְאֶלָּא' (but rather), implying that the objection is invalid and the simple reading of the verse stands.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's statement about inheritance
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's statement about inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'who inherits' does not mean the son inherits everything, but rather that when there is both a son and a daughter, they inherit together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'who inherits,' asking whether it means the son inherits everything.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah means when there is both a son and a daughter, they inherit together, not that the son inherits everything.

items.text: Abaye's objection and alternative derivation
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Abaye questions the need for a verse to teach that a son inherits all, and suggests the verse might teach that a daughter also inherits, but this is rejected as already derived from another verse.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the verse is unnecessary to teach that a son inherits all when he is the only child, as that is obvious.
Abaye suggests the verse might teach that a daughter also inherits, not just a son.
The Gemara rejects Abaye's suggestion, noting that the daughter's inheritance is already derived from the verse 'וְּכׇל בַּת יֹרֶשֶׁת נַחֲלָה' (and every daughter who inherits property).

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's derivation from the daughters of Zelophehad
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's derivation from the daughters of Zelophehad
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives from the daughters of Zelophehad's statement that a son precedes a daughter. The Gemara questions whether this was their specific plea, but concludes it is a clear derivation as taught originally.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives from the daughters of Zelophehad's statement that a son precedes a daughter.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the daughters of Zelophehad were merely stating their own plea, not establishing a general halachic principle.
The Gemara concludes that the derivation is clear and stands as originally taught.

items.text: Ravina's derivation from 'the closest'
items.text_en: Ravina's derivation from 'the closest'
items.desc_en: Ravina derives from the verse 'the closest to him' that a closer relative precedes. The Gemara questions what makes a son closer than a daughter, suggesting reasons like ייעוד or שדה אחוזה, but rejects them, concluding the derivation is as originally taught.

sub.desc_en: Ravina derives from the verse 'הקרוב אליו' (the closest to him) that a closer relative precedes in inheritance.
The Gemara asks what makes a son closer than a daughter, suggesting reasons of ייעוד (designation as a maidservant's child) and שדה אחוזה (ancestral field).
The Gemara rejects both suggestions: a daughter is not subject to ייעוד, and the rule of שדה אחוזה applies only where there is no son, so neither proves the son's greater closeness.
The Gemara concludes that the derivation stands as originally taught, without needing additional justification.

items.text: Alternative derivation from 'to your sons'
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from 'to your sons'
items.desc_en: An alternative derivation is offered from the verse 'to your sons after you', implying sons but not daughters. The Gemara objects that the same phrase in a blessing cannot exclude daughters, and answers that a blessing is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative derivation from the verse 'וְהִתְנַחַלְתֶּם אֹתָם לִבְנֵיכֶם אַחֲרֵיכֶם' (and you shall bequeath them to your sons after you), interpreting 'sons' to exclude daughters.

The Gemara objects that if 'sons' in the inheritance verse excludes daughters, then the same word 'sons' in the blessing verse 'לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ יְמֵיכֶם וִימֵי בְנֵיכֶם' (that your days and the days of your sons may be multiplied) would also exclude daughters, which is absurd.
The Gemara answers that a blessing (ברכה) is different — the term 'sons' in a blessing is not exclusive, but in the context of inheritance it is.

items.text: Derivation that paternal half-brothers inherit
items.text_en: Derivation that paternal half-brothers inherit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that paternal half-brothers inherit. Rabbah derives it via a verbal analogy from the brothers of Jacob. The Gemara questions why another verse is needed, and clarifies that Rabbah's statement was said regarding levirate marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that paternal half-brothers inherit and bequeath.
Rabbah derives the rule via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the brothers of Jacob, establishing that inheritance follows paternal lineage.
The Gemara objects that a separate verse already teaches that paternal family is called 'family' while maternal family is not, making Rabbah's derivation seemingly unnecessary.
The Gemara resolves that indeed Rabbah's statement was said regarding יבום (levirate marriage), not inheritance.

items.text: Introduction to the next Mishnah
items.text_en: Introduction to the next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss the next Mishnah about a man inheriting from his mother, asking for the source, and introduces a baraitha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the next Mishnah about a man inheriting from his mother and asks for the scriptural source, then cites a baraitha.

items.text: Opening kal vachomer for son's precedence in mother's estate
items.text_en: Opening kal vachomer for son's precedence in mother's estate
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that a daughter inherits two tribes, then uses a kal vachomer to argue that a son should inherit from the mother as well, and that the son precedes the daughter in the mother's estate just as in the father's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how a daughter inherits two tribes, explaining it refers to a case where her father and mother are from different tribes and both die.
The Gemara derives from a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that a son inherits from the mother and precedes the daughter, just as in the father's estate.

items.text: Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav's equal inheritance position
items.text_en: Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav's equal inheritance position
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei state in the name of Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav that son and daughter are equal in the mother's estate, applying the dayo principle to limit the kal vachomer.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei in the name of Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei in the name of Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei state in the name of Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav that son and daughter are equal in the mother's estate.
The reasoning is given: the dayo principle limits the kal vachomer so that the son does not gain priority over the daughter in the mother's estate.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution on dayo
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution on dayo
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the first Tanna rejects the dayo principle, which is Torah-based, and cites the example of Miriam to show that dayo is indeed applied. It then explains that the first Tanna does apply dayo generally, but here the verse 'mattot' equates the mother's tribe to the father's, overriding dayo.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the first Tanna (תנא קמא) rejects the principle of דיו (the dayo principle), which is Torah-based.
The Gemara cites a baraita from the story of Miriam to demonstrate that the dayo principle is indeed applied in Torah law.

The Gemara resolves that the first Tanna generally applies the dayo principle, but here the verse 'מטות' (tribes) equates the mother's tribe to the father's, overriding dayo and establishing that a son precedes a daughter in maternal inheritance.

items.text: Distinction via the verse 'mattot'
items.text_en: Distinction via the verse 'mattot'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first Tanna does apply dayo in general, but here the verse 'mattot' equates the mother's tribe to the father's, so the son precedes the daughter in the mother's estate as in the father's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the first Tanna does apply the principle of דיו (enough) in general, but here the verse 'מטות' (tribes) equates the mother's tribe to the father's, so the son precedes the daughter in the mother's estate as in the father's.

items.text: Stories of rabbis attempting to rule like Rabbi Zecharya
items.text_en: Stories of rabbis attempting to rule like Rabbi Zecharya
items.desc_en: Rav Nittai and Rav Tavla tried to rule like Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav, but Shmuel and Rav Nachman rebuked them. Rav Nachman threatened Rav Tavla and embarrassed Rav Huna bar Chiya, citing that Rav and Shmuel both held the halacha is not like Rabbi Zecharya.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nittai attempted to rule like Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav, but Shmuel rebuked him, saying 'Zecharya is nullified.'
Rav Tavla also ruled like Rabbi Zecharya, citing Rav Chinana bar Shelemia in Rav's name; Rav Nachman threatened to expel Rav Chinana from his ear if he did not retract.
Rav Huna bar Chiya attempted to rule like Rabbi Zecharya, citing Rav Huna in Rav's name; Rav Nachman embarrassed him, noting he only dared after Rav Huna's death.
The gemara concludes that Rav Nachman held like Rav and Shmuel, who both said the הלכה (binding law) is not like Rabbi Zecharya ben Hakatzav.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's encounter and final derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's encounter and final derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai, leaning on Rabbi Simlai, met Rabbi Yehuda Nasi, who asked for the source that a son precedes a daughter in the mother's estate. Rabbi Yannai cited the verse 'mattot', but Rabbi Yehuda Nasi challenged him with the implication that a firstborn would then take a double portion in the mother's estate.

sub.desc_en: The gemara describes Rabbi Yannai leaning on Rabbi Simlai as they encountered Rabbi Yehuda Nasi, who commented on their appearance.
Rabbi Yehuda Nasi asked Rabbi Yannai for the scriptural source that a son precedes a daughter in the mother's estate.
Rabbi Yannai answered by citing the verse 'mattot', which equates the mother's tribe to the father's tribe, so just as a son precedes a daughter in the father's estate, so too in the mother's.
Rabbi Yehuda Nasi objected that if the analogy is complete, then just as a firstborn takes a double portion in the father's estate, so too in the mother's — which is not the halacha.

items.text: Gemara's initial derivation from 'לו'
items.text_en: Gemara's initial derivation from 'לו'
items.desc_en: Abaye derives from the verse 'בכל אשר ימצא לו' that the firstborn takes a double portion only from what belongs to him, not from what belongs to his wife.

sub.desc_en: Abaye derives from the verse 'בכל אשר ימצא לו' that the firstborn takes a double portion only from what belongs to him, not from what belongs to his wife.

items.text: Challenge and alternative derivation from 'אונו'
items.text_en: Challenge and alternative derivation from 'אונו'
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised: perhaps the exclusion applies only when a bachelor marries a widow, but if he marries a virgin, he takes her property. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers with a derivation from 'ראשית אונו' – 'אונו' excludes her strength.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the derivation: perhaps the exclusion of the wife from inheriting applies only when a bachelor marries a widow, but if a bachelor marries a virgin, he does take her property.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers with a derivation from the verse 'ראשית אונו' (the first of his strength), interpreting 'אונו' to exclude her strength, thus the husband does not inherit her property even when he marries a virgin.

items.text: Refutation and resolution with dual derivation
items.text_en: Refutation and resolution with dual derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'ראשית אונו' is needed for the law of a firstborn after miscarriages. It answers that the extra word 'אונו' teaches both laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the word 'אונו' is needed to teach that a firstborn after miscarriages inherits, excluding a child whose father's heart is not pained by his birth.
The Gemara resolves that the verse could have said 'ראשית און' without the extra 'אונו', so the extra word teaches both laws.

items.text: Further challenge and Rava's derivation from 'משפט הבכורה'
items.text_en: Further challenge and Rava's derivation from 'משפט הבכורה'
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised: perhaps the exclusion applies only to a widower marrying a virgin, but a bachelor marrying a virgin takes her property. Rava answers with a derivation from 'לו משפט הבכורה' – the law of the firstborn applies to the man, not the woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further challenge: perhaps the exclusion of the husband from inheriting the wife's property applies only to a widower (אלמון) who marries a virgin, but a bachelor (בחור) who marries a virgin would take her property.

Rava answers by citing the verse 'לו משפט הבכורה' (to him is the law of the firstborn), deriving that the law of the firstborn applies to the man (the husband) and not to the woman (the wife), thus excluding the bachelor's inheritance of the virgin's property.

items.text: Derivation of husband inheriting wife from 'שארו'
items.text_en: Derivation of husband inheriting wife from 'שארו'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: 'שארו' refers to his wife, teaching that a husband inherits his wife. The verse 'וירש אותה' shows he inherits her, not she him. Abaye reinterprets the verse to read 'ונתתם את נחלתו לקרוב אליו שארו וירש אותה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a husband inherits his wife, and cites a baraita that interprets 'שארו' as his wife, teaching this law.
The baraita raises the possibility that the wife might also inherit her husband, and rejects it by citing the verse 'וירש אותה' — he inherits her, not she him.
Abaye resolves the textual difficulty by reinterpreting the verse as 'ונתתם את נחלתו לקרוב אליו שארו וירש אותה', reading the words in a different order.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's forced reading, calling it a 'sharp knife cutting verses'. He explains that the verse means 'ונתתם את נחלת שארו לו', employing the principle of subtracting and adding to interpret.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's forced reading of the verse, calling it a 'sharp knife cutting verses'.
Rava explains that the verse means 'ונתתם את נחלת שארו לו' (you shall give the inheritance of his relative to him), employing the principle of גורעין ומוסיפין (subtracting and adding) to interpret.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael's dispute with proofs
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael's dispute with proofs
items.desc_en: The baraita is attributed to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yishmael says it is unnecessary, citing verses about inheritance not passing from tribe to tribe, and the example of Pinchas inheriting his wife's land, and Segub's cities.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a baraita attributed to Rabbi Akiva, who derives from the verse 'וְיָרַשׁ אוֹתָהּ' that a husband inherits his wife.

Rabbi Yishmael argues that the derivation is unnecessary, citing the verse about a daughter inheriting from one tribe to another, which implies the husband's inheritance through the transfer of property.
Rabbi Yishmael cites two additional verses that prohibit the transfer of inheritance from tribe to tribe, reinforcing the principle that a husband inherits his wife.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael (citing the example of Pinchas)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael (citing the example of Pinchas)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael cites the story of Pinchas inheriting his wife's land, demonstrating that a husband inherits his wife.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael (citing the example of Segub)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael (citing the example of Segub)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael cites the example of Segub, whose son Yair inherited cities, further supporting the principle that a husband inherits his wife's property.

items.text: Opening proof: Yair inherited from his wife
items.text_en: Opening proof: Yair inherited from his wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by asking how Yair could have had cities if he wasn't from Seguv, and answers that he married a woman who died and he inherited her property, establishing that a husband inherits his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Yair could have had cities if he was not from Seguv.
The Gemara answers that Yair married a woman who died and he inherited her property, establishing that a husband inherits his wife.

items.text: Rejecting alternative interpretations with multiple verses
items.text_en: Rejecting alternative interpretations with multiple verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara systematically rejects the possibility that the verses only refer to inheritance through a son (סיבת הבן) and not a husband, by citing additional verses that impose prohibitions (לאו ועשה) and show that even a husband's inheritance is forbidden, culminating in the question of why two verses are needed if both cases are the same.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'ואומר' adds, and proposes that perhaps the verse only prohibits inheritance through a son (סיבת הבן) but allows a husband to inherit, then cites a supporting verse to reject this.
The Gemara suggests that the verse imposes both a negative prohibition (לאו) and a positive command (עשה), and cites another verse to support this.
The Gemara proposes that the verse imposes two negative prohibitions (לאוין) and a positive command (עשה), and cites the verse about Elazar's death to demonstrate that a husband inherits.
The Gemara suggests that perhaps Elazar married a woman who died and Pinchas inherited her, but then cites the verse about Segub fathering Yair to show that a husband inherits.
The Gemara objects that if all cases are the same, why are two separate verses needed, implying that the verses must teach different laws.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge: perhaps husband does not inherit
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge: perhaps husband does not inherit
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye by suggesting that the verses only refer to inheritance through a son, and that Yair and Pinchas simply bought the land, so no proof of husband's inheritance exists.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye by suggesting that the verses only refer to inheritance through a son, and that Yair and Pinchas simply bought the land, so no proof of husband's inheritance exists.

items.text: Abaye's rebuttal: Pinchas could not have bought it
items.text_en: Abaye's rebuttal: Pinchas could not have bought it
items.desc_en: Abaye rejects Rav Pappa's suggestion regarding Pinchas, arguing that if Pinchas bought the land, it would return in the Jubilee year, leaving a righteous man buried in a grave not his own. He then proposes that the land came to Pinchas from the field of devoted things (שדה חרמים).

sub.desc_en: Abaye rejects Rav Pappa's suggestion that Pinchas bought the land, arguing that if so, the field would return in the Jubilee year, leaving a righteous man buried in a grave not his own.
Abaye proposes instead that the land came to Pinchas from the field of devoted things (שדה חרמים), which does not return in the Jubilee.

items.text: Abaye's conclusion: inheritance still transfers tribes
items.text_en: Abaye's conclusion: inheritance still transfers tribes
items.desc_en: Abaye concludes that even with the field of devoted things, the inheritance still transfers from the mother's tribe to the father's tribe, and rejects the possibility that the transfer is acceptable because the land was already transferred (כבר הוסבה).

sub.desc_en: Abaye concludes that even with the field of devoted things, the inheritance still transfers from the mother's tribe to the father's tribe.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the case is different because the land was already transferred (כבר הוסבה) from the mother's tribe.
Abaye rejects the objection, stating that the claim of 'already transferred' (כבר הוסבה) is not accepted.

items.text: Rav Yemar's challenge: the need for the 'already transferred' principle
items.text_en: Rav Yemar's challenge: the need for the 'already transferred' principle
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar argues to Rav Ashi that without the principle of 'already transferred' (כבר הוסבה), the verses cannot be reconciled, because even if a woman marries within her father's tribe, the inheritance still moves from her mother's tribe to her father's tribe, unless she marries a man whose father is from her mother's tribe and mother from her father's tribe.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar opens by stating that if one accepts the principle of 'already transferred' (כבר הוסבה), the verses can be reconciled for both inheritance through a son and through a husband.
Rav Yemar challenges that without the 'already transferred' principle, even if a woman marries within her father's tribe, the inheritance still moves from her mother's tribe to her father's tribe.
Rav Yemar proposes that the only way to avoid the inheritance transfer is if the woman marries a man whose father is from her mother's tribe and whose mother is from her father's tribe.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse says 'to one of the family of the tribe of his father and mother' instead of just 'to one of the family of the tribe of his father', and explains that if it were written that way, one might think it applies even in the reverse case, so the verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse specifies 'to one of the family of the tribe of his father and mother' instead of just 'to one of the family of the tribe of his father'.
The Gemara explains that if the verse were written without 'and mother', one might think it applies even in the reverse case (mother's tribe), so the verse teaches otherwise by adding 'and mother'.

items.text: Baraita on inheritance through a son vs. through a husband
items.text_en: Baraita on inheritance through a son vs. through a husband
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that discusses the verse 'and the inheritance shall not pass from tribe to tribe' – it states that the verse speaks of inheritance through a son. The baraita then argues: if it were only about inheritance through a husband, another verse would suffice; therefore, this verse must be about inheritance through a son.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that there are two baraitot: one about inheritance through a son and one about inheritance through a husband, and then cites the verse 'and the inheritance shall not pass from tribe to tribe' to argue that it speaks of inheritance through a son.
The baraita poses a rhetorical question: do you say the verse speaks of inheritance through a son, or perhaps only through a husband?

The baraita resolves that the verse 'and the inheritance shall not pass from tribe to another tribe' already addresses inheritance through a husband, so the earlier verse must be about inheritance through a son.

items.text: Baraita interpreting the verse about inheritance transfer
items.text_en: Baraita interpreting the verse about inheritance transfer
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'and the inheritance shall not transfer from one tribe to another tribe' refers to transfer through a husband (i.e., a husband inheriting his wife and thereby moving property to his tribe). It contrasts this with transfer through a son, which is addressed by another verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'and the inheritance shall not transfer from one tribe to another tribe' refers to transfer through a husband.

The baraita asks whether the verse refers to transfer through a husband or through a son, and answers that transfer through a son is already addressed by another verse, so this one must refer to a husband.
The gemara asks how we know the verse refers to a husband, and cites a proposed proof from the word 'איש' (man), but rejects it because both husband and son are called 'איש'.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes a proof from the word 'ידבקו' (they shall cleave), but the gemara rejects it because both husband and son are described with 'ידבקו'.
Rava resolves by citing 'ידבקו מטות' (tribes shall cleave), and Rav Ashi adds that the phrase 'ממטה למטה אחר' (from one tribe to another) excludes a son, who is not 'another' tribe.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yannai citing Rabbi, with a tradition from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yannai citing Rabbi, with a tradition from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu transmits a tradition that a husband does not inherit property that was only ראוי (expected) to his wife, as opposed to מוחזק (already possessed), citing the case of Segub who married a woman who died before inheriting, and Yair inherited from her.
A second proof is brought from Elazar's wife who died before inheriting, and Pinchas inherited from her, showing the same principle.

The gemara explains why the second verse was needed: to counter the possibility that Yair inherited through marriage, and to show that a son inherits even property that was only ראוי (expected) to his father.
A tanna states that the rule of 'בני אחות' (sons of a sister) applies, but not 'בנות אחות' (daughters of a sister).

items.text: Gemara's search for the scriptural hint
items.text_en: Gemara's search for the scriptural hint
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the baraita knows the verse refers to a husband and not a son. Several suggestions are made: the word 'ish' (man), the word 'yidbeku' (they shall cleave), and the phrase 'yidbeku mattot' (the tribes shall cleave). Finally, Rav Ashi says that a son is not 'other' (acher) relative to his mother's tribe, so the verse must refer to a husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the baraita derives that the verse 'from one tribe to another tribe' refers to a husband and not a son.
Rabba bar Rav Sheila suggests the word 'איש' (man) indicates the husband, but the Gemara objects that both husband and son are called 'איש'.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak suggests the word 'ידבקו' (they shall cleave) indicates the husband, but the Gemara objects that both husband and son are described with 'ידבקו'.
Rava suggests the phrase 'ידבקו מטות' (the tribes shall cleave) indicates the husband.
Rav Ashi resolves the question by noting that a son is not 'אחר' (other) relative to his mother's tribe, so the verse must refer to a husband.

items.text: Proof that a husband does not inherit ra'uy
items.text_en: Proof that a husband does not inherit ra'uy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing a chain back to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, derives from the verse about Yair that a husband does not inherit property that was only due to his wife (ra'uy). The case: Segub married a woman who died before her parents, and when the parents died, Yair (Segub's son) inherited the property, not Segub.
