A second proof from Pinchas is brought, and the Gemara explains that the second verse is needed to rule out the possibility that Yair inherited through his own marriage or through a field of devoted property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing a chain back to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, derives from the verse about Yair that a husband does not inherit property that was only due to his wife (ra'uy), using the case of Segub who married a woman who died before her parents, and when the parents died, Yair (Segub's son) inherited the property.
A second proof is brought from the verse about Elazar and Pinchas, showing that Pinchas inherited property that was only due to his father Elazar (ra'uy), not Elazar himself.

The Gemara explains that the second verse is needed to rule out the possibility that Yair inherited through his own marriage or through a field of devoted property, concluding that a husband does not inherit ra'uy.

items.text: Sons of a sister inherit, not daughters
items.text_en: Sons of a sister inherit, not daughters
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the sons of a sister (i.e., a woman's sons from a previous marriage) inherit from her, but not the daughters of a sister.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the sons of a sister inherit from her, but not the daughters of a sister.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Sheshet's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Sheshet's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halakha is derived from the verse, and Rav Sheshet answers that it is to give precedence (to a son over a daughter in inheritance).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halakha is derived from the verse.
Rav Sheshet answers that the verse teaches to give precedence (to a son over a daughter in inheritance).

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's teaching: analogy between first and second inheritance
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's teaching: analogy between first and second inheritance
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak taught before Rav Huna that the verse 've-yarash' compares secondary inheritance to primary inheritance: just as in primary inheritance a son precedes a daughter, so too in secondary inheritance a son precedes a daughter.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's teaching
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's teaching
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak taught before Rav Huna that the verse 'וְיָרַשׁ' (and he shall inherit) compares secondary inheritance to primary inheritance: just as in primary inheritance a son precedes a daughter, so too in secondary inheritance a son precedes a daughter.

items.text: Rabba bar Chanina's teaching and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rabba bar Chanina's teaching and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Chanina taught before Rav Nachman that inheritance is apportioned only by day, not by night. Abaye objects: if so, one who dies at night would not be inherited by his sons? The Gemara clarifies that the teaching refers to the law of inheritance (din nachalot), as a baraita states that the entire passage is for judgment.

sub.text: Rabba bar Chanina's teaching before Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Chanina's teaching before Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Chanina teaches before Rav Nachman that inheritance is apportioned only by day, not by night, based on the verse 'וְהָיָה בְּיוֹם הַנְחִילוֹ אֶת בָּנָיו' (and it shall be on the day he bequeaths to his sons).
Abaye objects: if inheritance only applies by day, then one who dies at night would not be inherited by his sons, which is absurd.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabba bar Chanina's teaching refers to the law of inheritance (דין נחלות), not the actual transfer of property, as a baraita states that the entire passage is for judgment.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on three visitors and the law of day
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on three visitors and the law of day
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda's ruling: three who enter to visit a sick person may, if they wish, write (a will) or adjudicate; two may write but not adjudicate. Rav Chisda adds that this applies only by day.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that three visitors to a sick person may, if they wish, write a will or adjudicate, while two may write but not adjudicate.
Rav Chisda adds that this ruling applies only by day, not at night.

items.text: Nighttime court rule and its rationale
items.text_en: Nighttime court rule and its rationale
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that at night, even three judges may write the verdict but not execute judgment, because they also serve as witnesses and a witness cannot become a judge. The interlocutor confirms this is the intended meaning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that at night, even three judges may write the verdict but not execute judgment, because they also serve as witnesses and a witness cannot become a judge.
The interlocutor confirms that this is indeed the intended meaning of the earlier statement.

items.text: Dispute on when a kinyan can be retracted
items.text_en: Dispute on when a kinyan can be retracted
items.desc_en: An explicit dispute is recorded: Rabba says a kinyan can be retracted as long as the judges are still seated; Rav Yosef says it can be retracted as long as they are still engaged in that matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: until when can a formal acquisition (קִנְיָן) be retracted?
Rabba rules that the kinyan can be retracted as long as the judges are still seated.
Rav Yosef rules that the kinyan can be retracted only as long as the judges are still engaged in that same matter.

items.text: Rav Yosef's proof from visiting the sick
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's proof from visiting the sick
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that his view is more reasonable, citing Rav Yehuda: three who enter to visit a sick person may, if they wish, write a will or execute judgment. If retraction were possible as long as seated, there would be a concern that the sick person might retract.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef opens by asserting that his own view is more reasonable, citing Rav Yehuda's teaching about three who visit a sick person.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching (cited by Rav Yosef)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching (cited by Rav Yosef)
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites Rav Yehuda's rule that three visitors to a sick person may, if they wish, write a will or execute judgment.
Rav Yosef argues that if retraction were possible as long as the judges are seated, there would be a concern that the sick person might retract.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge to Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge to Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he stated this teaching before Rav Kahana, questioning: according to Rav Yosef, is it satisfactory? There is still a concern that the sick person might retract! The Gemara begins to answer that the case is where they have concluded their session.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he presented this teaching before Rav Kahana and raises a challenge: according to Rav Yosef's position, is it satisfactory? There is still a concern that the sick person might retract!
The Gemara answers that the case is where they have concluded their session (סליקו), so retraction is no longer possible.

items.text: Transition and ruling
items.text_en: Transition and ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara transitions from one topic to another, noting that the Sages stood and sat back down. It then rules like Rav Yosef regarding a field, with the terms 'inyan' and 'mechetza'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara transitions from one topic to another, noting that the Sages stood and sat back down.
The Gemara rules like Rav Yosef regarding a field, with the terms 'ענין' (topic) and 'מחצה' (half).

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah teaches 'the woman with her son' when it already taught 'the man with his mother' and 'the man with his wife'. It answers that this teaches that a woman with her son is analogous to a woman with her husband: just as a husband does not inherit his wife in the grave, so too a son does not inherit his mother in the grave to pass on to paternal brothers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah teaches 'the woman with her son' when it already taught 'the man with his mother' and 'the man with his wife'.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that a woman with her son is analogous to a woman with her husband: just as a husband does not inherit his wife in the grave, so too a son does not inherit his mother in the grave to pass on to paternal brothers.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's tradition on Torah law
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's tradition on Torah law
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon that by Torah law, a father inherits his son and a mother inherits her son, as derived from the verse 'matot' which equates the mother's tribe to the father's tribe.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan transmits a tradition from Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon that by Torah law, a father inherits his son and a mother inherits her son.
The tradition derives this law from the verse 'מטות' (tribes), which equates the mother's tribe to the father's tribe, so just as a father inherits his son, a mother inherits her son.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Rabbi Yehuda ben Shimon
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Rabbi Yehuda ben Shimon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a mishnah stating that a woman transmits inheritance to her son and her husband, and maternal brothers transmit but do not inherit. Rabbi Yehuda ben Shimon responds that he does not know who taught that mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Rabbi Yehuda ben Shimon by citing a mishnah that states a woman transmits inheritance to her son and husband, and maternal brothers transmit but do not inherit.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Shimon responds that he does not know who taught that mishnah.

items.text: Analysis of the mishnah's authorship
items.text_en: Analysis of the mishnah's authorship
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the mishnah could be Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav's, who does not expound the word 'matot'. It then rejects this because the mishnah mentions 'sons of a sister' and not daughters, and Rabbi Zecharya holds that son and daughter are equal in maternal inheritance. The Gemara further argues that if the mishnah were his, it would be inconsistent regarding a woman inheriting her son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah could be attributed to Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav, who does not expound the word 'matot'.
The Gemara objects that the mishnah cannot be Rabbi Zecharya's because it mentions 'sons of a sister' and not daughters, and Rav Sheshet explains this is to establish priority.
The Gemara argues that if the mishnah were Rabbi Zecharya's, it would contradict his view that son and daughter are equal in maternal inheritance.
The Gemara resolves that from either perspective—whether the Tanna expounds 'matot' or not—the mishnah's position on a woman inheriting her son is inconsistent with Rabbi Zecharya's view.

items.text: Resolution: the mishnah expounds 'matot' but limits a woman's inheritance
items.text_en: Resolution: the mishnah expounds 'matot' but limits a woman's inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the mishnah does expound 'matot', but the verse 'every daughter who inherits' teaches that she inherits but does not transmit inheritance to her son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the mishnah indeed expounds 'matot', but the verse 'every daughter who inherits' teaches that she inherits but does not transmit inheritance to her son.

items.text: Mishnah: the order of inheritance
items.text_en: Mishnah: the order of inheritance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the order of inheritance: a son precedes a daughter, and his descendants precede her; a daughter precedes brothers; brothers precede paternal uncles; and the father precedes all his descendants.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by presenting the order of inheritance, citing the verse and listing the priority: a son precedes a daughter, his descendants precede her, a daughter precedes brothers, brothers precede paternal uncles, and the father precedes all his descendants.

items.text: Gemara: baraita expanding the definition of descendants
items.text_en: Gemara: baraita expanding the definition of descendants
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that from 'ben' (son) we include a son's son, daughter's son, etc., and from 'bat' (daughter) we include a daughter's daughter, son's daughter, etc., by expounding the word 'lo' (to him) as 'ayin alav' (look upon him).

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that from the word 'בן' (son) we include all male descendants, and from 'בת' (daughter) we include all female descendants, by expounding the word 'לו' (to him) as 'עיין עליו' (look upon him).

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says inheritance goes up to Reuben, not Jacob, and Abaye explains that a tribe never entirely ceases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says inheritance goes up to Reuben rather than directly to Jacob.
Abaye explains that a tribe never entirely ceases, so inheritance traces through the tribe to Reuben.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling against daughter inheriting with son's daughter
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling against daughter inheriting with son's daughter
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says that anyone who says a daughter inherits alongside a son's daughter is not listened to, as it is a Sadducean practice, citing a baraita about the 24th of Tevet.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states in the name of Rav that anyone who says a daughter inherits alongside a son's daughter is not listened to, even if a prince, because it is a Sadducean practice.
A baraita is cited that on the 24th of Tevet the rabbis returned to their court, because the Sadducees had been saying that a daughter inherits alongside a son's daughter.

items.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's debate with a Sadducee elder
items.text_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's debate with a Sadducee elder
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai confronts the Sadducees, and one elder argues that if a son's daughter inherits from her grandfather, then his own daughter should certainly inherit.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai confronts the Sadducees and asks them for the source of their position.
A Sadducee elder argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori): if a son's daughter inherits through her father, then his own daughter should certainly inherit directly.

items.text: Proof from the genealogy of Seir and resolution of Anah's identity
items.text_en: Proof from the genealogy of Seir and resolution of Anah's identity
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai cites a verse showing that Zibeon fathered Anah through his mother, proving that a son's daughter does not inherit. The Gemara then resolves a potential contradiction by identifying Anah as the same person.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai cites the verse from Seir's genealogy to prove that Zibeon fathered Anah through his mother, demonstrating that a son's daughter does not inherit.
The Gemara objects that perhaps there were two different individuals named Anah, undermining the proof.
Rabbah (or alternatively Rav Pappa) states a teaching that even King Shapur did not say, identifying the authority as Shmuel (or Rabbah).
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing the verse 'הוּא עֲנָה' (he is Anah), indicating that it is the same Anah as originally mentioned.

items.text: The elder's response and Rabban Yochanan's rebuke
items.text_en: The elder's response and Rabban Yochanan's rebuke
items.desc_en: The elder asks if he is dismissed with this answer, and Rabban Yochanan calls him a fool, implying the proof is insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Sadducee elder asks Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai if he is dismissed with this answer, expressing dissatisfaction.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai calls the elder a fool, rejecting his argument as insufficient.

items.text: Victory of the Sages over the Sadducees
items.text_en: Victory of the Sages over the Sadducees
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that the Sages defeated the Sadducees in a debate about inheritance, establishing that a daughter's daughter inherits in the presence of brothers, but a daughter does not. This day was made a holiday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that the Sages defeated the Sadducees in a debate about inheritance, establishing that a daughter's daughter inherits in the presence of brothers, but a daughter does not, and this day was made a holiday.

items.text: Proof from the Tribe of Benjamin
items.text_en: Proof from the Tribe of Benjamin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami explains that the verse about Benjamin's inheritance teaches that they stipulated that a daughter's daughter should not inherit with brothers. This supports the earlier ruling.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami interprets the verse about Benjamin's inheritance to prove that they stipulated a daughter's daughter should not inherit alongside brothers, supporting the earlier ruling.

items.text: One Who Leaves No Son Incurs Divine Wrath
items.text_en: One Who Leaves No Son Incurs Divine Wrath
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that anyone who does not leave a son to inherit him incurs divine wrath, as derived from a verbal analogy between 'transferring inheritance' and 'day of wrath'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that one who leaves no son to inherit him incurs divine wrath, derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'והעברתם את נחלתו' (you shall transfer his inheritance) and 'יום עברה' (day of wrath).

items.text: Dispute: Son vs. Disciple
items.text_en: Dispute: Son vs. Disciple
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi debate the meaning of a verse: one says it refers to one who leaves no son, the other to one who leaves no disciple. The Gemara attempts to identify which opinion belongs to which rabbi, citing evidence from Rabbi Yochanan's own statement and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's practice, concluding that Rabbi Yochanan's statement is from his teacher, resolving the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi over the meaning of the verse 'אֲשֶׁר אֵין חֲלִיפוֹת לָמוֹ' (who have no changes): one says it refers to one who leaves no son, the other to one who leaves no disciple.
The Gemara attempts to determine which opinion belongs to which rabbi, suggesting that Rabbi Yochanan is the one who said 'disciple' based on his own statement about a tenth-born son.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Yochanan said 'disciple', then Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi must have said 'son' — but this contradicts evidence from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's practice.

The Gemara cites that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi only visited a house of mourning for one who died without sons, citing the verse 'בְּכוּ בָכֹה לַהֹלֵךְ' (weep for the one who goes) and Rav Yehuda's interpretation that this refers to one who dies without a male son, proving that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi actually said 'disciple'.
The Gemara objects again: if Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said 'disciple', then Rabbi Yochanan must have said 'son' — but this contradicts the earlier evidence from Rabbi Yochanan's own statement.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's statements: one is his own opinion (that the verse refers to a son), the other is from his teacher (that it refers to a disciple).

items.text: David and Yoav: Leaving a Son Like Oneself
items.text_en: David and Yoav: Leaving a Son Like Oneself
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Chama explains why the verse uses 'lying down' for David and 'death' for Yoav: David left a son like himself, while Yoav did not. The Gemara objects that Yoav did have a son, but clarifies that he did not leave a son comparable to himself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Chama asks why the verse uses 'שכיבה' (lying down) for David and 'מיתה' (death) for Yoav, and answers that David left a son while Yoav did not.
The Gemara objects that Yoav did leave a son, citing the verse listing Obadiah ben Yechiel among Yoav's descendants.

The Gemara resolves the objection by clarifying that the distinction is not about having any son, but about leaving a son comparable to oneself: David left a son like himself (Solomon), while Yoav did not.

items.text: Poverty and Illness: Seeking a Sage
items.text_en: Poverty and Illness: Seeking a Sage
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Chama teaches that poverty is worse than fifty plagues, and that one with a sick person in the house should go to a sage for mercy. These are aggadic teachings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Chama teaches that poverty within a person's house is worse than fifty plagues, citing a verse from Job.
Rabbi Pinchas bar Chama teaches that one with a sick person in the house should go to a sage for mercy, citing a verse from Proverbs.

items.text: Question: Grandfather vs. Uncles
items.text_en: Question: Grandfather vs. Uncles
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the father precedes all descendants. Rami bar Chama asks: in the case of a grandfather and uncles (e.g., Abraham and Ishmael regarding Esau's estate), who comes first? Rava attempts to answer from the Mishnah, but the Gemara cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: whoever comes first in inheritance, his descendants precede him, and the father precedes all his descendants.
Rami bar Chama asks: in the case of a grandfather and uncles (e.g., Abraham and Ishmael regarding Esau's estate), who comes first?
Rava attempts to answer from the Mishnah's statement that the father precedes all his descendants.
The Gemara cuts off Rava's answer, indicating that the discussion is incomplete or that Rami bar Chama's question remains unresolved.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara comments that due to his sharpness, Rami bar Hama did not examine the Mishnah carefully before posing his question.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara comments that due to his sharpness, Rami bar Hama did not examine the Mishnah carefully before posing his question.

items.text: Rami bar Hama's question and resolution
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama's question and resolution
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama asks: in the case of a grandfather and a brother (e.g., Abraham and Jacob inheriting from Esau), who comes first? Rava cites a Mishnah that the father precedes all his descendants, and Rami bar Hama clarifies that this refers to the father's own descendants, not his son's. The Gemara then supports this with a logical inference from the rule that one who precedes in inheritance gives precedence to his descendants.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Hama asks: between the father's father (grandfather) and the father's brother, who inherits first?
Rava answers by citing a baraita: the father precedes all his descendants, meaning the grandfather precedes the father's brother, who is a descendant of the grandfather.
The Gemara provides additional support from the Mishnah's rule: if Isaac were alive he would precede Jacob, so now that Isaac is dead, Jacob (as Isaac's descendant) precedes Esau's other heirs.
The Gemara supports this with a logical inference from the rule that one who precedes in inheritance gives precedence to his descendants.

items.text: Mishnah: Daughters of Zelophehad
items.text_en: Mishnah: Daughters of Zelophehad
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the daughters of Zelophehad took three portions in the inheritance: their father's portion (with those who left Egypt), his portion with his brothers in the property of Hepher, and the extra portion due to Zelophehad being a firstborn.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the daughters of Zelophehad took three portions in the inheritance: their father's portion with the Exodus generation, his portion with his brothers in the property of Hepher, and the firstborn's double portion.

items.text: Gemara's opening question
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishna follows the opinion that the land was divided among those who left Egypt, citing a Tannaitic source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Mishna follows the opinion that the land was divided among those who left Egypt, citing a Tannaitic source.

items.text: Rabbi Yoshiyah's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yoshiyah's opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiyah argues that the land was divided among the Exodus generation, citing the verse 'לִשְׁמוֹת מַטּוֹת אֲבֹתָם יִנְחָלוּ' and interpreting 'לָאֵלֶּה' to exclude minors.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yoshiya's opinion that the land was divided among those who left Egypt, based on the verse 'לִשְׁמוֹת מַטּוֹת אֲבֹתָם יִנְחָלוּ', and explains that 'לָאֵלֶּה' excludes minors.

items.text: Rabbi Yonatan's opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan's opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan argues that the land was divided among those who entered the land, citing the verse 'לָאֵלֶּה תֵּחָלֵק הָאָרֶץ' and explaining that this inheritance is unique: the dead inherit the living.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is difficult for Rabbi Yoshiya?
Rabbi Yonatan explains that the verse 'לִשְׁמוֹת מַטּוֹת אֲבֹתָם יִנְחָלוּ' teaches that this inheritance is unique: the dead inherit the living.

items.text: Rabbi's parable
items.text_en: Rabbi's parable
items.desc_en: Rabbi offers a parable of two priestly brothers with different numbers of sons who go to the threshing floor, take portions, then return to their father and divide equally, illustrating the inheritance principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers with a mashal (parable) of two priest brothers with one and two sons, who go to the granary and take shares, then return to their father and divide equally.
Rabbi describes two priestly brothers with different numbers of sons who go to the threshing floor and take portions according to their sons.
Rabbi concludes the parable: the brothers return to their father and divide the portions equally, illustrating the inheritance principle.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar begins his opinion, but the text is cut off; the section ends here.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds a statement (likely a continuation or alternative view).

items.text: Resolution of the division of the land
items.text_en: Resolution of the division of the land
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the land was divided to fulfill two verses: those who left Egypt and those who entered the land each receive a portion according to their status. A person who was both receives a portion from both groups.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the land was divided to fulfill two verses: those who left Egypt and those who entered the land each receive a portion according to their status, and a person who was both receives from both groups.

items.text: Status of specific groups
items.text_en: Status of specific groups
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Joshua and Caleb, the spies who remained faithful, received their portion. The complainers and Korach's assembly received no portion, but their children inherited through the merit of their fathers or mothers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Joshua and Caleb received their portion in the land, while the complainers and Korach's assembly received none, but their children inherited through the merit of their fathers or mothers.

items.text: Proof that the verse refers to the Exodus generation
items.text_en: Proof that the verse refers to the Exodus generation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the phrase 'by the names of the tribes of their fathers' refers to the Exodus generation, and answers that it is derived from the verse 'I will give it to you as a possession'—an inheritance from their ancestors, spoken to the Exodus generation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the phrase 'לִשְׁמוֹת מַטּוֹת אֲבֹתָם' (by the names of the tribes of their fathers) refers specifically to the Exodus generation, suggesting it might instead refer to the tribes themselves.

The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְנָתַתִּי אֹתָהּ לָכֶם מוֹרָשָׁה אֲנִי ה׳' (I will give it to you as a possession, I am the Lord) indicates an inheritance from their ancestors, and this was spoken to the Exodus generation.

items.text: Mnemonic for the following discussion
items.text_en: Mnemonic for the following discussion
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided to aid memory for the subsequent topics: לָרַב, צְלָפְחָד, וְיוֹסֵף, אִיכְּפַל, מְנַשֶּׁה, יְחַשֵּׁב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic (סִימָן) listing key terms for the following discussion: לָרַב, צְלָפְחָד, וְיוֹסֵף, אִיכְּפַל, מְנַשֶּׁה, יְחַשֵּׁב.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: According to the view that the land was divided among the Exodus generation, this explains the verse 'to the many you shall increase their inheritance and to the few you shall diminish their inheritance'—which implies division based on the original census.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: According to the view that the land was divided among the Exodus generation, this explains the verse 'to the many you shall increase their inheritance and to the few you shall diminish their inheritance'—which implies division based on the original census.

items.text: Question on the verse for the opinion of 'those who entered the land'
items.text_en: Question on the verse for the opinion of 'those who entered the land'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: according to the opinion that the land was divided among those who entered the land, what does the verse 'to the many you shall increase their inheritance' mean?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: according to the opinion that the land was divided among those who entered the land, what does the verse 'to the many you shall increase their inheritance' mean?

items.text: Rav Pappa's question and answer about the daughters of Zelophehad
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question and answer about the daughters of Zelophehad
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: according to the opinion that the land was divided among those who entered the land, why did the daughters of Zelophehad complain? They would not receive anything. The Gemara answers: they complained to receive a portion in the property of the one who died without heirs (חפר).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: according to the opinion that the land was divided among those who entered the land, why did the daughters of Zelophehad complain? They would not receive anything.
The Gemara answers: they complained to receive a portion in the property of the one who died without heirs (חפר).

items.text: Question and answer about the sons of Joseph
items.text_en: Question and answer about the sons of Joseph
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that the land was divided among those who entered the land, why did the sons of Joseph complain? They all received portions. The answer is: they complained because they had many dependents (טפלים).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that the land was divided among those who entered the land, why did the sons of Joseph complain? They all received portions.
The Gemara answers: they complained because they had many dependents (טפלים) who were not counted among the original recipients.

items.text: Abaye's inference that everyone received a portion
items.text_en: Abaye's inference that everyone received a portion
items.desc_en: Abaye infers from the fact that only the daughters of Zelophehad and the sons of Joseph complained that everyone else received a portion. He rejects the possibility that someone who did not receive a portion complained but was not recorded, because the sons of Joseph complained and were not helped, yet their complaint was recorded.

sub.desc_en: Abaye infers from the fact that only the daughters of Zelophehad and the sons of Joseph complained that everyone received a portion.
The Gemara objects that perhaps someone who did not receive a portion complained but was not recorded because his complaint was not helped.
Abaye rejects the objection by noting that the sons of Joseph complained and were not helped, yet their complaint was recorded.

items.text: Resolution: the sons of Joseph's complaint teaches a lesson
items.text_en: Resolution: the sons of Joseph's complaint teaches a lesson
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the sons of Joseph's complaint was recorded to teach a good lesson: one should beware of the evil eye. Joshua told them to hide in the forest so that the evil eye would not control them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the sons of Joseph's complaint was recorded to teach a good lesson: one should beware of the evil eye, and Joshua told them to hide in the forest so that the evil eye would not control them.

items.text: Joseph's descendants are immune to the evil eye
items.text_en: Joseph's descendants are immune to the evil eye
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the descendants of Joseph are not subject to the evil eye, based on a verse and a teaching of Rabbi Avahu, and Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina derives this from the blessing of fish.

sub.desc_en: The Sages declare that they are from Joseph's seed, which is immune to the evil eye, citing the verse 'בן פורת יוסף' and Rabbi Avahu's midrashic reading of 'עולי עין' (rising above the eye).

sub.text: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina's alternative derivation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina's alternative derivation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina derives Joseph's immunity from the blessing 'וידגו לרוב' (may they multiply like fish), comparing fish hidden by water to Joseph's descendants who are likewise protected from the evil eye.

items.text: Joshua and Caleb received their portion from the spies
items.text_en: Joshua and Caleb received their portion from the spies
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that Joshua and Caleb received their portion in the land from the spies, as derived from the verse that says they 'lived' from among the men, meaning they lived in their portion.

sub.desc_en: Ulla explains that Joshua and Caleb received their portion in the land from the spies, as derived from the verse that says they 'lived' from among the men, meaning they lived in their portion.

items.text: Dispute over the complainers and Korah's assembly
items.text_en: Dispute over the complainers and Korah's assembly
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: one source says the complainers and Korah's assembly had no portion, while another says Joshua and Caleb took their portion. The Gemara resolves this by noting a dispute: one Tanna compares the complainers to the spies, while another does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the complainers and Korah's assembly had no portion in the land.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says Joshua and Caleb took their portion from the complainers and Korah's assembly.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting a dispute: one Tanna compares the complainers to the spies, while another does not.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about the complainers
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about the complainers
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if the complainers are compared to the spies, would Joshua and Caleb have doubled their portion and inherited all of Eretz Yisrael? Abaye clarifies that they refer to the complainers within Korah's assembly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: according to the opinion that compares the complainers to the spies, would Joshua and Caleb have doubled their portion and inherited all of Eretz Yisrael?
Abaye clarifies that the comparison refers only to the complainers within Korah's assembly, not to all complainers.

items.text: Dispute over whether the land was divided for those who left Egypt or those who entered
items.text_en: Dispute over whether the land was divided for those who left Egypt or those who entered
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa questions Abaye about the division of Menashe's portions: for those who say the land was divided for those who left Egypt, there are ten portions; for those who say for those who entered, there are eight. The Gemara resolves the discrepancy by noting that there were additional brothers of the father.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: according to the view that the land was divided for those who left Egypt, the verse 'וַיִּפְּלוּ חַבְלֵי מְנַשֶּׁה עֲשָׂרָה' (the portions of Menashe fell ten) makes sense — six portions for the six paternal houses and four for themselves, totaling ten.

Rav Pappa continues: but according to the view that the land was divided for those who entered the land, only eight portions would be expected — six for the paternal houses and two for themselves, not ten.

Abaye responds: according to your own reasoning, even for the view of those who left Egypt, there would be only nine portions, so you must say they had an additional brother of the father; similarly, here they had two additional brothers of the father, making ten.

items.text: The inheritance of the daughters of Zelophehad
items.text_en: The inheritance of the daughters of Zelophehad
items.desc_en: A baraita explains the verses regarding the daughters of Zelophehad: they inherited their father's portion, their grandfather's portion, and the firstborn's portion. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that they also took the portion of their father's brother, and for those who say there were two brothers, that is derived from 'achuzat nachalah'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verses to show that the daughters of Zelophehad inherited their father's portion, their grandfather's portion, and the firstborn's double portion.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that they also took the portion of their father's brother, and for those who say there were two brothers, that is derived from 'achuzat nachalah'.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about the count of families
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about the count of families
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: what does the verse count? If it counts dependents, there were many; if it counts paternal houses, there were only six.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye what the verse counts: if it counts dependents (טפלים), there were many; if it counts paternal houses (בתי אבות), there were only six.

items.text: Gemara's initial claim: daughters took a firstborn's portion
items.text_en: Gemara's initial claim: daughters took a firstborn's portion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that the daughters of Zelophehad received a firstborn's portion, implying that the land of Israel was considered held property (מוחזקת).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that the daughters of Zelophehad received a firstborn's portion, implying that the land of Israel was considered מוחזקת (held property).

items.text: Contradiction about the basis of inheritance: merit of ancestors vs. themselves
items.text_en: Contradiction about the basis of inheritance: merit of ancestors vs. themselves
items.desc_en: Mar's statement that the sons inherited by merit of their fathers is contradicted by a baraita saying they inherited by their own merit. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between those who left Egypt and those who entered the land, or by age (over or under twenty).

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the sons inherited by merit of their paternal grandfather and maternal grandfather.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says the sons inherited by their own merit, not their ancestors'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between those who left Egypt (inherited by ancestors' merit) and those who entered the land (inherited by their own merit).
Alternatively, the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between those over twenty years old (inherited by their own merit) and those under twenty (inherited by ancestors' merit).

items.text: Question: How can a firstborn take a double portion in land that was not yet held?
items.text_en: Question: How can a firstborn take a double portion in land that was not yet held?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a firstborn would take a double portion in the land of Israel, since it was not yet held property (ראוי). Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that it refers to tent pegs (יתדות אוהלים), which are movable property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a firstborn can take a double portion in land that was only ראוי (not yet held property).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel answers that the double portion refers to tent pegs (יתדות אוהלים), which are movable property, not land.

items.text: Rabbah's objection and alternative answer
items.text_en: Rabbah's objection and alternative answer
items.desc_en: Rabbah objects based on a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says the daughters took four portions, implying land. Rabbah concludes that the land of Israel is considered held property (מוחזקת).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects by citing Rabbi Yehuda's statement that the daughters of Zelophehad took four portions, implying land inheritance, which challenges the earlier assumption.
Rabbah resolves the objection by asserting that the land of Israel is considered מוחזקת (held property), so the firstborn's portion applies even to land that was not yet physically possessed.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Chidka: Moses knew the daughters inherit but not about the firstborn's portion
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Chidka: Moses knew the daughters inherit but not about the firstborn's portion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chidka reports that Shimon HaShikmoni said Moses knew the daughters were heirs but was unsure about the firstborn's portion. The section also compares this to the case of the wood-gatherer, where Moses knew the punishment but not the method of execution, teaching that worthy people cause Torah sections to be written through their actions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chidka reports that Shimon HaShikmoni said Moses knew the daughters of Zelophehad inherit but was unsure whether they take a firstborn's portion.
The baraita states that the section of inheritances was worthy of being written through Moses, but the daughters of Zelophehad merited that it be written through their case.

The baraita compares this to the wood-gatherer: Moses knew the punishment was death but not the method, and the wood-gatherer's guilt caused the section to be written through him, teaching that worthy people cause Torah sections to be written.

items.text: Gemara's question about the uncertainty of the land inheritance
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the uncertainty of the land inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the daughters of Zelophehad were uncertain about the inheritance of Eretz Yisrael, given the principle that merit is rolled through the worthy. It explains that they were uncertain about the nature of the inheritance—whether it is a permanent inheritance from ancestors or a temporary possession. They received two answers: it is both an inheritance and something that is inherited but not passed on, as hinted in the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that merit is rolled through the worthy and liability through the liable.
The Gemara asks: if Eretz Yisrael was already assured, what were the daughters of Zelophehad uncertain about?
The Gemara explains that they were uncertain about the nature of the inheritance: whether it is a permanent inheritance from ancestors or a temporary possession that is inherited but not passed on.
The Gemara resolves that they received both answers: it is both an inheritance from ancestors and something that is inherited but not passed on, as hinted by the verse.

items.text: Dispute about the order of standing before the leaders
items.text_en: Dispute about the order of standing before the leaders
items.desc_en: The verse describes the daughters standing before Moses, Eleazar, the princes, and the entire congregation. Rabbi Yoshiyah argues that the verse should be reinterpreted (seres) to mean they stood before all of them simultaneously. Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer says they were sitting in the study hall and then stood before all of them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the literal sequence of the verse: how could the daughters stand before Moses, Eleazar, the princes, and the entire congregation without receiving a response at each stage?
Rabbi Yoshiyah answers that the verse should be reinterpreted (סרס) to mean they stood before all of them simultaneously.
Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer answers that the leaders were sitting in the study hall, and the daughters went and stood before all of them together.

items.text: Dispute about dividing honor in the presence of the teacher
items.text_en: Dispute about dividing honor in the presence of the teacher
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: one opinion holds that honor is divided to the student in the presence of the teacher, the other holds it is not. The halakha is stated both ways, and the resolution is that it depends on whether the teacher grants the student honor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute is between the two opinions about dividing honor to a student in the presence of the teacher.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between two halakhic statements by distinguishing whether the teacher granted the student honor.

items.text: The daughters of Zelophehad were wise, exegetes, and righteous
items.text_en: The daughters of Zelophehad were wise, exegetes, and righteous
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the daughters were wise, exegetes, and righteous. Their wisdom is shown by speaking at the right time: when Moses was teaching the laws of yibbum, they argued that if they are considered like a son, they should inherit; if not, their mother should be subject to yibbum. Moses then brought their case before God.

sub.desc_en: A baraita opens by declaring that the daughters of Zelophehad were wise, exegetes, and righteous.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak explains their wisdom: they spoke at the opportune moment when Moses was teaching the laws of יבמין (yibbum), arguing that if they are considered like a son they should inherit, otherwise their mother should be subject to yibbum, prompting Moses to bring their case before God.

items.text: Their exegetical skill: they would have refrained if there were a son
items.text_en: Their exegetical skill: they would have refrained if there were a son
items.desc_en: The daughters were exegetes because they said that if their father had a son, they would not have spoken. A baraita is cited that says 'daughter', but Rabbi Yirmeyah emends it to 'son'. Abaye adds that even a son's daughter would have prevented their claim.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that the daughters of Tzelofchad were exegetes (דַּרְשָׁנִיּוֹת) because they said: if their father had a son, they would not have spoken.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says 'בת' (daughter) rather than 'בן' (son).
Rabbi Yirmeyah answers that the baraita should be emended: erase the word 'בת' (daughter) and read 'בן' (son).
Abaye adds that even if their father had a son's daughter (a granddaughter), they would not have spoken.

items.text: Their righteousness: they married only worthy men and a miracle of fertility
items.text_en: Their righteousness: they married only worthy men and a miracle of fertility
items.desc_en: The daughters were righteous because they married only worthy men. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that even the youngest was not married before forty. The Gemara questions this based on Rav Chisda's statement about fertility, and answers that due to their righteousness, a miracle occurred like with Yocheved.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the daughters of Tzelofchad were righteous because they married only worthy men, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that even the youngest was not married before age forty.
The Gemara objects: Rav Chisda's statement about fertility says a woman married after forty can no longer bear children, so how could the daughters have had children?
The Gemara resolves: because they were so righteous, a miracle occurred for them like for Yocheved, who conceived Moses at an advanced age.

items.text: Yocheved's miraculous rejuvenation
items.text_en: Yocheved's miraculous rejuvenation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Yocheved, who was 130 years old, could be called a 'girl' (בת). Rabbi Chama bar Chanina identifies her as Yocheved, who was conceived on the road and born between the walls. Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevida explains that she was called 'girl' because signs of youth appeared on her: her flesh became firm, wrinkles smoothed, and beauty returned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a 130-year-old woman can be called a 'girl' (בת).
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina identifies the woman as Yocheved, who was conceived on the road and born between the walls.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevida explains that she was called 'girl' because signs of youth appeared: her flesh became firm, wrinkles smoothed, and beauty returned.

items.text: Amram's remarriage to Yocheved
items.text_en: Amram's remarriage to Yocheved
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse says 'And he took' (וַיִּקַּח) instead of 'And he returned' (וַיַּחְזוֹר). Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevida explains that Amram performed an act of marriage: he seated her in a bridal canopy, with Aaron and Miriam singing before her, and ministering angels saying 'A mother of children is joyful.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse uses 'took' (וַיִּקַּח) instead of 'returned' (וַיַּחְזוֹר).

Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevida explains that the verse teaches that Amram performed a new act of taking (ליקוחין) for Yocheved, seating her in a bridal chamber with Aaron and Miriam singing and angels proclaiming 'mother of children is joyful'.

items.text: Order of listing: greatness vs. wisdom
items.text_en: Order of listing: greatness vs. wisdom
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts two listings: one follows their greatness, the other their wisdom. This supports Rabbi Ami's ruling that in a session (ישיבה) one follows wisdom, but in a banquet (מסיבה) one follows age. Rav Ashi adds that this applies only when one excels in wisdom or age respectively.

sub.desc_en: The Stam notes a contrast: elsewhere the Torah lists the daughters of Tzelofchad by their greatness, but here by their wisdom.
This supports Rabbi Ami's ruling: in a study session follow wisdom, but at a festive meal follow age.
Rav Ashi qualifies that this applies only when one is distinguished in wisdom or age respectively.

items.text: Daughters of Tzelafchad were equal
items.text_en: Daughters of Tzelafchad were equal
items.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the daughters of Tzelafchad were equal (שקולות), as the verse says 'and they were' (וַתִּהְיֶינָה) – a single existence for all of them.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the daughters of Tzelofchad were equal, as the verse says 'and they were' — a single existence for all of them.

items.text: Permission to marry any tribe
items.text_en: Permission to marry any tribe
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that the daughters of Tzelafchad were permitted to marry into any tribe, as the verse says 'they may be wives to whom is good in their eyes.' The restriction 'only to the family of their father's tribe' is explained as good advice that they should marry only those suitable for them.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that the daughters of Tzelofchad were permitted to marry into any tribe, citing the verse 'they shall be wives to whoever is good in their eyes'.
The Gemara questions how to reconcile this with the verse 'but they shall be wives to the family of their father's tribe'.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that the verse offers good advice that they should marry only those suitable for them.

items.text: Scope of the prohibition: fathers vs. sons
items.text_en: Scope of the prohibition: fathers vs. sons
items.desc_en: Rabba raises an objection from a baraita that expounds 'Say to them' (those at Sinai) and 'for your generations' (future generations), concluding that both 'fathers' and 'sons' are needed because each has unique aspects. The baraita states that regarding fathers it says 'any daughter who inherits' – implying a restriction. Rabba resolves that this applies only to the daughters of Tzelafchad, not to all generations.

sub.desc_en: Rabba raises an objection by citing a baraita that expounds 'Say to them' (those at Sinai) and 'for your generations' (future generations), showing that both 'fathers' and 'sons' are needed because each has unique aspects.

The baraita specifies that regarding fathers it says 'any daughter who inherits' – implying a restriction, and that many commandments were given to sons that were not given to fathers, justifying the need for both terms.
Rabba resolves the objection by stating that the restriction applies only to the daughters of Tzelafchad, not to all generations.

items.text: Proof from 'this thing'
items.text_en: Proof from 'this thing'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the phrase 'this thing' (זֶה הַדָּבָר) indicates that the prohibition applies only to that generation. The Gemara asks: does 'this thing' in the context of slaughtering outside also apply only to that generation? It answers that there it says 'for your generations' (לְדֹרֹתָם), indicating permanence.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the verse 'every daughter inheriting an inheritance' was said regarding the fathers, not the sons.
The Gemara asks: what is the scriptural indication for this distinction?
Rava explains that the phrase 'זֶה הַדָּבָר' (this thing) indicates the prohibition applies only to that generation.

sub.text: Rabba Zuti's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rabba Zuti's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rabba Zuti objects to Rav Ashi: if so, does the phrase 'זֶה הַדָּבָר' regarding slaughtering outside also apply only to that generation?
The Gemara resolves: there it is different because the verse explicitly says 'לְדֹרֹתָם' (for your generations), indicating permanence.

items.text: Gemara's question about the scope of "zeh hadavar"
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the scope of "zeh hadavar"
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase "zeh hadavar" regarding the heads of tribes implies that the law applies only to that generation. It argues that a gezerah shavah is unnecessary here because the context itself indicates it is for all generations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'זה הדבר' (this is the matter) regarding the heads of tribes implies that the law applies only to that generation.
An initial answer is given: that case derives a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) from the other instance of 'זה' (this).

items.text: Explanation of the gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Explanation of the gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the gezerah shavah between the two instances of "zeh hadavar": one here and one regarding the priests, teaching that the law applies to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel, and similarly here to the heads of tribes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) is, and introduces a baraita.
The baraita explains the gezerah shavah: just as the phrase 'זה הדבר' regarding the priests applies to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel, so too here it applies to the heads of tribes, and vice versa.

items.text: Derivation of vow annulment by three laymen
items.text_en: Derivation of vow annulment by three laymen
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the gezerah shavah teaches that vow annulment requires three laymen. The Gemara addresses the apparent contradiction with "heads of tribes" by citing Rav Chisda's teaching that a single expert can also suffice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement from the baraita that the gezerah shavah (גזירה שוה) teaches that the same participants—Aaron, his sons, and all Israel—apply in both contexts.
The Gemara asks what halachic conclusion is derived from this comparison.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the comparison teaches that the annulment of vows (הפרת נדרים) requires three laymen (הדיוטות).
The Gemara objects that the verse explicitly mentions 'heads of tribes' (ראשי המטות), implying experts, not laymen.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the requirement for three laymen applies only when there is no expert; but a single expert (יחיד מומחה) can also annul vows, reconciling the verse's mention of 'heads of tribes'.

items.text: Derivation of questioning consecrated items
items.text_en: Derivation of questioning consecrated items
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet explains that the gezerah shavah also teaches that there is a possibility of questioning (annulling) consecrated items (hekdesh).

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet explains that the gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) also teaches that there is a possibility of questioning (annulling) consecrated items (הקדש).

items.text: Beit Shammai's objection and alternative uses
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's objection and alternative uses
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Beit Shammai, who deny questioning of hekdesh, must use the two instances of "zeh hadavar" for other purposes: one for the laws of slaughtering outside the Temple, and one for the distinction between a sage and a husband in vows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since Beit Shammai deny the possibility of questioning hekdesh (consecrated property), what do they do with the two instances of 'zeh hadavar' (this is the matter) in the Torah?

The Gemara answers: Beit Shammai use one instance of 'zeh hadavar' for the laws of slaughtering outside the Temple (to distinguish between slaughtering and pinching the neck), and the other for the distinction between a sage (who can permit vows) and a husband (who can annul vows).

items.text: Beit Shammai's source for three laymen
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's source for three laymen
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Beit Shammai, who reject the gezerah shavah, derive the law of vow annulment by three laymen. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives it from a different verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Beit Shammai, who reject the gezerah shavah (verbal analogy), derive the law that vow annulment requires three laymen.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives the law from a different verse, providing Beit Shammai's alternative source.

items.text: Opening baraita: Ben Azzai's teaching
items.text_en: Opening baraita: Ben Azzai's teaching
items.desc_en: The baraita states that 'mo'adei Hashem' is stated (implying a specific derivation), but Shabbat Bereishit is not stated. Ben Azzai adds that 'mo'adei Hashem' is stated, but hatarat nedarim is not stated.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that the phrase 'mo'adei Hashem' is stated (implying a specific derivation), but Shabbat Bereishit is not stated.
Ben Azzai adds that 'mo'adei Hashem' is stated, but hatarat nedarim (annulment of vows) is not stated.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Natan's inquiry to Rav Sheshet about the first clause
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Natan's inquiry to Rav Sheshet about the first clause
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Natan knew the baraita but not its explanation. He traveled to Rav Sheshet and asked: what does 'mo'adei Hashem is stated, Shabbat Bereishit is not stated' mean? Rav Sheshet answered: the festivals require sanctification by the court, but Shabbat Bereishit does not require court sanctification, lest one think it does because it is written alongside the festivals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yosei bar Natan knew the baraita but did not know its explanation.
Rabbi Yosei bar Natan traveled to Rav Sheshet and asked: what does 'mo'adei Hashem is stated, Shabbat Bereishit is not stated' mean?

Rav Sheshet answered: the festivals require sanctification by the court, but Shabbat Bereishit does not require court sanctification, lest one think it does because it is written alongside the festivals.

items.text: Explanation of the second clause and resolution of a contradiction
items.text_en: Explanation of the second clause and resolution of a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Ben Azzai's statement: festivals require experts (mumchin) for sanctification, but hatarat nedarim does not require experts. A difficulty is raised from the verse 'rashei ha-mattot', which implies a court. Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yochanan answers: it refers to a single expert (yachid mumcheh).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Ben Azzai's second clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Ben Azzai's second clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ben Azzai's statement 'festivals were said, hatarat nedarim was not said' means festivals require experts (mumchin) for sanctification, but hatarat nedarim does not require experts.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: the verse 'rashei ha-mattot' (heads of the tribes) implies a court of experts is required for hatarat nedarim.
Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse refers to a single expert (yachid mumcheh), not a full court.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that there were no better festivals for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur, when the daughters of Jerusalem would go out in borrowed white garments to avoid shaming those without. The Gemara asks: Yom Kippur is understandable as a day of forgiveness and the giving of the second tablets, but what is special about the fifteenth of Av?

sub.desc_en: The mishnah cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement that the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur were the best festivals, when Jerusalem's daughters would go out in borrowed white garments to avoid shaming the poor.
The Gemara asks: Yom Kippur is understandable as a day of forgiveness and the giving of the second tablets, but what is special about the fifteenth of Av?

items.text: First answer: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel – permission for inter-tribal marriage
items.text_en: First answer: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel – permission for inter-tribal marriage
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel explains: the fifteenth of Av was the day when the tribes were permitted to marry into each other. The derivation is from the verse 'zeh ha-davar' – this matter shall only apply to that generation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel explains that the fifteenth of Av was the day when the tribes were permitted to marry into each other, deriving this from the verse 'זה הדבר' (this matter) — indicating the prohibition applied only to that generation.

items.text: Second answer: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan – permission for the tribe of Benjamin
items.text_en: Second answer: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan – permission for the tribe of Benjamin
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan says: it was the day when the tribe of Benjamin was permitted to enter the congregation, based on the oath at Mitzpah that 'no man from us shall give his daughter to Benjamin as a wife', and they derived 'from us' but not from our sons.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that the fifteenth of Av was the day the tribe of Benjamin was permitted to enter the congregation, derived from the oath at Mitzpah that 'from us' but not from our sons.

items.text: Third answer: Rav Dimi bar Yosef quoting Rav Nachman – end of the generation of the wilderness
items.text_en: Third answer: Rav Dimi bar Yosef quoting Rav Nachman – end of the generation of the wilderness
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef quoting Rav Nachman says: it was the day when the generation of the wilderness finally died out, as the Master said that until the last of them died, the divine communication to Moses had not resumed.

sub.text: Rav Dimi bar Yosef quoting Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef quoting Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef quoting Rav Nachman answers that the fifteenth of Av was the day when the generation of the wilderness finally died out, citing the principle that divine communication to Moses had not resumed until the last of them perished.

items.text: First opinion: cessation of the generation of the wilderness
items.text_en: First opinion: cessation of the generation of the wilderness
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a source that the fifteenth of Av was the day when the decree against the generation of the wilderness ended, as the verse about the death of the men of war is juxtaposed with God speaking to Moses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the fifteenth of Av was when the decree against the generation of the wilderness ended, citing the juxtaposition of the death of the men of war with God speaking to Moses.

items.text: Second opinion: removal of Jeroboam's guards
items.text_en: Second opinion: removal of Jeroboam's guards
items.desc_en: Ulla says the fifteenth of Av was the day when Hoshea ben Elah removed the guards that Jeroboam had stationed on the roads to prevent Israel from making pilgrimage.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the fifteenth of Av was the day when Hoshea ben Elah removed the guards Jeroboam had placed on the roads to prevent pilgrimage.

items.text: Third opinion: burial of the slain of Beitar
items.text_en: Third opinion: burial of the slain of Beitar
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana says the fifteenth of Av was the day when the slain of Beitar were given burial, and on that day the blessing 'Hatov vehametiv' was instituted in Yavneh.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana states that the fifteenth of Av was the day when the slain of Beitar were given burial.

Rav Mattana explains that on that day the blessing 'הטוב והמטיב' (the Good and the Beneficent) was instituted in Yavneh, with 'הטוב' (the Good) because the bodies did not decompose, and 'המטיב' (the Beneficent) because they were given burial.

items.text: Fourth opinion: cessation of wood-cutting for the altar
items.text_en: Fourth opinion: cessation of wood-cutting for the altar
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef say the fifteenth of Av was the day when they stopped cutting wood for the altar, as from that day the sun's strength waned. Rav Menashe adds that this day is called 'Yom Tevar Magal'. The Gemara then discusses the significance of adding or not adding study from this point onward.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that the fifteenth of Av is the day when they stop cutting wood for the altar.

sub.text: Supporting baraita citing Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita citing Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol explaining that from the fifteenth of Av the sun's strength wanes, so they stopped cutting wood for the altar.
Rav Menashe adds that this day is called 'Yom Tevar Magal' (the day of breaking the sickle).
The Gemara asks the meaning of the term 'יסיף' (will cease) in the statement about adding or not adding study from this point onward.
Rav Yosef explains that 'יסיף' means 'may his mother bury him' — a curse for one who does not increase his Torah study.

items.text: Seven who spanned the generations and the exception of the tribe of Levi
items.text_en: Seven who spanned the generations and the exception of the tribe of Levi
items.desc_en: A baraita lists seven people who spanned the entire world from Adam to Eliyahu. The Gemara questions how Achiya HaShiloni could have seen Amram, given that all of that generation died in the wilderness. Rav Hamnuna answers that the decree did not apply to the tribe of Levi, as their census was from age thirty.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists seven people who spanned the entire world from Adam to Eliyahu, each seeing the next.
The Gemara questions how Achiya HaShiloni could have seen Amram, given the verse that only Kalev and Yehoshua survived the wilderness generation.
Rav Hamnuna answers that the decree of death in the wilderness did not apply to the tribe of Levi, as their census was from age thirty, not twenty.

items.text: Objection from other tribes and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from other tribes and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that people from other tribes also lived long, citing Yair ben Menashe and Machir ben Menashe who were born in Jacob's time and lived until the entry into the land. Rabbi Nechemya explains that the verse says 'about thirty-six', referring to Yair who was as significant as a full Sanhedrin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that people from other tribes also lived long, citing a baraita that Yair ben Menashe and Machir ben Menashe were born in Jacob's time and lived until the entry into the land, and Rabbi Yehuda interprets the verse 'about thirty-six' literally.
Rabbi Nechemya resolves the objection by noting the verse says 'about thirty-six', referring to Yair ben Menashe who was as significant as a full Sanhedrin.

items.text: Alternative answer: exclusion of those under twenty and over sixty
items.text_en: Alternative answer: exclusion of those under twenty and over sixty
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an alternative answer: the decree did not apply to those under twenty or over sixty, as derived from the term 'u'malah' compared to valuations.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an alternative answer: the decree of death in the wilderness did not apply to those under twenty or over sixty, deriving the upper limit from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'וּמַעְלָה' from the laws of valuations (ערכין).

items.text: Inquiry about the division of the land
items.text_en: Inquiry about the division of the land
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: was the land of Israel divided according to tribes or according to the heads of households?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: was the land of Israel divided according to tribes or according to the heads of households?

items.text: Gemara's initial proof from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's initial proof from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the verse 'between many and few' to support the idea that the land was divided by value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a proof from the verse 'between many and few' to support the idea that the land was divided by value.

items.text: Baraita on the future division and the method of lottery
items.text_en: Baraita on the future division and the method of lottery
items.desc_en: A baraita describes that the Land of Israel will be divided into thirteen tribes, initially it was divided into twelve, and it was divided by money, lottery, and Urim VeTummim. Rabbi Yehuda notes the value difference between Judea and Galilee. The process involves Eleazar, Joshua, and all Israel, with lots for tribes and boundaries.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the Land of Israel will be divided into thirteen tribes, though initially it was divided into twelve.

The baraita states that the division was by money, citing the verse 'בֵּין רַב לִמְעָט' (between the many and the few), and Rabbi Yehuda adds a note about the value difference between Judea and Galilee.
The baraita adds that the division was by lottery, citing 'אַךְ בְּגוֹרָל' (but by lot), and by Urim VeTummim, citing 'עַל פִּי הַגּוֹרָל' (according to the lot).
The baraita explains the procedure: Eleazar wears the Urim VeTummim, Joshua and all Israel stand before him, and two urns are placed before him—one for tribes and one for boundaries.
The baraita describes how Eleazar, with divine inspiration, declares that Zebulun and the boundary of Acco come up together, and then draws lots confirming this.
The baraita repeats the process for Naphtali and the boundary of Ginosar, and states that this was done for every tribe.

items.text: Comparison of this world and the World to Come
items.text_en: Comparison of this world and the World to Come
items.desc_en: The baraita contrasts the division of land in this world, where one may have only one type of field, with the World to Come, where each person will have land in mountain, lowland, and valley, as per the verse about the gates of the tribes.

sub.desc_en: The baraita contrasts the division of land in this world, where each person receives only one type of field, with the World to Come, where each will have land in mountain, lowland, and valley, and God Himself divides it.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that the land was divided by tribes, concluding that the division was per tribe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that the land was divided by tribes, concluding that the division was per tribe.

items.text: Question about the thirteenth tribe
items.text_en: Question about the thirteenth tribe
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the thirteenth tribe is for, and Rav Chisda answers it is for the prince (nasi), citing a verse. Rav Pappa suggests it might be a mere servant, but Abaye rejects this based on another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The master said the land will be divided into thirteen tribes — for whom is the extra portion?
Rav Chisda answers that the extra portion is for the prince (nasi), citing the verse 'and the workers of the city shall serve him from all the tribes of Israel'.
Rav Pappa suggests to Abaye that the extra portion might be merely for a servant (רונגר בעלמא).
Abaye rejects this, citing the verse 'and the remainder for the prince from this and from that, for the holy portion and for the city's holding', which indicates the prince's own portion.

items.text: Clarification of 'by money'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'by money'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of the money valuation, rejecting that it was for quality (beauty vs. ugliness) and concluding it was for proximity and distance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the purpose of the monetary valuation mentioned in the baraita?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the valuation was for quality (beauty vs. ugliness), arguing that the division was not about aesthetic judgment.
The Gemara concludes that the monetary valuation was to compensate for differences in proximity and distance of the land portions.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the method of valuation
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the method of valuation
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua: one says they valued the land by money, the other says by land.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a Tannaic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says they valued the land by money (בכספים).
Rabbi Yehoshua says they valued the land by land (בקרקע).

items.text: Exception of Joshua and Caleb from the lottery
items.text_en: Exception of Joshua and Caleb from the lottery
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'but by lot' excludes Joshua and Caleb, meaning they did not receive their portions by lot but by divine command, as shown by verses.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'אך בגורל' (but by lot) excludes Joshua and Caleb from the lottery.
The Gemara asks: What does this exclusion mean? If it means they received no portion at all, that is impossible since they clearly received portions.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that they received nothing, arguing that if others received portions, surely they themselves received portions.
The Gemara resolves: The exclusion means they did not receive their portions by lottery, but rather by divine command (על פי ה׳).
The Gemara cites the verse for Joshua: 'על פי ה׳ נתנו לו את העיר אשר שאל, את תמנת סרח בהר אפרים' (by the mouth of the Lord they gave him the city he asked for, Timnat Serach in Mount Ephraim).

items.text: Opening discussion on Seraḥ and Caleb
items.text_en: Opening discussion on Seraḥ and Caleb
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction in the spelling of 'Seraḥ' and explains Caleb's acquisition of Hebron as its suburbs, not the city itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in the spelling of the city name 'Seraḥ' and 'Ḥeres'.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by explaining that the city was initially called 'Ḥeres' (hard) and later 'Seraḥ' (rotten), referring to the quality of its fruit.
An alternative version reverses the order: initially the fruit rotted, later it became hard.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: Hebron was a city of refuge, yet Caleb received it as an inheritance.
Abaye explains that Caleb received only the suburbs (פַּרְוורַהָא) of Hebron, not the city itself, as supported by the verse about its fields and courtyards.

items.text: Mishnah: Inheritance laws
items.text_en: Mishnah: Inheritance laws
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that sons and daughters are equal in inheritance, but a son takes a double portion in the father's estate and daughters are supported from the father's estate.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that sons and daughters are equal in inheritance, but a son takes a double portion in the father's estate and daughters are supported from the father's estate.

items.text: Gemara's first question and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'one son and one daughter for inheritance,' noting that a son precedes a daughter. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains it means both take from property that is due (ראוי) as from property in hand (מוחזק).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'one son and one daughter for inheritance,' noting that a son precedes a daughter, so they cannot inherit equally.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the Mishnah means both son and daughter take from property that is due (ראוי) as from property in hand (מוחזק).

items.text: Objection and Rav Pappa's answer
