items.text_en: Objection and Rav Pappa's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this is already taught regarding the daughters of Zelophehad, and questions the word 'but' (אֶלָּא). Rav Pappa explains the Mishnah means both take a portion in the firstborn's double share.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the principle of inheriting the ראוי (inheritance not yet possessed) is already taught from the daughters of Zelophehad, who took three portions including their father's share from the Exodus generation and his share with his brothers in the property of Hepher.
The Gemara further questions the meaning of the word 'אֶלָּא' (but) in the Mishnah, implying that the Mishnah's formulation is problematic.
Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah means both a son and a daughter take a portion in the firstborn's double share (בכורה), resolving the objection about the word 'אֶלָּא'.

items.text: Second objection and Rav Ashi's answer
items.text_en: Second objection and Rav Ashi's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this is also already taught, and questions 'but' again. Rav Ashi explains the Mishnah means that if one says 'so-and-so shall inherit all my property,' whether a son among sons or a daughter among daughters, his words stand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah already teaches that a firstborn takes a double portion, and further questions the meaning of 'but' in the Mishnah.
Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah means that if one says 'so-and-so shall inherit all my property,' whether a son among sons or a daughter among daughters, his words stand.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Ashi and Mar bar Rav Ashi's answer
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Ashi and Mar bar Rav Ashi's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rav Ashi's explanation aligns with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, but that is a disputed opinion and a later dispute overrides a prior anonymous ruling. Mar bar Rav Ashi explains the Mishnah means that sons and daughters are equal in the mother's estate and the father's, except for the double portion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rav Ashi's explanation aligns with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, but that is a disputed opinion and a later dispute overrides a prior anonymous ruling.

The Gemara objects that even if the Mishnah is a סתם (anonymous ruling) following Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, it is followed by a מחלוקת (dispute), and the rule is that a סתם followed by a מחלוקת does not establish the הלכה (binding law) as the סתם.
The Gemara asks further: what is the meaning of the word 'אֶלָּא' (but rather) in the Mishnah, which Rav Ashi's explanation does not adequately address.

Mar bar Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah means sons and daughters are equal in the mother's estate and the father's, except that the son takes a double portion in the father's estate but not in the mother's.

items.text: Baraita on 'double portion'
items.text_en: Baraita on 'double portion'
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the meaning of 'double portion' (פִּי שְׁנַיִם), suggesting it means double of one share, not double of all the property, and begins a logical argument.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'to give him a double portion' and interprets it as double of one share, not double of all the property.
The baraita poses a logical question: does 'double portion' mean double of one share or double of all the property?
The baraita transitions to a logical argument (kal vachomer) to resolve the question.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the Mishnah's ambiguity
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the Mishnah's ambiguity
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two possible interpretations of the Mishnah's phrase 'פי שנים כאחד'—whether it means double the portion of one brother or double of all property. It then cites a verse to rule in favor of the first interpretation, that the firstborn takes double the portion of one brother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two possible interpretations of the Mishnah's phrase 'פי שנים כאחד'—whether it means double the portion of one brother or double of all property.
The Gemara cites a verse to rule in favor of the first interpretation, that the firstborn takes double the portion of one brother.

items.text: Proof from biblical verses about the birthright
items.text_en: Proof from biblical verses about the birthright
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses about Reuben and Joseph to prove that the birthright grants a double portion. It also interprets the verse 'וַאֲנִי נָתַתִּי לְךָ שְׁכֶם אַחַד' to mean that Joseph received a double portion, and explains the terms 'חרבי' and 'קשתי' as prayer and supplication.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses from Chronicles and Chronicles to establish that the birthright (בכורה) grants a double portion, linking Joseph's double portion to the general rule.
The Gemara infers from the shared term 'בכורה' (birthright) that just as Joseph received a double portion, so too does every firstborn receive a double portion in inheritance.

The Gemara cites the verse where Jacob gives Joseph 'one portion' (שכם אחד) and interprets 'חרבי' (my sword) as prayer (תפילה) and 'קשתי' (my bow) as supplication (בקשה), showing Joseph's double portion was a reward for piety.

items.text: Addressing potential objections to the proof
items.text_en: Addressing potential objections to the proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara anticipates and refutes three possible objections: that the verse about Reuben is only for Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's teaching, that we cannot learn from 'בכורתו' to 'בכורה', and that Joseph's double portion itself is uncertain. Rav Pappa challenges Abaye, who responds with a verse showing Joseph's sons were counted as tribes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara anticipates the objection that the verse about Reuben's birthright being given to Joseph only teaches Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's principle, and refutes it by citing the verse.

The Gemara anticipates the objection that we cannot learn the rule of 'בכורה' (birthright) from 'בכורתו' (his birthright), and refutes it by citing the verse that explicitly says 'והבכרה ליוסף' (the birthright is Joseph's).

The Gemara anticipates the objection that even regarding Joseph himself, we do not know that he received a double portion, and refutes it by citing the verse 'I have given you one portion above your brothers'.

Rav Pappa objects to Abaye that the verse might only refer to a mere palm tree (a single field), and Abaye responds by citing the verse that Ephraim and Manasseh are counted as full tribes like Reuben and Simeon.

items.text: Why Jacob gave the birthright to Joseph
items.text_en: Why Jacob gave the birthright to Joseph
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo asks Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani why Jacob transferred the birthright from Reuben to Joseph. After dismissing the obvious answer that it was due to Reuben's sin, Rabbi Yonatan explains that the birthright was originally destined for Rachel, but Leah preceded her in prayer, and due to Rachel's modesty, God returned it to her.

sub.text: Rabbi Chelbo's question to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chelbo's question to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo asks Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani why Jacob took the birthright from Reuben and gave it to Joseph, dismissing the obvious answer of Reuben's sin.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani offers a parable of a homeowner who raised an orphan, but the orphan's later generosity is rejected as insufficient to explain Joseph's reward without Reuben's sin.
Rabbi Yonatan explains that the birthright was originally destined for Rachel, but Leah preceded her in prayer, and due to Rachel's modesty, God returned it to her.

items.text: Explanation of Leah's soft eyes and her prayer
items.text_en: Explanation of Leah's soft eyes and her prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת'. Rabbi Elazar says it means her gifts were long-lasting. Rav says it means literally soft, which is praise because she cried upon hearing that Esau was wicked and Jacob was righteous, causing her eyelashes to fall out. The Gemara also explains 'שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה' as referring to Esau's deeds being hateful to her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by the statement that Leah preceded Rachel in prayer, citing the verse 'וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת' (and Leah's eyes were soft).
The Gemara objects that if 'soft' is taken literally, it would be a disgrace, and the Torah does not speak in disgrace even of an unclean animal, let alone of righteous people.
Rabbi Elazar explains that 'soft' means her gifts (descendants) were long-lasting, not a literal description of her eyes.
Rav argues that 'soft' is indeed literal and is praise: Leah cried upon hearing that Esau was wicked and Jacob righteous, causing her eyelashes to fall out.
The Gemara asks what 'שְׂנוּאָה' (hated) means in the verse, and objects that a literal reading would be a disgrace.
The Gemara explains that 'שְׂנוּאָה' means Esau's deeds were hateful to Leah, and therefore God opened her womb.

items.text: Rachel's modesty and the switch with Leah
items.text_en: Rachel's modesty and the switch with Leah
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes Rachel's modesty: when Jacob told her he was her cousin, she warned him about Laban's deceit. Jacob gave her signs, but when Leah was brought in, Rachel gave the signs to Leah to prevent her sister's shame. This explains the verse 'וְהִנֵּה הִיא לֵאָה'—Jacob did not know it was Leah until morning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rachel's modesty consisted of, and relates that Jacob told Rachel he was her cousin and proposed marriage, but she warned him about Laban's deceitfulness.

Jacob asked what Laban's deceit was, Rachel explained that she had an older sister, Jacob said he was a brother in deceit, Rachel questioned if it was permitted for the righteous, and Jacob gave her identifying signs.
When Leah was brought in, Rachel gave her the signs to prevent her sister's shame, so Jacob did not know it was Leah until morning.

items.text: Question about the count of Jacob's descendants
items.text_en: Question about the count of Jacob's descendants
items.desc_en: Abba Chalifa asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba why the total count of Jacob's descendants is seventy when listed generally, but only sixty-nine when listed individually. Rabbi Chiyya answers that Dinah had a twin sister, as implied by the verse 'וְאֵת דִּינָה בִתּוֹ'.

sub.desc_en: Abba Chalifa asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba why the total count of Jacob's descendants is seventy when listed generally, but only sixty-nine when listed individually.
Rabbi Chiyya answers that Dinah had a twin sister, as implied by the verse 'וְאֵת דִּינָה בִתּוֹ' (and Dinah his daughter).

items.text: Interpretation of Benjamin as 'son of his mother'
items.text_en: Interpretation of Benjamin as 'son of his mother'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'and Benjamin his brother, the son of his mother,' and Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains that it refers to Jochebed, who was conceived on the road but born between the walls, as derived from the verse about Levi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'and Benjamin his brother, the son of his mother,' implying a rhetorical objection.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains that 'son of his mother' refers to Jochebed, who was conceived on the road but born between the walls, as derived from the verse about Levi.

items.text: Why Jacob sought to leave Laban after Joseph's birth
items.text_en: Why Jacob sought to leave Laban after Joseph's birth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo asks Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani why Jacob wanted to leave after Joseph was born. The answer is that Jacob foresaw Esau's descendants would only be defeated by Joseph's. Objections are raised from David's victory and from the Simeonites' attack on Amalek, resolved by identifying Yishai as a descendant of Menashe.

sub.text: Rabbi Chelbo's question to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chelbo's question to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo asks Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani why the verse singles out Joseph's birth as the moment Jacob sought to leave Laban.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani answers that Jacob foresaw Esau's descendants would only be defeated by Joseph's descendants, citing the verse comparing Jacob's house to fire and Joseph's to flame.
An objection is raised from David's victory over Esau's descendants (Amalek), which seems to contradict the claim that only Joseph's descendants could defeat them.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani resolves the objection by citing that David's warriors who defeated Amalek included leaders from Menashe, Joseph's son.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosef's objection from the Simeonites
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosef's objection from the Simeonites
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosef objects by citing that the Simeonites, not Joseph's descendants, attacked the remnant of Amalek.
Rabba bar Sheila resolves the objection by identifying Yishai, the leader of the Simeonite expedition, as a descendant of Menashe (Joseph's son), citing the verse listing Menashe's sons.

items.text: Tannaic baraita on firstborn's double portion
items.text_en: Tannaic baraita on firstborn's double portion
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that a firstborn takes a double portion in the foreleg, cheeks, and maw (priestly gifts), in consecrated animals, and in appreciation of property after the father's death.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a firstborn takes a double portion in the priestly gifts of foreleg, cheeks, and maw, in consecrated animals, and in appreciation of property after the father's death.

items.text: Examples of property appreciation
items.text_en: Examples of property appreciation
items.desc_en: The baraita explains that if the father left a cow that was rented out or grazing in a pasture and it gave birth, the firstborn takes a double portion; but if they built houses or planted vineyards, the firstborn does not take a double portion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita gives an example: if the father left a cow that was rented out or grazing in a pasture and it gave birth, the firstborn takes a double portion.
The baraita contrasts: if the heirs built houses or planted vineyards, the firstborn does not take a double portion.

items.text: Gemara's question on priestly gifts
items.text_en: Gemara's question on priestly gifts
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the firstborn can take a double portion in the foreleg, cheeks, and maw, since if they came into the father's possession it is obvious, and if not, they are ' ראוי' (not yet possessed). The answer is that we deal with recognized priests where the animal was slaughtered during the father's lifetime, and the opinion holds that gifts not yet separated are considered as separated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the firstborn can take a double portion in the foreleg, cheeks, and maw, since if they came into the father's possession it is obvious, and if not, they are 'רָאוּי' (not yet possessed) and the firstborn does not take in 'רָאוּי' as in 'מוּחְזָק' (possessed).

The answer explains that we deal with recognized priests where the animal was slaughtered during the father's lifetime, and the opinion holds that gifts not yet separated (מתנות שלא הורמו) are considered as separated (כמי שהורמו).

items.text: Consecrated animals and Rabbi Yosi HaGelili
items.text_en: Consecrated animals and Rabbi Yosi HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the firstborn can take a double portion in consecrated animals, since they are not the father's property. It answers that this refers to קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) according to Rabbi Yosi HaGelili, who holds they are the owner's money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that consecrated animals (מוקדשין) are not the father's property, so how can the firstborn take a double portion in them?
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) according to Rabbi Yosi HaGelili, who holds they are the owner's money (ממון בעלים).

items.text: Clarification of the cow example
items.text_en: Clarification of the cow example
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita mentions a rented or hired cow, which is not in the owner's domain, and then a grazing cow, which is even more obvious. It explains that the baraita teaches that a rented or hired cow is analogous to a grazing cow: both involve appreciation that comes naturally without additional expense.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita mentions both a rented/hired cow (not in the owner's domain) and a grazing cow (even more obvious), implying redundancy.
The Gemara answers that the baraita teaches that a rented or hired cow is analogous to a grazing cow: both involve appreciation that comes naturally without additional expense.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a firstborn does not take a double portion of appreciation that comes naturally, such as a field that becomes more fertile without expense.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a firstborn does not take a double portion of appreciation that comes naturally, such as a field that becomes more fertile without expense.

items.text: Attribution of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Attribution of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi, citing a baraita where Rabbi holds that a firstborn takes a double portion of appreciation after the father's death, but not of improvements made by the orphans.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, suggesting it is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A baraita is cited stating that a firstborn does not take a double portion in appreciation that occurred after the father's death.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states his opinion that a firstborn does take a double portion in appreciation after the father's death, but not in appreciation from the orphans' own efforts.

items.text: Debt cases
items.text_en: Debt cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: if they inherited a debt document, the firstborn takes a double portion; if a debt document is levied against them, he pays double; and if he says 'I will neither take nor give,' he may do so.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if they inherited a debt document, the firstborn takes a double portion; if a debt document is claimed against them, the firstborn pays a double portion; and if he says 'I will neither take nor give,' he is permitted.

items.text: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.text_en: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Sages derive from the verse 'to give him a double portion' that the double portion is like a gift, only acquired when it reaches his hand. Rabbi derives from 'double portion' that the firstborn's portion is equated to the plain portion, which is acquired even before it reaches his hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the reasoning of the Sages (who hold that the firstborn does not take a double portion in post-mortem appreciation)?

The Sages derive from the verse 'לָתֶת לוֹ פִּי שְׁנַיִם' (to give him a double portion) that the double portion is called a gift (מתנה), and just as a gift is only acquired when it reaches the recipient's hand, so too the firstborn's portion is only acquired when it reaches his hand.

Rabbi derives from the phrase 'פִּי שְׁנַיִם' (double portion) that the firstborn's portion is equated to the plain portion (חלק פשוט); just as the plain portion is acquired even before it reaches the heir's hand, so too the firstborn's portion is acquired even before it reaches his hand.

items.text: Reconciliation of verses
items.text_en: Reconciliation of verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages interpret 'double portion' to give him a portion in each boundary, and Rabbi interprets 'to give him' to allow the firstborn to opt out of taking and giving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The Sages also have the verse 'פי שנים' (a double portion) — how do they interpret it?
The Gemara answers: That verse is needed to give him a portion at each boundary.
The Gemara asks: Rabbi also has the verse 'לתת לו' (to give him) — how does he interpret it?
The Gemara answers: That verse teaches that if the firstborn says 'I will not take and I will not give' — he is permitted to do so.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that all agree a firstborn takes a double portion of natural growth like a tree that thickened or land that rose with silt; the dispute is over cases where a pit became full of water or a palm tree bore fruit, where one considers it natural improvement and the other a change.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that all agree a firstborn takes a double portion in natural growth like a palm tree that grew stronger or land that rose with silt, but they disagree about a pit that produced shoots or a palm that produced dates, where one considers it natural appreciation and the other considers it a change.
Rav Pappa distinguishes that the dispute is over cases where a pit became full of water or a palm tree bore fruit, where one opinion considers it natural improvement and the other a change.

items.text: Rabbah bar Chanah's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Chanah's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Chanah reports in the name of Rabbi Chiyya that if one acted according to Rabbi's opinion or according to the Sages' opinion, his action is valid.

sub.text: Rabba bar Chana citing Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Chana citing Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Chiyya that if one acts according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's opinion, it is valid, and if one acts according to the Rabbis' opinion, it is also valid.

items.text: Gemara's question about the rule of halakha like Rabbi
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the rule of halakha like Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt: does the principle 'halakha like Rabbi from his colleague' mean only from his colleague but not from his students, or even from his students?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt: does the principle 'halakha like Rabbi from his colleague' mean only from his colleague but not from his students, or even from his students?

items.text: Rav Nachman and Rava's positions on following Rabbi
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Rava's positions on following Rabbi
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rav says it is forbidden to act like Rabbi, holding that halakha follows Rabbi only from his colleague, not his students. Rav Nachman himself says it is permitted, holding it applies even from his students. Rava says it is forbidden but if done it is valid, interpreting the rule as 'leaning' rather than absolute.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Rav that it is forbidden to act like Rabbi, because the halakha follows Rabbi only from his colleague, not from his students.
Rav Nachman states his own view that it is permitted to act like Rabbi, because the halakha follows Rabbi even from his students.
Rava rules that it is forbidden to act like Rabbi, but if one did so it is valid, because the original statement was 'leaning' (מטין) rather than absolute.

items.text: Two baraitot on firstborn's share in appreciation
items.text_en: Two baraitot on firstborn's share in appreciation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman's baraita teaches that 'in all that is found for him' excludes appreciation by heirs after the father's death, but includes natural appreciation of assets, and attributes this to Rabbi. Rami bar Hama's baraita excludes both types of appreciation, attributing it to the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman's baraita teaches that the verse 'בכל אשר ימצא לו' (in all that is found for him) excludes appreciation by heirs after the father's death, but includes natural appreciation of assets, and attributes this to Rabbi.
Rami bar Hama's baraita teaches that the verse excludes both natural appreciation of assets and appreciation by heirs, and attributes this to the Rabbis.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on firstborn and loans
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on firstborn and loans
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says a firstborn does not take a double portion in a loan. The Gemara asks: to whom does this apply? If to the Rabbis, who deny appreciation in hand, a loan is even less. So it must be for Rabbi. But a baraita says a firstborn takes double in a loan and interest, contradicting both. The Gemara resolves that the baraita is for the Rabbis, and Shmuel's ruling is necessary lest one think a loan is like collected.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling that a firstborn does not take a double portion in a loan.
The Gemara asks to whom Shmuel's ruling applies, and suggests that if it is for the Rabbis, who deny a firstborn appreciation in hand, a loan should certainly be excluded.
The Gemara concludes that Shmuel's ruling must apply to Rabbi, who grants a firstborn appreciation in hand.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says a firstborn takes double in both loan and interest, which contradicts both Rabbi and the Rabbis.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita is for the Rabbis, and Shmuel's ruling is necessary lest one think a loan is like collected property.

items.text: A ruling from the academy on loans and interest
items.text_en: A ruling from the academy on loans and interest
items.desc_en: They sent from there: a firstborn takes double in a loan but not in interest. The Gemara questions: to whom? If to the Rabbis, a loan is less than appreciation; if to Rabbi, he says he takes even interest. The Gemara concludes it is for the Rabbis, and a loan is considered as collected.

sub.desc_en: The academy sends a ruling: a firstborn takes double in a loan but not in interest.
The Gemara questions to whom the ruling refers: if to the Rabbis, who deny the firstborn appreciation, a loan is even less than appreciation.
The Gemara objects: if the ruling is for Rabbi, he holds that a firstborn takes even interest, contradicting the academy's exclusion of interest.
The Gemara resolves: the ruling is for the Rabbis, and a loan is considered as already collected (גבוי), so the firstborn takes it.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Rav's report and the Nehardeans' reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav's report and the Nehardeans' reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav tells Ravina that Ameimar lectured: a firstborn takes double in a loan but not in interest. Ravina comments that the Nehardeans follow their own logic, citing Rabba and Rav Nachman's dispute about whether a firstborn takes double in land or money after collection. Abaye then challenges both Rabba and Rav Nachman.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav reports to Ravina that Ameimar lectured: a firstborn takes double in a loan but not in interest.
Ravina comments that the Nehardeans follow their own logic, citing the dispute between Rabba and Rav Nachman about whether a firstborn takes double in land or money after collection.
Abaye challenges both Rabba and Rav Nachman, pointing out difficulties with each of their positions.

items.text: First objection to the distinction between land and money
items.text_en: First objection to the distinction between land and money
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why land is treated differently from money, since both were left by the father. It then cites the Western sages' reasoning that if the grandmother sold the land first, her sale is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why money is treated differently from land, since both were left by the father.
The Gemara cites the Western sages' reasoning that if the grandmother sold the land first, her sale is valid, implying a distinction between land and money.

items.text: Second objection attributed to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Second objection attributed to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a similar difficulty from Rav Nachman's perspective, questioning why land is singled out. It then cites Rav Nachman's ruling that if orphans collected land for their father's debt, a creditor can reclaim it from them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty for Rav Nachman: just as land is excluded because it was not left by the father, so too money is excluded for the same reason.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds a supporting ruling from Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: if orphans collected land for their father's debt, a creditor can reclaim it from them.

items.text: Resolution: the ruling follows Western sages, not accepted by Babylonians
items.text_en: Resolution: the ruling follows Western sages, not accepted by Babylonians
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that neither objection is valid, because the discussion is merely explaining the Western sages' reasoning, which the Babylonian sages do not accept. It then begins to explain the case of the grandmother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objections by stating that the discussion merely explains the Western sages' reasoning, which the Babylonian sages do not accept.
The Gemara introduces the case of the grandmother by asking what the grandmother case is, and begins to cite the relevant statement.

items.text: Opening case: bequest to grandmother, then to heirs
items.text_en: Opening case: bequest to grandmother, then to heirs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where someone says 'My property to my grandmother, and after her to my heirs.' The grandmother had a married daughter who died before both her husband and the grandmother. After the grandmother dies, the husband comes to claim the inheritance.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a man bequeaths his property to his grandmother and then to his heirs, and after the grandmother's death, the husband of the deceased daughter comes to claim the inheritance.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rav Anan dispute the meaning of 'my heirs'
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Anan dispute the meaning of 'my heirs'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says 'my heirs' includes even the heirs of my heirs, so the husband inherits. Rav Anan says 'my heirs' does not include heirs of heirs, so the husband does not inherit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets 'to my heirs' as including even the heirs of the heirs, meaning the husband inherits.
Rav Anan interprets 'to my heirs' as excluding the heirs of the heirs, so the husband does not inherit.

items.text: The ruling from the West: law follows Rav Anan, but not his reasoning
items.text_en: The ruling from the West: law follows Rav Anan, but not his reasoning
items.desc_en: The sages send from the West that the law follows Rav Anan that the husband does not inherit, but not for his reason. Rav Anan thought the husband would not inherit even if the daughter had a son, but actually if there were a son he would inherit. The real reason the husband does not inherit is because the property was ' ראוי ' (not yet in the wife's possession at her death), and a husband does not take ' ראוי ' like ' מוחזק '.

sub.desc_en: The academy rules in accordance with Rav Anan that the husband does not inherit, but not for his reason; rather because the husband does not take from ראוי (property not yet in possession) as from מוחזק (property in possession).

items.text: Gemara's inference: Rav Huna holds husband takes ' ראוי '
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: Rav Huna holds husband takes ' ראוי '
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the ruling that Rav Huna must hold that a husband does take ' ראוי ' like ' מוחזק ', since he said the husband inherits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Rav Huna must hold that a husband does take from ראוי (property not yet in possession) as from מוחזק (property in possession).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: the phrase 'after you' is like 'from now'
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: the phrase 'after you' is like 'from now'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar comments that this matter was opened by great scholars and concluded by lesser ones, and that one who says 'after you' is considered as saying 'from now'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar comments that this matter was opened by great sages and concluded by lesser ones, and that saying 'after you' is like saying 'from now'.

items.text: Rabbah explains the reasoning of the Westerners
items.text_en: Rabbah explains the reasoning of the Westerners
items.desc_en: Rabbah says the reasoning of the Westerners (who ruled that the husband does not inherit) is plausible: if the grandmother had sold the property before her death, the sale would be valid, showing the property was not yet in the wife's possession.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains the reasoning of the Western sages: if the grandmother sold the property before her death, the sale is valid, indicating she has full ownership.

items.text: Rav Pappa's final ruling: husband and firstborn do not take ' ראוי '
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's final ruling: husband and firstborn do not take ' ראוי '
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states the halakha: a husband does not take ' ראוי ' like ' מוחזק ', a firstborn does not take ' ראוי ' like ' מוחזק ', and a firstborn does not take a double portion in a loan, whether the land or money was collected.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that a husband does not take from ראוי (property not yet in possession) as from מוחזק (property in possession), and a firstborn does not take a double portion from a loan, whether they collected land or money.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a loan is with the property, the firstborn does not take a double portion of it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a loan that is with the property is divided equally, and the firstborn does not take a double portion.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the firstborn's portion of processed produce
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the firstborn's portion of processed produce
items.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav Asi says that if a firstborn protested his portion, it is a valid protest. Rabba and Rav Yosef debate whether the firstborn takes a double portion of grapes that were pressed into wine or olives that were pressed into oil, with Rav Yosef allowing even after pressing. The Gemara objects that pressing changes the substance, and resolves with Rav Ukva bar Chama's principle of paying damages for the grapes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav Asi states that if a firstborn protested his portion, the protest is valid.
Rabba limits Rav Asi's ruling to grapes that were picked or olives that were harvested, but not pressed; Rav Yosef extends it even to pressed produce.
The Gemara objects that pressing changes grapes into wine, so the firstborn cannot take a double portion of the wine.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rav Ukva bar Chama
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rav Ukva bar Chama
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the firstborn receives the value of the grapes as damages, not the wine itself.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the original context
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the original context
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the original statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, where Rav Ukva bar Chama's principle was applied to pressed grapes.

items.text: Dispute about the scope of a firstborn's waiver
items.text_en: Dispute about the scope of a firstborn's waiver
items.desc_en: Rav Asi states that if a firstborn took a portion equal to a simple son, he has waived his right. Rav Pappa and Rav Pappi dispute whether this waiver applies only to that field or to all property, based on whether the firstborn has a right before division.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states that if a firstborn (בכור) took a portion equal to a simple son (פשוט), he has waived (ויתר) his right to the double portion.
The Gemara asks what the scope of the waiver (ויתר) is.

sub.text: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa, citing Rava, answers that the waiver applies only to that specific field (אותה שדה).

sub.text: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi, citing Rava, answers that the waiver applies to all the property (כל הנכסים כולן).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappa's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappa's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Pappa's position: the firstborn has no right to the double portion before division (קודם חלוקה), so he only waived what came into his possession, not other property.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappi's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Pappi's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Pappi's position: the firstborn has a right to the double portion before division (יש לו קודם חלוקה), so by waiving in one field he waived in all.

items.text: Illustrative story about a firstborn's sale and waiver
items.text_en: Illustrative story about a firstborn's sale and waiver
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that the dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Pappi was not explicitly stated but inferred from a case where a firstborn sold his own and the simple son's property, and the orphans of the simple son were beaten by the buyers. Rava ruled that the firstborn's action was invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the dispute between Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa was not stated explicitly but inferred from a case.
The Gemara recounts the case: a firstborn sold his own property and that of the simple son, and the orphans of the simple son were beaten by the buyers.
The relatives object to the buyers: is it not enough that you bought their property, but you also beat them?
The parties came before Rava, who ruled that the firstborn's action was invalid.

items.text: Dispute about the firstborn's right before division
items.text_en: Dispute about the firstborn's right before division
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Mar and Mar about whether a firstborn who sold his portion before the estate was divided has done anything. A message from the academy rules that such a sale is void, indicating the firstborn has no right before division, but the halakha is that he does have a right before division.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between two sages named Mar about whether a firstborn who sold his portion before division has done anything, with one saying he has done nothing and the other saying he has done something regarding the entire estate.
The academy sends a ruling that a firstborn who sold before division has done nothing, implying that the firstborn has no right before division.
The halakha concludes that the firstborn does have a right before division, contradicting the academy's implication.

items.text: Mar Zutra's case of waiving the firstborn's share
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's case of waiving the firstborn's share
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra from Drishta divided a basket of peppers equally with his brothers, and Rav Ashi ruled that since he waived his right in part, he waived it in all the property.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra from Drishta divided a basket of peppers equally with his brothers.
Rav Ashi ruled that since Mar Zutra waived his firstborn share in part (the peppers), he waived it in all the property.

items.text: Mishnah: Stipulations against Torah law and gifts
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stipulations against Torah law and gifts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one says 'My son so-and-so, the firstborn, shall not take a double portion' or 'shall not inherit with his brothers', his words are void because he stipulates against Torah law. However, if he distributes his property as a gift, giving more to one and less to another, and equalizes the firstborn, his words stand; but if he says it is because of inheritance, his words are void. If he writes it as a gift, his words stand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a stipulation against Torah law regarding inheritance is void.
The Mishnah continues that if one distributes property as a gift, even equalizing the firstborn, his words stand, but if he calls it inheritance they are void.

items.text: Gemara: Does the Mishnah align with Rabbi Yehuda?
items.text_en: Gemara: Does the Mishnah align with Rabbi Yehuda?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a stipulation about monetary matters is valid. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says a condition about monetary matters is valid, unlike Rabbi Meir. The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, in the Mishnah the son does not waive his right, whereas in the baraita the woman waives her rights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that a stipulation against the Torah's inheritance law is void aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a condition about monetary matters (דבר של ממון) is valid.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda explicitly rules that a condition about monetary matters (such as waiving marital obligations) is valid, unlike Rabbi Meir.

The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the Mishnah is valid because in the baraita the woman actively waives her rights (מחלה), whereas in the Mishnah the son does not waive his right to the double portion.

items.text: Rav Yosef: Distinction in testimony about firstborn
items.text_en: Rav Yosef: Distinction in testimony about firstborn
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that if one says 'So-and-so, my son, is my firstborn', he takes a double portion; but if he says 'So-and-so is a firstborn', he does not, because he might mean the firstborn of his mother.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that if one says 'So-and-so, my son, is my firstborn', he takes a double portion; but if he says 'So-and-so is a firstborn', he does not, because he might mean the firstborn of his mother.

items.text: Cases of identifying a firstborn by father's statements
items.text_en: Cases of identifying a firstborn by father's statements
items.desc_en: Two cases are brought: one before Rabbah bar bar Chanah, where a witness claimed the father called the son 'foolish firstborn', and another before Rabbi Chanina, where the father said 'go to my son Shechvat, who is a firstborn and spits'. The Gemara questions whether these refer to the firstborn of the mother, and resolves that a firstborn of the father spits, while one of the mother does not.

sub.desc_en: A case is brought before Rabbah bar bar Chanah where a witness claims the father called the son 'foolish firstborn'.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah objects that the father might have meant a firstborn of the mother, since such a child is also called 'foolish firstborn'.
A second case is brought before Rabbi Chanina, where the father told people to go to his son Shechvat, who is a firstborn and spits.
The Gemara questions whether this too might refer to a firstborn of the mother.
The Gemara resolves that a firstborn of the father spits, while one of the mother does not, so the father's statement about spitting identifies a paternal firstborn.

items.text: Rabbi Ammi and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Tumtum's status
items.text_en: Rabbi Ammi and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Tumtum's status
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi rules that a tumtum (one with obscured genitals) who is torn and found to be a male does not take a double portion, because the verse requires being a son from the moment of birth. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that such a person is also not judged as a rebellious son, for the same reason.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi rules that a tumtum (one with obscured genitals) who is torn and found to be a male does not take a double portion, because the verse requires being a son from the moment of birth.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that such a person is also not judged as a rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה), for the same reason.

items.text: Three Amoraic statements excluding tumtum/androgynos
items.text_en: Three Amoraic statements excluding tumtum/androgynos
items.desc_en: Ameimar, Rav Sheizvi, and Rav Sherevya each derive from a verse that a tumtum or androgynos is not considered a 'son' for the laws of firstborn inheritance, circumcision on the eighth day, and the mother's impurity of childbirth, respectively.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar derives from the verse 'וְיָלְדָה לוֹ בָּנִים' that a tumtum or androgynos is excluded from the firstborn's portion, requiring a son at the time of birth.
Rav Sheizvi derives from the verse 'אִשָּׁה כִּי תַזְרִיעַ וְיָלְדָה זָכָר' that a tumtum or androgynos is not circumcised on the eighth day, requiring a male from birth.
Rav Sherevya derives from the verse 'אִשָּׁה כִּי תַזְרִיעַ וְיָלְדָה זָכָר' that the mother of a tumtum or androgynos is not impure from childbirth, requiring a male from birth.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Sherevya from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Sherevya from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that a woman who miscarries a tumtum or androgynos must observe the impurity periods for both a male and a female, which contradicts Rav Sherevya's claim that the mother is not impure from childbirth. The Gemara concludes this is a refutation of Rav Sherevya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that a woman who miscarries a tumtum or androgynos must observe impurity periods for both a male and a female, which contradicts Rav Sherevya's claim that the mother is not impure from childbirth, and concludes this is a refutation of Rav Sherevya.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Sheizvi and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Sheizvi and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the same baraita also refutes Rav Sheizvi's position regarding circumcision. It answers that the tanna is uncertain about the status of a tumtum/androgynos and rules stringently, but this does not resolve the difficulty regarding the baraita's wording.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the same baraita also constitutes a refutation of Rav Sheizvi's position regarding circumcision.
The Gemara answers that the tanna is uncertain about the status of a tumtum/androgynos and rules stringently, so the baraita does not refute Rav Sheizvi.

The Gemara objects that if the tanna is merely uncertain, the baraita should have also required the woman to observe the days of a menstruant (נִדָּה), and concludes that the difficulty remains unresolved.

items.text: Rava cites a baraita supporting Rabbi Ami
items.text_en: Rava cites a baraita supporting Rabbi Ami
items.desc_en: Rava states that a baraita is taught in accordance with Rabbi Ami, deriving from the words 'ben' and 'bekhor' that a tumtum is excluded from the firstborn laws, and a doubtful case is also excluded.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that supports Rabbi Ami, deriving from the words 'בן' (son) and 'בכור' (firstborn) that a tumtum and a doubtful case are excluded from the firstborn laws.

items.text: Clarifying the exclusion of 'safek'
items.text_en: Clarifying the exclusion of 'safek'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the exclusion of 'safek' from 'bekhor' comes to exclude the case where Rava previously taught that two women who gave birth to two males in hiding can write authorizations for each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara accepts the exclusion of 'tumtum' from 'ben' as per Rabbi Ami, but questions what the exclusion of 'safek' from 'bekhor' comes to exclude.
The Gemara answers that the exclusion of 'safek' comes to exclude the case where Rava taught that two women who gave birth to two males in hiding can write authorizations for each other.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge and Rava's retraction
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge and Rava's retraction
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Rava's earlier ruling with a tradition from Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yannai, which distinguishes between cases where the children were recognized and later mixed, versus never recognized. Rava then retracts his earlier statement and teaches the correct tradition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Rava's earlier ruling by citing a tradition from Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yannai, which distinguishes between cases where the children were recognized and later mixed (permitting authorization) versus never recognized (prohibiting authorization).
Rava retracts his earlier statement, publicly declares it an error, and teaches the correct tradition from Rabbi Yannai distinguishing between recognized and unrecognized children.

items.text: Inquiry from the people of Akra deAgma to Shmuel
items.text_en: Inquiry from the people of Akra deAgma to Shmuel
items.desc_en: The people of Akra deAgma ask Shmuel about a case where a man was presumed to be the firstborn, but the father declared another son as the firstborn. Shmuel responds that they may write an authorization.

sub.text: People of Akra deAgma's inquiry to Shmuel
sub.text_en: People of Akra deAgma's inquiry to Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The people of Akra deAgma ask Shmuel about a case where a man was presumed to be the firstborn, but the father declared another son as the firstborn.
Shmuel responds that they may write an authorization (הרשאה) to resolve the uncertainty.

items.text: Gemara's question on the mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah states 'this one to that one' without specifying which opinion the father follows. It suggests that the father is uncertain whether to follow Rabbi Yehuda or the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah writes 'this one to that one' without specifying which opinion the father follows, arguing that if he follows the Rabbis or Rabbi Yehuda, he should send accordingly.
The Gemara answers that the father is uncertain whether to follow Rabbi Yehuda or the Rabbis.

items.text: The baraita on 'yakhir' and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.text_en: The baraita on 'yakhir' and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets 'yakhir' to mean that a father can make his son known to others. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a father is believed to say 'this is my firstborn son,' and similarly for a son of a divorced woman or a חלוצה. The Rabbis disagree and say he is not believed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that interprets the verse 'יַכִּיר' (he shall recognize) to mean that a father makes his son known to others.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that a father is believed to say 'this is my firstborn son,' and similarly for a son of a divorced woman or a חלוצה (a woman who performed חליצה).
The Sages disagree and rule that the father is not believed to make such declarations.

items.text: The necessity of 'yakhir' for the Rabbis and Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: The necessity of 'yakhir' for the Rabbis and Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava: for Rabbi Yehuda, 'yakhir' is understood, but for the Rabbis, why is it needed? The Gemara answers that it is needed for identification. It then questions whether this is for giving a double portion, but notes that even a stranger could be given a gift. The Gemara explains it is for property that falls to him later. For Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can acquire something not yet in the world, 'yakhir' is needed for property that falls to him when he is dying.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava: for Rabbi Yehuda, the verse 'יַכִּיר' (he shall recognize) is understood, but for the Rabbis, why is 'יַכִּיר' needed?
The Gemara answers that 'יַכִּיר' is needed for identification (הֶיכֵּרָא).
The Gemara objects: what is the practical halachic consequence — to give him a double portion? Even a stranger could be given a gift, so identification is unnecessary.
The Gemara resolves: it is necessary for property that falls to him after this point (i.e., after the father's declaration), where a gift would not apply.
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can acquire something not yet in the world, why is 'יַכִּיר' needed?
The Gemara answers: it is needed for property that falls to him when he is dying (גּוֹסֵס), where the father cannot make a gift.

items.text: Baraita on presumption of firstborn status
items.text_en: Baraita on presumption of firstborn status
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if people presume someone is a firstborn and the father says another is the firstborn, he is believed. If they presume he is not a firstborn and the father says he is, he is not believed. The Gemara notes that the first clause follows Rabbi Yehuda and the latter clause follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if people presume someone is a firstborn and the father says another is the firstborn, he is believed; if they presume he is not a firstborn and the father says he is, he is not believed.
The Gemara notes that the first clause follows Rabbi Yehuda and the latter clause follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on declaring someone a son or slave
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on declaring someone a son or slave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules: if one says 'he is my son' and then 'he is my slave,' he is not believed. If he says 'he is my slave' and then 'he is my son,' he is believed, because he meant he serves me like a slave. The opposite applies at a customs house to avoid tax. A challenge is raised from a baraita where one who serves as a son or slave cannot change his statement. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that case involves a known slave called 'עבדא מצר מאה' (a slave worth 100 zuz).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one first says 'he is my son' and then retracts to 'he is my slave,' he is not believed; but if he first says 'he is my slave' and then says 'he is my son,' he is believed, because he meant the person serves him like a slave.
The gemara notes that the opposite ruling applies at a customs house: to avoid tax, the first statement is believed and the retraction is not.
A baraita is cited as a challenge: whether the person served as a son or as a slave, the father's retraction is never believed, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction: the baraita deals with a known slave called 'עבדא מצר מאה' (a slave worth 100 zuz), so the father's retraction is not believed because the slave's status is already established.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's question about a stolen slave claim
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question about a stolen slave claim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a question to Rav Yosef bar Chama about a case where one says 'you stole my slave' and the other says 'I did not steal; you sold him to me.' The daf cuts off mid-sentence.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Yosef bar Chama
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Yosef bar Chama
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a question to Rav Yosef bar Chama about a case where one claims 'you stole my slave' and the other responds 'you sold him to me,' but the text cuts off mid-sentence.

items.text: Retraction after an oath
items.text_en: Retraction after an oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the novelty of the ruling that one cannot retract after saying 'I will give it to you' and the other swears. It cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagree about retracting from a statement of trust, and concludes that the dispute applies to 'I will give' and the law follows the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one says 'You gave it to me as a gift' and the other says 'If you want, swear and take it,' and the claimant swears, the defendant cannot retract.
The Gemara asks what novelty the Mishnah teaches, citing a parallel Mishnah where Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether one can retract from a statement of trust.
The Gemara concludes that the novelty is that the dispute applies to the case of 'I will give it to you' and the law follows the Sages.

items.text: Collecting from slaves
items.text_en: Collecting from slaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a ruling to Rav Yosef bar Chama that one may collect from slaves, while Rav Nachman disagrees and says one may not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a ruling to Rav Yosef bar Chama that one may collect from slaves.
Rav Nachman disagrees and rules that one may not collect from slaves.

items.text: Third witness in second year
items.text_en: Third witness in second year
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that a third witness who testifies in the second year is valid. Rava says even in the first year. Mar bar Rav Ashi validates a grandfather, but the halacha does not follow him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a ruling to Rav Yosef bar Chama that a third witness who testifies in the second year of a loan is valid.
Rava adds that the third witness is valid even in the first year of the loan.
Mar bar Rav Ashi validates a grandfather as a witness, extending the principle further.
The Gemara concludes that the halacha does not follow Mar bar Rav Ashi's lenient ruling.

items.text: Witness who became blind
items.text_en: Witness who became blind
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that a witness who knew land boundaries before becoming blind is invalid. Shmuel says he is valid because he can orient by landmarks, but not for a cloak. Rav Sheshet says even for a cloak, by length and width, but not for a cup. Rav Pappa says even for a cup, by weight.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a ruling to Rav Yosef bar Chama that a witness who knew land boundaries before becoming blind is invalid.
Shmuel argues that such a witness is valid for land because he can orient by landmarks, but not for a cloak.
Rav Sheshet extends validity even to a cloak, since one can measure its length and width, but not to a cup.
Rav Pappa further extends validity even to a cup, since one can estimate its weight.

items.text: General rule for witness disqualification
items.text_en: General rule for witness disqualification
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from a baraita: a witness who became a relative, deaf, blind, or insane is invalid. But if the disqualification is temporary and reversed, he is valid. The general rule: if the beginning or end is invalid, he is invalid; if both beginning and end are valid, he is valid.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises an objection from a baraita listing cases where a witness who becomes a relative, deaf, blind, or insane is invalid.
The baraita continues with cases where the disqualification is temporary and reversed, making the witness valid.
The baraita concludes with a general rule: if the beginning or end of the witness's status is invalid, he is invalid; if both beginning and end are valid, he is valid.

items.text: Refutation of all previous opinions
items.text_en: Refutation of all previous opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara declares that the previous refutation (תיוובתא) applies to all opinions, indicating a conclusive rejection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara declares that the refutation (תיוובתא) applies to all previous opinions, conclusively rejecting them.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's first ruling: testimony about a child among sons
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's first ruling: testimony about a child among sons
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sent to Rav Yosef bar Chama that one who says about a child among sons is believed, but Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. Abaye explains the dispute as about inheritance designation (like Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka vs. Rabbis), while Rava objects and reinterprets it as about declaring the child a firstborn (like Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbis).

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's ruling sent to Rav Yosef bar Chama
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's ruling sent to Rav Yosef bar Chama
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a ruling that one who says about a child among sons is believed, while Rabbi Yochanan disagrees.
The Gemara asks what the ruling means.
Abaye explains that the dispute is about inheritance designation, aligning Rabbi Abba with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Yochanan with the Rabbis.
Rava objects that the terms 'believed' and 'not believed' are inappropriate for inheritance; the terms 'inherit' and 'not inherit' should have been used.
Rava reinterprets the dispute as about declaring the child a firstborn, aligning Rabbi Abba with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan with the Rabbis.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's second ruling: wife's share as one of the sons
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's second ruling: wife's share as one of the sons
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sent that a wife who is to take like one of the sons does so, and Rava clarifies this applies to present property and sons born after the statement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a ruling that a wife who is to take like one of the sons indeed takes accordingly.
Rava clarifies that the ruling applies only to present property and to sons born after the statement.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's third ruling: partial repayment with witnesses
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's third ruling: partial repayment with witnesses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sent a case where a debtor claims partial repayment but witnesses say full repayment; the creditor swears and collects half from free property but not from liened property. The Gemara discusses whether this aligns with Rabbi Akiva (who considers it returning a lost item) or Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar (who considers it a partial admission), with Mar bar Rav Ashi objecting to the latter.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's ruling (sent to Rav Yosef bar Chama)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's ruling (sent to Rav Yosef bar Chama)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba sends a ruling: in a case where a creditor claims no repayment, the debtor claims half repayment, and witnesses testify to full repayment, the creditor swears and collects half from free property but not from liened property, since lienholders rely on the witnesses.

The Gemara notes that even according to Rabbi Akiva, who considers the debtor a 'returner of a lost item' (משיב אבידה) and thus exempt from an oath, here the presence of witnesses supporting the creditor changes the case, so the creditor's claim is substantiated (אירתותי אירתת).

Mar bar Rav Ashi objects: on the contrary, even according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who considers the debtor a 'partial admitter' (מודה מקצת הטענה) and thus liable to swear, here the witnesses support the debtor, so he is certainly a 'returner of a lost item' (משיב אבידה) and exempt.

items.text: Halakhic conclusion and final query
items.text_en: Halakhic conclusion and final query
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules in the name of Rav Shimi bar Ashi that the halakha follows all of Rabbi Abba's rulings. Ravina asks Rav Ashi about Rav Nachman's opinion, and Rav Ashi responds that the ruling 'they do not collect' is taught, and Rav Nachman agrees. The Gemara then asks what the halakha excludes.

sub.text: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Shimi bar Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Shimi bar Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that the halakha follows all of Rabbi Abba's rulings sent to Rav Yosef bar Chama.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi about Rav Nachman's opinion on the matter.
Rav Ashi responds that the ruling 'אין גובין' (they do not collect) is taught, and Rav Nachman agrees.
The Gemara asks what the halakha excludes by stating that the ruling applies to all of Rabbi Abba's rulings.

items.text: Resolution of earlier contradictions
items.text_en: Resolution of earlier contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier refutations of Rav, Shmuel, Rav Sheshet, and Rav Pappa are not decisive; rather, the ruling is to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yochanan and the difficulty raised by Mar bar Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for the earlier refutations, arguing that each is either an addition or already refuted.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling is meant to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yochanan and the difficulty raised by Mar bar Rav Ashi.

items.text: Definition of gift at the beginning, middle, and end
items.text_en: Definition of gift at the beginning, middle, and end
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses one who divides his property verbally. Rabbi Yochanan defines three scenarios: 'give field X to Y and he shall inherit it' is a gift at the beginning; 'he shall inherit it and give it to him' is a gift at the end; 'he shall inherit it and give it to him and he shall inherit it' is a gift in the middle. This applies only to one person and one field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to define a gift at the beginning, middle, and end of a verbal property division.

Rabbi Yochanan, reported by Rav Dimi, defines the three scenarios: 'give field X to Y and he shall inherit it' is a gift at the beginning; 'he shall inherit it and give it to him' is a gift at the end; 'he shall inherit it and give it to him and he shall inherit it' is a gift in the middle.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's definitions apply only to one person and one field, not to one person with two fields or one field with two people.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's broader opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's broader opinion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar argues that the rule applies even to one person and two fields, or one field and two people, but not to two fields and two people.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states his broader opinion: the rule applies even to one person and two fields, or one field and two people, but not to two fields and two people.

items.text: Contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Ravin reports a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says one acquires, Rabbi Elazar says one does not acquire when the language is 'give field X to Y, and Y shall inherit field X'. Abaye questions Ravin about the contradiction within Rabbi Yochanan's own statements. The Gemara resolves that there are different Amoraim transmitting Rabbi Yochanan's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one acquires the field, while Rabbi Elazar rules that one does not acquire, when the language is 'give field X to Y, and Y shall inherit field X'.
Abaye challenges Ravin: Rabbi Elazar's positions are consistent, but Rabbi Yochanan's earlier statement (segments 3-4) contradicts his later ruling here.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that different Amoraim transmitted Rabbi Yochanan's opinion, so the apparent inconsistency is due to variant traditions.

items.text: Resh Lakish's stringent requirement
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's stringent requirement
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that one does not acquire until the donor explicitly says: 'So-and-so and so-and-so shall inherit field X and field Y that I have given them as a gift, and they shall inherit them.'

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that one does not acquire until the donor explicitly says: 'So-and-so and so-and-so shall inherit field X and field Y that I have given them as a gift, and they shall inherit them.'

items.text: Dispute among Rav Hamnuna, Rav Nachman, and Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Dispute among Rav Hamnuna, Rav Nachman, and Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna limits the rule to one person and one field; Rav Nachman extends it to one person and two fields or one field and two people; Rav Sheshet extends it even to two fields and two people, citing a baraita about giving a shekel to sons on Shabbat as support.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna limits the rule of a gift combined with inheritance to one person and one field, excluding one person with two fields or one field with two people.
Rav Nachman extends the rule to one person with two fields or one field with two people, but not to two fields and two people.
Rav Sheshet extends the rule even to two fields and two people.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita about giving a shekel to sons on Shabbat to support his position that the rule applies even to multiple fields and multiple people.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when one says 'give' or 'do not give' to heirs, they only receive a shekel, implying that a gift to multiple parties is not valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when one says 'give' or 'do not give' to heirs, they only receive a shekel, implying that a gift to multiple parties is not valid.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's case is not considered like two fields and two people, and resolves that it refers to one who is fit to inherit, following Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's case, which resembles two fields and two people, still rules that the recipient acquires.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to one who is fit to inherit, following Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a baraita where a gift to one person with a conditional inheritance to another is valid, and questions why it is not considered like two fields and two people.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a baraita about a gift with successive inheritance clauses and challenges that it should be invalid like two fields and two people, yet the baraita rules it valid.

items.text: Refutation of Rav Ashi's challenge
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Ashi's challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita also follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, but then objects that if so, the third inherits after the second's death, which contradicts Rav Acha's ruling that inheritance has no interruption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the baraita is explained as referring to a beneficiary who is a ראוי ליורשו (qualified heir) and follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, then the third inherits after the second's death, which is problematic.

Rav Acha's ruling is cited: according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, when the first recipient is a ראוי ליורשו (qualified heir), the second has nothing in place of the first, because the language is one of inheritance not gift, and inheritance has no interruption.

items.text: Conclusion of the refutation
items.text_en: Conclusion of the refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara declares that this is a conclusive refutation of all previous positions.

sub.desc_en: The gemara declares: this is a conclusive refutation of all the earlier positions.

items.text: Defense of Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Defense of Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether this is also a refutation of Reish Lakish, but notes that Rava ruled like Reish Lakish in three cases, and resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between within and after the time of speech.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the refutation also applies to Reish Lakish.
The Gemara rejects the question, implying it is not a valid refutation.
The Gemara cites Rava's ruling that the הלכה (binding law) follows Reish Lakish in three specific cases, showing Reish Lakish's position is authoritative.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a retraction made תוך כדי דיבור (within the time of speech) and one made after that interval.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on within the time of speech
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on within the time of speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the principle 'within the time of speech is like speech' applies except for idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The gemara rules: all statements made within תוך כדי דיבור (the time it takes to say a short phrase) are considered as if spoken, except for idolatry.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'So-and-so shall inherit me' where there is a daughter, or 'My daughter shall inherit me' where there is a son, his words are void because he conditions against Torah law. Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says: if he said it about one who is fit to inherit him, his words stand; if about one not fit, they do not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: a stipulation that contradicts Torah law is void.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka adds that if the designated heir is fit to inherit, the statement stands; if not, it is void.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference and question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference and question
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a son among sons or a daughter among daughters would be valid, but then notes that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, raising a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a son among sons or a daughter among daughters would be valid, since the Mishnah only invalidates a son in place of a daughter or vice versa.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, raising a contradiction.

items.text: Resolution via Rabbi Yishmael's baraita
items.text_en: Resolution via Rabbi Yishmael's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka might include even a stranger in place of a daughter, but a baraita from Rabbi Yishmael, his son, clarifies that the dispute is only about a son among sons or a daughter among daughters, not about strangers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka might include even a stranger in place of a daughter or a daughter in place of a son.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, states that his father and the Sages agreed that a stranger in place of a daughter or a daughter in place of a son is invalid.
The baraita concludes that the dispute is only about a son among sons or a daughter among daughters, where Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says he inherits and the Sages say he does not.

items.text: First answer: Tanna Kamma holds they disagreed
items.text_en: First answer: Tanna Kamma holds they disagreed
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a first answer: from the fact that Rabbi Yishmael said 'they did not disagree,' it implies that the Tanna Kamma holds they did disagree, thus the Mishnah is from Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and the Tanna Kamma is a different view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a first answer: from Rabbi Yishmael's statement that 'they did not disagree,' it implies that the Tanna Kamma holds they did disagree, so the Mishnah's first clause is from Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and the Tanna Kamma represents a different view.

items.text: Second answer: Mishnah is incomplete
items.text_en: Second answer: Mishnah is incomplete
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a second answer: the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's view, and it is missing a clause. The correct text is: 'If one says... he said nothing; but a daughter among daughters or a son among sons, if he said 'he shall inherit all his property,' his words stand, for Rabbi Yochanan says: if he said about one fit to inherit him, his words stand.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's view, and the text is missing a clause specifying that a son among sons or a daughter among daughters inherits if explicitly stated.

items.text: Halakhic ruling in favor of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling in favor of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel, and similarly Rava, that the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel, and Rava independently, that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

items.text: Scriptural basis and objection
items.text_en: Scriptural basis and objection
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's reasoning from the verse 'And it shall be on the day he bequeaths to his sons' that the Torah gave the father authority to bequeath to whomever he wishes. Abaye objects that this is derived from 'He may not give preference to the firstborn,' and the Gemara notes that verse is needed for another teaching of Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks for the scriptural basis of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's position and answers that the verse 'וְהָיָה בְּיוֹם הַנְחִילוֹ אֶת בָּנָיו' grants the father authority to bequeath to whomever he wishes.
Abaye objects that the same principle is already derived from the verse 'לֹא יוּכַל לְבַכֵּר' (the law of the firstborn).
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the verse 'לֹא יוּכַל לְבַכֵּר' is needed for a different teaching cited by Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Derivation that a father cannot give a firstborn's portion to another son
items.text_en: Derivation that a father cannot give a firstborn's portion to another son
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'he cannot give the firstborn's portion' is needed, since a kal vachomer from a simple son would seem to permit it. It answers that the verse 'on the day he bequeaths to his sons' teaches that a father may give to whomever he wishes, but the firstborn's portion is protected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'לֹא יוּכַל לְבַכֵּר' (he cannot give the firstborn's portion) is necessary.

The Gemara explains that the verse 'וְהָיָה בְּיוֹם הַנְחִילוֹ' (on the day he bequeaths to his sons) teaches that a father may give to whomever he wishes, but a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from a simple son would permit giving the firstborn's portion to another, so the verse 'לֹא יוּכַל לְבַכֵּר' is needed to forbid it.
The Gemara asks why the verse 'וְהָיָה בְּיוֹם הַנְחִילוֹ' is also necessary, since the verse 'לֹא יוּכַל לְבַכֵּר' alone would suffice.

The Gemara explains that without 'וְהָיָה בְּיוֹם הַנְחִילוֹ', a kal vachomer from the firstborn would suggest that a simple son cannot receive a bequest from his father, so the verse teaches that the Torah gave the father authority to bequeath to whomever he wishes.

items.text: Alternative derivation: the verse 'on the day he bequeaths' teaches the father's right
items.text_en: Alternative derivation: the verse 'on the day he bequeaths' teaches the father's right
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'on the day he bequeaths' is needed, since a kal vachomer from the firstborn would seem to forbid a father from giving to anyone else. It answers that this verse teaches that the Torah gave the father permission to bequeath to whomever he wishes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'וְהָיָה בְּיוֹם הַנְחִילוֹ' is needed, since a kal vachomer from the firstborn would seem to forbid a father from giving to anyone else.
The Gemara answers that the verse teaches that the Torah gave the father permission to bequeath to whomever he wishes.

items.text: Dispute over the halakha: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's opinion and the term 'hora'ah'
items.text_en: Dispute over the halakha: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's opinion and the term 'hora'ah'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika reports in the name of Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Chanina, and Rabbi that the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. Rabbi Abba objects, saying the term 'hora'ah' (teaching) was used, not 'halakha'. The Gemara explains the dispute: one holds that 'halakha' is preferable, the other that 'ma'aseh' (practice) is greater.

sub.text: Rabbi Zerika citing Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Chanina, and Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zerika citing Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Chanina, and Rabbi
