sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika reports in the name of Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Chanina, and Rabbi that the halakha (binding law) follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.
Rabbi Abba objects, asserting that the term 'הוֹרָה' (a teaching) was used, not 'הֲלָכָה' (a binding ruling).
The Gemara explains the dispute: one authority holds that 'הֲלָכָה' (a formal halakhic ruling) is preferable, while the other holds that 'מַעֲשֶׂה' (a practical precedent) is greater.

items.text: The rule: halakha is not learned from study or practice unless stated 'halakha lema'aseh'
items.text_en: The rule: halakha is not learned from study or practice unless stated 'halakha lema'aseh'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one cannot derive halakha from study or practice unless the teacher says 'halakha lema'aseh'. If asked and told 'halakha lema'aseh', one may act, provided he does not draw analogies. The Gemara questions the exception, since all Torah is learned by analogy. Rav Ashi explains it refers specifically to tereifot, where analogies are not made.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one cannot derive halakha from study or practice unless told 'halakha lema'aseh'; if told so, one may act but not draw analogies.
The Gemara questions the restriction against drawing analogies, since all Torah is learned through analogy.
Rav Ashi explains that the restriction applies specifically to cases of טריפות (animals with fatal defects), where analogies are not made.
A baraita supports Rav Ashi by stating that in cases of טריפות one does not say 'this is similar to that', as the same cut can cause death or survival.

items.text: Practical ruling: Rabbi Asi asks Rabbi Yochanan, and Rava's instruction to his students
items.text_en: Practical ruling: Rabbi Asi asks Rabbi Yochanan, and Rava's instruction to his students
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi asks Rabbi Yochanan if they should act on his 'halakha' statement. Rabbi Yochanan says no, until he says 'halakha lema'aseh'. Rava instructs Rav Papa and Rav Huna not to tear up his ruling if they find a flaw, but to come to him; after his death, they should not tear it up nor learn from it, lest he would have given a reason.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi asks Rabbi Yochanan whether they should act on his ruling when he says 'הלכה הכי (the law is thus)'.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that they should not act until he explicitly says 'הלכה למעשה (a ruling for practice)'.
Rava instructs Rav Papa and Rav Huna that if they find a flaw in his ruling, they should not tear it up but come to him, and if he has a reason he will tell them, otherwise he will retract.
Rava adds that after his death, they should neither tear up his ruling nor learn from it, because had he been there he might have given a reason.

items.text: Opening principle: the judge has only what his eyes see
items.text_en: Opening principle: the judge has only what his eyes see
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that one should not derive further rulings from a judge's decision, as a judge has only what his eyes see.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the principle that one should not derive further rulings from a judge's decision, because a judge has only what his eyes see.

items.text: Rava's question: does Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling apply to a healthy person?
items.text_en: Rava's question: does Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling apply to a healthy person?
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling, which allows a dying person to allocate property to a son who is not the firstborn, applies only to a deathbed declaration or also to a healthy person.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling applies only to a deathbed declaration (שכיב מרע) or also to a healthy person (בריא).

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Nathan's statement and Rabbi's response
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Nathan's statement and Rabbi's response
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya brings a proof from a Mishnah where Rabbi Nathan told Rabbi that they taught like Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka regarding sons inheriting the ketubah. Rabbi initially said the text reads 'yisbun' (they shall take), but later admitted it reads 'yirtun' (they shall inherit), proving that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling applies even to a healthy person.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's ruling that a husband can condition that his sons inherit his wife's ketubah applies only to a גוסס (dying person) or even to a healthy person.
Rav Mesharshiya brings a Mishnah where Rabbi Nathan tells Rabbi that their teaching follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, citing the clause about sons inheriting the ketubah.
Rabbi initially objects that the Mishnah reads 'יִסְּבוּן' (they shall take) not 'יִרְתוּן' (they shall inherit), but later admits he was wrong.
The Gemara resolves that the text must read 'יִרְתוּן' (they shall inherit) because otherwise the sons could not collect from liened property.
Rav Mesharshiya concludes that since Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds this view, it applies even to a healthy person (בריא).

items.text: Objection: how can one acquire something not yet in the world?
items.text_en: Objection: how can one acquire something not yet in the world?
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Abaye: whether the text reads 'yisbun' or 'yirtun', one cannot acquire something not yet in the world. Even Rabbi Meir, who allows acquisition of something not yet in the world, only allows it for something that exists but is not yet owned, not for something that does not exist at all. The Gemara answers that a court-imposed condition is different.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Abaye that whether the text reads 'יִסְּבוּן' or 'יִרְתוּן', one cannot acquire something not yet in the world, and even Rabbi Meir's leniency only applies to something that exists but is not yet owned, not to something that does not exist at all.
The Gemara answers that a court-imposed condition (תְּנַאי בֵּית דִּין) is different and allows acquisition of something not yet in the world.

items.text: Abaye's initial response: because it uses the language of inheritance
items.text_en: Abaye's initial response: because it uses the language of inheritance
items.desc_en: Abaye responds that the court's condition is effective because it uses the language of inheritance ('yirtun'), which takes effect automatically upon the sons' birth.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the court's condition is effective because it uses the language of inheritance ('יִרְתוּן'), which takes effect automatically upon the sons' birth.

items.text: Abaye retracts: proof from the daughters' clause
items.text_en: Abaye retracts: proof from the daughters' clause
items.desc_en: Abaye retracts his statement, citing a Mishnah where the husband obligates himself to support daughters from his property, which is a court-imposed condition even though it uses the language of a gift ('yihvyan'), not inheritance. This shows that the court's condition is effective regardless of the language used.

sub.desc_en: Abaye retracts his earlier statement, citing the Mishnah about daughters' support as a court-imposed condition (תנאי בית דין) that is effective even when phrased as a gift.
The Gemara adds that when one party receives as a gift and another as inheritance, even the Rabbis (who disagree with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka) would concede that the court's condition is effective.

items.text: Rav Nechumi or Rav Chananya bar Minyomei addresses Abaye
items.text_en: Rav Nechumi or Rav Chananya bar Minyomei addresses Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Nechumi (or Rav Chananya bar Minyomei) speaks to Abaye, continuing the discussion.

sub.text: Rav Nechumi (or Rav Chananya bar Minyomei) to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Nechumi (or Rav Chananya bar Minyomei) to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Nechumi (or Rav Chananya bar Minyomei) addresses Abaye, initiating a statement.

items.text: Gemara's question on the court that enacted the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the court that enacted the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling was enacted by one court or two different courts. It argues that if it were two courts, the analogy drawn in the Mishnah would be problematic, but a counter-argument suggests the later court could have modeled its enactment on the earlier one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's enactments were made by one court or two different courts.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of two courts, citing the Mishnah's opening which presents Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's midrash linking sons' inheritance and daughters' sustenance.
The Gemara explains that if one court enacted both rulings, the analogy from one enactment to the other is valid, but if two courts enacted them, the analogy would be problematic.
An objection argues that even if two courts enacted them, the later court could have modeled its enactment on the earlier one to avoid inconsistency.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: writing all property to wife makes her an administrator
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: writing all property to wife makes her an administrator
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that if a man writes all his property to his wife, he has only made her an administrator (apotropos), not a full heir.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that one who writes all his property to his wife has only appointed her as an administrator (אפוטרופא).

items.text: Extension to a minor son
items.text_en: Extension to a minor son
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the same principle applies to a minor son. Rav Chanilai bar Idi says in the name of Shmuel that even a minor son lying in a cradle is considered an administrator, not a full heir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the rule that one who writes all his property to his wife makes her only an administrator (אפוטרופוס) applies also to a minor son.

sub.text: Rav Chanilai bar Idi in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chanilai bar Idi in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanilai bar Idi reports in the name of Shmuel that even a minor son lying in a cradle is considered an administrator (אפוטרופוס), not a full heir.

items.text: Cases with others: son and another, wife and another, betrothed and divorced wife
items.text_en: Cases with others: son and another, wife and another, betrothed and divorced wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if a man writes property to his son and another person, the other receives it as a gift and the son as administrator. Similarly, if to his wife and another, the other gets a gift and the wife is administrator. However, if the wife is betrothed or divorced, she receives it as a gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the obvious case: when a man writes property to his son and another person, the other receives it as a gift and the son as administrator; similarly, if to his wife and another, the other gets a gift and the wife is administrator.
The Gemara concludes that if the wife is betrothed or divorced, she receives the property as a gift, not as an administrator.

items.text: Dispute between Ravina and Rav Avira on other cases
items.text_en: Dispute between Ravina and Rav Avira on other cases
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised about a daughter among sons, a woman among brothers, and a woman among the husband's sons. Ravina citing Rava says she does not acquire in all cases except a betrothed or divorced wife. Rav Avira citing Rava says she acquires in all cases except a woman among brothers or among the husband's sons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires about the status of a daughter among sons, a wife among brothers, and a wife among the husband's sons.
Ravina says in the name of Rava that in all these cases the recipient does not acquire the property, except for a betrothed wife or a divorced wife.
Rav Avira says in the name of Rava that in all these cases the recipient acquires the property, except for a wife among brothers and a wife among the husband's sons.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about a healthy person
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about a healthy person
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a healthy person (baria) also desires that his words be publicized, like a shkhiv mera, or not. The question is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a healthy person (בריא) also desires that his words be publicized immediately, like a shkhiv mera (שכיב מרע), or not, leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Baraita on a husband writing property to his wife
items.text_en: Baraita on a husband writing property to his wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a husband writes produce of his property to his wife, she collects her ketubah from the land; if he writes a half, third, or quarter, she collects from the remainder. If he writes all his property to her and a debt document emerges, Rabbi Eliezer says her gift is torn and she stands on her ketubah, while the Sages say her ketubah is torn and she stands on her gift, leaving her bald from both. Rabbi Yehuda the baker recounts a case where the Sages ruled accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The baraita is cited: if a husband writes produce of his property to his wife, she collects her ketubah from the land; if he writes a half, third, or quarter, she collects from the remainder.

The baraita continues: if he writes all his property to her and a debt document emerges, Rabbi Eliezer says her gift is torn and she stands on her ketubah, while the Sages say her ketubah is torn and she stands on her gift, leaving her bald from both.
Rabbi Yehuda the baker recounts a case where the Sages ruled accordingly, leaving the woman bald from both.

items.text: Gemara's inference and question
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and question
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if no debt document emerged, the wife acquires the gift. It asks: in what case? If it is a shkhiv mera, you said he only made her an appointee (apotropos). Rather, it must be a healthy person (baria).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if no debt document emerged, the wife acquires the gift, and then asks: in what case? If it is a shkhiv mera (שכיב מרע, a deathly ill person), you said he only made her an appointee (אפוטרופוס, apotropos). Rather, it must be a healthy person (בריא, baria).

items.text: Answers: Rav Avira and Ravina's resolutions
items.text_en: Answers: Rav Avira and Ravina's resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: actually it is a shkhiv mera, and Rav Avira establishes it in all cases, while Ravina establishes it regarding his betrothed wife and his divorced wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case is always a shkhiv mera (shkhiv mera), and then presents Rav Avira's and Ravina's alternative resolutions.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei said in the name of Rav Nachman: the halakha is that her ketubah is torn and she stands on her gift, leaving her bald from both.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the halakha follows the Sages: her ketubah is torn and she stands on her gift, leaving her bald from both.

items.text: Challenge from assessment and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from assessment and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: does Rav Nachman not follow assessment (umdana)? A baraita says if one thought his son died and wrote property to others, then the son returns, Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says the gift is invalid due to assessment, and Rav Nachman rules like him. The Gemara distinguishes: there, the wife wants the publicity that the property was written to her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: does Rav Nachman not follow assessment (אומדנא, circumstantial inference)?

A baraita is cited: if one thought his son died and wrote property to others, then the son returns, Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says the gift is invalid due to assessment (אומדנא), and Rav Nachman rules like him.
The Gemara distinguishes: there (in the case of the wife), she wants the publicity that the property was written to her, so the gift is valid despite the assessment.

items.text: Mishnah on writing property to sons and wife's ketubah
items.text_en: Mishnah on writing property to sons and wife's ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah: if one writes his property to his sons and writes to his wife any land, she loses her ketubah. The Gemara questions this, and Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina offer explanations: Rav says it is when he grants them through her, Shmuel says when he divides in her presence and she is silent, and Rabbi Yosei says when he says 'take this land for your ketubah.'

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if one writes his property to his sons and writes to his wife any land, she loses her ketubah.
The Gemara questions why merely writing her any land would cause her to lose her ketubah.
Rav explains that the case is where he grants the property to the sons through her (she acts as an intermediary), so she implicitly agrees to forfeit her ketubah.
Shmuel explains that the case is when he divides the property in her presence and she remains silent, indicating consent to forfeit her ketubah.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that the case is when he says to her: 'Take this land in satisfaction of your ketubah,' so she receives it as payment and forfeits the ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's opening statement
items.text_en: Gemara's opening statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling is based on the leniencies of the ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Mishnah's ruling is based on the leniencies of the ketubah (כתובה).

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and Baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei says a widow who accepted a share forfeits her ketubah even if not written, implying the first Tanna requires both writing and acceptance. It then brings a Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda that refutes all opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei says a widow who accepted a share forfeits her ketubah even without writing, implying the first Tanna requires both writing and acceptance.

The Gemara rejects the possibility that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yosei by citing a Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda that distinguishes between presence and acceptance, concluding that this refutes all opinions.

items.text: Rava asks Rav Nachman; Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman; Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman for his opinion among the conflicting views. Rav Nachman rules that once a husband makes his wife a partner among the sons, she forfeits her ketubah. This is supported by a statement from Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman what his opinion is among the conflicting views of Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina.
Rav Nachman answers that once a husband made his wife a partner among the sons, she loses her ketubah.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: A supporting tradition is cited: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi reports that Rav Nachman likewise ruled that making her a partner among the sons causes her to forfeit her ketubah.

items.text: Rava's inquiry about a healthy husband
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about a healthy husband
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether the same rule applies to a healthy husband, since a deathly ill husband's wife knows he has nothing and forgives, but a healthy husband's wife might think he will acquire again. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava inquires about the case of a healthy person: whether the wife's waiver is only assumed in a dying person who has no hope of recovery, but a healthy person might regain property, or perhaps she still has nothing now.

Rava asks whether the rule that a wife who was made a partner among the children loses her ketubah applies to a healthy husband, since a deathly ill husband's wife knows he has nothing and forgives, but a healthy husband's wife might think he will acquire again.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved with 'תיקו' (let it stand).
The gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Case of a husband giving produce to his wife
items.text_en: Case of a husband giving produce to his wife
items.desc_en: A man said to give half to one daughter, half to another, and a third to his wife in produce. Rav Nachman asked Rav Chisda, who cited Shmuel that even one date-palm for its produce forfeits her ketubah. Rav Nachman objects that Shmuel's case involved land, not mere produce, and Rav Chisda concedes that movables are excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a man allocated half to one daughter, half to another, and a third to his wife in produce; Rav Nachman asked Rav Chisda, who cited Shmuel's ruling that even one date-palm for its produce forfeits her ketubah.
Rav Nachman objects that Shmuel's case involved land, not mere produce, and Rav Chisda concedes that movables are excluded.

items.text: Case of a daughter's death
items.text_en: Case of a daughter's death
items.desc_en: A man gave a third to each daughter and a third to his wife. One daughter died, and Rav Pappi thought the surviving daughter takes only her third.

sub.desc_en: In a case where a man gave a third to each daughter and a third to his wife, and one daughter died, Rav Pappi considered that the wife takes only a third.
Rav Pappi thought that the surviving daughter takes only her third, not the deceased daughter's share.

items.text: Rav Kahana's argument on the wife's right to the gift
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's argument on the wife's right to the gift
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana argues that if the husband had repurchased the property, the wife would take it through her ketubah; therefore, even now she takes it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks: if the husband had repurchased the property, would the wife not take it through her ketubah?
Rav Kahana concludes: since if he had repurchased it she would take it, even now she takes it.

items.text: Case of dividing property between wife and sons with one tree left out
items.text_en: Case of dividing property between wife and sons with one tree left out
items.desc_en: A man divided his property between his wife and sons, leaving out one tree. Ravina thought the wife only gets that tree, but Rav Yemar argued that if she has no claim to the rest, she has no claim to the tree either; rather, since she descends to the tree, she descends to all the property.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a man divided his property between his wife and sons, leaving out one tree.
Ravina thought that the wife only gets that one tree.
Rav Yemar objects that if she has no claim to the rest, she has no claim to the tree either.
Rav Yemar resolves that since she descends to the tree, she descends to all the property.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a terminally ill person's gift to a stranger
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a terminally ill person's gift to a stranger
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if a terminally ill person writes all his property to another, we examine: if the recipient is fit to be his heir, he takes it as inheritance; if not, he takes it as a gift.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that when a terminally ill person writes all his property to another, we examine: if the recipient is fit to be his heir, he takes it as inheritance; if not, he takes it as a gift.

items.text: Rav Nachman's challenge and clarification of Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's challenge and clarification of Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman criticizes Rav Huna's formulation, suggesting he should simply state the halakha like Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. Rav Huna then clarifies that his ruling refers to a case where the dying person answered ambiguously, and Rav Nachman confirms this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman challenges Rav Huna's convoluted formulation, arguing that if he agrees with Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, he should simply state the halakha (הלכה) outright.
Rav Nachman proposes that Rav Huna's ruling refers to a specific case where the dying person gave an ambiguous answer, and Rav Huna confirms this interpretation.
Rav Huna confirms that Rav Nachman's interpretation of his ruling is correct.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's inference regarding the widow's sustenance
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's inference regarding the widow's sustenance
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava suggests that if the recipient is fit to be an heir, the widow is sustained from the property; if not, she is not. Rava objects, arguing that if inheritance (Torah law) provides sustenance, then a gift (rabbinic) certainly should.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's question before Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's question before Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava asks Rava what practical halacha follows from Rav Huna's rule, proposing that if the recipient is fit to inherit, the widow receives sustenance from the property, and if not, she does not.
Rava objects, arguing that if inheritance (Torah law) provides sustenance, then a gift (rabbinic) certainly should, so Rav Adda's distinction is flawed.

items.text: Rava's final ruling based on Rav Acha bar Avya's teaching
items.text_en: Rava's final ruling based on Rav Acha bar Avya's teaching
items.desc_en: Rava cites Rav Acha bar Avya: according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, if one says 'My property to you, and after you to so-and-so,' and the first is fit to be his heir, the second has nothing, because the language of gift is like inheritance, and inheritance has no interruption. Rava then questions Rav Nachman about the interruption, noting that the Torah says inheritance has no interruption.

sub.text: Rava's citation of Rav Acha bar Avya's teaching
sub.text_en: Rava's citation of Rav Acha bar Avya's teaching
sub.desc_en: Rava introduces Rav Acha bar Avya's teaching: according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, if one says 'My property to you, and after you to so-and-so,' and the first is fit to be his heir, the second has nothing, because the language of gift is like inheritance, and inheritance has no interruption.
Rava questions Rav Nachman: but the donor interrupted the inheritance by specifying 'after you,' while the Torah says inheritance has no interruption.

items.text: Opening case: gift with remainder clause
items.text_en: Opening case: gift with remainder clause
items.desc_en: A man says 'My property to you, and after you to so-and-so,' and the first recipient was his heir. When the first dies, the second claims the property. Rav Ulish thought the second takes it, but Rava rebukes him, citing a precedent from Rav Acha bar Rav Avya. Rav Ulish is embarrassed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a man said 'My property to you, and after you to so-and-so,' and the first recipient was his heir; when the first died, the second came to claim the property.
Rav Ulish thought before Rava that the second recipient also takes the property.
Rava rebukes Rav Ulish, saying that the judges of the partition (inferior courts) would rule this way, and cites a precedent from Rav Acha bar Rav Avya.
Rav Ulish was embarrassed, and Rava applied to him the verse 'I am the Lord, in its time I will hasten it.'

items.text: Mishnah: disinheriting sons
items.text_en: Mishnah: disinheriting sons
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who writes his property to others and leaves out his sons – his action is valid, but the Sages are not pleased with him. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: if the sons were not behaving properly, he is remembered for good.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one who writes his property to others and leaves out his sons – his action is valid, but the Sages are not pleased with him.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds: if the sons were not behaving properly, the father is remembered for good.

items.text: Gemara's question: do the Sages dispute Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: do the Sages dispute Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Sages (Tanna Kamma) disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Sages (Tanna Kamma) dispute Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position or not.

items.text: Attempted proof from Yosef ben Yoezer's story
items.text_en: Attempted proof from Yosef ben Yoezer's story
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story about Yosef ben Yoezer, whose son was not behaving properly. Yosef consecrated a room of dinars, and later the son sold it, finding a pearl. The court valued it and wrote that Yosef brought one and his son brought six (or removed seven). The Gemara debates whether this implies approval or disapproval of the son's actions, concluding no proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story about Yosef ben Yoezer, whose son was not behaving properly, and Yosef consecrated a room of dinars; the son later sold it and found a pearl.
The son's wife advises him not to sell the pearl to the king for a low price, but to bring it to the Temple treasurers and let them appraise it.
The treasurers appraised the pearl at thirteen rooms of dinars, and the son said: give me seven, and six are consecrated to Heaven.

sub.text: First version of the court's record
sub.text_en: First version of the court's record
sub.desc_en: The court wrote either that Yosef ben Yoezer brought one and his son brought six, or that Yosef brought one and his son removed seven.
The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'brought' implies approval of the son's actions, while 'removed' implies disapproval, concluding that no proof can be derived from this story.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling against transferring inheritance
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling against transferring inheritance
items.desc_en: Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda not to be involved in transferring inheritance, even from a bad son to a good son, and certainly not from a son to a daughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the resolution is regarding the dispute, then introduces a proof.
Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda not to be involved in transferring inheritance, even from a bad son to a good son, and certainly not from a son to a daughter.

items.text: Story of Yonatan ben Uzziel and Shammai's objection
items.text_en: Story of Yonatan ben Uzziel and Shammai's objection
items.desc_en: A man whose sons were not behaving properly wrote his property to Yonatan ben Uzziel. Yonatan sold a third, consecrated a third, and returned a third to the sons. Shammai came with his staff and wallet to protest, but Yonatan challenged him to undo the sale and consecration first.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces a story of a man whose sons were not behaving properly, who wrote his property to Yonatan ben Uzziel, and Yonatan sold a third, consecrated a third, and returned a third to the sons.
Shammai came with his staff and wallet to protest, and Yonatan challenged him to first undo the sale and consecration before undoing the return to the sons.

items.text: The case of Beit Horon and the rule about gifts that cannot be consecrated
items.text_en: The case of Beit Horon and the rule about gifts that cannot be consecrated
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier statement about a gift that cannot be consecrated is based on the incident of Beit Horon, where a man gave a courtyard and meal as a gift to circumvent his father's vow, but the recipient consecrated them. The Sages ruled that any gift that cannot be consecrated is not a valid gift.

sub.desc_en: Ben Uzziel exclaims that if not for the ruling, one cannot retrieve what one has given back, repeating his protest.
The Gemara asks what the original reasoning was, and answers that it is based on the incident of Beit Horon.
The Gemara cites a baraita about the incident of Beit Horon, where a man gave a courtyard and meal as a gift to circumvent his father's vow.
The recipient consecrates the gift, leading to a dispute about the validity of the gift.
The Sages rule that any gift which cannot be consecrated is not a valid gift.

items.text: Praise of Hillel's students and Jonathan ben Uzziel
items.text_en: Praise of Hillel's students and Jonathan ben Uzziel
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the eighty students of Hillel the Elder, their levels of greatness, and the vast knowledge of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the least of them. It then extols Jonathan ben Uzziel, the greatest, noting that birds flying over him while he studied Torah were burned.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Hillel's eighty students, categorizing them by greatness and naming the greatest (Jonathan ben Uzziel) and the least (Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai).
The Gemara details the vast Torah knowledge of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the least of the students, including all branches of Torah and the interpretation of 'great' and 'small' matters.
The Gemara concludes by a fortiori reasoning that Jonathan ben Uzziel, the greatest, was so holy that birds flying over him while he studied Torah were burned.

items.text: Mishnah: Declaring one's son or brother
items.text_en: Mishnah: Declaring one's son or brother
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man says 'This is my son,' he is believed, but if he says 'This is my brother,' he is not believed, and the alleged brother takes a share with him. If the declarant dies, the property returns to its original place; if the alleged brother acquires property from elsewhere, the other brothers inherit with him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one who declares 'this is my son' is believed, but if he says 'this is my brother' he is not believed, and the alleged brother takes a share with him.
The Mishnah adds: if the declarant dies, the property returns to its original place.
The Mishnah concludes: if the alleged brother acquires property from elsewhere, the other brothers inherit with him.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for what halakhic purpose the Mishnah's ruling applies, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers: for inheritance and to exempt his wife from levirate marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for what halakhic purpose the Mishnah's ruling that one who says 'this is my son' is believed applies.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers: the ruling applies to make him his heir and to exempt his wife from levirate marriage (ייבום).

items.text: Opening question and resolution
items.text_en: Opening question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's case of 'this is my son' is necessary, since it seems obvious. It explains that the case is needed to exempt the wife from yibbum, and distinguishes it from a case where the man is not known to have brothers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's case of 'this is my son' is necessary, since it seems obvious, and answers that it is needed to exempt the wife from yibbum (levirate marriage).
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where a dying man who says 'I have sons' is believed, but 'I have brothers' is not, implying the Mishnah's case is redundant.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing: there the man is not known to have brothers, but here the Mishnah's case applies even when he is known to have brothers.

items.text: First version of Shmuel's reason
items.text_en: First version of Shmuel's reason
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef quotes Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel: the reason 'this is my son' is believed is because a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed, invoking the principle of 'ho'il'.

sub.text: Rav Yosef quoting Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef quoting Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites Shmuel's reason: the statement 'this is my son' is believed because a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed, invoking the principle of הוֹאִיל (since he could divorce her now).

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects: the Mishnah's ruling is being made dependent on a ruling that is not itself established in a Mishnah or Baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that the Mishnah's ruling is being made dependent on a ruling that is not itself established in a Mishnah or Baraita.

items.text: Corrected version of Shmuel's reason
items.text_en: Corrected version of Shmuel's reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara retracts and presents a corrected version: Rav Yehuda said Shmuel said the reason is because the husband has the power to divorce her now, establishing the 'ho'il' principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara retracts the earlier version and presents the corrected statement: Rav Yehuda said Shmuel said the reason 'this is my son' is believed is because the husband has the power to divorce her now, establishing the 'הוֹאִיל (since)' principle.

items.text: Rav Yosef's deduction from 'ho'il'
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's deduction from 'ho'il'
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef now deduces that since we apply 'ho'il', a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed because he could divorce her now.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef deduces that since the principle of הוֹאִיל (since he could) is applied, a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed because he could divorce her now.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's contradiction and Rav Sheshet's reaction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's contradiction and Rav Sheshet's reaction
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports that Rabbi Yochanan says a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is not believed, which Rav Sheshet dismisses as blowing away Rav Yosef's 'ho'il' principle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports that Rabbi Yochanan rules a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is not believed.
Rav Sheshet dismisses Rabbi Yochanan's statement with a hand gesture, declaring that Rav Yosef's 'ho'il' principle is thereby blown away.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's statements and resolves it: one refers to believing him for the past (retroactively), the other for the future.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan is quoted by Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin as saying a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed, contradicting his earlier statement that he is not believed.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one statement applies retroactively (למפרע) and the other applies for the future (להבא).

items.text: Inquiry about splitting speech
items.text_en: Inquiry about splitting speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether if he said 'I divorced' for the past, we believe him for the future as well, debating whether speech can be split. It cites Rava's case about testimony for execution, distinguishing between two bodies and one body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether if a husband said 'I divorced' for the past (למפרע), we also believe him for the future (להבא), debating whether speech can be split.
Rav Mari and Rav Zevid dispute: one says we split speech (פָּלְגִינַן), the other says we do not split speech (לָא פָּלְגִינַן).

The Gemara objects by citing Rava's case: if a man says 'So-and-so had relations with my wife,' he and another witness join to execute the man but not the woman, showing speech is split between two bodies.
The Gemara resolves: we split speech between two bodies (e.g., two people), but within one body (e.g., one person's past and future status) we do not split speech.

items.text: Case of the dying man who says his wife is permitted to a High Priest
items.text_en: Case of the dying man who says his wife is permitted to a High Priest
items.desc_en: A dying man says his wife is permitted to a High Priest. Rava initially argues she is permitted based on Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed. Abaye objects, citing a contradictory version of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling. Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between retroactive and future effect, but Abaye questions relying on such a distinction. Rava then advises to be stringent.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a dying man is asked about his wife's status and says she is permitted to a High Priest.
Rava argues there is no concern, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a husband who says 'I divorced my wife' is believed.
Abaye objects, citing a contradictory version of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the husband is not believed.
Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between retroactive effect (למפרע) and future effect (להבא).
Abaye questions whether one can rely on such a forced distinction (שינוי).

sub.text: Rava to Rav Nachman bar Ammi
sub.text_en: Rava to Rav Nachman bar Ammi
sub.desc_en: Rava advises Rav Nachman bar Ammi to be stringent and treat the woman as prohibited.

items.text: Case of the dying man who says he has no brothers
items.text_en: Case of the dying man who says he has no brothers
items.desc_en: A man presumed to have no brothers says at death that he has no brothers. Rav Yosef argues she is permitted based on the presumption and his statement. Abaye objects that there may be witnesses overseas. The Gemara compares this to Rabbi Chanina's ruling about witnesses in a corner. Abaye further argues that leniency in the case of a captive woman does not apply to a married woman. Rava again advises to be stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a man presumed to have no brothers stated at death that he has no brothers.
Rav Yosef argues there is no concern: the man was presumed to have no brothers, and he himself stated so at death.
Abaye objects that there may be witnesses overseas who know he has brothers.
The Gemara questions whether this is not the same as Rabbi Chanina's ruling about witnesses in a corner, where the woman would be forbidden.
Abaye argues that leniency in the case of a captive woman does not apply to a married woman (אשת איש).

sub.text: Rava to Rav Nachman bar Ammi
sub.text_en: Rava to Rav Nachman bar Ammi
sub.desc_en: Rava instructs Rav Nachman bar Ammi to be stringent and forbid the woman.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah: 'This is my brother' is not believed
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah: 'This is my brother' is not believed
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one who says 'This is my brother' is not believed. It asks what the other brothers say: if they say 'He is our brother', why would he not take a share? If they say 'He is not our brother', the Mishnah's later clause about inheriting from elsewhere contradicts this. The Gemara resolves that they say 'We do not know'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that one who says 'This is my brother' is not believed.
The Gemara asks what the other brothers say in response to the claimant's statement.
The Gemara objects: if the brothers say 'He is our brother', why would the claimant not take a share with them?
The Gemara objects further: the Mishnah's later clause says that if property falls to him from elsewhere, the brothers inherit with him, implying they deny his brotherhood.
The Gemara resolves that the brothers say 'We do not know', which explains the Mishnah's rulings.

items.text: Rava's principle: 'I have a mana in your hand' and the other says 'I don't know' – exempt
items.text_en: Rava's principle: 'I have a mana in your hand' and the other says 'I don't know' – exempt
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the previous discussion that if one claims 'You owe me a mana' and the other says 'I don't know', he is exempt. Abaye begins to respond, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives a general principle: if one claims 'You owe me a mana' and the other says 'I don't know', the defendant is exempt from liability.
Abaye begins to respond to Rava's principle, but the text cuts off, leaving his objection or qualification incomplete.

items.text: Rava's query about appreciation of assets
items.text_en: Rava's query about appreciation of assets
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier ruling (that assets return to their original place upon the recipient's death) applies only when the recipient is like a bailee. Rava then asks about appreciation that occurs naturally, distinguishing between movable appreciation (like fruit) and fixed appreciation (like a tree growing stronger or land rising due to silt). The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier ruling (that assets return to their original place) applies only when the recipient is like a bailee (מנה לאחר בידך).
Rava asks about appreciation that occurs naturally (שבח ששבחו נכסים מאליהם) — whether it goes to the recipient or returns to the original owner.
The Gemara distinguishes movable appreciation (שבח המגיע לכתפיים) as clearly belonging to the recipient, like assets from elsewhere.
Rava's unresolved query focuses on fixed appreciation (שבח שאינו מגיע לכתפיים), such as a tree growing stronger or land rising due to silt.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah: Found will tied to thigh
items.text_en: Mishnah: Found will tied to thigh
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a person dies and a will (diyatikei) is found tied to his thigh, it is invalid. However, if he explicitly granted the property to another, whether an heir or a stranger, his words stand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a will found tied to the deceased's thigh is invalid, but if he explicitly granted the property to another, his words stand.

items.text: Definition of diyatikei and gift
items.text_en: Definition of diyatikei and gift
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita defining a diyatikei as one that says 'this shall stand and be,' and a gift as one that says 'from today and after death.' Abaye clarifies that the latter refers to a healthy person's gift that is like a dying person's gift, i.e., only takes effect after death.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by defining a דיאתיקי (will) as one that says 'this shall stand and be.'
The baraita defines a gift as one that says 'from today and after death.'
The Gemara questions: does only 'from today and after death' count as a gift, but 'from now' does not?
Abaye clarifies that the baraita refers to a healthy person's gift that is like a dying person's gift, i.e., only takes effect after death.

items.text: Dispute about writing a gift after death
items.text_en: Dispute about writing a gift after death
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that if a dying person says 'write and give a mane to so-and-so' and dies, we do not write and give, because he may have intended to transfer only through a document, and a document cannot be written after death. Rabbi Elazar warns to be careful with this ruling. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves that Rabbi Elazar said it, not Rabbi Yochanan, based on a message sent by Ravin. Rabbi Yochanan himself said 'tibadek' (it should be examined).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's definition of a gift, asking why only 'from today and after death' qualifies as a gift, but not 'from now'.
Abaye clarifies that the baraita refers to a healthy person's gift that takes effect only after death, like a dying person's gift, defined by the phrase 'from today and after death'.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that if a dying person says 'write and give a mane to so-and-so' and dies, we do not write and give, because he may have intended to transfer only through a document, and a document cannot be written after death.
Rabbi Elazar warns to be careful with this ruling, and Rav Sheizvi attributes the warning to Rabbi Yochanan instead.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak argues that Rav Sheizvi's version is correct: Rabbi Elazar said the ruling, and Rabbi Yochanan needed to testify about his colleague, not the reverse.
Ravin's message in the name of Rabbi Avahu confirms that Rabbi Elazar sent the ruling to the diaspora, while Rabbi Yochanan said 'tibadek' (it should be examined).

items.text: Resolution: yafeh koach (empowering) clause
items.text_en: Resolution: yafeh koach (empowering) clause
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi explains that 'tibadek' means a will can override a will; we examine if the dying person was empowering the recipient (yafeh koach). If so, we write; if not, we don't. Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects from a baraita about a healthy person, but resolves it himself: the baraita refers to a case where the donor empowered the recipient. The Gemara then asks what constitutes 'yafeh koach'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'תִּיבָּדֵק' (it should be examined) means in Rabbi Yochanan's statement.
Rav Dimi explains that 'תִּיבָּדֵק' means a will can override a will; we examine if the dying person was empowering the recipient (ייפוי כוח); if so, we write, if not, we don't.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects from a baraita about a healthy person, implying that for a dying person we do write and give, contradicting Rav Dimi's distinction.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel resolves his own objection: the baraita refers to a case where the donor empowered the recipient (ייפוי כוח).
The Gemara asks what constitutes 'ייפוי כוח' (empowering the recipient).

items.text: Opening statement and halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Opening statement and halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Chisda's statement about adding to a gift, and then records the ruling of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel and Rava citing Rav Nachman that the halakha is that one writes and gives (the document).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rav Chisda's statement about adding to a gift, applying it to the case of writing and signing a document.

sub.text: Gemara citing Rav Yehuda and Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara citing Rav Yehuda and Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara records the ruling of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel and Rava citing Rav Nachman that the halakha is that one writes and gives the document.

items.text: Mishnah: Writing property to sons and the law of sale
items.text_en: Mishnah: Writing property to sons and the law of sale
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding the need to write 'from today and after death' in a gift to sons. It then states the law that neither the father nor the son can sell the property during the father's lifetime, and the consequences if either does sell.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding the need to write 'from today and after death' in a gift to sons.
The Mishnah states that neither the father nor the son can sell the property during the father's lifetime.
The Mishnah details the consequences if the father or the son sells the property.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'from today and after death'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'from today and after death'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the validity of the phrase 'from today and after death' based on a parallel in Gittin where it creates a doubt. It resolves that here the intent is to grant the body from today and the produce after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the validity of the phrase 'from today and after death' by citing a parallel in Gittin where it creates a doubt about whether it is a valid get or not.
The Gemara resolves that in Gittin the doubt is whether it is a condition or a retraction, but here the intent is to grant the body from today and the produce after death.

items.text: Inquiry about the halakha like Rabbi Yosei and his reasoning
items.text_en: Inquiry about the halakha like Rabbi Yosei and his reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rav Nachman whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Nachman initially demurs, then Rav Huna asks the halakha while Rav Nachman explains the reasoning: the date of the document proves it. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Yosei's position that one need not write 'from today and after death'; the Gemara then introduces the story of Rabbah bar Avuh's illness and the visit of Rav Huna and Rav Nachman.

sub.text: Rav Huna's question to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's question to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rav Nachman to inquire of Rabbah bar Avuh whether the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei or not.
Rav Nachman objects that he does not even know Rabbi Yosei's reasoning, so how can he ask about the הלכה (binding law)?
Rav Huna proposes a division of labor: Rav Nachman will ask about the הלכה (binding law), and Rav Huna himself will later explain the reasoning.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's inquiry and Rav's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's inquiry and Rav's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbah bar Avuh, who responds in the name of Rav that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei.

sub.text: Rav Huna's explanation of the reasoning
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's explanation of the reasoning
sub.desc_en: After they leave, Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: the date of the document (זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל שְׁטָר) proves that the gift takes effect from the date of writing, so no explicit 'from today' clause is needed.
A baraita (תַּנְיָא) is cited in support, explicitly stating Rabbi Yosei's position with the same reasoning: the date of the document proves the timing of the gift.

items.text: Dispute about the need for 'from today' in a deed of acquisition (הקנאה)
items.text_en: Dispute about the need for 'from today' in a deed of acquisition (הקנאה)
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a deed of acquisition (הקנאה), and Rav Nachman rules it is unnecessary. Rav Pappi distinguishes between two formulations, Rav Chanina from Sura challenges the scribes' knowledge, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua clarifies that the dispute is about a document of 'record of matters' (דוכרן פתגמי).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether a deed of acquisition (הקנאה) requires the phrase 'from today'.
Rav Nachman rules that a deed of acquisition does not require 'from today'.

Rav Pappi distinguishes between two formulations: 'הקנינהו וקנינא מיניה' (he transferred and we acquired from him) does not require 'from today', while 'קנינא מיניה והקנינהו' (we acquired from him and he transferred) does require it.
Rav Chanina from Sura objects: is there anything we do not know that the scribes know? He notes that the scribes of Abaye and Rava were consulted and they knew the distinction.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua clarifies that the dispute is not about acquisition deeds but about a 'record of matters' (דוכרן פתגמי) document, where the sages disagree.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's report of Rav Zevid's tradition
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's report of Rav Zevid's tradition
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rav Zevid from Nehardea transmitted a different version of the tradition: Rava said in the name of Rav Nachman that neither formulation requires 'from today', and the dispute is only about a 'record of matters' document.

items.text: Case of the son selling during the father's lifetime and dying
items.text_en: Case of the son selling during the father's lifetime and dying
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new case: if the son sold the property during the father's lifetime and then died while the father was still alive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new case: if the son sold the property during the father's lifetime and then died while the father was still alive.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on acquisition of usufruct
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on acquisition of usufruct
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue whether a purchaser of usufruct (קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת) acquires ownership equivalent to the body of the property (קִנְיַן הַגּוּף). Rabbi Yochanan holds it is equivalent, Reish Lakish holds it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish state their opposing positions on whether a purchaser of usufruct (קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת) acquires ownership equivalent to the body of the property (קִנְיַן הַגּוּף).

items.text: Gemara's question: Why repeat the dispute?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why repeat the dispute?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this same dispute already appeared in the context of selling a field for its produce (הַמּוֹכֵר שָׂדֵהוּ לְפֵירוֹת), where Rabbi Yochanan said the buyer brings first fruits and recites, while Reish Lakish said he brings but does not recite. The Gemara questions why the dispute is repeated here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the same dispute already appears in a different context regarding bringing first fruits and reciting the declaration.

The Gemara explains that the dispute is repeated because each case has its own novel point: in the earlier case, the buyer of produce brings first fruits and recites because קניין פירות כקניין הגוף דמי (acquisition of produce is like acquisition of the body), while here the father's gift to his son involves a different consideration.

items.text: Answer: Each opinion needs to be stated here due to a novel case
items.text_en: Answer: Each opinion needs to be stated here due to a novel case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that even though generally he holds קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת is like קִנְיַן הַגּוּף, here it was necessary because one might think a father waives his rights to his son. Reish Lakish explains that even though generally he holds it is not equivalent, here it was necessary because one might think a person prefers himself even over his son.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that even though generally usufruct is equivalent to the body, here a special teaching was needed to counter the assumption that a father waives rights in favor of his son.

Reish Lakish explains that even though generally he holds קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת is not equivalent to קִנְיַן הַגּוּף, here it was necessary because one might think a person prefers himself even over his son.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection from a baraita about sequential gifts
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection from a baraita about sequential gifts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from a baraita: If one says 'My property to you, and after you so-and-so will inherit, and after him so-and-so,' and the second dies in the lifetime of the first, the property returns to the heirs of the first. Rabbi Yochanan argues that if Reish Lakish were correct, it should return to the heirs of the giver.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita about sequential inheritance, arguing that if usufruct is not equivalent to the body, the property should revert to the donor's heirs rather than the first recipient's heirs.

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish by citing a baraita about sequential gifts: if one says 'My property to you, and after you so-and-so will inherit, and after him so-and-so,' and the first recipient dies, the second acquires; if the second dies, the third acquires.
The baraita continues: if the second dies during the first's lifetime, the property returns to the heirs of the first.

Rabbi Yochanan argues: if Reish Lakish were correct (that the first recipient acquires the property fully), then when the second dies in the first's lifetime, the property should return to the heirs of the original giver, not to the heirs of the first.

items.text: Reish Lakish's answer: The phrase 'after you' is different
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's answer: The phrase 'after you' is different
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish responds that the case of 'after you' (אַחֲרֶיךָ) is different, as explained by Rav Hoshaya in Babylonia and by Rabbah bar Rav Huna before Rav. A supporting baraita is cited that indeed the property returns to the heirs of the giver.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish responds that the case of 'after you' (אַחֲרֶיךָ) is different, as explained by Rav Hoshaya in Babylonia and by Rabbah bar Rav Huna before Rav.
A supporting baraita is cited that indeed the property returns to the heirs of the giver.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction between the two baraitot
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction between the two baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the two baraitot present contradictory rulings of Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding the first recipient's rights. It resolves the contradictions by distinguishing between the body of the property and its produce, and between initial permission and post-facto validity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita presenting Rabbi's ruling that the second recipient can reclaim property sold by the first.
The baraita cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opposing view that the second recipient only gets what the first left unsold.
The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a second baraita where Rabbi permits the first to sell and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel restricts him to eating produce only.
The Gemara objects that each authority contradicts himself across the two baraitot.

The Gemara resolves the contradictions: Rabbi's rulings distinguish between the body of the property (גוּפָא) and its produce (פֵּירָא), while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's distinguish between לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and בדיעבד (after the fact).

items.text: Abaye's definition of a cunning wicked person
items.text_en: Abaye's definition of a cunning wicked person
items.desc_en: Abaye defines a 'cunning wicked person' as one who advises selling property in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient view, thereby harming the second recipient.

sub.desc_en: Abaye defines a 'cunning wicked person' as one who advises selling property in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient view, thereby harming the second recipient.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and its rationale
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and its rationale
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but adds that if the gift was given as a gift of a dying person (matnat shekhiv mera), the first recipient's actions are void. Abaye explains that such a gift takes effect only after death, and the 'after you' clause precedes it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but adds that if the gift was given as a gift of a dying person (מתנת שכיב מרע), the first recipient's actions are void.
Abaye explains that a gift of a dying person (מתנת שכיב מרע) takes effect only after death, and the 'after you' clause precedes it.

items.text: Challenge to Abaye's position and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Abaye's position and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's statement by citing a dispute where Abaye held that a dying person's gift takes effect at the moment of death, not after. The Gemara concludes that Abaye retracted his earlier view, as evidenced by a mishnah that a get given 'after death' is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's statement by citing a dispute where Abaye held that a dying person's gift takes effect at the moment of death, not after.
The Gemara suggests that Abaye retracted his earlier view, but then questions whether he retracted from that specific dispute or from another.
The Gemara resolves that Abaye must have retracted from the earlier dispute, citing a mishnah that a get given 'after death' is invalid, which supports Abaye's later position.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's ruling: even with slaves
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's ruling: even with slaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel even if the first recipient freed slaves, which might seem forbidden. The Gemara explains that this is obvious, but the ruling teaches that we do not assume the donor intended to prevent a transgression.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel even if the first recipient freed slaves, which might seem forbidden.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is necessary, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling teaches that we do not assume the donor intended to prevent a transgression.

items.text: Rav Yosef's ruling: even with shrouds
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling: even with shrouds
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel even if the first recipient used the property to make shrouds for a corpse, which might be forbidden. The Gemara explains that this is obvious, but the ruling teaches that we do not assume the donor intended to prevent a prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel even if the first recipient used the property to make shrouds for a corpse.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious, since the first recipient's use for a corpse is still a permissible use of the property.

The Gemara explains that the ruling teaches that we do not assume the donor intended to prevent the first recipient from creating an object of forbidden benefit (איסורי הנאה), so the ruling is not obvious.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's case and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's case and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda presents a case of an etrog given with an 'after you' clause, and says the first recipient's use of it for a mitzvah depends on the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, arguing that the dispute there was about whether the right to produce is like ownership of the body, but here the issue is different.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda presents a case of an etrog given with an 'after you' clause, and rules that the first recipient's use of it for a mitzvah depends on the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, arguing that the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was about whether the right to produce is like ownership of the body, but here the issue is different.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of giving an etrog if it cannot be used for the mitzvah. It concludes that everyone agrees one may fulfill the obligation with it; the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is only if the recipient sold or ate it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the recipient cannot fulfill the mitzvah (מצוה) of taking the lulav with this etrog, why was it given to him at all?
The Gemara answers: everyone agrees one may fulfill the obligation with it; the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is only about the case where the recipient sold or ate the etrog.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling on brothers and an etrog
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling on brothers and an etrog
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that if brothers jointly own an etrog as part of the household property, and one takes it and uses it for the mitzvah, he fulfills his obligation only if he is entitled to eat it (i.e., it is his share). This applies only if each brother has his own etrog, but not if they share a single fruit like a pomegranate.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that brothers who jointly own an etrog as household property: if one takes it and uses it for the mitzvah, he fulfills his obligation only if he is entitled to eat it (i.e., it is his share).
The gemara clarifies that this ruling applies only when each brother has his own etrog, but not when they share a single fruit like a pomegranate.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a conditional gift with return
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a conditional gift with return
items.desc_en: Rava states that if one says, 'This etrog is given to you as a gift on condition that you return it to me,' and the recipient takes it and uses it for the mitzvah, he fulfills his obligation only if he actually returns it. This teaches that a gift on condition of return is considered a valid gift.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a conditional gift of an etrog on condition of return is a valid gift, so the recipient fulfills the mitzvah only if he actually returns it.

items.text: Story of the woman and the date tree, and Rav Huna's objection
items.text_en: Story of the woman and the date tree, and Rav Huna's objection
items.desc_en: A woman who owned a date tree on Rav Bibi's land transferred ownership of the tree to him for her lifetime. Rav Bibi then transferred it to his minor son. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects, arguing that even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only allows a gift to another, not to oneself.

sub.desc_en: The gemara tells a story: a woman who owned a date tree on Rav Bibi's land, who resented her coming to cut it, transferred ownership of the tree to him for her lifetime, and he then transferred it to his minor son.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects: even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only permits a gift to another, not to oneself, so Rav Bibi's transfer to his own son is invalid.

items.text: Rava and Rav Nachman's discussion on consecration and return
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Nachman's discussion on consecration and return
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that if one says, 'This ox is given to you as a gift on condition that you return it to me,' and the recipient consecrates it and then returns it, it is both consecrated and returned. Rava questions what exactly is returned, and Rav Ashi resolves that the condition's wording determines whether the return is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites Rav Nachman's ruling that if one gives an ox as a gift on condition of return, and the recipient consecrates it and then returns it, the ox is both consecrated and returned.
Rava asks Rav Nachman: what exactly does the recipient return — the consecrated ox itself or its value?
Rav Nachman dismisses the question, implying that nothing is lacking — the return is valid as is.

Rav Ashi resolves the issue by distinguishing the wording: if the condition says 'that you return it' (without 'to me'), the ox itself is returned; if it says 'that you return it to me', the recipient must return something fit for the giver, i.e., the ox itself, not its value.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Yehuda/Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan on rejecting a gift
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Yehuda/Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan on rejecting a gift
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that if one writes his property to another and the recipient says 'I do not want them,' the recipient acquires it even if he protests. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, saying he does not acquire it. Rabbi Abba bar Memel states they do not actually dispute.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that if one writes his property to another and the recipient says 'I do not want them,' the recipient acquires it even if he protests.
Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, stating that the recipient does not acquire the property.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel resolves that Rav Yehuda/Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan do not actually dispute.

items.text: Initial distinction between protesting and silent recipient
items.text_en: Initial distinction between protesting and silent recipient
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a distinction: one who protests from the outset does not acquire, while one who is initially silent and later protests is in dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a distinction between one who protests from the outset and one who is initially silent and later protests.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak links the case to a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak links the case to a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the case of a gift delivered through a third party where the recipient was silent and later protested is the subject of a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages, as cited in a baraita about a man who writes his property to another and the recipient says 'I do not want them'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that the case of a gift delivered through a third party where the recipient was silent and later protested is the subject of a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages.

A baraita is cited: one who writes his property to another, including slaves, and the recipient says 'I do not want them' — the Tanna Kamma holds the slaves may eat תרומה (priestly portion) if the recipient is a priest, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the heirs have already acquired them.

items.text: Gemara's question on the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Tanna Kamma's position: does he hold that the recipient acquires even if he stands and protests?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Tanna Kamma's position: does he hold that the recipient acquires even if he stands and protests?

items.text: Rava or Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dispute
items.text_en: Rava or Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yochanan) clarifies that all agree that if the recipient protests from the outset he does not acquire, and if he is silent and later protests he does acquire. The dispute is only when a third party delivered the gift and the recipient was silent initially but later protested: the Tanna Kamma holds that silence effects acquisition, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that his later protest shows he never intended to acquire.

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yochanan) opens by stating that all agree that if the recipient protests from the outset (צוֹוֵחַ מֵעִיקָּרוֹ), he does not acquire the gift.
He continues that if the recipient was silent initially and protested later, all agree that he does acquire the gift.

He resolves the dispute by explaining that the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagree only when a third party delivered the gift and the recipient was silent initially but later protested: the Tanna Kamma holds that silence effects acquisition, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the later protest shows he never intended to acquire.

items.text: Baraita on sequential gifts from a deathbed declaration
items.text_en: Baraita on sequential gifts from a deathbed declaration
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a deathly ill person says 'Give 200 zuz to Ploni, 300 to Ploni, and 400 to Ploni' (without specifying order), the creditors collect from all equally. But if he says 'Give 200 to Ploni, and after him to Ploni, and after him to Ploni', the first recipient takes precedence, and a creditor collects from the last recipient first.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the first case: a deathly ill person lists sequential gifts without specifying order, so creditors collect from all recipients equally.

The baraita presents the second case: if the dying person specifies 'and after him', the first recipient takes precedence, and a creditor collects from the last recipient first, then from the preceding ones in order.

items.text: Baraita on gifts to a firstborn son and to a wife
items.text_en: Baraita on gifts to a firstborn son and to a wife
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a deathly ill person who gives 200 zuz to his firstborn son 'as is fitting for him' – the son takes the gift and his birthright. If he says 'with his birthright', the son may choose either. Similarly, if he gives 200 zuz to his wife 'as is fitting for her', she takes the gift and her ketubah; if he says 'with her ketubah', she may choose.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the case of a deathly ill person who gives 200 zuz to his firstborn son 'as is fitting for him' – the son takes the gift and his birthright.
The baraita adds that if the father says 'with his birthright', the son may choose either the gift or the birthright.
The baraita presents a parallel case: a deathly ill person who gives 200 zuz to his wife 'as is fitting for her' – she takes the gift and her ketubah.
The baraita begins the parallel rule for the wife: if he says 'with her ketubah', she may choose, but the text is cut off at the end of the section.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a dying man says 'Give 200 zuz to so-and-so, my creditor, as is proper for him.' The ruling is that the creditor takes the 200 zuz and also collects his debt. If he said 'in his debt,' he takes it as his debt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: a woman's hand is on top, and a dying man who says 'give 200 zuz to so-and-so my creditor, as is proper for him' takes the 200 and also collects his debt; if he said 'in his debt,' he takes it as his debt.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling: why does saying 'as is proper for him' allow the creditor to take the money and also collect his debt? Perhaps the dying man meant 'as is proper for him in his debt'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling: why does saying 'as is proper for him' allow the creditor to take the money and also collect his debt? Perhaps the dying man meant 'as is proper for him in his debt'?

items.text: Rav Nachman's answer citing Rabbi Akiva's principle
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer citing Rabbi Akiva's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman, citing Huna, explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who infers from extra language. Just as in a case where a seller specifies 'except for these' even though it's unnecessary, the extra language adds something, so here the dying man's extra phrase 'as is proper for him' adds that the creditor takes the money as a gift in addition to his debt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman, citing Huna, identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Akiva, who infers from extra language.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva and the Sages dispute whether a seller who specifies 'except for these' must provide a path, illustrating Rabbi Akiva's method of inferring from extra language.

The Gemara concludes that just as in the baraita the extra phrase adds something, so here the dying man's extra phrase 'כראוי לו' (as is proper for him) adds that the creditor takes the money as a gift in addition to his debt.

items.text: Baraita on a dying man's testimony and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Baraita on a dying man's testimony and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a dying man who says 'I have a maneh with so-and-so.'
