Rabbi Meir says witnesses write it down even if they don't recognize the debt, but when he collects he must bring proof. The Sages say they only write if they recognize, so he doesn't need proof. Rav Nachman cites Huna that Rabbi Meir's concern is that courts might err, but Rav Dimi from Nehardea rules that we do not worry about courts erring.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says witnesses write the dying man's statement even without recognizing the debt, requiring proof when collecting; the Sages say they write only if they recognize, so no proof is needed.
Rav Nachman cites Huna that the baraita's version is reversed: Rabbi Meir actually says witnesses do not write, and his concern is that courts might err.
Rav Dimi from Nehardea rules that the הלכה (binding law) is that we do not worry about courts erring.

items.text: Comparison with Rava's ruling on chalitzah and mi'un
items.text_en: Comparison with Rava's ruling on chalitzah and mi'un
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why we worry about courts erring in the case of chalitzah and mi'un documents, but not in the case of the dying man's testimony. The answer distinguishes: courts do not scrutinize the rulings of other courts, but they do scrutinize the testimony of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the ruling about the dying man's testimony differs from Rava's ruling about chalitzah and mi'un documents, where courts write documents even without recognizing the parties.
The Gemara objects that Rava's ruling might be based on concern for courts erring, which would contradict the earlier ruling.

The Gemara resolves that courts do not scrutinize the rulings of other courts (so chalitzah documents are written without concern), but they do scrutinize the testimony of witnesses (so the dying man's testimony requires recognition).

items.text: Mishnah and brief Gemara on a father's rights to produce
items.text_en: Mishnah and brief Gemara on a father's rights to produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a father may pluck and feed produce to whomever he wishes, but what he leaves plucked belongs to the heirs. The Gemara clarifies: plucked produce is for the heirs, but attached produce is not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a father may pluck and feed produce to whomever he wishes, but what he leaves plucked belongs to the heirs.
The Gemara clarifies that only plucked produce goes to the heirs, but attached produce does not.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita on appraising attached items
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita on appraising attached items
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says attached items are appraised for the buyer. Ulla resolves it by distinguishing between a son and another person, since a father's mind is close to his son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that rules attached items are appraised for the buyer.
Ulla resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a son and another person, since a father's mind is close to his son.

items.text: Mishnah: Inheritance rules for sons and daughters
items.text_en: Mishnah: Inheritance rules for sons and daughters
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man left older and younger sons, the older may not support themselves from the estate at the expense of the younger, and vice versa; they divide equally. Similarly for daughters, with an additional stringency that daughters are supported by sons but not by other daughters.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule for sons: older and younger sons divide the estate equally, and neither may support themselves at the expense of the other.

The Mishnah adds that if the older sons married using estate funds, the younger sons may also marry from the estate, but if the younger sons demand to marry in the same manner as the older sons did during the father's lifetime, they are not heard.
The Mishnah states the parallel rule for daughters: older and younger daughters divide equally and may not support themselves at the expense of the other.

The Mishnah adds that if the older daughters married using estate funds, the younger daughters may also marry from the estate, but if the younger daughters demand to marry in the same manner as the older ones did during the father's lifetime, they are not heard.
The Mishnah concludes with a stringency for daughters: daughters are supported by sons but not by other daughters.

items.text: Rava's ruling on an older brother who took from the estate
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on an older brother who took from the estate
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if an older brother clothed himself from the estate, what he did is done. The Gemara questions this from the Mishnah and explains that the Mishnah refers to a case of 'shrakha' (a loan), where the older brother's action is valid to prevent embarrassment.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if an older brother clothed himself from the estate, what he did is done.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that older brothers may not support themselves at the expense of the younger ones.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to a case of 'שרכא' (a loan), where the older brother's action is valid to prevent embarrassment.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling about 'שרכא' is obvious, but it teaches that the older brother's action is upheld to avoid his embarrassment.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's statement about older sons marrying
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's statement about older sons marrying
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'if the older ones married, the younger ones may marry.' Rav Yehuda explains that it refers to marriages after the father's death, but if the older ones married during the father's lifetime, the younger ones cannot demand the same after his death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by the phrase 'if the older ones married, the younger ones may marry.'
Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah refers to marriages after the father's death; but if the older ones married during the father's lifetime, the younger ones cannot demand the same after his death.

items.text: Question about a daughter who borrowed and married: purchaser or heir?
items.text_en: Question about a daughter who borrowed and married: purchaser or heir?
items.desc_en: Avuh bar Geniva asks Rava whether a husband who marries a daughter who had borrowed and consumed is considered a purchaser or an heir. Rava initially cites the Mishnah, but the Gemara distinguishes between support (which has publicity) and other debts.

sub.text: Avuh bar Geniva's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Avuh bar Geniva's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Avuh bar Geniva asks Rava whether a husband who marries a daughter who had borrowed and consumed is considered a purchaser (so the oral loan cannot be collected from him) or an heir (so it can).
Avuh bar Geniva clarifies the practical difference: if the husband is a purchaser, an oral loan cannot be collected from him; if he is an heir, it can.

sub.text: Rava's initial answer from the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rava's initial answer from the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rava cites the Mishnah (segments 4-5) as proof: 'If older daughters married, younger ones may marry' — implying the husband is a purchaser, since the younger ones take from the husband.
The Gemara rejects the inference: the Mishnah means that older daughters married to a husband, so younger ones may also marry a husband — not that they take from the husband.
Rabbi Chiyya's baraita explicitly states that younger daughters marry from the husband, supporting Rava's original inference.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: support (פרנסה) is different because it has publicity (קלא), so the husband is treated as a purchaser only for support, not for other debts.

items.text: Proof from Ravin's letter about a widow and daughter
items.text_en: Proof from Ravin's letter about a widow and daughter
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa brings a case from Ravin's letter where a widow's sustenance continues even after the daughter marries, proving the husband is an heir. Abaye notes that without Ravin's letter, they would have known from the Mishnah about items that do not return in the Jubilee.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites Ravin's letter to Rava, which states that when a man dies leaving a widow and a daughter, the widow continues to receive sustenance even after the daughter marries.
The gemara infers that if the husband is an heir, the widow's sustenance continues; but if he is a purchaser, it should not, proving the husband is an heir.
Abaye notes that even without Ravin's letter, they would have known the husband is an heir from the Mishnah listing items that do not return in the Jubilee, including the firstborn's portion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that a husband inherits his wife's property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that a husband inherits his wife's property.

items.text: Rava's question and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling
items.text_en: Rava's question and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava questions the practical application of the husband's inheritance right, citing a ruling by Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina that a husband can reclaim property sold by his wife during his lifetime.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions how the husband's inheritance right applies practically when the wife sold property during his lifetime.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina cites the enactment in Usha that a husband can reclaim property sold by his wife during her lifetime after her death.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution: husband as both heir and purchaser
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution: husband as both heir and purchaser
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Sages treated the husband as both an heir and a purchaser, applying whichever status benefits him in different contexts: regarding יובל he is an heir, regarding Rabbi Yosei's case he is a purchaser, and regarding Ravin's case he is an heir to protect the widow.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by stating that the Sages treated the husband as both an heir and a purchaser, applying whichever status benefits him in different contexts.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding purchasers' loss
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding purchasers' loss
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that in Rabbi Yosei's case, treating the husband as a purchaser causes loss to the purchasers. It answers that the purchasers brought the loss upon themselves by buying from a married woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that in Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's case, treating the husband as a purchaser causes loss to the purchasers, contradicting the principle that the rabbis treated him as a purchaser only for his own benefit.
The Gemara answers that the purchasers brought the loss upon themselves, since they should not have bought from a woman living under her husband's authority.

items.text: Mishnah: Inheritance with sons and daughters
items.text_en: Mishnah: Inheritance with sons and daughters
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when a man dies leaving sons and daughters, if the estate is large the sons inherit and the daughters are supported; if small, the daughters are supported and the sons must beg. Admon objects, and Rabban Gamliel agrees with him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens the chapter and states the general rule: when a man dies leaving sons and daughters, if the estate is large the sons inherit and the daughters are supported.
The Mishnah states the converse: if the estate is small, the daughters are supported and the sons must beg.
Admon objects to the rule, arguing that being male should not cause a loss of inheritance.
Rabban Gamliel endorses Admon's position, saying he agrees with him.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of 'large' estate
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of 'large' estate
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav defines 'large' as enough to support both sons and daughters for twelve months. Shmuel notes this is Rabban Gamliel's view, but the Sages say it must support them until they reach maturity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How much property is considered 'large' (מרובין) in the Mishnah's context?
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav defines 'large' as enough to support both sons and daughters for twelve months.
Shmuel notes that this definition reflects only Rabban Gamliel's view, not the consensus.
The Sages hold that 'large' means enough to support both sons and daughters until they reach maturity (בגרות).

items.text: Supporting tradition from Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Supporting tradition from Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Ravin and Rabbah bar bar Chanah report that Rabbi Yochanan defines 'large' as enough to support both until maturity; less than that is 'small'. The Gemara adds that if there is not enough for both until maturity, the estate is considered small.

sub.text: Ravin / Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ravin / Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ravin and Rabbah bar bar Chanah report that Rabbi Yochanan defines a large estate as one that can support both sons and daughters until the daughters reach majority, and less than that as a small estate.
The Gemara asks what the ruling is if the estate cannot support both groups until the daughters reach majority.

items.text: Rava's ruling on daughters' sustenance
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on daughters' sustenance
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that daughters receive sustenance until they reach majority, and the remainder goes to the sons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether daughters would take all the property for their sustenance.
Rava rules that daughters receive sustenance until they reach majority (בגרות), and the remainder of the estate goes to the sons.

items.text: Gemara's question on diminished or increased assets
items.text_en: Gemara's question on diminished or increased assets
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether heirs retain rights if assets were many and then diminished, or if they were few and then increased, questioning if the heirs are in control or removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether heirs retain rights if assets were many and then diminished (obviously they do), or if assets were few and then increased — are the heirs in control or removed from these assets?

items.text: Rabbi Asi's ruling on orphans' sale
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's ruling on orphans' sale
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that if orphans sold from diminished assets, the sale is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that if orphans sold from diminished assets (מועטין), the sale is valid, providing a supporting baraita for the preceding question.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about the widow
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about the widow
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Avahu whether a widow reduces the estate, given her sustenance rights, or if remarriage would negate that.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Avahu whether a widow reduces the estate, given her sustenance rights, or if remarriage would negate that.

items.text: Question about the wife's daughter
items.text_en: Question about the wife's daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a wife's daughter reduces the estate, considering she has rights even if married, but loses them upon death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a wife's daughter reduces the estate, considering she has rights even if married, but loses them upon death.

items.text: Question about the creditor
items.text_en: Question about the creditor
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a creditor reduces the estate, given his claim persists even after death, but collection is uncertain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a creditor reduces the estate, given his claim persists even after death, but collection is uncertain.

items.text: Alternative version of the creditor question
items.text_en: Alternative version of the creditor question
items.desc_en: Some pose the creditor question from a different angle, asking whether he reduces the estate.

sub.text: Alternative version of the Gemara's question
sub.text_en: Alternative version of the Gemara's question
sub.desc_en: Some pose the creditor question from a different angle, asking whether he reduces the estate.

items.text: Opening questions about the widow and daughter
items.text_en: Opening questions about the widow and daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises three questions: whether a stepdaughter reduces the inheritance, whether a widow reduces it, and which of the two takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises three questions: whether a stepdaughter reduces the inheritance, whether a widow reduces it, and which of the two takes precedence.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's ruling on the widow and daughter
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's ruling on the widow and daughter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Asi rules that the widow is treated like a daughter in a small estate: the widow is sustained and the daughter must beg.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Asi rules that the widow is treated like a daughter in a small estate: the widow is sustained and the daughter must beg.

items.text: Admon's statement and its interpretation
items.text_en: Admon's statement and its interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Admon's statement: he argues that being male should not cause him to lose out. Abaye and Rava debate whether the loss is due to Torah study or inheritance rights.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Admon's rhetorical question: should being male cause me to lose out?
The Gemara asks what Admon means by his statement.
Abaye explains that Admon argues: because I am male and fit to study Torah, should I lose out?
Rava objects: if Torah study were the criterion for inheritance, only those who study would inherit.
Rava resolves: Admon argues that because he is male and fit to inherit large estates, he should not lose out in small estates.

items.text: Mishnah on tumtum inheritance
items.text_en: Mishnah on tumtum inheritance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when there are sons, daughters, and a tumtum, in a large estate the males push the tumtum to the females, and in a small estate the females push him to the males.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the rule for a tumtum inheriting alongside sons and daughters: in a large estate the males push him to the females, in a small estate the females push him to the males.

items.text: Mishnah on conditional inheritance for a child
items.text_en: Mishnah on conditional inheritance for a child
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a man who stipulates that if his wife bears a son he gets a maneh, if a daughter she gets two hundred, and if a tumtum he gets nothing unless he says 'whatever my wife bears'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a man who stipulates inheritance for his child based on the child's gender, with specific amounts for a son or daughter, and rules that a tumtum receives nothing unless the father says 'whatever my wife bears'.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: does 'push him' mean he takes like a daughter? But the Mishnah says a tumtum gets nothing. Abaye answers: 'push him' means he gets nothing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: does 'push him' mean he takes like a daughter? But the Mishnah says a tumtum gets nothing.
Abaye answers: 'push him' means he gets nothing.

items.text: Rava's answer and the baraita
items.text_en: Rava's answer and the baraita
items.desc_en: Rava says 'push him' means he does have something, and the Mishnah's case of a tumtum getting nothing follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that a tumtum has no sanctity.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that 'they push him' means the tumtum does receive a share, contrary to Abaye.
Rava explains that the Mishnah's ruling that a tumtum receives nothing follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that a tumtum has no sanctity (קדושה).

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a tumtum inherits like a son and is sustained like a daughter. This supports Rava: he inherits like a son in a small estate and is sustained like a daughter in a large estate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection by citing a baraita that states a tumtum inherits like a son and is sustained like a daughter, which seems to contradict the Mishnah's ruling.
Rava resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita means the tumtum inherits like a son in a small estate and is sustained like a daughter in a large estate, consistent with his view.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of Abaye's and Rava's difficulty
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of Abaye's and Rava's difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier difficulty by explaining that the phrase 'nourished like a daughter' means she is eligible for sustenance but not actually given it, just as 'inherits like a son' means eligible to inherit but not actually inheriting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Abaye, what does the phrase 'nourished like a daughter' mean? And by your reasoning, according to Rava, what does 'inherits like a son' mean?

The Gemara resolves: just as 'inherits like a son' means eligible to inherit but does not actually inherit, so too 'nourished like a daughter' means eligible for sustenance but is not actually given it.

items.text: Question on daughter's preference and resolution
items.text_en: Question on daughter's preference and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah implies a daughter is preferred over a son, citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that one who leaves no son incurs divine wrath. It resolves that for inheritance a son is preferred, but for benefit (like the gift in the Mishnah) a daughter is preferred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a daughter is truly preferred over a son, citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that one who leaves no son incurs divine wrath.
The Gemara distinguishes: regarding inheritance, a son is preferred; regarding benefit (having a daughter first as a good omen), a daughter is preferred.
The Gemara resolves that for inheritance a son is preferred, but for benefit (like the gift in the Mishnah) a daughter is preferred.

items.text: Samuel's explanation: firstborn daughter as good omen
items.text_en: Samuel's explanation: firstborn daughter as good omen
items.desc_en: Samuel explains the Mishnah deals with a firstborn daughter, citing Rav Chisda that a daughter first is a good sign for sons, either because she raises her brothers or because she wards off the evil eye. Rav Chisda adds that he personally prefers daughters over sons.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the mishna deals with a firstborn daughter, citing Rav Chisda that a daughter first is a good sign for sons.
Some say the daughter raises her brothers, and others say the evil eye does not prevail over her.
Rav Chisda states that for himself, his daughters are preferable to his sons.

items.text: Alternative attribution to Rabbi Yehuda and its rejection
items.text_en: Alternative attribution to Rabbi Yehuda and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda. It first considers Rabbi Yehuda of 'Bakol' who says Abraham had a daughter named Bakol, but rejects this because that Rabbi Yehuda only says a daughter is not lacking, not that she is preferred over a son. It then considers Rabbi Yehuda of the baraita about supporting daughters, but this is also rejected as it does not match the Mishnah's preference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative attribution: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara asks which Rabbi Yehuda is intended.
The Gemara suggests it is Rabbi Yehuda of 'Bakol', who says Abraham had a daughter named Bakol.
The Gemara objects: that Rabbi Yehuda only says Abraham was not lacking a daughter, not that a daughter is preferred over a son.
The Gemara suggests it is Rabbi Yehuda of the baraita about supporting daughters, who says it is a מצוה (commandment) to support sons and a קל וחומר (a fortiori) for daughters.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution of the baraita about twins
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution of the baraita about twins
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a baraita where a woman bears twins (male and female) and the son takes six dinars, the daughter two. Rav Ashi explains this involves a man who said 'if a male first, 200; if a female after him, nothing; if a female first, 100; if a male after her, 100.' Since it's unknown which was first, the male takes 100 (certain), and the remaining 100 is disputed money divided equally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a baraita where a woman bears twins (male and female) and the male takes six dinars, the female two, seeking its explanation.

Rav Ashi explains that the baraita involves a man who said 'if a male first, 200; if a female after him, nothing; if a female first, 100; if a male after her, 100'; since the birth order is unknown, the male takes 100 (certain), and the remaining 100 is disputed money divided equally.

items.text: Ravina's explanation of the baraita with only one maneh
items.text_en: Ravina's explanation of the baraita with only one maneh
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a baraita where the twins yield only one maneh total. Ravina explains this involves a case where the man said 'if you bear a male, 100; if a female, 100' (using the term 'מבשרני' meaning 'inform me').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a baraita where if she bore a male and female, he has only 100 dinars — how is that found?
Ravina answers: in the case of 'Mevasreni' (one who says 'inform me').

items.text: Baraita on the messenger's promise
items.text_en: Baraita on the messenger's promise
items.desc_en: The baraita states that if one says 'Whoever informs me of the sex of my wife's child, if it is a male he shall receive a maneh,' and she gives birth to a male, he receives a maneh. The Gemara notes that the baraita also includes a case where the child is both male and female, and explains that this is to exclude a stillborn (nefel).

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the case of a messenger's promise: one who promises a maneh for news of a male or female child receives it accordingly, and if both are born, only one maneh is given.

The Gemara questions why the baraita includes a case of both male and female, since the original promise did not mention that scenario, and explains that the baraita implies the promise also covered that case.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita's inclusion of both male and female is to exclude a stillborn (nefel) from the promise.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on granting to a fetus
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on granting to a fetus
items.desc_en: A man said to his wife 'My property is for this child that you are carrying.' Rav Huna ruled that this is a grant to a fetus, and one who grants to a fetus does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: A man said to his wife, 'My property is for this child that you are carrying.'
Rav Huna ruled that this is a grant to a fetus, and one who grants to a fetus does not acquire.

items.text: Rav Nachman's objection from the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection from the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman challenged Rav Huna from the baraita where one says 'If my wife gives birth to a male, he shall receive a maneh,' and the child receives it. Rav Huna responded that he does not know who taught that mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna by citing a baraita where one says 'If my wife gives birth to a male, he shall receive a maneh,' and the child receives it, implying that a fetus can acquire.
Rav Huna responds that he does not know who taught that mishnah, thereby dismissing its authority.

items.text: Attempt to attribute to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Attempt to attribute to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Huna could have said the mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can acquire something not yet in the world. However, the Gemara rejects this: Rabbi Meir only said so for something that exists in the world, not for something that does not yet exist.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Huna could have answered the objection by attributing the mishnah to Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can acquire something not yet in the world.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion: Rabbi Meir only permits acquisition of something that already exists in the world, not something that does not yet exist.

items.text: Attempt to attribute to Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Attempt to attribute to Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a fetus can acquire (as in the case of a fetus disqualifying from terumah). The Gemara rejects this: inheritance is different because it comes automatically.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah could be attributed to Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a fetus can acquire property.
The Gemara rejects the attribution: inheritance is different because it comes automatically, unlike a gift.

items.text: Attempt to attribute to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.text_en: Attempt to attribute to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that a gift to an heir is valid. The Gemara rejects this: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka only said so for something that exists in the world, not for something not yet in the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that a gift to an heir is valid.
The Gemara rejects this: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka only said so for something that exists in the world, not for something not yet in the world.

items.text: Combined suggestion of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Combined suggestion of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka who holds like Rabbi Yosei. The Gemara questions whether he indeed holds that view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah could be attributed to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds like Rabbi Yosei regarding an unborn child's acquisition.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka actually holds like Rabbi Yosei, casting doubt on the suggestion.

items.text: Final resolution: the baraita is about a messenger
items.text_en: Final resolution: the baraita is about a messenger
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita deals with a messenger (מבשריני), not a grant to a fetus. The Gemara objects: if so, the later clause about an heir is problematic. Another suggestion: the baraita is about a child that has already been born (שילדה). The Gemara objects: the language 'whatever she will give birth' (כל שתלד) would then be incorrect; it should say 'whatever she gave birth' (כל שילדה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita deals with a messenger (מבשריני) rather than a grant to a fetus.
The Gemara objects: if the baraita is about a messenger, the later clause about an heir is problematic.
The Gemara suggests that the baraita deals with a child that has already been born (שילדה).
The Gemara objects: the language 'whatever she will give birth' (כל שתלד) would then be incorrect; it should say 'whatever she gave birth' (כל שילדה).

items.text: Rav Huna's position on 'when she gives birth'
items.text_en: Rav Huna's position on 'when she gives birth'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous assumption by asking why not say 'when she gives birth'? It then cites Rav Huna's consistent view that even a conditional gift to a fetus ('when she gives birth') does not effect acquisition, contrasting with Rav Nachman who holds that such a conditional gift does work, and Rav Sheshet who holds that both direct and conditional gifts to a fetus work.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not say the gift was conditional on 'when she gives birth' (לִכְשֶׁתֵּלֵד).
The Gemara explains that Rav Huna consistently holds that even a conditional gift to a fetus ('when she gives birth') does not effect acquisition.
Rav Nachman holds that a direct gift to a fetus does not work, but a conditional gift ('when she gives birth') does work.
Rav Huna holds that even a conditional gift to a fetus does not work.
Rav Sheshet holds that both direct and conditional gifts to a fetus work.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's proof from a baraita about a convert's estate
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's proof from a baraita about a convert's estate
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita: if a convert dies and Israelites seize his property, then hear he has a son or his wife is pregnant, they must return everything. If they return it and then hear the son died or the wife miscarried, the second seizure effects acquisition but the first does not. Rav Sheshet argues that if a fetus does not acquire, why would the second seizure be needed? The first seizure should have already been valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet opens by asking for a source and then cites a baraita about a convert who dies, whose property is seized by Israelites, and who then is discovered to have a son or a pregnant wife, requiring return of the property.
The baraita continues: if they return everything and then hear the son died or the wife miscarried, the second seizure effects acquisition but the first does not.
Rav Sheshet argues: if a fetus does not acquire, why would the second seizure be needed? The first seizure should have already been valid.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's distinctions to reject the proof
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's distinctions to reject the proof
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava offer alternative explanations for the baraita, rejecting Rav Sheshet's inference. Abaye says inheritance that comes automatically is different (the fetus inherits by Torah law, not by human gift). Rava says the first seizure was weak because the Israelites were hesitant from the start, knowing the fetus might have a claim. The Gemara then asks what practical difference exists between their views, and answers: a case where they heard the son died but he did not actually die until later.

sub.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes the baraita by noting that inheritance that comes automatically (ירושה הבאה מאליה) is different from a gift, so the fetus inherits by Torah law, not by human acquisition.
Rava offers an alternative explanation: the Israelites' initial seizure was weak (ריפויי מרפייאן) because they were hesitant from the start, knowing the fetus might have a claim.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Abaye's and Rava's explanations.
The Gemara resolves the question: the difference lies in a case where they heard the son died but he did not actually die until later, testing the strength of the initial seizure.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah: a one-day-old inherits but a fetus does not
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah: a one-day-old inherits but a fetus does not
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah: a one-day-old child inherits and bequeaths, implying a fetus does not. Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah means a one-day-old inherits from the mother to bequeath to paternal brothers, but a fetus cannot do so. The Gemara asks for the reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that a fetus can acquire by citing a Mishnah that a one-day-old inherits and bequeaths, implying a fetus does not.
Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah means a one-day-old inherits from the mother to bequeath to paternal brothers, but a fetus cannot do so.
The Gemara asks for the reason why a fetus cannot inherit from the mother to bequeath to paternal brothers.

items.text: Opening statement: A son who dies immediately does not inherit his mother to pass on to paternal brothers
items.text_en: Opening statement: A son who dies immediately does not inherit his mother to pass on to paternal brothers
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a son dies immediately after birth, he does not inherit his mother to pass the inheritance to his paternal half-brothers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a son who dies immediately does not inherit his mother to pass on to paternal brothers.

items.text: Challenge and resolution: The case of Parches who convulsed three times
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution: The case of Parches who convulsed three times
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that the son died immediately, citing a case where a child convulsed three times. Mar bar Rav Ashi explains that this was like the tail of a lizard that twitches after being cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that the son died first, citing a case where a child convulsed three times after birth.
Mar bar Rav Ashi explains that the convulsions were merely reflexive twitching, like the tail of a lizard that twitches after being cut off, not a sign of life.

items.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef: A one-day-old son reduces the firstborn's portion, but not a fetus
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef: A one-day-old son reduces the firstborn's portion, but not a fetus
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava states that a son who lives even one day reduces the firstborn's portion, but a fetus does not, as the verse says 'and they bore for him' (וְיָלְדוּ לוֹ). Similarly, a son born after the father's death does not reduce the firstborn's portion.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava states that a one-day-old son reduces the firstborn's portion, but a fetus does not.
The Gemara explains the reason: the verse 'וְיָלְדוּ לוֹ' (and they bore for him) implies only a child already born.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef adds that a son born after the father's death also does not reduce the firstborn's portion, because the verse requires 'וְיָלְדוּ לוֹ' (they bore for him) while the father was alive.

items.text: Alternate version: A firstborn born after the father's death does not take a double portion
items.text_en: Alternate version: A firstborn born after the father's death does not take a double portion
items.desc_en: In Pumbedita they taught that a firstborn born after the father's death does not take a double portion, as the verse requires 'he shall recognize' (יַכִּיר), which is impossible. The halakha follows all these statements of Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Stam introduces two alternate versions of the teaching, one from Sura and one from Pumbedita.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava rules that a firstborn born after the father's death does not take a double portion.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: He provides the reason: the verse requires 'he shall recognize' (יַכִּיר), which is impossible for a posthumous child.
The Stam concludes that the halakha follows all these statements of Mar bar Rav Yosef in the name of Rava.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: One who transfers property to a fetus does not acquire
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak: One who transfers property to a fetus does not acquire
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who transfers property to a fetus does not acquire it. If one objects from our Mishnah, the answer is that it is because a person's mind is close to his son.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who transfers property to a fetus does not acquire it.
The gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah that seems to contradict this ruling.
The gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah's case is exceptional because a person's mind is close to his son.

items.text: Shmuel's opinion and the halakha: One who transfers to a fetus does not acquire
items.text_en: Shmuel's opinion and the halakha: One who transfers to a fetus does not acquire
items.desc_en: Shmuel told Rav Chana Bagdata'ah to gather ten people and declare that one who transfers property to a fetus acquires it, but the halakha is that he does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel instructs Rav Chana Bagdata'ah to gather ten people so he can declare publicly that one who transfers property to a fetus acquires it.
The gemara rules that the halakha (הלכה) is that one who transfers property to a fetus does not acquire it.

items.text: Case of a man who said 'my property to sons that will be born from you' and the dispute about a minor's share
items.text_en: Case of a man who said 'my property to sons that will be born from you' and the dispute about a minor's share
items.desc_en: A man said to his wife 'my property to sons that will be born from you.' An older son asked what will be with him, and the father said 'go acquire like one of the sons.' The unborn sons certainly did not acquire. The dispute is whether the older son has a share alongside the sons (the unborn ones). Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Meisha, and Rabbi Yirmeya say he has a share; Rabbi Avahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha say he does not. Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Yirmeya for the halakha, and Rabbi Yirmeya says it follows them because they are older, but Rabbi Avahu retorts that it depends on reasoning, not age, and sends him to Rabbi Avin for the explanation.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where a man said 'my property to sons that will be born from you,' and his older son asked about his own share; the father told him to acquire like one of the sons, but the unborn sons certainly did not acquire.
The gemara asks whether the older son has a share alongside the unborn sons or not.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Meisha, and Rabbi Yirmeya's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Meisha, and Rabbi Yirmeya's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Meisha, and Rabbi Yirmeya rule that the older son does have a share alongside the unborn sons.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha rule that the older son does not have a share alongside the unborn sons.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu's question to Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's question to Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Yirmeya whether the halakha follows their group or the other group.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the halakha follows their group because they are older, not the other group who are younger.
Rabbi Avahu objects that the halakha depends on reasoning, not on the age of the disputants.
Rabbi Avahu sends Rabbi Yirmeya to Rabbi Avin to learn the reasoning behind the ruling.

items.text: Introduction of the 'you and a donkey' principle
items.text_en: Introduction of the 'you and a donkey' principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case where one says 'acquire like a donkey' or 'you and a donkey', and presents the dispute between Rav Nachman, Rav Hamnuna, and Rav Sheshet regarding whether the capable party acquires half or all, or nothing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where one says 'acquire like a donkey' and questions whether the recipient acquires anything.
The Gemara cites the dispute: for 'you and a donkey', Rav Nachman says the capable party acquires half, Rav Hamnuna says nothing, and Rav Sheshet says everything.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's proof from terumah
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's proof from terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet proves his position from a baraita where Rabbi Yosei rules that one may add to the outer part of a gourd when tithing, because the inner part is considered the main part. The Gemara questions this as a case of 'you and a donkey', and answers that terumah from the inferior is valid by Torah law, citing Rabbi Ila'a's derivation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet introduces his proof from a baraita where Rabbi Yosei rules that one adds to the outer part of a gourd when tithing, because the inner part is primary.
The Gemara objects that this case is a classic 'you and a donkey' situation, where the outer part is inferior and the inner part is superior.
The Gemara answers that terumah from the inferior is valid by Torah law, citing Rabbi Ila'a's derivation from the verse about not bearing sin when removing the fat.

items.text: Challenge from a case of betrothal
items.text_en: Challenge from a case of betrothal
items.desc_en: Rav Avya raises a challenge from a case where a man betrothed five women with a basket of figs, including two sisters, and the Sages ruled that the sisters are not betrothed, implying that unrelated women are betrothed. This seems to contradict the 'you and a donkey' principle. The Gemara resolves that the man specified 'the one fit for intercourse among you shall be betrothed to me'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya cites a case where a man betrothed five women including two sisters with a basket of figs, and the Sages ruled only the sisters are not betrothed, implying the unrelated women are betrothed.
The Gemara objects that if unrelated women are betrothed, this contradicts the 'you and a donkey' principle, since the sisters are invalid like a donkey.

Rav Ashi resolves that the case was where the man specified 'the one fit for intercourse among you shall be betrothed to me', so the sisters are excluded by the condition, not by the 'you and a donkey' principle.

items.text: Case of 'my property to you and your son'
items.text_en: Case of 'my property to you and your son'
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that when a man says 'my property to you and your son', the wife acquires half, based on the verse regarding Aaron and his sons. Abaye challenges that Aaron is a distinct heir, whereas a wife is not an heir, so she should only take like one of the sons.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the case of a man who said to his wife 'my property to you and your son', and Rav Yosef rules that she acquires half.

Rav Yosef cites a baraita where Rabbi learns from the verse 'וְהָיְתָה לְאַהֲרֹן וּלְבָנָיו' (and it shall be for Aaron and for his sons) that half goes to Aaron and half to his sons, analogizing to the wife and son.
Abaye objects that Aaron is a distinct heir (בן חלוקה), so the Torah specified he takes half, but a wife is not an heir, so she should only take like one of the sons.

items.text: Supporting precedents and distinction
items.text_en: Supporting precedents and distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites precedents where Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan enforced a half share for a wife, and a case of royal gifts to gatekeepers and guards where Rabbi ruled half each. The Gemara distinguishes that in the royal case, the original practice was to write only to gatekeepers, and the guards assisted, so the king intended equal shares.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Abaye's distinction by citing precedents where Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan enforced a half share for a wife in similar cases.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports a case of royal gifts to gatekeepers and guards where Rabbi ruled each receives half.
The Gemara distinguishes that in the royal case, the original practice was to write only to gatekeepers, and the guards assisted, so the king intended equal shares.

items.text: Challenge from a meal-offering case
items.text_en: Challenge from a meal-offering case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a challenge from a case where one vows to bring a meal-offering of one hundred tenths in two vessels, and the ruling is that he brings sixty in one vessel and forty in another, implying unequal division, which contradicts the principle of equal division in 'you and your son'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a challenge from a case where one vows to bring a meal-offering of one hundred tenths in two vessels, and the ruling is that he brings sixty in one vessel and forty in another, implying unequal division, which contradicts the principle of equal division in 'you and your son'.

items.text: Gemara's question on bringing a large korban in two vessels
items.text_en: Gemara's question on bringing a large korban in two vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if one brought fifty units in each of two vessels, he fulfills his obligation, but only after the fact. It suggests that if each vessel is considered a half-offering, it should be permitted initially. The Gemara answers that the person intended for a large korban from the start, and using two vessels is due to necessity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah permits bringing a large korban in two vessels only בדיעבד (after the fact), arguing that if each vessel is considered a half-offering, it should be permitted לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara answers that the person intended for a large korban from the start, and using two vessels is due to necessity, so only what is possible is brought.

items.text: Halakha like Rav Yosef in field, topic, and half
items.text_en: Halakha like Rav Yosef in field, topic, and half
items.desc_en: A brief ruling that the halakha follows Rav Yosef in three specific areas: field, topic, and half.

sub.desc_en: The Stam rules that the halakha follows Rav Yosef in three areas: field, topic, and half.

items.text: Case of sending silk pieces to his home
items.text_en: Case of sending silk pieces to his home
items.desc_en: A man sent silk pieces to his home. Rabbi Ami rules that items suitable for sons go to sons, and for daughters to daughters, unless there is a daughter-in-law, in which case they go to her, provided the daughters are married.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a man sent silk pieces to his home.
Rabbi Ami rules that items suitable for sons go to sons, for daughters to daughters, but if there is a daughter-in-law, they go to her.
Rabbi Ami qualifies that if the daughters are unmarried, the items go to them, not the daughter-in-law.

items.text: Does 'my sons' include a daughter?
items.text_en: Does 'my sons' include a daughter?
items.desc_en: A man said 'my property to my sons' and had a son and a daughter. The Gemara debates whether 'sons' excludes the daughter (to remove her from the inheritance) or includes her as a gift. Abaye, Rava, and Rav Yosef bring verses to prove that 'sons' can include a daughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a man said 'my property to my sons' and had a son and a daughter, and questions whether 'sons' excludes the daughter from inheritance or includes her as a gift.

Abaye cites the verse 'וּבְנֵי דָּן – חֻשִׁים' (Dan's sons – Hushim) to prove that 'sons' can include a single child, but Rava rejects this by citing the school of Hezekiah that Hushim was as numerous as reeds.
Rava cites the verse 'וּבְנֵי פַלּוּא – אֱלִיאָב' (Pallu's sons – Eliab) and Rav Yosef cites 'וּבְנֵי אֵיתָן – עֲזַרְיָה' (Ethan's sons – Azariah) to prove that 'sons' can refer to a single child.

items.text: Does 'my sons' include a grandson?
items.text_en: Does 'my sons' include a grandson?
items.desc_en: A man said 'my property to my sons' and had a son and a grandson. Rav Chaviva and Mar bar Rav Ashi debate whether 'sons' includes a grandson. A baraita supports Mar bar Rav Ashi that one who vows not to benefit from 'sons' may benefit from grandsons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a man said 'my property to my sons' and had a son and a grandson, raising the question whether people call a grandson 'son'.
Rav Chaviva asserts that people do call a grandson 'son'.
Mar bar Rav Ashi argues that people do not call a grandson 'son'.
A baraita supports Mar bar Rav Ashi: one who vows not to benefit from 'sons' may benefit from grandsons.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on adult children improving the estate
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on adult children improving the estate
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if adult children improve inherited property, the profit is shared equally unless they explicitly say they are working for themselves. The Gemara adds that this applies only when the improvement comes from the property itself, but if from their own effort, the profit is theirs alone.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that adult children who improve inherited property share the profit equally unless they explicitly declare they are working for themselves, and the same applies to a widow improving her husband's estate.

sub.text: Rav Chaviva bar Rav Yosef bar Rava in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Chaviva bar Rav Yosef bar Rava in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Chaviva bar Rav Yosef bar Rava reports in the name of Rava that the Mishnah's rule applies only when the improvement comes from the property itself, but if the improvement comes from the children's own effort, the profit is entirely theirs.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Chanina's statement that seems to contradict Rava's distinction.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's statement on minimal inheritance
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's statement on minimal inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite Rabbi Chanina's opinion that even if a father left only a small amount, the rule applies, but the segment is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's distinction by citing Rabbi Chanina's statement that even minimal inheritance triggers the rule, but the citation is cut off.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier ruling about watchmen
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier ruling about watchmen
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the profit from watchmen goes to the middle, since watchmen are hired for protection, and even minors can guard, so the profit is not due to the heir's effort.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the profit from watchmen (אודייני) goes to the middle, since it is due to the heir's own effort.
The Gemara answers that watchmen are different because they are hired for protection, and even minors can guard them, so the profit is not due to the heir's effort.

items.text: Case of heirs who say 'see what father left'
items.text_en: Case of heirs who say 'see what father left'
items.desc_en: If heirs explicitly say they are working for themselves, the profit is theirs. The Gemara recounts a case where Rav Safra used his father's money for business, and Rava ruled in his favor because he was a great scholar who wouldn't neglect his studies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if heirs explicitly say 'see what father left, we are working and eating,' any profit is theirs.
The Gemara recounts that Rav Safra used his father's money for business, and Rava ruled in his favor because as a great scholar he would not neglect his studies for others' profit.

items.text: Widow who improves property
items.text_en: Widow who improves property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a widow who improves property improves for the middle. Rabbi Yirmeya explains this applies to a woman who inherits, not a widow managing orphans' property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a widow who improves property improves for the middle (half profit).
The Gemara asks: what business does a woman have with orphans' property (to which this rule would apply)?
Rabbi Yirmeya answers: the Mishnah refers to a woman who inherits property (not a widow managing orphans' property).

items.text: Why the ruling about a woman inheritor is necessary
items.text_en: Why the ruling about a woman inheritor is necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the ruling is obvious, but it teaches that even though it is not her usual way to toil, she is not considered to have explicitly stipulated for herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the ruling is not obvious, suggesting that since a woman is not accustomed to toil, her silence might be considered an explicit stipulation.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling teaches that even without explicit stipulation, she is not considered to have stipulated for herself.

items.text: Widow who says 'see what my husband left'
items.text_en: Widow who says 'see what my husband left'
items.desc_en: If the widow explicitly says she is working for herself, the profit is hers. The Gemara explains that this teaches that she does not forfeit her rights even though people might say she is toiling for the orphans.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a widow explicitly says 'see what my husband left me, I am working and eating,' the profit is hers.
The Gemara asks: this is obvious — why does the Mishnah need to state it?

The Gemara explains: one might think that since it is a praiseworthy matter for her to work for the orphans, she is considered to have waived her rights; the Mishnah teaches that she does not forfeit her profit.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's ruling about marrying off an adult son
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's ruling about marrying off an adult son
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that if a father marries off his adult son in the house, the son acquires the property. This applies specifically to an adult son, a virgin, his first wife, and if the father married him off first.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that a father who marries off his adult son in the house grants the son acquisition of the property, with four conditions: the son is adult, the bride is a virgin, she is his first wife, and the father married him off first.

items.text: Cases of designating a house and upper story
items.text_en: Cases of designating a house and upper story
items.desc_en: If a father designates a house and upper story for his son, the son acquires the house but not the upper story. Questions about a house and portico, or two houses one inside the other, remain unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the obvious case: if a father designated a house and an upper story for his son, the son acquires the house but not the upper story.
The Gemara raises an unresolved question about a house and a portico (אכסדרה).
The Gemara raises another unresolved question about two houses one inside the other.
The Gemara concludes that both questions remain unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Challenge and resolution about designating a house and utensils
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution about designating a house and utensils
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised: if a father designates a house and utensils, the son acquires the utensils but not the house. Rabbi Yirmeya resolves that this refers to a case where the father's treasure was stored there. Nehardeans, Rav Yehuda, Rav Pappi, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi add further examples of what constitutes a 'house' for this purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a baraita: if a father designates a house and utensils for his son, the son acquires the utensils but not the house, contradicting the earlier ruling that designating a house grants acquisition.
Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the challenge by explaining that the baraita refers to a case where the father's treasure was stored in the house, so the son does not acquire the house itself.
The Nehardeans add that even a dovecote can be considered a 'house' for this halacha (הלכה).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda and Rav Pappi's example
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Pappi's example
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Pappi add that even a pot of a certain plant (הרסנא) can be considered a 'house'.
Mar Zutra, when marrying off his son, hung a sandal in the designated house to indicate acquisition.
Rav Ashi, when marrying off his son, hung a flask of oil in the designated house to effect acquisition.

items.text: Mar Zutra's three halachic statements without reason
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's three halachic statements without reason
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra states that the Sages established three matters as halacha without giving a reason: the previous ruling, Shmuel's ruling that a husband who writes all his property to his wife only makes her an overseer, and Rav's ruling about a deposit given in the presence of all three parties.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra opens by stating that the Sages established three matters as הלכה (binding law) without giving a reason.

sub.text: Mar Zutra citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra lists the first matter: the previous ruling, and the second: Shmuel's ruling that a husband who writes all his property to his wife only makes her an overseer (אפוטרופוס).
Mar Zutra lists the third matter: Rav's ruling that a deposit given in the presence of all three parties is acquired.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Brothers as partners
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Brothers as partners
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one of the brothers who are partners falls into a trade (specifically a royal appointment), the earnings go to the common fund. If he falls ill and recovers, his medical expenses are his own.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that if one of the brothers who are partners falls into a trade (specifically a royal appointment), the earnings go to the common fund; if he falls ill and recovers, his medical expenses are his own.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the royal appointment
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the royal appointment
items.desc_en: The Gemara specifies that the trade mentioned is a royal appointment. A baraita teaches that if one brother was appointed as a tax collector or strategos, the earnings go to the brothers if the appointment came due to the brothers, but to himself if due to his own merit. The Gemara questions why the case of 'due to the brothers' is obvious, and explains it is needed to counter the claim that his sharpness caused it.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna specifies that the trade mentioned in the Mishnah refers to a royal appointment.

A baraita teaches that if one brother was appointed as a tax collector or strategos, the earnings go to the brothers if the appointment came due to the brothers, but to himself if due to his own merit.
The Gemara questions why the case of 'due to the brothers' is obvious and needs to be stated.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is needed to counter the claim that his sharpness caused the appointment, so it teaches that it still goes to the brothers.

items.text: Baraita: Brother studying Torah or a trade
items.text_en: Baraita: Brother studying Torah or a trade
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one brother took 200 zuz to study Torah or a trade, the other brothers can say: if you are with us, you have sustenance; if not, you do not. The Gemara questions why they cannot give him sustenance wherever he is, and supports Rav Huna's principle that the blessing of the house is in its majority, concluding that they give him according to the blessing of the house.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one brother took 200 zuz to study Torah or a trade, the other brothers can say: if you are with us, you have sustenance; if not, you do not.
The Gemara questions why the brothers cannot give him sustenance wherever he is.
The Gemara supports Rav Huna's principle that the blessing of the house is in its majority.
The Gemara concludes that they give him according to the blessing of the house.

items.text: Illness: negligent vs. unavoidable
items.text_en: Illness: negligent vs. unavoidable
items.desc_en: Ravin sent in the name of Rabbi Il'a that the Mishnah's ruling that medical expenses are from his own applies only if he fell ill through negligence, but if unavoidable, from the common fund. The Gemara defines negligence as per Rabbi Chanina: everything is in Heaven's hands except colds and injuries, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: if a brother fell ill and was healed, the medical expenses come from his own pocket.

sub.text: Ravin in the name of Rabbi Il'a
sub.text_en: Ravin in the name of Rabbi Il'a
sub.desc_en: Ravin sent in the name of Rabbi Il'a that the Mishnah's ruling applies only if he fell ill through negligence, but if unavoidable, the expenses come from the common fund.
The Gemara asks: what constitutes negligence in this context?
The Gemara answers with Rabbi Chanina's principle: everything is in Heaven's hands except colds and injuries, as per the verse, so negligence is failing to guard against these.

items.text: Mishnah: Shoshvinut among brothers
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shoshvinut among brothers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if some brothers acted as shoshvinim (best men) during their father's lifetime, when the shoshvinut is returned, it returns to the common fund, as shoshvinut is collected in court. But sending jugs of wine or oil is not collected in court, as they are acts of kindness.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that shoshvinut (best-man gifts) among brothers during the father's lifetime return to the common fund and are collectible in court, but sending jugs of wine or oil is not collectible because it is an act of kindness.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction and resolution via Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction and resolution via Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: if the father sent shoshvinut, it returns to him; if shoshvinut was sent to the father, it returns from the common fund. Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves that our Mishnah also deals with shoshvinut sent to the father. The Gemara questions the wording 'brothers who made some shoshvinut' and suggests emending to 'for some of them', and explains that 'returns' means 'when it comes to collect, it is collected from the common fund'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: if the father sent shoshvinut, it returns to him; if shoshvinut was sent to the father, it returns from the common fund.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves that our Mishnah also deals with shoshvinut sent to the father.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'brothers who made some shoshvinut', not 'shoshvinut sent to the father'.
The Gemara suggests emending the Mishnah to read 'for some of them'.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'the shoshvinut returns', implying return of the actual gift.
The Gemara explains that 'returns' means 'when it comes to collect, it is collected from the common fund'.

items.text: Alternative resolution: Rabbi Asi distinguishes between explicit and unspecified
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: Rabbi Asi distinguishes between explicit and unspecified
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi offers another resolution: the baraita deals with an explicit case (the father sent shoshvinut), while the Mishnah deals with an unspecified case (the father sent shoshvinut without specifying), so it returns to the common fund.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an explicit case (the father sent shoshvinut specifying it is for him) and an unspecified case (the father sent shoshvinut without specifying), so the latter returns to the common fund.

items.text: Shmuel's explanation and discussion on returning gifts
items.text_en: Shmuel's explanation and discussion on returning gifts
items.desc_en: Shmuel says the Mishnah deals with a yavam (levir), who does not take in the estate what is ראוי (not yet in possession). The Gemara questions whether the other brother must pay, and cites a baraita about returning kiddushin depending on custom. Rav Yosef bar Abba in the name of Mar Ukva in the name of Shmuel says that if the wife died, they return; if the husband died, they do not, because she can say...

sub.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the Mishnah deals with a yavam (levir), who does not take in the estate what is ראוי (not yet in possession).
The Gemara questions whether the other brother must pay, since the yavam can claim 'give me my shoshbin gift so I can rejoice with him'.
The Gemara cites a baraita about returning kiddushin depending on local custom.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Abba in the name of Mar Ukva in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Abba in the name of Mar Ukva in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Abba citing Mar Ukva citing Shmuel resolves that if the wife died, they return the kiddushin; if the husband died, they do not, because she can claim...

items.text: Opening question: Can the woman say 'Give me my husband'?
items.text_en: Opening question: Can the woman say 'Give me my husband'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: just as a woman can say 'Give me my husband and I will rejoice with him' (to avoid returning gifts), can she say 'Give me my shoshvin and I will rejoice with him'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the woman's claim 'Give me my husband and I will rejoice with him' extends to the shoshvin (best man) as well.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: The case is where he already rejoiced
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: The case is where he already rejoiced
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the case is where the shoshvin already rejoiced with the groom for seven days of feasting, but did not manage to pay before he died, so the woman cannot claim 'Give me my shoshvin'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a shoshvin who already rejoiced with the groom for seven days of feasting but died before paying, so the woman cannot claim 'Give me my shoshvin'.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on returning betrothal gifts
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on returning betrothal gifts
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the principle 'Give me my husband' is a dispute between Tannaim. It cites a baraita: Rabbi Natan says that if the betrothed woman dies, gifts are returned according to local custom; if the man dies, they are not returned because she can say 'Give me my husband'. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says that in either case, gifts are returned according to custom, and she cannot say that.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the principle 'Give me my husband' is a dispute between Tannaim.

The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Natan rules that if the woman dies, gifts are returned according to custom; if the man dies, they are not returned because she can say 'Give me my husband'. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that in either case, gifts are returned according to custom.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's statement seems identical to the first Tanna, so the only difference must be the principle 'Give me my husband'.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita is missing text: the first Tanna (Rabbi Natan) actually distinguishes between when the woman dies (gifts returned) and when the man dies (gifts not returned, because she can say 'Give me my husband').

sub.text: Gemara's completion of the emended baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's completion of the emended baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the emended baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that in both cases gifts are returned according to custom, and she cannot say 'Give me my husband'.

items.text: Reinterpretation: The dispute is about whether betrothal money is given for consummation
items.text_en: Reinterpretation: The dispute is about whether betrothal money is given for consummation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous explanation and reinterprets: all agree that she can say 'Give me my husband' when he dies. The dispute is when she dies, and it revolves around whether betrothal money is given for consummation (לטיבועין) or not. Rabbi Natan holds it is not, so gifts are returned; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds it is, so gifts are not returned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous explanation, asserting that all agree the woman can say 'Give me my husband' when he dies.

The Gemara resolves that the dispute is only when she dies, and it revolves around whether betrothal money is given for consummation (לטיבועין) or not: Rabbi Natan holds it is not, so gifts are returned; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds it is, so gifts are not returned.

items.text: Clarification: The baraita refers to gifts (סבלונות), not betrothal money
items.text_en: Clarification: The baraita refers to gifts (סבלונות), not betrothal money
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the baraita's statement 'where they are accustomed to return, they return' refers to gifts (סבלונות), not the betrothal money itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly says 'where they are accustomed to return, they return,' implying it discusses betrothal money, not gifts.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita actually refers to gifts (סבלונות), not the betrothal money itself.

items.text: Parallel dispute among Tannaim: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Parallel dispute among Tannaim: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita where Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei dispute a case of betrothal with a loaf. The Gemara analyzes the case: it cannot be when she died (no ketubah), nor when he died (she could say 'Give me my husband'), nor an Israelite woman who committed adultery. It concludes it is a case of a priest's wife who was raped, and the dispute is again about whether betrothal money is given for consummation. Rabbi Yosei is uncertain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a parallel dispute among Tannaim regarding betrothal with a loaf, citing the positions of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that the bride collects her ketubah but returns the surplus betrothal money to the groom.
Rabbi Yosei states that if he betrothed her with twenty, he gives her thirty half-shekels; if with thirty, he gives her twenty half-shekels.

items.text: Practical ruling: Rav Nachman and others on returning gifts and betrothal money
items.text_en: Practical ruling: Rav Nachman and others on returning gifts and betrothal money
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that wherever they are accustomed to return gifts, they return. In Nehardea, they return gifts; in the rest of Babylonia, gifts are returned but betrothal money is not. Rav Pappa states the halakha: whether he died, she died, or he retracted, gifts are returned but betrothal money is not; if she retracts, even betrothal money is returned.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that wherever the custom is to return gifts, they are returned.
The Gemara explains that the custom of returning gifts applies in Nehardea.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef both state that in the rest of Babylonia, gifts (מוהרי) are returned but betrothal money (קידושי) is not.
Rav Pappa rules the הלכה (binding law): whether he died, she died, or he retracted, gifts are returned but betrothal money is not; if she retracts, even betrothal money is returned.

items.text: Reason for not returning betrothal money: decree and Rav Ashi's rejected view
items.text_en: Reason for not returning betrothal money: decree and Rav Ashi's rejected view
items.desc_en: Ameimar says betrothal money is not returned as a decree lest people say betrothal takes effect on her sister. Rav Ashi says the divorce document proves otherwise, but this is rejected as a fabrication.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar rules that betrothal money (קידושי) is not returned, as a decree lest people mistakenly think betrothal can take effect on the sister of the betrothed.
Rav Ashi objects that the divorce document (גט) itself proves the betrothal is dissolved, so the decree is unnecessary.
The Gemara rejects Rav Ashi's view as a fabrication (בדותא), because some heard of this reasoning and some did not.

items.text: Five laws of shoshvinut
items.text_en: Five laws of shoshvinut
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to list five laws regarding the shoshvin (best man) gift: it is collected in court, returns in its season, and has no issue of usury.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists five laws of the shoshvinut (best man gift): it is collected in court, returns in its season, and has no issue of ribbit (usury).

items.text: Completion of the shoshvina gift's legal status
items.text_en: Completion of the shoshvina gift's legal status
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the shoshvina gift is not subject to shemittah cancellation, usury, or the firstborn's double portion, treating it as a loan-like obligation but with unique features.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating three legal features of the shoshvina gift: it is not cancelled by shemittah, the firstborn does not take a double portion from it, and it is collected in court.

The Gemara explains that the gift is like a loan (כְּמִלְוֶה דָּמְיָא), so it is collected in court, has no usury concern because the giver did not intend it as a loan, and shemittah does not cancel it because the verse 'lo yigosh' does not apply.
The Gemara explains that the firstborn does not take a double portion because the gift is considered ראוי (not yet possessed), and the firstborn does not take a double portion from ראוי.

items.text: Rav Kahana's rule for shoshvina attendance and Abaye's custom
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's rule for shoshvina attendance and Abaye's custom
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana states general rules for when a shoshvina must attend a feast, and Abaye reports the local custom in Genana regarding how much the shoshvina must pay if he fails to attend.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana states the general rule for a shoshvina (best man): if he is in town or hears the drum, he must attend; if he does not hear the drum, he must be informed, and if he fails, he must pay compensation.

Abaye reports the custom of the people of Genana regarding the amount a shoshvina must pay if he fails to attend: up to a zuz he eats what he brings, up to four zuz he pays half, and beyond that each according to his importance.

items.text: Baraita on reciprocity in shoshvina gifts
items.text_en: Baraita on reciprocity in shoshvina gifts
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one party changes the terms of the shoshvina arrangement (e.g., from public to private, from virgin to widow, from second to first wedding, or from one to two weddings), the other party can insist on the original terms.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the first two cases: if one party changed from public to private or from virgin to widow, the other can insist on the original terms.
The baraita continues with two more cases: if one party changed from a second wedding to a first wedding, or from one wedding to two weddings, the other can insist on the original terms.

items.text: Baraita on types of Torah scholars
items.text_en: Baraita on types of Torah scholars
