items.desc_en: A baraita describes three types of scholars: the master of aggadah (wealthy in public lectures), the master of pilpul (wealthy in coins and sharp arguments), and the master of traditions (wealthy in oil and cumin), all needing the master of wheat (Talmud).

sub.desc_en: A baraita classifies three types of Torah scholars—master of aggadah (wealthy in public lectures), master of pilpul (wealthy in coins and sharp arguments), and master of traditions (wealthy in oil and cumin)—all of whom need the master of wheat, which is Talmud.

items.text: Amoraic interpretations of 'All the days of the poor are evil'
items.text_en: Amoraic interpretations of 'All the days of the poor are evil'
items.desc_en: Multiple amoraim (Rabbi Zeira citing Rav, Rava, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) offer competing interpretations of Proverbs 14:15, identifying the 'poor' and 'good-hearted' with various types of people, including scholars, spouses, and temperaments.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav interprets 'All the days of the poor are evil' as referring to a Talmud scholar, and 'a good-hearted person always feasts' as referring to a Mishnah scholar.
Rava reverses the interpretation, citing Rav Mesharshiya that 'moving stones' refers to Mishnah scholars and 'splitting wood' refers to Talmud scholars.
Rabbi Chanina interprets the verse as referring to a man with a bad wife versus a man with a good wife.
Rabbi Yannai interprets the verse as referring to a fastidious person (איסטניס) versus a person with a good disposition.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse as referring to a merciful person versus a cruel person.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets the verse as referring to a narrow-minded person versus a broad-minded person.

items.text: Opening discussion on the verse 'All the days of the poor are evil'
items.text_en: Opening discussion on the verse 'All the days of the poor are evil'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi questions the verse, noting that Shabbat and festivals are good days. The Gemara resolves with Shmuel's statement that a change in routine is the beginning of illness. Ben Sira adds that even nights are bad for the poor, with poetic description.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi questions the verse 'All the days of the poor are evil' by noting that Shabbat and festivals are good days.
Shmuel resolves that a change in routine (even for good days) is the beginning of illness, so the poor person's days remain bad.
Ben Sira adds that even nights are bad for the poor, with a poetic description of his lowly dwelling and vineyard.

items.text: Mishnah: Sivlonot sent to the father-in-law
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sivlonot sent to the father-in-law
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man sends gifts (sivlonot) to his father-in-law's house and then eats a wedding meal there, even worth a dinar, the gifts are not recoverable. If he did not eat, they are recoverable. Many gifts meant to return with the wife are recoverable; few gifts for her use in her father's house are not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of sivlonot (gifts sent to the father-in-law): if the groom ate a wedding meal there, even worth a dinar, the gifts are not recoverable; if he did not eat, they are recoverable; many gifts meant to return with the wife are recoverable; few gifts for her use in her father's house are not.

items.text: Gemara's initial clarifications on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial clarifications on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava specifies that the Mishnah's 'dinar' is precise; less than a dinar does not render gifts non-recoverable. The Gemara then raises questions: what if he drank instead of ate? What if his agent ate? What if the gift was sent to him?

sub.desc_en: Rava specifies that the Mishnah's term 'דינר' (dinar) is precise, excluding less than a dinar, and the Gemara clarifies that this is not obvious because the Mishnah might have used 'dinar' merely as a typical example.

The Gemara raises three questions: whether drinking is equivalent to eating, whether the groom's agent eating counts, and whether receiving the gift at his own home (sent to him) is equivalent to eating at the father-in-law's home.

items.text: Ma'aseh with Rav Yehuda and Shmuel, and ruling from Usha
items.text_en: Ma'aseh with Rav Yehuda and Shmuel, and ruling from Usha
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel recounts a story of a man who sent many gifts, drank a cup of hot water at his father-in-law's door, and died. Rabbi Acha Sar HaBirah brought the case to the sages in Usha, who ruled: sivlonot that are meant to be consumed are not recoverable; those not meant to be consumed are recoverable. The Gemara infers that even drinking counts, but questions whether this applies to less than a dinar or to gifts sent to him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel recounts a story of a man who sent many gifts to his father-in-law, drank a cup of hot water at the door, and died.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha Sar HaBirah and the sages in Usha
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha Sar HaBirah and the sages in Usha
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha Sar HaBirah brought the case to the sages in Usha, who ruled that sivlonot meant to be consumed are not recoverable, while those not meant to be consumed are recoverable.
The Gemara infers from the story that even drinking counts as consumption that forfeits the gifts.
The Gemara asks whether the story also implies that drinking even less than a dinar's worth of consumption forfeits the gifts.
Rav Ashi answers that perhaps they ground a pearl worth a thousand zuz and gave it to him to drink, so the value was far more than a dinar.
The Gemara asks whether the story also implies that gifts sent to the groom (not just consumed at the father-in-law's house) are forfeited.

The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting that the door of the father-in-law's house is considered like the father-in-law's house itself, so the case does not prove the rule for gifts sent elsewhere.

items.text: Question about appreciation of sivlonot
items.text_en: Question about appreciation of sivlonot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if sivlonot appreciate in value, who gets the profit? Since if they still exist they return to the sender, the appreciation is his; but if they were lost or stolen he must pay, so perhaps the appreciation belongs to the recipient. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question (תיקו) about whether the appreciation of sivlonot belongs to the sender or the recipient, given that if they still exist they return to the sender but if lost the recipient must pay.

items.text: Rava's question on sivlonot that did not wear out
items.text_en: Rava's question on sivlonot that did not wear out
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if sivlonot are meant to wear out but have not yet worn out, what is the law? The Gemara attempts to prove from the Usha ruling that they are not recoverable even if not worn out, but rejects this, saying the ruling only applies when they have worn out. Another proof from the Mishnah about few gifts is answered by Rava that it refers to specific items like a basket and a sieve.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if sivlonot (gifts sent to the bride's family) are meant to wear out but have not yet worn out, what is the law regarding their recoverability?
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Usha ruling that sivlonot that are meant to wear out are not recoverable, implying even if not worn out.
The Gemara rejects the proof, clarifying that the Usha ruling applies specifically when the sivlonot have worn out.
The Gemara attempts another proof from the Mishnah's ruling that few sivlonot are not recoverable, implying even if not worn out.
Rava answers that the Mishnah's ruling about few sivlonot refers specifically to items like a basket (יֵיבָא) and a sieve (סְבַכְתָּא), which are meant to wear out quickly.

items.text: Two stories by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
items.text_en: Two stories by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav tells a story of a man who sent new wine, oil, and linen garments to his father-in-law on Shavuot, illustrating either the abundance of Eretz Yisrael or that if one claims, his claim is valid. Another story: a man whose wife was said to be promiscuous followed her into a ruin to test her, saying he smelled radish in the Galilee.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav tells a story of a man who sent new wine, oil, and linen garments to his father-in-law on Shavuot.
The Gemara asks what lesson this story teaches.
The Gemara suggests the story teaches the abundance of Eretz Yisrael.
The Gemara alternatively suggests the story teaches that if one claims, his claim is valid.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav tells a story of a man whose wife was said to be promiscuous, and he followed her into a ruin to test her.
The man tells his wife he smells radish in the Galilee, as a pretext to test her fidelity.

items.text: Case of a man who gave a gift based on a mistaken assumption
items.text_en: Case of a man who gave a gift based on a mistaken assumption
items.desc_en: A man gave a gift from the writings of Jericho and ate from it. The property was destroyed and the woman died. The Sages ruled that since he only entered to inspect her, if she dies he does not inherit her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a man gave a gift based on inspecting a woman, and the Sages ruled that since he only entered to inspect her, he does not inherit her.

items.text: Discussion of returning gifts and food
items.text_en: Discussion of returning gifts and food
items.desc_en: Ravin Sava stated before Rav Pappa that if the woman dies or the man dies, he returns the gifts but not the food consumed. If she returns, she returns even a vegetable. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua added that they assess the value of meat at a low price, up to a third.

sub.text: Ravin Sava's statement before Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Ravin Sava's statement before Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Ravin Sava states that if the man dies, gifts of סיבלונות (betrothal gifts) are returned, but food and drink are not.
Ravin Sava adds that if the woman retracts, she returns even the smallest item like a bundle of vegetables.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua rules that the value of meat consumed is assessed at a cheap price, defined as up to one-third below market.

items.text: Mishnah: Gift of a terminally ill person
items.text_en: Mishnah: Gift of a terminally ill person
items.desc_en: If a terminally ill person writes all his property to others and leaves any land, his gift stands. If he leaves no land, his gift does not stand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a dangerously ill person who writes all his property to others, leaving any land, his gift stands; if he leaves no land, it does not.

items.text: Gemara: Who is the Tanna who follows assessment?
items.text_en: Gemara: Who is the Tanna who follows assessment?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who follows assessment. Rav Nachman says it is Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, as taught in a baraita: If one thought his son died and gave away all his property, and the son returns, Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says the gift is not valid because he would not have given it had he known.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that we follow the presumed intention (אומדנא) of the giver.
Rav Nachman identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, citing a baraita where he rules that a gift given under mistaken belief that his son died is invalid.

A baraita is cited: if a father gave away all his property thinking his son died, and the son returns, Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rules the gift is invalid because he would not have written it had he known.

items.text: Alternative opinion: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
items.text_en: Alternative opinion: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet says it is Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, as taught in a baraita about one who says 'write a get for my wife' while going to execution, and later they added the case of one traveling or going on a ship, and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds even one who is dangerously ill.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, citing a baraita where he includes a dangerously ill person in the rule about writing a get.
The baraita cites the early ruling about one going to execution, the later addition of travelers, and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's addition of the dangerously ill.

items.text: Reasons for rejecting each opinion
items.text_en: Reasons for rejecting each opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rav Nachman does not hold like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri: there he said 'write', which is explicit. And why Rav Sheshet does not hold like Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya: a clear assessment is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Nachman does not attribute the Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri.
The Gemara explains that the case of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is different because the person explicitly said 'write,' indicating clear intent.
The Gemara asks why Rav Sheshet does not attribute the Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya.
The Gemara explains that the case of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya involves a compelling presumption (אומדנא דמוכח), which is different from the Mishnah's situation.

items.text: Introduction to a baraita about a sick person
items.text_en: Introduction to a baraita about a sick person
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that discusses a sick person lying in bed who is asked about his property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna taught the baraita about a sick person who is asked about his property.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's analysis of conditional gift
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's analysis of conditional gift
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a person gives a gift conditionally, thinking he has no son or that his wife is not pregnant, but later it turns out otherwise; the gift is void. The Gemara questions whether this follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya or the Rabbis, and explains that the word 'דומה' (it seems) makes the case unique, and that the Mishnah teaches that the person is not just recalling his pain but making a condition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a gift given conditionally is void when the condition is revealed to be false.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and not the Rabbis.
The Gemara answers that even according to the Rabbis, the word 'דומה' (it seems) makes the case unique.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah teaches this case at all.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that the person is not merely recalling his pain but making a condition.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's derivation from the Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's derivation from the Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a verse (Numbers 27:8) to prove that the gift of a deathly ill person (מתנת שכיב מרע) is from the Torah, interpreting 'והעברתם' as a transfer similar to inheritance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites Rav's derivation from the verse 'וְהַעֲבַרְתֶּם אֶת נַחֲלָתוֹ לְבִתּוֹ' (Numbers 27:8) to prove that the gift of a deathly ill person (מתנת שכיב מרע) is from the Torah, interpreting 'העברה' (transfer) as analogous to inheritance.

items.text: Rav Nachman's alternative derivation and discussion
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's alternative derivation and discussion
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh derives the same law from a different verse (Numbers 27:9), using 'ונתתם'. The Gemara explains why Rav Nachman does not use Rabbi Zeira's verse, citing Rabbi's teaching about the unique case of a daughter transferring inheritance between tribes, and why Rabbi Zeira does not use Rav Nachman's verse, saying it is just the normal style of the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh derives the law of a deathbed gift from the verse 'וּנְתַתֶּם אֶת נַחֲלָתוֹ לְאֶחָיו' (and you shall give his inheritance to his brothers), arguing there is another 'giving' like this one.
The Gemara asks why Rav Nachman does not use Rabbi Zeira's verse 'וְהַעֲבַרְתֶּם' (and you shall transfer).
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְהַעֲבַרְתֶּם' is needed for Rabbi's teaching that a daughter uniquely transfers inheritance between tribes, since her son and husband inherit her.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Zeira does not use Rav Nachman's verse 'וּנְתַתֶּם' (and you shall give).
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וּנְתַתֶּם' is just the normal style of the verse and not a special derivation.

items.text: Additional derivations from King Hezekiah and Achitophel
items.text_en: Additional derivations from King Hezekiah and Achitophel
items.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya and Rami bar Yechezkel each derive the concept of a deathbed gift from biblical narratives: Hezekiah being told to command his house, and Achitophel commanding his house before hanging himself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya derives the concept of a deathbed gift from the verse where Hezekiah is told 'צַו לְבֵיתֶךָ' (command your house), interpreting it as a mere command (צַוָּאָה בְּעָלְמָא) regarding his estate.
Rami bar Yechezkel derives the same concept from Achitophel's action: 'וַיְצַו אֶל בֵּיתוֹ' (he commanded his house) before hanging himself, also interpreted as a mere command.

items.text: Achitophel's three instructions and the dispute about 'barur'
items.text_en: Achitophel's three instructions and the dispute about 'barur'
items.desc_en: The Sages teach three things Achitophel commanded his sons: not to quarrel, not to rebel against the Davidic dynasty, and regarding the festival of Shavuot – whether to plant 'barur' (clear) or 'balul' (mixed) wheat. Mar Zutra and the Nehardeans debate the correct reading, concluding that even mixed wheat with a north wind is considered 'barur'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three instructions Achitophel gave his sons: avoid quarrels, do not rebel against the Davidic dynasty, and on Shavuot, plant 'barur' (clear) wheat.
Mar Zutra objects that the correct reading is 'balul' (mixed) rather than 'barur'.

sub.text: Nehardeans in the name of Rabbi Yaakov
sub.text_en: Nehardeans in the name of Rabbi Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans resolve the dispute by stating that neither literal 'barur' nor literal 'balul' is meant; even mixed wheat with a north wind is considered 'barur'.

items.text: Discussion on wind directions and agricultural omens
items.text_en: Discussion on wind directions and agricultural omens
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba tells Rav Ashi that they learned from Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi about the smoke direction on the last day of Sukkot indicating rainfall. The Gemara raises a contradiction with a baraita about wind directions' effects on wheat and olives, and resolves it by distinguishing between different regions (ours vs. theirs).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba tells Rav Ashi that they learned from Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi about the smoke direction on the last day of Sukkot indicating rainfall and its effects on the poor and wealthy.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi's teaching continued
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi's teaching continued
sub.desc_en: The teaching continues detailing the effects of smoke direction south, east, and west on the poor and wealthy.
The Gemara raises a contradiction with a baraita about wind directions' effects on wheat and olives.

sub.text: Rav Yosef / Mar Zutra / Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef / Mar Zutra / Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: A mnemonic is offered: the table in the north and the menorah in the south, each increases its own produce.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between different regions: ours vs. theirs.

items.text: Abba Shaul's teaching on Shavuot as an omen
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's teaching on Shavuot as an omen
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul says that a clear Shavuot (עצרת ברור) is a good sign for the entire year. Rav Zevid adds that the first day of the year (Rosh Hashanah) indicates the weather for the whole year, and the Gemara asks what practical difference this makes.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Abba Shaul's teaching that a clear Shavuot (עצרת ברור) is a good omen for the entire year.
Rav Zevid adds that the first day of the year (Rosh Hashanah) indicates the weather for the entire year.
The Gemara asks what practical difference this omen makes.

items.text: Continuation of earlier discussion
items.text_en: Continuation of earlier discussion
items.desc_en: The segment concludes a previous statement about the prayer of the High Priest, serving as a transition to the new topic.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the previous discussion about the prayer of the High Priest (כהן גדול), serving as a transition to the new topic of a gift of a dying person (מתנת שכיב מרע).

items.text: Rava's statement in the name of Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's statement in the name of Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rava reports that Rav Nachman considers a deathbed gift to be merely rabbinic, to prevent mental distress.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Rav Nachman considers a deathbed gift (מתנת שכיב מרע) to be merely rabbinic in origin, instituted to prevent mental distress.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Nachman's view by citing a ruling where he treats a deathbed gift as irrevocable, implying it is biblical. The resolution is that the Sages gave it the force of biblical law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman's view by citing a case where he ruled that a deathbed gift cannot be revoked, implying it is biblical.
The Gemara resolves that although the gift is rabbinic, the Sages gave it the force of biblical law, making it irrevocable.

items.text: Rava's second statement in the name of Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Rava's second statement in the name of Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rava reports that Rav Nachman rules that a deathbed gift of usufruct without transfer of ownership is invalid; the recipient must be given the property itself.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava reports Rav Nachman's ruling that a deathbed gift of mere usufruct (residence or fruit) without transfer of ownership is invalid; the recipient must be given the property itself.

items.text: Gemara's inference and question
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and question
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Rav Nachman applies the same rules to deathbed gifts as to gifts by a healthy person, and then questions this by citing a contradictory statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Rav Nachman applies the same rules to deathbed gifts as to gifts by a healthy person, and then questions this by citing a contradictory statement from Rava citing Rav Nachman.

items.text: Effectiveness of a dying person's instruction regarding a loan
items.text_en: Effectiveness of a dying person's instruction regarding a loan
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a dying person who says 'Give my loan to so-and-so.' It questions whether this is effective even though the loan is not physically present. Rav Pappa explains it is because the heir inherits the loan, while Rav Acha bar Rav Ika argues that the loan is considered present and cites Rav Huna's rule about acquisition in the presence of all three parties.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a dying person's instruction to give his loan to someone is effective, even though the loan is not physically present for acquisition.
Rav Pappa explains that the instruction is effective because the heir inherits the loan, so the dying person can direct its transfer.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika argues that the loan is considered present for acquisition, citing Rav Huna's rule that if one says 'I have a maneh in your hand, give it to so-and-so' in the presence of all three parties, the recipient acquires it.

items.text: Inquiry about a tree and its produce
items.text_en: Inquiry about a tree and its produce
items.desc_en: A question is raised: if one gives a date palm to one person and its produce to another, does the giver retain the place of the produce? The Gemara then asks a further case: if one gives a tree to another but excludes its produce for himself, what is the ruling?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: if one gives a date palm to one person and its produce to another, does the giver retain the place of the produce (מקום פֵּירֵי) as a reservation (שיור) or not?
The Gemara poses a second hypothetical: if one gives a tree to another but excludes its produce for himself (using the phrase 'חוץ מפירותיו'), what is the ruling regarding the place of the produce?

items.text: Rava's resolution: retaining produce for oneself is a valid reservation
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: retaining produce for oneself is a valid reservation
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman resolves the inquiry: if one gives the tree to another and its produce to yet another, it is not a reservation of the place of produce. But if one gives the tree to another and reserves the produce for himself, it is a valid reservation, because a person is generous with himself.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the inquiry: if one gives the tree to another and reserves the produce for himself, it is a valid reservation because a person is generous with himself.

items.text: Support from Resh Lakish's ruling on selling a house
items.text_en: Support from Resh Lakish's ruling on selling a house
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba tells Rav Ashi that they teach this principle from Resh Lakish, who ruled that if one sells a house to another and says 'on condition that the upper story is mine,' the upper story remains his.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba tells Rav Ashi that they derive the principle of shiyur (retaining rights) from Resh Lakish's ruling: one who sells a house and says 'on condition that the upper story is mine' retains the upper story.

items.text: Inquiry about a house and a diyota as a reservation
items.text_en: Inquiry about a house and a diyota as a reservation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether giving a house to one and a diyota (balcony) to another constitutes a valid reservation (shiur) in a gift. Rava cites Rav Nachman that if one says 'except for the diyota,' it is a reservation, following Rav Zevid's reasoning that the diyota includes space for projecting beams, thus reserving that space.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether giving a house to one person and a balcony (דיוטא) to another constitutes a valid reservation (שיור) in a gift, and if not, whether saying 'except for the balcony' does.

Rava reports Rav Nachman's ruling that if one says 'except for the balcony,' it is a reservation, following Rav Zevid's reasoning that the balcony includes space for projecting beams, so here too saying 'except for its fruits' reserves the place of fruits.

items.text: Distinction between 'dividing' and 'deliberating' in a shekhiv mera's gift
items.text_en: Distinction between 'dividing' and 'deliberating' in a shekhiv mera's gift
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quotes Rav Nachman: If a shekhiv mera writes all his property to others, we examine his intent. If he was dividing (mechallek), upon death all acquire, but if he recovers, he retracts all. If he was deliberating (nimlakh), upon death all acquire, but upon recovery he only retracts the last gift, as he scrutinizes and then gives.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quotes Rav Nachman's rule: if a shekhiv mera (שכיב מרע, a person on his deathbed) writes all his property to others, we examine his intent; if he was dividing (מחלק), upon death all acquire, but if he recovers, he retracts all.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman (continued)
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman (continued)
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman continues: if he was deliberating (נמלך), upon death all acquire, but upon recovery he only retracts the last gift.
The gemara objects: perhaps in the 'deliberating' case he is merely scrutinizing and then giving, so why would he retract only the last?
The gemara resolves: the default assumption about a shekhiv mera (שכיב מרע) is that he scrutinizes carefully and then gives, so the 'deliberating' case is exceptional.

items.text: Concern for hidden assets when a shekhiv mera recovers
items.text_en: Concern for hidden assets when a shekhiv mera recovers
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi quotes Rav Nachman: If a shekhiv mera writes all his property to others and recovers, he does not retract, because we suspect he may have assets in another country. Rav Chama and Mar bar Rav Ashi explain how to reconcile this with the Mishnah that requires some land to be left for the gift to stand.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Minyomi quotes Rav Nachman that a shekhiv mera who writes all his property to others and recovers does not retract, because we suspect he may have assets in another country.
The Gemara asks how to reconcile Rav Nachman's ruling with the Mishnah that requires some land to be left for the gift to stand.
Rav Chama answers that the Mishnah applies when the shekhiv mera explicitly says 'all my property,' indicating no hidden assets.
Mar bar Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah applies when it is established that he has no other assets.

items.text: Whether partial retraction constitutes retraction of the entire gift
items.text_en: Whether partial retraction constitutes retraction of the entire gift
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether retracting part of a gift counts as retracting the whole. A baraita is analyzed: if all to the first and some to the second, the second acquires but the first does not. The Gemara concludes this applies when the giver recovered, not died. Rav Yemar and Rav Ashi debate the logic, and the halakha is that partial retraction is retraction of the whole.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether partial retraction of a gift constitutes retraction of the entire gift.
A baraita is cited: if all property was given to the first and some to the second, the second acquires but the first does not.
The Gemara infers that the baraita refers to a case where the giver died, implying partial retraction is retraction of the whole.
The Gemara rejects the inference, stating the baraita refers to a case where the giver recovered from his illness.
The Gemara supports this by noting the baraita's second clause: if some to the first and all to the second, the first acquires but the second does not.
The Gemara argues: if the giver died, both recipients should acquire, but the baraita says the second does not, so it must be a case of recovery.
Rav Yemar objects to Rav Ashi: even assuming recovery, if partial retraction is retraction of the whole, the second's acquisition is explained.
Rav Yemar argues: if partial retraction is not retraction of the whole, the case would be like a dividing gift, and neither recipient should acquire.

The halakha is that partial retraction constitutes retraction of the whole; the first clause of the baraita applies whether the giver died or recovered, but the second clause applies only when he recovered.

items.text: Inquiries about hekdesh, hefker, and charity upon recovery
items.text_en: Inquiries about hekdesh, hefker, and charity upon recovery
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises three unresolved questions (teiku): whether a shekhiv mera who dedicates all property to hekdesh, declares it hefker, or distributes it to the poor and then recovers, can retract. The doubt is whether the finality of these acts overrides the assumption that one does not fully intend to give away everything.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the first unresolved question: whether a shekhiv mera who dedicates all property to hekdesh (הקדש) and then recovers can retract, given the doubt whether one fully intends to give to hekdesh versus to oneself.

The Gemara raises the second unresolved question: whether a shekhiv mera who declares all property hefker (הפקר) and then recovers can retract, given the doubt whether the act's inclusivity (even for the poor) indicates final intent.

The Gemara raises the third unresolved question: whether a shekhiv mera who distributes all property to the poor and then recovers can retract, given the doubt whether charity (צדקה) is inherently final or subject to the same self-interest limitation.
The Gemara concludes all three questions with 'תיקו' (teiku — unresolved), leaving them standing.

items.text: Terms of gift and inheritance
items.text_en: Terms of gift and inheritance
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet states that the terms 'yitol', 'yizkeh', 'yachzik', and 'yikneh' are all expressions of gift. A baraita adds 'yachsin' and 'yirat' for one who is fit to inherit, following Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. The Gemara then begins a new inquiry.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet states that the terms 'yitol', 'yizkeh', 'yachzik', and 'yikneh' are all expressions of gift.
A baraita adds that the terms 'yachsin' and 'yirat' are also gift expressions for one fit to inherit, following Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

items.text: Gemara's questions on ambiguous gift terms
items.text_en: Gemara's questions on ambiguous gift terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a series of unresolved questions (teiku) about the interpretation of phrases like 'yihane bahen' (he shall benefit from them), 'yera'eh bahen' (he shall appear in them), 'ya'amod bahen' (he shall stand in them), and 'yisha'en bahen' (he shall lean on them) in the context of a gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the phrase 'יֵהָנֶה בָּהֶן' (he shall benefit from them) means the entire property is given as a gift or only that he may derive some benefit from them.
The Gemara asks about the phrase 'יֵרָאֶה בָּהֶן' (he shall appear in them).
The Gemara asks about the phrase 'יַעֲמוֹד בָּהֶן' (he shall stand in them).
The Gemara asks about the phrase 'יִשָּׁעֵן בָּהֶן' (he shall lean on them), and concludes all these questions are unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's contradictory rulings on a seller's right to retract
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's contradictory rulings on a seller's right to retract
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires about a seller who sold all his property and then stood up. Rav Yehuda quotes Rav with two seemingly contradictory statements: one that he cannot retract, and one that he can. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases where the coins are still in hand (he can retract) and where they were used to pay a debt (he cannot).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a seller sold all his property and then stood up, what is the law — can he retract?
Rav Yehuda quotes Rav stating that if the seller stood up, he cannot retract.
Rav Yehuda also quotes Rav stating the opposite: if the seller stood up, he can retract.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first case is where the coins are still in hand (he can retract), the second where they were used to pay a debt (he cannot).

items.text: The case of Issur the convert and his son Rav Mari
items.text_en: The case of Issur the convert and his son Rav Mari
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a shekhiv mera's admission (hoda'ah) can transfer property. It brings the case of Issur the convert, who had 12,000 zuz deposited with Rava. His son Rav Mari was conceived before conversion but born after, making him a non-heir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a shekhiv mera's admission (הודאה) can transfer property, and brings the case of Issur the convert who had 12,000 zuz deposited with Rava, and his son Rav Mari who was conceived before conversion but born after.
Rava asks how Rav Mari could acquire the money, noting that inheritance and gift of a shekhiv mera are treated equally, so since Rav Mari is not an heir, he cannot receive a gift.
Rava lists other acquisition methods (משיכה, חליפין, אגב קרקע, מעמד שלשתן) and explains why each fails in this case.
Rav Ika objects, asking why Issur could not simply admit (יודה) that the money belongs to Rav Mari, thereby transferring it through הודאה (admission).
While they were discussing, an admission (אודיתא) emerged from Issur's house, and Rava became upset, saying they were teaching litigants arguments and causing him loss.

items.text: Rava's analysis of how Rav Mari could acquire the money
items.text_en: Rava's analysis of how Rav Mari could acquire the money
items.desc_en: Rava analyzes the possible methods for Rav Mari to acquire the 12,000 zuz: inheritance (he is not an heir), gift (the rabbis equated a shekhiv mera's gift to inheritance, so if he cannot inherit, he cannot receive a gift), meshikhah (the money is not in his possession), halipin (currency cannot be acquired by exchange), agav karka (he has no land), or ma'amad shloshtan (he would not go if summoned).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks how Rav Mari can acquire the 12,000 zuz, and rejects inheritance and gift because the rabbis equated a shekhiv mera's gift (מתנת שכיב מרע) to inheritance, so if Rav Mari cannot inherit, he cannot receive a gift.

Rava rejects meshikhah (משיכה) because the money is not in Rav Mari's possession, halipin (חליפין) because currency cannot be acquired by exchange, agav karka (אגב קרקע) because Rav Mari has no land, and ma'amad shloshtan (מעמד שלשתן) because Issur would not go if summoned.

items.text: Rav Ika's objection and Issur's admission
items.text_en: Rav Ika's objection and Issur's admission
items.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami objects: why not have Issur admit that the money belongs to Rav Mari, and Rav Mari could acquire it through admission (hoda'ah)? While they were discussing this, Issur's admission emerged from his house. Rava became upset, saying they were teaching people arguments and causing him loss.

sub.text: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Rav Ami objects: why not have Issur admit that these coins belong to Rav Mari, and Rav Mari could acquire them through admission (הודאה)?
While they were discussing this, Issur's admission emerged from his house, resolving the objection.
Rava became upset, saying they were teaching people arguments and causing him loss.

items.text: Opening statement and dispute
items.text_en: Opening statement and dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one left any amount of land, the gift stands. Rav Yehudah citing Rav says 'any amount' means land sufficient for one's sustenance, while Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba says it means movables sufficient for one's sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one left any amount of land, the gift stands.
The Gemara asks how much 'any amount' means.
Rav Yehudah citing Rav answers that 'any amount' means land sufficient for one's sustenance.
Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba answers that 'any amount' means movables sufficient for one's sustenance.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's harmonization
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's harmonization
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira praises the elders' traditions, explaining that land is needed so one can lean on it, and movables similarly so one can lean on them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira praises the elders' traditions, explaining that land is needed so one can lean on it, and movables similarly so one can lean on them.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to Rabbi Zeira's harmonization, arguing that the Mishnah explicitly says 'land' and 'any amount', so the interpretations are forced.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to Rabbi Zeira's harmonization, arguing that the Mishnah explicitly says 'קרקע (land)' and 'כל שהוא (any amount)', so the interpretations are forced.

items.text: Abaye's counter-challenge
items.text_en: Abaye's counter-challenge
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's objection by citing a Mishnah about freeing a slave where 'land' is mentioned but the context shows it includes movables, and Rabbi Shimon's opinion further complicates the matter.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's assumption that 'קרקע' (land) in the Mishnah always means specifically land, citing a case where a master writes all his property to his slave and the Mishnah uses 'קרקע' but the context includes movables.
Rabbi Shimon adds that the slave is always freed unless the master explicitly excludes even one ten-thousandth of the property, further complicating the definition of 'קרקע'.

items.text: Rav Dimi's statement on movables as shiur
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's statement on movables as shiur
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Elazar: The Sages ruled that movables can serve as a reservation (שיור) regarding a slave, but not regarding a ketubah. This sets up the central question of the daf.

sub.text: Rav Dimi bar Yosef citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that the Sages ruled movables can serve as a reservation (שיור) regarding a slave but not regarding a ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the mishnah in Peah mentions 'land of any size' (קרקע כל שהוא) – it is due to the first clause. It then addresses a challenge from a mishnah about first shearing where 'any amount' (כל שהן) has a defined minimum, resolving that the term is relative to the Tanna Kamma's large measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah in Peah mentions 'land of any size' only because the first clause (Rabbi Akiva's statement) requires it, not because the term 'any size' has a fixed minimum.
The Gemara objects by citing a mishnah about first shearing (ראשית הגז) where 'any amount' (כל שהן) has a defined minimum of a mane and a pras, challenging the claim that 'any size' lacks a minimum.
The Gemara resolves that in the shearing case, the term 'any amount' is relative to the Tanna Kamma's large measure, so it is not a true minimum but a rhetorical contrast.

items.text: Clarification of gift terminology
items.text_en: Clarification of gift terminology
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the legal implications of different phrases used in gifts: 'my movables to so-and-so' excludes grain, 'all my movables' includes grain and the upper millstone but not the lower, and 'all that is movable' even includes the lower millstone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one says 'my movables to so-and-so,' the recipient acquires all utensils except grain.
The Gemara adds that if one says 'all my movables,' the recipient even acquires grain and the upper millstone, but not the lower millstone.
The Gemara concludes that if one says 'all that is movable,' the recipient even acquires the lower millstone.

items.text: Inquiry: Is a slave like land or movables?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Is a slave like land or movables?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is a slave legally classified as land (מקרקע) or movables (מטלטל)? Rav Acha bar Avya brings a proof from a mishnah about selling a city, where slaves are not sold with the city unless specified. The Gemara refutes the proof by distinguishing between movable and immovable land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: Is a slave legally classified as land (מקרקע) or as movables (מטלטל)?

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Avya to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Avya to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya proposes a proof from a mishnah about selling a city: slaves are not sold with the city unless specified, implying they are movables.
Rav Ashi refutes the proof: even if a slave is like land, the mishnah distinguishes between movable land (קרקע נייד) and immovable land (קרקע דלא נייד), so the slave is not sold with the city.

items.text: Proof from slave manumission and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Proof from slave manumission and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Ravina brings a proof from a mishnah: one who writes all his property to his slave goes free; if he reserved any land, the slave is not free. Rabbi Shimon disagrees. Rav Dimi's statement is cited again, and Rava explains to Rav Nachman: a slave is movable, so movables can be a shiur for movables; a ketubah is like land, so movables cannot be a shiur for land.

sub.desc_en: Ravina proposes a proof from a mishnah about one who writes all his property to his slave, citing the rule that if any land is reserved the slave is not freed, with Rabbi Shimon's dissenting opinion.

sub.text: Citation of Rav Dimi bar Yosef citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Citation of Rav Dimi bar Yosef citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Elazar states that movables are considered a valid reservation (שיור) regarding a slave, but not regarding a ketubah.

Rava explains to Rav Nachman that a slave is movable (מטלטלא), so movables can serve as a reservation for movables, but a ketubah is like land (מקרקעא), so movables cannot serve as a reservation for land.

items.text: Opening statement: reason for the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Opening statement: reason for the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about a shkhiv mera is not because the gift is like a get, but because of the principle that a shkhiv mera's gift is valid only if he leaves some property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah's ruling is not based on the principle of a get (bill of divorce) but on the rule that a shkhiv mera's gift is valid only if he leaves some property.

items.text: Rav Nachman's list of five who must write all their property
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's list of five who must write all their property
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman lists five cases: a shkhiv mera, a slave, a wife, sons, and a mavrachat. Each is supported by a baraita or amoraic statement showing that if they leave any property, the gift is not fully effective.

sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman lists five categories of people who must write all their property for their gift to be effective: a shkhiv mera, a slave, a wife, sons, and a mavrachat.
Cites the Mishnah that a shkhiv mera who writes all property to others and leaves any land retains the gift; if no land is left, the gift is void.
Cites the Mishnah that one who writes all property to his slave frees him; if any land is left, the slave is not freed.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel for a wife
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel for a wife
sub.desc_en: Cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that one who writes all property to his wife only makes her an overseer (אפוטרופוס), not a full owner.
Cites the Mishnah that one who writes all property to his sons and leaves any land to his wife causes her to lose her ketubah.
Cites Mar that a mavrachat (a woman fleeing her husband) must write all her property for the gift to be valid.

items.text: Discussion: movables as shiyur, except for ketubah
items.text_en: Discussion: movables as shiyur, except for ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that in all these cases, movables can constitute a shiyur (remainder), except for a ketubah where the Sages instituted that only land counts. Amemar adds that if movables are specified in the ketubah and still exist, they too count as shiyur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that in all these cases, movables can constitute a shiyur (remainder), except for a ketubah where the Sages instituted that only land counts.
Amemar adds that if movables are specified in the ketubah and still exist, they too count as shiyur.

items.text: Definition of 'property' (nikhsei) – includes slaves, land, garments, coins, documents
items.text_en: Definition of 'property' (nikhsei) – includes slaves, land, garments, coins, documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that the term 'nikhsei' includes slaves, land, garments, coins, and documents, citing various mishnayot and a story about Rav Pappa. It then records a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chiyya bar Avin about the number of types of documents.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asserting that the term 'נִכְסַי' (my property) includes slaves, land, and garments, citing mishnayot for each.
The Gemara proves that coins (זוּזֵי) are called 'נִכְסֵי' by citing a mishnah and a story where Rav Pappa transferred coins to Rav Shmuel bar Acha via land acquisition.
The Gemara proves that documents (שְׁטָרָא) are called 'נִכְסֵי' by citing Rabba bar Yitzchak's rule about two types of documents and their legal effect.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin reports in the name of Rav Huna that there are three types of documents, adding a third case about a seller who writes the document in advance.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's inquiry into what qualifies as 'property'
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's inquiry into what qualifies as 'property'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a document can be written for a seller even without the buyer present, and that movable property is acquired together with land. The Gemara then questions whether various items—animals, birds, phylacteries, and a Torah scroll—are considered 'property' (נכסי) for the purposes of this rule, citing relevant Tannaitic sources.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a document may be written for the seller even without the buyer present, and that movable property is acquired together with land through money, document, or possession.
The Gemara cites a baraita proving that animals and birds are called 'property' (נכסי) for the rule of consecration.
The Gemara cites that phylacteries are called 'property' and then raises an unresolved question about whether a Torah scroll is considered 'property' since it may be sold for Torah study or marriage.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic) for the following stories
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic) for the following stories
items.desc_en: A brief mnemonic lists the names of the rabbis and figures appearing in the subsequent cases: Zutra, the mother of Amram, two sisters, Rav Tovi, Rav Dimi, and Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The gemara provides a mnemonic listing the names of the rabbis and figures appearing in the subsequent cases: Zutra, the mother of Amram, two sisters, Rav Tovi, Rav Dimi, and Rav Yosef.

items.text: Case of the mother of Rav Zutra bar Toviya
items.text_en: Case of the mother of Rav Zutra bar Toviya
items.desc_en: The mother of Rav Zutra bar Toviya wrote her property to him because she intended to marry Rav Zevid. She married and was divorced. Rav Beivai bar Abaye initially questioned the gift, but Rav Huna bar Yehoshua argued that even according to the view that a 'mavrachat' (one who transfers property to avoid creditors) acquires, here the intent was clearly conditional on marriage, which failed.

sub.desc_en: The mother of Rav Zutra bar Toviya wrote her property to him because she intended to marry Rav Zevid, and she married and was divorced.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye questions the gift, arguing that since the stated reason (marriage) occurred, the gift should stand, but the divorce undermines the condition.

Rav Huna bar Yehoshua rejects the objection, stating that even according to the view that a 'mavrachat' (one who transfers property to avoid creditors) acquires, here the intent was clearly conditional on marriage, which failed due to divorce.

items.text: Case of the mother of Rami bar Chama and Rav Ukva bar Chama
items.text_en: Case of the mother of Rami bar Chama and Rav Ukva bar Chama
items.desc_en: The mother of Rami bar Chama wrote her property to him at night, but in the morning wrote it to Rav Ukva bar Chama. Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman each ruled in favor of one brother. Rav Sheshet challenged Rav Nachman, who cited Shmuel's principle: if a shikhiv mera would retract if he recovered, he can retract from his gift. Rav Sheshet questioned whether this applies to a gift to another, and Rav Nachman confirmed that Shmuel explicitly said it applies both to himself and to another.

sub.desc_en: The mother of Rami bar Chama wrote her property to him at night, but in the morning wrote it to Rav Ukva bar Chama; each brother obtained a ruling from a different Amora — Rav Sheshet for Rami and Rav Nachman for Rav Ukva.
Rav Sheshet confronts Rav Nachman, asking why he ruled for Rav Ukva, given that the mother was a שְׁכִיב מְרַע (a deathly ill person) and thus her retraction should be invalid.
Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's principle: any gift that a שְׁכִיב מְרַע would retract if he recovered, he can retract from it even while still ill.
Rav Sheshet objects that Shmuel's principle might apply only when the שְׁכִיב מְרַע retracts in favor of himself, not when he gives to another person.
Rav Nachman resolves the objection by stating that Shmuel explicitly said the principle applies both to retracting for oneself and for another.

items.text: Case of the mother of Rav Amram the Pious
items.text_en: Case of the mother of Rav Amram the Pious
items.desc_en: The mother of Rav Amram the Pious had a bundle of promissory notes. On her deathbed, she said they should go to her son Rav Amram. Her brothers challenged that he did not perform a kinyan (formal acquisition). Rav Nachman ruled that the words of a shikhiv mera are considered as if written and delivered.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the case: the mother of Rav Amram the Pious had a bundle of promissory notes, and on her deathbed she declared they should go to her son Rav Amram.
The brothers of Rav Amram came before Rav Nachman and objected that Rav Amram did not perform a formal acquisition (משיכה) to take possession of the notes.
Rav Nachman rules that the words of a shikhiv mera (שכיב מרע, a deathly ill person) are considered as if written and delivered, so no formal acquisition is needed.

items.text: Case of the sister of Rav Tovi bar Rav Mattana
items.text_en: Case of the sister of Rav Tovi bar Rav Mattana
items.desc_en: The sister of Rav Tovi bar Rav Mattana wrote her property to him in the morning. Later, Rav Achadvoi bar Rav Mattana cried to her, saying one is a Torah scholar and the other is not, so she wrote it to him as well. Rav Nachman ruled that since she would have retracted if she recovered, she can retract from the gift, citing Shmuel's principle.

sub.desc_en: The sister of Rav Tovi bar Rav Mattana writes her property to him in the morning, but later, at Rav Achadvoi bar Rav Mattana's tearful plea that one brother is a Torah scholar and the other is not, she writes it to him as well.
Rav Nachman rules that since she would have retracted if she recovered, she can retract from the gift, citing Shmuel's principle that one who would retract if they recovered may retract the gift.

items.text: Case of the sister of Rav Dimi bar Yosef
items.text_en: Case of the sister of Rav Dimi bar Yosef
items.desc_en: The sister of Rav Dimi bar Yosef had an orchard. Whenever she was ill, she would transfer it to him. The Gemara begins this case, which continues in the following amud.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of the sister of Rav Dimi bar Yosef, who would transfer her orchard to him whenever she fell ill.

items.text: The story of the woman who retracted her gift
items.text_en: The story of the woman who retracted her gift
items.desc_en: A woman on her deathbed instructed others to acquire property from her, but later recovered and retracted. Rav Nachman ruled that since she was a מצוה מחמת מיתה (one who gives due to impending death), she may retract.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that a woman on her deathbed sent for a relative to acquire property, but when she recovered she retracted.
The woman came before Rav Nachman, who summoned the relative; when he did not come, Rav Nachman threatened him with a curse.
Rav Nachman asked the witnesses about the woman's words, and upon hearing she lamented her impending death, ruled that she was a מצוה מחמת מיתה (one who gives due to impending death) and may retract.

items.text: Mar Zutra's statement in the name of Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's statement in the name of Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra reports that Rav Nachman said a partial gift of a sh'khiv m'ra is both like a healthy person's gift (irrevocable if he recovers) and like a dying person's gift (no kinyan needed).

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports Mar Zutra's statement in the name of Rav Nachman that a partial gift of a sh'khiv m'ra has a dual nature: like a healthy person's gift (irrevocable if he recovers) and like a dying person's gift (no kinyan needed).

items.text: Rava's correction of the tradition
items.text_en: Rava's correction of the tradition
items.desc_en: Rava rejects Mar Zutra's version and insists that Rav Nachman actually said a partial gift requires a kinyan, like a healthy person's gift.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects Mar Zutra's version of Rav Nachman's statement, insisting that Rav Nachman actually said a partial gift is like a healthy person's gift and requires a kinyan (formal acquisition).

items.text: Rava's objection and Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman with a baraita about a sh'khiv m'ra who left some land; Rav Nachman answers with Shmuel's ruling that if one gave all his property, even with a kinyan, he may retract if he recovers.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenged Rav Nachman from a baraita: if a dying person left any land, the gift stands — implying no acquisition was needed; but if no land was left, the gift does not stand, which would be inexplicable if acquisition had been performed.

Rav Nachman answered by citing Shmuel's ruling: a dying person who writes over all his property to others, even with acquisition, may retract if he recovers, because it is known he only gave due to impending death.

Rav Nachman resolves the objection by citing Shmuel's ruling that a sh'khiv m'ra who gave all his property, even with a kinyan, may retract if he recovers, because it is clear he only gave due to the expectation of death.

items.text: Further objections and resolutions
items.text_en: Further objections and resolutions
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya and Ravina bring additional cases (the mother of the Rochal family, and a case of giving a get or money) that seem to contradict Rava; Rava resolves each by saying the case involved a מצוה מחמת מיתה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya challenged Rava from a story of a sick woman who gave a bed worth twelve maneh to her daughter, and the sages upheld her words despite no acquisition.
Rava answered that the case involved a מצוה מחמת מיתה (one who gives due to impending death), which does not require acquisition.

items.text: Rav Huna's distinction and the halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Rav Huna's distinction and the halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua distinguishes between a partial gift (requires kinyan) and a gift of all property (no kinyan needed if the giver dies). The Gemara concludes that a partial gift of a sh'khiv m'ra requires a kinyan even after death, while a מצוה מחמת מיתה does not require a kinyan and is revocable if he recovers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua distinguishes between a מצוה מחמת מיתה (one who gives instructions due to impending death) in general, which requires a kinyan, and the cited baraitot which deal with one who divides all his property, which the Sages treated as a gift of a sh'khiv m'ra (deathbed gift) that does not require a kinyan.

The Gemara concludes the halakha: a partial gift of a sh'khiv m'ra requires a kinyan even after death, while a מצוה מחמת מיתה (instructions due to impending death) does not require a kinyan and is revocable if he recovers, even if a kinyan was performed.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a deathbed gift with a קנין
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a deathbed gift with a קנין
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: the school of Rav says such a gift rides on two horses (ארכביה אתרי ריכשי) – it is like a healthy person's gift in that if he recovers he cannot retract, and like a deathbed gift in that he can orally assign a loan. Shmuel says he does not know what to do with it, suspecting the donor intended only a formal document, which is invalid after death.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: the school of Rav says a deathbed gift with a קנין (formal acquisition) rides on two horses, while Shmuel says he does not know what to do with it.
The school of Rav explains the dual nature: it is like a healthy person's gift in that if he recovers he cannot retract, and like a deathbed gift in that he can orally assign a loan.
Shmuel explains his uncertainty: he suspects the donor intended only a formal document, which is invalid after death.

items.text: Contradiction raised against Rav and Shmuel from a baraita
items.text_en: Contradiction raised against Rav and Shmuel from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita sent by Ravin in the name of Rabbi Abahu: a deathbed patient who said 'write and give a maneh to so-and-so' and died – we do not write and give, because he intended only a document. Yet Rav Yehuda said Shmuel ruled that we do write and give. This creates contradictions for both Rav and Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that it will raise a contradiction against Rav and against Shmuel from a baraita.

sub.text: Baraita cited by Ravin in the name of Rabbi Abahu
sub.text_en: Baraita cited by Ravin in the name of Rabbi Abahu
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita sent by Ravin in the name of Rabbi Abahu: Rabbi Elazar sent to the exile that a deathbed patient who said 'write and give a maneh to so-and-so' and died – we do not write and give, because he intended only a document, and there is no document after death.
The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda who said that Shmuel ruled: the halacha is that we do write and give.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita creates a contradiction for both Rav and Shmuel.

items.text: Resolution of the contradictions
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: Rav's contradiction is resolved by distinguishing whether a קנין was performed (then irrevocable) or not (then revocable). Shmuel's contradiction is resolved by the case of יפוי כח (empowering the recipient), where the gift is valid even after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rav's contradiction by distinguishing whether a קנין (formal acquisition) was performed (then irrevocable) or not (then revocable).
The Gemara resolves Shmuel's contradiction by invoking the case of יפוי כח (empowering the recipient), where the gift is valid even after death.

items.text: Rava's question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak about Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Rava's question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak about Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava, sitting before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, asks: Did Shmuel really say that a deathbed gift with a קנין is invalid? But Rav Yehuda said Shmuel ruled that a deathbed patient who wrote all his property to others, even with a קנין, can retract if he recovers – implying the gift is revocable, contradicting Shmuel's earlier position.

sub.text: Rava's question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rava's question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether Shmuel really said that a deathbed gift with a קנין is invalid, citing Rav Yehuda's report that Shmuel ruled a deathbed patient who wrote all his property to others can retract if he recovers.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak questions Rava about the gesture
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak questions Rava about the gesture
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava what the earlier gesture meant, and Rava explains it was a case of one who enhances his power (meyapeh et kocho).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the scene: it was known that there was no formal acquisition (קִנְיָן) except due to the impending death, and the earlier sage gestured with his hand and remained silent.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava what the earlier gesture meant.
Rava explains that the gesture referred to a case of one who enhances his power (מְיַפֶּה אֶת כֹּחוֹ).

items.text: Definition of meyapeh et kocho
items.text_en: Definition of meyapeh et kocho
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda defines the phrase 'meyapeh et kocho' as a case where the recipient says 'we acquired from him adding to this gift,' indicating an enhancement of the gift's validity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a concrete example of the phrase 'meyapeh et kocho' (enhancing one's power).
Rav Chisda defines the case: the recipient says 'we acquired from him adding to this gift,' indicating an enhancement of the gift's validity.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on multiple gifts
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on multiple gifts
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: if one wrote and transferred possession to one person, then wrote and transferred to another, Rav says the first acquires (like a healthy person's gift), while Shmuel says the second acquires (like a shekhiv mera's gift).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: if one wrote a will for one person and then wrote for another, citing Rav Dimi's principle that one will annuls another.
The Gemara asks about a case where one wrote and transferred possession to one person, then wrote and transferred to another, presenting Rav's and Shmuel's opposing rulings.
Rav rules that the first recipient acquires, comparing this to a healthy person's gift (מתנת בריא).
Shmuel rules that the second recipient acquires, comparing this to a shekhiv mera's gift (מתנת שכיב מרע).

items.text: Why the dispute is necessary despite earlier disagreement
items.text_en: Why the dispute is necessary despite earlier disagreement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why this dispute is needed since they already argued about a shekhiv mera's gift with a kinyan. It explains that each case is necessary to avoid assuming one would concede to the other in the other case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this dispute is necessary, since they already argued about a shekhiv mera's gift with a kinyan (formal acquisition).
The Gemara explains that each case is necessary to avoid assuming one would concede to the other in the other case.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a shekhiv mera with a kinyan
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a shekhiv mera with a kinyan
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a version from Sura and Pumbedita: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the house of Rav sent to Shmuel asking about a shekhiv mera who wrote all his property to others with a kinyan, and Shmuel replied that nothing follows the kinyan (i.e., the gift is valid as a shekhiv mera's gift).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces two versions of the tradition, one from Sura and one from Pumbedita.

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reporting the house of Rav's question
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reporting the house of Rav's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba reports that the house of Rav sent to Shmuel asking about a shekhiv mera (שכיב מרע, a deathly ill person) who wrote all his property to others with a kinyan (קניין, formal acquisition).
Shmuel replies that nothing follows the kinyan (קניין), meaning the gift is valid as a shekhiv mera's gift and the kinyan does not convert it to a healthy person's gift.

items.text: Rav Chisda's clarification of the rule
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's clarification of the rule
items.desc_en: People initially thought that the rule about a certain acquisition applies only to others but not to oneself. Rav Chisda reports that Rav Huna explained it applies both to oneself and to others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the initial assumption that the rule applies only to others but not to oneself.
Rav Chisda reports that Rav Huna explained the rule applies both to oneself and to others.

items.text: Case of improper acquisition
items.text_en: Case of improper acquisition
items.desc_en: A man who acquired property from another came before Rav Huna, who said he could do nothing because the acquisition was not done in the proper manner.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces a case of a man who acquired property from another and came before Rav Huna.
Rav Huna responds that he can do nothing because the acquisition was not performed in the proper manner (לכתחילה).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on 'in life and in death'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on 'in life and in death'
items.desc_en: A gift document containing the phrase 'in life and in death' is debated: Rav says it is like a dying person's gift (taking effect after death), while Shmuel says it is like a healthy person's gift (taking effect immediately). The Nehardeans rule in accordance with Rav.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case of a gift document containing the phrase 'בחיים ובמות' (in life and in death), and records the dispute: Rav says it is like a dying person's gift (taking effect after death), while Shmuel says it is like a healthy person's gift (taking effect immediately).
Rav explains his position: since the document says 'במות' (in death), the gift takes effect after death, and the phrase 'בחיים' (in life) is merely a sign that the giver was alive.
Shmuel explains his position: since the document says 'בחיים' (in life), the gift takes effect from life, and the phrase 'ובמות' (and in death) is like saying 'from now and forever.'
The Nehardeans rule that the halacha follows Rav.

items.text: Rava's statement and Amemar's rejection
items.text_en: Rava's statement and Amemar's rejection
items.desc_en: Rava says that if the document says 'from life' (mechayim), the recipient acquires immediately. Amemar rules against Rava, and Rav Ashi explains that this is obvious since the Nehardeans already ruled like Rav, but Amemar teaches that even Rav would agree in that case.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if the document explicitly says 'from life' (מחיים), the recipient acquires the gift immediately.
Amemar rejects Rava's ruling, stating that the halacha does not follow Rava.
Rav Ashi questions Amemar, pointing out that the Nehardeans already ruled like Rav, so Amemar's rejection of Rava is obvious.
Rav Ashi explains that Amemar's statement is necessary to teach that even Rav would agree in the case where the document says 'from life' (מחיים), so the ruling is not obvious.

items.text: Rav Nachman sends a case to Rabbi Yirmeya
items.text_en: Rav Nachman sends a case to Rabbi Yirmeya
items.desc_en: A case came before Rav Nachman in Nehardea, but he sent it to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba in Shum Tamya, saying that since this is Shmuel's territory, they cannot rule like Rav.

sub.desc_en: A case came before Rav Nachman in Nehardea, and he sent it to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba in Shum Tamya, reasoning that since this is Shmuel's territory, they cannot rule like Rav.

items.text: Rava's ruling and the woman's complaint
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and the woman's complaint
items.desc_en: A woman came before Rava, who ruled according to his own opinion. She troubled him, so he told his scribe to write a document including a clause that she could hire workers or deceive them. The woman cursed him, accusing him of misleading her, and his clothes were soaked in water, but he was not freed from the curse.

sub.desc_en: A woman came before Rava, who ruled according to his own opinion, and she troubled him.
Rava tells his scribe to write a document including a clause that she could hire workers or deceive them.
The woman curses Rava, accusing him of misleading her.
Rava's clothes were soaked in water, but he was not freed from the curse.

items.text: Mishnah: Burden of proof for a dying person's gift
items.text_en: Mishnah: Burden of proof for a dying person's gift
items.desc_en: If a gift document does not state that the giver was a dying person, and the recipient claims he was dying while the heirs claim he was healthy, Rabbi Meir says the recipient must bring proof, while the Sages say the burden is on the one seeking to take from another.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: if a gift document does not specify the giver was a dying person (שכיב מרע), Rabbi Meir requires the recipient to prove the giver was dying, while the Sages place the burden of proof on the one seeking to take from another.

items.text: Gemara: Case of a gift document with ambiguous language
items.text_en: Gemara: Case of a gift document with ambiguous language
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a gift document that said 'when he was sick and lying in bed' but did not include the phrase 'and from his illness he departed to his eternal home,' raising the question of its legal status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case of a gift document that used ambiguous language indicating illness but omitted the standard phrase about death, raising the question of its legal status.

items.text: Rava's ruling and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava states that if a person is found dead and his grave is present, it serves as proof of death. Abaye objects, arguing that if a ship (where most are lost) is treated with stringencies of both life and death, then a sick person (where most recover) should certainly be treated as alive.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a person is found dead and his grave is present, the grave serves as proof of death.

Abaye objects with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if a ship (where most are lost) is treated with stringencies of both life and death, then a sick person (where most recover) should certainly be treated as alive.

items.text: Attribution of Rava's view to Rabbi Natan
items.text_en: Attribution of Rava's view to Rabbi Natan
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua identifies Rava's ruling as following Rabbi Natan's opinion in a Tosefta. The Tosefta presents a dispute: Rabbi Yaakov says the one who takes possession from others needs no proof, but others need proof to take from him; Rabbi Natan says the burden of proof depends on whether the person was healthy or a shakhiv mera (deathly ill).

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua identifies Rava's ruling as following Rabbi Natan's opinion.
The Tosefta is cited, presenting Rabbi Yaakov's and Rabbi Natan's dispute about the burden of proof for a shakhiv mera (deathly ill) versus a healthy person.

items.text: Application to impurity: Rabbi Elazar's ruling
items.text_en: Application to impurity: Rabbi Elazar's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that the same dispute applies to impurity laws. He cites a Mishnah: in summer, a field is a private domain for Shabbat but a public domain for impurity; in winter, it is a private domain for both.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that the same dispute applies to impurity laws, citing a Mishnah about a field in summer being a private domain for Shabbat but a public domain for impurity.
The Mishnah concludes that in winter, the field is a private domain for both Shabbat and impurity, completing the citation.

items.text: Rava's qualification of the impurity ruling
items.text_en: Rava's qualification of the impurity ruling
items.desc_en: Rava qualifies Rabbi Elazar's ruling: the distinction between summer and winter applies only if the rainy season has not yet passed; if it has passed, the field is a private domain for both Shabbat and impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rava qualifies Rabbi Elazar's ruling: the distinction between summer and winter applies only if the rainy season has not yet passed; if it has passed, the field is a private domain for both Shabbat and impurity.

items.text: Conclusion: Sages' general principle
items.text_en: Conclusion: Sages' general principle
items.desc_en: The Sages state the general rule: the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from another.

sub.desc_en: The Sages state the general principle that the burden of proof falls on the one who seeks to extract property from another.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rav Huna vs. Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rav Huna vs. Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says 'proof' means witnesses, while Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna say it means authentication of the deed. This sets up the central debate of the daf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asking what 'proof' (ראיה) refers to in the context of a dying man's gift.
Rav Huna states that 'proof' means bringing witnesses to testify that the donor was healthy at the time of the gift.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's position
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's position
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna argue that 'proof' means authenticating the deed (קיום השטר) to verify it was written by a healthy person.

items.text: Rav Huna's view linked to Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Natan
items.text_en: Rav Huna's view linked to Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Natan
items.desc_en: Rav Huna's position is explained as being based on the dispute between Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Natan, with Rabbi Meir aligning with Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis with Rabbi Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna's view (that proof requires witnesses) is based on the dispute between Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Natan.
The Gemara aligns Rabbi Meir with Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis with Rabbi Yaakov.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's view linked to the dispute about admitting a deed
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's view linked to the dispute about admitting a deed
items.desc_en: Their position is explained as being based on the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding whether one who admits to a deed needs to authenticate it. Rabbi Meir says no, the Rabbis say yes.

sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's position (that proof is via deed authentication) is based on the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis regarding whether one who admits to a deed needs to authenticate it.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why repeat the dispute?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why repeat the dispute?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this dispute is repeated, since it already appears in a baraita about disqualifying a deed. It explains that both cases are necessary: the Rabbis' leniency in the baraita might not apply here, and Rabbi Meir's stringency here might not apply there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this dispute is repeated, since it already appears in a baraita about disqualifying a deed.
The Gemara explains that the baraita's case is needed because the Rabbis' leniency there might not apply here, where the witnesses are not strong.
The Gemara explains that the present case is needed because Rabbi Meir's stringency here might not apply in the baraita's case.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling and Abaye's challenge
