items.desc_en: Rabbi Shabtai says in the name of Chizkiya that the two lines refer to the handwriting of the witnesses, not a scribe, because a forger would not go to a scribe to forge.

sub.text: Rabbi Shabtai in the name of Chizkiyah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shabtai in the name of Chizkiyah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shabtai reports in the name of Chizkiyah that the two lines refer to the witnesses' own handwriting, not a scribe's, because a forger would not go to a scribe.
The gemara explains the reasoning: a forger would not go to a scribe to forge, so the handwriting must be the witnesses' own.

items.text: Three opinions on the minimum gap
items.text_en: Three opinions on the minimum gap
items.desc_en: Three Amoraim give different examples of the minimum forgery-vulnerable gap: Rav Yitzchak ben Elazar says two lines and four spaces, Rav Chiyya bar Ami says two lines and three spaces, and Rabbi Avahu says one line and two spaces.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the minimum gap size, and Rav Yitzchak ben Elazar answers with an example of two lines and four spaces.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ami citing Ulla
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ami citing Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla gives a different example, indicating two lines and three spaces.
Rabbi Avahu provides a third example, holding that the minimum is one line and two spaces.

items.text: Rav's distinction and the Gemara's objection
items.text_en: Rav's distinction and the Gemara's objection
items.desc_en: Rav says the rule applies only between witnesses and the text, not between witnesses and the asherta (validation). The Gemara objects that both cases are equally susceptible to forgery. The answer is that witnesses might sign on a blank space (atyuta), but a court would never sign on a blank space.

sub.desc_en: Rav distinguishes the rule: it applies only between witnesses and the text, but between witnesses and the asherta (validation) even a large gap is valid.
The Gemara objects: both cases are equally susceptible to forgery, as a forger could write whatever he wants and have witnesses sign.
The Gemara answers that the space is filled with scribbling (tyuta), but then objects that the same could be done between witnesses and the text.
The Gemara resolves: witnesses might sign on a blank space (atyuta), but a court would never sign on a blank space, so the asherta is secure.

items.text: Concern about erasing the blank space
items.text_en: Concern about erasing the blank space
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further concern: perhaps the forger will erase the blank space and write above it, then have witnesses sign. Rav's ruling that a document with witnesses on an erasure is valid is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: one might cut off the top, erase the cross-out, write whatever he wants, and have witnesses sign; and Rav ruled that a document with witnesses on an erasure is valid.
Rav rules that a document whose witnesses signed on an erasure is valid, implying the concern is not applicable.

items.text: Question on Rav Kahana and Rav Tavyomei's traditions
items.text_en: Question on Rav Kahana and Rav Tavyomei's traditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rav Kahana's tradition (citing Shmuel) works well, but asks what Rav Tavyomei (citing Rav) would say. It answers that Rav holds that in such a case, the document is validated not from the erasure but from the witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana's tradition citing Shmuel works well, but asks what Rav Tavyomei citing Rav would say.
The Gemara answers that Rav holds that in such a case, the document is validated not from the erasure but from the witnesses.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the leniency (allowing a gap of one line) applies only between the witnesses and the text, but between the witnesses and the erasure, even one line invalidates the document.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the leniency of allowing a one-line gap applies only between the witnesses and the text, but between the witnesses and the erasure (אשרתא), even a single line invalidates the document.

items.text: Reason for the distinction
items.text_en: Reason for the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the rationale: between witnesses and the erasure, one might erase the top, write himself and his witnesses on one line, and such a document is valid. But between witnesses and the text, one might erase the top, write whatever he wants, and have witnesses sign below, which is invalid because the document and witnesses are on separate lines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the distinction is made: between witnesses and the erasure, one might erase the top, write himself and his witnesses on one line, and such a document is valid.

The Gemara answers that between witnesses and the text, one might erase the top, write whatever he wants, and have witnesses sign below, which is invalid because the document and witnesses are on separate lines.

items.text: Objection and resolution
items.text_en: Objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not worry that one might write himself and his witnesses on one line and claim he intended to enlarge the witnesses? It answers that in such a case, the document is validated from the upper witnesses, not the lower ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not worry that one might write himself and his witnesses on one line and claim he intended to enlarge the witnesses?
The Gemara answers that in such a case, the document is validated from the upper witnesses, not the lower ones.

items.text: Rav's original statement
items.text_en: Rav's original statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav's original ruling: a document that comes with its text and witnesses on an erasure is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a document whose text and witnesses appear on an erasure is valid.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: if a document has witnesses on an erasure, the borrower might erase and rewrite the text. Abaye explains that Rav holds witnesses only sign on an erasure if it was erased in their presence, preventing forgery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if a borrower could erase and rewrite, the difference between one erasure and two erasures would be detectable, so why worry?
The Gemara counters: what if the borrower originally placed ink where the witnesses would sign, then erased it, so that when he later erases the whole area it appears as two erasures?
Abaye explains that Rav holds witnesses only sign on an erasure that was made in their presence, preventing the forgery scenario.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if the text is on parchment and witnesses on an erasure, it is valid. The Gemara objects that the borrower could erase and rewrite, but the baraita explains that witnesses write a clarifying statement. The Gemara then questions where this statement is written, concluding it is between the witnesses.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if the text is on parchment and witnesses on an erasure, it is valid.
The Gemara objects: the borrower could erase the witnesses' signatures and write whatever he wants, making the document appear as if both text and witnesses are on the erasure.
The baraita explains that the witnesses write a clarifying statement: 'We, the witnesses, signed on an erasure, but the document was written on parchment.'
The Gemara asks where this clarifying statement is written, and concludes it is written between the witnesses.

items.text: Challenge from the reverse case
items.text_en: Challenge from the reverse case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the text is on an erasure and witnesses on parchment, it is invalid. Why not write a clarifying statement? The Gemara answers that here the erasure is not witnessed, so the concern of multiple erasures applies, but that concern only applies when witnesses sign on the erasure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the text is on an erasure and witnesses on parchment, the document is invalid; why not write a clarifying statement to make it valid?
The Gemara answers: the concern of multiple erasures applies only when witnesses sign on the erasure, not when they sign on the parchment, so the clarifying statement would not help.

items.text: Further attempts at forgery and rebuttals
items.text_en: Further attempts at forgery and rebuttals
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests bringing another parchment to match the erasure, but is rejected because erasures differ. It then suggests delaying the document to age the erasure, but Rabbi Yirmeya objects due to concern for court error.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests bringing another parchment to match the erasure by erasing it similarly.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion because erasures on different parchments do not look alike.
The Gemara suggests having the witnesses sign in court and then erasing to match the original erasure.
Rabbi Hoshaya rejects the suggestion because a fresh erasure does not resemble an older one.
The Gemara suggests delaying the document to age the erasure.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects because of concern that a court might err by relying on the aged erasure.

items.text: Introduction of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's opinion
items.text_en: Introduction of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's opinion
items.desc_en: The mishnah cites Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's view on tied documents, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi responds to his words.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah cites Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's opinion on tied documents, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi responds to his words.

items.text: Distinction between pashut and mekushar dates
items.text_en: Distinction between pashut and mekushar dates
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a pashut (simple) document dates by the actual years of the king's reign, while a mekushar (folded) document adds an extra year to each regnal year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference between a pashut (simple) document, which dates by actual regnal years, and a mekushar (folded) document, which adds an extra year to each regnal year.

items.text: Potential forgery using mekushar
items.text_en: Potential forgery using mekushar
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: a borrower might take a loan with a mekushar document, repay part of it, have the document torn (creating a 'tevara'), and then later present a pashut document claiming the loan was recent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: a borrower might take a loan with a mekushar document, repay part of it, have the document torn (creating a 'tevara'), and then later present a pashut document claiming the loan was recent.
The Gemara explains that when the loan term arrives, the borrower could present a pashut document and claim the loan was recent.

items.text: Rabbi's initial ignorance of mekushar
items.text_en: Rabbi's initial ignorance of mekushar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi was familiar with mekushar documents, citing an incident where he initially mistook one for a post-dated document until Zunin explained the custom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi was familiar with mekushar documents, citing an incident where he initially mistook one for a post-dated document.
Zunin explains to Rabbi that the custom of that nation is to count regnal years differently in mekushar documents.
The Gemara resolves that after hearing from Zunin, Rabbi became familiar with mekushar documents.

items.text: Document dated by 'Archan'
items.text_en: Document dated by 'Archan'
items.desc_en: A document was dated 'in the year of so-and-so Archan.' Rabbi Chanina says to check when Archan became governor. Rav Hoshaya explains the custom: first year called 'Archan', second 'Digon'. Rabbi Yirmeya adds that if he was deposed and reinstated, they would call him 'Archan Digon'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case of a document dated 'in the year of so-and-so Archan,' and Rabbi Chanina rules that one must check when Archan became governor.
The gemara objects: perhaps his reign was long, so the year alone is insufficient to date the document.
Rav Hoshaya explains the custom: in the first year they call him 'Archan,' in the second year 'Digon,' so the title itself indicates the year.
The gemara objects: perhaps he was deposed and then reinstated, which would confuse the counting.
Rabbi Yirmeya resolves that if he was deposed and reinstated, they would call him 'Archan Digon,' so the title still indicates the correct year.

items.text: Braita on Greek number prefixes
items.text_en: Braita on Greek number prefixes
items.desc_en: A braita discusses nazirite vows using Greek number prefixes (Heina=1, Digon=2, etc.) and another braita on houses that are round or polygonal (Digon, Trigon, etc.) not being susceptible to plague, while a Tetrigon (square) is, derived from verses about walls.

sub.desc_en: A braita lists Greek number prefixes for nazirite vows: Heina=1, Digon=2, Trigon=3, Tetrigon=4, Pentigon=5, attributed to Somkhos.
A second braita states that round or polygonal houses (Digon, Trigon, Pentigon) are not susceptible to plague (נגעים), but a Tetrigon (square) is susceptible.
The Gemara derives the requirement for four walls from the verse: the repetition of 'קיר' (wall) above and below yields two each, totaling four.

items.text: Rabbi's error and lashon hara
items.text_en: Rabbi's error and lashon hara
items.desc_en: Rabbi initially thought a mekushar document had no date, but Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi found the date hidden between folds. Rabbi then blamed the scribe Yehuda the tailor, but was rebuked for lashon hara. The Gemara explains why praising someone can also lead to lashon hara, and concludes with Rav Amram's statement that one cannot avoid three sins daily, including lashon hara.

sub.desc_en: A mekushar document came before Rabbi; Rabbi said it had no date, but Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi suggested the date might be hidden between the folds, and upon opening it, the date was found.
Rabbi was embarrassed and blamed the scribe Yehuda the tailor for the error.
Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi rebuked Rabbi for speaking לשון הרע (evil speech) by blaming the scribe.
On another occasion, Rabbi praised Yehuda the tailor's handwriting, and again Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi rebuked him for לשון הרע.
The Gemara asks: In the first case, there is clearly לשון הרע, but in the second case where Rabbi praised the scribe, what לשון הרע is there?
The Gemara answers based on Rav Dimi's teaching: one should never speak of a friend's good qualities, because from praising him one may come to speak of his bad qualities.
Rav Amram said in the name of Rav that a person cannot avoid three sins daily: sinful thoughts, distraction in prayer, and לשון הרע.
The Gemara objects: Can it enter your mind that a person cannot avoid actual לשון הרע daily? (Implying that the statement must refer to something less severe, like dust of לשון הרע.)

items.text: Severity of lashon hara
items.text_en: Severity of lashon hara
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement about 'all' refers to the 'dust of lashon hara' (avak lashon hara), not actual lashon hara. Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that most people sin in theft, a minority in forbidden relations, and everyone in the dust of lashon hara.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's 'all' refers to the dust of lashon hara (אבק לשון הרע), not actual lashon hara.

items.text: Dispute about custom and kefeida
items.text_en: Dispute about custom and kefeida
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Tanna Kamma ignores local custom. Rav Ashi explains that the dispute is only in a place where both simple and folded documents are used; if one requests a simple document and receives a folded one, or vice versa, the Tanna Kamma considers it a deal-breaker (kefeida), while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel considers it merely a matter of location (mar'eh makom).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Tanna Kamma ignores local custom entirely.

Rav Ashi explains that the dispute applies only where both simple and folded documents are used; if one requests a simple document and receives a folded one, or vice versa, the Tanna Kamma considers it a deal-breaker (קְפֵידָא), while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel considers it merely a matter of location (מַרְאֶה מָקוֹם).

items.text: Abaye's list of those who hold mar'eh makom
items.text_en: Abaye's list of those who hold mar'eh makom
items.desc_en: Abaye states that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar all hold the principle of mar'eh makom. He cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon says a betrothal is valid if the groom misled the bride to her benefit, and a Mishnah where Rabbi Elazar validates a get received from a different location than specified.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar all hold the principle of מראה מקום (showing location).

items.text: The case of a simple document with one witness
items.text_en: The case of a simple document with one witness
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that a simple document with one witness is invalid, as it seems obvious. Abaye explains it is necessary for a case where one witness is in writing and one is oral. Amemar validates such a document, and when Rav Ashi asks about Abaye's statement, Amemar says he neither heard nor agrees with it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that a simple document with one witness is invalid, as it seems obvious, while the case of a folded document with two witnesses is necessary.
Abaye explains that the Mishnah's statement is necessary for a case where one witness is in writing and one is oral, teaching that even such a document is invalid.
Amemar validates a document with one witness in writing and one oral, contradicting Abaye's position.
Rav Ashi asks Amemar about Abaye's statement, seeking Amemar's view on it.
Amemar responds that he neither heard nor agrees with Abaye's statement.

items.text: Unfinished objection
items.text_en: Unfinished objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins an objection with 'Ela kashya' (But it is difficult), but the argument is cut off, likely continuing on the next amud.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty with the previous discussion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's inference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's inference
items.desc_en: The Mishnah implies that two witnesses in a connected document are like one witness in a simple document, both being invalid by Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited as the starting point of the discussion.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that two witnesses in a connected document are like one witness in a simple document, both invalid by Torah law.

items.text: First question: joining a written and oral witness
items.text_en: First question: joining a written and oral witness
items.desc_en: The colleagues ask Rabbi Yirmeya whether one written witness and one oral witness can join. He responds humbly that his opinion leans toward allowing them to join.

sub.desc_en: The colleagues ask Rabbi Yirmeya whether one written witness and one oral witness can join together.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the question's scope
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the question's scope
sub.desc_en: The gemara clarifies that the question only arises according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who allows two written and two oral witnesses to join, but the doubt is whether one written and one oral witness also join.
Rabbi Yirmeya responds humbly that his opinion leans toward allowing them to join.

items.text: Second question: joining witnesses from different courts
items.text_en: Second question: joining witnesses from different courts
items.desc_en: The colleagues ask Rabbi Yirmeya whether witnesses who testified in two different courts can join. He again responds that his opinion leans toward allowing them to join.

sub.desc_en: The colleagues ask Rabbi Yirmeya whether two witnesses who testified in separate courts can join by having the courts come together.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the question's framing
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the question's framing
sub.desc_en: The gemara clarifies that the question only arises according to Rabbi Natan, who allows joining within one court, but not according to the Tanna Kamma who rejects joining even within one court.
Rabbi Yirmeya responds humbly that his opinion leans toward allowing the witnesses to join.

items.text: Third question: joining judges from different courts
items.text_en: Third question: joining judges from different courts
items.desc_en: Mar bar Chiyya reports that the colleagues asked about judges from different courts joining. Rabbi Yirmeya again responds that his opinion leans toward allowing them to join.

sub.text: Mar bar Chiyya's report of the colleagues' question
sub.text_en: Mar bar Chiyya's report of the colleagues' question
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Chiyya reports that the colleagues sent a question to Rabbi Yirmeya: if two witnesses testified in one court and then again in another court, may one judge from each court join together to form a panel?

The gemara clarifies the inquiry: according to Rabbi Natan, the question is unnecessary since even witnesses from the same court cannot join, but according to the Tanna Kamma (first Tanna) who disputes Rabbi Natan, the question is whether witnesses cannot join but judges can, or whether the same rule applies to both.
Rabbi Yirmeya responds with his characteristic humility, stating that his opinion leans toward permitting the judges to join.

items.text: Fourth question: writing a validation formula when one judge dies
items.text_en: Fourth question: writing a validation formula when one judge dies
items.desc_en: Ravina reports that the colleagues asked whether a court that validated a document must write 'we were in a session of three, and one is not here' when one judge dies. Rabbi Yirmeya responds that they must, and this led to his admission to the study hall.

sub.desc_en: Ravina reports that the colleagues sent to Rabbi Yirmeya asking whether a court that validated a document must write 'we were in a session of three, and one is not here' when one judge dies.
Rabbi Yirmeya responds humbly that his opinion inclines that they must write the formula.
The gemara notes that because of this response, Rabbi Yirmeya was admitted to the study hall.

items.text: Mishnah: interpreting contradictory amounts in documents
items.text_en: Mishnah: interpreting contradictory amounts in documents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that when a document states conflicting amounts (e.g., '100 zuz which are 20 selas'), the lower amount is followed, but the higher amount is written as a safeguard against erasure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule for a document with conflicting amounts: the lower amount is followed.
The Mishnah adds that when the word 'כסף' (silver) is written and then erased, the minimum amount is two units.
The Mishnah resolves that when the top and bottom amounts differ, the lower (bottom) amount is followed, and the higher amount is written as a safeguard against erasure.

items.text: Gemara: interpreting 'kesef' and 'dehav' in documents
items.text_en: Gemara: interpreting 'kesef' and 'dehav' in documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the minimum amounts implied by terms like 'kesef' (silver) and 'dehav' (gold), and clarifies that they refer to minted coins, not ingots.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the minimum amounts implied by various formulations of 'kesef' (silver) in documents.
The Gemara questions why 'kesef' alone cannot refer to a silver ingot (נסכא) rather than a coin.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the document explicitly uses the term 'מטבע' (minted coin), excluding ingots.
The Gemara further questions why 'kesef' cannot refer to small silver coins (פריטי).
Rav Pappa answers that the baraita refers to a place where small silver coins (פריטי) are not in circulation.
A baraita lists the minimum amounts implied by various formulations of 'dehav' (gold) in documents.
The Gemara questions why 'dehav' alone cannot refer to a gold ingot (נסכא) rather than a coin.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the document explicitly uses the term 'מטבע' (minted coin), excluding ingots.

items.text: Initial question and answer about 'gold in dinars'
items.text_en: Initial question and answer about 'gold in dinars'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether 'gold in dinars' could mean gold coins (peritei) and answers that people do not make gold coins. It then questions if it means 'crushed gold' worth two gold dinars, and Abaye responds that the writer's hand is on the lower (i.e., the less valuable) interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether 'gold in dinars' could refer to gold coins (פריטי), and answers that people do not make gold coins.
The Gemara questions whether 'gold in dinars' means crushed gold worth two gold dinars, and Abaye responds that the writer's hand is on the lower (less valuable) interpretation.

items.text: Parallel question about 'silver in dinars' and resolution
items.text_en: Parallel question about 'silver in dinars' and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a similar question about the phrase 'silver in dinars' in the first clause, asking if it means silver ingots worth two silver dinars. Rav Ashi resolves both by noting the first clause uses 'dineirei' and the second uses 'dinarin', implying a linguistic distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a parallel question about the first clause 'silver in dinars', asking why it cannot mean silver ingots worth two silver dinars.
Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by pointing out a linguistic distinction: the first clause uses 'דינרי' (dineirei) while the second uses 'דינרין' (dinarin), implying different meanings.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about the distinction between 'dineirei' and 'dinarin'
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about the distinction between 'dineirei' and 'dinarin'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for proof that there is a difference between 'dineirei' and 'dinarin'. It cites a baraita about a woman with uncertain births or discharges, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel uses the terms 'dineirei zahav' (gold dinars) and 'dinarin' (dinars) to show the distinction, demonstrating that 'dineirei' means actual gold coins while 'dinarin' means silver coins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for proof that there is a distinction between the terms 'דינרי' (dineirei) and 'דינרין' (dinarin).
The Gemara cites a baraita about a woman with uncertain births or discharges, establishing the basic halacha of bringing one offering and being exempt from further obligations.

sub.text: Supporting baraita (continued) — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's story
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita (continued) — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's story
sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts a story where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel uses the terms 'דינרי זהב' (gold dinars) and 'דינרין' (silver dinars) to demonstrate the distinction between the two forms, showing that 'דינרי' means actual gold coins while 'דינרין' means silver coins.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on that day, the prices of bird-offerings stood at four pairs (a quarter each). This sets the context for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on that day, the prices of bird-offerings stood at four pairs (a quarter each).

items.text: Baraita: Learning the lower from the upper
items.text_en: Baraita: Learning the lower from the upper
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: One may learn the lower (word) from the upper (word) if they differ by one letter, but not by two letters, e.g., 'ḥanan' from 'ḥanani' and 'anan' from 'anani'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one may learn the lower word from the upper word if they differ by one letter, but not by two letters, giving examples of 'ḥanan' from 'ḥanani' and 'anan' from 'anani'.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on two-letter difference
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on two-letter difference
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why two letters are not allowed: perhaps a four-letter name might occur, making it half the name. But then one letter would also be problematic for a two-letter name. Rather, the reason for two letters is that a three-letter name might occur, making it the majority of the name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two-letter differences are forbidden, proposing that a four-letter name might occur, making it half the name.
The Gemara objects that by the same logic, a single-letter difference would be problematic for a two-letter name, making it half the name.
The Gemara resolves that the reason for forbidding two-letter differences is that a three-letter name might occur, making it the majority (רוב) of the name.

items.text: Rav Pappa's clear case
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's clear case
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that it is obvious to him: if 'sefel' is above and 'kefel' is below, everything follows the lower (word).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa declares that it is obvious to him: when 'sefel' is written above and 'kefel' below, the document follows the lower word.

items.text: Rav Pappa's dilemma
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's dilemma
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa raises a dilemma: if 'kefel' is above and 'sefel' is below, what is the law? Do we suspect a fly (that erased a letter) or not? The matter stands unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa raises a dilemma: if the word 'קפל' (kefel) is written above and 'ספל' (sefel) below, do we suspect a fly erased a letter, or not?
The gemara concludes that the matter stands unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Case of ambiguous numbers
items.text_en: Case of ambiguous numbers
items.desc_en: A document had written 'six hundred and zuz'. Rav Sherevya sent it before Abaye: does it mean six hundred istirai and a zuz, or six hundred prutot and a zuz? Abaye replied: Remove prutot, as they are not written in a document – for they are commonly used for bargaining.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a document had written 'six hundred and a zuz', and Rav Sherevya sent it before Abaye.
Rav Sherevya asks whether the document means six hundred istirai and a zuz, or six hundred prutot and a zuz.
Abaye replies: remove prutot, as they are not written in a document – for they are commonly used for bargaining.

items.text: Opening discussion on writing sums in a document
items.text_en: Opening discussion on writing sums in a document
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how to write a sum of money in a document to prevent forgery, concluding that the lowest line of writing is authoritative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to write a sum of money in a document to prevent forgery, presenting two possible formulations.
The Tanna Kamma rules that the lower line of writing is authoritative, resolving the question.

items.text: Abaye's warning about signing at the bottom of a scroll
items.text_en: Abaye's warning about signing at the bottom of a scroll
items.desc_en: Abaye advises not to display one's signature at the end of a scroll, lest someone find it and write a false promissory note above it, as a signed document is collectible from unencumbered property.

sub.desc_en: Abaye warns not to display one's signature at the bottom of a scroll, lest someone find it and write a false promissory note above it, as such a document is collectible from unencumbered property.

items.text: Story of the tax collector and Abaye's signature
items.text_en: Story of the tax collector and Abaye's signature
items.desc_en: A tax collector asked Abaye to show his signature so he could exempt rabbis from tax. Abaye signed at the top of the scroll, but the collector drew a line through it, and Abaye remarked that the rabbis had already preceded him.

sub.desc_en: A tax collector came before Abaye and asked him to show his signature so that he could exempt rabbis from tax.
Abaye showed his signature at the top of the scroll.
When the collector drew a line through the signature, Abaye remarked that the rabbis had already preceded him.

items.text: Abaye's rule for writing numbers at the end of a line
items.text_en: Abaye's rule for writing numbers at the end of a line
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that from three to ten, one should not write the number at the end of a line, lest it be forged. If it happens, one should repeat the word several times until it falls in the middle of a line.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that from three to ten, one should not write the number at the end of a line, and if it happens, one should repeat the word several times until it falls in the middle of a line.

items.text: Two stories of detecting forged additions to documents
items.text_en: Two stories of detecting forged additions to documents
items.desc_en: Two cases came before Abaye where a forger added a letter to a document to change its meaning. In the first, a vav was added to turn 'third of an orchard' into 'and an orchard'; in the second, a vav was squeezed in to change 'Achi' to 've'Achi'. In both cases, Abaye detected the forgery by the spacing and extracted a confession.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a document originally read 'a third of an orchard' and a forger erased the roof and leg of the letter beit to turn it into a vav, changing the phrase to 'and an orchard'.
The forger came before Abaye, who asked why the vav had so much space around it, then bound the forger until he confessed.

items.text: Story of a forged document with Rava's and Rav Acha bar Adda's signatures
items.text_en: Story of a forged document with Rava's and Rav Acha bar Adda's signatures
items.desc_en: A document signed by Rava and Rav Acha bar Adda was brought before Rava. The defendant claimed his signature was forged, and Rava extracted a confession. Rava then asked how the forger managed to replicate Rav Acha bar Adda's shaky hand; the forger explained he placed his hand on a wall or stood on a stool to write.

sub.desc_en: A document signed by Rava and Rav Acha bar Adda was brought before Rava; the defendant claimed his own signature was forged and that he never signed before Rav Acha bar Adda.
Rava had the forger bound and he confessed.
Rava asked the forger how he managed to forge Rav Acha bar Adda's shaky handwriting.
The forger explained that he placed his hand on a wall, or alternatively stood on a stool, to steady his hand and replicate the shaky signature.

items.text: Mishnah: Writing a get or receipt without the other party
items.text_en: Mishnah: Writing a get or receipt without the other party
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a get may be written for a husband even without his wife present, and a receipt for a wife even without her husband, provided the scribe knows them. The husband pays the fee.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a get may be written for a husband without his wife present, and a receipt for a wife without her husband, provided the scribe knows them, and the husband pays the fee.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rules for writing documents
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rules for writing documents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists which documents may be written without both parties present, and who pays the scribe. It covers loans, sales, marriage, tenancy, and court documents, with a dissenting opinion from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a loan document may be written for the borrower even without the lender present, and the borrower pays the scribe.
The Mishnah states that a sale document may be written for the seller even without the buyer present, and the buyer pays the scribe.
The Mishnah states that betrothal and marriage documents may only be written with both parties' consent, and the groom pays the scribe.
The Mishnah states that tenancy and contract documents may only be written with both parties' consent, and the tenant pays the scribe.
The Mishnah states that arbitration documents and all court acts may only be written with both parties' consent, and both pay the scribe.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissents, ruling that for arbitration documents, two separate documents are written, one for each party.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's missing condition
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's missing condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a missing condition from the Mishnah: that the scribe must know the names of the parties. Rav Yehuda quoting Rav explains that the scribe must know the husband's name in the get and the wife's name in the receipt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's condition 'provided that he knows them' refers to.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that the scribe must know the husband's name in the get and the wife's name in the receipt.

items.text: Discussion on the scope of name recognition
items.text_en: Discussion on the scope of name recognition
items.desc_en: Rav Safra, Rav Acha bar Huna, Rav Huna bar Chinana, and Abaye debate whether the requirement applies only to the husband's name in the get and the wife's name in the receipt, or vice versa. Abaye clarifies that Rav's statement applies equally to both names in each document.

sub.text: Rav Safra, Rav Acha bar Huna, and Rav Huna bar Chinana's question
sub.text_en: Rav Safra, Rav Acha bar Huna, and Rav Huna bar Chinana's question
sub.desc_en: The rabbis question whether Rav's requirement applies only to the husband's name in the get and the wife's name in the receipt, or vice versa.
The gemara objects that if the husband's name is not required in the receipt, a woman might write a receipt for another man's husband.
The gemara objects that sometimes a woman might write a receipt and give it to a man who is not her husband.
Abaye clarifies that Rav's statement applies equally to both names in each document, resolving the question.

items.text: Concern about two men with the same name
items.text_en: Concern about two men with the same name
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern about two men named Yosef ben Shimon living in the same city, who might write a get for the wrong wife. Rav Acha bar Huna quotes Rav that such men must divorce their wives only in each other's presence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that two men named Yosef ben Shimon living in the same city might write a get for the wrong wife.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna quotes Rav that such men must divorce their wives only in each other's presence.

items.text: Concern about a person assuming another's name
items.text_en: Concern about a person assuming another's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara worries that someone might go to another city and claim the name Yosef ben Shimon, then write a get for the wrong wife. Rav Huna bar Chinana quotes Rav that if a name is established in the city for 30 days, there is no concern. Abaye and Rav Zevid discuss what to do if the name is not established.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: perhaps a person might go to another city, assume the name Yosef ben Shimon, and write a גט (bill of divorce) for the wrong wife.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana quotes Rav that if a person's name has been established in the city for thirty days, there is no concern about such deception.
The Gemara asks: if the name has not been established for thirty days, what is the law?
Abaye answers that if people call him by that name and he responds, that is sufficient to establish the name.
Rav Zevid answers that a deceitful person (רמאה) is careful about his own deceit, so he will not risk exposure by using an unestablished name.

items.text: Anecdote about a mistaken identity in a document
items.text_en: Anecdote about a mistaken identity in a document
items.desc_en: A story is told about a document signed by Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, where a woman claimed she was not the one involved. Rav Yirmeya explains that he had questioned it but was told the woman had a harsh voice. Abaye concludes with a general principle from the Sages.

sub.desc_en: A story is told about a document signed by Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, where a woman came before him claiming she was not the one involved.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba explains that he had questioned the identity but was told the woman had a harsh voice.
Abaye concludes with a general principle from the Sages, though the text cuts off before stating it.

items.text: Torah scholar's testimony and the case of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
items.text_en: Torah scholar's testimony and the case of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with the principle that once a witness has testified, he cannot retract. It then relates a story where Rav Yirmeya bar Abba was a signatory on a document, and a woman claimed she was not the one who appeared before him. Abaye concludes that although a Torah scholar is not expected to be meticulous, once he has examined and testified, his testimony stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that once a witness has testified, he cannot retract, and notes that a Torah scholar is not expected to be meticulous.

sub.text: Story of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: A story is related where Rav Yirmeya bar Abba was a signatory on a document, a woman claimed she was not the one who appeared before him, and Abaye concludes that although a Torah scholar is not expected to be meticulous, once he has examined and testified, his testimony stands.

items.text: Abaye's advice for a Torah scholar betrothing a woman
items.text_en: Abaye's advice for a Torah scholar betrothing a woman
items.desc_en: Abaye advises that when a Torah scholar goes to betroth a woman, he should bring an unlearned person with him to prevent the woman from being switched with another.

sub.desc_en: Abaye advises that a Torah scholar who goes to betroth a woman should bring an unlearned person with him, lest they substitute another woman for him.

items.text: The husband pays the scribe's fee
items.text_en: The husband pays the scribe's fee
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the husband pays the scribe's fee for the ketubah. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis from the verses 'and he shall write' and 'and he shall give'. Nowadays, the Sages imposed the fee on the woman to prevent delay in marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the husband pays the scribe's fee, and answers that the verse says 'and he writes' and 'and he gives'.
The Gemara explains that nowadays the rabbis placed the burden on the woman so that the husband will not delay the divorce.
The Gemara explains that nowadays the Sages imposed the fee on the woman to prevent delay in marriage.

items.text: Clarifications on writing various documents
items.text_en: Clarifications on writing various documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses apparent redundancies in the Mishnah's list of documents that may be written without the other party present. It explains that each case is necessary: for a loan document with a business transaction, for a seller selling due to land's poor quality, for a Torah scholar who wants to betroth a relative, and for a fallow field in a sharecropping contract.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's rule that a loan document may be written without the lender present is obvious, implying it needs no special teaching.
The Gemara answers that the case is necessary when the loan is part of a business transaction (עיסקא), where the lender might not be present.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's rule that a seller's document may be written without the buyer present is obvious.
The Gemara answers that the case is necessary when the seller is selling his field because of its poor quality, where the buyer might be reluctant to be present.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's rule that betrothal documents may not be written without both parties is obvious.

The Gemara answers that the case is necessary even for a Torah scholar (צורבא מרבנן) who wants to betroth a relative, where the father-in-law might be willing but the document still requires both parties.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's rule that sharecropping and tenancy documents may not be written without both parties is obvious.
The Gemara answers that the case is necessary when the field is fallow (בורה), where the sharecropper might be eager to work it but the document still requires both parties.

items.text: Definition of 'shtarot berurin' and the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages
items.text_en: Definition of 'shtarot berurin' and the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'shtarot berurin' as documents of claims (according to the local translation) or as arbitration documents where each party selects a judge (according to Rav Yirmeya bar Abba). It then analyzes the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who requires two separate documents, and the Sages, who allow one. The Gemara initially suggests they argue about coercion in a Sodomite measure, but concludes that all agree coercion applies; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's concern is that one party does not want his rights combined with the other's, as it would make him feel like a lion lying in wait.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'shtarot berurin' means.
The local translation explains that 'shtarot berurin' are documents of claims.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba defines 'shtarot berurin' as arbitration documents where each party selects a judge.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that two separate documents must be written, one for each party.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Sages is about whether we coerce a person to accept a Sodomite measure.

The Gemara rejects this, concluding that all agree coercion applies; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's concern is that one party does not want his rights combined with the other's, as it would make him feel like a lion lying in wait.

items.text: Mishnah: Partial repayment and deposited document; dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Mishnah: Partial repayment and deposited document; dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a debtor partially repays and deposits the document with a third party, stipulating that if he does not pay by a certain date, the third party should give the document to the creditor. Rabbi Yosei rules that the third party must give it, while Rabbi Yehuda rules he should not. The Gemara explains they argue about whether an asmachta (conditional commitment) is legally binding. Rav Nachman reports that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, but Rabbi Ami notes that Rabbi Yochanan taught this twice, yet the final ruling is not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of partial repayment with a deposited document and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara asks what is the underlying principle of their dispute.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei holds that an asmachta (conditional commitment) is legally binding, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it is not.
Rav Nachman reports in the name of Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Ami objects, noting that Rabbi Yochanan taught the ruling in favor of Rabbi Yosei twice, implying he cannot contradict it.
The Gemara concludes that despite the earlier tradition, the final ruling is not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure for a document that has been erased
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure for a document that has been erased
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins the next topic: if a debtor's document is erased, he brings witnesses before the court, and the court issues a validation document stating that so-and-so's document was erased on a certain date.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents the case of one whose document was erased, and the procedure of presenting witnesses to the court to validate the document.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on validating a shtar machuk
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on validating a shtar machuk
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions that a document is validated by witnesses declaring 'So-and-so and so-and-so are its witnesses.' The Gemara cites a Baraita that defines the exact formula for such validation, and adds that if the document also states that the court examined the witnesses and found their testimony consistent, the document is valid without further proof.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a document is validated by witnesses declaring 'So-and-so and so-and-so are its witnesses.'

The Baraita defines the exact formula for validating a shtar machuk (erased document) and adds that if the document states the court examined the witnesses and found their testimony consistent, it is valid without further proof; otherwise, proof is required.

items.text: Distinction between torn and erased documents
items.text_en: Distinction between torn and erased documents
items.desc_en: The Baraita states that if a document is torn (nikra) it is invalid, but if it is accidentally torn (nitkarah) it is valid. If it is erased or smudged but the impression remains, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita states that a document torn intentionally (נִקְרַע) is invalid, but if torn accidentally (נִתְקָרַע) it is valid; if erased or smudged but the impression remains, it is valid.

items.text: Definition of a court tear vs. accidental tear
items.text_en: Definition of a court tear vs. accidental tear
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that a 'court tear' (nikra) is a tear made by the court, while an accidental tear (nitkarah) is any other tear. He further specifies that a court tear is made in the place of the witnesses, the date, and the signature (or, according to Abaye, in a crisscross pattern).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes a court tear (נִקְרַע) from an accidental tear (נִתְקָרַע).
Rav Yehuda defines a court tear as one made by the court, and an accidental tear as any other tear.
The Gemara asks what constitutes a court tear in practice.
Rav Yehuda specifies that a court tear is made in the place of the witnesses, the date, and the signature (תּוֹרֶף).
Abaye says a court tear is made in a crisscross pattern (שְׁתִי וָעֵרֶב, like warp and woof).

items.text: Case of Arabs seizing land and request for duplicate documents
items.text_en: Case of Arabs seizing land and request for duplicate documents
items.desc_en: A group of Arabs came to Pumbedita and were seizing people's land. The landowners came before Abaye and asked him to write them new documents, so that if one was lost they would have another. Abaye refused, citing Rav Safra's rule that one may not write two documents for the same field, lest the creditor collect twice.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where Arabs seized land in Pumbedita, and the landowners asked Abaye to write them duplicate documents as a safeguard.
Abaye refused, citing Rav Safra's rule that one may not write two documents for the same field, lest the creditor collect twice.

items.text: Abaye's suggestion to write on the erasure and Rav Acha's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's suggestion to write on the erasure and Rav Acha's objection
items.desc_en: When the landowners persisted, Abaye told his scribe to write the document with the text on the erased part and the witnesses on the paper, which is invalid. Rav Acha bar Minyomi objected, noting that if the impression is recognizable, the document is valid. Abaye clarified that he meant only an 'alef-beit' (a mere form), not a valid document.

sub.desc_en: Abaye, pressured by the landowners, tells his scribe to write a document with the text on the erased part and the witnesses on the paper, which is invalid.
Rav Acha bar Minyomi objects that if the impression of the erased text is recognizable, the document is valid according to the baraita.
Abaye clarifies that he meant only an 'alef-beit' (a mere form), not a valid document.

items.text: Baraita on writing a duplicate for a lost document
items.text_en: Baraita on writing a duplicate for a lost document
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Baraita: If someone says 'my loan document is lost,' even if witnesses confirm they wrote and signed it, one does not write a duplicate for a loan document. However, for a sale document, one may write a duplicate, except for the guarantee clause.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if someone claims his loan document is lost, even with witness confirmation, a duplicate loan document is not written.
The baraita clarifies that the prohibition applies only to loan documents, but for sale documents a duplicate may be written, except for the guarantee clause.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that documents of sale and purchase are not written, and that if one gives a gift and the recipient returns the document, the gift is revoked. The Sages disagree, holding that the gift remains valid.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that documents of sale and purchase are not written, and that if one gives a gift and the recipient returns the document, the gift is revoked.
The Sages disagree, holding that the gift remains valid.

items.text: Gemara's question on the guarantee clause
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the guarantee clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the guarantee clause is excluded from the list of documents that may not be written, and what the reason is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the guarantee clause is excluded from the list of documents that may not be written, and what the reason is.

items.text: Rav Safra's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Safra's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Safra explains that the reason is because two documents are not written on one field, lest a creditor seize the field, and the debtor produce one document to collect from other buyers, then produce another to collect again, leading to double collection.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra answers the gemara's question by explaining that the reason for the rule is that two documents are not written on one field, lest a creditor seize the field and the debtor produce one document to collect from buyers, then produce another to collect again, leading to double collection.

items.text: Objection and Rav Nachman's principle
items.text_en: Objection and Rav Nachman's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: once the creditor's document is torn, how can he collect again? It cites Rav Nachman's rule that any collection document must state that the creditor's document was torn, and similarly for court orders and appraisals, implying the document is indeed torn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: once the creditor's document is torn, how can he collect again?
The Gemara cites Rav Nachman's rule that any collection document must state that the creditor's document was torn, and similarly for court orders and appraisals, implying the document is indeed torn.

items.text: Answer: collection through ancestral right
items.text_en: Answer: collection through ancestral right
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the second collection is not based on the torn document but through the ancestral right of the seller, so the tearing does not prevent it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the second collection is not based on the torn document but through the ancestral right of the seller, so the tearing does not prevent it.

items.text: Rav Acha's question and answer
items.text_en: Rav Acha's question and answer
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina why the debtor needs to tell the creditor to 'rub' the land and then collect; why not simply collect twice with two documents? The answer is that otherwise there would be too many litigants against him.

sub.text: Rav Acha mi-Difti's question to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha mi-Difti's question to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha mi-Difti asks Ravina why the debtor needs to tell the creditor to 'rub' the land and then collect; why not simply collect twice with two documents?
The Gemara answers that if he did so, there would be too many litigants against him.

items.text: Alternative proposal and conclusion
items.text_en: Alternative proposal and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes writing a valid document and a cancellation for the seller, but the rabbis before Rav Papa and Rav Ashi conclude that this implies that a receipt is not written, so the original concern stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative: write a valid document and a cancellation for the seller, declaring all future documents on this land invalid except the one issued now.

sub.text: Rabbis before Rav Papa and Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rabbis before Rav Papa and Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: The rabbis before Rav Papa and Rav Ashi conclude that this proposal implies that a receipt (שובר) is not written, so the original concern remains.

items.text: Gemara's defense of writing a receipt for a field sale
items.text_en: Gemara's defense of writing a receipt for a field sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a receipt is written for a field sale but not for a loan: with a field, the creditor might seize it from the buyer, and the buyer might then seize other purchasers' fields without a receipt; eventually the purchasers would reclaim their fields, but in the meantime the creditor consumes the produce. Alternatively, the sale was without guarantee. The Gemara objects that the same logic should apply to loan documents, but distinguishes: with a loan, people say the creditor was appeased with money; with a field, everyone knows a field creditor is not appeased with money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by explaining that generally a receipt is written, and here the reason is that the creditor might seize the field from the buyer, and the buyer might then seize other purchasers' fields without a receipt.
The Gemara objects that ultimately the purchasers would reclaim their fields.
The Gemara answers that in the meantime the creditor consumes the produce.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the sale was without guarantee (שלא באחריות).
The Gemara objects that the same logic should apply to loan documents.
The Gemara distinguishes: with a loan, people say the creditor was appeased with money; with a field, everyone knows a field creditor is not appeased with money.

items.text: How to write 'excluding the guarantee'
items.text_en: How to write 'excluding the guarantee'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to write the clause 'excluding the guarantee' in a deed. Rav Nachman explains the formula: 'This deed is not to collect from encumbered property or from free property, but only to establish the field in the buyer's hands.'

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the deed includes the clause 'excluding the guarantee'.
The Gemara asks how to write this clause in practice.
Rav Nachman provides the formula: 'This deed is not to collect from encumbered property or from free property, but only to establish the field in the buyer's hands.'

items.text: Dispute: Is 'guarantee' a scribal error?
items.text_en: Dispute: Is 'guarantee' a scribal error?
items.desc_en: Rafram argues that the word 'guarantee' in a deed is a scribal error; if it were not written, the buyer could collect. Rav Ashi disagrees, saying 'guarantee' is not a scribal error, and 'excluding the guarantee' means the deed simply does not include a guarantee clause.

sub.desc_en: Rafram argues that the word 'guarantee' (אחריות) in a deed is a scribal error; if the clause excluding guarantee were not written, the buyer could collect from the seller's property.
Rav Ashi disagrees, asserting that 'guarantee' is not a scribal error; the phrase 'excluding the guarantee' simply means the deed was written without a guarantee clause.

items.text: Case of an agent who bought land without guarantee
items.text_en: Case of an agent who bought land without guarantee
items.desc_en: A woman gave money to an agent to buy land for her; he bought it without guarantee. She came before Rav Nachman, who ruled: 'I sent you to fix, not to break. Go buy it from him without guarantee, then sell it back to her with guarantee.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case: a woman gave money to an agent to buy land for her, and he bought it without guarantee; she came before Rav Nachman.
Rav Nachman rules that the agent must buy the land from the seller without guarantee and then sell it back to the woman with guarantee, because he was sent to fix, not to break.

items.text: Dispute: Returning a deed cancels the gift?
items.text_en: Dispute: Returning a deed cancels the gift?
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that if a donor returns the deed to the recipient, the gift is cancelled; the Sages say the gift remains valid. Rav Asi explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: it is as if the donor said 'this field is given to you as long as the deed is in your hand.' Rabba objects: if so, the same should apply if the deed is stolen or lost. Rabba then reinterprets the dispute as being about whether documents are acquired by delivery (the Sages hold they are not, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds they are).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says returning the deed cancels the gift; the Sages say the gift remains valid.
Rav Asi explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: the donor is considered to have said 'this field is given to you as long as the deed is in your hand.'
Rabba objects: if Rav Asi's explanation is correct, the same logic should apply if the deed is stolen or lost, which is not the case.
Rabba reinterprets the dispute: they argue about whether documents (אותיות) are acquired by delivery (מסירה) — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds they are, the Sages hold they are not.

items.text: Dispute: Adjudicating by deed or by possession
items.text_en: Dispute: Adjudicating by deed or by possession
items.desc_en: A baraita states: One who comes to be judged with a deed and with possession is judged by the deed – the words of Rabbi. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: by possession. Rav Dimi explains that they dispute whether documents are acquired by delivery.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute: one who comes to be judged with a deed and with possession is judged by the deed (Rabbi) or by possession (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel).
Rav Dimi explains that the dispute is about whether documents (אותיות) are acquired by delivery (מסירה).

items.text: Opening dispute: acquisition of documents by delivery vs. signature
items.text_en: Opening dispute: acquisition of documents by delivery vs. signature
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the core disagreement: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that documents are not acquired by delivery, while Rabbi holds they are acquired by delivery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the core disagreement: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that documents are not acquired by delivery, while Rabbi holds they are acquired by delivery.

items.text: Abaye's challenge: contradiction within Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge: contradiction within Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Abaye questions the resolution of the Mishnah according to Rav's explanation, pointing out that it leads to a contradiction in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's own views.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav, saying that according to Rav's resolution the Mishnah's dispute is meaningless, and Rav dismissively tells him to argue.
Abaye clarifies that his objection is not about the Mishnah's resolution but that it creates a contradiction within Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's own views.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: case of a relative or invalid witness
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: case of a relative or invalid witness
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah deals with a case where one witness is found to be a relative or invalid, and the dispute is between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar: Rabbi follows Rabbi Elazar (delivery witnesses are decisive), Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel follows Rabbi Meir (signature witnesses are decisive).

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the difficulty by stating that the Mishnah deals with a case where one witness is found to be a relative or invalid.

Abaye explains that the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel follows the earlier dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar regarding whether delivery witnesses or signature witnesses are decisive.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Avina's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Avina's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba's statement that Rabbi Elazar admits a forged-from-within document is invalid raises an objection. Rabbi Avina resolves that all agree on a document explicitly stating the witnesses' testimony was found forged; the dispute is only over a document with no witnesses at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Abba stated that Rabbi Elazar admits a forged-from-within document is invalid, contradicting the proposed resolution.

Rabbi Avina resolves: all agree a document explicitly stating the witnesses' testimony was found forged is invalid; the dispute is only over a document with no witnesses at all, where Rabbi follows Rabbi Elazar (עדי מסירה כרתי) and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel follows Rabbi Meir (עדי חתימה כרתי).

items.text: Alternative resolution: dispute over admission of writing the document
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: dispute over admission of writing the document
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation: the dispute is about whether one who admits writing a document needs to authenticate it. Rabbi says no, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says yes.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces an alternative resolution: the dispute is about whether one who admits writing a document needs to authenticate it.
The gemara states that Rabbi holds one who admits writing a document does not need to authenticate it, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds he does.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita shows Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel taking opposite positions on authentication, contradicting the previous explanation. Rava resolves that in a case of a validated document all agree they divide; the dispute is over an unvalidated document, and the baraita must be reversed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a baraita shows Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel taking opposite positions on authentication, contradicting the previous explanation.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi would not follow the mishna of two holding a garment, which says they divide.

sub.text: Rava's answer in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava's answer in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava citing Rav Nachman resolves that in a case of a validated document all agree they divide; the dispute is over an unvalidated document, and the baraita must be reversed.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must be reversed to align with Rava's explanation.

items.text: Final alternative: dispute over clarifying the debt
items.text_en: Final alternative: dispute over clarifying the debt
items.desc_en: Another explanation: the dispute is about clarifying the debt, illustrated by the story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and Rabbi Abba, where the need for witnesses to testify about repayment is debated, and the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a final alternative explanation: the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is not reversed but concerns the need to clarify the debt.

sub.text: Narrative illustration (story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and Rabbi Abba)
sub.text_en: Narrative illustration (story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and Rabbi Abba)
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the case of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef who owed money to Rabbi Abba, and when he claimed repayment before witnesses, Rav Yitzchak Nappaha required those witnesses to testify, despite the principle that a lender who gave with witnesses need not repay with witnesses.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak Nappaha's response and ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak Nappaha's response and ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak Nappaha explains that he follows the ruling of Rav Adda bar Ahava citing Rav, that one who claims repayment before named witnesses must bring them to testify, and notes that Rav Giddel cited Rav that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and even Rabbi did not dispute this.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the previous amud's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the previous amud's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier statement about 'clarifying' refers to clarifying the document, and the speaker confirms he also meant clarifying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the previous amud's statement, asking whether it meant 'to clarify' (לְבָרֵר) the document.
The speaker confirms that he also meant 'to clarify' (לְבָרֵר), resolving the Gemara's question.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: dispute on partial repayment
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: dispute on partial repayment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says the debtor should exchange the note (for a new one), Rabbi Yosei says he should write a receipt. Rabbi Yehuda argues that this forces the debtor to guard the receipt from mice, while Rabbi Yosei responds that this is preferable and the creditor should not suffer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who partially repaid a debt, with Rabbi Yehuda requiring exchanging the document and Rabbi Yosei requiring writing a receipt (שובר).
Rabbi Yehuda objects that with a receipt, the borrower must guard it from mice (i.e., risk of loss).
Rabbi Yosei responds that it is better for the borrower to guard the receipt, and the lender's power should not be weakened.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling in the name of Rav
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling in the name of Rav
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says the halakha follows neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei; rather, the court tears the original note and writes a new one with the original date.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav rules that the halacha follows neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei; rather, the court tears the original document and writes a new one with the original date.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman (or Rav Yirmeya bar Abba) challenges Rav Huna: if Rav had heard the baraita that says witnesses tear the note and write a new one with the original date, he would have retracted his ruling.

sub.text: Rav Nachman (or Rav Yirmeya bar Abba) to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman (or Rav Yirmeya bar Abba) to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman (or Rav Yirmeya bar Abba) asks Rav Huna whether Rav would have retracted had he heard the baraita that witnesses tear the document and write a new one with the original date.

items.text: Rav Huna's response
items.text_en: Rav Huna's response
items.desc_en: Rav Huna responds that Rav had indeed heard the baraita but did not retract his ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna responds that Rav had indeed heard the baraita but did not retract his ruling.

items.text: Gemara's question on witnesses' agency
items.text_en: Gemara's question on witnesses' agency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how witnesses who have already performed their agency can write another document, contrasting the power of a court to extract money with that of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how witnesses who have already performed their agency can write another document, contrasting the power of a court to extract money with that of witnesses.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption by citing Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that witnesses may write even ten documents for one field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous assumption by citing Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that witnesses may write even ten documents for one field.

items.text: Two answers: gift deed or no liability
items.text_en: Two answers: gift deed or no liability
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef and Rava each offer a resolution: Rav Yosef says it refers to a gift deed, while Rava says it refers to a deed without אחריות (liability).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the case of witnesses who may write multiple deeds refers to a gift deed (שטר מתנה), where no monetary loss is involved.
Rava answers that the case refers to a deed without אחריות (liability), so the seller bears no financial responsibility.

items.text: Baraita on partial repayment and receipt
items.text_en: Baraita on partial repayment and receipt
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says witnesses tear the old deed and write a new one with the original date, while Rabbi Yosei says they write a receipt. Two reasons are given for writing a receipt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita: for a partial repayment of a thousand-zuz loan, Rabbi Yehuda says witnesses tear the old deed and write a new one with the original date, while Rabbi Yosei says they leave the deed in place and write a receipt (שובר).
The baraita gives two reasons for writing a receipt: to pressure the debtor to repay the balance, and to allow the creditor to collect from the original date.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Yosei's objection
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Yosei's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei argues with Rabbi Yehuda: if the new deed is dated from the first time, he disputes one point; if from the second, he disputes two.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda also dates the new deed from the first time, so why does Rabbi Yosei object?
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei's objection is conditional: if Rabbi Yehuda dates from the first time, he disputes one point; if from the second, he disputes two.

items.text: Baraita on delayed deeds written on Shabbat
items.text_en: Baraita on delayed deeds written on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a deed dated on Shabbat or Yom Kippur is a delayed deed and valid according to Rabbi Yehuda, but Rabbi Yosei invalidates it. Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent from Tzippori where Rabbi Yosei validated such a deed.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule: a deed dated on Shabbat or Yom Kippur is a delayed deed and valid according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yosei objects and invalidates such a deed.
Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent from Tzippori where Rabbi Yosei himself validated such a deed.
Rabbi Yosei responds that his validation was limited to that specific case, not a general rule.

items.text: Rabbi Pedat's resolution on the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Pedat's resolution on the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei's response, and Rabbi Pedat explains that all agree that if the deed's 'season' (עונה) is found to coincide with Shabbat or Yom Kippur, it is a valid delayed deed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei's response to Rabbi Yehuda seems to concede the very point Rabbi Yehuda was making.
Rabbi Pedat resolves the difficulty by explaining that all agree that if the deed's 'season' (עונה) is found to coincide with Shabbat or Yom Kippur, it is a valid delayed deed.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on writing a receipt for a postdated note
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on writing a receipt for a postdated note
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute in the Mishnah about postdated notes is limited to that case. Rabbi Yehuda holds that one does not write a receipt, leading to potential abuse, while Rabbi Yosei holds that one does write a receipt, also leading to potential abuse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute in the Mishnah is limited to a postdated note (שטר מאוחר), and explains Rabbi Yehuda's position that one does not write a receipt (שובר), so no abuse results.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei's position that one does write a receipt (שובר), leading to potential abuse.

items.text: Rav Huna's qualification and rejection
items.text_en: Rav Huna's qualification and rejection
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua limits the permission to write a receipt to a partial payment, not the full amount. The Gemara rejects this and rules that even for the full amount, a receipt may be written.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's qualification
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's qualification
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua limits the permission to write a receipt (שובר) to a partial payment, not the full amount.
The Gemara rejects Rav Huna's distinction and rules that a receipt may be written even for the full amount.

items.text: Story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and the dispute between Rav/Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan/Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and the dispute between Rav/Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan/Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: A story illustrates the dispute: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef sought payment from Rabbi Abba, who demanded his note first. Rav Yitzchak cited Rav and Shmuel that no receipt is written. Rabbi Chanina bar Papi countered with Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish that a receipt is written. Ravin reported Rabbi Ila'a's ruling that a receipt is written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef was owed money by Rabbi Abba, and when he came before Rabbi Chanina bar Papi to demand payment, Rabbi Abba demanded his note first.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef claims his note was lost and offers to write a receipt (שובר), citing Rav and Shmuel that no receipt is written.
Rabbi Chanina bar Papi dismisses Rav and Shmuel's authority and counters with Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish that a receipt is written.

sub.text: Ravin's report in the name of Rabbi Ila'a
sub.text_en: Ravin's report in the name of Rabbi Ila'a
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Ila'a also rules that a receipt is written, supporting the position of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.
The Gemara concludes that a receipt is written, reasoning that if not, the debtor would lose his note and the creditor would unjustly benefit.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a receipt is written, reasoning that otherwise the lender would unjustly benefit if the note is lost. Abaye objects that if a receipt is lost, the borrower would unjustly benefit. Rava answers that the borrower is a servant to the lender, implying the lender's claim is stronger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a receipt (שובר) is written, reasoning that otherwise if the lender's note is lost, the lender would unjustly benefit.
Abaye objects that if a receipt (שובר) is lost, the borrower would unjustly benefit.
