Rava answers that the borrower is a servant to the lender (עבד לוה לאיש מלוה), implying the lender's claim is stronger.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's distinction between loan and sale documents
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's distinction between loan and sale documents
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna rules that postdated loan documents are valid, but postdated sale documents are invalid due to the risk of the seller claiming the land was repurchased. The Gemara objects that the same risk applies to loans if no receipt is written, but Rav Hamnuna assumes no receipt is written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah from elsewhere that early-dated loan documents are invalid, but postdated ones are valid.
Rav Hamnuna distinguishes between loan documents (postdated valid) and sale documents (postdated invalid), explaining the risk that the seller might claim the land was repurchased.
The Gemara objects that the same risk applies to loan documents: the borrower could claim he already repaid if no receipt was written.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Hamnuna holds the position that no receipt is written, so the risk does not apply to loans.

items.text: Practical solutions for postdated notes and receipts
items.text_en: Practical solutions for postdated notes and receipts
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar asks Rav Kahana why they now write postdated notes and receipts. Rav Kahana explains that Rabbi Abba instructed scribes to write in the note that it was postdated. Rav Ashi asks why they do not do so now, and Rav Safra instructed scribes to write the date of the receipt if known, otherwise write it undated. The daf ends with Ravina's question to Rav Ashi.

sub.text: Rav Yemar's question to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar's question to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar asks Rav Kahana why they now write both postdated notes and receipts, which seems contradictory.
Rav Kahana explains that Rabbi Abba instructed scribes to write in the note that it was postdated, thereby preventing fraud.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks why they do not currently follow Rabbi Abba's practice of writing the postdating clause.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's answer citing Rav Safra
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's answer citing Rav Safra
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains that Rav Safra instructed scribes to write the date of the receipt if known, otherwise write it undated, so the receipt is valid whenever it appears.
The daf ends with Ravina beginning to ask Rav Ashi a question, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Gemara's question on current practice
items.text_en: Gemara's question on current practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why scribes do not follow the earlier practice of writing the date of acquisition in deeds of transfer. Rava bar Rav Sheila explains that the Sages instituted a leniency, and whoever fails to do so loses out.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why scribes do not follow the earlier practice of writing the date of acquisition in deeds of transfer, and Rava bar Rav Sheila explains that the Sages instituted a leniency, and whoever fails to do so loses out.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Sheila's instruction to scribes
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Sheila's instruction to scribes
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Sheila instructs scribes writing deeds of transfer: if they know the date of the acquisition, write it; otherwise, write the date they are standing, to avoid appearing false.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Sheila instructs scribes writing deeds of transfer to write the date of acquisition if known, otherwise the current date, to avoid the document appearing false.

items.text: Rav and Rav Huna's instruction to scribes
items.text_en: Rav and Rav Huna's instruction to scribes
items.desc_en: Rav and Rav Huna instruct their scribes to write the place where they are standing when writing the document, even if the transaction occurred elsewhere, to avoid falsehood.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Rav Huna instruct their scribes to write the place where they are standing when writing the document, even if the transaction occurred elsewhere, to avoid falsehood.

items.text: Rava: Splitting a large loan document into two smaller ones
items.text_en: Rava: Splitting a large loan document into two smaller ones
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if someone holds a document for 100 zuz and asks to split it into two documents of 50 zuz each, we do not do so. The reason is that the Sages instituted a practice beneficial to both lender and borrower: the lender can pressure the borrower for payment, and the borrower can partially pay and have the document reduced.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a lender holding a 100-zuz document cannot have it split into two 50-zuz documents.
Rava explains that the Sages instituted a practice beneficial to both lender and borrower: the lender can pressure for payment, and the borrower can partially pay and have the document reduced.

items.text: Rava: Combining two small loan documents into one large one
items.text_en: Rava: Combining two small loan documents into one large one
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if someone holds two documents of 50 zuz each and asks to combine them into one document of 100 zuz, we do not do so. The reason is the opposite: the lender benefits by not having his document reduced, and the borrower benefits because the lender cannot pressure him for payment as easily.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if someone holds two documents of 50 zuz each and asks to combine them into one document of 100 zuz, we do not do so.

The Gemara explains that the rabbis instituted this rule as a benefit for both parties: the lender benefits because his document is not reduced (preventing partial payment), and the borrower benefits because the lender cannot pressure him for payment as easily.

items.text: Rav Ashi: Reducing a loan document's value
items.text_en: Rav Ashi: Reducing a loan document's value
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that if someone holds a document for 100 zuz and asks to reduce it to 50 zuz, we do not do so. The concern is that the borrower may have already paid part of the debt, and the lender might later produce the original document claiming it is a different one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that if someone holds a document for 100 zuz and asks to reduce it to 50 zuz, we do not do so.
The Gemara explains the concern: the borrower may have already paid, and the lender might later produce the original document claiming it is a different one.

items.text: Mishnah: Brothers with inherited property and people with identical names
items.text_en: Mishnah: Brothers with inherited property and people with identical names
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses two brothers, one poor and one rich, who inherit a bathhouse or olive press. If they rent it out, the income is shared equally; if they use it themselves, the rich brother can tell the poor one to hire workers. It then discusses two people with the same name in one city: they cannot collect debts from each other, and if a document is found saying 'the document of Yosef ben Shimon is paid,' both are considered paid. To avoid confusion, they should use triple names, or a sign, or write 'kohen.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of two brothers inheriting a bathhouse or olive press, ruling that if rented out the income is shared equally, but if used themselves the rich brother can tell the poor one to hire workers.
The Mishnah states that two people with the same name in one city cannot collect debts from each other, nor can another person collect from them using a document with that name.
The Mishnah rules that if a document is found saying 'the document of Yosef ben Shimon is paid,' both men's debts are considered paid.
The Mishnah concludes with the solution: to avoid confusion, they should use triple names, or a sign, or write 'kohen.'

items.text: Gemara: A document that came before Rav Huna's court
items.text_en: Gemara: A document that came before Rav Huna's court
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins discussing a specific case: a document that came before Rav Huna's court, which was written 'I, so-and-so, borrowed a maneh from you.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of a document that came before Rav Huna's court, written in the first person as a debtor's admission.

items.text: Rav Huna's statement
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the word "מִמְּךָ" in a get includes even the Exilarch or King Shapur, meaning the husband himself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the word 'מִמְּךָ' (from you) in a get includes even the Exilarch or King Shapur, meaning the husband himself.

items.text: Rav Chisda's request and the baraita support
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's request and the baraita support
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda tells Rabba to investigate Rav Huna's statement, as Rav Huna will need it later. Rabba finds a baraita where Abba Shaul says a get without a date is valid if it says "גֵּרַשְׁתִּיהָ הַיּוֹם", implying "הַיּוֹם" means the day it was issued; similarly, "מִמְּךָ" means from the husband who issued it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda tells Rabba to investigate Rav Huna's statement, as Rav Huna will need it later.
Rabba finds a baraita where Abba Shaul rules that a get without a date is valid if it says 'גֵּרַשְׁתִּיהָ הַיּוֹם' (I divorced her today).
The gemara infers that just as 'הַיּוֹם' (today) in the baraita means the day the get was issued, so too 'מִמְּךָ' (from you) in Rav Huna's statement means from the husband who issued it.

items.text: Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that Abba Shaul might follow Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that witnesses of delivery are essential, so there is no concern about the get being found; but here we should worry about the get being lost and found (נפילה).

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Abba Shaul might follow Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that witnesses of delivery are essential, so there is no concern about the get being found; but here we should worry about the get being lost and found (נפילה).

items.text: Response: no concern for נפילה
items.text_en: Response: no concern for נפילה
items.desc_en: The Gemara responds that we are not concerned about the get being lost and found (נפילה), and proves this from a mishna about two people with the same name who can collect debts from others, implying no fear of a lost document being used fraudulently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara responds to Abaye's objection that we are not concerned about the get being lost and found (נפילה).

The Gemara cites a mishna about two people with the same name who can collect debts from others, implying no fear of a lost document being used fraudulently, to prove that we are not concerned about נפילה.

items.text: Abaye's distinction
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction
items.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes: we are not concerned about a single document being lost (נפילה דחד), but we are concerned about a document lost among many (נפילה דרבים).

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the objection by distinguishing: we are not concerned about a single document being lost (נפילה דחד), but we are concerned about a document lost among many (נפילה דרבים).

items.text: First dispute: transferring documents by delivery
items.text_en: First dispute: transferring documents by delivery
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what underlies the disagreement between our Mishnah (which says one cannot collect with a transferred document) and the Baraita (which says one can). It answers that they dispute whether documents (אותיות) are acquired by delivery (מסירה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute between the Mishnah and the Baraita regarding collecting with a transferred document.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna of our Mishnah holds that documents (אותיות) are acquired by delivery (מסירה), while the Tanna of the Baraita holds they are not.

items.text: Alternative explanation: need to bring proof
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: need to bring proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a second answer: everyone agrees that documents are acquired by delivery, but they dispute whether the recipient must bring proof of the transfer. This is supported by a dispute between Abaye and Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a second answer: everyone agrees that documents are acquired by delivery, but they dispute whether the recipient must bring proof of the transfer.

sub.text: Supporting dispute between Abaye and Rava
sub.text_en: Supporting dispute between Abaye and Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding whether one who acquires documents by delivery must bring proof of the transfer.

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate the proof from brothers
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate the proof from brothers
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a Baraita about a brother holding a debt document to argue that one must bring proof; Rava distinguishes brothers because they are suspected of taking each other's documents. The Gemara then explains Abaye's reasoning and the necessity of the Baraita.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks for the source of his position that one must bring proof, citing a Baraita about a brother who holds a debt document.
Rava distinguishes brothers because they are suspected of taking each other's documents, so the Baraita does not apply to others.
In an alternative version, Rava cites the same Baraita to prove that only brothers need to bring proof, not others.
The Gemara explains that Abaye needed the Baraita to teach that even brothers must bring proof, despite the suspicion that they might be careful with documents.

items.text: Second dispute: writing a loan document without the lender
items.text_en: Second dispute: writing a loan document without the lender
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses another Baraita that says brothers can collect from others and from each other. It explains that the dispute is about whether one may write a loan document for a borrower without the lender present, with our Tanna permitting it and the Baraita's Tanna requiring the lender's presence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: regarding the Baraita that says brothers can collect from others and from each other, what is the underlying dispute?
The Gemara explains that the dispute is about whether one may write a loan document for a borrower without the lender present.

The Tanna of our Mishnah holds that one may write a loan document for a borrower without the lender, because the borrower might go to a scribe and witnesses and say 'write me a document, for I want to borrow from Yosef ben Shimon my friend,' and after they write and sign, he takes it and says 'give me the hundred that you lent me.'
The Tanna of the Baraita holds that one may not write a loan document for a borrower unless the lender is present with him.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with a Baraita on found receipts
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with a Baraita on found receipts
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a Baraita that says if a receipt for Yosef ben Shimon's debt is found, both debts are cancelled, which seems to contradict the Mishnah's rule that no one else can collect. Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Hoshaya explain it refers to a triplicated document (משולשין), and Abaye offers an alternative reading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Baraita's ruling that if a receipt for Yosef ben Shimon's debt is found, both debts are cancelled, which seems to contradict the Mishnah's rule that no one else can collect.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the Baraita refers to a triplicated document (משולשין), where the receipt is written in a way that identifies the specific debt.
The Gemara objects: why not simply look at the name written on the receipt to identify which debt is cancelled?
Rav Hoshaya clarifies that the document is triplicated in the loan document (שטר) but not in the receipt (שובר), so the receipt does not specify which debt it cancels.

Abaye offers an alternative reading of the Baraita: the receipt was found among the borrower's documents and states 'Yosef ben Shimon's debt upon me is paid,' so both debts are cancelled, and the Tosefta adds that if both are priests, they should write generations.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on ambiguous statements of repayment
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on ambiguous statements of repayment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a father who says a document among his is paid, and Rava distinguishes between saying 'your document is paid' (only the largest is paid) and 'your debt is paid' (all are paid). Ravina challenges this with an analogy to fields, and Rava responds with the principle that the holder of the document has the lower hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a father tells his son that one of his documents is paid but he does not know which, ruling that all documents are paid; if two documents are found for one debtor, the larger is paid and the smaller is not.
Rava distinguishes between saying 'your document is paid' (only the largest is paid) and 'your debt is paid' (all documents are paid).
Ravina challenges Rava with an analogy to fields: if one says 'my field is sold to you' versus 'a field that I have is sold to you', would the same distinction apply?

Rava resolves the challenge by invoking the principle that the holder of the document has the lower hand (יַד בַּעַל הַשְּׁטָר עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה), meaning the debtor's ambiguous statement is interpreted in the creditor's favor.

items.text: Opening of the next Mishnah: lending with a guarantor
items.text_en: Opening of the next Mishnah: lending with a guarantor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one lends with a guarantor, he cannot collect from the guarantor first, introducing a new topic.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the rule that a lender who lends with a guarantor (ערב) may not collect from the guarantor first.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a creditor stipulates he may collect from whomever he wishes, he may collect from the guarantor. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if the borrower has assets, the creditor may not collect from the guarantor in any case, and adds a case about a guarantor for a wife's ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that if a creditor stipulates he may collect from whomever he wishes, he may collect from the guarantor.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if the borrower has assets, the creditor may not collect from the guarantor in any case.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a case about a guarantor for a wife's ketubah, requiring the husband to vow benefit from her lest they collude to reclaim assets.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Nachman's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Nachman's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the reason for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling. Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that the guarantor says 'I entrusted a man to you, you entrusted a man to me.' Rav Nachman objects that this is Persian law, but then clarifies that the real issue is that Persian courts give no reason for their rulings. He explains that 'he shall not collect from the guarantor' means he may not sue the guarantor first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that the guarantor says 'I entrusted a man to you, you entrusted a man to me,' implying the lender should first pursue the borrower.
Rav Nachman objects that this reasoning is Persian law, not Jewish law.
The Gemara counters that Persian courts actually go after the guarantor, not the borrower.
Rav Nachman clarifies that the problem is Persian courts give no reason for their rulings, so the analogy is invalid.
Rav Nachman explains that 'he shall not collect from the guarantor' means he may not sue the guarantor first, but may collect from him after the borrower.

items.text: Supporting baraita
items.text_en: Supporting baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Nachman's interpretation: a creditor may not sue the guarantor first unless he stipulated otherwise.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Nachman's interpretation: a creditor may not sue the guarantor first unless he stipulated otherwise.

items.text: Biblical source for guarantor's obligation
items.text_en: Biblical source for guarantor's obligation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna derives the guarantor's obligation from the verse 'I will be his guarantor; from my hand you shall demand him.' Rav Chisda objects that this is a mere acceptance of responsibility (קבלנות). Rabbi Yitzchak cites a different verse, and the Gemara adds another verse about the dangers of guarantorship and advice for the guarantor.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna opens by asking for the biblical source of the guarantor's obligation and cites the verse 'אנכי אערבנו, מידי תבקשנו' (I will be his guarantor; from my hand you shall demand him).

Rav Chisda objects that Rav Huna's verse describes a קבלן (guarantor who accepts full responsibility), not a simple guarantor, citing the verse 'תנה אותו על ידי, ואני אשיבנו' (Place him in my hand, and I will return him).

Rabbi Yitzchak provides a different biblical source for the guarantor's obligation, citing the verse 'לקח בגדו כי ערב זר, ובעד נכריה חבלהו' (Take his garment because he guaranteed a stranger, and for a foreign woman take a pledge from him).
The Gemara adds a supporting verse from Proverbs warning about the dangers of guarantorship and advising the guarantor to either release his own assets or gather many friends to help.

items.text: Amemar and Rav Ashi on the mechanism of guarantor's obligation
items.text_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi on the mechanism of guarantor's obligation
items.desc_en: Amemar suggests that the guarantor's obligation depends on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding אסמכתא. Rav Ashi objects that we see daily that אסמכתא does not acquire yet the guarantor is obligated. Rav Ashi explains that the guarantor obligates himself due to the benefit of being trusted.

sub.desc_en: Amemar proposes that the guarantor's obligation depends on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding אסמכתא (conditional commitment).
Rav Ashi objects that daily practice shows אסמכתא does not acquire, yet the guarantor is obligated.
Rav Ashi resolves that the guarantor obligates himself due to the benefit of being trusted (הנאת מהימנותא).

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's condition
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's condition
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when the borrower has no assets. The Gemara notes a contradiction from the Mishnah's own wording and resolves it by explaining that the Mishnah is missing a clause: the first Tanna agrees that if the borrower has assets, the creditor may not collect from the guarantor, but a קבלן is always liable.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when the borrower has no assets, but if he has assets, the creditor may not collect from the guarantor.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's later clause implies the first Tanna holds the ruling applies regardless of the borrower's assets, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's limitation.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah is missing a clause: the first Tanna agrees that if the borrower has assets, the creditor may not collect from the guarantor, but a קבלן (guarantor who accepts full liability) is always liable.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that if the borrower has assets, neither the creditor nor the guarantor may collect from the guarantor's property.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if the borrower has assets, neither the creditor nor the guarantor may collect from the guarantor's property.

items.text: General rule: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's rulings are halakha except three
items.text_en: General rule: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's rulings are halakha except three
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan's rule that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches in the Mishnah, the halakha follows him, except for three cases: Eruv, Tzidon, and the final proof.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Chanah reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches a ruling in the Mishnah, the הלכה (binding law) follows him, except for three cases: עָרֵב (guarantor), צַיְדָן (Tzidon), and רְאָיָה אַחֲרוֹנָה (final proof).

items.text: Rav Huna: Distinction between language of ערב and קבלן
items.text_en: Rav Huna: Distinction between language of ערב and קבלן
items.desc_en: Rav Huna categorizes various formulations: phrases like 'Lend him and I will be guarantor' are language of ערבות (ordinary guarantee), while phrases like 'Give him and I will be a kablan' are language of קבלנות (a stronger form of guarantee).

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna lists phrases like 'Lend him and I will be guarantor' as language of ערבות (ordinary guarantee).
Rav Huna lists phrases like 'Give him and I will be a kablan' as language of קבלנות (stronger guarantee).

items.text: Question: Mixed formulations
items.text_en: Question: Mixed formulations
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: what is the status of phrases like 'Lend him and I will be a kablan' or 'Give him and I will be a guarantor'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: what is the status of mixed formulations — 'הַלְוֵהוּ וַאֲנִי קַבְּלָן' (lend him and I am receiver) and 'תֵּן לוֹ וַאֲנִי עָרֵב' (give him and I am guarantor)?

items.text: Three Amoraim's answers to the dilemma
items.text_en: Three Amoraim's answers to the dilemma
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak rules that the language determines the type: 'ערבות' means guarantee, 'קבלנות' means kablanut. Rav Chisda says all are kablanut except 'Lend him and I will be a guarantor'. Rava says all are ערבות except 'Give him and I will pay'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak rules that the language used determines the type: 'ערבות' (guarantee) language makes it a guarantee, 'קבלנות' (kablanut) language makes it kablanut.
Rav Chisda says all formulations are kablanut except 'Lend him and I will be a guarantor'.
Rava says all formulations are ערבות (guarantee) except 'Give him and I will pay'.

items.text: Mar bar Amemar's tradition and qualification
items.text_en: Mar bar Amemar's tradition and qualification
items.desc_en: Mar bar Amemar reports in the name of Abba that for 'Give him and I will pay', the creditor has no claim against the borrower. The Gemara qualifies: the borrower is not absolved until the guarantor actually gives the money.

sub.text: Mar bar Amemar to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar bar Amemar to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Amemar reports in the name of Abba that for the formula 'תן לו ואני נותן' (Give him and I will pay), the creditor has no claim against the borrower.
The Gemara qualifies that the borrower is not absolved from the creditor until the guarantor actually gives the money into the creditor's hand.

items.text: Case: Judge who attached guarantor's property before suing borrower
items.text_en: Case: Judge who attached guarantor's property before suing borrower
items.desc_en: A judge attached the guarantor's property before suing the borrower. Rav Chanin bar Rav Yeiva removed him. Rava explains: a person's assets are his guarantors, and the Mishnah teaches that a creditor may not collect from the guarantor first.

sub.desc_en: A judge attached the borrower's property for the creditor before suing the borrower, and Rav Chanin bar Rav Yeiva removed him.
Rava praises Rav Chanin bar Rav Yeiva, explaining that a person's assets are his guarantors, and the Mishnah teaches that a creditor may not collect from the guarantor first.

items.text: Case: Guarantor for orphans who paid before informing them
items.text_en: Case: Guarantor for orphans who paid before informing them
items.desc_en: A guarantor for orphans paid the creditor before informing the orphans. Rav Pappa says paying a debt is a mitzvah, and orphans are not obligated to perform mitzvot. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua says perhaps the creditor seized the guarantor's assets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a guarantor for orphans paid the creditor before informing the orphans.
Rav Pappa rules that paying a debt is a מצוה (commandment), and orphans are not obligated to perform מצות (commandments), so the guarantor cannot collect from them.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua objects: perhaps the creditor seized the guarantor's assets (צררי — bundles of money) by force, so the guarantor's payment was involuntary and he can collect from the orphans.

items.text: The difference between Rav Huna and Rav Pappa
items.text_en: The difference between Rav Huna and Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the opinions of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua and Rav Pappa regarding a guarantor who pays before being sued. It answers that the difference is when the debtor admits the debt or when the guarantor was excommunicated and died in that state.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the opinions of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua and Rav Pappa regarding a guarantor who pays before being sued.
The Gemara answers that the difference is when the debtor admits the debt or when the guarantor was excommunicated and died in that state.

items.text: Halakhic ruling sent from the academy
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling sent from the academy
items.desc_en: A message is sent from the academy that the halakha follows Rav Huna bar Yehoshua in the case of excommunication and death in that state.

sub.desc_en: The academy sends a ruling that the halakha follows Rav Huna bar Yehoshua in the case of excommunication and death in that state.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a guarantor who holds the debt document, which seems to contradict Rav Pappa. It resolves that the case is different because the guarantor wrote 'I have received from you' (התקבלתי ממך), indicating he paid willingly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a guarantor who holds the debt document, which seems to contradict Rav Pappa.
The Gemara resolves that the case is different because the guarantor wrote 'התקבלתי' (I have received from you), indicating he paid willingly.

items.text: Dispute about a guarantor for a gentile
items.text_en: Dispute about a guarantor for a gentile
items.desc_en: Rav Mordechai and Rav Ashi debate whether a guarantor who paid a gentile creditor before being sued is suspected of collusion (צררי). Rav Mordechai cites Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava that for a gentile, since the creditor pursues the guarantor, we do not suspect collusion. Rav Ashi counters that for a gentile, since their law follows the guarantor, we do suspect collusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a guarantor for a gentile paid the gentile creditor before the orphans (the heirs) were sued.

sub.text: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that Avimi from Hagronya said in Rava's name: even for one who suspects collusion (צררי) with a Jew, for a gentile, since the creditor pursues the guarantor, we do not suspect collusion.

Rav Ashi counters: on the contrary, even for one who does not suspect collusion with a Jew, for a gentile, since their law follows the guarantor, if the guarantor had not taken collateral (צררי) from the outset, the gentile would not have accepted him.

items.text: The case of Moshe bar Atzri and Abaye's advice
items.text_en: The case of Moshe bar Atzri and Abaye's advice
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story about Moshe bar Atzri, a guarantor for his daughter-in-law's ketubah. Abaye advised divorcing her so she could collect from her father and then remarry. Rava objected due to the mishnah about vowing benefit. Abaye dismissed the concern. Later it was revealed he was a priest, and Abaye commented on poverty following the poor. The Gemara questions Abaye's consistency with his own statement about a 'wicked cunning person' and distinguishes between a son and a Torah scholar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah about a guarantor for a woman's ketubah and introduces the story of Moshe bar Atzri, a guarantor for his daughter-in-law's ketubah, whose son was a Torah scholar in financial distress.
Abaye suggests that the son divorce his wife so she can collect her ketubah from her father (the guarantor) and then remarry.
Rava objects citing the mishnah that one who divorces must vow benefit from the wife, and Abaye dismisses the concern by noting that not every divorce happens in court.
It is revealed that the son is a priest, so the divorce plan fails, and Abaye comments on the proverb that poverty follows the poor.
The Gemara questions Abaye's consistency, citing his own statement that advising someone to sell assets according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is a 'wicked cunning person'.
The Gemara distinguishes between a son and a Torah scholar, explaining that the advice is permissible for a son but not for a Torah scholar.

items.text: Distinction between guarantor and receiver for ketubah
items.text_en: Distinction between guarantor and receiver for ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Moshe bar Atzri was a receiver (קבלן), not a guarantor, since a guarantor for ketubah is not liable. It then addresses the dispute about a receiver for ketubah: if the husband has assets, he is liable; if not, he is not. Two answers are given: either the husband had assets that were lost, or a father binds himself for his son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Moshe bar Atzri appears to be a guarantor (ערב), yet a guarantor for a ketubah is not liable.
The Gemara answers that Moshe bar Atzri was a receiver (קבלן), not a guarantor, so the objection is resolved.
The Gemara questions how the case fits the opinion that a receiver for a ketubah is only liable if the husband has assets.
The first answer suggests that the husband had assets at the time of the guarantee but they were subsequently lost.
The second answer explains that a father binds himself for his son, so the receiver is liable regardless of the husband's assets.

items.text: Summary of disputes and final halakha
items.text_en: Summary of disputes and final halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara summarizes the disputes: a guarantor for ketubah is never liable; a receiver for a creditor is always liable; a receiver for ketubah and a guarantor for a creditor are disputed. The final halakha is that a guarantor is always liable except for a guarantor for ketubah, because it is a mitzvah and he did not cause a loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara summarizes the three categories of guarantors and receivers, noting the unanimous and disputed positions.
The Gemara rules that a guarantor is always liable except for a guarantor for ketubah, because he performed a מצוה (commandment) and caused no loss.

items.text: Rav Huna's statement about a dying person and Rav Nachman's objection
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement about a dying person and Rav Nachman's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a dying person who consecrates all his property and says 'I have a maneh of so-and-so in my hand' is believed, because one does not act deceitfully with consecrated property. Rav Nachman objects, citing Rav and Shmuel that a dying person who says 'give' is believed, but if he does not say 'give', he is not believed, indicating one may act deceitfully with his children.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a dying person who consecrates all his property and claims a debt is believed, because one does not act deceitfully with consecrated property.
Rav Nachman objects, citing Rav and Shmuel that a dying person is believed only if he says 'give', indicating one may act deceitfully toward his children, unlike consecrated property.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection to Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection to Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a person is likely to say 'give' even when not intending to satisfy his creditor, so Rav Huna's logic is flawed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a person is likely to say 'give' even when not intending to satisfy his creditor, so Rav Huna's logic is flawed.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Huna's case and challenge from Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Huna's case and challenge from Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna's ruling applies when the creditor holds the debt document. It then challenges Rav and Shmuel, who would rule that if the debtor says 'give' without holding a document, the heirs should not pay, since an oral loan is not collected from heirs or purchasers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna's ruling applies specifically when the creditor holds the debt document.
The Gemara challenges Rav and Shmuel: if the debtor says 'give' without holding a document, why would the heirs pay, since an oral loan (מלוה על פה) is not collected from heirs or purchasers?

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution: distinction based on document validation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution: distinction based on document validation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by stating that in both cases the creditor holds a document; the difference is whether the document is validated. If the debtor says 'give,' he has validated the document; if not, he has not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by stating that in both cases the creditor holds a document; the difference is whether the document is validated. If the debtor says 'give,' he has validated the document; if not, he has not.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling and its apparent reversal
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling and its apparent reversal
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if a dying person says 'a mana is in my hand for so-and-so,' and the orphans claim they repaid, they are believed; but if he says 'give a mana to so-and-so,' they are not believed. The Gemara objects that the opposite seems logical, since 'give' implies the father concluded the matter, making repayment more likely.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if a dying person says 'a mana is in my hand for so-and-so,' orphans claiming repayment are believed, but if he says 'give a mana to so-and-so,' they are not believed.

The Gemara objects that the opposite seems logical: 'give' implies the father concluded the matter, making repayment more likely, while 'in my hand' suggests he did not conclude, so repayment is less likely.

items.text: Corrected version of Rabbah's ruling
items.text_en: Corrected version of Rabbah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara retracts and presents the correct version: if the orphans say 'Father later told us he repaid,' they are believed when he said 'a mana is in my hand' (since he might recall), but not when he said 'give' (since if he had repaid, he would not have said 'give').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara retracts the earlier version of Rabbah's ruling and presents the corrected version: when orphans say 'Father later told us he repaid,' they are believed if he said 'a mana is in my hand' (since he might recall), but not if he said 'give' (since if he had repaid, he would not have said 'give').

items.text: Rava's inquiry and resolution regarding a dying person's admission
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry and resolution regarding a dying person's admission
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a dying person's admission requires formal witnesses or a directive to write, and whether a dying person might be deceptive. He then resolves that a dying person is not deceptive, and his words are considered as written and delivered.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a dying person's admission requires formal witnesses or a directive to write, and whether a dying person might be deceptive.
The gemara resolves that a dying person is not deceptive, and his words are considered as written and delivered.

items.text: Mishnah: Collection from encumbered vs. free property
items.text_en: Mishnah: Collection from encumbered vs. free property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who lends with a document collects from encumbered property (sold to others), while one who lends with witnesses collects only from free property (still in the debtor's possession).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that a lender with a document collects from encumbered property, while one who lends with witnesses collects only from free property.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: collection from free property and the guarantor case
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: collection from free property and the guarantor case
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a loan by a signed note is collected from free property, and a guarantor who signed after the document is also collected from free property. A story is brought about Rabbi Yishmael and ben Nannas debating the guarantor's liability, with ben Nannas comparing it to a bystander who tells a creditor to release a debtor, which is not a valid guarantee.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a loan collected via a signed note is collected from free property, and a guarantor who signed after the document is also collected from free property.

The Mishnah recounts a story where Rabbi Yishmael ruled the guarantor collects from free property, but ben Nannas objected, comparing the guarantor to a bystander who tells a creditor to release a debtor, which is not a valid guarantee, and distinguished a valid guarantor as one who says 'lend to him and I will give you.'
Rabbi Yishmael adds a digression: one who wishes to become wise should engage in monetary laws, and one who wishes to engage in monetary laws should serve ben Nannas.

items.text: Ulla's view: Torah law liens property for all loans
items.text_en: Ulla's view: Torah law liens property for all loans
items.desc_en: Ulla argues that by Torah law, both oral and written loans should be collected from liened property because the lien is Torah-based. The reason oral loans are only collected from free property is to protect buyers from loss, but written loans are collected from liened property because the buyers knew of the debt.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that by Torah law, both oral and written loans should be collected from liened property.
Ulla explains that the reason is that the lien is Torah-based (שיעבודא דאורייתא).
The Gemara asks why the Sages ruled that an oral loan is collected only from free property.
Ulla answers that it is to protect buyers from loss (פסידא דלקוחות).
The Gemara objects that if so, a written loan should also be limited to free property for the same reason.
The Gemara resolves that in the case of a written loan, the buyers brought the loss upon themselves (אינהו נינהו דאפסידו אנפשייהו) because they had notice of the debt.

items.text: Rabbah's view: no Torah lien, written loans collect to prevent door-closing
items.text_en: Rabbah's view: no Torah lien, written loans collect to prevent door-closing
items.desc_en: Rabbah argues that by Torah law, no loan creates a lien on property; both oral and written loans are collected only from free property. The reason written loans are collected from liened property is to prevent the door from being closed in borrowers' faces. Oral loans are not collected from liened property because they lack publicity.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that by Torah law, neither a written nor an oral loan creates a lien (שיעבודא) on property, so both are collected only from free property.
Rabbah explains that written loans are collected from liened property only to prevent the door from being closed in borrowers' faces (שלא תנעול דלת בפני לווין).
The Gemara objects: if the reason is to prevent door-closing, then oral loans should also collect from liened property.
The Gemara resolves: an oral loan lacks publicity (קלא), so it cannot create a lien that would affect purchasers.

items.text: Contradiction from Rabbah's other statement and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from Rabbah's other statement and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rabbah's statement about collecting land versus money, and from Ulla's statement about collecting from inferior land. It resolves that Rabbah was merely reporting the view of the Western sages, not his own opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rabbah's own statement about collecting land versus money.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of swapping Rabbah's and Ulla's positions, citing Ulla's statement about collecting from inferior land.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbah was merely reporting the view of the Western sages, not his own opinion.

items.text: Amoraic dispute: Rav and Shmuel vs. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute: Rav and Shmuel vs. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel hold that an oral loan is not collected from heirs or buyers because the lien is not Torah-based. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish hold that an oral loan is collected from both heirs and buyers because the lien is Torah-based.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel state that an oral loan is not collected from heirs or buyers because the lien is not Torah-based.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish state that an oral loan is collected from both heirs and buyers because the lien is Torah-based.

items.text: Challenge from the pit-digger case and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the pit-digger case and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that oral loans are collected from heirs, citing a baraita where a pit-digger's heirs are liable for the ox's value. Rabbi Ila'a says the case is where the digger stood in judgment. Rav Adda bar Ahavah says the ox was made a treifa. Rav Nachman says the judges sat at the pit's mouth and convicted him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that oral loans are collected from heirs, citing a baraita where the heirs of a pit-digger are liable for the ox's value even though the pit-digger himself was exempt.
Rabbi Ila'a citing Rav answers that the case is where the pit-digger stood in judgment and was convicted before his death, so the obligation was already fixed.
The Gemara objects that the baraita says the ox 'killed him' (הרגו), implying immediate death without a prior court case.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah answers that the ox was made a טריפה (mortally wounded animal), so the pit-digger died from the injury but not immediately, allowing time for a court case.
The Gemara objects citing Rav Nachman that a Tanna taught the baraita with the phrase 'died and they buried him' (מת וקברו), which implies immediate death.
Rav Nachman resolves that the case is where judges were sitting at the mouth of the pit and convicted the digger immediately, so the obligation was fixed before death.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling on oral loans
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling on oral loans
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states the halakha: an oral loan is collected from heirs but not from purchasers, to prevent locking the door before borrowers, and because it lacks publicity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that an oral loan is collected from heirs but not from purchasers, to prevent locking the door before borrowers and because it lacks publicity.

items.text: Rabba bar Natan's inquiry about a confirmed handwriting
items.text_en: Rabba bar Natan's inquiry about a confirmed handwriting
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Natan asks Rabbi Yochanan whether a confirmed handwriting in court allows collection from liened property; Rabbi Yochanan answers it still only collects from free property.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Natan asks Rabbi Yochanan whether a confirmed handwriting in court allows collection from liened property.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that even with confirmed handwriting, the debt collects only from free property.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's objection from the Mishnah of invalid gittin
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's objection from the Mishnah of invalid gittin
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects from a Mishnah about invalid gittin where a get written in the husband's handwriting without witnesses is valid and collects from liened property. The Gemara distinguishes because there the husband obligates himself from the time of writing.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects by citing a Mishnah listing three invalid gittin, including one written in the husband's handwriting without witnesses, and Rabbi Elazar's statement that such a get is valid and collects from liened property.
The Gemara distinguishes the case of the get, because there the husband obligates himself from the time of writing, unlike the case of a loan by oral agreement.

items.text: Rav's contradictory rulings on a guarantor and Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Rav's contradictory rulings on a guarantor and Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: Rav initially rules that a guarantor who signs before the witnesses collects from liened property, but later says even before witnesses he collects only from free property. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first case is where it says 'so-and-so is guarantor', the second where it says 'and so-and-so is guarantor'. Rabbi Yochanan holds that in both cases he collects only from free property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: a guarantor who signs after the witnesses' signatures collects only from free property.
Rav rules that a guarantor who signs before the witnesses collects from liened property, but after the witnesses collects only from free property.
Rav elsewhere rules that even if the guarantor signs before the witnesses, he collects only from free property.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first case is where the document says 'so-and-so is guarantor' (פלוני ערב), the second where it says 'and so-and-so is guarantor' (ופלוני ערב).
Rabbi Yochanan holds that in both cases the guarantor collects only from free property, even if the document says 'and so-and-so is guarantor'.

items.text: Rava's objection from the case of witnesses signing a greeting in a get
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the case of witnesses signing a greeting in a get
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a case where witnesses sign a greeting in a get, which is invalid. Rabbi Abahu explains that 'greet' is invalid but 'and greet' is valid. The Gemara applies this to the guarantor case: if it says 'and so-and-so is guarantor', it is like 'and greet' and valid. The Gemara then notes this is like Rav's ruling, and rephrases Rabbi Yochanan's statement as 'and so said Rabbi Yochanan'.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a case where witnesses sign a greeting in a get, which is invalid because we suspect they signed only for the greeting.

sub.text: Rabbi Abahu's answer in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abahu's answer in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu clarifies from Rabbi Yochanan that if the greeting is written as 'greet' (שְׁאִילוּ) it is invalid, but if written as 'and greet' (וּשְׁאִילוּ) it is valid.

sub.text: Gemara's application to the guarantor case
sub.text_en: Gemara's application to the guarantor case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara applies the distinction to the guarantor case: if the document says 'so-and-so is guarantor' (without a vav), it is like 'greet' and invalid; if it says 'and so-and-so is guarantor' (with a vav), it is valid.

sub.text: Gemara's note on Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's note on Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this ruling aligns with Rav's position, and rephrases Rabbi Yochanan's statement as 'and so said Rabbi Yochanan'.

items.text: The dispute about a choked guarantor and the halakha
items.text_en: The dispute about a choked guarantor and the halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether Rabbi Yishmael's ruling applies to a guarantor who was choked (i.e., obligated by a handshake). Rabbi Yochanan confirms that Rabbi Yishmael disagreed even in the case of a choked guarantor, and the halakha follows him even in that case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the case that came before Rabbi Yishmael, and Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that even though Rabbi Yishmael praised ben Nannas, the halakha follows ben Nannas.
The Gemara raises a question: what is the ruling regarding a guarantor who was choked (obligated by a handshake) — does Rabbi Yishmael's dispute apply there as well?
Rabbi Yaakov reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yishmael disagreed even in the case of a choked guarantor.
The Gemara asks whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yishmael in this case or not.
Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yishmael disagreed even in the case of a choked guarantor, and the halakha follows him even in that case.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel's ruling on a choked guarantor with a kinyan
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel's ruling on a choked guarantor with a kinyan
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel: if a guarantor was choked and a kinyan was performed, he is obligated; implying that a regular guarantor does not need a kinyan. This disagrees with Rav Nachman.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that a guarantor who was choked (i.e., a guarantor who was already obligated) and a kinyan was performed from him, becomes obligated.
The gemara infers from Shmuel's statement that a regular guarantor (without being choked) does not require a kinyan to become obligated.
The gemara notes that this ruling of Shmuel disagrees with Rav Nachman, who holds a different position.

items.text: Distinction between court-appointed and regular guarantor
items.text_en: Distinction between court-appointed and regular guarantor
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a court-appointed guarantor does not require a formal acquisition (kinyan), but a regular guarantor does require one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a court-appointed guarantor (ערב דבית דין) does not require a formal acquisition (קינין), but a regular guarantor does require one.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on guarantor at time of loan vs. after
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on guarantor at time of loan vs. after
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that a guarantor at the time of the loan does not require a kinyan, but one after the loan does. A court-appointed guarantor never requires a kinyan, because the benefit of being trusted causes him to commit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara issues a final ruling (הלכתא): a guarantor at the time of the loan does not require a formal acquisition (קינין), but one after the loan does; a court-appointed guarantor does not require one because the benefit of being trusted induces him to commit.
